are prepared to play their part, to use

document? It came from Liverpool. I
was amazed at it; in fact it put me in

Northern Ireland farmers.
As a Member of this House I am prepared to give every Minister all the support of which I am capable, but I am not

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to call
the attention of the House to the
question of unemployment assistance.
When this subject was before the House
on a former occasion I was not able to
get any information from the Minister of
Labour, but I have now been supplied
with the information from London. On
that occasion I asked him if the abolition
of the means test applied to unemployment assistance. At that time he was
not able to give me the answer. In
referring to this matter I might bring
in the household means test. In the
British House of Commons on November
6 the Prime Minister made a short statement on the household means test for
unemployment assistance and supplementary pensions. The Government has
reached a united conclusion to introduce
legislation before Christmas which will
make the test one of personal need. I
want you to take a note of the words,
"before Christmas.'
""
If the applicant is not a householder,
and is living with relations, regard will
be had to the constitution and circumstances of the home in assessing his personal needs, but inquiries into the
resources of other members of the household will in any case be greatly reduced
and will often be unnecessary. No applicant without resources of his own will
be left dependent on other members of
the household for means to buy clothing
and other personal requirements. The
Assistance Board is working out the
detailed application of these principles in
order that draft Regulations may be
submitted as soon as the necessary legislation is passed.
The new test will be based on the
following principles: The needs and
resources of the applicant will continue
to be aggregated with those of his wife
and of any dependants, but the resources
of any other member of the household
will no longer be aggregated with those.
of the applicant. If the applicant is
the householder, a standard contribution
by non-dependent members of his household towards rent and other overheads
will be assumed and taken into account
as part of the applicant's resources. This
means that inquiry will normally be
limited to the needs and resources of the
applicant, his wife and dependants.
That means the individual will be the
sole source of inquiry if a single man,
and, if married, his wife and any
children under the age of 14 who are
wholly dependent upon him.

introduce changes in the administration

Report of the Select Committee.
Resolved, "That the Interim Report of
the Select Committee on Unemployment
be now taken into consideration."-(The
Prime Minister.)
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I beg
to move, "That the Interim Report
should receive the immediate and sympathetic consideration of the Government
as a matter of urgent public importance."
I should like first of all to thank the
Prime Minister for calling the House together in order that the Interim Report
of the Unemployment Committee might
be considered. I know that he is as much
concerned as any of us about the unemployment problem, and I hope in the discussion which will follow we will be able
to convince him, if indeed convincing is
that our recommendations, if
necessary,
adopted, would help to ease the situation.
The report may sound a little alarming, but it simply states bare facts, and
there is no use disguising them, no matter
how unpalatable they may be. At the
outset I would like to pay a warm
tribute to the care and attention which
the Committee gave to this particular
phase of their inquiry. Altogether thirty
sessions were held, and we paid visits to
three flax processing establishments.
Every aspect of the linen trade was carefully examined, and we were all so impressed with the evidence put before us
that we were in agreement and the report
is a unanimous one.
methods. These men
believe that in
youth, with its energy, initiative and
enthusiasm lies the best hope of securing
stability, progress and success.
It has been said that private enterprise,
which has built up this Ulster of ours,
should develop these new methods, and
that the Government should not be asked
to undertake work of this description. I
am all in favour of private enterprise
doing things, but evidence has been produced to show that private enterprise instead of being encouraged is throttled by
legislation, and its very existence is
threatened. Then I suggest it is the duty
of the Government to use every means
possible to relieve that stranglehold and
to give all the assistance in its power.
As to the recommendations put forward, I do not propose to say very much,
but I should tell the House that what

trade rests largely in new and up-to-date
The Committee in their report have expiained the position of private concerns
as regards the erecting of flax factories, so
I need not dwell on that matter; but in
the Committee's opinion there is a very
strong case why the Government, be it
the Imperial or the Ulster Government,
should undertake to erect factories in
Northern Ireland and in support of their
contention they cite the factories erected
in Great Britain. These factories have
been built in order to promote the growing and handling of flax in entirely new
areas, and it would be interesting to
know whether the money to erect these
factories is taken from the contribution
sent from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain. Of course we recognise that
these factories are a war project, but I
can see nothing in the regulations governing the erection of these factories, to prevent the British Government at the end
of the war handing them over to private
enterprise, at a valuation. Thus the
traders across the water would be placed
in an advantageous position as compared
with those in Northern Ireland. Since
the report was drawn up I have seen that
more factories are to be built in England
in addition to the eight now operating;
also that there is a move to introduce flaxgrowing into Wales.
Members may have noted that the
Government of New Zealand propose to
spend £500,000 on the initiation of a
linen industry in that country. If, as we
have pointed out, private enterprise is
unable to erect factories in Northern Ireland, then something should be done by
the Government to save an established
industry of world renown.
Report of Select Committee 2698
Unemployment-
14 JANUARY 1941
The report also deals with the saving
of flax seed which, I think, is a most
important matter. Lord Woolton has
told us how necessary it is to save shipping space, and our own Minister of Agriculture and other Members representing
agricultural constituencies, have stressed
the need for more feeding stuffs.
Yet we
have here at our very doors what they are
crying out for. Are we going to make no
effort to save this feeding stuff? Are we
to continue to spend money on fertilisers
and seed, and waste all this valuable feeding stuff by throwing it into a dam? Are
we not progressive and enterprising enough
to depart from the old customs which are
so wasteful? Why after a few years, the
money received for seed that could be
saved, would go a long way towards paying for the erection of the suggested
factories.
I will only touch on one other point,
because I know that other members of the
Committee with practical knowledge will
deal with points not referred to by me.
That is the question of export trade. We
have recommended that an examination
of the export markets should be made with
the object of aiding the currency drive and
being ready for the post-war period.
There are many markets formerly closed
to us, which we think will be open at the
close of hostilities, and we should lose no
opportunity in finding out what kind of
goods they are in the habit of getting so
that we shall be in a position to produce
similar or alternative goods, and meet the
demand. We should see if the methods
adopted by Russia in the establishment
of the Arcos system would be of any
service to us, and it might be that a study
of the barter system might yield gratifying results. After the war the whole
economic system of the
the world will
doubtless be altered, and we should be
ready for the changes when they come.
The report, as I have stated, merely
records the hard facts. No personal
opinions are expressed, and whilst the
report deals chiefly with the present
serious situation, we must not forget the
future. I do not agree with those who

The PRIME MINISTER (Mr.
Andrews): In the first place I desire to
thank the hon. Member for Woodvale
for the gracious and generous tribute he
paid to me at the beginning of his speech,
but it must be my duty clearly and
definitely to oppose the Amendment
which he has advocated because I feel
that to pursue the course outlined in
it would be very detrimental to the
interests of Ulster. It would deprive
Ulster of almost all those men who have
served her for a great many years, many
of them for nineteen years, and I feel
that would not be in the interests of
In the first place it would deprive
Ulster of the services in future of those
men who have maintained through all
the difficult years our constitutional
position unimpaired. It would also
deprive Ulster of those men who in very
trying circumstances, unnecessarily trying circumstances, have preserved law
and order, and further, it would deprive
Ulster of those men who have extended
our social services to an extent never
before contemplated. Our unemployment and unemployment assistance
schemes have been widened so as to embrace almost everyone who needs their
help. There were no widows' and
orphans' pensions when this Government
came into existence, and we all know
what a vast benefit they have been to
our fellow citizens, young and old, for
whom we have the greatest possible sympathy. Again, we have increased the
amount given in old-age pensions, and,
further, we have introduced a measure of
contributory pensions.
Yet one of the two Members responsible for this Amendment has stated that
the Government have done nothing in
the past to help the position, and
that he is content that we should be
judged by our success or our failure. I
accept that challenge. I say we have
not failed. I say we have succeeded in
a very difficult situation. I would like also
to point out to hon. Members how the
Government have improved our educational system. We have brought to the
children of this Province a system of
which we have every right to be proud.
Further, I say without hesitation, that
we have encouraged industry and agriculture to an extent never before known.
I go on to say that it is because we have

hon. Members on this side of the House,

Mr. JOHNSTON: I rise with some
hesitation after all the eloquence we have
heard this afternoon. At the same time,
I think this should console me; that of
all the Members of the Select Committee,
which is a very good Committee, I was
the only one who had any first-hand
knowledge of the linen business. When
we came to examine the question of unemployment in Northern Ireland we
found, to my intense astonishment, that
over half the unemployment in Northern
Ireland was in the linen trade. Over
37,000 persons in the linen trade and
its ancillary trades were unemployed
when we got the figures in September
last. It is really astonishing to think
that in our staple industry, of which we
are so proud, 37 per cent. of the employees should be on the dole. When
we came to examine the causes of that
unemployment we found that the main
cause was want of raw material. This
want of raw material did not happen
just at once.
From the evidence we got I am of the
opinion that that is due to the long
drawn out policy of the Ministry of
Agriculture during the last ten years.
The Ministry of Agriculture had
policy, and, from their point of view,
may have been a good policy. But their
model, instead of being Northern Ireland, was Denmark, and flax did not
figure in their programme. On more
than one occasion it was stated that flax
was not a farmer's crop. The Ministry
argued that flax for the linen trade
could be brought from abroad, where it
was grown better and more cheaply, and
that they could do far better for the
farmers of Northern Ireland by concentrating on cattle. Consequently, when
any approach was made to the Ministry
of Agriculture for any further help in
the growing of flax, except in the case
of pedigree seed, every objection that
could possibly be put forward was put up
against it.

I myself went to the Ministry of
Agriculture and tried to see what could
be done. That was in 1937, before the
outbreak of war, but I found the most
insuperable difficulties put forward to
any scheme for helping to increase the
acreage of flax. I was in such despair
that I immediately went and with others
started a place at Armoy to see if by
I want to say this from my knowledge
of the linen trade; that the Government
cannot escape responsiblity for the predicament the linen trade is in at present.
It never has been in such a predicament
in its long history. This great trade of
ours is practically now totally unemployed
as far as flax is concerned. The Ministry
of Agriculture banked on there being
no war, and if there had not been a war
they might have pulled it off. The
cotton trade of Lancashire can get its
supplies from overseas because they come
from Africa and America and other warm
countries. Similarly with hemp and
jute, but flax is a European crop, and
there is no other country available for its
supply. Once Europe is involved in war
our supplies of flax cease. That is the
one thing the Ministry of Agriculture left
out of their calculation, and I say it must
burn into the minds of the Ministry and
their officials that never again must
Northern Ireland be allowed to do without a home-grown crop of flax.
The question between the Ministry of
Agriculture and the flax trade was the
price to the farmer. There was no reason
why that could not have been got over,
but, granting my premise as to the policy
of the Ministry, I cannot believe that
they look upon flax-growing as a serious
proposition for Northern Ireland. The
point is, what is the best thing to be
done? The Ministry of Agriculture are
urging that 100,000 acres of flax be grown
in Northern Ireland in the coming year
in order that looms in the Province may
be employed. Up to the present they
have not put forward any scheme or
method whereby that 100,000 acres can be
processed, nor has it been worked out how
the farmers who grow the flax and want
to sell it on foot can dispose of it. I
wish to impress upon the Government that
the Report presented to-day does, if not
entirely, show how that 100,000 acres can
be processed with advantage to the linen
trade, the spinner and the Government.
In the first place, the ordinary method
of treating the few thousand acres
usually grown in Northern Ireland can be
continued, and the flax, useful enough,
would help to do a medium class trade.
There is, however, a section of the trade,
to which the Prime Minister and I belong,
the fine end, which would be left high and
Report of Select Committee 2734
Unemployment-
14 JANUARY 1941
dry without any material whatsoever to
spin this year or next year unless the
new process of retting flax in reinforced
concrete tanks by a new method is adopted
here. From our experience in Armoy we
are convinced that out of the crop grown
locally good flax can be produced, flax
equal to good Beigian, suitable for the
fine end of the trade. We have proved
that point beyond all possibility of doubt.
I would, therefore, urge the Government
to see to it that at least 30,000 acres of the
coming crop is processed by the new
method. It is utterly impossible at the
present time for private enterprise to do
this. That was fully brought out in
evidence given before the Committee.
If you start a rettery and, say, spend
£8,000 or £10,000 on putting it down
you are, by war legislation, only allowed
to make £1,000, or 8 per cent. on your
capital, whichever amount is the greater.
That being so there is not sufficient money
allowed to make extensions for possible
contingencies or for interest on the money
spent. Any more money you make is
taken by the Government as excess profit.
That being so, it is imperative that the
Government should give sufficient money
to put down the flax factories in order to
enable the crop to be processed next year.
There is no time for delay if the work is
to be done in time for next year's crop.
If this work is carried out at once a good
deal of that object can be attained. The
machinery could be made in Northern
Ireland, but the manufacturers will have
to receive time in which to carry out the
orders. The Government will have to
make up its mind at once and adopt this
report in order that sufficient flax may
be processed for the fine spindles if there
is going to be any work for the spindles
during 1940-1941.
There is a new method of treating flax,
or rather the adaptation of a very old one.
It happened when we were at war with
Napoleon in 1812-the processing of flax
without putting it through the process of
retting. The work can be done very
satisfactorily by putting down turbine
scutchers and other modern plant. Green
flax is very suitable for making many
things. If more green flax were processed
in Northern Ireland we could get more
Government orders. If this process was
carried out we could also save the seed
which, by the old process, is thrown away
and wasted. That is a new thing which,
I think, is confined to the British Isles.
The Government should encourage that
to the utmost of their ability, and see
what further progress can be made in this
method by the use of more modern
machinery than our forefathers had.
I would implore the Government not to
look upon this matter in a small way; if
they are going to do it they should not
spoil or cramp it because of money. The
Government will not save money by doing
it in a small way, and I do not think they
will lose money if they tackle it in a large
way, because the seed that will be saved
can be used as seed and also for feeding
purposes. In one or two years that would
meet the expenditure which the Government would have to undertake.
I have spoken fairly strongly to the
Government, and I hope they will make
up their minds to treat this matter in a
very broad way. If it should cost one
million pounds in two years they should
not hesitate. The future of my livelihood, the livelihood of the Prime Minister,
and that of thousands of our people, is
at stake. I hope the Government will
decide to do something in a big way.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Salaries of Ministerial Offices Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am asking the House to pass through all its
stages this Measure to provide, for a
salary of £1,000 being paid to a Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Agriculture and a similar sum to be paid
to a Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Commerce. As hon. Members
know the work of these two departments
has enormously increased. In England
there has been a very rapid increase. also,
and in Great Britain the matter is being
dealt with by the establishment of new
Ministries. I feel that a more economical
and satisfactory way of dealing with the
matter here is by making these two additional appointments, which I hope hon.
Members on both sides of the House will
be good enough to approve.
I may say on the question of Finance
that if hon. Members feel that this is
going to be an additional burden upon
the Exchequer I hope to be able to make
adjustments so that the total charge from
the Ministerial Offices Vote will certainly
not be more than formerly. I beg to
move.

has given a manly and straight answer to

This House is not tied by what happened
in the past. When you have passed this
Bill making two new offices at £1,000 a
year each, that is an end of the matter.
It is now 1941, and I notice that the
principal Act was passed in 1921. We did
without these offices for twenty years, and
when we complained about the number
of Ministerial offices we were told they
were fixed by the House, and that the

Mr. NIXON: I am still opposing the
Bill, and will continue to do so to the
iast stage. This Bill was handed to the
House yesterday, and it has been treated
a matter of great public urgency.
To-day the Prime Minister moved
Motion, which was carried, suspending the
Standing Orders of the House in order
that this Bill, which invents two new jobs
in an already over-staffed Parliament at
a time when the nation is standing up to
the greatest and most ruthless war in
history, might be taken. Serving soldiers
are being recalled from the front at
Bangor, or some other local place, and
have to give up their commissions in order
to take places in the Government as
authorised by this Bill. The members of
the Government should be ashamed of
themselves. However, it is part of what
is going on.
The most important thing this House
is now concerned with is new jobs and
new salaries. Going along the streets of
Belfast it grieves one to see the useless
people who are on a salaried list. I do
not say they are all on the salaried list
of the Northern Parliament. I do not
know where this kind of thing is going
to end. I would spend the last penny
I have in helping to win the war, but
when one sees money thrown away and
squandered it makes one wonder. I will
again oppose the Bill in the Lobby.
Nobody is more out to win the war
than myself and the people whom I
represent working people and others.
who are not working people, but who,
nevertheless, are willing to sacrifice everything. When sacrifices are wasted by
the invention of useless and unnecessary
jobs it is enough to make those who have
given their lives to defend us turn in
their graves.
It is in keeping with what
we have been used to in this House, and,
what, I am sorry to say, will still continue.
I am sorry I have to go so strongly against
the Prime Minister in this matter. I
could understand if he came in and
asked us to reduce the number of
positions. From various quarters the
suggestion has come that he will not fill
these positions, or something to that
effect. That is of no use at all, because
once you create positions with salaries
attached they will be filled even if not
at the moment.

not only want to get these people unemployed back into employment, but we

and on the Continent knows that if flax
is going to be handled by that method
there is an inevitable lag of at least nine
months before the flax can become available for use in the spinning mills. Therefore, however meritorious this method
may be, it is not the quickest way of getting flax processed so that the people can
be got back into the mills. I calculate
that if the Government and the trade or
some body that might be set up representing all parties, proceeded to handle the
bulk of the 1941 flax crop by that method it
would be the month of May, in 1942,

is wholeheartedly the hope of myself and

that they may be able to devise some

Northern Ireland. We have been at a

the remainder of our industrial population is engaged in the textile industry
and so is not, in the present circumstances, able to make that contribution
to the war effort which not only they
but the rest of the population would so
gladly desire to make.
We are all very satisfied to be part
and parcel of the United Kingdom, but
the defence of the United Kingdom is
a matter for the Imperial Government.
The provision of munitions and supplies generally is a matter which has been
undertaken by the Imperial Parliament
and confided, so far as we are concerned,
to the Ministry of Supply. The Ministry
has undertaken the purchase of all the
supplies required by the different Forces
in order to carry on the war.

which may exist
hon. Members
among
on this point.
It is true that all flax grown within,
or imported into, the United Kingdom.
becomes the property of the British
Government. The Ministry of Supply is
the sole purchaser. The flax is distributed through the agency of the Flax
Control of the Ministry of Supply, but

Unemployment-
Report of Select Committee 2776
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
This Committee, which sits under the
chairmanship of Colonel Llewellin, the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Aircraft Production, was set up as a
sub-committee of the Production Council,
under the British War Cabinet, and is
responsible for the allocation of all
essential raw materials in the United
Kingdom.
the
The hon. Member will, I am sure,
appreciate that in allocating essential
raw materials in time of war,
Priority Committee must have regard,
not to claims submitted on a geographical
basis, but to the use to which the material
is intended to be put. As the hon.
Member is aware, the guiding principle
followed by the British Government is
that Government and export orders must
be given priority over ordinary home
trade. As the supply of flax is not
sufficient to meet all the Government
orders which would normally be fulfilled
in linen as well as the export trade, it
naturally follows that the Committee has
not been able to allocate any flax for the
home market. From what I have said,
it will be seen that the distribution of
the flax supply as between Scotland and
Northern Ireland is governed solely by
the extent to which Government contracts
and export orders are placed either in
Scotland or Northern Ireland.
It is well known that Scotland is
equipped to undertake many types of
Government orders which our machinery
is not capable of handling, and, having
regard to the limited supplies available,
our obvious policy has been to secure as
large as possible a share of the supplies
for export trade. The Board of Trade
is responsible for submitting claims to
the Priority Committee for the allocation
of raw materials for the United Kingdom
export trade, and I am glad to say that
that Department has recognised the
special importance of the high-quality
trade carried on by Northern Ireland,
particularly with the United States.
Hon. Members will realise, therefore,
that we are doing our utmost to obtain
such contracts as we are capable of handling in Northern Ireland, and to obtain
as large a supply of flax as can be made
available under present conditions for
export trade. We cannot, however, act
independently of the special organisation
established by the War Cabinet and obtain
flax for purposes or in quantities beyond
those which I have mentioned.
As to what share of flax Northern
Ireland obtains in addition to the allocation for export trade, this depends on
the purchasing Departments, such as the
Admiralty, the Ministry of Aircraft Production and the Ministry of Supply, to
whom the supplies for service requirements
are allocated in the first instance.
Prior to the war the Scotch trade
catered far more for Government requirements and home consumption than the
trade in Northern Ireland. Our trade
lay principally in the export trade, but
we also catered very largely for consumption within the United Kingdom. Consequently, when flax had to be conserved
for Government requirements we were
not in as good a position to tender for
Government contracts as the trade in
Scotland. We must remember that
while the Government does its best to
promote the securing of Government contracts in our own area, we are entirely
dependent on the efforts of our local
manufacturers to obtain these contracts.
We can bring the Government and our
local manufacturers together, but the
actual placing of the orders lies between
them.
Before the war broke out we had taken
steps to counteract this state of affairs,
and were able to persuade the Government
to alter the terms of their specification.
Instead of only taking the dry spun yarns,
which had hitherto been supplied by the
Scotch trade, we induced them to accept
the wet spun yarns capable of being spun
by our mills in Northern Ireland.
Further, we persuaded them to accept a
yarn made from hemp and so preserve
the scanty supplies of flax for the
spinning of the finer articles for which
flax is absolutely essential.
I am very glad to say that as a result
of those representations millions of yards
-I am not speaking extravagantly-of
cloth were placed in Northern Ireland.
While we may consider we have not been
fairly treated in comparison with
Scotland in regard to the allocation of
orders I do not think we would like to
seek consolation in another man's
misfortune. I do not think the Scottish
trade is in any better position than we
are. I have here a trade paper in which
it is stated:

The spinning end, however, is in a
decidedly more serious position, as substitutes cannot be so readily employed,
or are not at present available, in this
case. The volume of yarn business
passing, which, of course, is regulated
by licences issued, is quite inadequate,
and spinners are faced with the problem
of more and more machinery becoming
idle. So far as prices are concerned, it
seems that a new list will be issued in
the near future and will probably be
somewhat lower than previously, but
this interests spinners very little as it
is work which is required. They feel
that if they could only see ahead, instead of the present system of working
completely in the dark, the present
restricted production might be tolerable,
but as it is, there is not a single bright
feature in the whole position.
So I feel that the representations we
have been able to make to the Government
have secured us as large a share of
Government business as we are equipped
to make. The extent to which we have
been able to secure these contracts is not
unsatisfactory. We have to remember
that human nature has to be taken into
account. If people undertake Government work it means they have to readjust
their factories to a very large extent, and
the workpeople have to acquire a dexterity
in handling material and making articles
to which they have not been accustomed.
The manufacturer knows that if he
succeeds and is able to get contracts and
execute them the personal gain is removed
owing to the excess profits tax.
There is another thing which has a
bearing on the matter. Some manufacturers realise that their stock is
irreplaceable. They have to conserve their
stock in order to spread it over as long a
period as possible. By doing so they will
be in touch with their customers when
supplies are again available and will be
able to take advantage of the business
which will spring up. It is very hard to
find fault with them for doing so, because
if they did not take up that attitude they
would simply dispose of their stock and
have a complete breakdown or gap until
the end of the war when supplies would
again become available.

Johnston and Mr. Headley had previous
military experience. Before the appointment of Captain Collins' successor was
recom-

if it would in any way serve the interests

Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL: I confess
to

Report of Select Committee 2804
HOUSE OF COMMONS

as the bad, unhealthy home industry.
We are aware that for many years
certain parts of the linen industry were
done in the homes of the people. Since
I first entered this House I have been
keen for every effort to keep the people
on the land. One of the disasters of
modern civilisation is the tendency to
drift into the big cities and centralise
all your industries in the big cities. It
may be it is more economic. It may be
there are increased opportunites for comfort. At the same time, once a slump
comes it throws out of employment enormous numbers of people.
This is only a portion of the question
that has been referred to this Committee
on Unemployment. If I am not out of
order I would like to make a suggestion.
I do not know whether Members here all
realise the deplorable condition of men
who are unemployed. It has fallen to
my lot repeatedly to have to make reports
on injured unemployed men, who have
been out of work two or three years.
They have a slight injury. I am not
accusing them for a moment, but the
slightest trace of injury makes them unfit
and they are off work. They are then
asked after a certain length of time to
get a letter from the medical attendant
that they are now fit for what is called
light work, a thing which I really do not
understand for I do not see anything else
done. But I suggest it is part and parcel
of the duty of our Government to do
something to keep these people fit for
employment when employment becomes
available.
fit for it and not break down within a
few days. As I see it, if things go on
we will soon have an enormous number
of totally unemployable and unhealthy
people.
I have seen the present Prime Minister
when he was Minister of Labour introducing a training scheme for youths.
Why not have training for every man?
I am not asking for military drill. I
am asking for some sort of physical
exercise that will keep the muscles in
reasonable condition. It has more than
once been my unfortunate lot when
asked if one of these men was fit for
ordinary work to state that he is not fit
to do it, because he has not a decent
muscle in his body. Now, if there were
centres where they could practise mild
physical exercises suitable to their condition it would keep them in condition
so that they would be fit for a job if it
is offered to them, and if they were asked
to do some sort of work they would be
To be quite straight this means, in my
view, compulsion. People ought to be
obliged while getting unemployment
money to do something as a duty to keep
themselves as fit as possible for workfirst, to themselves; secondly, to their
families, and thirdly, to the community
when work becomes available. If the
Government is going to provide some
system to enable that to be done, then
if the men refuse they should not at the
same time receive unemployment money.
I do not like the word compulsion, but
it seems to me essential that that should
be done. I have already drawn attention
to the entirely demoralising effect it has
on youths under 18 brought up on the
unemployment bureau, to be able to put
out their hands and get a certain amount
of money month by month for doing
nothing. They acquire the undesirable
idea that money can be had without
work. I am not asking the unemployment pay to be stopped. I am asking
if a man will not do something to keep
himself fit he should not get paid.
Training and games might be available
for these young people where they might
be taught something-anything you
like, but they should have to do something.
I do not wish to occupy the time of
the House. I know this is perhaps a
little outside the exact line of the Report
on the linen industry, but it has a very
considerable bearing on it as far as the
youth are concerned. The latest number
I have is 2,500. It is quite possible to
provide something to finance that 2,500,
but it is a very different thing to provide
labour for 50,000 or 60,000. I urge
strongly that we should look into this
whole question of the moral effect of unemployment on the nation. If we go on
as we are doing we will become a nation
of invalids and people incapable of work
altogether.

that the subject matter of the Report is
of such paramount importance that they
could not hold it over until the other part
or parts of their Report were ready. Let
us hold fast now to the realities of the
present position. This is not the time
for recriminations or even for a full-dress
debate on the unemployment problem, but
a time for immediate action along the
lines of the Report.
The Committee are to be congratulated
on the expeditious way in which they set
about the business referred to them.
They have not only discovered the cause
of the canker of unemployment, but they
have produced what, in the opinion of
many Members of this House and in the
opinion of many people outside, is a
practical solution of the unemployment
problem as far as the linen industry is
concerned. I would like to point out to
the Members of this House what seems
There may have been undue delay in
dealing with the great problem of unemployment and I am not saying there has
not been-but let us not cloud the issue
and delay the matter further. Our job
now is to see that the Government, which
set up this Committee, accepts that Committee's Report and loses no time in
putting it into operation. The sands are
fast running out; in fact, they have
almost run out already, and we have to
accomplish the task set before us of
producing 100,000 acres of flax in 1941.
If an incendiary bomb falls on the roof
of our house, the first thing we think of
is putting it out. After we have done
so, and not before, we can criticise the
preparations made by the Minister of
Defence and the Minister of Public
Security. But let us not wait to deal
with the incendiary bomb until we have
criticised the preparations made. And
so let us say to the Government, as I say:
"Go ahead immediately with the recommendations made; it is action we want
to-day, not only sympathetic consideration, for unless that consideration
develops into action the problem of
unemployment will soon become much
worse."
The Select Committee mean business.
We back benchers mean business, and we
will brook no delay on the part of the
Government in dealing with this Report.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) As far as
I am concerned as a back bencher I
would have very little sympathy with the
Government if they tried either to shelve
or postpone operations in connection with
it. I have listened to many speakers from
both sides of the House, and I am glad
to know that however much some of these
may disagree with the terms of the
Report they are all at one in trying to
solve, the unemployment problem.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am grateful
to the hon. Member for North Armagh,
because he of all the speakers allowed me
to answer an accusation which is very
often made against my Ministry, and I
hope to show it is not accurate.. I know
it is the impression, but the position is
this. He made one remark the other day
in the course of his speech which is true,
that is to say, that flax is not truly an
agricultural crop. It is the raw material
for industry. I think in looking at this
matter we should look at it impartially
and objectively, if I may put it so, and
also at the question of how industry has
handled their own raw material in the
past. Every industry is entitled and has
a perfect right to get its raw material at
the cheapest possible price wherever it
can secure it. That is natural. But if in
the process of getting the raw material
at a low price they discourage the production of the raw material so that
eventually the raw material disappears
from the market the responsibility is
with the industry. That stands to
reason. If one took some industry in
England, the Government could not be
responsible say for the production of iron
ore for the steel industry. It is primarily
the responsibility of the industry.

Having said that I think it is obvious

Ministry, some of them a very long time

One. was a scheme by which the farmer
was paid £2 an acre. Now there were
never any conditions to that £2 an acre.
The advocates of that scheme said if the
farmer was paid £2 an acre he would
grow more, flax. There was no price fixing
when that scheme was put forward, and
therefore there was nothing to prevent
the price of flax falling in the end to
the price it was before the £2 was given.
It is really to my mind a form of subsidy
to a trade over which the Government
has no control.
It is only right to point out to the
House that when the Government gives a
subsidy as is done in the many marketing
schemes, conditions are attached. In the
case of milk, where the consumer has to
pay more, the producer must fulfil certain
conditions before he receives the subsidy.
In the case of other products of the farm,
such as cattle, eggs and things of that

certain conditions. Under this £2 an
acre scheme no Government could stand

It will be necessary in dealing with the

tackled the flax position at the beginning

We had very long conversations with the

easy for people who have not had experience of dealing with this aspect of
the case to arrive quickly at a right
decision in connection with the matter.
The truth is that the flax crop is affected
by many causes. There is climate, there
is soil, there is purity of seed, there is
the availability of an adequate water
supply. All these matters have got to
be taken into consideration, because they
so seriously affect the crop if they are
not available; if they are available they
ensure that the crop can be satisfactorily
harvested.

HOUSEHOLD MEANS TEST.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether officers of his Department call on employers and demand to
know the wages paid to their workers on
the grounds that such workers lodge in
houses with old people who apply for
supplementary pensions, although such
workers are not blood relations or even
step-children of the pensioners; whether
this administration is in harmony with
the pledges given on behalf of the
Government when the household means
test was sanctioned by a majority of the
House.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): Officers of my Department do
not make inquiries of the nature referred
to by the hon. Member. Officers of the
Assistance Board do, however, make such
inquiries, but only in cases where the
wage earner is a member of the pensioner's household. The terms of the
existing Act require that in determining
the amount of a supplementary pension
the resources to be taken into account
shall include resources of all members of
the applicant's household. The household may include persons (for example,
sons-in-law or adopted children) who
have no blood relationship to the
applicant.
As I previously promised the hon.
Member, if he will give me particulars of
any cases of hardship that have come to
his notice I will see that they are carefully and sympathetically considered.

SENDING YOUNG GIRLS TO
EMPLOYMENT IN GREAT BRITAIN
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether it is a fact that he
is compelling young girls of 18 to 23
years of age to take up employment in
Great Britain as munition workers at
wages from 30s to 35s per week; whether
he is aware that food and lodgings cost
them 25s per week; whether large numbers of them who find themselves unfit
for this class of work and desirous of
returning to their homes in Belfast are
denied facilities to do so; whether numbers of them have been stranded in Great
Britain without means of subsistence;
whether the alternative, in case of refusal
to take the work, is stoppage of unemployment benefit; and whether he has
made any arrangement to facilitate the
return of these girls to their homes.
pelling young girls to take up munitions.
work in Great Britain.
Mr. GORDON: In answer to the hon.
Member, it is not a fact that I am com-
The facts are that last month for the
first time we got a request for a number
of young women for employment on such
work, and 52 (out of a much larger
number interviewed) volunteered to go.
They were all over the age of 21, except
one or two, who were about 20. There
was no stoppage of benefit whatever in
the case of those who did not volunteer.
The wages offered were 35s per week
and overtime to bring them up to 42s
per week while learning. After learning,
there were piece-work rates which would
bring in 39s for a 47-hour week, with
considerable opportunities for overtime
at higher rates.
Of the 52 selected, 49 actually started
work. Of these, one returned home
owing to illness and another owing to a
death in the family. In the latter case,
the firm paid her fare home.
I am not aware of any obstacles being
placed in the way of any girls who found
themselves unable to do the work and
wished to return home.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
on the streets of Liverpool last week six
of these girls were wandering about with
no home and no money for food? Is it
not also a fact that men returning to the
city of Belfast owing to the completion of
their jobs in England had to make a collection around certain individuals so as to
provide the girls with lodging money until
such times as they would return to
Birmingham, the place of their employment?
Mr. GORDON: I must confess that this
is the first I have heard of this matter.
My information is that the firm is giving
a free gift of 10s to each girl on arrival
and defraying the cost of the first week's
lodgings, which comes to about 25s. That
is the information I have received.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do you think it is

who have been employed in mills in
Northern Ireland across Channel under

Would he himself send his own daughter
under the same conditions?
Mr. GORDON: It is awfully difficult
to answer that question owing to the fact

INDUSTRIAL REGISTRATION.
4. Rev. PROFESSOR CORKEY asked
the Prime Minister whether he has
observed a statement made on the 21st
instant by Mr. Bevin, Minister of Labour
in the Imperial Parliament, in which he
said that we had now reached the stage
when it would be necessary to have industrial registration by age-groups, and
by this means to make a list of those who
should be called upon to serve the State
in national industry, and whether it was
the purpose of the Government of Northern Ireland to have this system of industrial registration extended to this area.
Mr. GORDON: I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply. I am aware
of the steps which the Imperial Minister of
Labour proposes to take to meet the
shortage of labour in Great Britain. As
the hon. Member is, however, aware, the
supply of labour in Northern Ireland is
considerably in excess of the demand except in the case of a few skilled trades,
for which compulsory registration has
already been put in force. Nevertheless,
I am taking steps to secure that power
will be given to me to make a similar
Order in Northern Ireland should that
course become necessary.

“NORTHERN WHIG'S "
EXCLUSIVE" INFORMATION
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether the "Northern Whig
of 7-1-41, in an article on the present
calling together of Parliament claimed
exclusive information regarding the policy
of the Government in respect to the
supply of turbine scutchers, and other
matters; whether these claims are well
founded, and whether there is any direct
or indirect leakage so far as Government
Departments are concerned.
""
The PRIME MINISTER: I have seen
the article to which the hon. Member
refers, and I am not aware of any direct
or indirect leakage from Government
Departments of information on the policy
of the Government. The hon. Member
will appreciate that the forecasts which
appear from time to time in our Press are,
in many cases, merely an anticipation of
what the policy of the Government is
likely to be.

When making these appointments it

The PRIME MINISTER: As hon.
Members know, negotiations have been
proceeding for several months between our
Government and the British Treasury
and the Ministry of Supply, with a view
to the establishment of tank and chemical
retteries and green fibre processing plants
in appropriate places in Northern Ireland
on somewhat similar lines to those which
have been established by the British
Government in Great Britain.
In dealing with this matter our Government has had the advantage of the views
of the Flax Development Committee, composed of farmers, spinners and others
interested in the industry, and of the
Select Committee of this House which,
as hon. Members know, obtained
evidence from all parties concerned.
My colleagues and I felt that it was
desirable that we should also have the
benefit of the opinions of the representatives of the linen trade. We, therefore,
had several conferences with a large deputation appointed by the trade and at these
conferences the whole position was fully
and helpfully explored. At a conference
heid on the 17th of this month it was
decided that a deputation appointed by
the trade, and accompanied by the
Secretaries of the Ministries of Agriculture and of Commerce, would proceed to
London with a view to having the matter
finally disposed of, the urgency of a quick
decision being recognised by all. I am
glad to be in a position to announce that
an agreement has been arrived at which
has the approval of the British Treasury
and the Ministry of Supply, our Government and the representatives of the trade
Prime Minister's Statement 2864

The scheme is as follows:
1. The Ministry of Supply, through the
agency of our Ministry of Commerce, will
provide and equip with the necessary plant
and machinery, either for the treatment
of green flax, or for the production of
retted fibre, processing factories in areas
where no adequate handling facilities are
now available.
2. The units may be accommodated in
new building or in an existing one
adapted for the purpose.
The estimates
and plans will be subject to approval by
the Ministry of Commerce.
a
3. The factories will be located in areas
approved by the Ministry of Agriculture,
such areas being those where processing
facilities do not exist or are inadequate.
4. The factories will be leased on
reasonable terms to approved firms for a
period of five years with a break at the
cessation of hostilities. No rental will
commence to accrue until 1st January,
1942.
5. The operators will have the option of
purchasing the factories on agreed terms,
at the cessation of hostilities.
6. The flax straw will be purchased for
these factories from farmers who cannot
ret it, in accordance with an agreed plan
based on the yield and quality of the
fibre.
7. The Northern Government will continue to pay 75 per cent. of the labour
costs involved in the provision of new flax
dams and the cleaning out of existing
dams on the usual relief scheme conditions
except that owing to the urgency of the
matter the Government has also agreed to
the removal of the valuation limit and the
present occupational restrictions in connection with this work.

The first effort made to give this protection to small householders was to provide masonry protection-bricks, cement
bound-in the backyards or somewhere
immediately in the vicinity of the dwelling-
That type of shelter was all the more
necessary because it was quite plain in
the course of the last few months that
the enemy has been tending to use
heavier bombs, and a lot of small house
property simply cannot stand against the
resulting blast. Further, with the small
communal shelter in the street or at the
rere of the house it is easier to get those
who shelter in it out than where the shelter
has been built into small houses which
might well fall down on the top of the
shelter. The roofs of these communal

question of ladders, but a good many premises have equipped themselves in that
way. There is one point I would like to
take this opportunity of emphasising as
best I can. The subject of fire prevention in the present phase of the enemy's
activities means dealing with the incendiary bomb before it has got to be a fire,
and it cannot be stressed too often that
the task is simple if it is taken early.
The point I want to stress is that that
task presents a very difficult administrative problem. Every person who has
studied it knows that. That has been
found to be so in Great Britain as well
as here, and it has to be faced. We are
facing it, and we have to do our best with
it from the administrative point of view.
But the important thing is this, and
again it is the experience not only of my
own Department but of the Department
in Great Britain, that the people can
make their own arrangements much more
effectively once they are given some
guidance as to what equipment they
should get than if they are dragooned
along the lines of some official regulation.
I am not saying that in the hope that
there will not be any official regulations,
but in the belief that if the people of this
country tackle the problem themselves
they will be able to evolve a system which
will be as efficient, subject to suitable
supervision, as one can arrive at in any
other way, and a great deal more efficient
than if everyone assumed that this protection ought to work from the top rather
than from the bottom.

POOR-LAW RELIEF IN BELFAST.
1. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
in recent weeks the Commissioners of Poor
Law for Belfast have discontinued relief
to applicants notwithstanding the fact
that in some cases the applicants were
married men with dependants and have
been A.R.P. volunteers since the outbreak
of war; whether he will instruct the
Belfast Poor Law Commissioners that the
utmost sympathetic consideration will in
future be given to this type of applicant;
whether he will consider making such
representations to those gentlemen at once
in the case of Mr. Patrick Devlin, 54
M'Donnell Street, who is a senior post
warden, and is a married man with a
dependant wife, and whose grant of relief
was withdrawn on Friday, the 17th
instant.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I can assure the hon.
Member that the circumstances of each
case are fully considered by the Commissioners before outdoor relief is discontinued, and I am satisfied that the Commissioners deal with these cases most
sympathetically, but, of course, having in
mind that they are spending the ratepayers' money.
It is a fact that outdoor relief has been
refused to
persons who are A.R.P.
wardens, but in each case it was because
the income to the house was sufficient or
because the man concerned was not considered a suitable case for relief.
With regard to the case of Patrick
Devlin, this is a man of 28 years, with no
children, who has been on poor relief and
unemployment assistance for 9 years.
Relief was discontinued on January 11th
of this year.
Mr. BYRNE: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, are those who
have been getting outdoor relief and are
trying to keep a house over their heads,

1941 FLAX-SEED PRICES.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
reduced prices for 1941 of flax-seed, and
what increased allocations of seed to produce blue flowering flax will be made, and
whether the farmers of Northern Ireland
prefer this to the white flowering variety,
and would grow more flax if the supplies
of the former were substantially increased.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): As the hon. Member
will see from the published price lists flaxseed prices are from 2/6d to 5/- a bag less
than last year.
In most districts in Northern Ireland
farmers prefer blue flowering flax to
white; in certain parts of Antrim, however, the preference is for white flowering.
The proportion of blue to white is twice
as great this year as last. Every ounce of
blue flowering flax that is available is
being obtained.
Mr. BROWN: While thanking the
noble Lord for his reply, may I ask will
he take steps to ensure that there is an
equitable distribution all over Northern
Ireland?
Lord GLENTORAN: Yes, sir.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
the right hon. Gentleman can give an
assurance that there will be flax seed
available. for the 100,000 acres for which
he asked?
Lord GLENTORAN: We hope so.
We think there is ample seed available
for the 100,000 acres.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the noble
Lord in case the supply of flax seed in
Northern Ireland is not sufficient is there
any reciprocal arrangement whereby
seed could be got from elsewhere? If so,
would the noble Lord intimate to the
House the procedure to be adopted if we
have not sufficient seed to meet the
requirements of the 100,000 acres?
Lord GLENTORAN: As far as the
first part of the question is concerned, we
are getting seed from all parts of the
world where it is grown. We are getting
it from Canada, Australia and England.
As regards the second part of the question, I am glad to say the matter of
procedure has not arisen and I hope it
will not arise.
Mr. BEATTIE: The point I want to
emphasise is that the seed is there, but
representations may have to be made for
it. The noble Lord can have it on proper
representations being made. Is the seed
suitable to the soil of Northern Ireland
so that a large yield may be obtained?
Could I have an answer to that?
Lord GLENTORAN: Yes, every possible. step will be taken to get all available seed.

Dear Dr. Howell,
It is good to hear from you after all
these years: actually thirteen years
have passed since I left London, and I
have got on well here. We have still
a bit to go in one or two of our services
before we can wave our hats in the air,
but in time we should "get there."
Now, with regard to your letter, I
am glad to be able to recommend Dr.
Walker for the post of Temporary
Deputy Medical Officer of Health and
Tuberculosis Officer.
Dr. Walker is a man of ability and is
not afraid of a spot of work. There
was recently some difficulty at the
Tuberculosis Committee, and Dr.
Walker sent in his resignation.
Frankly, that particular Committee

It is as well that the Minister and the

fact that the Minister has already acted

at one time representing and advising a
client, and then later on having to deal

withdrawn; the fact that, according to
the disclosures here this afternoon, he
has acted on several occasions in regard to
the transfer or sale of certain land which
was part of a bigger estate; the fact that
he is still acting in a legal capacity for

connection with the sale of this Rathmore
site to the Corporation; the fact that this
man's departure to America seems to have
been facilitated by somebody to allow him
to escape from justice-in view of all these
things, I submit respectfully and friendly,
but firmly, that the Minister of Home
Affairs should resign, or if he does not the
Cabinet should hold a meeting after this

resign. If they do not do that, what
they ought to do, at the very least, is to
reconsider Cabinet policy and submit a
fresh statement to this House in regard
to what the future is going to be, and
what the relationship of Cabinet Ministers
to their private pursuits is going to be
in future.

15 JULY 1942
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 25th February, 1941.
The Fourth Session of the Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed
to meet on 25th February, 1941, in the
Fifth year of the Reign of King
George VI, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Five Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland) in
the Chair.
Brigadier-General H. G. Young,
C.I.E., D.S.O., acting as Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Acting
Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.
Papers Presented.
Ministry of Education:
The Public Elementary School
(Teachers' War Service) Regulations,
1940, Amending Regulation, No. 1, 1941.
(By Act).
Ministry of Finance:
Estimate of a further sum required to
be voted for the service of the year ending
March 31st, 1941. (By Command.)
Accounts of the Government Loans
Fund for the year ended March 31st, 1940,
together with the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor-General thereon.
(By Act.)
Ministry of Home Affairs:
Inspectors' Reports for 1940 of each
Private and Public Mental Hospital in
Northern Ireland. (By Act.)
SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
A
King's Speech
Sessional Orders
HOUSE OF COMMONS
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime
or misdemeanour; and this House will
proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein,
or thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS AND
RECORDS.
Ordered, That the Votes, Proceedings
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered, That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL.
A Bill" for the more effectual preventing Clandestine Outlawries," was read
the First time.
Resignation of Major D. G. Shillington.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to inform the
House that I have received the following
letter:-
February, 24th, 1941.
Dear Mr. Speaker,
Acting on medical advice, I beg herewith to tender to you my resignation
from Parliament.
I had hoped to have been able to
resume my full duties, but now, owing to
health reasons, I find this is impossible.
It is with regret, therefore, that I now
place my resignation in your hands.
Yours sincerely,
D. GRAHAM SHILLINGTON.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The struggle in which the Empire is
engaged for liberty and justice has
entered
its second year.
upon
The
people of Northern Ireland have responded willingly to all the calls which
have been made upon them. Large
numbers of men and women have voluntered for His Majesty's Forces; the
civil defence services have been well
maintained, and the energy and initiative of employers, reinforced by the
adaptability of our workers, point to the
value of the contribution which is being
made on the Home Front.
The most friendly relationship exists
between the civil population and the
members of His Majesty's Services,
whose presence in Northern Ireland all
our people view with much pleasure,
and whose comfort and happiness while
stationed here are our desire.
Ministers have been active to secure the
fullest co-operation with the Forces of
My
King's Speech
King's Speech
25 FEBRUARY 1941
the Crown in connection with the varied
administrative problems which arise.
The Local Defence Volunteers have
been pursuing their training under
military direction and guidance and
have reached a stage of efficiency which
reflects credit on all ranks of the Force,
and is viewed with satisfaction by the
General Officer commanding the troops
in Northern Ireland.
Considerable progress has been made
with civil defence measures. It is
evident that the community as a whole
is becoming increasingly alive to the
vital importance of this subject.
Hitherto the necessity to call the civil
defence services into action has fortunately not arisen, but I have no doubt
that, if it should, all sections of the
people will acquit themselves with the
same courage and resource as have been
displayed in Great Britain, and which
have evoked the admiration of the
world.
I have been impressed by the splendid
response which has already been made
by our farmers to the appeal by my
Government for an increase in the area
under the plough so as to provide more
foodstuffs from our own soil.
The
coming year will make even greater calls
upon our resources, but I am confident
that our farmers will redouble their
efforts to grow more food and also to
increase the acreage under flax in order
to provide to the greatest extent possible
the raw material upon which our linen
industry depends.
I am glad to learn that our textile
trades are being utilised to a greater
degree in supplying the needs of the
Forces of the Crown, and that they
have thus been able, within the past
few months, to provide additional employment for our workers. Notwithstanding the cessation of flax supplies
from the Continent, it has been found
possible to arrange an allocation of
flax yarns for the manufacture of linen
for the export trade, the maintenance of
which is of such vital importance to the
national effort. It is gratifying to
know that the total number of unemployed has fallen, during the past year,
by fifteen thousand.
My Ministers have been able to conclude a satisfactory arrangement with
departments of the Imperial Government under which flax processing
factories will be erected in areas where
the need is greatest, and I hope that
the adoption of these modern methods
will have a beneficial effect on our linen
industry and make a substantial contribution to relieving unemployment.
A measure will be laid before you to
make the household means test for
Unemployment Assistance and Supplementary Pensions more favourable to the
claimants and also to disregard certain
War Savings in computing the resources
of such claimants for these purposes.
You will be invited to consider proposals
for the preservation of certain superannuation rights in the case of persons
transferring to war employment, and
for the amendment of the Education
(Emergency Provisions) Act, passed
last Session, so as to authorise the payment of a grant, in appropriate cases,
of the entire cost of the protection of
schools and training colleges against
damage from air attack. You will also
be asked to consider an amendment of
the Fisheries Acts for the purpose of
modifying the law relating to the discharge of flax water into rivers and
lakes.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The reduction to 60 of the age at
which women may become entitled to
contributory old age pensions resulted
in the grant of pensions to a large
number of women who were either
themselves insured or who were the
wives of men who had reached the age
of 65 and had qualified for contributory
pensions. The introduction of the
Supplementary Pensions Scheme last
August did much to ameliorate cases of
hardship amongst old age pensioners.
It is of the utmost importance at this
time that there should be the minimum
of interruption in the country's
machinery of production, and it is,
therefore, satisfactory to record that
very few stoppages have taken place.
The settlement of disputes has been
greatly facilitated by the establishment,
under the Emergency Powers (Defence)
Acts, of the National Arbitration
Tribunal (Northern Ireland).

I am pleased to learn that no difficulty

the education of those children who were

country districts.
It is a matter of satisfaction that the

Debate on the Address.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I beg to
move:-
"That a humble Address be presented to his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth :
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
In rising to move the Address I should
like at the beginning to point out that
in a time of war even this House cannot
escape the effects. In peace times one of
the main or major functions of this
House is to deal with legislation, but at
a time like the present when not only
our ancient liberties but our very
existence as a people are being put to the
arbitrament of the most ruthless war
perhaps the world has ever seen, the
functions of this House have also to
undergo certain modifications, and so it
is that in the Gracious Speech we do not
find any long recital of legislative
measures to be proposed for the attention
of the House during the session.
There are nevertheless some such
measures. There is one first of all to
deal with the household means test, and
a Bill is to be introduced along similar
lines to those of the Bill before the
Imperial Parliament. There is every
reason to hope that that Bill will remove
what has been regarded as a serious
grievance on the part of those directly
affected. I do not know to what extent
the Exchequer will be affected by the
provisions of that Bill, but I think it is
something to be proud of that at a time.
when the burdens of war are so gigantic,
the Government and our people feel
strong enough to deal with a grievance
of this kind and to find the wherewithal
to do it.
Another measure that is to come
before Parliament is a Bill to safeguard
the right of superannuation of persons
proceeding from civil employment to war
employment. The Government is anxious
through this measure to make sure that
any possible handicap in the way of anyone failing or being prevented from
doing work in the particular sphere for
which he is qualified at a time like this,
shall be removed.
Then there is to be a Bill to make
provision that as regards air raid protection in the case of certain schools and
training colleges there shall be a charge
on the Exchequer and not even a partial
charge upon local authorities in cases
where the Government is satisfied that
that is the proper course to adopt.
There is only one other legislative
measure referred to in the Gracious
Speech, and that is a measure to deal
with the discharge of flax water
into certain streams and rivers. This
has been the cause of a considerable
amount of bitterness, indeed a feeling
of very definite bitterness, for a good
while back. It was not only the law,
but it was the way in which prosecutions
were sometimes brought, and it was the
attitude and general approach of the
fishery authorities in this matter that
embittered flax growers in certain districts. There is no doubt that in those
districts the state of the law and the
way in which prosecutions were brought
before the courts did act as a deterrent
to the extensive sowing and growth of
flax. May I appeal to the Government
to have this Bill drafted and brought
before this House at the earliest possible moment so that the farmers may
know that everything is being done that
can be done in a reasonable way to
remove their
and
grievances
their
difficulties in this connection.
A great part of the Gracious Speech
is taken up with a review of the general
situation. It is pointed out that the

country is in a peaceable state, that the

creditable.

There is a reference to enlistment in
His Majesty's Forces. I think, having
regard to the ever increasing attractions
in the nature of work of one kind and
another and remunerative rates of pay, it
is something to congratulate our people
upon that the response to the call for men
for the different services has been met so
well and that enlistments have been so
good. Sometimes I think critics of these
figures overlook the fact that a good
number of our young men did join up
voluntarily in the anti-aircraft
and
various other units which since the war
started have become an integral part of
the standing forces.
There is a reference to the enthusiasm
and the efficiency of the Local Defence
Volunteer Force. After that force was
established there was a certain feeling of
grievance on the part of some of the
members. I often heard criticisms and
contrasts drawn as between the terms of
service in that force and the "B" Special
Constabulary. Well, as the imminence of
danger has increased, and as throughout
the world a fuller knowledge of all that
our fellow citizens on the other side of
the Channel have been suffering and
undergoing as this has come home to
our people I think these grousers have disappeared. The volunteers deserve a
special word of commendation and
encouragement, and I think there is only
one spirit amongst the men here and that
is a desire that when the hour comes they
may be ready.
May I say that a considerable, change,
I had almost used the word improvement,
in the general attitude of our people to
the whole war situation has taken place.
I would not like to say that even yet
that change has penetrated and found its
way to every individual in the community. I think, speaking of the vast
majority of our people, the truth has
dawned on them increasingly that we are
at war, that war has broken out not on
some distant shore but on these islands of
ours, and that in that war we are all
involved. Our homes are at stake. The
safety of our families is at stake. It is
total war, a war not waged by the enemy
according to any of the recognised
standards of humanity, a war in which
the only rights are those enjoyed by the
enemy and where the stronger trample
the weaker.
Then there is a reference to the presence
amongst us of larger numbers of His
Majesty's forces. At first I think the
feeling evoked by the presence of these
men was largely one of novelty and
curiosity and that sort of thing, but as
time has gone on, as I have already
pointed out, the presence of these men
has brought home to our people the sense
of the danger to us all. These men have
been heartily welcome, and the general
testimony is and I meet a good many
of them from time to time-that they
have been received with open arms and
warm words everywhere they have gone.
They have received nothing but kindness.
and the greatest of hospitality. Perhaps
mention should also be made of the way
in which the military authorities connected with these men have tried as far
as possible to accommodate themselves
to the conditions that they found here,
and to fit in their activities and their demands with the activities of the different
Government departments and of the
various interests with which they have
come in contact.
Mention is made in the Gracious
Speech of the co-operation that has been
forthcoming on the part of the heads of
business firms throughout our community, and there is also a reference to
the adaptability of the workers. May I
say in regard to labour generally that
I think we are only beginning to come
face to face with our real labour
problems, and without being too explicit
about the position in certain districts I
would draw the attention of the House
to the fact that in some districts already
there is keen competition for the labour
available there as between one kind of
national work and another kind of
national work. There is not a moment
to be lost in drawing up a scheme for
real organisation and systematic utilisation and apportionment as between one.
kind of national work and another of the
labour that is available, otherwise there
is no doubt that in some districts at any
rate certain kinds of national work are

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
going to be seriously prejudiced and

There is a reference to the very considerable reduction in the volume of unemployment during the past twelve
months, but I think there is still hanging round the labour exchanges far too
big a fringe of men who, physically and
in every other way, are just not fit for
employment as things are. I have been
seriously wondering whether the time is
not coming when these men should be
sifted and classified not merely according to their actual registration at the
labour exchange for their more remote
antecedents as labourers or workers, but
that a field should be taken and spades
put into the hands of a good proportion
of them. They could be set to work, if
it was only for an hour a day, not as a
penalty or anything of the kind, but
with a view to bringing them back to a
physical condition in which their services
would be of real use to the community
and the nation at a time like the present.
It is perhaps invidious when all classes
of the community are expected to give
us all they can to single out any particular class, but I do think that the
Gracious Speech was justified in making
a special reference an honourable
mention, shall I say to the farming community. The vast majority of our
farmers have not only been doing all
they can, but are determined to go on
doing all they can, to give their services
to the nation loyally. They do not ask,
as far as I am in touch with their feelings, for favourable consideration of any
kind, but they do ask, and I think the
nation cannot afford to give them less, the
utmost facilities available having regard
to all the conditions prevailing for the
production of more and still more food for
the people and more raw material for
the great linen industry.
In regard to that linen industry I
need only say that it has been passing
through, and is still in, a difficult
period, but there is no use at this stage
in crying over spilt milk and trying to
apportion blame on this one or that one.
The circumstances are such that it is only
by the unreserved co-operation of all the
interests involved in that industry that a
satisfactory issue can be obtained.

way I have covered the points to which

had all so long been accustomed to thinking of the State as being possessed of
inexhaustible resources, of being some

We might almost say at the moment
that the portents are sinister. By that
I mean that sore trials and severe and
desperate tests are ahead of our people.
We do not know in what form or when
