Mr. DOWLING (in morning dress):
In seconding the Motion before the
House, the first thing I would like to say
is that we are beginning this new Session
with a new Prime Minister possessing
many qualifications of a high order, but
I believe the one qualification which
stands out prominently beyond all others
and the one that appeals strongly to the
people of Northern Ireland is that he is
a businessman first rather than
politician. That does not mean he is not
to have anything to do with politics; far
from it, because when political questions
no longer arise in Northern Ireland the
people will have become deaf, dumb, and
blind, or have ceased to exist. That being
so, his success will largely depend on his
reactions to what will be demanded, and
how far this will serve the best interests
of the people he is called upon to govern.
In all these matters we have confidence
that he will stand up to the test.
Already the Prime Minister has made
an excellent start by exchanging positions
of Ministers, adding one new Minister of
exceptional experience and appointing
three new junior Ministers. I am going
to take the risk of saying that in my
opinion the Government has been
materially strengthened by these appointments, and most of us, if not all, will
be greatly disappointed if our prediction
turns out to be wrong. To the junior
Ministers I would say, "A very great
opportunity has been given to you of
serving your country in a way that will
be most acceptable, and I hope you will
take full advantage of it without undue
delay".
The Gracious Speech which has just
been read deals mainly with matters
which have arisen out of the war. Now,
in an emergency of such magnitude, it
was only to be expected that a great deal
of dislocation would occur to normal
peace-time activities. I do not consider it
necessary to mention in detail the various
difficulties with which the people, whether
in their homes or in their business have
had to contend, because I know of no one
young or old who has not experienced
some inconvenience due to war, indeed it
is not only a matter of inconvenience but
often enough great personal sacrifice.
Notwithstanding this, however, I have
yet to find even the person who may be
suffering acutely due to this war, who
would put forward the demand to the
British Government that it should enter
into peace negotiations with one or other
of our enemies to-day.
We have all had to realise, therefore,
that the Government faced with such
opponents, one at least whose chief desire
is the destruction of everything the
British Empire stands for, had to introduce unusual measures considered necessary in order to safeguard the lives and
interests of our people. These measures,
it is only right to say, have not always
been administered with that sympathy or
consideration which the circumstances
demanded; increased hardships are. sometimes inflicted where already general war
conditions, however carefully and sympathetically applied, had hit many people
severely. When this happens the best
efforts and intentions of the Government
are frustrated and complaints are.
magnified. I think it would be well if
some of our administrators would
remember they are the servants of the
people. Really good administrators never
require to be reminded of this, and we
have many who are beyond reproach.
The Gracious Speech quite properly
calls attention to decided improvements
in social services, providing supplementary pensions, unemployment assistance.
up to a higher limit, and new and more
equitable conditions regarding the means
test. These changes are heartily welcomed
and will dispose of injustices of long
standing which this House had previously
no power to ameliorate or remove.
I am also glad to find in the Gracious
Speech reference to His Majesty's Forces
stationed in our midst, and I would join
in expressing thanks to all who have so
willingly taken a part in co-operating
with our Civil Defence measures, and for
the help and instructions so freely given.
to our Local Defence Volunteers.
What of the future? Here, I do not
hesitate to say the war and everything
necessary to ensure complete victory in
the shortest possible time must occupy
first place in our minds and hearts. No
room exists for divided opinions on this
question. At the same time, I agree
with those who express the view that a
victorious peace must be a peace that will
enable our people, however placed to-day,

Debate on the Address

to return as quickly as possible to a
normal and contented life, freed from the

benefit, but rather lining up to be given
the name and address of the employer in
their own area in Northern Ireland who

The Gracious Speech refers to the
splendid response of our farmers in providing foodstuffs, and they are entitled to
our thanks and appreciation. They are
now called upon to produce still more food
and to interest themselves in the growing
of flax in addition. I believe they will
equally respond to this appeal, provided
the Government play fair with them.
which they have not always done, with
serious consequences to the best interest
of all. The growing of flax in sufficient
quantities should enable the linen industry to overtake a considerable amount
of the ground they have lost between the
last Great War and the present one, and
the arrangements made with the Imperial
Government for financing flax processing
factories should, when these are
pleted, enable much greater employment
to be given in the textile industry.
com-
It has been stated, and not without
some foundation, that 60 per cent. of the
trouble hitherto in the textile industry
was due to internal and controllable
causes. If this is true then immediate
steps should be taken to put the
industry's own house in order. The
Government's recent decision to assist the
industry in matters at present beyond the
control of this trade, is a gesture which
should act as a stimulus to every section
of this industry to get together and frame
a policy that will bring a success more in
keeping with its past history. If lack of
co-operation exists in the linen industry
it exists in many others, even down to our
home industries. Speaking generally, it
is anti-employment and anti-progressive,
and no country can produce its best
results under such adverse conditions.
While we all desire to see the farmers
and the linen trade forging ahead and
prospering beyond measure, we must not
overlook the fact that these interests do
not stand alone, or that their solution
solves the whole unemployment problemvery far from it; and do not let anyone
imagine that the moment peace returns
all will be well. In a war such as the
present, unemployment and general dislocation are bound to arise. The fact that
the unemployment figures to-day are more
favourable than twelve months ago is satisfactory up to a point. This is, of course,
largely due to war work, and some of it
will continue during the whole course of
the war, and some will finish at a much
earlier date.
The unemployment, however, between
the last war and this one in almost every
branch of industry has been extremely
severe, and the cause of this must be investigated and reported upon before our
Government can put forward the claim
that they have done everything possible
to find a solution. It is clear that no
complete solution can be applied during
the war, but only when peace returns.
Therefore now is the time to investigate
into causes. We all agree that depression
in one trade or several trades affects
adversely other trades, and we can never
have an improved universal standard of
living where acute unemployment occurs
at intervals in almost every trade.

us, therefore, take the necessary steps

Mr. BEATTIE: Before proceeding,
might I be allowed to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder
of the Address in Reply to the King's
Speech. In moving the Address in Reply
I think it is the duty of the proposer to
give, to the best of his ability, an outline of the principles which have been
promulgated to guide the Government in
its business during the session. I regret
that the mover on the present occasion
did not make any reference to that grand
principle which has been in operation.
since I came into this House. I do not
say that about the seconder. He has
given time and attention to the things
which matter. He has tried to put first
things first, and I hope the Government
will act very quickly on what he has said.
The mover mentioned many things in
which I believe, but if he had taken his
text from the Sermon on the Mount it
would have been more appropriate than
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
25 FEBRUARY 1941
to move the Address in Reply.on blood
and slaughter. We are all anxious and
willing to help and to make every effort
to bring this war to an early and successful termination; but we want, if possible,
to bring it into a real Christian world.
If Christianity had prevailed throughout
the nations I doubt very much whether
we would have been suffering under the
cloud of a world war as at present. The
mover, being one of its disciples, is
partly responsible for the Christianisation.
of the world, and I think it would have
been better if he had concentrated on
things that matter and left alone the
things which do not matter. This is the
first time I have deviated from the
Gracious Speech, but in view of the
utterances of the mover I was compelled
to make these comments. This is the
first time I have transgressed to that
extent.
What did the mover of the Address
say about unemployment? Absolutely
nothing. He has now departed from
the House, and it is the first time in the
history of the House that the mover of
an Address has left before the Prime
Minister has spoken. This House must
get down to the first things first. If we
are a unit of Great Britain, why have
we in our midst to-day 60,000 unemployed? Why are we losing the energy
and labour power of these people? Is it
because our value as a unit of Great
Britain is not appreciated, or is it due
to the failure of the right hon. Gentlemen who are responsible for the lives and
the well-being of the people in this area?
I say there is a dual responsibility.
The Minister of Labour has, from the
commencement of the war, been implored
from this side of the House to get into
his stride and start working on behalf
of the unemployed in Northern Ireland.
What has he done? He has taken the
easiest way out. He has gone to London
and met representative people there, but
has he brought anything of a substantial
nature to the unemployed workers in
Northern Ireland? No, he has not; he
has only brought desolation, loneliness,
and the breaking up of family life by
agreeing, when in London, to the
transfer of labour from Northern Ireland to Great Britain. I say, without
fear of challenge from any quarter, that
if the Minister of Labour had been just
to labour he would have told the British
Minister that we have a supply of labour
in Northern Ireland equal to a certain
percentage of productivity, and that if
he was willing to establish factories here
our people would be willing to give 100
per cent. production. That would have
been a business-like way for the Minister
of Labour to approach the matter, and
I am more certain now than ever that
it would have been the proper way. I
say that because to keep our factories in
production it is necessary to have them
scattered over as wide an area as possible.
Northern Ireland would have been a
very good area in which to erect factories
for the production of things of national
importance. Instead of that we have the
heads of families sent to Scotland,
England and Wales, and the wives and
families are also going to the same areas
while the skill they possess could have
been used at home and they would also
have been able to keep intact parental
control. That is the Minister of Labour's
solution of the unemployment problemship them away. It is the same system
as was adopted by the British Government
in the bad old days when they reduced
the population of Ireland from eight to
three-and-a-half millions. They shipped
the people away to foreign countries and
made every provision for the shipment.
In the year 1941 our Minister of Labour
is doing exactly what was done in those
evil days by a Government which failed to
recognise the valuable asset in Ireland,
next door to Great Britain. In those days
they shipped them to America, and now
we are calling upon America to give us
very necessary help. Many thousands of
the sons and daughters of the people who
were shipped away are now giving us 100
per cent. support from the American production market so that we may be relieved
of the great hardships we are enduring at
the moment. I say that the present shipment of people from one country to
another owing to the failure or laziness of
individuals to think out the best way to
serve those people is a tragedy, and I hope
that shipment of labour will discontinue.
Then we are told that the household
means test is to be abolished. That
is a ridiculous statement for anyone to make. The household means
test is going to remain. It is going to
remain with the support of people who in
years gone by stood with me for 100 per
cent. abolition. I regret that these people
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
because of getting into positions in
Government circles have run away from
the ideas they themselves propagated
from platform to platform. We have an
intimation in the Speech that we are to
follow the lines of Great Britain. Why
should we be compelled to tolerate the
household means test for either old age
pensions or public assistance? We are
poorer by far than Great Britain. Our
mode of life is different to that in Great
Britain. We are asked to carry out a
step-by-step policy from the point of view
of conditions of life and purchasing power
on the same footing as Great Britain. It
cannot be done. The lives of the two
peoples are different. Their dietary is
different. The conditions under which
they live are different, and their earning
power is different. The Government would
be well advised to abolish in its entirety
the household means test. If it does it
will give a sensible lead to the British
Parliament.
We are told about the voluntary
system of recruiting. I did not hear the
numbers that had joined the British
Army. I have not heard those figures
from any quarter, but I have heard in
peace time. large numbers of people
giving great lip service to their loyalty,
people who in days of trial and difficulty
would respond at the first moment when
the call was made. I can see in Northern
Ireland to-day many hundreds,
thousands, of such people who must not
have heard that call. I have challenged
these people, and they say the home
front must be guarded. The home front
is a very good excuse for many people.
If I had been a super-loyalist such as
these people claim to be I do not think
in times of difficulty and trouble for the
British Empire I would be found in
civilian attire.
yes
We have, as stated in the King's
Speech, got in our midst large numbers
of the British Army. I am pleased to
know that the civil population are extending Irish hospitality, kindness and
courtesy to the troops who are away from
home. But too much hospitality sometimes does not tend to the betterment of
the physical fitness of the members of
the Army, Navy and Air Forces. I have
noted the rationing system on the civil
population. The people. are undergoing
a heavy strain owing to the rationing of
foodstuffs, but I have noticed also that
the civil population, although crying out
about the rationing scheme that is
applied under Order, supply food and
refreshments in canteens to members of
the services who are not rationed, and
who are provided with a dietary which is
sufficient to keep them in physical fitness
to meet any emergency. There is a
danger in over-hospitality. That danger
is that one might become over-fed which
creates less efficiency. I give that as a
warning. Too much hospitality in the
line, of feeding can be given to the troops
here. I do not think that is desirable in
the interests of the Army and Navy in
our area.
The next thing I want to mention is
the Local Defence Volunteers. Why
should the volunteers still remain a force
of that kind in Northern Ireland? If you
are going step by step with Great Britain
why not bring all classes of the community into the force on the same basis
as the Home Guard in England? Why
do you not designate our force as the
Home Guard? What is the reason? I
will try to give the reason now. It is
known to everyone who has any connection with the Province that the percentage of Catholics in the L.D.V.s is
very low. I have made inquiries why that
is so.
It matters not whether you are a
Protestant or Catholic, Methodist
Episcopalian, if an invasion comes you
will all get the same punishment. Every
man, no matter what religion he belongs
to, should be enrolled in the home force
in order to keep out the invader. Why
is there one section of our community not
enrolled? It is because the L.D.V.s
come under the heading of Ulster Special
Constabulary.
or
I want to see in Northern Ireland a
united force known as the Home Guard
under the direct supervision of the military authorities, with a personnel at the
head of the force equal to the requirements and duties they may be called upon
to discharge. The right hon. Gentleman,
the Minister of Public Security, is new
to his job, and no one would assist him
more than I would. I wish every citizen in

If he makes the change I suggest I am
certain he would have the support of
90 per cent. of the community. Why
am I not a member of the force? The
Ulster Special Constabulary, on the for-

mation of this Government, was recruited

As to the cost of living, I may say
as a member of a tribunal established by
this House that that tribunal has given
service in the national interest. We have
large numbers of complaints from people
regarding the failure of employers to

Through the agency of the Minister of
Labour employers and workmen are able

favourably by the workers' side I do not
know. The cost of living is soaring to
such an extent that the working class,
at least the stabilised class in the community, are in a very serious position
at the moment.
A large percentage of the people of
Northern Ireland have got no increase
in wages since the commencement of the
war, and therefore their position is very
unhappy in regard to this question of the
increased cost of living. I hope the
Prime Minister will see his way to give

sufficient to meet the reduced purchasing
power of their wages or salaries since the
war commenced. I hope the right hon.
Gentleman gets that point, as he and the
Minister of Finance are the two gentlemen concerned. I hope he will give a

were
I wish now to refer to factories. I
would point out that we who
members of the Select Committee on
Unemployment, which
which has now been
terminated, feel in regard to the

Again, it has been stated that our

I do not think we would. When it is
realised that the production of every
man is equal to five tons and there are
70,000 people unemployed it is easily seen
what the national interests are losing by
those men walking the streets. The
sooner we get them usefully employed
the better.
The Minister of Labour has just returned. I am sorry he was not here
before, but it seems to be the practice
now to be absent when anything of importance is to be said. It may not seem
important to the right hon. Gentleman,
but it is all-important to me. My concern

I believe he is the right man in the right

I come now to the sentence in which
it is stated that there is to be a modification of the law relating to the discharge

The PRIME MINISTER (Mr.
Andrews): It is a great pleasure to me
to join with the hon. Member for Pottinger in congratulating the mover and
the seconder of the Address in Reply to
the Gracious Speech on the excellent
speeches they made. They have performed what is always recognised to be a
very delicate, difficult and trying Parliamentary duty in the very best way
possible. Having dealt with the various
suggestions made in the Speech itself with
tact, judgment and good taste they, in my
opinion, upheld the traditional dignity of
an occasion such as this.
I have gone so far in company with the
hon. Member for Pottinger that I regret
it is now necessary for me to take exception to a good deal he has said. I suppose
it was too much to expect that he would
bless the Gracious Speech unreservedly,
having regard to the fact-I think I am
entitled to say this-that he is the most
active Member of our Opposition, but I
did not think he would go so far as to
criticise somewhat severely almost every
thought expressed in the Gracious Speech.
I have said on several occasions of late
that I was anxious that we should leave
party controversy aside during this war,
and I think it will be admitted that there
is nothing really controversial in the
Gracious Speech.
My colleagues and I
feel that we in Ulster should lay aside
party politics, as I have said, while this
gigantic struggle in which our Empire is.
engaged rages. We should all remember
what is at stake: our Empire, our national
security, our freedom, our independence,
our democratic form of Government, our
trade unions, and our very civilisation; in
fact everything that has been built up
through the generations that have gone
and which we in this part of the United
Kingdom have the privilege of enjoying.
May I mention a few of the more
important matters dealt with in the
Gracious Speech? It is stated that large
numbers of men and women have joined
the forces of the Crown. We all regret
that already a considerable number of
them have made the supreme sacrifice.
The relations which exist between the civil
population and the members of the Forces
are of the most friendly character. That
must give great satisfaction to everyone of
us no matter upon which side of the House
we happen to sit. It is also gratifying to
feel that our Civil Defence services have
been established on a sound foundation,
and, further, that our Local Defence
Volunteers, to which the hon. Member
for Pottinger referred, are under competent officers in a very advanced
state of training. I am perfectly certain
that if the worst should happen and they
are called into action their local knowledge will be of the greatest value to the
forces of the Crown. The hon. Member
stated that this was a party force.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
25 FEBRUARY 1941
Mr. BEATTIE: Pardon me. Do not
misrepresent me. I want that statement
corrected. I do not want any ambiguity.
I said the "B" Special force was a party
one, not the L.D.V's.
The PRIME MINISTER: Then the
hon. Member is satisfied with the way in
which the L.D.V's have been enlisted and
formed.
Mr. BEATTIE: With your permission,
Mr. Speaker, I said I was dissatisfied because the way in which it has been formed
has prevented me and thousands of others
from joining. You have a Territorial Act
applicable to Northern Ireland. Why do
you not form a Home Guard under that
Act as it is formed in England and bring
in all classes of the community?
The PRIME MINISTER: I was quite
right then in my original statement. The
hon. Member was referring not only to
the "B" Specials, but also to the L.D.V's.
I want to be quite frank with the hon.
Member. In Ulster we have difficulties
with which to deal; difficulties which do
not exist in Great Britain. In forming
any force in Ulster we have to be careful
that we put arms and ammunition only
into the hands of men who can be
depended upon. We have to make doubly
sure that if trouble should come, which
we all hope and pray will not, these arms
and ammunition will not be used to help
the enemy.
That is why the force has
been raised, not on a political or religious
basis, but simply on a basis which will
ensure that it will be a loyal force. A
loyal force it is and one on which we can
depend.
I now wish to say a few words in reference to the great efforts which our farmers
are making to provide food, which will be
doubly necessary in the future; also the
raw materials required to provide, in the
form of linen, the needs of the Forces and
to maintain our great export trade,
especially with America. That is a matter
of vital public importance. The hon.
Member referred to the work of the Select
Committee. I wish, again, to pay my
tribute to the work which that Committee
has done. It must be gratifying to everyone to know that already the main provisions of the first Report have been given
effect to, and, through arrangements with
the appropriate departments in Great
Britain, a considerable number of
processing factories are to be established in Northern Ireland in order
to deal with the 100,000 acres of
flax which we are justified in expecting
will be grown during the present year.
The Committee has also presented us with
a second Report which deals with drainage and certain other matters.
I should have. thought that the hon.
Member for Pottinger would have
expressed some satisfaction at the fact
that during the past year the unemployment figures have fallen by 15,000. I am
thankful to be able to announce to-day
that the February returns show a further
fall of 7,000, which makes a total reduction of 22,000. This leaves the total
number of unemployed not over 70,000,
as the hon. Member for Pottinger
thought, but just over 61,000.
Mr. BEATTIE: I think I said between
60,000 and 70,000.
The PRIME MINISTER: And I am
hopeful as regards the future unless something very unexpected happens. The
winter is giving place to spring, and we
have reason to believe that a great deal
of unemployment in our seasonal
industries, such as farming, will be done
away with. It will be recollected by the
House that a few weeks ago the Government was able to announce that it
intended to restore the road grants to
local authorities. This should enable
them to give more work than they were
able to do during the past year.
Mr. HENDERSON: They cannot get
the material.
The PRIME MINISTER: I know that
a great deal of material is required at the.
present time for carrying out building
work in connection with the defence of
Ulster, and of course that must be given
first place. I am hopeful, however, that
after that has been supplied there will
be available for road improvement and
road maintenance such material
as is
necessary. Another reason why I look
forward to the future with hope so far
as Northern Ireland is concerned is the
belief that the recent visit of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Commerce,
to London will be productive of good
results. I am glad in that respect, if in
no other, that the hon. Member for
Pottinger and myself are in entire agreement.

So much
unemployment. As the hon. Member for
Pottinger has referred to our great social

ago when walking down High Street I

if you cannot the State, in a large

Mr. NIXON: Was he on the dole?
The PRIME MINISTER: The statement to which I refer is absolutely true.
It is a fact that since this Government
came into being almost twenty years ago
-this cannot be denied our great social
services, which mean so much to our
working people, have been added to,
widened and extended almost beyond
measure. Then again, my hon. Friend
has expressed some approval, qualified
approval of our Supplementary Pensions.
Act. I should like to inform hon.
Members that that Act has meant that
supplementary pensions are being paid
to no fewer than 35,000 persons at a cost
of £675,000 per annum.
In addition to
that, 6,200 additional women have
obtained contributory old-age pensions,
owing to the reduction of the qualifying
age to 60, at an annual cost of £161,200.
It cannot be said that this Government,
of which I am proud to be a member, has
not done everything humanly possible to
help our people during the years they
most require aid.
But a strange thing is that we can never
satisfy some hon. Members opposite. I
do not quite understand the logic of my
hon. Friend (Mr. Beattie), because he
said that this was a poorer country than
Great Britain, and yet he went on to say
that we ought to do better in many
directions than is done in Great Britain.
I cannot follow his argument.
There is another statement he made
to-day to which I feel I must refer, and
that is his objection to people from this
part of the United Kingdom, who cannot
get work here at the moment, being sent
temporarily to Great Britain to do necessary war work there. In the first place,
Englishmen do not refuse to go to Scotland, and Scotsmen do not object to go
to England. I cannot, therefore, see why
Northern Ireland men should not go, and
go willingly, to any other part of the
Kingdom, especially in these times.
Further, I would point out to the hon.
Member that the transfer of labour from
one part of the Kingdom to another, in
other words the mobility of labour, is a
recognised principle in trades union
circles, as I am sure the hon. Member
knows quite well.
Mr. BEATTIE: I want you to bring
factories here.
The PRIME MINISTER: Nobody
would be more delighted to see these
people coming back than I would, but
still we are at war, and in my opinionand I do not hesitate to say it with all
the responsibility attached to the position
I occupy-if there is no work here for
them during the war they ought to be
glad and proud to go and do work whereever it is available.
In the next place there is a word or
two I would like to say about the means
test to which my hon. Friend has referred. Of course, I know that for a great
many years the means test has been the
stock-in-trade of the opposition, not only
in this House but in the Imperial House
as well. I had hoped that the hon.
Debate on the Address
Adjournment
25 FEBRUARY 1941
Member would have come forward to-day
and welcomed the easing of the position.
It is an undoubted fact that the position
is being eased. But the hon. Member
comes along and talks about the household means test as if that test, which was
objected to by many in the days gone
past, was going to remain as of old. That
is not so. The position is going to be
entirely changed. Amongst other things
it will be provided that in assessing the
amount which claimants shall receive the
old household test for unemployment
assistance and supplementary pensions
shall be very largely replaced by the personal needs test under which only the
applicant's own resources and those of
the applicant's wife or husband and dependents will in general be taken into
account.
I have frequently heard other Members
speak about this means test as a thing
which divided households and families.
There may have been some trouble as to
that in the past, but my view for what
it is worth as regards the test which is
going to be applied in the future is that
it will be a test to unite families because,
after all, if an aged father or mother
requires help why should the son, or even
the daughter if she can afford it, not
assist the State in providing for the aged
parents? Again, if one brother requires
help why should another brother not help?
It is not my view of family life that such
should not take place. No, I feel beyond
all doubt that this easing of the means
test is desirable and will leave the means
test in a position which can and should
be defended by every right-thinking man.
May I say in conclusion, that in Ulster
we all desire to play our part in this tragic
war, this deplorable war, the stakes in
which are immeasurable. We can best
play that part, as I said at the beginning
of my remarks, by putting aside for the
time being party considerations and
uniting in a desire to do everything
humanly possible to bring victory as
quickly as it can be brought.

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 26th February, 1941.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
KING'S SPEECH.
Adjourned Debate on the Address.
Order read for resuming adjourned
debate on Question (25th February):
"That an Humble Address be presented to his Grace, the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as follows:
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our humble
thanks to your Grace for the Speech
which your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."-(Rev. Robert
Moore.)
Question again proposed.
Mr. NIXON: So far as the Gracious
Speech is concerned it was a comparatively
mild document. Some things in it have
my approval, and some things have not.
But the Speech was more conspicuous for
what it omitted than for what it contained. The Motion for an Address was
moved and seconded in the usual way by
Members on that side, and in the absence
of the Member who moved it I will go no
further in that respect. The Speech
itself was divided into paragraphs, each
dealing with and confined to the subject
of that paragraph, which, of course, is
the proper way to present anything. To
go from one subject to another
is the only way it can be followed.
I think one of the clearest-headed men I
ever met was the late Chairman of Ways
and Means. There were never any mixed
ideas coming from him. One paragraph
followed another and each dealt with the
particular subject to which it was related.
But some of our would-be critics and
journalists seem to think that you should
not go from one subject to another, but
that you should mix them all up. However, that does not take me into
the Speech proper.
One of the first and principal things
referred to was the war, and I think I
will make a suggestion from this side of
the House to-day without any notice to
any person, somewhat similar to the suggestion I made on a previous occasion and
which was accepted and carried out by
Mr. Speaker on the instructions of the
late Prime Minister. The House will
recollect that after the Royal Air Force
won the first battle of Britain, I suggested
that this House congratulate the authorities. The late Prime Minister acceded to
that suggestion, and Mr. Speaker sent a
suitable message of congratulation from
the whole House. Now I think that the
time has come to send a message to
General Wavell or the proper authority
on the occasion of the great victories in
Egypt. The Prime Minister of the
Commonwealth of Australia is in London
at the present time, and I will leave the
idea to our own Prime Minister. I know
everyone in the House would approve that
a message should be sent, congratulating
General Wavell and the Australian troops
in Egypt on their valour.
You know we have had great victories
recently. I know well enough there is a
lot of serious work before us, but we have
had great victories. I do not think any
of us expected the great victories we have
had in Africa and are going to have.
There is no
reason why we should be
depressed. We do not know yet what war
in our midst is. The people of England
do. It might be our turn anytime. I
hope we are ready for it, but I will have
something to say on that subject later on.
It has always been a sort of official
policy to smother criticism on the ground
that you might convey something useful
to the enemy.
That is the excuse that
has often been put forward, but the real
motive is to cloak incompetence. I was
restrained for a very long time since the
war broke out. I am not going to restrain
myself in the same way any longer. At
the same time I am not going to give
away anything that I think would be
useful to the enemy. I will certainly not
take advantage of my position as a
Member of the House to do that. Neither
am I going to let that excuse stand
between me and my right to expose incompetence and the danger, as I see it,
from incompetence. But every one of
you that is fair-minded must know that
I foresaw this long before any of you and

warned the House about Hitler. And anyone who is only finding out now about the
character of Hitler-well, I do not give

The Prime Minister talked yesterday

to do that at all.

attacking the Independents.

meter and his wife could not turn it off

That means one of two things, either he

he gave the order, he never took steps to
see that it was carried out. That is a
poor prospect if there should be an air raid
on the city of Belfast. If there is an
attack the whole city will be involved at

city as well, and every A.R.P. post or
district will be on its own.
The House will recollect that I asked
the Minister if any of the A.R.P. posts
had a ladder. That is the first thing
required. You will get instructions about
ladders and you will hear lectures, but
there is no use in trying to evade the issue.
In any other Department a man might
get through by bluffing me, but that
cannot be done here. A raid might take
place to-night. If so, the first thing an
A.R.P. post would require would be a
ladder and a handcart. I was at a meeting not long since listening to an A.R.P.
lecture, and I gave a lecture, too, when
I got my opportunity. The meeting was
composed of the best of men, but if a
report of an attack had come in with the
statement that a number of people were
trapped, not one of them had a ladder, a
pick, or a rope.
That is after seven or eight months
with the Minister in charge. These are
most essential and important things.
There would be no use relying on the fire
brigade, because they might be busy elsewhere and not be available. None of the
men have been supplied with bandages or
disinfectants, although at some of the
posts I understand there is a little cabinet
with these things in it. These are most
important and essential things.
The conclusion of the whole matter is this, either
the Minister does not give the orders
which he is supposed to give, or he does
not see that they are carried out.
The last day I talked about shelters.
I refer, of course, to the shelters up the
side streets, not to the shelters in the
centre of the city. I gave it as my opinion
that they were generally useless because
no one went into them when there was an
alert. I have studied them and made inquiries since, and I never heard anyone
I try to be practical. Supposing an
hon. Member went into one of those
shelters in the side streets at nine o'clock
last night with a mother, a baby, and a
couple of little children up to their ankles
in water or ice until 2 o'clock this
morning, where would they be now?
That is the practical way of looking at
it; there is no other way. The Minister
tells us that his experts approved of these
shelters. I do not know who his experts
were. I do not know what constitutes
an A.R.P. expert. There is nothing an
A.R.P. expert could not learn in a
month. I go further than I did last day

I suggested then that there should be
something done in a kitchen or other

able to support the roof in case it collapsed. Then the people would not be
all gathered together; they would be

that, and if there was a direct hit there
would not be such a tragedy.
It is very remarkable that the new
shelters being built in England are of
steel. I dare say most hon. Members
have seen photographs of them. One
can be brought into the kitchen, or other
suitable room, in parts and erected there.
A mattress can be placed in it, and it is
guaranteed to carry the roof. There is
some sense in that, because you can sit
in your own room, at the heat of your
own fire, or lie on your own mattress.
Do not get up and tell us that anyone
could go
into one of these shelters in the
streets at 9 o'clock at night and stay
there until 2 o'clock the next morning.
It would be far better to die in your
own house than to die as the result of
going in there.
The first advice we got from the
London experts came through the late
Prime Minister. He told us he was talking to a London expert, who told him
that in the event of a raid the safest
thing to do was to go into the fields. I
pointed out that neither he nor I, nor
three-quarters of the population, would
survive one night in the fields, and we
heard no more about that expert.

pension as a blind person for a number of
years and has now passed the three score
years and ten is automatically ruled out
of receiving any supplemental pension
because of the fact that at one time or
another he received a blind person's
pension.
I do not think it ever was the intention
of the Government that these most
deserving people in our community who
have reached 70 years of age and over
should be deprived of their supplemental
pension. The Government ought to see to
it that the law is so interpreted that these
blind people, who, if anything, are more
deserving than those who have their sight,
should be treated decently and be allowed
their supplemental pension. I hope that
if necessary this Government will introduce new legislation in order to remove
what in my opinion is a very serious
grievance under which these old-age
pensioners, who
who were formerly blind
pensioners, are suffering. The Government
may say to me, "We cannot introduce
legislation. We can only follow step by
step with Great Britain". If I am told
that as soon as Great Britain introduces
B
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Elliott]
a Bill to pay blind pensioners over 70 a
supplemental pension we will do likewise
I shall not be very grateful for that,
because, if there had never been a Parliament here at all, once that Bill was
passed by the Imperial Parliament these
people would automatically become
entitled to their pension.
This Government did not wait on the
Imperial Government giving them a lead
on the transport problem. Our Government said, "No. We will show them the.
way transport ought to be run. We will
go a step ahead of Great Britain and
introduce a Bill that will make the
Imperial authorities sit up and take
notice." They did so, and they have had
to pay for it. If the Government here
can introduce legislation dealing with
transport it is not beyond the bounds of
possibility that the Government should
introduce a short Measure to remove this
interpretation under which the most
deserving people in our community are.
being penalised. As long as I am
Member of this House I shall advocate
the claims of blind people for better treatment than they are receiving. I hope
that soon this anomaly, which I believe
exists only in the minds of officials who
are debarring blind persons from
receiving what they are entitled to, will
be made right.
a
The Government seem to be satisfied
with what has been done in regard to civil
defence measures. I am not an authority
on this question and I do not intend to
say anything further than that, while a
great deal has been done, I believe there
still remains a great deal to be done to
make this civil defence force perfect.
Every one in this House ought to support
the Minister of Public Security in his
efforts to perfect this organisation.
Reference has been made to the
unemployed. As one of those who looked
to the setting up of the Select Committee
on Unemployment with a great deal of
misgiving, may I say that I believe
that
is one Committee that was
well worth while establishing. In
my opinion that Committee has done
more to remove unemployment from
Northern Ireland than the Government
has done since it came into office twenty
years ago. I want to be perfectly candid
about it. This Committee went to work
with a will and tackled their job as a lot
of businessmen ought to tackle any job.
They deserve. the best thanks of the community for the successful efforts they put
forth, and for their two Interim Reports.
The Government immediately set to
work to put the first part of the first
Interim Report into operation. But because they have put the linen business on
its feet, I do not want the Government to
hang up the other part of the Report as
they did the Transport Report. Now
that we have got the linen business going
I want to see the Government tackling
the second Interim Report dealing with
drainage. It is a Report with which I
am in entire agreement: It is a splendid
Report, and I hope the Government will
be as ready and as enthusiastic in putting
it into operation as they were in the case
of the first Interim Report.
I am out to support those who think
this Unemployment Committee should be
continued or reorganised. I believe the
appointment of the Committee was the
best thing the Government ever did, and
in my opinion it should be re-appointed.
I speak as a Member who did not serve on
the Committee and who was not asked to
act on it, but I give every credit to the
members of the Committee for the energy
they put into their work and for bringing
in Reports which are a credit to themselves and to Northern Ireland. I hope
that Committee will be continued, and I
shall give any Motion brought forward to
re-appoint it my whole-hearted support.
When they brought that Committee into
being, I believe it was the best day's work
the Government of Northern Ireland ever
did for the unemployed.
I notice that in connection with flax
production flax factories are to be established in Northern Ireland. That is
carrying out the suggestion of the Committee. I would like to say to the linen
merchants and the linen lords of Northern
Ireland that I hope when the war is over
and the days of peace return these factories will continue to operate, and that
when the Northern Ireland farmer is
producing his own flax they will not revert
to the practice of bringing flax from
foreign countries. When peace returns,
I hope the linen lords will not forget the
men who stuck to them in the days of
war, and that we shall receive from them
the same encouragement and help that is
being given now.

Debate on the Address
26 FEBRUARY 1911
It takes both the farmer and the
linen merchant to make a success of
the business. We as agriculturists are
prepared to forget the past and the way
we were treated when our flax was thrown
at us in the markets and they would not
buy it at any price. If the linen men
will stand by us now in the interests of
the whole community, we on our part are
prepared to do our utmost to bring prosperity back to the linen trade of Northern
Ireland.
Now that the first Interim Report has
been acted upon, I hope the Government
will not delay in putting into operation
the second Interim Report, because I
believe that many thousands of people
could be employed in Northern Ireland
in reclaiming land now waterlogged and
opening water courses. I believe that,
in spite of all our aeroplanes and battleships and armies, the last shot in this war
will be fired by the land, and that food
production will play at least as important
a part in the winning of the war as any
of the three great fighting Services. So
we want the Government to utilise these
unemployed people by helping us on the
land. If they will stand in with us now
and tackle this drainage question in the
way suggested in the Interim Report they
can do a great deal to encourage and help
us.
I again ask the Government to reconsider the question of employing labour
on the land and not allow Northern
Ireland to be depleted of its farm workers.
I support the Motion whole-heartedly.
Mr. AGNEW: After all the speeches
that have been made from the various
parts of the House it is rather difficult
for me to follow. I notice that in the
very first line of the King's Speech it is
stated that the present struggle is for
liberty and justice. I am opposed to
aggression, and I hope the Government of
Northern Ireland will see to it that
liberty and justice are guaranteed to every
citizen of this Province. Civil defence is
a matter of urgency. In view of what
has been stated in the House to-day by
Members representing Belfast constituencies I would like to call the attention
of the Minister of Public Security to
matters affecting A.R.P. outside the city
of Belfast.
I feel there has been some slackness in
dealing with this problem in the area in
which I live. I have taken a keen interest
in this particular matter, and I find that
up to the present time there has been no
shelter accommodation provided for those
who may be caught on the streets during
a raid. We must realise that, after all,
our main duty is to give protection to the
civil population who are innocent victims
of the war, and if this protection is withheld a serious responsibility rests on the
authorities concerned. I have been in
contact with my own local authority and
I would ask the Minister of Public
Security to give serious consideration to
this matter, so far as Armagh and district
are concerned, so that we may have some
degree of security and protection for the
people. We all know the horrors through
which many citizens in Great Britain have
had to pass. We sympathise with them,
but while we are sympathetic we must not
forget ourselves. The Department concerned should when dealing with this
matter remember the district to which I
have referred. I hope that out of all this
welter of sorrow and suffering peace will
return to a stricken world.
Reference is made in the King's Speech
to the farming community. Assistance
should be rendered to farmers, both small
and large, in order that they may provide
the necessary food. Certain Regulations
in force to-day are detrimental to them,
and I trust that the Department will
grant some concession in the very near
future. In view of the statement made
by the Minister of Agriculture in reference to producing more food I hope the
Minister of Labour will keep sufficient
numbers of agricultural workers in reserve
in Northern Ireland. Even though we
may be told there is a surplus it is not
right to send these men across to England
because, according to what we are told by
the Government, food production is one
of the main lines of defence. The
Minister should realise that.
I now come to the question of flax
production, which is a very important
feature in the life of Northern Ireland.
I should like to know, now that we are
going to produce 100,000 acres of flax,
that all our idle textile workers throughout Northern Ireland will be able to return to employment. In my constituency
thousands of textile workers are idle.
Should prosperity come some of them will
not be found in Armagh or South
Armagh, because they have been sent
across to England. We are also told
that the textile industry is providing
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
materials for His Majesty's Forces. I do
not know. When I view the situation
in the city of Armagh, Keady and South
Armagh I find that this work has not
reached those areas. We have a splendid
spinning mill, factory and other mills in
Keady district which are lying idle. I
should like to know when the responsible
Minister will visit that particular area
to see what can be done to relieve the
serious unemployment which prevails.
That part of Northern Ireland has been
forgotten. Belfast, through its industrial
activities and situation, claims pride of
place. I hope in the distribution of
work-it has long been promised-that
Armagh will not be overlooked.
We
want to see a revival of industry there,
but unless the Government take action
and are really sincere our hopes will fall
to the ground.
There is one strange statement in the
King's Speech, and one which has been
emphasised by the Prime Minister. It
is that the unemployment figure has
fallen by 15,000. I should like to know
if these 15,000 are engaged on work of
national importance or placed in industry in Northern Ireland. Are the
wages they earn being spent in Northern
Ireland? We can take it for granted
that the majority of the workers have
been sent across to England, and that 50
per cent. of their earnings are being
spent there. How can we build up our
industries or bring prosperity if we have
to pay for permits, photographs, fares,
and subsistence allowances for men sent
to England? While we sit contentedly
and allow things like that to go on, how
can prosperity come about?
I have protested against sending men
to England. Men are asked: "Are you
willing to accept an offer of employment?" Naturally, a man who is unployed has to say "Yes" whether he is
willing to go or not. If he says "No"
he will be disallowed benefit as not
available for work, or he will be disallowed as having refused an offer of
suitable employment. That is the
position. In view of the time and
energy wasted in sending men across the
water-there are many regulations to be
complied with before they reach the boat
-I should like to see that particular
Department of the Ministry of Labour
co-operating with other Departments.
new
During my three years in this House
I have heard the same story in the King's
Speech about prosperity. It makes me
rather doubtful now. What is the use
of promises? Is the Government really
anxious to see the industries I have mentioned thriving? Is it anxious to see
industries developed? Has it
tackled the problem in the same spirit as
the district area commissioners in England? It has not; it has allowed things
to become worse. The only way it has
found of solving the unemployment is by
what I call conscripting labour under the
threat of men losing benefit, and sending them to England, Scotland, and
Wales. That is not a Christian way of
facing the problem. We are told that
we are part and parcel of the United
Kingdom, and that we have the same
rights and privileges as the citizens of
Great Britain. If that is so how is it
that this Government has failed to bring
a share of the prosperity to Northern
Ireland? I should like an answer to
that question. It is not because we
have not the necessary labour. The
workers are here, and if you bring work
to Northern Ireland the workers are
prepared to do their share. It is up to the
Government to see to it that the people
of Northern Ireland are given work at
home. That is not too much to ask.
We are told that legislation will be
passed in order to ease the position in
regard to the means test, but, unfortunately, not to abolish it. Those of us
who are in daily contact with the people
affected by the means test know that it
will not be such a beautiful present. On
the last occasion we were told the same
thing, but many anomalies were found.
It is strange that the means test only
applies to the working class people. Oldage pensioners are subject to a means test.
If they have been thrifty during their
life when they reach the age of 70, or
even 60 or 65, and are entitled to a
supplementary pension their thrift counts
against them. Governments when granting pension do not put in force a means
test affecting officials with £500 or £600
a year. But here, unfortunately, the
working classes with little means find a
means test. It is inhuman.
The fact that a pensioner resides with
his married son or married daughter
should not be taken into account.
We
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
26 FEBRUARY 1941
wish to have these defects remedied.
Some degree of security should be given
to our old people. Let us place the amount
it takes to carry on the war beside the
sum required to grant pensions. If we do
so we will find it is a very small figure in
comparison with the war expenditure.
When it comes to a matter of comfort
for the unemployed or old-age pensioners
it is unfortunate that the Government
have no thought or charity towards them.
We all like freedom, justice, liberty and
the right to live, but unless the Government becomes more active in Northern
Ireland there will only be freedom to
starve.
Another matter to which I wish to refer
is air-raid precautions in schools. At the
moment I feel children are not safe. In
the Armagh area during an alert we find
children are sent home. Anything can
happen. What I want to see is this, that
in view of the fact that children attending
schools are the men and women of
to-morrow, finance should not be. an
obstacle in guaranteeing that every
school, particularly in urban districts and
vulnerable areas, may have that degree
of security they are entitled to, and that
there will be no liability in so far as the
local authorities are concerned. I would
like the Minister of Public Security also
to realise that where expenditure has to
be met for air-raid precautions as far as
the local authorities are concerned in
dealing with that problem he will look
into one of the main issues to-day, that
many of the local authorities have very
serious financial liabilities to meet and
putting an additional burden in any
shape or form for such precautions would
be a very serious detriment to local
government throughout Northern Ireland.
Finally, I would like to say that the
King's Speech, remarkable for many
statements and, as usual, promises, holds
out absolutely no hope for the workers of
Northern Ireland. It would have been
nice for us on this side of the House
to-day to have read in the King's
Speech that the Government could give
a guarantee that the prosperity so often
promised has materialised. It would
have been nice to have read that. There
is no mention of it. We are told something may be done. We have heard that
too often. What we want the Government to realise is this, that the solution
of the unemployment problem is not
tackled in the proper spirit. You cannot keep secure the home front and the
home life of the citizen by breaking up
the family life. Prosperity can only
come when the heads of the various departments of the Government realise
that industry must come here. It is your
duty, seeing you tell us so often that we
are part and parcel of the United Kingdom to do it, and if you fail the
responsibility is not on our side of the
House. It is not the responsibility of
the unemployed.
You have had long
enough to do it and I feel you have
failed miserably.
Mr. THOMPSON: I feel sure that
every Member of the House deeply
regretted to learn yesterday that the
Member for Central Armagh has
retired. He was one of the most loved
Members of this House and I am certain
it is the wish of every Member that he
will be still spared to do useful work for
the community.
I would like to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the
Address in reply to the King's Speech.
Both gentlemen dealt faithfully with a
rather difficult task for the Speech was
more conspicuous for the things it did not
say than for what was said. Therefore, I
congratulate the gentlemen on their
achievement. The Member for Windsor
hoped that men would step out of the
Army into work. I pray this may be

ensure this. I wish I could be sure that
the Government have in hand schemes
that will be capable of being put

Roads have got into a deplorable condition
chiefly owing to the great strain put upon

discussions been opened with Municipal

post-war period? Have any arrangements
been thought out for a complete new
housing programme? Have any schemes
been discussed with local authorities for
this work?
I could enumerate scheme after scheme
that should and could be prepared now so
that when peace does come we will at once
be ready to absorb our unemployed-not
waiting for weary months to elapse while

HOUSE OF COMMONS

plans are being prepared and financial

bodies and the Government. A bold
housing scheme must be faced immediately
the war is over. There never could be a

The railways are making profits, so is the
road transport. If co-operation and
vision were brought into play now these
concerns, with a closer working arrangement, could greatly enhance their dividends. It will be a shame if the opportunity of greater co-operation in service.
is allowed to pass without full advantage
being taken of the splendid opportunities
now available.
These are all matters that could be
usefully planned during the coming
Session. What about post-war finance?
Surely we can see at least a part of the
way now as to what our programme can
be. It would not take a very clever
financier to visualise to some extent the
financial needs in the immediate years
after the conflict is won-as won it surely
will be. Does any man expect to see a
reduced income tax for several years after
the war, or a reduced city rate? Do we
ever expect to see the old days of pre-war
competition coming back? I sincerely
hope they are gone for ever. The days of
co-operation and a greater understanding
of each others needs are the things that I
hope a post-war period will usher in. A
new understanding in all branches of industry, including both employer and
employee, a clearer understanding of each
others needs.
"There is enough in the world to-day
for every man's need, but not enough for
every many's greed." If this could be
impressed on the mind of the people
something really might happen. If the
Government provide the tools the community will deliver the goods. The British
Government have already set up a Com.
mission to study the post-war period. Are
we just going to wait and accept whatever
may be coming to us-good little boys
waiting for the meal to be served; little
Jack Horners or are we going to have
our own drive and our own initiative and
build up something suitable for Ulster's
special and peculiar needs. A friend of
mine last week went into a down-town
store. He wanted to buy buckets and
other things necessary in his business.
The buckets were there in the shop, but
they could not sell them to him for some
unearthly reason of the Ministry of
Supply. The gentleman had to go minus
his buckets. I went into a large store a
fortnight ago to buy a kettle for our firewatchers. The kettles were there by the
hundred in the shop and yet they could
not sell them, simply because the Ministry
of Supply again would not give permission.
Mr. BEATTIE: Did you not vote for
that?
Mr. THOMPSON: And now we are
informed that the linen quota is being
reduced to 20 per cent. If we do not take
steps to control our own supplies disaster
is staring us full in the face. The Ministry
of Shipping has refused to put the Belfast
ship chandlers on the shipping list.
Belfast, the fourth largest shipping centre
in the United Kingdom, is refused a
privilege that is granted to the cross-
Channel ports-a most unfair position. I
drew the late Minister of Commerce's
attention to the fact. Nothing has been
done. I have never got an answer why
such an unfair position is tolerated. The
present Minister has promised to investigate, but valuable time is being lost to
the Belfast firms-over a year's valuable
trading. These are a few things as I see
them requiring the attention of the
Government, and I hope during the
coming Session a considerable amount of
attention will be given to them.

is a matter of interest to every member

ing. I have noticed it growing during

The whole-hearted support of the
entire community will be best obtained
by removing the realm of civil defence
from party debate, and I am sorry that
it should have been made the subject of
party debate here. I do not suggest
there should be no criticism. I think

facts or their importance to the community, then one is justified in saying

back rather than advanced.
some
Civil defence is a matter of deeds
rather than words. If it had been a
matter of words it would have been far
advanced by the words which we have
heard in this House to-day. The hon.
Member for Shankill was good enough to
inform me what he would do if the
district he represents had been raided.
He said he would lead the people to
hunt me out of the country. He
spoke vehemently and fluently, and if
vehemence and fluency stand for an
apprehension of civil defence problems
his help would be most valuable, but he
is making a mistake if he imagines that
he discharges his responsibility by talking in that strain.
He has said a great deal about shelters,
a matter I will have to notice further in
a moment. I do not think he has so far
any experience of high explosives, but
when the raid to which he referred occurs,
as well it may, he will probably find a
virtue, even in an uncomfortable shelter
he has not dreamt of as yet. When it
comes to leading the survivors either to
Stormont or anywhere else I trust he
will find it convenient to explain to them
what part he has played in assisting them
to prepare for the onslaught.
He has
been a member for two years of the
statutory authority responsible, for civil
defence in Belfast until last November,
and I have yet to learn in what way he
advanced the cause of civil defence in
Belfast.

organisation of civil

there should be no standard of comfort in

the houses opposite which they are erected.
We believe they provide very much

moment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 27th February, 1941.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
UNREGISTERED MILK
PRODUCERS.
1. Mr. MALCOLM PATRICK asked
the Minister of Agriculture if he realises
the serious position of a great number of
farmers who send their milk to the
creameries, and because they are not
registered milk producers are not receiving a ration allowance under the new
Regulations. Further, does he realise
that the milk produced by these men is
passed for cleanliness at the creamery
and put into the same tank as the milk
supplied by the registered producers?
Further, if these farmers are deprived
of a feeding stuff allowance there will be
a shortage of milk, as a large proportion.
of the stock held will have to be disposed
of as the farmers concerned have not
holdings large enough to produce the
necessary feeding stuffs.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): The answer to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is in the affirmative. I am glad to have
this opportunity to clear up certain misunderstandings which appear to exist
with regard to the supply of imported
feeding stuffs. The present supply is
not sufficient to provide for all livestock,
consequently it has become necessary to
decide what order of priority should be
given to the various classes, having
regard to national requirements. It is
not possible to provide for all milk cows
unless we are prepared to cut off supplies
to pigs and poultry completely, and it
has therefore been decided that cows producing graded milk, which goes either
directly into the liquid market or is
available for that purpose, must have
first preference. Ungraded milk is used
mainly for the manufacture of butter,
and as it is much easier to import butter
than feeding stuffs, such milk is of
secondary importance. Whilst I have
every sympathy with the owners, I am
sorry it is not possible to provide imported feeding stuffs for cows producing
ungraded milk, and they must depend
upon home-grown feeding stuffs.
The balance of the imported feeding
stuffs is allocated to breeding sows, pigs,
and poultry, and although the quantity
per head is only one-third of normal,
yet it will help to maintain these very
valuable classes of livestock.
The necessity for a very substantial
increase in the acreage of home-grown
feeding stuffs is becoming more evident
every day, and if farmers are to maintain
their present numbers of livestock
during next winter, they must plough
every acre of suitable land and make as
much silage as possible.
FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE AND
HORSE RACING.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture if, in view of the
fact that racing has been prohibited in
ten counties in Eire owing to foot-andmouth disease, he will take the steps
necesary to ensure that no horses from
these infected areas will be allowed to
run at the Down Hunt Steeplechase at
Downpatrick on the 2nd April next and
so avoid the risk of spreading this deadly
plague with its consequent heavy loss to
the farmers of County Down.
Lord GLENTORAN: My Ministry
has already made an Order dealing with
gatherings such as that referred to by
the hon. and gallant Member. This
Order fully covers Downpatrick or any
other race meeting, including point-topoint meetings. The hon. and gallant
Member can rest assured that
my Ministry has ample powers and will take all
necessary precautions to avoid any risk
of the spread of foot-and-mouth disease
in Northern Ireland.
RATIONING OF FEEDING STUFFS.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can give full
information regarding the rationing of
feeding stuffs and the benefit to producers of A, B and C milk; whether the
same consideration will be given to producers of butter and buttermilk as to
registered milk producers, and whether
serious dissatisfaction has been caused
by the rationing scheme.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
27 FEBRUARY 1941
Lord GLENTORAN: Animal feeding
stuffs are being rationed on the following
basis: :-
Cows producing Grade A, B or C milk
-7 lbs. per day.
Breeding sows-5 lbs. per day.
Pigs-2 lbs per day.
Poultry-1 oz. per day.
This allocation exhausts the total
available supplies of imported feeding
stuffs, and I regret that it is not therefore possible to provide rations for other
classes of livestock.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I think there is
a general appreciation amongst stock
owners of the fact that, under the
difficult circumstances and with the very
limited amount of feeding stuffs available, my Ministry has secured through
fair
the rationing scheme as
a distribution of supplies as possible.

COST OF BANN DRAINAGE
SCHEME.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the
estimated cost of the Bann Drainage
Scheme, the total cost actually paid or to
be paid; the amount paid by the
Treasury and the amount paid or to be
paid by the various county councils; the
number of acres of land reclaimed by the
scheme and the number of acres improved; the number of inches by which
the level of Lough Neagh has been
reduced, and the number of inches by
which it could have been reduced by a
little extra sinking.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The estimated cost of the
Bann Drainage Scheme is £891,000, the
amount actually paid to date being
approximately £860,000. In accordance
with the provisions of the Drainage Act
(N.I.), 1929, the amount payable by the
county councils concerned, viz., Antrim,
Armagh, Down, Londonderry
Tyrone, is £200,000. This amount is
repayable by annuities over a period of
60 years. I am satisfied that the estimate
will cover the cost of the actual works
which are now approaching completion.
and
In the year 1876-77, which was the
worst from the point of view of rainfall,
approximately 50,000 acres were actually
under water and an additional 25,000
acres so saturated as to render cultivation
impossible. In the winter of the year
1938-39, when the amount of the rainfall
closely approached in intensity and duration that of the winter of 1876-77, it is
calculated that the works carried out
reduced the flood level by no less than 34
inches. No serious flooding occurred, with
resultant benefit to approximately 40,000
acres.
PENSIONS TO BLIND PERSONS.
7. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is satisfied with
the schemes put into operation by local
authorities in accordance with the Blind
Pensions Act (Northern Ireland), 1938;
whether the amounts paid to blind persons
are sufficient for maintenance seeing that
they vary from 2s 6d to 7s 6d; whether
the system of investigation carried out
by the county councils is satisfactory and
the amounts laid aside by the councils
are sufficient to give sustenance; and
whether in view of meagre allowances
granted by county councils a Commission
of Inquiry will be set up to discuss the
position of blind pensioners.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The schemes submitted annually to my Ministry by
county councils in accordance with the
terms of the Blind Persons Act, 1938,
are framed in general terms and give the
councils a wide discretion as to the form
of assistance to be given. There is
nothing in the schemes to limit the assistance which may be given. The amounts
paid to blind persons vary in individual
cases as the county councils and county
borough councils treat, and are required
to treat, each particular case on its
merits after investigation of the circumstances of the applicant.
As to the actual amounts provided by
councils, the hon. Member will appreciate that without an investigation into
the circumstances of each case, I am not
in a position to state whether the amounts
approved are, or are not, sufficient. I
have no reason to assume that the financial assistance afforded is not sufficient
or that cases are not properly investigated, but if the hon. Member is aware
of any blind person who is not receiving
sufficient help from a county or county
borough council, or whose case has not
been fully investigated, I will be prepared to have the matter reopened.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I would refer the hon. Member
to the discussion in this House last
Session, when a promise was made to
issue a further circular to county councils
and county borough councils on the
question of affording blind persons
adequate assistance. Such a circular was
issued, and I am glad to be able to say
that practically every county council
and county borough council has made
increased provision in its estimates in
respect of assistance to blind persons
during the coming financial year.

8. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received

Gentleman not give something more

to be arrived at?

Sir DAWSON BATES: I think there

Mr. THOMPSON: Can the Minister
give some general undertaking that the
matter will come before us this Session ?
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
learned Recorder is against this legislation, and is it not a fact that the
principle of the Bill means that when an

the person is not able to enter a defence?
Mr. THOMPSON: Can the Minister

Sir DAWSON BATES: The matter
will be attended to, but as the hon.
Member for Woodvale has pointed out
there is a difference of opinion on certain

Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.

MANAGER OF ENNISKILLEN
EXCHANGE AND WORKERS.

Mr. GORDON: A notice is exhibited

"Claimants wishing to make inquiries or

Mr. GORDON: As far as can be

I have no quarrel with the Civil

Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Cabinet Offices
[Mr. Warnock]
not seem to take very much interest in
the question of the cost of our services,
though it is a matter of vital importance.
The House of Commons is the custodian
of public money, and it appears to me
to be appropriate that this question
should be raised not in any spirit of
hostility at all. I do not wish to see the
salaries of civil servants decreased or
their living affected. I do not want any
of their privileges to be touched at all,
but I do want to see that the numbers
of the Civil Service shall be brought
within reasonable limits.
On a later occasion, on the Appropriation
Bill, I shall summarise and investigate
the whole position, and will put before
the House figures which will stagger them.
The increase during the past six years
has been absolutely staggering, and cannot be defended. The truth of the matter
is that the Civil Service has got too big.
An increase in numbers does not make for
efficiency. That is the point I wish to
make. I do not want anybody touched;
I do not want any salary touched or any
privilege interfered with, but I want to
see the Civil Service brought within
reasonable bounds and the numbers curtailed.
There is not one Department in this
Government, with the exception, I think,
of the Ministry of Education, in which
the staff has not grown and swollen
enormously. You know, as everybody
in the House knows, that while additional burdens have been cast upon some
Ministries, in many cases there have
been no additional burdens at all, and yet
there has been a gradual increase in staff
year after year. What is the cause of
it? The cause is a defect in the system.
We have no check. The Ministry of
Finance should be divided into two
sections, and there ought to be an absolutely definite check as there is in England.
You have the Ministry of Finance which
controls the Civil Service checking itself.
That is the cardinal defect of this system.
There is no person and there has never
been any person to say "No" to this staff
increase.
The staff of the Establishment Branch
of this Ministry increased from 90 to 155
over a period of six years. That is an
indication of the growth of the Civil
Service. The staff of the Establishment
Branch in 1934-35 numbered 90, while in
1939-40 it was 155. Those are facts from
which we cannot get away.
There is a very strong case for an
inquiry-I will not put it higher than
that into the growth of the Civil Service
in Northern Ireland. I know that the
higher civil servants-I came in contact
with them while in office-are extremely
competent, extremely high-minded, and
efficient. I would not wish for better.
Neither have I any
criticism to offer
upon
the lower ranks of the Civil Service. My
criticism is that the service has grown too
big, and there is no person and never has
been any person to say "No." The
Ministry of Finance should have some
particular section whose sole duty it would
be to say "No" to expenditure.
The cost of the services of this country
has increased enormously. I am not putting it too high when I say that in
relation to our population, we
are the
most expensively governed country in the
world. That is a reproach which could
and ought to be removed, and the preventing of it will not hurt the Civil
Service, but will help it. I am grateful
to you for the latitude you have given
me. I hope I have not transgressed
too far. In drawing attention to this
matter I submit that there is a case for
inquiry. I hold that any person drawing
attention to this matter is simply fulfilling
his duty as a public servant and as a
guardian of the finances of Northern
Ireland.

CLASS I. No. 3.
GOVERNMENT HOSPITALITY.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £250 be
granted to His Majesty for the service of
the year ending 31st March, 1941, as a
grant in aid of the Government
Hospitality Fund."
Major SINCLAIR: As the Committee
will remember, Government hospitality,
on anything but a very small scale, was
not envisaged during the current year.
In giving his blessing to the original
Estimate of £10, the hon. Member for
Woodvale, with his usual perspicacity,
foretold that a Supplementary Estimate
would be necessary, and, in fact, pay.
ments on this account have amounted to
£451 to date, exceeding the balance in
the fund at the beginning of the year
by £114. The increased Estimate has
been occasioned by the unexpectedly
large amount of entertaining made
necessary by visits of representatives of
Imperial Departments in connection with
the war effort. The sum now asked for
is to cover this excess expenditure and to
ensure the adequacy of the fund during
the remainder of the financial year. It
is hoped, however, that this amount will
be in excess of requirements, and that,
unless something unforeseen occurs, next
year's expenditure under this head really
will be substantially reduced.
