CLASS II. No. 4.
PUBLIC WORKS AND BUILDINGS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £29,600 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending 31st March,
1941, in respect of Public Works and
Buildings, including annuities and other
expenses in connection with drainage."
Major SINCLAIR: Of the increases
shown in this Estimate, nearly £30,000
is attributable to additional protective
measures undertaken by the Government
mainly as a result of the critical situation arising out of the capitulation of
France. Prior to that event, the possibility of air attack on objectives of primary
war importance had appeared to constitute the only serious menace to our
Province, and protection against such
attack had, therefore, been restricted to
buildings situated in relatively small
areas. The occupation by the enemy of
the Channel ports and air bases in
Northern France made the danger of
widespread air attack, and even of invasion, much more probable. Guided by
information or advice received from
Imperial Civil and Service Departments
it was decided, and I am sure hon. Members will agree that this advice could not
be ignored, to provide protection
Government buildings against air or land
attack. The expenditure on A.R.P. in
Government buildings is estimated to
require an additional £21,000, and the
defence measures against possible land
attack some £8,000 to £9,000.
in
There is also included in the Estimate
a figure of about £9,000 for the provision
of accommodation for internees in Belfast
and Londonderry prisons, consequent
upon
their recent transfer from the
auxiliary prison in Strangford Lough.
The sum of £4,000 for additional accommodation for the staff of the Assistance
Board arises by reason of the additional
work involved in connection with Supplementary Pensions under the Old Age and
Widows' Pensions Act passed by this
House last year. Minor items in sub-head
A bring the gross total of this particular
sub-head to over £43,000, but against this
there are savings amounting to over
£5,000, representing provision made in
original Estimate for other works either
postponed or for which accounts will not
come in course of payment in the present
financial year.
The net total of the subhead is, therefore, £38,500.
Sub-head C requires little comment,
but I should perhaps make it clear that
the increase under the heading of insurance does not indicate any change in
the rate of insurance but is due to an
increase in the capital value of the property insured, mainly in order to take
account of the change in values owing to
the war.
As regards sub-head D, hon. Members,
in their private capacities, will be only
too well acquainted with the increases in

1 wanted to raise the conduct of the

letter is as follows:-
26th February, 1941.
The Ministry of Home Affairs,
Stormont,
Belfast
Dear Sirs,
On the 20th inst. we received a
Requisition Order from you for seven
lorries. We immediately notified you
that it would be impossible for us to
comply with this order without our
commitments to the Admiralty,
Military, Air Force and other high
priority orders being left short of coal.
On the 24th inst. we had a visit from
Mr. Warren in connection with this
matter, and we informed him our reason
for declining to comply with the order
was that, knowing the disastrous consequences it would create, we personally declined to accept such a heavy
responsibility, and if you insisted on
requisition you would have to impound
these lorries, and thereby accept full
responsibility for the subsequent break
down of our deliveries.
At the same time we advised you that
your requisition to Messrs. Wm. M.
Barkley & Sons, Ltd., of one lorry, and
Messrs. John Milligan & Co., Ltd., for
two lorries, came under the same category, as we had to call on their help
continuously for assistance.
Notwithstanding our warning you
have forcibly commandeered, and we
have nothing further to add.
This is the serious part:
We might further say that Mr.
Warren gave us his personal guarantee
these lorries were not for the Road
Transport Board. This morning we
find these lorries at the Road Transport
Board's premises in University Street.
Yours faithfully,
JOHN KELLY, Ltd.
The next letter reads:-
26th February, 1941.
The Ministry of Home Affairs,
Stormont,
Belfast.
Dear Sirs,
Further to my letter of this date,
we learn with astonishment that one
of the lorries you commandeered from
us yesterday-
I find that there were actually two
lorrieswas to-day at Messrs. E. T. Green's
Marlborough Street Mills, and another
of these lorries loaded coal on the
Queen's Quay from Messrs. F. E.
Harcourt & Co., Ltd., consigned to
Robinson's Cottage Hospital, Ballymoney.
It is difficult to reconcile this with
your statement that it would not be
used by the Transport Board, and
more particularly with Mr. Warren's
statement that the justification for
commandeering these lorries was it was
for very high priority work, higher
even than our work with the
Admiralty and Army.
We think this will require a considerable amount of explanation.
That letter is signed by one of the
directors of Messrs. John Kelly, Ltd.
The lorries were commandeered by Mr.
Warren on behalf of the Ministry of
Home
Affairs, and what happened?
You talk about the Gestapo in Germany.
The police take possession of lorries, and
instead of taking them into Messrs.
John Kelly's yard and unloading the
bags there they deliberately threw the
bags out on the street-a firm that is
giving great service. This is from the
principals of Messrs. Kelly, Ltd. I have
every right to believe them. I know they
would not give a Member of Parliament
a statement that was false. The bags
were thrown on to the footpath, and the
police drove the lorries away and handed
them over to the Transport Board.
The Board used these lorries, after the
statement that they were not for the
Transport Board, to drive a competitor's
coal from Donegall Quay to Ballymoney
Cottage Hospital. Look at the scandalous
waste of petrol. In my opinion this was
done deliberately. I am quite satisfied
the railway companies could very easily

The Navy, the Army, and the Air

Coal for Ballymoney could have been

Instead of that they take these lorries
down to Ballymoney and take them from
people using them for Government work.
It may be the Government's policy to
try to facilitate the Road Transport
Board at the expense of firms giving
great service to the State. I think it is

murder you could not have worse than

What right had Mr. Warren to tell

lorries were not for the Transport Board?
I could mention other things, and I do

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I wish to

properly and people treated fairly and

The facts are as stated. We had a

Oral Answers to Questions.
DIFFICULTIES OF PETROL
SUPPLY.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
difficulties with which distributors of
petrol, as well as commercial and agricultural users, are confronted when
getting their supplies from the "Pool";
whether he is aware that cash must be
sent with the order, and that this must
be sent by post; whether he is also aware
that even in a case of extreme urgency this
is insisted on, and although a user in
urgent need of a supply went to the office
of the "Pool" and tendered his coupons
with a cheque for the full amount he
was sent home and told the order and
cheque must be sent by post, thus
causing a delay of at least 24 hours; and
whether the Minister will take steps to
see that this arrangement will be speedily
terminated and petrol supplies distributed as in pre-war times.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I was not aware of
the difficulties mentioned by the hon.
Member. would explain to him,
however, that the Government of
Northern Ireland has no control over the
operations of the Petroleum Board,
which, I am informed, is a trade
organisation responsible to the Imperial
Department concerned. I have therefore
caused a copy of his question to be transmitted to the Secretary for Petroleum.
REQUISITIONING OR PURCHASE
OF LORRIES.
2. Mr. WARNOCK asked the Minister
of Finance whether he will refuse to
advance any money to the Northern
Ireland Road Transport Board for the
purchase of vehicles requisitioned by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and whether
he considers it proper or in the public
interest to take vehicles from traders to
hand them over to a Board which has
already involved the country in a
liability of some two million pounds.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Barbour): The vehicles referred to
are not being purchased by or for the
Road Transport Board. No question of
the advance of money to the Board
therefore arises.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the position is that these
vehicles were requisitioned by the
Ministry of Home Affairs for urgent
war work and were paid for out of
funds provided by the Imperial Government. The operation of the vehicles
has been entrusted to the Road Transport Board for use for Service requirements. This arrangement was initiated
by a committee consisting of Imperial
and Northern Ireland Departmental
representatives, and in my mind such a
course has been necessitated as the only
manner of providing essential assistance
to the Service Departments in a matter
of the utmost importance to the war
effort.

WAVING TO INTERNEES.
3. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been directed to a police prosecution of
a Belfast woman for waving her hand at
the armoured car conveying internees
from the "Al Rawdah" prison ship to
Crumlin Road Jail; whether he has considered the views expressed by the Resident Magistrate in Belfast in dismissing
the prosecution, and whether he can
state who was the police officer who
directed this prosecution.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
My attention has been directed to the
prosecution to which the hon. Member
refers, and I have considered the Press
which certain views
report in
attributed to the Resident Magistrate
who dealt with the case.
were
The prosecution was for conduct calculated to lead to a breach of the peace.
The action which led to the prosecution
occurred when internees conveyed in
buses were approaching the Crumlin
Road Jail. A crowd had assembled and
the excitement was such that a small
incident might have precipitated a
serious disturbance. In the circumstances I have no doubt that the member of the force who apprehended the
defendant acted in the genuine belief
that his action was necessary to maintain the peace.
As the peace was maintained owing to
the prompt action of the police in dealing with the crowd I incline to the view
that the case might have been met by
a warning, and without recourse
Court proceedings. It is, however, easy
to be judgmatic far from the event,
and, in fairness to the police, I should
to
point out that the defendant's conduct
did not invite the more lenient course
as she ignored a warning given to her
at the scene of the Occurrence and
refused to state her name and address
until taken to the barrack.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, it is not usual
or in the interests of the service to give
the information thereby sought, and I
see nothing to warrant any departure
from this practice in this particular
case.
Mr. BYRNE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that this lady's husband was passing at the time she was
guilty of this serious crime, and if such
a thing occurred in Norway or France
or any other country, what would be
said in the English Press?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I was not
aware the lady's husband was passing
at the time.
REQUISITIONING OF MOTOR
VEHICLES.
4. Mr. WARNOCK asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the Ministry of
Home Affairs has served a large number
of requisitioning notices on owners of
motor goods vehicles in Northern Ireland
requiring them to deliver their vehicles
forthwith to an officer of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, and whether he has handed
over a number of such vehicles to the
Northern Ireland Road Transport Board.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In pursuance of the
powers delegated to the Ministry of Home
Affairs by the Secretary of State, requisitioning notices have been served on
certain owners of motor goods vehicles
which are required for use in connection
with a large number of urgent works
which have been undertaken by Imperial
Government Departments.
The question was considered by a Committee on which all the Imperial Departments concerned were represented, and it
was decided that the work could not be
accomplished with the necessary despatch
save by requisitioning and that the most
effective way to operate the transport so
obtained was to utilise the services of the
Northern Ireland Road Transport Board.
The vehicles requisitioned are in the

that recently a very large number of

SENDING OF WORKERS TO GREAT

the 1/2/41 to 22/2/41; whether all of

these men had some knowledge of labouring work; and whether it is the intention

public utility schemes to carry out.

ride many miles on cycles to the work,

in Northern Ireland.
Mr. GORDON: I regret that it would

precise information of the employment
mentioned. I may, however, say that

when the local supply is exhausted men

BELFAST CITY COUNCIL BUS
DRIVERS.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if the
Transport Department of the Belfast
City Council refuse to allow bus drivers
to join the Army unless such men previously resign; whether there are unemployed bus drivers available for the
Transport Department, and other unemployed men who could easily be trained
to drive buses.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Schedule of Reserved Occupations
provides that driving omnibuses is a reserved occupation for persons who are 25
years of age, or are over that age; consequently, no bus driver who is of such an
age will be attested for service with the
Army.
It is not, therefore, within the discretion
of the Belfast County Borough Council
to say whether such a person may join
the Army, and the question of whether
any omnibus drivers are unemployed at
present does not arise.
I would, however, like to remind the
hon. Member that the training of an
omnibus driver is not a simple matter.
A candidate must first be proficient at
driving motor-cars or goods vehicles
before his training as an omnibus driver
can begin, and before he can be licensed
as a driver he must show that he possesses
traffic sense; that he is physically fit, and
that his eyesight is good. He must also
pass practical tests to demonstrate his
ability to drive every type of omnibus
used by the undertaking in which he
hopes to obtain employment, and must
also show that he has a thorough knowledge of the traffic regulations.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's lengthy reply, if a patriotic
lorry driver, who can drive a tank, wants
to join the Army-to throw in his weight
-why should he be held back by the
Belfast Corporation, or why should they
refuse to allow him to join unless he
resigns?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think that
question ought to be directed to the
Secretary of State for War and not to me.

EFFICIENCY OF L.D.V..
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he stated in
the House on 24th July, 1940, that
"The defence of this part of the United
Kingdom against enemy attack is the
business of the armed forces of the Crown
over whose disposition and employment
neither the Government nor this Parliament has any jurisdiction; and whether,
in view of that statement, he will state
whether the L.D.V. are trained,
equipped, and armed to repel invasion,
and whether this force is now under the
control of the Imperial Government.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The answer to
the first part of the hon. Member's
question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part of
the question, the Local Defence Volunteers are being trained, equipped and
armed to assist the regular troops in
defeating the enemy should he come to
Northern Ireland.
In reply to the last part of the
question, the force would, in the event
of it being used to repel invasion, come
under the control of the military
authorities. At present it is under the
control of this Government, though its
training is being carried out under the
direction of the General Officer Commanding. When the Imperial Government thinks a change in this position.
would benefit the national cause it has
only to say so. As I said in this House
the 19th November, 1940, "the
readiness of this Government to agree to
military control of and a military status
for the Local Defence Volunteer Force
has been made plain to the military
authorities and to the Imperial Government, and, as I have previously indicated to the House, this Government is
willing to facilitate any steps in this
direction which the Imperial Government may consider desirable."
on

ARMY OF THE NILE
CONGRATULATED.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report
that I have carried out the request
made to me by the House through the
Prime Minister by sending a letter to
Captain Margesson, Secretary of State
for War, and that I have received a
reply. Although I may incur the
censure of the House I think it only fair
Sittings of the House
Supplementary Estimates
4 MARCH 1941
that I should read the letter I sent to
the right hon. Gentleman. It was as
follows: :-
My dear David,
At the unanimous request of the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland I am sending you the following
message: .-
On this, the earliest opportunity
after the opening of Parliament, the
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland unanimously wish
to express their intense admiration for
the heroic Imperial Forces composing
the Army of the Nile, only matched
by the wonderful deeds of gallantry
performed by the Royal Navy and
Royal Air Force.
Right hon. and hon. Members also
wish to extend heartiest congratulations to those forces which are So
successfully carrying on operations in
Eritrea, Abyssinia and Italian Somaliland, surmounting all difficulties and
inflicting heavy defeats on the enemy
on all fronts.
They have watched with particular
pride the prominent part taken in all
these operations by our forces from all
parts of the British Empire.
(Signed) HARRY MULHOLLAND,
Speaker.
The right hon. Gentleman wrote me a
very nice private letter and enclosed his
official reply, which stated:-
Dear Mr. Speaker,
:-
I have received and thank you for
your letter of the 27th February, in
which you communicate to me a message unanimously adopted by the
House of Comons of Northern Ireland
for transmission to those concerned.
I shall have the greatest satisfaction
in having your message telegraphed to
the Commander-in-Chief, Middle East.
Yours sincerely,
(Signed) DAVID MARGESSON.

It is easy to be generous at other

normal work. Yet "while on duty"
Supplementary Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
the cost of meals consumed is borne by
the Government as employer, "in line
with the practice adopted in most, if

The reply was unfortunately worded,
being open to the interpretation that
all meals were supplied during the 24
hours of duty. This, we are informed,
is not the case. The public funds are
drawn on only for supper and breakfast. It is natural, however, that
many should ask: "Then why should
the L.D.V., who is neither a Government servant nor the employee of a

differently?" The fact that outside
L.D.V. duties involve more uncomfortable conditions than those
obtaining in Government offices adds
point to the question. It would be a
more equitable arrangement if, as
across the Channel in the Home Guard,
a small allowance were made to all
L.D.V.s irrespective of where their
duties are performed. This would
dispose of the charge of preferential
treatment. Thousands of taxpayers
and ratepayers perform their daily
jobs with none of the securities on
which public officials lay so much
emphasis, and certainly if they want
a recreation ground they have to dip
into their own pockets to provide it.
I am not going to read the rest of this
article, but in its concluding words it
urges
a greater care on the part of all
engaged not only in Government
departments but in the spending of
public moneys generally. There was
never a time when vigilance in this
regard was more necessary than at the
present time.

is very easy to say how a force could be

draw the attention of the Committee to

Army Council Instruction No. 924, 15th
August, 1940, paragraph 20-the hon.
and gallant Member for East Down must
be familiar with it—says:
In normal circumstances it is
anticipated that volunteers will in most
cases be able to provide their own food
without difficulty and without extra
expense to themselves. Where, however, extra expense is necessarily
incurred by the volunteer in the performance of his duties, he will be
eligible for subsistence allowance, if he
desires to claim it, provided that he is
employed on a continuous period of
duty in excess of 5 hours, and that the
hours of duty are duly authorised by
the battalion commander. Where the
continuous period of duty is in excess
of 5 hours but not more than 10 hours,
subsistence allowance may be claimed
at the rate of 1s 6d a head, and, where
the, period is in excess of 10 hours, at
the rate of 3s a head. Claims for these
allowances will be certified by the Home
Guard unit commanders and passed to
T.A. Associations for payment.
That instruction of the Army Council
is still current. I understand the War
Office has it under very careful consideration at the moment and they are anxious
so far as possible to provide the necessary
meals on some. communal basis, which is
more satisfactory, where it can be
managed, than the paying out of small
sums of money. Hon. Members will see
that in order to qualify for this allowance
extra expense has to be necessarily
incurred by the volunteer in the performance of his duty. A certain number
of continuous hours of duty have to be
served. It is also the view of the Army
Council that in normal circumstances it
is anticipated that volunteers will in most
cases be able to provide their own food

Another misapprehension I think in
some people's minds, as pointed out by

L.D.V. all over were performing precisely
similar duties. That is not quite right.
This question of feeding is linked very
closely with the nature of the role assigned
to the different units. Broadly speaking
units here as in Great Britain are of two
kinds those who man road posts and
observation points outside, whom I will
refer to as outside units. And those
recruited in factories and public utility
concerns and Government buildings whose
primary role is to preserve the buildings
in which they are stationed and the immediate surroundings, and whom I will
call for brevity inside units.
in
The role of the inside units is quite
different from that of the outside
units. Whether future experience will
necessitate some modification of the role
of the inside units, time alone can tell.
But at the moment the different nature
of the roles has a bearing on this question
of subsistence and feeding. Because,
take the case of this building. If there
is to be a guard-and I think all
members will agree there should be a
guard-it ought to be one which has no
loopholes in it. When the staff leave at
the end of the day. the guard should be
here, and so it comes about that in the
case of this inside unit in this particular building the members of the
L.D.V. are on duty for a considerably longer time than is the case
outside units. A man on duty here,

home at the ordinary time.
He has to
work the next day and only goes home

ordinary work ends to-day, that is the
normal Civil Service employment, until he
off duty next morning a considerable
goes
period has elapsed, well over the 10

an L.D.V., whenever he is on duty for

a thing occurred. This is the letter:
War Office,
Dear Nixon,
Whitehall, S.W.1.
9th Nov., 1940.
You wrote to Eden on 18th
October about the rejection by the
Recruiting Officer of William James
Hanna, 41 Belgrave Street, Belfast. I
have had inquiries made, and I understand that the Regulations at the
moment regarding enlistment into the
Northern Ireland regiments are that all

from the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
In view of a police report of several

entering illegally,
Recruiting
Officer had no alternative but to refuse
Mr. Hanna's enlistment.
Yours sincerely,
the
Edward Greig.
The point is that all these convictions
were made before he went to the
reformatory, and they should have been
forgiven and wiped out. They should
never have been supplied to the Army
authorities, I think the police probably
inadvertently supplied them, because
otherwise how is a boy who has been in
a reformatory ever to earn his living. He

know it is a very annoying thing, just as

Mr. BEATTIE: I agree with the pay
and allowances of officers of the Borstal
Institute being increased on the basis of

if we can continue to deal with the

there must be additional work for them
to do. Instead of there being more work

to juveniles are carried out with the
object of reforming them. I think the
increase in juvenile crime is not so much
due to the juveniles themselves or to their
parents, who are SO often blamed.
Juvenile crime should not exist in any
well regulated state of society. Juveniles
in themselves are not bad, but it is the
atmosphere in which they are brought up
-not always the atmosphere of the home,
but that of the outside world-that creates
that inherent feeling that he must get
something he sees other people enjoying.
That is due to the poverty of the majority
of working-class people for whose children
these institutions are maintained by the
State. I feel that if the State would only
tackle the problem of the poverty of the
people from whose homes these children
come, money spent in that way would be
well worth while.
Listening to the Member for Woodvale
regarding the after life of these boys, I
felt that these Borstal institutions are a
bar to a boy's prospects in life.
The
fact that he has been an inmate in a
borstal institution is a record against him
in everything that is likely to be useful to
him in after life. The circle in which he
has grown up and in which he moves
knows that he has spent a period in a
Borstal institution, and the fact that they
can cast the finger of scorn against that
individual is sometimes the means of
dragging him from the happy position he
may have attained and placing him again
on the downward path.
I notice that you have another place
of detention. I am sorry I was not in
the Committee when the right hon.
Gentleman was giving a detailed explanation of the Estimate, but I should
like to know why this additional accommodation was necessary. I presume it
is due to the increased number of
offenders that have been sent by the
magistrates to the Borstal Institution.
Sometimes I wonder whether the magistrates can see the two sides of the life
of a young offender or whether it is
because of the conduct of the parents
that the boy is taken away from them.
I know that the Resident Magistrates
are very sympathetic and considerate to
the boys who come before them, and
that they do everything within their
power to bring about an improvement in
the habits of the boys before they decide
to send them to the Borstal Institution.
But I have never yet found whether
both sides of the life of the boys are
taken into consideration. Sometimes I
think the magistrates inflict punishment
on the boys because of the sins of the
parents and I do not agree with that
angle. The Borstal Institution is well
managed by the staff, and there is no
spending of money that is not warranted, no matter who the visitor may
be. But the best teachers and the best
supervision in the world will never keep
a boy from juvenile crime, of which we
hear so much talk in the courts and elsewhere. We want to clear evil associations from the life of the community
and give an equal opportunity to everyone to go through life unstained and
untainted by anything of an incriminating kind. If we can do that I think
we shall have spent our time and our
money in a useful direction.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]

There is a saving which will be very

and Dental Benefit Councils, Boards of

They say he is not fit for employment,

the part of the right hon. Gentleman's
Department, and it certainly is not in
the interest of the public purse that such
a system should be allowed to continue.
The man is either fit or unfit.
When an approved society puts a
report against a member they immediately send him to a medical referee for
examination when an examination has
already been carried out by the panel
doctor. The panel doctor says he is
unfit, but the board of medical referees
in 90 per cent. of the cases say the man
is fit. There is a contradiction amongst
members of the medical profession, and
we should not allow the right hon.
Gentleman to waste money in that way.
The medical referee will always go
against the claimant. I have seen very
few reports from the medical referees
favourable to the claimant.

Valuable money is being spent on this

Adjournmentunnecessary and useless system. Where
are we going to be after the war when

I sometimes wonder whether this Ministry is going to fulfil the functions for
which it was appointed. I said very
little for twelve months after the Minister
and his Parliamentary Secretary were
appointed. I did not make any awkward
criticism of the Estimates or of the Department, but I am beginning to think that
the right hon. Gentleman is imbued with
the idea that he is the beginning and the
end of all things so far as dealing with
the question of unemployment is concerned. His method of dealing with the
question is so distasteful and disheartening
to me that I feel the time has arrived
when I should express myself in the way
I did when the right hon. Gentleman's
predecessor was in control. Not only has
the right hon. Gentleman let down the
working classes, but he has also let down
his own
staff who were able to save
the fund for the benefit of those who unfortunately are out of employment.
I am going to say now that in that
Department there are more senior transferred officers sitting on the stools they
occupied on the first day they came than
in any other Ministry. They have not
been allowed to make any headway whatever. No other Department has overlooked the rights of the staff so much as
the right hon. Gentleman's. In the
Ministry of Agriculture promotions are
taking place every month, senior positions
are given to junior officers, and every
position that is worth filling is filled by
those who have less service and less ability
than the officers who are domiciled in
the Ministry of Labour for all time.
The Ministry of Labour is the only
Department that has to give personal
attention to the public. The public
are very hard taskmasters, and the
Ministry of Labour has to deal with
the public directly and not by letter.
I think Public Security is the only
Department that has taken two of those
officers from the Ministry of Labour,
whereas there are ten or twelve men
whom I remember in the Imperial Service
still sitting in the grade in which they
entered the Ministry. If the right hon.
Gentleman had been doing his duty those
men would not have been in the lowly
paid grade that they still occupy.

BLACK-OUT OFFENCES IN
BELFAST.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
number of householders in Belfast who
have been prosecuted for black-out
offences during the past six months.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): The
number of householders in Belfast who
have been prosecuted for black-out
offences during the past six months is
4,500. This figure does not include cases
relating to motor vehicles or the use of
torches.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Minister aware
that I can get some A.R.P. men to prove
that the biggest offenders in Belfast are
the officers in Victoria Barracks and has
the Minister any jurisdiction there?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The heads of the
various services have assured me of their
co-operation for the purpose of securing a
perfect black-out. I know that every
person who is approached for offending
against the regulations is always ready
and able to find some person worse than
himself.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that policemen are sent out with instructions that so
many cases must be presented to the
station sergeant on their return from
duty?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: No, sir. I do
not think that is a fact.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman make inquiries as to what instructions with regard to the black-out
regulations are given to policemen before
going on duty?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: If the hon.
Member can give me a case where that is
so, I will have it inquired into.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's reply that the person who
made the complaint had committed an
offence would the Minister be surprised
to know that the person who made this
complaint is one of his most efficient
A.R.P. officials, and is not a bit afraid to
give his name if the Minister thinks he
wants it? He was never prosecuted.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I did not refer to
the gentleman who gave the information
to the hon. Member. I was only referring
to the general tendency on the part of
those who have committed breaches of the
regulations to point out some person worse
than themselves. I am quite sure, as the
hon. Member says, the person who gave
him the information was speaking of what
he considered to be the facts.

ACCOUNTS OF THE SPECIAL

Mr. MacDERMOTT: I have been

The accounting system for the Special
Constabulary contains the usual safeguards considered necessary for Government accounting. No system can, however, be devised that will be proof
against deliberate fraud on a small scale
and for limited periods. Such dishonesty usually comes to light sooner or

an investigation into the accounts of the
Special Constabulary as suggested by the
hon. Member.

Oral Answers
SNOW-PLOUGHS TO CLEAR ROADS.
10. Mr. BAILEY asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government will
take steps to induce the county councils of
Northern Ireland to purchase snowploughs to clear the roads in time of
snow; whether he is aware that owing to
the lack of this equipment many thousands
of galions of milk were lost in Northern
Ireland owing to the fact that a great
number of the roads were blocked for over
a fortnight during the very heavy snowstorm in January and February.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Government has considered the
problem of the clearance of snow from
roads, in the light of the situation which
arose recently.
In Great Britain a statutory obligation
is placed on highway authorities to clear
snow from roads. No similar obligation
is placed on highway authorities in
Northern Ireland.
It is proposed to introduce legislation
placing a statutory obligation on road
authorities in Northern Ireland, to deal
with this matter, and I have in mind
including in such legislation provisions
requiring county councils to provide and
keep available for immediate use necessary
machinery such as snow-ploughs.

I am

Government work.

MITTEE'S APPOINTMENT.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The question

Flax Development Committee is entirely
one for that body and is not a matter in

to tank retting; one reason for this being
that already the Linen Industry Research Association is engaged on investigations into the utilisation of green
flax, and that, moreover, certain private.
interests are carrying out experiments
on a commercial basis on the possibilities
of green flax.
The Committee have pointed out, however, that under their existing arrangements they are prepared to purchase
green straw direct from the farmer.

FARMERS AND USE OF TRACTORS.
15. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware of the fact
that a farmer who owns and operates a
tractor is not allowed to draw goods for
his own use on either a tractor or a
trailer attached thereto on a country road
without having a goods vehicle licence;
whether in view of the hardship thus
inflicted on these agriculturists who at
the present time. are putting forth every
effort to further the increased tillage
campaign now in progress, he will take
immediate action to have. this matter
regularised and exempt such vehicles from
goods licence duty.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Under the Motor Vehicles and Road
Traffic Act (Northern Ireland), 1934, all
goods vehicles used on public highways
for the carriage of goods must be licensed
by the police, and a tractor drawing goods
is a goods vehicle. As the hon. Member
is aware, inspection and licensing of goods
vehicles were imposed by Parliament to
ensure that vehicles are not permitted to
be used in an unsafe condition on public
roads, thereby endangering the travelling
public.
The licence fees prescribed are merely
sufficient to cover the costs of inspection,
including the periodical examination of
the vehicles, and I am not prepared to
differentiate between the licence fees paid
by different classes of the community,
particularly as it is a growing practice
with farmers to convert old motor cars
into tractors and use them with trailers,
and it is essential that such vehicles
should be regularly examined to ensure
their fitness.
The fee for licensing a new tractor is
only 1s for the first year, and the fee
for the licence for each successive year is
only £1.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I would like to ask
whether it is a fact that these vehicles
are exempt from goods licence duty in
England?

Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE

produce to the local Food Executive

number of colonies of bees in their
possession.

THE 1940 FLAX CROP.
17. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether in the event of
flax grader
not accepting the
declaration of the farmer that the flax
offered by him for sale was of 1940
growth and insisting on putting this flax
in the 1939 grade with corresponding
lower price, he will state who is the final
authority to decide a case such as this.
Lord GLENTORAN: The grading of
flax is a service carried out at each flax
market by officers of the Ministry of
Supply. At each market an inspector
of the Ministry of Supply is also in
attendance and if any grower is dissatisfied with the grading of his flax
appeal can be made to this officer.
Further, the local administrator of the
Northern Ireland Flax Control attends
most markets and a final appeal can be
made to him. Where a farmer is still
dissatisfied with the decision
on the
point mentioned by the hon. Member,
and brings the matter to the attention
of my Ministry, we make the necessary
representations to the local administrator. I may add that in any cases in
which we have approached the local
administrator up to date, the representations put forward by my Ministry have
been accepted.
FIRMS PROCESSING FLAX SEED.
18. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
number of firms in Northern Ireland
processing flax seed for this season's
sowing; whether deliveries of such are
being made up to requirements, and
whether in view of any firm not delivering this seed in time for sowing, he
will take steps to have late deliveries paid
for at a reduced rate and allow same to
be sold to farmers for feeding purposes
at its commercial value.
Lord GLENTORAN: Seven firms in
Northern Ireland are engaged in the
processing of flax seed for this season's
sowing. The disinfection of the seed is
being carried out under the control of
my Ministry and we are satisfied that
all the seed from the firms in question
will be available for this season's sowing.
The second part of the hon. Member's
question does not, therefore, arise.

I know that the right hon. Gentleman

a job in regard to administration as the

they have to come into personal contact
with the individuals, they are up against

when I enter departments under his
management and in those branches find
the same officials that I found in the
years 1912, 1913, 1914, and right up to
1920. When I look to see what advancement they have made I find they have
made very little in regard to their grade.
We have all watched the development
of the Ministry of Agriculture, and now
we are watching the development of the
Ministry of Public Security. I feel that
the openings provided by those two
branches of the Service should have been
given to those tried and trusted servants
in the Ministry of Labour who have been
waiting for the last twenty years for the
promotion they are entitled to receive. I
do not want to give them what the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned the last
day-stripes. I am not looking for stripes
for them. All I am looking for is justice,
and I am hoping that the Parliamentary
Secretary and his chief will endeavour to
see that justice is done to those servants
who have maintained a high standard of
efficiency in the Ministry of Labour since
the establishment of this Government.
That was really the object I had in view
when I spoke on the last day. I am
making that appeal now because I think
it should not fall on deaf ears.
There are
fourteen, or perhaps fewer, going out of
the Service in the way they came into it.
That is not, in my opinion, the way those
officials should go out. They should go
out in a grade equal to the ability they
have shown and equal to the services they
have rendered.

He complained that members of my

Departments, the release of officers for

during the financial year to officers in

volunteering. Under the conditions at

into operation in this way. If you are
offered a job and refuse to go that is all
there is about it at the time, but in a few
days you get a notice to the effect that
you have refused an offer of suitable

employment and you are

I am in full agreement with the training scheme, although I was opposed to it
at the beginning because the training had
to be carried out in Great Britain. Since
the Minister has adopted a training
scheme at home I think it is a very useful
thing for these young men in order to

class of employment they would not have

that trainees should be compulsorily put
into craftsmen's positions. Craftsmen
have a claim on certain classes of work in
industry, and without the will and consent of those craftsmen no trainee should
be put in there by force.
I am very sceptical of the benefit to be
derived from sending to Great Britain of
so much of the class of labour we will
very soon require for our own services.
The scarcity is becoming so pronounced
that the Minister of Labour has said that
if it should be necessary he will, with the
acquiescence of the trade unions, bring
conscription in and compel men to go on
the land. At the same time he has exported anything up to 3,000 highly skilled
land workers to Great Britain to dig
trenches and foundations for the new
factories to be erected in that country.
Do you not think that is a very unwise
policy to pursue?

Northern Ireland of placing these trainees

better than the man who has had no
previous training.
As regards the question of training
allowances, the rates are:-Men aged 21
and over-To the trainee personally an
allowance of 8s per week plus the cost of
his board and lodging. In addition the
trainee is given a free mid-day meal at
the centre on six days in the week.
Dependants' allowances are also payable at the rates of 30s per week for an
adult, with 4s per week for each of the
first two dependent children, and 3s per
week for each dependent child in excess
of two.
Young men aged 18 to 20-To the
trainee personally an allowance of 6s per
week with the cost of board and lodging,
free meals and dependents' allowances as
for those of 21 and over.
The Member for Pottinger said the
market on the other side was not just as
favourable for Irish boys as it was for
boys from Scotland and England. There
might be a certain amount of truth in
that, but it is not generally the case. I
myself had an opportunity of visiting a
good many of these training establishments and having a friendly chat with
boys from Northern Ireland who were
being trained there. In at least two of
the training centres I visited I saw boys
in their best clothes who were not working
there. They had got a half-day off from
the factory where they were engaged.
They were former trainees, and they had
come back again to encourage the other
boys who were undergoing a course of
training to stick to their job because there
were possibilities of good positions being
found for them after their period of
training had expired.
Both the Minister and myself have had
letters from these boys. I had a letter
from a boy belonging to Newry who had
got a splendid job in an aviation factory.
He started at five guineas a week. I will
admit he was an exceptional boy, but his
employer was so well pleased with the
progress he had made and the likelihood
of his turning out to be a good craftsman
that he thought he was well worth a wage
of five guineas a week. I think hon.
Members will agree that the opportunities
for boys getting a job like that in Northern Ireland are few and far between.

BLACK-OUT CLOTH FOR A.R.P.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state
the amount spent on black-out cloth for
various A.R.P. services in the city of
Belfast; whether the cloth was obtained
through the usual system of advertising;
whether there was a standard pattern
and whether the material supplied was
subject to a proper test to see if it came
up to standard.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): I am
informed that the amount spent on
black-out cloth for various A.R.P. services in the city of Belfast up to the
present date is £1,974 16s 4d. The cloth
was obtained through the usual system
adopted throughout by the former
A.R.P. Committee and the Belfast
Civil Defence Authority by inviting
quotations from at least six firms.
Under this system a standard pattern is
not specified, but each firm is required.
to submit with its quotation a sample of
the goods it proposes to supply. The
material supplied was, I am informed,
iu all cases where necessary subjected to
a proper test to ensure that it came up
to the sample submitted.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's reply that in all cases where
necessary it is subjected to a proper test,
what is the expression "necessary" calculated to convey in that particular
connection?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I take it from
information received from the Civil
Defence Authority
Authority that where any
question arises as to the sufficiency or
insufficiency of the sample, it would be
a matter of a definite technical test. I
also take it that in cloth seen by the
senses to correspond to sample no
question arises, and it would not be subject to actual technical test.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not usual for the
Corporation to get a standard pattern
and to send the pattern and the cloth
to the testing house in the technical
institute?

in the Belfast Civil Defence organisation.
Their duties are to organise and coordinate all the services in their districts,
and there is no specified service under
their individual control. There is not

STRENGTH AND COST OF R.U.C. IN
BELFAST.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he can state
the total number of all ranks of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary stationed in
the borough of Belfast, the number of
constables, sergeants, head constables,
district inspectors and county inspectors;
the number of different ranks attached to
Waring Street headquarters, with their
respective ranks; the number attached to
the Commissioner's headquarters and their
respective ranks; the total number of the
detective branch and their respective
ranks; what were the respective totals of
above for the year 1924; what is the
number of auxiliary policemen and their
respective ranks at present attached to
the Royal Ulster Constabulary and doing
full time duty, and what is the total cost
of all ranks to the Exchequer for the
preservation of law and order in the city
of Belfast.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I feel that it
would not be in the public interest in
present circumstances to give details of
police dispositions, and consequently I am
unable to give the hon. Member the
complete information asked for in his
question. He will find in the published.
Estimates of my Department particulars
of personnel of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, down to the rank of head
constable, who form the headquarters of
the Inspector General.
The total number of Royal Ulster
Constabulary and full-time Ulster Special
Constabulary serving in the city of Belfast
taken together is at present approximately
500 less than in 1924.
The total number of members of the
Ulster Special Constabulary mobilised for
full-time duty with the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is approximately 900
throughout Northern Ireland.
The accounts kept by my Department
are framed so as to deal with the Royal
Ulster Constabulary and the Ulster
Special Constabulary as a whole, and not
by way of a division of the cost between
Belfast and the rest of the country. For
this reason I regret that I am not in a
position to give the hon. Member a figure
for the total cost of the preservation of
law and order in the city.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask is
it not a fact that the regulations and

are set down by Act of Parliament, and
is it a fact that the quota for the city of
Belfast in regard to officers and men is

SUPPLEMENTARY AID TO BLIND
PERSONS' DEPENDANTS.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
amount of supplementary aid paid by the
Armagh County Council to dependants of
blind pensioners; whether the maximum
sum of 5s granted by that Council as
supplementary aid is sufficient for the
needs of the blind, in view of the acute
conditions prevailing.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Armagh County
Council pays supplementary allowances to
93 blind pensioners, the average amount
payable being 4s per week. Each case is
dealt with on its merits after careful
investigation by the Blind Persons Act
Committee of the Council, and I have. no
reason to suppose that the Committee
does not act sympathetically. If the hon.
Member has any particular case in mind
I shall be happy to have inquiries made.
The total estimated expenditure in
assistance to blind persons in County
Armagh during the coming financial year
is £2,907, as compared with an expenditure of £678 during the financial year
1939-40.
PUBLIC HEALTH ACT AND
BLIND PERSONS.
6. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Public Health
Act, 1925, applies to Northern Ireland
in relation to blind persons, and whether
he can state if his department follows a
step-by-step policy in all social services.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Public
Health Act, 1925, now largely embodied
in the Public Health Act, 1936, did not
apply to Northern Ireland. Section 176
of the latter Act, which has reference to
blindness, is an enabling Section and
allows local authorities to make such
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
arrangements as they may think desirable for assisting in the prevention of
blindness, and, in particular, for the
treatment of persons suffering from any
disease of, or injury to, the eyes. In
Northern Ireland, however, authority
was given by the Local Government Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, to Boards of
Guardians to send to a hospital or
infirmary poor persons requiring special
medical or surgical treatment. Consequently, persons suffering from eye
diseases are enabled to received suitable
treatment, and, in fact, cases frequently
arise of persons being sent to eye hospitals. It appears unnecessary, therefore, to introduce in Northern Ireland
any further legislation on the matter.
RATES IN NEWRY URBAN AND
RURAL DISTRICTS.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
grounds on which he made the statement
in the House on the 4th instant, that the
increases in the rates in the various urban
and rural districts in Newry Union,
ranging from ls to 5s 8d in the £, are
due mainly to the payment of outdoor
relief to persons whose unemployment
benefit has been stopped because they
have (as alleged) refused, without good
reason, to accept offers of suitable employment, or because they have left
suitable employment voluntarily without
just cause; whether he can state the
source from which he received this information; whether he can give the
House the details of all these cases; and
whether he can state the exact proportion of the rate increases referred to that
were brought about by these refusals of
offers, of employment or the leaving of
employment without just cause.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I explained in my reply to the hon. Member's
previous question on this matter, the
rate increases referred to by him have
resulted mainly from the increased demand of the Newry Board of Guardians
in respect of outdoor relief, which
is estimated to cost £17,000 in 1941-42,
an increase of more than £5,000 as compared with the current financial year.
In addition, provision has been made in
the demand to meet an estimated debit
balance of £4,000 at the end of the
current
financial year. This debit
balance is due mainly to excess expenditure on outdoor relief incurred
during the current year, and for which
the guardians have not made any
provision.
From information which has been
furnished by the Board of Guardians,
and from consultation which I have had
with my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Labour, it is clear that the very substantial increase in expenditure has been
caused mainly by the granting of outdoor
relief to able-bodied persons whose unemployment benefit has been stopped for
the reasons indicated in my previous
reply. I am informed that during the
past six months nearly 1,100 claims
were disallowed at Newry Employment
Exchange owing to the persons concerned
having refused to take suitable work
when it was offered to them, and I am
sure that the hon. Member will
appreciate that it would be impossible
to give the House details of these cases.
I regret that statistics are not available
which would show the exact proportions
of the rate increases which are
attributable to the granting of outdoor
relief to persons who had refused
suitable employment.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister
supply me with the particulars asked for
if he cannot give them to the House, as
I am in a position to dispute his
information?

of the Select Committee which has functioned, not altogether with success, for
some years past in the Imperial Parliament; but whereas at Westminster
effective criticism of the Estimates in
Committee of Supply is impracticable.
owing to their voluminous character, with
the result that debates on Estimates are

FINANCIAL SECRETARY
Sinclair): Part I of this
Resolution covers certain amendments of
existing provisions in our Exchequer and
Financial Provisions code, the first of
which is the proposal to provide for an
increase in the amount which may be
temporarily advanced from the. Exchequer
to make good calls which may be made
upon the Civil Contingencies Fund. This
Fund is used for meeting urgent expenditure in anticipation of covering approval
by Parliament. For a considerable time
the fixed capital of £100,000, which is
available in the Fund, proved sufficient
to meet these demands, but on the outbreak of war it was found necessary to
increase. the margin by means
temporary advances from the Exchequer.
In last year's Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Act power was taken to
supplement the fixed capital of £100,000
by means of Exchequer advances to the.
extent of another £100,000, making in
all a margin of £200,000.
of
311 Financial Provisions [Money]- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Major Sinclair]
It is now proposed to increase the
amount available to £350,000, of which
£100,000 will be represented by the fixed
capital and the balance of £250,000 made
up of temporary advances from the
Exchequer. It is thought prudent to
provide for this increase in view of the
continued uncertainty of the situation
created by the war, but it will be a condition that any advances which may have
to be made to the Fund will be repayable
to the Exchequer not later than 30th
September, 1942.
I. (b) of the Resolution deals with
matters of administration in connection
with Ulster Savings Certificates. It has
been a source of considerable satisfaction
to all members of the Committee that it
has been found possible to hand over the
entire proceeds of our National Defence
Issue to the Imperial Treasury for war
purposes, but circumstances arising out
of the large amounts raised as a result
of the war savings campaign necessitate
some widening of our statutory powers.
The powers contained in our 1933 Act
permitted the investment of the proceeds
of Ulster Savings Certificates in
authorised securities, and it was this
power which enabled us to remit the
National Defence Issue proceeds to the
Imperial Exchequer in exchange for
Treasury Certificates charging eventual
repayment of the amount of such
remittances on the Consolidated Fund
of the United Kingdom, with interest
at the rate corresponding to that given
by us on Savings Certificates issued to
members of the public. The 1933 Act
also, continuing an earlier Act, provides
that we should set aside annually to a
Sinking Fund the amount required to
meet the accrued interest due to the
public on Savings Certificates outstanding
As a result it would normally become
necessary for us to set aside a very substantially increased provision based on
the present huge total of the National
Defence Issue, in addition to the provision required for interest on the older
issues of Savings Certificates, and to
charge this amount against revenue in
our Budget. On the other hand, it is
evidence that interest accruing on the
Treasury Certificates held by us will
eventually cover practically to the full
extent our corresponding liability to the
public, and it is proposed to take power
to enable us to offset these two items,
that is, to set one off against the other,
and to restrict our Budget provision for
the Sinking Fund accordingly.
The opportunity of amendment of the
1933 Act will also be taken to bring up
to date certain clauses with respect to
which the powers contained, while
sufficient for their purposes at the time,
require amplification in changed circumstances. My right hon. Friend will explain the details on the Second Reading.
I (c) is merely declaratory and is considered necessary only for the removal of
an administrative difficulty in regard to
the form of presentation of our annual
Capital Accounts, and the intention is to
place beyond doubt that the Capital
Fund is an asset held by the Ministry of
Finance which bridges to the extent
required any gap between the total of
Exchequer borrowings and the amount
of assets held in the shape of investments
and repayable advances.
Part II of the Resolution makes provision for meeting the liabilities which
will be imposed on our Government
when the War Damage Bill becomes law.
For instance, if the Government holds a
mortgage on any property for which
contributions are payable the Government will have to indemnify the contributor in accordance with the terms of
the Bill. Sub-paragraph (b) of this
part of the Resolution empowers the
Government to contribute to county
councils and county boroughs up to 50
per cent. as in Great Britain, of the contributions which those authorities will
have to pay as premiums against war
damage to roads. I beg to move.

operating at Derry have dealt with this
task and to the way in which, without
thought of self, they have spent themselves night and day in beating back
this scourge.
I would also like to acknowledge the
tremendous assistance which my officers
have received from all ranks of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. From the moment
the disease first made its appearance the
police have been ready to do anything, to
go anywhere in order to help to prevent
its spread, and I know how very effective
their advice has been in persuading
farmers and other residents in the affected
area to refrain from all unnecessary
movement which could only increase the
risk of infection. I am very glad indeed
to have this opportunity of acknowledging their assistance.
Nor must I forget the manner in which
the military authorities have endeavoured
to help us in stamping out the disease. On
this particular aspect of the outbreak I
cannot, of course, speak too freely, but
hon. Members will at once appreciate
what it meant to my Ministry to have the
heads of the Forces prepared to co-operate
in restricting the movement of large
bodies of men and vehicles either through
or out of the scheduled area. Such help
has been invaluable.
The Committee will note that the provision for premium bulls, which owing to

sub-head c (2) of the supplementary.
I am very glad that it has been found
possible to continue our Premium Bulls

the welfare of our live-stock industry, and

breeding.

War Bonuses to Civil Servants.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: I beg to
move:
That in the opinion of this House any
increases in the amount of war bonuses
paid to members of our Civil Service
ought, in the interests of economy and
equity, to be based on the family allowance system, which has been recognised
as practical, equitable and economic in
the case of unemployment insurance
benefits, and which has been adopted
by His Majesty's Government in the
payment of wages to the Army, Navy
and Air Forces.
This is the first occasion on which I
have ventured to move a Motion in this
House, and I would not do so now did I
not regard this matter as of considerable
importance from the point of view of
national interests. I would like, first of
all, to remind the House that the principle
of paying war bonuses to families has gone
far beyond the merely experimental or
theoretical stage. It has been in operation
in a considerable number of countries and
in one form or another has been used by
different groups of people for upwards of
100 years. After the last war this policy
received a very great impetus in France
by reason of the fact that artisans in
France and many of the peasants were
unable to maintain their families owing
to the rise in the cost of living, and at
that time in France a very interesting
policy was worked out by industrialists
whereby by means of an equalisation Bill
it was made possible to pay to the wives
of workers a sum additional to wages and
in proportion to the number of children
in the home.
own
Since that time this policy has been
adopted in a great number of other
countries and in nearly every country in
Europe except Turkey and our
country. It has been adopted in various
spheres of Government Departments and
with Government approval since the last
war. In addition to that it has been in
operation for a considerable number of
years in Australia-I am referring now
to industry rather than to Government
services and also in New Zealand, and
as late as 1938 the New Zealand Government raised the payment to families
from 2s per dependent child to 4s. The
House will be interested to know that in
our own country this policy of recognising the claims of families and of children
has been acknowledged by our own Government already in several Departments of
its work. For example, the income-tax
authorities, although they are very
voracious as all income-tax payers know,
do make abatements to payers who have
children of an educable age, and in that
way they have recognised to some extent
the principle of family allowances.
Of far greater significance, however, is
the fact that the Imperial authorities, at
least since the beginning of this war,
have adopted this principle in the payment of all the Forces of the Crown. It
is very important at all times, and
particularly in war time, that those who
are defending us with their lives should be
loyal, that they should be contented,
that there should be no unrest among
the troops, and one of the methods by
which the Imperial Government have
tried to obviate the possibility of unrest
was by giving our soldiers and our sailors
and our airmen grants for their children
while they were away on service. Just
shortly before the actual outbreak of war
it was announced by Mr. Hore-Belisha,
Minister of War at that time, that the
family allowance to a man with a wife
would be 17s; a man with a wife and
one child, 22s 'ôd in addition to pay. A
331 War Bonuses to Civil Servants HOUSE OF COMMONS War Bonuses to Civil Servants 332
[Rev. Professor Corkey]
man with a wife and two children would
get 26s, and a man with a wife and three
children 28s.
Recently in one of our canteens I
happened to come into contact with three
young men who had come up from Eire
to enlist in our Forces, fine, big, strong
fellows they were, and I was pleased to
meet them and welcome them coming as
they were on such a mission. I asked
them how it was they did not enlist in
the Forces of Eire. The reply was
rather significant. "Well," they said, "you
know Dev does not make as good provision for our children as the Imperial
authorities." It is a small illustration,
perhaps, but it is a real illustration of the
significance and value of this principle as
a principle of justice and fair play. Our
Imperial Government in a very large
department of its service has already
recognised this principle, and my point
is that the principle itself is thus not one
that can simply be laughed out of court
as a mere phantasy of idealism. The
principle is in operation. Further, as
we all know, it is a principle that has
been sanctioned by the Imperial authorities and by our own Northern Government in the calculation of grants and the
limitation of grants that are given by the
Unemployment Assistance Board.
I might mention in passing that the
payments of these benefits to people out
of work has one rather unfortunate consequence. It so happens that owing to
the fact that benefits are calculated in
this way the amount which a man receives
as unemployment insurance benefit is
actually greater than the amount which
he will receive as wages when he is in
employment. But in spite of the
anomaly, in spite of the inconvenience,
and in spite of that unfortunate result
our Imperial authorities and our own
Government are so satisfied with this
principle of family allowances that they
have never thought to change it in that
respect.
I will just mention one more fact along
these lines. It was reported in the paper
yesterday. It would appear that our own
Government is at present engaged in preparing trainees for various types of work
to which they have not been accustomed
-a splendid scheme which has my hearty
approval. I hope thousands and thousands
of young men will be trained-well for
the encouragement of these young people
and in order to secure loyalty and contentment they are not only to be paid
allowances but here is a sentence. from
the report: "These amounts," it says,
"may be increased by 4s for each of the
first two additional children and by 3s
for each child in excess of two". That
appeared in our papers just yesterday.
Our Northern Government so far from
discrediting and discounting this principle
of family allowances are already recognising it, not only in the payment of
unemployment insurance as I have
already pointed out, but in this new
scheme they encourage the training of young
people engaged in war service. These facts
will be sufficient, I think, to convince the
Members of the House that this is no
mere theoretical fancy of my own, that
this principle of family allowances is no
mere policy of idealists. It is practical.
It has been in operation. It is used by
our Own Government, and my suggestion is that in another department
it should be put in operation. There
is just one additional type of facts that
I would mention in commending the
principle of family allowances to the
House. This principle has been in operation in the great Methodist Church in
the payment of their ministers for over
150 years. It is in operation in many
dioceses in the Church of England. It is
in operation at present in the sister
church to my own, the English Presbyterian Church. Just the. other day steps
were taken in my own church, the
to
Presbyterian Church in Ireland,
establish a central fund in the church for
the payment of family allowances.
I think it is likely that a policy which
has thus commended itself not only to our
own Government and the Government
across the water, but also the churches
for a very long time has something in it
which is worth looking into. Well, to
come more closely to the Motion and the

to the House, the first reason is one which
I think should commend the Motion to
the Prime Minister and also to the

that it is economical, and that war
bonuses can be paid according to this
principle more economically than in any
other way.
Before I develop that perhaps you will
allow me to point out the limited scope

What are these bonuses anyhow? What

This is not a recompense given to men

dealt with in various countries where the
scheme operates.

has been brought before the House by the
Member for the University, there was no

has said with such eloquence and fairness.
I must say I find myself very much in
agreement with what the Member for
Woodvale has said in reference to the
Motion. The Member for South Down
expressed the opinion that the family
allowance system, as advocated in the
Motion, would be a tax on bachelors. I
think it would work entirely the other
way, because both hon. Members who have
spoken said that while they advocated increased consideration being given to the
married man, especially under present

exercised in carrying out the public services. As the conditions under which we
are working at the present time are, we

be carried on by temporary civil servants,
and I think it would be a factor in engaging temporary civil servants to engage
those to whom the least liability attached.
Nevertheless, many of the points which
the Member for the University has raised
cannot be disputed, and I think all of us
realise the many advantages of any
efficient scheme that can be devised for
the proper upbringing of the rising
generation. But we must not close our
eyes to the practical difficulties which
have prevented any scheme of the kind
being adopted generally in the United
Kingdom. It is quite true, as the Member for the University reminded us, that
his Motion is confined to the application
of this scheme of family allowances to
additional bonuses which may be granted
during the course of the present war, but

effected by the manner in which he proposes to apply the scheme, he also tells us
that the majority of civil servants are
without family and that, therefore, they
would not enjoy the benefits of this family
allowance scheme. They would thus have
to forego any advantage of the bonuses
which might be granted.
Bonuses must not be confused with
salaries. Bonuses are granted with the
idea of helping civil servants to meet the
increased cost of living under war conditions, and therefore a civil servant without any family obligations would have to
forego part of the bonus he would be
entitled to to meet that extra cost of living
in order that the civil servant with family
obligations might receive more. Although,
as the hon. Member for the University
said, the scheme has been applied in certain instances in the United Kingdom, I
do not think it can be claimed that it has
made much progress. The main difficulty
lies in the fact that the scheme does not
commend itself to the trade unions. Both
hon. Members, in the course of their
remarks, referred to the fact that an
analogous scheme, although not exactly
the same, was under consideration in the
House of Lords at Westminster only a
few days ago, and Lord Moyne, who was
replying to the Motion, said it could not
be put into operation without the support
of organised labour, in view of the risk
of considerably affecting the present wage
structure.
I now come specifically to the application of the scheme to civil servants as
defined in the Motion before the House.
Hon. Members are, of course, aware that
conditions in our Civil Service have been
governed, broadly speaking, by those
obtaining in the Imperial Civil Service.
There is one point I hope hon. Members
will always bear in mind, and that is
that here in Northern Ireland we have

is one of the most serious things we have
to face; one of the most horrible plagues
in existence.. The hon. Member for
Woodvale is very happy that he has never
seen it. I have come across it, and it is
a most tragic thing to see on a man's

his grandfather reared up, and sheep and
all those cattle which are almost members
of his family-it is a most tragic thing
to walk in and destroy those animals

not tell hon. Members that no compensation could pay for animals one has reared.

utmost sympathy not only with our own
farmers, but the farmers of England and
of Eire in the trying times through
which they are passing. As far as we are
concerned we are in this position that the
issue raised by the hon. Member for
Woodvale does not arise at the moment,
because our entire export is to Great
Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Educational Services
[Lord Glentoran]
Britain. Great Britain will not accept
any animals from a country which has
foot-and-mouth disease, and we have no
alternative but to stamp out the disease
at the earliest possible moment.
Mr. NIXON: If you can.
Lord GLENTORAN: If we can.
Therefore the major question does not
affect us nearly to the same extent. I
would like to say, however, that for years
past hundreds of thousands of pounds
have been spent by the British Government on experiments to try to capture
the microbe of foot-and-mouth disease,
and retain it in such a manner as to
inoculate cattle, exactly like the microbe
of influenza, but so far without success.
The microbe is so small they cannot
isolate it. These experiments have gone
a small distance. They can give the
animal the disease, but it can get it again
and so it goes on. We know where five
or six outbreaks were caused by one man
going round in the course of his visits.
There is nothing more virulent than the
microbe of foot-and-mouth disease.
Therefore I think we can congratulate
ourselves that we have kept the disease
at one end of our country. It would be
terrible that it should get any further. I
would like the hon. Member to know that
this question of whether we have to kill
the animals in time or try to cure them is
one that is giving the gravest concern
every day. Let me show you the difficulty
we are up against. Foot-and-mouth
disease has been traced to animals
slaughtered in the Argentine and brought
over here iced. It has been traced in the
bones of animals brought over here and
used for feeding purposes. When we are
dealing with this virulent disease we are
up against a very grave proposition. Hon.
Members can be assured of this fact that
farmers have my sympathy, and if we can
do anything to alleviate their troubles we
certainly will do it.
Question put, and agreed to.

who had left school. We were impressed
by the urgent need for the extension and
development of youth welfare organisations. Juvenile delinquency appeared to
be on the increase, and conditions
inseparable from war such as the blackout and the general emotional atmosphere,
accentuated the need to give healthy
occupation and recreation to the young.
Steps were taken to enlist the

voluntary school managers in a movement
for the formation of clubs for boys and
girls who had left school; and at the
same time the Ministry encouraged those
interested in the problems of youth to
extend the clubs and movements already
in existence and to create new ones. It
is too early to say what measure of success

that education committees and both

been engaged. The Ministry has undertaken to make grants equal to one-half

Rev. Professor CORKEY: It is

STRIKE IN BELFAST.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn".-
(Lord Glentoran.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I wish to raise a
matter about which I have given the
Minister of Labour notice the strike
which has been going on in Belfast since
Friday last. I am rather perturbed about
this matter in view of the seriousness of
the situation and the necessity for providing the implements necessary for the
British Empire in its fight against Hitler.
Five or six thousand men are on strike,
and I believe. it is spreading. With all
due respect to the Minister of Labour I
say that if I were Minister I would have
had this thing settled one way or the
other. These men have a just grievance.
I understand that men employed in the
Sirocco Works had their services dispensed
with. In the ordinary course they went
to Harland & Wolff's to seek employment,
which they got. After receiving the.
employment two of the men
were dismissed and told to go back to the Sirocco
Works. I am told that the firm wrote
and told Harland & Wolff's to dismiss
them. It is a deplorable thing to throw
men on to the street in order to compel
them to go back to another firm. The
strike is spreading. I understand that
the apprentices are out on strike owing
to the very thing which this Government
has been trying to encourage-the trainee
system. Apparently what the right hon.
Gentlemen and Members of this House
have done is not going to be accepted in
Northern Ireland.
I believe, that if the men and the
employers were called together-their
hearts are in the fight against Hitlersomething could be done in reference to
the trainees and apprentices which would
bring about a settlement of a dispute
which is likely to spread to all the shops
in Belfast. Several meetings have been
held since Friday, and I was amazed to
learn that up to the present no settlement
had been arrived at. Yesterday I had
the pleasure. of being in touch with some
of the delegates in connection with the
Engineering Trades Union. I was
astonished to find that the Minister had
not stepped in and brought both parties
together. Something should be done
immediately, because we cannot afford to
lose one minute in so far as production
of ships, tanks and other things is concerned. I feel that there has been some
laxity, and I would appeal to the entire
Cabinet to try to get the employers and
the men together, so that this strike may
be settled immediately, not only for the
benefit of the citizens of Northern
Ireland, but for the benefit of the
Empire.
Mr. NIXON: I have heard all about
this strike from people concerned. I had
hoped that the Government would have
settled it to-day, and I am amazed that
they have not done so. The Minister of
Labour was telling us about his power:
this is a case in which he can exercise that
power. I do not want to say anything
about the merits of the dispute now, because it might not be the right thing to
do, but I am satisfied that there is not one
single person who, if he heard the case,
would not say that the men are right. I
do not say right in their demand, because
no demand has been made. It is a case
of certain people using power that they
have no right to use, and that they should
not be allowed to use.
Generally speaking, the heads of firms.
in Belfast are reasonable and considerate,
but they are not so in this particular case.
Nor can I say the same thing about the
heads of a lot of the country firms, parti-
