The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I am placed in an exceedingly
difficult position by this matter having
been raised in the House. The hon.
Member for Shankill is wrong. I have
been in contact with both the work people
and the employers since the inception of
this strike, and less than an hour ago I
was on the 'phone with a representative
of the workers. The hon. Member is
wrong. A strike of this magnitude and
of this character cannot be settled with a
wave of the hand, and in the circumstances I think the less said the better.
Negotiations have taken place, and are
taking place. A meeting of the men will
be held to-morrow, and I hope that as a
result of the meeting a satisfactory solution of the whole problem will be reached.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not want to enter
into the merits of this dispute, but I do
say there is great danger in the interference of the Government between
worker and employer. Nevertheless if
the conciliation officer of the Ministry,
whom I know as a very capable gentleman, has been in touch with the two
bodies concerned, and has failed up to the
moment, then perhaps some other effort
must be made. It is sad to think that
our streets are filled with men whose skill
could be usefully employed in the national
interest. Looking at it from my point of
view, I feel that the strike should never
have taken place. That is the strike in
which adult labour is concerned. I think
it is wrong and it is unadvisable that men
whose services have been dispensed with
by a firm, and who found useful employment in the national interest, should be
compelled to return to the firm by which
they had been dismissed, in order to serve
the interests of the employers who
dispensed with their services when they
had not work to keep them moving.
The other side of the question relates
to trainees. It is a difficult problem.
It is not as easy to solve as one would
think. I was an apprentice myself for
a period of seven years, and the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Labour has had similar experience. We
had to deal with disputes affecting
apprentices during the last war. I have
every sympathy with apprentices who
find themselves highly qualified to carry
out certain work, but who are bound by
the conditions of their appointment as
apprentices to conform to certain regulations, and who see trainees, after a
period of three months, getting 69s as
against their 40s.
But the circumstances of the moment
warrant the employment of these
trainees; we require that class of labour.
While I have every sympathy with the
apprentices in their present position, I
must point out that they have a binding
contract, whereby after the war, their
skill and ability will be protected in
their trade, which will be reserved for
their skilled labour. After the war, on
the other hand, the trainee will have to
revert to his former position or walk the
streets. There is something in that dispute that should be considered from the
point of view of the national interests.
As to the first dispute to which I have
referred, I hope that the right hon.
Gentleman has impressed upon the
parties concerned the importance of its
being settled immediately. I hope that
the hour of settlement will be reached
to-night, and that the men will return
to work to-morrow morning.

The hon. Member for Woodvale then

I think
he must have come prepared to attack

which I gave in moving the Estimates,

to take them off the streets.
I think in order to support my Estimate
and to make my case, it would be advisable for me to refer to what took place in
Great Britain shortly after war had
broken out. In this particular connection
in Great Britain the Imperial Government recognised that the strain of war
must create a very serious menace to
youth. They decided that the Board of
Education there should undertake the
direct responsibility for youth welfare and
they appointed the National Youth Committee to advise the President of the Board
of Education on this matter. A special
grants board has been organised there to
administer grants for the maintenance,
development and recreation of the young
people and expenditure by approved local
education authorities will under a certain
section of the Education Act of 1921 be
approved.
What is more, His Majesty the King
took a very deep interest in this whole
question. He addressed a letter to the
Prime Minister, Mr. Chamberlain, stating
that he had learned with pleasure of the
National Youth Committee, that he had
long taken a close, personal interest in
work of this kind, and he hoped it would
be continued and extended despite the
handicaps imposed by the war. Over
here where our problems were very much
the same his Grace the Governor expressed
the opinion that this matter was one of
vital importance, and he sent a message to
a public meeting in Belfast commending
the scheme for the welfare of the young
people of Northern Ireland. Then we
wondered how we were going to tackle
this question and found that under the
Physical Training and Recreation Act of
1938 which we had more or less suspended
except for certain commitments during the
war, we were enabled to continue our
good work in a slightly different direction,
but with the aim of helping the young
people who were unemployed, or even
those who were employed, to spend their
evenings not in the black and darkened
streets, especially in the winter, exposed

for their recreation, providing clubs for
them, premises, equipment; some place
where they could go under good leadership and good guidance; in decent surroundings and in good companionship.
We feel, as I feel most strongly, that
no work that could be carried on during
the war is of more importance than this.

recently when he referred to the fact
that in a certain city the crime returns
showed that the number of specially

I must say the Ministry's regulations
in regard to school attendance have not
been put into operation. The responsibility is put on the regional education
authorities, and as the officers are neighbours of the parents of the children the
attendance regulations are ignored to a

better school attendance, but also to instil

of the education authorities to carry out

Royal Ulster Constabulary

£69,426, and, in addition, there are

to

know that to the members of the "B”
Class Special Constabulary on patrol

and questions have been asked from
time to time as to these payments
being in arrear. Sometimes the delay
was as much as two or three weeks,
and on looking into the matter
I discovered that the delay was
largely due to congestion, consequent
on the fact that claims for some
13,000 men had to be dealt with
quarterly and all at a time. The staff
was not able to cope with that and we
then considered the best thing to do
rather than providing extra staff to deal
with what was only periodic heavy duty,
was to stagger the payments so that onethird of the force would get a payment
each month. In other words one-third of
the force got a month's payment at the
beginning of February of this year and
another third got two months at
beginning of March. For that amount
we had to draw this year extra payments
so as to find the payments made at the
beginning of February and the beginning
of March. There will be so much less to
be found in the. next financial year, and
the result will be that one-third of the
force will get their each month
pay
instead of the whole force each quarter.
I hope that in consequence payments will
be made with greater promptitude than
was hitherto possible.

Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the Prime Minister the order of business
for to-morrow.
I should also like to ask the right hon.
Gentleman to notify the House of the
termination of the strike that unfortunately occurred in the city of Belfast.
I understand that the strike has now
been settled. This strike should never
have taken place. It is regrettable that
these things happen.

regrettable that these things happen,
but I am very gratified to be able to

has been settled. I understand that the

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 13th March, 1941.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CULTIVATION OF STORMONT
ESTATE.
1. Mr. DOWLING (for Rev. Professor
Corkey) asked the Minister of Finance
whether in view of the clamant and
reiterated appeals to farmers and others
to cultivate more land and grow more
food, he will consider the question of
cultivating a very much larger proportion of the Stormont Estate, or leasing
part of it to the Plot Owners' Association
for the present emergency and one year
after, thus setting a good example in
this matter to all others.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The cultivation of the
Stormont Estate has been carried out in
consultation with the Ministry of
Agriculture. A substantial part of the
Estate is utilised for experimental
purposes under the control of that
Ministry and practically the whole of the
remaining arable area has been ploughed
up for the growing of flax and food crops.
As regards the second part of the hon.
Member's question, he may not be aware
that part of the Estate has already been
assigned to and is under cultivation by
the Belfast Garden Plots Association.
DISALLOWANCES BY ASSISTANCE
BOARD.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Labour whether
he is aware of the large number of disallowances issued by the Assistance
Board on grounds not normally";
whether the Assistance Board intends to
disallow on grounds "not normally" on
a large scale without considering the
acute industrial situation; whether he
can state the number of disallowances
issued by the Board through area officers,
and who is the officer at headquarters.
responsible for the said disallowances.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I have made inquiries from
the Assistance Board, and I am informed
that no separate record is kept of the
disallowances on "not normally" grounds
of applications for unemployment
assistance.
In considering whether any applicant
fulfils the "normally" condition, the
officers of the Board take careful account
of his industrial record and his opportunities of obtaining employment.
Under the statutes responsibility for
decisions on applications is placed not
on any particular officer, but on officers
of the Board generally; and, in fact,
disallowance action is taken by various
officers.
VISITS TO AREA OFFICES.
3. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Labour whether he
can state how many visits have been made
by the members of the Assistance Board
to area offices in Northern Ireland, and
whether, in view of the acute position of
the unemployed the Minister will recommend to these members the necessity of
having personal contact in the said areas
in order to see things in their proper
light.
Mr. GORDON: I have made inquiries
from the Assistance Board and I am informed that particulars are not kept of
visits paid by members to the various area
offices of the Board in Northern Ireland.
The Board keeps in close touch with the
position in the various areas through its
organisation, and by personal visits by
members. Members of the Board have,
in fact, visited every area office in Northern Ireland during the last six months.

to bring the strike to an end. If I can

Mr. BARBOUR: It is not customary
on the occasion of the moving of the
annual Vote on Account to do other than
draw attention to the general trend of
the estimates in comparison with the
expenditure of the current year. It will
be seen that as against a reduction of
about half a million pounds, which was
registered last year when the Vote on
Account was taken, we now find an
increase of approximately the same sum.
Hon. Members will wish to know
whether this increased sum arises from
war causes or whether it is to some extent
due to an expansion of what I may call
our normal services, and I should explain
that when in March last credit was being
taken for a reduction this was due to the
curtailment of many normal services
which were not essential for war purposes.
The position to-day is rather different in
that we are faced with substantial
increases in expenditure due to wartime
developments on civil defence.
These increases from wartime causes
more than offset the savings on normal

I am asking the Ministry of Labour

My Dear Friend,

We will have a little talk about the legal

The legal aspect does not frighten me at

was describing an interview I had had

The Minister was wrong in reference
to another point. That was that I said
the air-raid shelters would not stop blast
if such a thing occurred. I want the
Minister and everyone else to stick to
the point. I do not say that air-raid
shelters would not stop the blast-that
is not why I call them useless-my point
is that if people had to spend a cold night
in these air-raid shelters they would not
live long after the experience. That is
my complaint, and I adhere to it.
Take the case of a woman with a baby
in her arms, with another child so high,
and yet another so high. She and her
children have to go into one of these
shelters from nine o'clock to four on a
winter's night. They would not live
after an experience of that kind.
I am
not making the point that these shelters
would not stop some of the blast, but
that the people could not exist in them.
I am trying to be constructive, and I find
that everyone is coming round to my
way of thinking. What is really wanted
is the strengthening of a room in every
house where the people cannot afford to
do it themselves. I would not do it for
people who could afford to do it themselves. Strengthen a room in
every
house, on the lines of the new air-raid
shelters that are being provided across
the water.
The Table of this House is pretty
strong. If something pretty strong on
those lines were set up in the kitchen
or some other suitable apartment the
people could put a mattress under it,
lie there, and have the heat of their
own fire. Then if their house did fall
there would be no part of it squeezing
them to death. That is my remedy, and
I want anyone who does not agree with
me to contradict me if he can.
I can
get no one amongst the ordinary people
to disagree with me. What good would
pushing this do me if there were
logical support for it? I have put the

would rather be in the shelters outside
than in anything they could put up in
their own houses, I would drop this at

with me if they want to do so, but they
are not entitled to make out that I said
something I did not say.

for Shankill, and if the money that has
been paid in unemployment benefit had
been spent in the development and
471 Ministerial Offices [Money]- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Mr. Byrne]
reclamation of land, in the erection of
houses, and for other purposes, we would
not be in the position we are in to-day.
Another matter in which the Government has been stingy is this. They have
ceased to give any encouragement from
the Road Fund. To-day our roads are
getting into a deplorable state. That is
caused by the. Government refusing to
give grants. Anyone walking in the
streets of Belfast to-day will find that the
streets are getting into a deplorable condition. We are not allowed to spend any
money on them, the reason being that
the Government have stopped the grants
which would give employment. Another
matter to which I want to call the attention of the Minister of Home Affairs is
that many people have. been deprived of
outdoor relief. That is a great mistake.
I meet numbers of these people who have
been a considerable time out of work.
There are many of them living in houses
at small rents, but when unemployment
assistance ceases there is nothing for them
but the union. The people could be kept
much more cheaply in their houses with
a little assistance than in the union. We
know every Irishman detests having to
go to the workhouse.
There is only one other matter. I want
on behalf of the people I represent to
enter again a protest against the unfair
treatment we receive in the matter of
education. I have. appealed for years for
an increase in the grants we have been
getting. We have 74,000 children in this.
city to cater for and only get half of
what Protestants get notwithstanding
that we pay our entire, share of the rates.

PROVIDING SIRENS AND A.R.P.
EQUIPMENT.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether the sirens to give
air-raid alarms are provided out of public
funds; and, if so, whether residents in
Greenisland area have received circulars
from the A.R.P. officers there to the
effect that officers of the organisation will
cail on the residents for subscriptions for
the purpose of providing a siren and other
A.R.P. equipment for the Greenisland
district.
I
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): Sirens
and other equipment are provided out of
public funds in
in accordance with the
vulnerability and importance of the
various areas in Northern Ireland.
have no objection whatever to the purchase
of additional equipment by private subscription in cases where the local inhabitants wish to supplement the provision
made from public funds, provided always
that such additional purchases do not
interfere with the supply of essential
equipment to places where it is more
urgently needed, and are not such as
would interfere with the operational
control of the area as a whole.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
reply, did the Minister give his sanction
to a scheme to make a public collection for
the purchase of a siren and other A.R.P.
equipment for the district in question?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The position.
with regard to the siren in this district is
shortly as follows: Sirens are generally
supplied out of public funds on the same
basis that exists in Great Britain.
Usually the standard is that a siren is
supplied when the population exceeds
3,000 within a mile radius of the site of
the siren. Here that particular standard
is followed, though in special cases the
Ministry is prepared to give a siren to a
smaller centre of population where there
is some particular circumstance warranting that. In this case the population was
very much below the usual figure, but
representations were made to us on behalf
of the inhabitants at the beginning of this
year. We pointed out that we could not
justify a siren out of public funds, but
in view of the anxiety of the population
and seeing the representative undertook
to collect for the siren we said if they
got the siren we would go the length of
allowing the cost of installing it to rank
for a grant. We did not initiate the
scheme for the payment of the siren by
the local inhabitants, but we did say if
they got a siren, if we could not give them
priority, we would assist in linking it up.
Mr. NIXON : Did the Minister
approve of this: "The Government have
sanctioned the scheme on condition that
the cost, about £50, shall be locally
defrayed. An A.R.P. representative will
call in the course of a few days to receive
your subscription"?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: No. All we did
was to say if they provided the siren and
defrayed the expense, we would allow the
cost of installing it to rank for grant.
That is as far as we can go.
Mr. NIXON: Since they went so far
and the scheme has the approval of the
Ministry, will the Minister see that the
accounts of the collection are properly
audited and this place supplied with
equipment on the same basis as other
places?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: It is supplied
with equipment on the same basis as other
places. It is not for the Ministry to audit
a purely private subscription, but when
the siren is purchased we allow the cost
of installing it to rank for grant.

FILLING OF A.R.P. PAID JOBS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether vacancies for
permanent paid jobs in A.R.P. are filled
by suitable persons, such as journalists,
clerks, etc., who have lost their positions.
in civil life owing to the war.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Paid positions
in the civil defence services are, I believe
without exception, filled on a temporary
or acting basis, and not as permanent
appointments.
So far as I am concerned, my control
over local authorities and others charged
with the selection of persons to fill such
posts is aimed at securing that the most
suitable persons available are chosen. I
have no statistics showing the percentage
of vacancies filled by persons who were
previously unemployed owing to the war,
but I understand a very considerable
number of the appointments made belong to this category.

Mr. BEATTIE: It would be well that
Members of the Committee should have
an idea as to what this Bill really amounts
to.
I am not casting any reflection on
the majority of Members, but I do not
believe they take the keen interest in
financial matters here that they should.
On many occasions things are put before
us with the object of getting the necessary power on matters of finance, and we
afterwards find Members on both sides
criticising the wasteful expenditure of
this money under laws which they themselves passed. I have found that this is
the case in most of the criticisms I have
heard in the House. There was no one
gave the Civil Contingencies Fund more
support than I did up to a particular
figure. That figure, in my opinion, was
the maximum. I would not agree to give
plenary powers to any right hon. Gentleman with regard to matters of finance
and the spending of money.
This Committee have conceded a further request of
the right hon. Gentleman's Department
for an extension of that figure.
As I have said already, we have now
a growing menace in our area in regard
483 Financial Provisions Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Mr. Beattie]
to the financial side of the workings of the
Province. We are now spending over
fourteen millions per year and a very
large percentage of that sum is going to
waste. A large majority of Members
disagree with that waste. The Public
Accounts Committee, who are the
guardians for the Members of the House,
have not got a rightful place within the
confines of the finances of our Government,
because as a Public Accounts
Committee we are subordinate to the
Comptroller and Auditor-General in the
things he finds fault with, not the things
the Members find fault with. We can
only examine the items set forth by the
Audit Department. Look at the millions
spent outside that Public Accounts Committee which we never hear anything
about. We spend a great part of our
time on questions such as buildings, transport and that sort of thing, but I would
like to get into the internal working of
the bigger things. While we only deal
with thousands we are spending millions,
and it is as regards the millions where I
find the greatest danger is threatened.
The right hon. Gentleman may put
before the Committee the argument
that an examination of the accounts
has proved beyond the shadow of a doubt
that the finances, with the exception of a
few thousand pounds, are in a sound
position. It is not correct to make that
statement because the Public Accounts
Committee have not access to the internal
workings of a large portion of the expenditure that takes place. Therefore,
on this Exchequer and Financial Provisions Bill I would like an expression of
opinion from Members, especially on the
other side, because I view with alarm the
growing expenditure. I have been very
uneasy for some time past. Years ago I
used to accept the statement that the
growing expenditure was due to increased
social services. Well, it may have been
due to that at that period, but it cannot
be said it is true to-day. Our social services are to-day running on an economic
basis.
I think the suggestion thrown out by
me about an Estimates Committee would
have been a guarantee and protection to
the public at large against this growing
expenditure of the departments. The
appointment of such a committee would
have been justified. In view of the
failure of the Government to accept that
suggestion, I must say here and now
that the Government have something to
hide. I am going to be the ferret on
this occasion and find out if I possibly
can what the Government are hiding
from the public and members of the
Committee. I have pointed my finger in
one direction where there 18 a real
menace to the financial standing of this
area, and that is in the new appointment of Minister of Public Security.
If I
I know the Minister will not take this

had found a levelling process put into

Government should make representations to the Imperial Government to
introduce legislation to ensure that all
men in Northern Ireland who joined
the Army, Navy, or Air Force, since
the 1st January, 1938, be reinstated in
the employment they left, on being discharged from service, on the same terms
and conditions as men who have been
conscripted in Great Britain.

Generally speaking, we cannot say that
our recruiting effort is as good as we would
like it to be. It has been very good, and
in some districts it has been particularly
good. In the district I come from, I do
not think it could be better. I do not see
how they could get any more men, even
if they had conscription, but if anyone
approaches men to join the Army they can
always say: "Why should I give up my
job to join the Army and perhaps not get
it back when I return from the war. I
might find someone else in my job." Some
employers in Northern Ireland would
agree to do what the Motion asks without
legislation, but some would not. Some
employers are not doing it in respect of
men who joined up in this war and were
discharged on medical grounds, but are
still able to work. Some men would not
get back the job they had before they
joined up, but would be given a worse job.
The object of this Motion is to correct this
state of affairs.
I said our recruiting effort is nothing
like what it might have been or what it
was during the last war. There was a
recruiting campaign here last summer,
and it was badly mismanaged at the
start. At the very start of the recruiting
campaign His Majesty's Lieutenant for
the County of Down advertised for all
deputy-lieutenants to meet him in Glengall Street. That is where he started his
recruiting campaign, and as far as County
Down is concerned he put a political complexion on it from the very start. That
was Lord Londonderry. His Majesty's
Lieutenant for the City of Belfast did not
do that. He called his first meeting in
the City Hall. He was right and Lord
Londonderry was wrong, and the recruiting campaign in County Down was largely
a failure from the start.
I was in Bangor on the night of the
great recruiting rally there, and I was on
the promenade when the procession went
past. There were two outstanding incidents at the meeting. One was that the
Mayor of Bangor said he had joined.
up for the second time. But he never
went on either occasion. The second
thing was that a soldier's wife was
arrested for attacking the platform party,
and was trailed along the promenade to
the barracks. That is about all that
happened. All you could hear amongst
the people on the promenade was this:
"It is a wonder they have not got
Ribbentrop with them again." That is
not going to be forgotten, and if people
think it is they are greatly mistaken.
I do not want to cast up these things;
I only refer to them for the purpose of
trying to drill into the heads of everyone
who undertakes anything like this that
they should keep it as far from politics
as ever they can. A campaign like that
is not to be started in Glengall Street,
but in the City Hall or some other
neutral ground, and then it might have
some chance of success. The Minister of
Agriculture stumped through all
Northern Ireland. He was the principal
speaker. I am not out to belittle his
efforts, but undoubtedly he represents the
worst recruiting district in Northern
Ireland, or at least one of the worst.
Nobody at all got a chance at these recruiting meetings. Harry Midgley did
appear, and got a great reception at the
Ulster Hall.
I myself was invited to the same meeting and would have gone, but when I
took up that day's paper I saw that the
gentleman at the top of the bill was a
man who was defeated by 8,000 votes in
the constituency in which he was born.
The rest of us were not worth mentioning, so I stayed away and wrote to the
organiser of the meeting, a very decent
man, as to why I stayed away. He is a
very true and broad-minded man. I
refer to Colonel D. C. Lindsay. That
is why I stayed away and took no part
in that meeting. I never will take part
in a meeting that has a political basis
when it should not have a political basis.
When I saw at the top of the bill a man
who was defeated by 8,000 votes and who
would be defeated now by 20,000 votes,
notwithstanding the noise he makes, I
thought that was no place for me.
You know well who he was. I could

all events, I do not need to say anything
more to recommend this Motion to the

to accept it, and I think he will accept

being so, there is no necessity for me to

Mr. NIXON: With the permission of

that is the law in Great Britain I can

Britain you have conscription, and owing
to the nature of the present war everyone

that light they are as much in the war.
You have conscription there, and if they
let the police force go they have no
recruits to take their places, because the

But we are different here. We have
no conscription. Not alone that, but we
have an ample supply of recruits, so
much so that the standard of recruiting,
that is the height, had to be raised to
keep them out, a lot higher than ever it
was in the Royal Irish Constabulary.
The standard for the Royal Irish Constabulary was 5 feet 9 inches. I do not
know what the standard at the moment
is in the R.U.C., but it is very much

it. Supposing that the police were

and conditions as the police were allowed
to join during the last war, in Northern

after a little training and going out
under a senior man, would do the duties
quite well. In that case you would

conscripted and where there is no one to

UNSHAVEN MENTAL PATIENTS
IN TYRONE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I gave notice to!
the Minister of Home Affairs that I
intended to raise the question of Omagh
Hospital, County Tyrone. To my amazement I read this in an English newspaper:
FOUR HUNDRED MENTAL PATIENTS MUST
GROW BEARDS.
Yesterday members of the Tyrone
Mental Hospital Committee objected to
a requisition for £18 for razor blades
for the patients, Mr. Rowley Elliott,
M.P., the chairman, saying he thought
Tyrone Mental Patients-
Supply of Razor Blades
18 MARCH 1941
this was an occasion on which economy
might be practised especially as the
patients did not go outside the grounds
and meet the public. "Shaving is a
luxury," observed Mr. J. F. Gamble,
M.P.
When I read that in the paper I was
astounded. The member for South
Tyrone said publicly that the men who
are prisoners in Nazi concentration
camps grew beards. We know that some
horrible things are done in Germany.
We know people are butchered and get
brutal treatment. It has been the custom
in this Tyrone Mental Hospital to supply
the patients with safety razor blades to
enable them to keep themselves in a
healthy condition. The hon. Member for
South Tyrone suggested instead that these
poor people-400 of them should grow
beards down to their knees. The hon.
Member for North Tyrone said shaving
was a luxury. Why does he not practice
what he preaches? If it is a luxury then
there is no Member in the House would
look better than the Member for North
Tyrone with a beard on his face because
he has no hair on his head. Look at the
asset and drawing power he would be if
he would grow a beard.
There may be just cause for this attempt at economy, but I am surprised
that the two Members should for one
minute consider the idea of economising
for a paltry £18 at the expense of 400
patients. The Member for South Tyrone
tried to intimidate me, but notwithstanding that intimidation I decided to raise
this question in the House to-day. This
request for razor blades was made, I am
told, by the medical officer of the hospital.
If there is one man who should know
what the patients require it is the medical
officer who has to look after them. I am
told there is a barber there. If the
hospital committee do not want to supply
the patients with safety blades and thus
save £18 then I contend that the Minister
of Home Affairs, who is responsible for
the health and well-being of these poor
people, should step in and supersede
them. If there is one board that should
be superseded it is this one.
Mr. ELLIOTT: What about Whiteabbey Sanatorium?
Mr. HENDERSON: Ninety-nine per
cent, of the members of the Tuberculosis
Committee running that sanatorium were
Unionist friends of the hon. Member. I
was one of those who helped to bring
about the inquiry that was held. I think
that the committee, if they had done
things properly, could have done without
that inquiry. In any case there was an
inquiry held. I am not to blame for
that; it was the hon. Member's Unionist
friends. Outside Germany nothing like
this has taken place for the past 22 years.
Can the hon. Member visualise a room as
large as this containing 50 mental
patients, all growing long beards? In the
first place it is unhealthy. The hon.
Member himself looks spick and span
without a beard. He is a picture of
happiness, but if he had a beard trailing
to the ground he would not be happy,
especially if he got the same itch as the
hon. and learned Member for St. Anne's.
I believe he got some particular salve as a
cure for the itch he had. I will try to
find out what the cure was. If the
Member for South Tyrone took the itch
-not the political itch-and had a long
beard he would feel very uncomfortable.
The Press of the whole world published
this thing. It is not a good advertisement for the two hon. Members. I always
looked on them as very humane men. I
think they have done some good. The
hon. Member for South Tyrone is a great
temperance advocate, but when I read
this in the paper I felt he had been
imbibing something stronger than
lemonade. (Hon. Members: No, no.)
I thought he must have been imbibing
strong drink otherwise he would not
have used words like those I have quoted.
I protest against this thing. This Government have control over all the mental
hospitals in the Province. When the
medical officer made the recommendation
one would have thought the suggestion
would have been accepted. Supposing
the opponent of the Government in the
North Down election was to get hold of
that paragraph and put out 30,000 or
40,000 bills showing what the loyalist
candidate-I do not call him the official
Unionist-stands for, what would be the
result? It is just a sample of what the
patients in the North Down mental hospital would receive if the official or loyalist
candidate is returned.
Mr. ANDREWS: There is no North
Down mental hospital.
Mr. HENDERSON: If there is not
one in North Down there should be one

hands, and, secondly, there was the fact
that they were practically unobtainable.
The hon. Member does not tell the whole
story. He refrains from mentioning the
suggestion made by me as chairman that
as we had a very good electric supply we
ought no longer to tolerate this putting

mental patients but ought to get electric

it would be much better if there were no

razor blades into the hands of mental

dishonourable thing as the hon. Member
for Shankill would try to make out.
If the Minister of Home Affairs thinks
that the members of the Mental Hospital
Committee, which represents both Tyrone
and Fermanagh, are not discharging their
duty, I for one. will not have the slightest
hesitation in asking him to put in a

Member for Shankill, I am glad he has

We are prepared as a Committee to admit

It is not a matter of having fires in the

order to keep the institution at its
normal heat. When the war started we
had 500 tons of coal in reserve, but
that has all been used up. Our contractor has been giving us all the coal he
possibly can, we have been doing all we
can to get a further supply of coal, and
if the institution is not as comfortable as
it was in normal times it is through no
fault of the Committee.
We are doing our very utmost to get
coal in order to keep the hospital as
comfortable as possible, not only for the
poor, unfortunate people who are patients
but also for the attendants and nurses
who are doing very fine work, and doing
it very well indeed. I would like to
assure the House, and particularly the

Committee are not unsympathetic either
towards the patients or the nursing staff.
We want to do what we can for them,
and any time the Minister's officials or
medical inspector can point out to us something more that we can do to make the
patients more comfortable than they are I
for one will do my best to give them my
support. I can assure the House that
the patients in that and every other
similar institution have my whole-hearted
sympathy and that I will do my utmost
within the bounds of possibility to see
that they get all the comforts we can
give them.

the
Mr. AGNEW (for Mr. Beattie) asked
the Minister of Labour whether he can
state under what section of the Unemployment Assistance Acts the Board
have power to disallow claimants on the
grounds "that you are not an insured
person within the meaning of
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Pensions
Acts, therefore you are not a person
to whom the Unemployment Assistance.
Board can grant assistance,' and
whether he will state where the power of
disallowance is given to the Board.
""
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
(Mr. Gordon): The ground for disallowance referred to in the hon.
Member's question is given in Section 31
(1) (b) of the Unemployment Assistance
Act (Northern Ireland), 1934, which
lays down that a person is not within
the scope of the Act, and therefore not
entitled to be considered for an allowance,
unless he is either:
-
(i) a person whose normal occupation is employment in respect of which
contributions are payable under the
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Contributory Pensions Acts (Northern
Ireland), 1925 to 1932; or
(ii) a person who not having
normally been engaged in any remunerative occupation since attaining
the age of 16 years might reasonably
have expected that his normal
occupation would have been such employment as aforesaid but for the industrial circumstances of the district
in which he resides.

31 of the Unemployment Assistance Act,
a person because he has had no insurable

have expected that his normal occupation

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): The answer to the first

The expression of opinion of the members
of the Killinchy branch of the Ulster
Farmers' Union corresponds to that made
by farmers in many parts of the United
Kingdom. The matter was raised and
discussed in the Imperial House of
Commons on the 4th March as the hon.
Member is doubtless aware, and the reply
by the Secretary of State for the Home
Department was to the effect that on
balance the extension of summer time will
be to the advantage of the community as
a whole. Whilst the circumstances in
Northern Ireland differ to a certain extent from those in Great Britain, owing
to the greater proportion in Northern Ireland of those engaged in agriculture, it is
felt that the inconvenience caused by
having the time in Northern Ireland
different from that in other parts of the
United Kingdom would be so great that
it would not justify the Government of
Northern Ireland in making separate
arrangements in this respect.

necessary to synchronise our time with

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): I am
informed the total number of men connected with the First-Aid Post and the
Mobile Aid Post and other mobile
casualty services based on Spiers Place
is 112, of whom 62 are drivers; the
maximum number required for duty at
any one time is 41, of whom 13 are
drivers; and the number maintained
constantly on duty is 15 by day and 17
by night, the number of drivers being 6
and 8 respectively. The six drivers on
duty during the day are paid whole-time
personnel. Those on duty at night are
part-time volunteers.
With regard to the last part of the
question I am informed that 34 sets of
helmets and respirators have been issued
to drivers, and that 73 helmets and 99
respirators are retained at this depot for
the use of personnel on duty. Protective
clothing and other equipment is also kept
at the post in sufficient quantities to equip
those on duty.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Determination of Needs Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The
FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): This is a somewhat
complicated Bill, and if I fail to make
any point clear I am sure the House will
be satisfied that my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour will be able to
elucidate any points raised in the debate.
The Bill gives effect to three pledges.
First, that of the Prime Minister when
Minister of Finance, that new money
lent to the nation during the war would
be left out of account in calculating the
resources of applicants for unemployment
assistance or supplementary pensions up
to a total of £375 in each case; secondly,
that of Mr. Winston Churchill, that the
household means test would be abolished
subject to certain reservations; and
thirdly, that of the Government of Northern Ireland, that any improvements.
which were made in the social services
in Great Britain would be made also in
Northern Ireland.
The first part of the Bill deals with
the household means test, and provides
that new Regulations shall be drafted
by the Assistance Board and made by
525 Determination of Needs Bill-
20 MARCH 1941

Second Reading
cant with dependants. This, together
with the change now proposed under
Rule 1, will have the effect of increasing
the allowance made by the Board in such
the Ministry of Labour in conformity
with
the rules set out in the First
Schedule to the Bill. The effect of
these Regulations is explained in the
White Paper. Briefly, the position will
be as follows:-
:-
Hitherto the resources of all members
of the household have been added
together before arriving at the amount
of assistance to be given. Under this
new Bill the resources of the applicant,
the applicant's wife or husband and of
any member of the household dependent
on the applicant will be the only
resources taken into account, with one
exception to which I will refer.
If the applicant or the husband or
wife of the applicant is the householder,
the Board's allowance in a normal case
will
include the full amount of the
rent, but if there are wage earners in
the household they will be treated as
making a contribution towards the
general overhead expenses of the household. The maximum amount deemed
to be contributed in this way will be 78
where the member is earning 55s a week
or more, and where the income is less than
55s the amount will diminish so that a
member of the household with only 208
a week will be treated as making no contribution towards the expenses.
If the applicant's father or mother, or
son or daughter is the. householder and
the weekly income of the householder is
£6 or more, the applicant will be deemed
to receive free board and lodging in the
household, and the allowance which he
will receive from the Board will be based
on his personal needs. For the purpose
of arriving at the income, the father's
and mother's resources are aggregated
where one of them is the householder.
The figure of £6 will be increased if there
is more than one person other than the
applicant dependent on the householder,
and may be decreased in a case in which
the applicant is under 18.
In any other case, for instance, where
the applicant is living with his son-in-law,
the applicant's needs will be deemed to
include the need to make a contribution
towards the rent of the house. The
amount of this contribution will be prescribed in the Regulations and, in the
normal case, will probably be the proportion of the rent on a per capita basis,
subject to a maximum amount of 5s for
a single person or 7s in a case of an applicases.
Turning to the second part of the Bill,
the House will be aware that under existing legislation certain resources of an
applicant are already ignored for the
purposes of the means test, in connection
with unemployment assistance, supplementary pensions or assistance to blind
persons by local authorities. In addition,
it is now proposed that holdings of Government securities issued after 2nd
September, 1939, of Savings Certificates,
of money on loan to the Treasury without interest, and of deposits in the Post
Office and Trustee Savings Banks
acquired since the outbreak of war, up to
a maximum of £375, will also be disregarded.
If these savings have been acquired
through the realisation of other investments between the outbreak of war and
the 14th August, 1940, they will still be
ignored, but if acquired in this way since
that date they will be taken into account
in computing the resources of an applicant. The purpose of this is to provide
that after the 14th August, 1940, only
genuine new savings lent to the Government will entitle the applicant to this
privilege. I should say that 14th August
is an arbitrary date selected in Great
Britain for their Act for reasons I need
not now particularise. The object of the
pledge given in this connection was twofold-to encourage the lending for the
prosecution of the war of all money
available after essential household needs
had been met, and to discourage the
spending of that money on non-essentials
with the consequent danger of price
inflation and the retention of labour in
industries not contributing to the war
effort. The legislation now introduced is
designed to confer an exclusive benefit on
the war-saver.
The last part of the Bill provides for
the winding up of the Unemployment
Assistance Fund and the transfer of allowances and expenses to the Votes of the
Ministry of Labour. This will result in
considerable simplification of accounting
procedure. Hon. Members will see, however, that it is not proposed to wind up
the fund until directions are given to this
effect by the Ministry of Finance. The

abolition of the fund will affect our Reinsurance Agreement and the repercussions on the Agreement are at present

be no means test at all, but they do not
know what they are talking about. If
there were no means test at all any man
or woman no matter what his or her

All I wish to add is that to relieve our
local authorities of an obligation which is
upon the local authorities in Great
Britain would be to create a very
embarrassing financial situation, because
it would really be tantamount to relieving
our ratepayers of the obligation which the
ratepayers in Great Britain willingly bear
and putting upon our Exchequer an obligation which is not borne by the British
Exchequer. For us to put a proposal like
that up to the British Treasury in war
times above all others, which would have
the effect of reducing our contribution by
the amount that we relieve the local
authorities of would neither be reasonable
nor just, nor would it, in my opinion,
be agreed to by the British Treasury. I
do not see why it should. I think, having
regard to the undertaking which I have
given to hon. Members, that the Government will put pressure on those local
authorities which are not doing their
duty in this direction, a duty which other
local authorities are doing willingly,
ought to satisfy the Committee.

dismissed from the Force.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The numbers
of sergeants and other ranks whose
contract of service was not renewed, or
who have resigned since the detection of
the irregularities which led to the conviction of Sub-District Commandant
Saunders, are 8 and 17 respectively.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, verification of accounts includes
not only the normal accounting checks
applied in approved systems of Government accounting, but also the administrative checks applied during the performance of duty to ensure that irregular
claims are not put forward. This
verification is carried out in one way or
another by all supervisory ranks of the
Force, and is not confined to officers of
higher rank that District Commandant.
In all cases where financial irregularities come to light full inquiry is made as
to whether any responsibility rests on
the supervising officers concerned. I am
glad to say that in the present instance
the District Commandant and other
senior officers are regarded as entirely
free from blame in the matter.
BELFAST HARBOUR POLICE.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he is now in a
position to make a statement on the pay
and allowance of the Belfast Harbour
Police.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I am glad to be
able to inform the hon. Member that the
Belfast Harbour Commissioners have intimated their intention of increasing, as
from 1st January last, the temporary war
bonus now paid to sergeants and
constables in the Harbour Police Force,
from 5s to 10s per week. As the hon.
Member is aware, I have, for some time
past, been giving consideration to the
status and remuneration of the members
of the Harbour Police in relation to that
of the members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, alongside whom they are at
present employed in the Harbour Estate.
So far as pay is concerned the conclusion
I had reached was that the pay of
sergeants and constables in the Harbour
Police Force should be equated as nearly
as possible to that of members of the
corresponding grades of the R.U.C. with
service of similar duration.
My right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance has consented to a payment from
Government funds, which with the increased bonus will enable each sergeant
and constable of the Harbour Police Force
to receive by way of pay, war bonus and
special allowance, at least the net pay,
including any war bonus now payable,
which is received by a sergeant or
constable of the R.U.C. with the same
length of service. This arrangement will
come into force as from January 1, 1941,
and will continue while the Harbour
Police Force remains under Government
control for operational and disciplinary
purposes.
With regard to allowances as distinct
from pay and war bonus, I do not consider there is a case for payment to the

INTERNEES IN CRUMLIN ROAD
PRISON.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the. Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state how
many internees in Crumlin Road Prison
are on hunger strike; whether a barricade
of wire netting has been installed in the
visiting room which makes conversation
between internees and their relatives
inaudible unless it is conducted in
stentorian tones; and whether the
internees, when on the prison ship, Al
Rawdah, were allowed to speak to visiting relatives without a fence of wire
netting between them.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I understand that a
certain number of the internees in
Crumlin Road Prison have threatened to
go on hunger strike, but so far as I am
aware. they have not yet put that threat
into effect. I have myself inspected the
visiting room at the prison and am quite
satisfied that, although the wire netting
prevents contact between the internee
and the visitor, it does not in any way
interfere with conversation.
As regards the Al Rawdah, conditions
were entirely different and the number of
visitors to the internees for whom provision had to be made on the ship was
very much smaller.
Oral Answers

Mr. CAMPBELL: Will the right hon.
Gentleman say are the. interviews between
the internees and visitors conducted at all
times within sight and hearing of
warders? If that is so what useful
purpose does this fence of wire netting
serve.?
Sir DAWSON: I tried to explain to
the hon. Member it is to prevent physical
contact between the internees and visitors
for obvious reasons.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the Minister
say would the mere fact that a warder
is present all through not be a sufficient
guarantee against any risk of that kind?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, we have
a very large number of visitors, sometimes 50 a day, and I am not prepared
to provide a warder for each internee
when the visit in going on.

LOCAL DEFENCE VOLUNTEER
FORCE.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Public Security
whether he is now able to make a statement as to the status and control of the
Local Defence Volunteer Force.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I was authorised
yesterday by the Imperial Authorities
to state that after careful consideration
His Majesty's Government have come to
the conclusion that it is in the interests
of administrative efficiency and convenience that the force should continue
to be maintained as a branch of the
Constabulary Force under the control of
the Government of Northern Ireland
until such time as it may be necessary
for the military authorities to assume
control of the force for operational
purposes.
This decision settles authoritatively a
question which has been pending for some
time. As the House will be aware from
my previous statements on the subject,
this Government, while willing to
facilitate the assumption of military
control and expressing a preference for
that course,
course, have realised throughout
that the paramount consideration must
be what is best and most expedient in
the interests of the whole nation. We
accordingly made it plain to the Imperial
Government that, whatever they might
determine, we would help to implement
it in any way we could, and now that a
decision has been reached by those best
able to judge of the national interest we
shall do all in our power to make the
force as ready and efficient as possible
for its purpose.
In this we shall have
the invaluable, and, I think I may also
the increasing assistance of the
military authorities.
May I take this opportunity of expressing the hope that during the critical
days which lie ahead there may be added
to this practical aid the support and
good-will of all hon. Members whatever
their individual views and predilections
on the matter may have been.

Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
fact that this is a time of national

House should not sit continuously. The
workers have been told to take no holidays
and why should Members of Parliament,
who should be doing everything possible
to bring about the destruction of the
Nazis, get such a long holiday? Why
we should ask the taxpayers to pay for

that Members of Parliament have one

much. I protest against this lengthy
holiday which the
Minister of
Agriculture has just moved. We should

de to further the war effort. Any amount
can be done. If leaders on the other side

here increased by another 25 per cent.
We are lacking in leadership. I protest
against this adjournment for such a

Ministers and Directorships
Ministers and Directorships
27 MARCH 1941
Mr. HENDERSON: I want to take
this opportunity of raising the question
mentioned by the Member for Woodvale
about members of the Cabinet holding
directorships in private companies. This
is a matter vitally affecting good government. You cannot have a Government,
run on proper lines unless you run it
on modern lines. I contend that the
statement made by the Prime Minister
to-day that it is in the interests of the
country that Cabinet Ministers should
retain directorships in private companies
is entirely wrong. No other country
would tolerate it. We are a small community, and because that is so it is
necessary that Cabinet Ministers should
resign their directorships. Some Members
of the Government are directors in seven
or eight companies.
Is it fair to the citizens of Northern
Ireland that if any question arose in the
future in regard to the system of transport, we should have sitting here men who
are directors of railway companies? The
railways may take over the Road Transport Board when it becomes bankrupt
after the war. Supposing the Government decided to have State controlled
transport, an action they ought to have
taken in view of the fact that they introduced Communist ideas a few years ago
by putting private owners off the road,
would the members of the Cabinet of
Northern Ireland not be interested 100
per cent. ?
I do not like to be too hard on the new
Prime Minister, but he had no skin on
his face when he made the statement he
made to-day. Methods of that sort,
which are a great abuse of Parliamentary
privileges, can only come from right hon.
Gentlemen opposite. If any Cabinet
Minister in the British Parliament was a
director of a private company he would
at once resign his position. In our
country, the plea put forward by the
leader on the other side of the House when
he goes on the hustings is that we go step
by step with Great Britain in all legislation introduced. Then why have we
got out of step in this instance? It is
not nice to say this, but there could be
great abuse because of the interest the
right hon. Gentleman takes in six or seven
private companies.
The hon. Member for Woodvale referred to one Member of this House who
has first-class knowledge of everything in
connection with the introduction of the
Budget. If there were to be increases
imposed, look at the advantage that
Cabinet Minister has. I know this will
go on. Will the right hon. Gentleman
kindly behave himself and not adopt
cornerboy methods in this House? It is
rather regrettable that the Prime Minister, when a hon. Member is on his feet,
especially one of the intelligent Members
on this side, should engage in conversation. I will wait until the conference
between the Prime Minister and Mr.
Deputy Speaker is over. Do you know
that that is tantamount to insulting
Members on this side of the House? A
good Prime Minister should listen, and
if he has anything to talk about he should
go into his own room or the room of the
Deputy Speaker. To talk here is bad
taste. I do not know where he was educated, at Queen's University or Methodist
College, but I am afraid his education has
been sadly neglected. I appeal to the
right hon. Gentleman, for whom I have
great respect, to pay a little attention.
Mr. GORDON: You do not always
listen.
Mr. HENDERSON: I am the best
listener in the House. The Members of
this House should try to be a little bit
intelligent and listen. The conduct of
some Cabinet Ministers and deputy
leaders of this House is not what you
would get at a football meeting. It is
with regret I say that, and I want to
apologise to the footballers for trying to
compare them with the right hon. Gentlemen opposite. If this Government only
ran this country the way some football
committees run their clubs, it would be
a great boon to the overburdened
taxpayers.
As long as we Independent Unionists.
are in this House we will protest. The
time will come when we will have control
of the destinies of Ulster, and then no
matter who adorns the Front Government
Bench he will have to resign his directorship of private companies. This would
not be
be tolerated anywhere. Outside
murder, the Cabinet of Northern Ireland
can get away with anything. I humbly
protest on behalf of the intelligentsia,
that is, the
the Independent Unionists,
against the tactics adopted by the Government of Northern Ireland. There is not
a member of the Cabinet who is not
affected. The Prime Minister had the

decency to resign from one of the companies, but he is still interested in the
railways.

Mr. HENDERSON: You are one of

I appeal to the right hon. Gentleman,

would not go as far as the hon. and

were the best that could be found in the

If I had £1,700 or £1,800 a year, as some
right hon. Gentlemen have, or £3,000
or £4,000 like the Prime Minister, I
would not want to be a director of
private companies. I could live in the
lap of luxury, and I would be quite satisfied on that salary to do my duty. The
Government are not doing their duty as
long as they retain directorships of
private companies as they cannot give
the attention to their duties that they
should give. If they love Ulster as they
say they do they should resign. I know
they always bleat about their loyalty and
love for Ulster. If they continue to act
as directors of private companies when
Cabinet Ministers we can only come to
the conclusion that their love for Ulster
is for what they can take from her.
In view of the fact that no other government tolerates this thing, Cabinet
Ministers should have a little decency
and resign their directorships. If they
do so we on this side will be the first to
congratulate them on making the
sacrifice.

of subsistence allowances to married men

men have been sent to a particular job
in Limavady, the rate of wages being 24d
an hour less than in other districts. The
result is that they find it difficult to live.
They have requested me to bring this
matter before the House and see that some
treatment will be meted out to them.
They have to go a long journey from their
homes-
Notice taken that ten Members were
not present; House counted, and ten
Members being present-
Mr. AGNEW: I ask the Minister of

this matter of the payment of subsistence
allowance to men who have been sent to
England by the labour exchanges. Another matter is the payment of the fares
by the local exchanges of workers to the
places where they are to be employed.
According to my information some men
who have received fares through the

think that system operates as regards

following the step-by-step policy in insurance matters it is only right that the

and see that the men who have to leave

employed in Limavady.

Another matter that is causing very
serious alarm, particularly in my own

Unemployment Assistance Board because
the persons concerned were not normally
insured. Most of these people have
served 40 years in the textile industry.
In one case a dressmaker, at the age of
58 years, was brought before the appeals
tribunal and told by the chairman:
"You will get a month." The same
thing occurred yesterday in the Armagh
district. A number of cases were
allowed as being normally insured, but
that only applies for one month. We
can realise the plight of these people who
have reached a certain age. They are
what I would call unemployed and are
faced with a very serious difficulty. It
may be that in accordance with a certain
section of the Act they are disallowed,
but I feel that the Assistance Board
should be more sympathetic. These
people, I know, can appeal to the
tribunal, but once that body disallows
the claim it is final. In my own area
I find that a large number of disallowances have been made.
a
One particular case deals with
married woman who, with a disabled

She spent something like 45 years in the

Here is another case. A girl of 17

because the normal aspect of insurability

employed. If I had time I could

This is a very serious matter. These

I must say that the discretion of the

instances lacking.
I feel that the Minister of Labour has

industry I do not know what the end will

The Prime Minister says he is sympathetic, but there is as much sympathy in

of an important job, if we are

Is 8d per hour. The hours are 47 per

COMPILATION OF VOTERS' LISTS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
registration clerks employed by the Clerk
of the Crown and Peace for compiling
voters' lists, who lost their employment
owing to the war, are still unemployed;
whether there is a rule that people who
lost their work owing to the war have a
special claim on suitable work arising out
of the war; and whether he will look into
this matter and see that justice is done
to these men.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As the hon. Member
is no doubt aware, in accordance with the
provisions of the Local Elections and
Register of Electors (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1939, the compilation of
voters' lists has been suspended as a war
economy measure while the Act remains
in force.
•
I understand that it has been the
practice of the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace, Belfast, to employ certain persons
for some months each year in a temporary
capacity to assist him in the preparation
of the lists. It will be appreciated, however, that the arrangement was a personal
one and that the employment of the persons referred to is not a matter over which
I have any control.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman have a consultation with the
Minister of Labour with a view to having
these faithful servants of the Unionist
Party placed in permanent appointments
for the duration of the war?
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the right
hon. Gentleman not answer that question?
These people were the backbone of this
country, and now they are thrown on the

for them?

Oral Answers to Questions.
R.U.C. SERGEANTS AND WAR
BONUS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he is aware
that considerable discontent exists
amongst the sergeants of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary in view of the fact
that they have been ignored in the
allotment of any war bonus; whether
he is also aware that the increased cost
of living affects the sergeants in the same
way as head constables and constables;
that the heavy responsibilities of the
sergeants have been considerably increased owing to war-time duties, and
that up to the present this has not been
recognised in any tangible form.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): The
answer to the first part of the hon.
Member's question is in the negative. I
have no doubt that the sergeants of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary realise that
their basic pay is exactly the same as that
of sergeants of police in Great Britain,
and that the war bonus or supplementary
allowance of 5s per week which was given
last year, primarily in consideration of
the increased cost of living, was in Great
Britain granted to constables only.
In regard to the second part of the
hon. Member's question, I am aware that
the increased cost of living affects all
ranks, though not to the same extent.
The effect is naturally greatest on those
with least pay, and it is for this reason
that here, as in Great Britain, the war
bonus or supplementary allowance has
been granted to constables and not to
sergeants, whose minimum basic rate of
pay is £5 per week irrespective of
allowances.
So far as head constables of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary are concerned, I
should add that the recent slight adjustment of the scale of their remuneration
was not in the nature of a war bonus or
supplementary allowance, but was made
in order to bring the permanent scale of
pay for this rank into line with the
average standard in the corresponding
rank in Great Britain.
As for the last part of the hon.
Member's question, I appreciate that the
war has brought additional duties to
many, both inside and outside the public
service. In the Royal Ulster Constabulary the sergeants in common with
all other ranks have met any extra demands which may have been made upon
them with alacrity and a keen desire to
serve. In Great Britain the demands of
war conditions have been much heavier
than here and have necessitated a
modification of the conditions of service
entailing substantially longer working
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
22 APRIL 1941
hours and the abrogation of certain
privileges in respect of overtime. This
has been met by a war duty allowance
of 4s a week to sergeants and 3s a week
to constables in Great Britain. In Northern Ireland, however, the conditions.
which led to the grant of this allowance
do not apply at present.
So far as the cost of living is concerned
I may add that I realise that it has shown
a tendency to increase since the supplementary allowance or war bonus was
granted to constables, and should it be
decided to grant an allowance of this kind
to sergeants in Great Britain my Department will give sympathetic consideration
to the question of making a corresponding grant in Northern Ireland.
PAYMENT OF TRAINEES.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that the
Imperial Minister of Labour is paying a
weekly amount of 60s 6d per week to
trainees during their course of training;
and whether he can state why only 26s
per week is being paid to a similar class
of persons in Northern Ireland who are
the Technical
receiving training at
College, Belfast, under the Government
training scheme.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In answer to the hon. Member's
question, I should inform him that the
Northern Ireland Government is paying for
Northern Ireland trainees at the British
training centres exactly the same amount
as is paid by the British Government for
British trainees. The allowances for
trainees at our local technical schools had
to be fixed with some regard to the wages
they would have a reasonable chance of
obtaining when they completed their
course.
I must remind the hon. Member that,
while the trainee in Great Britain will
not get anything for dependants beyond
the 60s 6d now paid to him, the local
trainee will, if he has an adult dependant,
get 15s in addition to his 26s. If he has
dependent children he will get an extra
4s for each of the first two and 3s for
each child after that.

If the hon. Member has in mind any
local trainee who wishes to transfer to a
British centre and take a more comprehensive course at the higher rates of
pay, I will do my utmost to facilitate
him.
WAR
DAMAGE COMPENSATION.
Mr. CAMPBELL (by private notice)
asked the Attorney-General if he could
define the legal position with regard to
the provision of public compensation for
the dependants of ordinary members of
the public who were killed in the recent
air-raids and the provision of public compensation for ordinary members of the
public who were injured in those raids or
who suffered loss through the destruction
or damage of household goods or business
stock in those raids.
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): As the hon. Member is aware,
the provision of compensation in respect
of war injuries and damage is a matter
under the control of the Imperial Government. It is dealt with by Imperial
Statutes and Statutory Orders; the necessary moneys will be provided out of funds
voted by the Imperial Parliament; and
the various schemes of compensation will
normally be administered by Imperial
Government Departments.
The hon. Member will also appreciate
that the Statutes and Statutory Orders
dealing with the subject are of necessity
extremely lengthy and elaborate. Thus,
the recent War Damage Act, 1941, which
became law at the end of last month and
which deals only with damage to property
and not with compensation for personal
injuries, consists of 102 sections and five
schedules. Accordingly, within the limits
of the reply to a Parliamentary question
it is only possible to deal with the position
in the barest outline.
COMPENSATION FOR PERSONAL INJURIES
AND FOR THE DEPENDANTS OF PERSONS
KILLED IN AIR RAIDS.
Compensation for personal injuries and
for the dependants of persons killed in air
raids is provided for by the Personal Injuries (Civilians) Scheme, 1940.
(S. R. & O., 1940, No. 1307).
The scheme applies to Civil Defence
Volunteers and all "gainfully occupied
persons," that is to say, persons engaged
in any occupation and wholly or substantially dependent thereon for a livelihood, and also persons who, though
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
temporarily unemployed, are normally so
engaged and dependent.
The scheme is administered by the
Ministry of Pensions.
Under the scheme a person to whom the
scheme applies who sustains an injury
which incapacitates him for work for
seven days or longer is entitled to what
is called an injury allowance. These
injury allowances will be according to a
scale of weekly rates set out in the scheme,
varying according to whether the injured
person is married or unmarried and increased allowances will be paid in respect
of all dependent children under 15 years
of age.
These injury allowances will be
administered by the Assistance Board on
behalf of the Ministry of Pensions and
persons injured in air raids should make
application for the appropriate injury
allowances to the local area office of the
Assistance Board.
Injury allowances will be paid so long
as the injured person is incapacitated but
not for longer than six months.
If it is seen that his disablement is
likely to be serious and prolonged he will
then be entitled to a pension at a weekly
rate set out in the scheme.
The amount of pension payable will
depend on the percentage degree of disablement as assessed by a Medical Officer
or a Medical Board and the rates of
pension may be increased by additional
allowances in respect of wives and
dependent children.
In the case where a person to whom
the scheme applies has been killed in an
air raid the scheme provides for a pension
to his widow and also for allowances in
respect of dependent children. There is
also provision for pensions to parents and
orphan brothers and sisters in cases
where the parent or brother or sister is
in need and the person killed had been
regularly contributing to their support.
In addition to the provisions in regard
to gainfully occupied persons the scheme
also contains provisions as to pensions for
children and young persons who have
sustained injuries causing serious and prolonged disablement and also as
to
allowances under certain conditions for
women performing household duties who
have sustained injuries causing serious
and prolonged disablement.
All these various pensions and allowances will be administered by the
Ministry of Pensions, and widows and
dependants of persons killed in air raids
should at once make application to the
local office of the Ministry of Pensions,
Howard Street, Belfast.
COMPENSATION FOR DAMAGE TO BUILDINGS.
Compensation for damage to buildings
is provided for by Part I of the War
Damage Act, 1941, which became law on
the 26th March last.
This part of the Act is to be administered by a body called the. War Damage
Commission and compensation may take
one of two forms, either (a) what is
termed a cost of works payment, or (b)
what is termed a value payment.
If the war damage is such as to involve
a total loss of the premises, that is to say,
if the reinstatement would be likely to
require works costing more than the
difference of the value of the premises
after the execution of the works and the
site value, then the compensation will
normally take the form of a value payment.
If, however, the damage involves less
than a total loss, so that repair or
reinstatement is an economic proposition,
the compensation will normally take the
form of a cost of works payment.
Cost of works payments will ordinarily
be made as soon as reasonably possible
after the completion of the reinstatement
works.
The making of value payments will be
deferred, but such payments will carry
interest at 2 per cent. per annum.
The Act, however, contains provisions
enabling the Commission in certain cases
to make interim payments not exceeding
£800 to persons in need of funds
to enable them to secure housing
accommodation for themselves or their
families or to secure premises for carrying
on their trade or business.
In addition to cost of works payments
and value payments, additional payments
called temporary works payments, may be
made in order to cover the cost of any
works reasonably executed for temporarily
meeting the circumstances created by the
damage.
Claims for compensation for damage to
buildings will fall to be made to the War
Damage Commission. Until any further
Oral Answers
Recent Air Raid
22 APRIL 1941
directions are issued they should be made
on Form W.D.I and lodged with the
Commissioner of Valuation, Armagh
House, Ormeau Avenue, Belfast, within
30 days of the damage being sustained.
DAMAGE TO HOUSEHOLD GOODS AND
BUSINESS STOCKS.
With regard to damage to household
goods, Part II of the War Damage Act,
1941, provides that the Board of Trade is
to operate a scheme of insurance called
"The Private Chattels Scheme" which
will cover war damage to household
goods. This insurance scheme will not
come into operation until 1st May, 1941,
but section 68 of the Act enables the
Board of Trade to make payments in
respect of war damage occurring prior to
that date to such goods as would have
been insurable if the scheme had been in
operation.
Claims in respect of damage to furniture and household goods should also be
made on Form W.D.1 and lodged with
the Commisisoner of Valuation, Armagh
House, Ormeau Avenue.
As regards business stocks in trade,
these were, of course, insurable under
the Commodity Insurance Scheme which
was put into operation by the Board of
Trade in pursuance of the provisions of
Part II of the War Risks Insurance Act,
1939. Insurance under this scheme was
compulsory in respect of stocks
over
£1,000 in value and in respect of foodstuffs over £200 in value. In regard to
stocks of smaller value, insurance under
the scheme was optional.
Merchants and shopkeepers whose
stocks have sustained damage will be able
to claim under these insurance schemes,
and should send in their claims in the
first instance to the insurance office
through which the policy was taken out.
Small shopkeepers of limited means who
did not avail themselves of the opportunity of insuring their stocks under this
scheme and who are in a position to set
up again may apply to the Assistance
Board which has a certain limited power
to make advances in such cases.
The Assistance Board has also power
to make advances for the provision of
essential personal clothing or for the provision of tools vital to a man's employment, and where a person has dwelling
accommodation for the provision of essential household furniture.

RECENT AIR RAID.
Sympathy with Bereaved and Afflicted.
Tribute to Defence and other Workers.
Motion made and Question proposed:
