Recent Air Raid
Recent Air Raid
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The PRIME MINISTER: During the
past week the city of Belfast and
some of the other towns and country
districts have been subjected to a very
vicious and brutal attack by a cruel,
aggressive and inhuman foe, and I feel,
therefore, it will be the wish of hon.
Members on both sides of the House that
we should not proceed with the ordinary
business to-day, but that I should
endeavour in some measure briefly to
express the sympathy which in our hearts.
-deep down in our hearts-we all feel
with those who are bereaved through the
passing of those who were very dear and
near to them. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I feel also that we desire to
express our sympathy with those who
have suffered physical disablement, and
further, we wish to sympathise with those
who in large numbers have lost their
homes, and some of whom even have been
deprived of their business establishments.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) With all
these we sympathise to a degree that I
cannot adequately express.
I feel at the same time that we should
express our gratitude to my distinguished
and esteemed Colleague the Minister of
Public Security-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) for the arrangements which he
has made during recent months for
dealing with a catastrophe which he and
we all hoped would not arise-
Mr. BEATTIE: Question.
The PRIME MINISTER-
-but which
the
it was our duty to be prepared for. We
also wish to-day to thank the civil defence
and voluntary workers, His Majesty's
Forces, the members of our Royal Ulster
Constabulary, the "B" Specials,
Ulster Home Guard, and last, but not
least, our Women's Voluntary Service.
I hope I have not left out anyone, because
I know it is to all who have helped that
we desire to extend our thanks to-day.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Our people, in my opinion and in the
opinion of all in Ulster for whom I have
any right to speak, have simply
been magnificent. I have seen them at
the funeral of their dear ones yesterday;
I have seen them in their wrecked homes;
I have seen them on the streets, and I
cannot express the admiration which in
my own heart I feel for each and all of
those whom I have come across. Their
moral is unbroken, they are strong and
steadfast and true, and they are determined to see this thing through until
victory, be it soon or late, comes. With
all reverence I say God bless and protect
them all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. CAMPBELL: I only intervene to
say a very few words, but I do so with
the conviction that in rendering our
homage to the dead and voicing our
solicitude and sympathy with the living
sufferers, we are giving expression to the
innermost wishes of every element of our
population. Death during
during this past
week has taken its toll from the houses
of the well-to-do in Belfast, and a far
fuller toll from the homes in the narrow
streets where life crowds thick and where
the struggle for existence never ends
from the cradle to the
grave. Those
streets are to-day streets of sorrow. Some
have become the hecatombs of innocent
and helpless victims of this cruel blast
of war-swept into eternity in the
twinkling of an eye.
We reverence and mourn for those who
have gone, and in all sincerity, speaking
on behalf of every member of this community, we tender our sympathy to those
who will long miss them. We sorrow
and we suffer also with the living who
have been hurt or who have been
damaged in worldly goods. We have
gratitude deep and deserved for the devoted workers and volunteers who during
those fierce, dark hours when death was
hovering over part of Belfast and who
day and night since then have been
facing extreme peril to serve and succour
their fellow-beings. The men worked
heroically; the women were no less
heroic. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This last week has been a very grim
testing time for our citizens, but they
have bethought themselves during that
trying period how they could help their
neighbours. Amid their agony and
tribulation a fine civic spirit, a rich
comradeship, a true understanding
among the people have shone with
brightness. There have been manifestations of goodwill and practical generosity
and sympathy from across the Border,
and we should not conclude to-day without an expression of our earnest and
grateful acknowledgment of those manifestations. One touch of nature makes
the whole world kin.

22 APRIL 1941
a
Mr. ELLIOTT: I should like as
representative of a rural constituency to
support and endorse the well-earned
tribute paid by the Prime Minister and
the hon. and learned Member for
Central to all those who worked so
indefatigably to meet the situation which
had arisen in Belfast. Our sympathies
go out to those who have suffered the loss
of home and friends. I can speak as one
of those who share in that suffering
because I personally have suffered a great
deal, but some of my friends have lost
practically their all. But what I want
particularly to speak of is the case of the
evacuees coming to us from the city of
Belfast. We welcome those evacuees, and
in all our constituencies and homes they
are heartily welcome. We shall do our
utmost to make up what they have lost.
I should like here to draw the attention
of the Minister of Public Security to the
fact that it is being found difficult to get
food supplies in the rural districts to provide for this new population. I think
immediate steps should be taken by the
Food Controller to relieve the situation so
that there may be food available for the
women and children who have come into
our midst. We are doing all we can to
help, and I am glad to say that the doors
of County Tyrone and other counties are
wide open to receive those who have
suffered loss and have been bereft of their
homes.
It is difficult to find a flock without one
black sheep, and I would like to draw the
attention of the Minister of Home Affairs
to one fact. Exorbitant rents have been
charged by some people for vacant houses
throughout the length and breadth of the
country. I know of one or two cases in
which the houses have been lying vacant.
The rents were in the neighbourhood of
3s or 4s a week in pre-war days, and these
poor people who have been bereft of their
homes are being asked rents five and six
times more than they were in pre-war
days. There should be a clear pronouncement made by the Government on this
very important question so that we who
are glad to see these people in the country
and others who are evidently not so glad
will not be able to profiteer unduly
because of the condition of these unfortunate people.
I hope that steps will be taken to see
that every available unoccupied building
in Northern Ireland which is habitable
and can house the homeless people will be
utilised to the full, and that the people
will not be asked to pay any more than
the value of the houses in pre-war days.
I leave that to the Government. I will
expect them to take steps to have this
matter put in order so that better control
may be exercised over the vacant houses
in he country.
Mr. NIXON: As a representative who
remained with the people, I want to
endorse everything the Prime Minister
has said about the valour of the people
and the way the various services worked.
Language could not describe it. The
Prime Minister made an unintentional
omission. He forgot-I know it was
unintentional-to congratulate the fire
brigades that came here from Eire. They
were working in our district, and there
is nothing but praise for them.
I had hopes at one time-sometimes, of
course, the wish is father to the thought
-that perhaps we would be spared.
Ordinary people who give information to
the enemy are prosecuted, but high-up
people seem never to stop it. One gentleman called John Holness, the secretary of
the Victoria Unionist Association,
broadcast through the B.B.C. to the
world what we were doing. That has been
kept up ever since. The day after the
Minister of Commerce was appointed
there was a broadcast about contracts that
were to come to Northern Ireland. The
Minister and the House will recollect that
I put down a question about it. I had
only one intention-to stop it. But
nothing was done. That has continued
up to the present, and there was a statement in the "News-Letter" yesterday
about some gentleman who is over from
London in that connection. You never
hear what Germany is doing. Any little
hopes I had, and they were very slender,
that we would be spared were dispelled.
I lost them long ago.
I talk to a great many people of all
denominations and all shades, and they
are all very brave. There is no weakening of the morale of the people. I am
among them every day, and I am not
going to leave them. There is not going
to be any surrender on the part of the
people. But everything is not going to
be whitewashed. I have not the slightest
notion of allowing that. We know
rightly what took place. I met one
Recent Air Raid
Recent Air Raid
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
cynical individual who sneers at almost
everybody. I do not think he means it,
but he has a very unpleasant way of
expressing himself. I dealt with him
once before, and I may have to do it
again. This is not an occasion for
laughing. The hon. Member for South
Armagh knows that better than I do.
There were a few things mentioned here
before, and I would not mention them
again if it was not necessary. A Defence
Committee was set up of very sensible
Members of this House. I was not on
it myself, but that was my own fault;
rather it is not a fault, because I anticipated the Committee would never be
consulted. They have hardly been consulted about anything that is of practical
value. They are ignored all the time.
It is time we stopped that.
The chief of the Belfast Fire Brigade
broke down. He is a very decent man.
I was a member of the Police Committee
when he was appointed. I supported the
deputy chief of the Fire Brigade, Mr.
Robinson, but I was beaten by one vote.
I have nothing to say about Mr. Smith.
He has been most kind to me ever since,
and I would not refer to this except as an
illustration of the folly that is pursued
in bringing here people from outside who
know nothing about the country and
nothing about what they are doing, except swank. I was told by a gentleman
named McKeown, who is
very well
known and who sometimes lectures, that
if the A.R.P. wardens had had a ladder
they could have saved a certain church.
But they had no ladder to get up to the
incendiaries. Two days before I bought
a 44-foot ladder, but nobody came for it.
At all events, it was too far to bring it to
the church. You know how I struggled
to get ladders for these men.
an
Another thing I have been talking
about is the provision of helmets for
volunteer workers and ambulance drivers.
I could produce in five minutes
ambulance driver who was out all night
without a helmet, and out of nine
ambulance drivers five of them had no
helmets. I have them here to prove it.
They went out, but they want helmets
and equipment. I am not mentioning
these things to cast a slur on anybody,
because that is quite unnecessary.
No
one should say anything except in the
hope of doing some good, and that is my
only object in mentioning these things. I
do not care whom I censure if I am doing
any good. I have given both praise and
censure, and I can stand over everything
I have said. Nothing could exceed the
work of the members of the A.R.P.
organisation. I was down at the hall,
and it was marvellous to see boys and
girls carrying stretchers.
I hope that from now onwards our
energies will not all be directed to
politics, and that there will be no more
clarion calls. We do not want any more
of them. Get on with the war, and
when it is won I do not care who makes
clarion calls or who gets into office. Get
on with the war, and let us have no
sneering.
Mr. BROWN: I desire to support the
expressions of sympathy that have gone
forth from both sides of the House to
those who have suffered in this terrible
air raid. In the area I represent we
have done our best to aid the refugees
who have arrived in our midst. In my
opinion, this House should review the
whole position. The time has come for
a secret session of this House to be held,
similar to those which have taken place in
connection with the Imperial House of
Commons. I am not going to discuss
here any matters that might be of
assistance to the enemy, but I think there
should be a secret session of the House
to enable us to discuss various matters.
We are all moved to the very depths by
the fortitude shown by our people. None
of us listened unmoved to the B.B.C.
broadcast on what happened in Belfast
which was made by a gentleman who
comes to this House very frequently.
I am afraid the Government has only
now awakened to the importance of the
Ministry of Public Security. Unfortu
nately the Government allowed a whole
year to pass before the Ministry of Public
Security was set up, although we on the
back benches begged and beseeched them
to do so. Then we had another example
of the slight importance the Government
attached to the Ministry of Public
Security in the announcement of the
appointment of a half-time Parliamentary
Secretary to that Ministry. No one
doubts the great work that has been done
by the Ministry of Public Security, but
it has not been given the importance that
should be attached to it. I hope the
Government will regard that particular

Department as being of much greater
importance in the future. I hope there

It was unfortunate that we should have

importance at the present time. The

Mr. AGNEW: On behalf of my
colleague and myself, and in the name of
the working class community, we offer
our heartfelt sympathy to the citizens of
Belfast in the great tragedy that has
overtaken them. We realise that the
horrors of war visit the homes of rich and
poor alike, and that both rich and poor
are brought into line. We know that
death and suffering came into the homes
of the working classes particularly. We
sorrow with them, and we hope this
expression of our sympathy will be
accepted by them and will help them to
bear the burden they have to carry. We
realise we are the innocent victims of war,
and we do not forget those who rendered
them such great service in their hour of
trial. They are entitled to our deepest
gratitude. We are grateful to the A.R.P.
and various other Services, and to those
who came across the Border from Eire to
combat the dangers to the citizens of
Belfast.
But while we sorrow with our unfortunate people, we must realise that many
of them have been driven from their
homes and have had to seek refuge in
other places throughout Northern Irelnad. As they have had to leave their
own homes we must see to it that there is
no exploitation of these poor refugees by
landlords charging rents they cannot
afford to pay. This is a war that affects
rich and poor alike, and when refugees
from Belfast reach other towns and villages
in Northern Ireland I would like to see
both rich and poor taking their share in
housing them and preventing overcrowding. This is a matter I would like
the Minister of Public Security to
seriously consider, because I am afraid
that in some of our towns and villages
conditions are bad. Overcrowding does
exist, while in the houses of the rich,
where there is ample space and accommodation, no refugees have been taken
in. Is that the spirit which animates
those who are in a position to relieve
distress?
I must say that Armagh City did its
duty to the utmost of its ability in endeavouring to help refugees in their time
of sorrow. I should also like to take this
opportunity of paying a tribute to the
Manager of the Armagh Labour Exchange
and his staff, and to the officials of the
Assistance Board for the splendid work
they did in rendering aid to those who
came from Belfast. I hope this expression
of sympathy from the working-class
movement will reach the citizens of
Belfast, and especially those who have
been bereaved. I trust the various points
that have been mentioned to-day will be
considered by the Ministry, so that those
who have been bereaved will be protected
and safeguarded against any exploitation,
and that rich and poor alike will do their
duty to the suffering citizens of Belfast.

just typical of our Belfast people who

I am perfectly sure that we in this

We have a great deal to be thankful for.
We have to be thankful for the spirit of

We are not a bit downhearted. We
can keep our chins up and look forward

es we have our lives? We have a great

Mr. MacDERMOTT: I do not think
the present would be an opportune time to
debate any fine points, or to enter into
any controversy. A number of points of
a specific kind have been raised by hon.
Members, but I would be in a better
position to deal with them, in the light of
recent experiences, when I have had a
better opportunity of collating and sifting
all the information, much of which has
still to come to hand. I am sure on this
occasion hon. Members will not expect of
me any full review of the air raid over
Northern Ireland which took place last
Tuesday night. For one thing the facts,
as I have mentioned, have not been
completely gathered, and for another, it
would for reasons of an obvious and
vital character-be unwise at present to
speak at length on the subject.
I may say that over Belfast, judged
by all comparative standards, the raid
was one of very great severity. It involved extensive damage to industrial
and commercial premises, and also to
residential property. It caused much
desolation and distress, and, I regret to
say, a heavy loss of life. It is not the
usual practice to publish figures for
separate localities, but in view of the prevalence of exaggerated rumours as to the
position in Belfast I think it well that I
should tell the House what the latest
information in my possession is with
regard to casualties.
The dead as at present known number
500. The number of seriously injured
is 420, and the slightly injured 1,142.
I should warn hon. Members that these
figures may require revision. The figure
for fatal cases is based on the number of
bodies recovered to date. I fear that
more are still to be recovered, and that
there will be a number of missing to be
added to the figure I have given, but I
think I may say that I have told the
House the worst, and that the addition
to be made will be but a fraction of the
number I have
have quoted. They are
grave and heavy figures and show in some
measure the weight of the attack which
the city of Belfast had to suffer. I mention them because I have heard on all
hands alarming rumours about figures,
without any foundation, far and away
beyond those I have mentioned.

As the Minister concerned, I should
like to say a word as to how this savage
and barbarous assault was met by the
services of the Civil Defence Authority.
It was their first major battle, and I am
glad to be able to tell the House that
they emerged from it with flying colours.
It was Mr. Herbert Morrison who stated
recently that he had not seen a town
attacked by the enemy in which one
could not find something in some department of civil defence that might have
been done better, and no doubt the raid
of which I am speaking has afforded
much valuable experience from which the
services will profit in future. Still, it is
no exaggeration to say that the Civil
Defence services, as a whole, acted with
great gallantry and efficiency. Fires
were fought, the wounded, the homeless,
and distressed were succoured, demolished
buildings were searched and cleared with
a persistence and courage beyond praise.
The mighty task of coping with the
vast tide of suffering and distress was
shouldered by the welfare services,
assisted by many men and women of
good-will throughout the country. The
magnitude of this task is hard to describe
and difficult to estimate in advance, but
some idea of what was accomplished may
be
from the

Defence Authority in Belfast. On

60,000. On Friday the number
between 40,000 and 50,000; Saturday

The question of the homeless and distressed is still with us, but plans are
being formed to meet the future in the
light of the experience so recently
gained, and with the realisation that the
aftermath of the battle raises problems
as difficult and as important as those
which the battle itself presents. In this

the emergency arrangements made by
many local authorities outside the

who were billeted upon them at very short
notice, and to the kindness of the people
who, on many occasions, did not wait on
any formal arrangements.
I think it is but right and fitting on
this occasion that I should take the
opportunity on behalf of my Department
of expressing the thanks of the community to all who have served it so well
and faithfully both during and after the
attack. To the wardens-who worked
better than in any exercise; to the
regular and auxiliary fire services who
fought the. flames with a great devotion
to duty; to the casualty and hospital

explosive, death nor ghastly wounds deter
them from their purpose; to the rescue
parties who toiled incessantly, and often
in great danger, in their humane work;
to the staffs of report and control centres,
the officers in charge, the mappers, the
clerks, the telephonists, the messengers,

efficiency under difficult and trying conditions; to the police who were everywhere.
helpful in many ways; to the teachers,
the Women's Voluntary Service and
numerous others who at the rest centres
and other places helped to clothe, feed

the staffs and workers of the various

manifest will to serve.

men-our thanks are due, not only for

I should also like to take this opportunity of expressing my appreciation of
the help so readily given from outside this
country. As part of the United Kingdom we knew we should expect its full
sympathy and support in any suffering
which the Battle of Britain would impose
upon us. The help afforded by our
southern neighbour, Eire, was not related
to any bond of war or to any political
consideration. It was above and beyond
politics. It was based on a common
humanity, and we gratefully accepted
and acknowledge it as such.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
It is but right that I should also
acknowledge the invaluable assistance
given by the military authorities. Their
ready response and their magnificent
work will never be forgotten. The good
humour, the kindness and consideration
shown by the British soldier in aiding the
work of the civil authorities will long live
in the memory of us all.
In the last few days it has been my
duty and my privilege to visit many
centres of destruction and to see the
bearing of those who have suffered most.
The fortitude of these people, many of
whom have lost everything, has been an
experience which leaves one amazed and
very humble. I have seen in place after
place flags fixed to ruins in defiance of the
power of death and destruction to quench
the spirit. I have seen men and women
homes
remaining by their shattered
rather than feel that they were helping
the enemy by quitting them. I have
seen wardens and others who have carried
on notwithstanding the loss of their own
homes and their own families.
It is, of course, inevitable that a heavy
and murderous attack falling upon a
people unaccustomed to such methods of
warfare should produce a considerable
degree of shock and alarm. Yet my own
experience, and that of others, has established the strange but definite fact that it
is those who have been "blitzed" worst
who have reacted best and most quickly.
It is for the rest of us not only to admire
their sterling courage but to follow their
shining example so that the work of
rehabilitation may be swift, and the
normal life of the community restored as
fully and as quickly as possible. All can
and must assist to this end, and already
much has been accomplished. We here
have joined the line of battle in the
greatest cause of history, and I do not
think we shall break the ranks.
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope that the
advice tendered to the Government by the
hon. Member for Woodvale will be
accepted, otherwise they will be very unfaithful to the people of Northern Ireland. I understand that we have Royal
vistors in our midst, and that they have

people who have come through this dreadful experience. I believe that a warning
was given that no publication regarding
this visit was to be made in the newspapers, yet I regret to say I read about
it last night. That is a great mistake. I
should also feel better satisfied if the Government would accept the advice of the

I am saying now to the Government
that their actions in the future must be
guarded.
from the commence-
Right from the
ment of the war the Government of
Northern Ireland have invited publicity
time after time for the purpose of trying
to impress upon the British electorate the
important part that Ulster was playing
in the national effort. The Government
may attend the funerals of the victims.
They may try to the best of their ability
to help and relieve the suffering and distress caused by the blitz, but once and
for all they will have to drop the political
prejudices which they hold and which
they have been showing in the period of
time through which we have passed.
Everybody knows what Ulster is doing
and of her anxiety to perform her task
in the days of national crisis. I hope
that in future there will be nothing more
said of Ulster's part in the war and of
what firms in Ulster are doing. These
things only attract a very cruel enemy to
make an attempt to stem that movement
which we are trying to carry on under
very great difficulties.
The Minister of Public Security has no
right to laurels in connection with the
recent blitz. One of the reasons why I
did not want to speak to-day was because
I felt that I might be tempted to be
severe in regard to the organisation
of his Department. Had it not been
for the civil population and civil organisation events would have been much
worse. The Belfast people are best able
to complete their organisation within their
own areas and districts, and the outer
world knows of the good people that the
city possesses. I believe that the Ulster
people have the material and the organising ability to run a sufficiently strong and
powerful civil defence to give full satisfaction to the community at large.

Again I want to express the hope that
the right hon. Gentleman will take the
hint of the hon. Member for Woodvale
and will not scour England, Scotland and
Wales to get people to carry out duties
which could be carried out by good men
at home in a faithful and very efficient
fashion. We have now had the experience.
We can all be wise after the event.
I want to finish now, because the longer
I go on my feelings seem to be rising
within me. I am taking the experience
of the past as a guide for the future. I
hope the Government will do likewise,
that they will drop their political propaganda and their publicity stunts at
least for the duration of the war, and not
endanger the lives of the civil population.
If they do that I am satisfied that we may
feel safer in the future than we have
been in the past. I wish to associate
myself with everything that has been said.
by my colleagues and by other hon.
Members of the House. Let us hope it
will be a long time before we have to go
through a similar experience.

Financial Statement, 1941-42.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): After the grave happenings at
home of a fortnight ago when so heavy
an avalanche of death and destruction
descended upon our city, and in the field
of warfare abroad our fighting forces have
been subjected to extreme pressure of
attack from overwhelming numbers, it is
difficult to recall our thoughts and focus
our attention upon domestic matters of
normal routine and the economical discharge of the ordinary functions of
government. But even in the gravest
national crises our daily needs, the maintenance of law and order, the care of
our young, aged and infirm, all our social
and commercial services must be carried
on as efficiently and with the same, control
of public expenditure as though we were
enjoying the blessings of peace and
security. And so now the duty falls to
my lot to review the financial affairs of
our Province. for the past year, and propose to you how best the financial requirements for the following year may be met.
Unfortunately on the present occasion,
except for one or two modifications of
past practice, it is not a case of studying
whether improvement can be effected in
our social services, or how the burden on
our taxpayers can be lightened, but how
enormous

forced upon us in order to preserve our

In opening this my first Budget as
Minister of Finance I want first of all to
acknowledge how greatly my task has
been facilitated by the importance of the
service to our Province rendered by my
predecessor. It was he who as Minister
of Labour negotiated with the Imperial
Government our Reinsurance Agreement, thus assuring to those of our
people who were unable to secure
The Budget-
Financial Statement
29 APRIL 1941
employment the continuity of similar
alleviation of their necessities as is
afforded to our fellow citizens in the
United Kingdom under the Unemployment Insurance. Acts. More recently as
Minister of Finance he had to solve the
exacting problem of maintaining our
financial structure unimpaired in the
difficulties caused by war conditions. My
right hon. Friend was able to establish
war-time financial arrangements with the
Treasury, safeguarding the position of
Northern Ireland, and was responsible
for the inauguration of the War Savings
Campaign. These are only some of his
achievements, but they illustrate the
complex nature of his efforts as Ulster's
first war-time Minister of Finance. His
aim was always to secure that
finances were maintained on a sound footing while, at the same time, the Province
should make every contribution in its
power to the war effort.

For some time past the Government
has been concerned that our great linen
industry should have been so dependent
upon foreign countries for its supplies of
raw material. As from 1st July, 1938,
large grants were made to enable a Flax
Development Committee to be set up by
various sections of the linen industry to
investigate and demonstrate methods of
cultivating and processing flax crops,
and much valuable work has been done
by that committee. The Ministry of
Agriculture has tackled with great energy
the difficult task of increasing the area of
flax cultivation, which was 21,000 acres
in 1939 and 46,000 acres in 1940, to
100,000 acres in 1941, and, I am glad to
say, it is very hopeful of success. This
larger supply of flax will effect a smaller
degree of unemployment in the spinning
industry. More recently a Select Committee of this House recommended that
the establishment of tank retteries
and improved scutching plants should
be facilitated, which recommendation
received prompt approval, and the
Ministry of Supply of the
of the United
Kingdom also took prompt action in cooperation with members of the industry,
and it is hoped that additional
new
plants will be completed in time. to enable
the increased crop of this year to be
harvested and processed ready for the
mills during next winter.
Hon. Members are aware that for
various reasons there has been no improvement in the linen industry since last.
year's Budget was introduced. This is
not confined to the spinning but extends
also to the weaving end, but there has
been a welcome change for the better in
the position of the making-up trade which
was so severely hit by the restriction on
home consumption under the Limitation
of Supplies Orders. This improvement is
in no small measure due to the arrangement under which block contracts are
placed by the Ministry of Supply, through
the Ministry of Commerce, and allocated
among the various firms and sections of
the industry by a committee operating
under the ægis of the Ministry of Commerce.
I should like to comment particularly
on the closer relations which now exist
between the Ministry of Commerce of
Northern Ireland and the Ministry of
Supply of the United Kingdom; this is a
development which, we hope, will
strengthen Northern Ireland's contribution to the national effort and provide

and under our war-time policy of curtailing expenditure on peace-time services as
far as possible, no new loans are being

The Government is grateful to those
persons who generously lend their money
free of interest to the State for the
duration of the war and welcomes the
efforts and enthusiasm of some persons of
moderate means who have come forward
and sponsored this form of lending, but
interest-bearing loans must inevitably be
the main bridge across the gap betwee:1
revenue and expenditure. As the Chancellor of the Exchequer has emphasiset,
it is by the extent to which we succeed
in narrowing this gap that the success of
our war-time financial management must
be measured.
Amid the devastating welter of suffering and destruction of war one can find
one slightly redeeming feature as far as
the peoples of the British Empire are
concerned, namely, the advance which it
has not infrequently brought in social
legislation. Two outstanding examples in
the present war are the payment of supplementary pensions and the modification
of the means test; as the Committee
knows, our Government has, in accordance with our declared policy in matters
of this kind, followed the Imperial Government in making the same ameliorations
in Northern Ireland.
The increased and tangible expressions
of practical sympathy now reaching
United Kingdom ports from across the
Atlantic, and as a sequel the more
strenuous efforts made by the enemy to
intercept these supplies, have resulted in
gravely aggravated losses to our shipping.
Imports of food will require to be kept at
the lowest possible sufficing minimum, and
the maximum amount of food must, therefore, be produced at home. The deservedly important place in our economy of
agriculture, our greatest industry, has
been convincingly demonstrated, and I
hope when the war is over the energetic
response made by our farmers to the community's appeal will not be allowed to be
forgotten.

Before, however, arriving at
amount available for the Imperial Contribution I have to consider, first, whether
any changes in our revenue should be
made.
The first change which I have to
announce affects the taxation of agricultural tractors. In Great Britain a farmer
is able to use his tractor for hauling from
one part of his farm to another part of
the same farm agricultural produce or
articles required for the farm on payment
of a 5s rate of duty. In Northern Ireland this concession has not hitherto
applied, but the ordinary taxation rate on
agricultural tractors is half the duty paid
in Great Britain. After consultation
with my right hon. Friends, the Ministers
of Home Affairs and Agriculture, I have
decided to grant as from 1st May a similar
concession here to that which operates in
Great Britain, without altering the other
rates of duty for agricultural tractors.
This concession is estimated to reduce our
revenue by £7,000 per annum.
I also propose to introduce a Clause in
the Finance Bill to make it quite clear
that trailer pumps used for A.R.P. purposes are not liable to trailer tax, since
some doubt exists on this point.
The United Kingdom Finance Bill will
include a Clause to exempt from aggregation for the purpose of estate duty gifts
made to the Exchequer, and I propose
that a similar exemption shall operate in
Northern Ireland.
Hon. Members may be aware that the
promoters of an entertainment which is
run by a non-profit making society and is
provided for partly educational purposes
may secure exemption from entertainments duty. At present the Ministry of
Finance interpret "partly educational"
in a more exact sense than is the case in
Great Britain, and consequently in the
past it has occurred that an entertainment
which secured exemption in Great Britain
was taxable in Northern Ireland.
pose as from the 1st June next to take
a wider view of these words which occur
in the Finance (Entertainments Duty)
Act, 1939, and I hope that this change of
interpretation will be some encouragement
to the promoters of cultural entertainments in our Province.

I have no further changes in taxation
to announce to-day. Account has been
taken of the effect of the concessions I
have enumerated in the figures which I
have given to hon. Members, and consequently it only remains for me now to

arrived at.
The Committee will remember that an
arrangement was made at the beginning
of the war with the Treasury in London,
which has operated ever since, that all
approved expenditure on Consolidated
Fund and Supply Services over a certain
figure will be refunded to us by the
Imperial Exchequer. This arrangement
is intended to take account of what may
broadly be termed war expenditure which.
is borne, for one reason or another, on
our Exchequer. This year it is estimated
that over £3,000,000 will be spent by our
Government on what are, properly speaking, war services, the chief being Civil
Defence and L.D.V. Consequently, hon.
Members will see in Table 6 an item of
£3,297,000-the estimate this year of the
receipt from the Imperial Government in
respect of excess war expenditure.
Consequently, it is necessary for me to
add this receipt of £3,297,000 to the provisional balance of £8,530,000 which I
have already given to the Committee,
which gives a total of £11,827,000, of
which the very gratifying figure of
£11,750,000 is our provisional contribution to the Imperial Exchequer for the
year, and £77,000 is the provision for
surplus remaining to us. To those hon.
Members who may be surprised at the size
of this contribution I would point out
that our contribution last year, which was
generally welcomed, was £6,000,000, and
since then, as I have shown to hon.
Members to-day, the estimates of our
reserved revenue have increased by
£6,500,000. These extra taxes were
imposed entirely for war purposes, and it
is right, therefore, that their yield should
be reflected in an increased contribution.

Resolved, "That the Second Interim
Report of the Select Committee
Unemployment be now taken into consideration."(The Prime Minister.)
on
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move, "That
the Second Interim Report should receive
the immediate and sympathetic consideration of the Government as a matter of
urgent public importance." The Second
Interim Report deals solely with land
drainage.. The Committee have made
recommendations to the House from the
evidence which was presented to them
during their sittings, and they have compiled from that evidence recommendations
which they believe will go some way to
alleviate some of the difficulties and
obstacles that are now in the way of the
successful operation of drainage on the
land. This Report which the Committee
has presented to the House is selfexplanatory. I am sure no Member is
desirous of listening to me giving a
repetition of the Report, but there is one
thing I would like to say.
That is that the Committee appreciate to
the full the helpful services rendered to
them by the members of the county
councils and other organisations who
appeared before them and placed their
views at the disposal of the Committee.
We had representatives of all the county.
councils; we had the Ulster Farmers'
Union; we had a branch of the Farmers'
Union; we had many and varied witnesses,
and in making our recommendations we
were guided by the evidence they gave.
We have compiled recommendations to
which I hope the Government, in their
wisdom, will give sympathetic consideration.
Your Committee, while not claiming to
be land experts, had amongst them men
who understand the requirements of the
land, and men who gave their time and
attention to the work of the Committee
and helped in the framing of the final
recommendations. In giving that eulogy
to the representatives of the farmers on
the Committee I must not forget the
other members who represented different
phases of industry. Although they were
not in touch with the land question
to the same extent as were the represena
tatives of the farmers, nevertheless the
combination of the two interests went to
make what in my opinion was
up
perfect committee and, I believe, one of
the finest reports that has been presented
to the Government on the question which
the committee reviewed.
While it may be a rather drastic
measure to be swallowed with one gulp I
feel that if the. Government accept the
views of the committee, as expressed in
the recommendations, it will not go far
wrong. You will see in the report something about the heavy cost incurred
before schemes were actually started. We
were alarmed and surprised to find the
large amount of money that had to be
expended on schemes of a certain value
before one sod was turned in connection
with them.
We believe in the recommendations
we have put forward that the schemes
can be relieved of the heavy financial
burden which they had to bear before
being put into operation. One might
think that I, being a member of the
Opposition, was being inconsistent in
fathering the recommendations of this
Committee, on the lines set out in the
report, but my own personal views are
not a matter for discussion within the
Committee. Therefore, being one who
stands in favour of a majority vote I
accepted the recommendations on behalf
of all members. Our very worthy chairman was taken away from us by virtue
of an appointment under the Government, but, nevertheless, he was able to
be with us until the final conclusions had
been arrived at and put into print. As
vice-chairman the duty of carrying the
matter further was left to me. That is
the reason why I am presenting this

The PRIME MINISTER (Mr.
Andrews): It will make the position of
the Government clear and probably
shorten the debate if at this stage I state
the views of the Government.
The Government have carefully considered the report of the Select Committee
on land improvement schemes to which
the hon. Member has referred. These
schemes may be grouped into two main

major or arterial drainage work.

sure it
As regards the first, I feel
would be the desire of the whole House
to congratulate my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Agriculture and his predecessor on the valuable work which has
already been undertaken in this connection by the Department. As regards the
future the Government are prepared to
accept the recommendation of the Select
Committee that the valuation limit should
be removed, and in future the Government grant will be fixed at 75 per cent.
of the cost of labour involved in these
minor schemes irrespective of valuation.
The Government also propose that
these grants will be paid in respect of all
labour employed on schemes approved by
the Ministry. The effect of this is that
the grants will not be restricted, as heretofore, in respect of labour engaged
specially through the employment
exchanges. Further, payment of the.
grant will be made on the estimated
labour costs as determined and approved
by the Ministry of Agriculture.
The Government are confident that
these important changes in the conditions
and the machinery for administering the
land improvement schemes will meet with
the full approval of hon. Members and
will be welcomed by our farming
community.
As regards major arterial drainage
schemes, the Government have already
undertaken a considerable amount of
work in this direction, especially in connection with the River Bann. On the
other hand, our county councils, as the
drainage authorities, have not felt themselves able for financial reasons to initiate
many schemes of this character.
As the House is no doubt aware, preliminary
have already
surveys have already been
carried out for ten arterial drainage
schemes on behalf of county councils, and
the Government have now come to the

be placed in full possession of the facts,
it is desirable that a complete arterial
drainage survey should be undertaken
over Northern Ireland.
They therefore propose that a Drainage
Commission should be set up with the
object of undertaking this survey and of
advising the Government which schemes.
should be given priority with a view to
increasing the acreage under cultivation
during the period of the war.
It is proposed that the terms of reference of this
Commission should be as follows:
(i) to carry out an arterial drainage.
survey over Northern Ireland;
(ii) to consider and report to the
Government on-
(a) the arterial drainage schemes.
which should be undertaken and the
order of priority in which they should
be executed;

would contribute to an increase in the
acreage under cultivation during the
period of the war;
in

the existing administrative

matters.
The personnel of the Commission will
be constituted as follows:-
(1) A representative from each of the
Ministries of Finance, Home Affairs and
Agriculture, the Ministry of Finance
Government

I also propose
that the Financial
Secretary of the Ministry of Finance will

have already undertaken,

Dr. DOUGAN: In the part of the
country from which I come flooding has
been present as long as I can remember.
During my work I have to tour the
country and I can see what is happening.
I can tell the House that the fields in
that part of Central Armagh are in a
state of swamp, and a great proportion
of the land is unfit for cultivation due
to lack of drainage. Many farmers have
taken advantage of the grants given for
the purpose of drainage, but it is useless
for a farmer to drain his land unless the
man below him drains his too. That
being so, the Government should consider
making it compulsory for every farmer
to have his land properly drained.
The causes of flooding are manifold.
It is, first of all, due to lack of field
drainage; and, secondly, more particularly due to the stopping up of main
drains and small rivers. The banks of
many small rivers have fallen in and
have created fords, thus blocking the
water back. Farmers to whom I have
spoken about this matter complain that
the main drainage of the small rivers is
insufficient to carry away the water
drained from their farms.
A scheme such as is now proposed
would have been wrong until recently,
for the simple reason that the Bann was
then undrained and was unable to take
away the flood water. Since the draining of the Bann has been carried out the
river is capable of taking away the huge
floods which occur. In former years in
the valley of the Bann flood water would
lie for from four to six weeks and would
sour the land; now the flood water is
taken away in as many days.

constitutes a war effort, and, looking at

to take the viewpoint of the Member for

As a Member of the Select Committee
I desire to thank and to congratulate the
Government for acting so speedily in
adopting this Interim Report. Nothing
amazed me more in this debate than the
arguments put forward by some hon.
Members that this Report had nothing
to do with the war effort. If the Government required any justification for their
act they need only refer to the speech
last Sunday of Mr. Winston Churchill
when he spoke of the importance of the
battle of the Atlantic to keep the people
of these islands provided with food.
Surely when the Government take a step
of this kind they are making a very important and valuable contribution
towards the success of the battle. of the
Atlantic, which we are all confident will
be won by Great Britain. Therefore, the
Government need make no apology to
anyone for adopting this Report, because
they are making a most vital contribution
to the winning of the war.
In this morning's "Northern Whig
and Belfast Post," "Belfast News-
Letter," and "Irish News" you will find
a statement by Lord Cornwallis, chairman
of the Kent War Agricultural Committee,
who stated that the British Minister of
Agriculture had just told him that this
matter of getting more food for our
people had become so important that
money ceased to matter. In other words,
the food position is so serious that here
is the British Minister of Agriculture.
stating that money has ceased to matter.
That alone would justify the Government
in proceeding, as they are going to proceed, with these proposals. Even if there
was no war these recommendations are
perfectly economic and sound, but they
are a thousand times more so in view of
the developments in the war situation in
the last few days.
It is perfectly clear that in this war, as
in the last war, food is going to be the
vital and deciding factor in winning the
war. Therefore I am pleased that the
Government has taken the big view in
this matter and has decided to adopt
these proposals. I am particularly pleased
that the Government has adopted this
scheme, because in a ten-point programme
for the solution of the unemployment
problem which I placed before this House
in September last one of my points was
this: .-

scrub, drainage of land, etc., to all
owners or occupiers of land irrespective
of their valuations or whether they are
exclusively or partially engaged in
farming.

Mr. JOHN E. BAILEY: I should like
to thank the Prime Minister and the
Government for accepting this Report. I
feel, as a great many others do, that some
way should be found of relieving the flooding which is converting thousands of acres
of good land into bogland. It is impossible
for the farmers to pay the heavy rate
struck by the Drainage Board. This
rate ranges from 15s to 30s, and it is
impossible for farmers to pay that amount
over a period of 20 and sometimes 30 to
35 years.
I wish to draw the attention of the
Government to the fact that there are a
great many weirs across the main rivers.
These weirs cause considerable flooding.
I know of one weir which has caused
the flooding of 155 acres of land for a
long number of years. I also know of
another weir on the same river, the river
Bann, which has blocked up the river at
certain times and labourers could not get
crops from their plots of ground. For a
short time one man had to leave his
cottage owing to the flooding that took
place due to the weir stopping the flow
of water. It is no use cleaning rivers
unless the weirs are taken away. I again
thank the Government for accepting this
report.

I think briefly that is the statement.
Now in my humble opinion, and in the

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): The
hon. Member for Woodvale has referred

might be summarised by the slogan,
"Stay put." That advice-and it was
Evacuation of Houses
Public Shelters
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
never anything more than a request to the
population was made under circumstances
of very considerable emergency.
A great
many people had been rendered homeless,
and the problem of the authorities was
how to deal, not only in Belfast, but
outside it, with the large numbers who
had not a roof over their heads. Their
task, difficult at all times, was increased
considerably by the fact that it was
known that there were a number of people
leaving the city and who still had habitable and uninjured houses in which to
dwell, and it was essential in the interests
of the community and particularly in
the interests of those who were homeless
and distressed, that the numbers of those
leaving who were not homeless should be
reduced as much as possible.
It was in those circumstances that I
asked the public to "stay put," and I
think it is still a good slogan for all who
want the life of the city to continue, to
adopt. In other words I would think
that those whose houses are habitable
and who have no special reason for leaving
should remain in them. But it was never
intended to convey that those who want
to get their children to safe places were
being compelled in some way to abstain
from taking steps in that direction. It
is unfortunate that more children were
not out before, and it is unfortunate that
those who were out came back in great
numbers. It is also unfortunate that the
re-evacuation which had commenced before the heavy attack occurred, should
not have got further. It is further unfortunate that masses of people who had
to be dealt with as a result of the raid
should have temporarily made it impossible to continue the plan of evacuation
which had been commenced.
It is the Government's intention, as soon
as the reception areas are clear, that the
plan of evacuation of children, and of
mothers in some cases, should continue.
Meantime, I quite realise that many
people want out for the purpose the very
understandable purpose of putting their
children and those who had no place to
live in a position of safety. I also realise
that those are the people very often who
want to come back to their own houses as
soon as possible.
The hon. Member is under a misapprehension if he thinks that it was the Government's intention that persons with
young children were going to be ordered
to remain in places of danger at all costs.
My anxiety and that of my colleagues is
that
young children and persons who have
no part to play in the life of the community should be got to places of comparative safety as soon as it can be done.
All hon. Members will realise, I know perfect well, that until the reception areas
are sorted out it is going to be difficult to
have a full scale planned evacuation.
However, as soon as it can be done it will
be done. In the meantime I think the
hon. Member will agree as regards those
who have habitable houses and have no
special reason for leaving them, that it is
in the interests of the community that as
far as possible they should stay put. It
reduces fire risk in the city enormously. I
appreciate that there are many honourable
men whose anxiety has been to put those
for whom they are responsible and who
have no particular work to do in the service
of the community, in a place of safety.
I would like to say a word as regards
shelters, which the two hon. Members
spoke of. I would not like the impression
to get abroad, either here or elsewhere,
that there is no safety in shelters for the
community in Belfast. I would like to
we

have to work with such materials as I can

get.
shelter, which has been used extensively

establish in the light of experience, does

Mr. MacDERMOTT: I did not say
they could not be used in Belfast. I said
they could not be used in terrace houses
in the streets of Belfast because the
Anderson shelter needs to be dug in. If
it is to be effective the bulk of it has to be
below ground level. Where I have seen
them used to the best advantage in Great
Britain has been in houses which have

mentioned relates only to houses in
Belfast which have no gardens or no

Anderson shelters could not be got, and
that of course is involved with the question of supply and the steel position.
The hon. Member for Shankill also
raised the question of the Morrison
shelters. Those are steel tables that go
inside the house. Needless to say since
that type was evolved we took up the
matter with Great Britain to see if we
could get the necessary steel and necessary supplies. I am not going to say we
will not succeed, but I do not want to
lead hon. Members to think we will get
them early. It is a matter we will do all
in our power with regard to because I
think that type of shelter does give a
considerable degree of protection from the
debris load of houses. Whether it could
be used extensively in the small houses
in Belfast is another matter. It is 6ft.
6ins. long and 4ft. 6ins. wide, and that
would leave little space in a lot of houses.
Mr. NIXON: What about the yards?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The matter is
under the Government's consideration,
and if we can get these shelters we will
certainly have them. I do not think hon.
Members should be left under the impression that what has been referred to
as the Morrison shelter is the best kind
of shelter for small houses of the kitchen
type or parlour houses. My own feeling
definitely is that the communal masonry
shelter affords a higher degree of protection. The hon. Member for Shankill
also referred to underground shelters.
Belfast is in a peculiar position with
regard to underground shelters. As hon.
Members know there are very few basements and an underground shelter of that
kind is practically impossible. I should.
say also that the underground shelter of
the basement type is often not as good or
secure as it looks. The people in London
did prefer them, they felt secure, but I
think the general conclusion now is that
the well-built surface shelter is certainly
safer. Some go so far as to say that the
percentage of casualties in these shelters
was less than in the basement shelters.
There is the other type of shelter, which
is the real underground shelter, and
which is bomb proof. I cannot produce
that in Belfast; in fact, I cannot produce
it anywhere. I have inquired into the
matter. I had reports drawn up, and I
am afraid it is not a feasible proposition.
I think a great deal can be achieved by
extending the number of shelters, not
massing too many people in any one
shelter.
Mr. HENDERSON: What about tunnelling into the Divis mountain and
Cave Hill?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I called for a
report on that, and it is not quite as
easy or as practical as one would think.

He does not know the

Mr. SPEAKER: On the point of
Constitutional procedure, if a right
hon. Gentleman or an hon. Member makes
a slip during a debate it is quite in order
for him, on finding that he has made a
slip and said something he did not intend
to say, or given a false impression of
what was in his mind, to request the
Editor of Hansard to leave it out. If the
Editor of Hansard is in doubt about the
matter he comes to me, as Speaker, and
asks for my advice and instruction. In
a case of this kind, where in the course of
ordinary debate a word may be let slip in
an innocent manner, my anxiety is that
it should not get into Hansard, but should
be taken out altogether.
In the peculiar circumstances which the
Member for Woodvale has mentioned,
where he thought he had perhaps let out a
word which he did not mean to, I thought
it was my duty, in the interests of public
safety, to take immediate action and leave
out what I knew he would not like to be
left in. Accordingly, I consulted with
the Editor of Hansard and we left out a
sentence or two. I also considered it my
duty to write to the Member for Woodvale
telling him what I had done, and he wrote
back telling me the matter had worried
him, and that he thoroughly approved of
the action I had taken.
But, strictly speaking, I have no right
to interfere with Hansard at all. This
House is supreme and can do anything it
likes. That is why I want the House to
give me authority to examine the speeches

it should not reach. That is a matter for

Oral Answers to Questions.
LIABILITY FOR RENT OF
DAMAGED PREMISES.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Attorney-General whether he can state
if public compensation is available to
tenants whose dwellings or shops were
rendered untenantable by the recent air
raids, and who had to acquire other
dwellings, shops or stores for furniture,
and whether he can state the liability of
such tenants for the rent of the premises
they were obliged to quit.
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Black): In answer to the first part of the
hon. Member's question, the compensation provided for by the War Damage
Act, 1941, is in general compensation for
actual physical damage to property and
goods and does not cover the expense of
acquisition of other dwellings, shops or
stores for furniture.
a
Section 8, Sub-section 3, however, of
the Act provides that in the case of a
person who will in due course become
entitled to receive compensation or
share in compensation and is in need of
funds the War Damage Commission
may make him interim payments not
exceeding £800 in order to secure housing accommodation for himself or his
family, or in order to secure premises for
the carrying on of his trade or business.
As regards the second part of the
question, the hon. Member will appreciate that the legal position as between
landlord and tenant will vary in different
cases, and that it would be impossible to
give an answer which would cover every
conceivable case. If the premises are
held at a weekly or a monthly rent the
tenant can ordinarily determine the
tenancy by a week's or a month's notice.
In the case of a longer tenancy the hon.
Member will recollect that under Section
40 of the Landlord and Tenant Rent
Amendment Act (Ireland), 1860 (Deasy's
Act), if a dwelling-house or other building held under a contract of tenancy not
containing an express covenant to repair
is destroyed or becomes incapable of
beneficial occupation or enjoyment, by
fire or other inevitable accident, the
tenant may surrender the premises and
escape liability for future rent. The
hon. Member will also recollect that the
Rent Restrictions Acts contain various
provisions affecting the mutual rights of
landlords and tenants in cases to which
these Acts apply. Thus Section 7 of the
Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions
Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, provides
for the suspension of certain increases of
rent while the house is not in a reasonable state of repair, and Section 8, Subsection 4 of the same Act, enacts that
where the rent of the smaller type of
dwelling-houses which remained up to
1940 and still remain under the protection of the earlier Acts has been increased
by the maximum amount permitted in
respect of cost of repairs the landlord
shall be responsible for keeping the house
in a reasonable state of repair as if he
had entered into an express covenant in
that behalf.
LANDLORD AND TENANT (WAR
DAMAGE).
2. Mr. THOMPSON askel the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
it is the intention of the Government to
introduce legislation similar to the Landlord and Tenant (War Damage) Act,
1939, now in force in Great Britain; and,
if so, whether he will undertake to have
the necessary legislation introduced during
the present Session.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is the intention
of the Governemnt that legislation similar
to the measure to which the hon. Member
refers shall be introduced, and steps are
being taken to have it introduced during
the present Session.
HELMETS FOR A.R.P. PERSONNEL
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he can state

why the paid personnel of the A.R.P.
services in Belfast are not allowed to
carry their steel helmets and gas masks
from and to their place of residence.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): It has
not yet been possible to make a personal
issue of steel helmets and service or
civilian duty respirators to every paid
and unpaid member of the Civil Defence
Services, and, accordingly, it is essential
that sufficient steel helmets and respirators of appropriate type should be kept
available at certain posts to equip those
persons who are called to duty at any
particular time.
As far as the supply position permits,
personal issues of helmets and respirators
have been and are being made to paid and
unpaid personnel, and, where such issues
have been made, the equipment can be
taken home.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman think it is fair that the voluntary services and paid services under
A.R.P. here should be minus the most
important part of their equipment-the
steel helmet, while in Great Britain they
have at their command 11,000,000 steel
helmets, not only for the A.R.P., but for
reserves, and in view of the preferential
treatment of these A.R.P. services as
against Northern Ireland will the right
hon. Gentleman see that steel helmets are
supplied to every worker paid or unpaid
who has taken up work under A.R.P. in
Northern Ireland?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The non. Member
has referred to Great Britain in a manner
that indicates not quite the relation between the position there and the position
here with regard to the Civil Defence
Services, but I may say so far as the
position here is concerned we have already
covered the various establishments, and
we are making every effort to get a steel
helmet for every person entitled to one.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman tell the House the number of
deaths due to persons not being supplied
with steel helmets in the last blitz? Will
he gives the deaths that might not have
taken place?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: As the hon.
Member will surely appreciate I cannot
give any such figure, but I think it is a
pretty small part of the total death roll.

Mr. BEATTIE: The first thing I have
got to do is to extend my congratulations
to the Minister of Finance on the introduction of his financial statement. I am
trying to get at a true perspective of this
matter at the present time. The statement set out that the authority which is
budgeting carries with it the right to
gather in revenue, and it also sets out the
form in which that revenue would be
spent. We have the right to gather in
not for ourselves but for others, and
much of the money gathered in does not
belong to us at all. It is taken from the
people of the Six Counties and claimed
by the present Government as a part
of the Imperial contribution and handed
to the British Government in that form.
I think we have got to get down to bedrock to see what power we actually possess

in levying taxation on the area which we
represent. For the last 17 years the same
financial wizardry has been carried on in
the introduction of these financial statements. The present Minister is keeping
up the high reputation of the wizards
who have gone before.
I remember one night in a music hall
in the city of Belfast witnessing three
comedians, and the principal playboy said
that he owed £1 to each of the other
comedians, but he did such a financial
bit of jugglery with lending and borrowing that he finally came out clear of any
debt to his two partners on the stage
although he had no money to pay any
debt when he went on. That is the position the Northern Government are in.
They have been handling other people's
money and have given out this financial
statement to prove to the people at large
that they are what you would call superpatriots-patriots of a kind. They say,
"As long as it is other people's money
we will hand it back, but when it comes
to a matter of affecting our own finances
we will have to see what we can get in
return". After watching that movement
for the last 17 years I have come to the
conclusion that the loyalty of past and
present Governments was conditional. It
was conditional on this ground—“If we
can get nothing out of the pool we will
have to retard the help we were giving in
the past". We are told we have a
revenue coming into the Exchequer of 27
millions odd and that we have 19 millions
odd of an estimated expenditure. That
leaves a balance of eight million pounds
which is put down for the Imperial contribution. Then we are told that war
expenditure over and above the basic
expenditure of peace time is over 31
million pounds, but we are not concerned
with war expenditure at all because
Britain has recouped us to that extent.
We are transferring back to Britain that
34 million pounds which is war expenditure. This makes a total contribution or
surplus of £11,827,000.
I do not know what form of bookkeeping the right hon. Gentleman carries
on in his own premises, but I am sure
when handling other people's money he
does not call it his own. If he is handing over the people's money, which he is
entitled to hand over, he would not have
the cheek or be brazen enough to say,
"I will give you this as a contribution
towards the efforts you are making in
the great war." He would hand it over
as a right. The British Government has
a right to certain surpluses in Northern
Ireland under the 1920 Act, and they
will keep that claim on the financial
position in this area. They have placed
a financial obligation on the people
through different forms of taxation and
they claim the right to say what standard
of life the Northern Ireland people will
enjoy up to a particular figure of 13
million pounds. No matter what we
gather in from additional taxation which
the people have to bear, our normal services on a peace-time basis cannot exceed
that 13 millions. That is what we are
allowed under the Joint Exchequer
Board.

I said then that it did not matter what
we were, the same umbrella covered all
of us, and that if the German Air Force
came over they would not consider
whether we were Unionists, Liberals,
Socialists or Communists; but all would
suffer alike. If it is a good thing for the

the city of Belfast. Four and a half
million pounds is not an exorbitant sum

of this country. We propose to spend
three millions, but it would take ten
millions to put us into a position equal to
that of London and other cities in Great
Britain. I claim we have a right to hold
this eleven millions which the Minister
proposes to hand over to Great Britain
and spend it on the protection of our
people. If the Government give it away
they are unfaithful to the people of the
Six Counties. We should recognise that
our responsibilities at home cannot be
neglected for the sake of being favourably
spoken of in high places in London.
If I were in London I would tell you
to go and mind your own home first, and
when you have got everything into proper
working order in your own area then
come to me and I will gladly receive
any help you can possibly give. If the
people of London knew we were sacrificing
our own people in connection with A.R.P.
and other essential services they would
not agree to receive this money, although
it is really their own money, in the
manner you expect it should be received
on the other side.
A large number of houses have been
destroyed, and there are a considerable
number that will never be habitable. In
this Budget I would have thought some
consideration would have been given for
the discomfort those people are suffering
and will continue to suffer until the period
when rebuilding takes place. No matter
from what angle the right hon. Gentleman
may look at the matter, there is an additional expense placed on every person
who is dislodged from his own home. That
is an additional tax the whole community
does not bear. I want the right hon.
Gentleman to be more generous and more
liberal to these people than he has been
up to the present. I know families who
have lost half of their households, and
the breadwinners have been taken away.
The guiding hand in the home has been
lost, and in this Budget there is no compensation provided for the mother.
You have certainly provided a pension
for the mother if the father is gone, but
what provision have you made for the
children when the mother has gone? Not
one solitary thing has been done for the

The first change which I have to
announce affects the taxation of agricultural tractors. In Great Britain a
farmer is able to use his tractor for
hauling from one part of his farm to
another part of the same farm agricultural produce or articles required for
the farm on payment of a 5s rate of
duty. In Northern Ireland this concession has not hitherto applied, but
the ordinary taxation rate on agricultural tractors is half the duty paid in
Great Britain. After consultation
with my right hon. Friends, the
Ministers of Home Affairs and Agriculture, I have decided to grant as from
1st May a similar concession here to
that which operates in Great Britain,
without altering the other rates of duty
for agricultural tractors.-(Official
Report, April 29th, 1941, Vol. 24, Col.
661).
To grant a concession on exactly the
same lines as in Great Britain would
operate most unfairly against the farmers
in Northern Ireland. I say that because
the farms here are smaller as compared
with those across the water. Farmers in
Northern Ireland have, in many cases,
more than one farm; they may have two,
three or even four. I have four farms.
instances the farms are some
In many
little distance away from each other, probably a mile or two miles. If the Minister
for the 5s licence is only going to allow

that would mean a man who has more
than one farm would require a tractor for
each. I am sure the right hon. Gentleman does not mean that, and I hope he
will clarify the statement he made. What
I trust he intends is that a farmer who

for hauling stuff from one part of his

I am sure the Minister does not intend

If that is so then he would require to
have a tractor for each of his holdings.
If that concession is granted it will be a

sound.

There is one other matter. It is a
question of air-raid precautions, but I do
not want to go into details. Take the
position in Northern Ireland in regard
to Anderson and Morrison shelters. I
was never a great believer in the
Anderson shelter, but I am told by people
from England that the Morrison indoor
steel table shelter is most valuable.
There is no reason whatever why it should
not be manufactured in Northern Ireland. We have little blacksmiths' shops,
engineering shops, garages, etc., throughout the country which could help to turn
them out. I suggest we should take a
survey of our capacity and abilities in that
direction, and that the Government
should take into consideration the
question of having them manufactured
in Northern Ireland. I am assured by
those who have had experience of
Morrison Shelters across the Channel that

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Superannuation (Teaching Services)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): Before considering the
terms of the Bill at present before the
House, hon. Members will expect to be
acquainted with the circumstances out
of which the Bill has arisen. Certain
Teachers' Superannuation (Amendment)
Schemes were framed in the year 1936
745 Superannuation (Teaching) Bill-

6 MAY 1941
Second Reading
to provide for the decision of the
Government that the payment of a lump
sum benefit should be made to teachers
on retirement calculated on the basis of
1-30th of the annual salary for each year
of service after the 1st July, 1936. A
further concession to certain teachers was
made last year, and this was to the effect
that all full-time pensionable service
not earlier than the 1st February, 1922,
and up to the 1st July, 1936, should also
be taken into account for the purpose of
the additional allowance. Amending
schemes for the various classes of
teachers were accordingly laid before the
House last June to give effect to this
decision, and these provided, among
other things, that the teachers concerned
can, if they desire to enter the scheme,
contribute from July, 1939, an additional
contribution of 1 per cent. per annum of
their salary for certain defined periods,
but that no payments of additional
allowance to retired teachers in respect of
pre-1936 service would be made until the
end of the war.
As a result of these conditions, the
Teachers' Superannuation Fund receives
during the war years considerable annual
additions to its income, while the liability
on the Fund towards which these contributions are made will not emerge until
after the war. It is desirable, therefore,
that these additional sums should meantime be invested and treated as capital
until such time as the payment in respect
of additional allowances falls to be made
after the war. The investments can then
be realised and utilised as income for the
purpose of helping to meet such allowances then due for payment.
Sub-clause (1) of Clause 1 provides for
the investment of the money received
each year, but the amount to be invested
is taken not as the actual amount of
additional contributions received-the
reckoning of which would be a tedious
process not worth the staff time involved
-but as the excess over £80,000, which
figure was the approximate contribution
income of the Teachers' Superannuation
Fund in the years immediately preceding
the 1st April, 1940.
Sub-clause (2) empowers the Ministry
of Finance to realise, after the war, all
or part of this investment, and use it as
income of the Fund towards meeting the
payment to teachers who retire during
the war years of the arrears of additional
allowance.
I beg to move.

I think that is a reasonable

the
high cost of living that these
pensioners have to suffer, without any

Superannuation Schemes (War Service)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. GORDON: This short and noncontentious Bill to which I am asking the
House to give a Second Reading to-day
is, to a great extent, self-explanatory so
that I feel I need not occupy the time of
hon. Members with a lengthy speech.
However, a few words on its purpose may
be helpful.
Stated briefly, the object of the Bill is
to make it easier for people to join the
Crown forces or to undertake employment
for war purposes by rendering it possible
for certain superannuation rights, which
they might otherwise lose, to be preserved.
A number of private firms as well as
public or semi-public bodies have established superannuation schemes to provide
pensions for the employees on attaining
a certain age. It frequently happens,
too, that the schemes include life assurance benefits by means of a system of
group insurance.
Hon. Members will, I feel sure, agree
that it would be a great pity if a man
were deterred from joining up or undertaking war work because of the danger of
forfeiting rights in a superannuation
scheme on giving up his normal employment.
But in some cases the statutory or other
rules under which such schemes operate
would not, as matters stand at present,
permit of his rights being preserved and
this Bill accordingly proposes to give the
necessary power to the trustees or other
persons administering the schemes to
make arrangements for preventing loss
of benefits.
Separate provision has already been
made in Acts passed by this Parliament
for teachers and the staffs of local
authorities who are, therefore, excluded
from the scope of this Bill by sub-section
(5) and the schedule.
The Bill follows closely the lines of an
Act already passed in Great Britain.
That Act was discussed very fully with
the National Advisory Council which
represents both employers' and workers'
organisations. Moreover, certain satisfactory undertakings were given by the
Life Assurance Offices to the British
Government as to the manner in which
they will deal with policies covering any
employees affected by the provisions of
this Bill. I am glad to be able to say
that those undertakings have been
extended to include Northern Ireland as
well.
In view of the desirability of furthering all efforts to direct available manpower into the most profitable, channels
during the present emergency and of
helping to remove any obstacles which
might hinder our common task, I commend this Bill to the House and trust
that it will soon be placed upon the
Statute Book. I beg to move.
Members: Hear, hear.)

but I am sure that every Member of this

I say to-day that if this war terminates

She has now to take the tool makers from

Woodvale when he mentioned the bus

Army We can do without buses, and
we can do without much motor traffic,
but the Army cannot do without its
