We have had an experience in the past.
Do not let us have another in the future.
Let us strengthen what we now recognise
are the weak points. Let us do everything humanly possible to strengthen
them with the material we have. We can
justly make a percentage allowance without injuring our own position here. I
am rather surprised that the Government
should hesitate for one moment to accept
this Motion. I could say something, but
I do not want to irritate or to bring in
any contentious matter in connection with
the Motion. We will have to compare
the position to-day with that in the late
war, and we will have to compare the
Royal Irish Constabulary with the Royal
Ulster Constabulary; we will have to
compare the position as it is to-day with
the position in 1916, 1917 and 1918.
During 1916 we had armed rebellion in
Ireland. We had then the Royal Irish
Constabulary, whose numbers were fixed
according to Act of Parliament. Nevertheless, with all our home difficulties and
the trials which the civil population had
to face, the governing authority in
Ireland at that time allowed from that
civil force over 600 men to join up. They
were the only force in Ireland at that
time for the preservation of law and
order. I want hon. Members to bear that
in mind. Altogether some 600 of them
joined up, and over 350 were decorated
on the field, but 150 never returned.
Their name as a force stands in the roll of
history amongst the fighting forces, and
their names and their force have to be
honoured for all time amongst Englishspeaking peoples.
Now let us compare our own force
with them. We have, in it to-day many
young Ulstermen who are anxious to do

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I would

In this war there is no difference between
any single service and another, whether it
is civil or military or naval; whether you
serve in the fire brigade, as an air raid
warden, or in the police force. The whole
of the population is in the front line, and
one's duty in this war lies in the service
in which one is trained. You can best do
your part in winning this war by remaining where you are most wanted.
The Member for Pottinger urged that
our police should be released to the extent
of 15 per cent. to join His Majesty's
Forces. Has the hon. Member considered
what is the duty of a policeman here today? His duty is solely to maintain civil
law and order. A policeman is not
trained in a matter of months. It takes
a matter of years to train an efficient

Another matter the hon. Member

I contend that we here cannot afford
to release people who are required to
maintain law and order. The maintenance of law and order is not the duty
of the Army. The duty of the Army is
to defeat the enemy in the field, and the
duty of the police is to maintain quiet
and order behind the lines so that the
soldiers will not be troubled to take over
the civilian control, which is best left to
those who know how to deal with it.
The hon. Member rightly paid a

Subsequent events have proved that they

to-day after what we
we have just experienced would be nothing less than
folly.

When it comes to the police one has to
remember, as has been pointed out by
the hon. and gallant Member for East
Down, that this war is not being fought
merely between the armed forces of the
combatants. The war is being fought on
many different fronts, and one of the
most important is the home front. We
have had many reminders of that. Never
has it been so much the case in the past.
It is essential that we should be as strong
on the home front as on any other, and
it is particularly essential owing to the
fact that the technique of fifth column
methods has been brought to such a
pitch by the enemy. That means there
should be protection against the day
when the home front, by invasion or
otherwise, may be tested.
The hon. Member for Pottinger in his
very forceful introduction of this Motion
suggested that the question was whether
this Government was out to help His
Majesty's Forces or was against them. As
I have indicated, it is far bigger than
that. The question is not merely how
we can help the armed forces of the
Crown-a very important matter in itself
-but how we can assist the national
effort to bring the war to a victorious

Mr. MacDERMOTT: Of course in

We live in difficult times. We have a
subversive element in our midst which has
only been kept within bounds by the

a day. Experience and careful training
are essential if he is to perform his

Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): In moving the Second
Reading of this Bill I should like at first
to describe the present position as to the
dam-retting of flax, and also to explain
why the Government thought it necessary
to bring in this Bill. The present situation is governed by Section 80 of the
Fisheries (Ireland) Act, 1842. That
Section provides that:
or
No person shall throw, empty, or
cause to run or flow into any river
lake any dye stuff, or other
deleterious or poisonous liquid, or
shall throw into such river or lake any
lime, spurge, or other deleterious or
poisonous matter, or shall steep in
such river or lake any flax or hemp,
and if any person shall so offend he
shall forfeit and pay for every such
offence any sum not exceeding ten
pounds; provided always, that nothing
in this Act contained shall extend or
be construed to render any person
liable to the penalties hereby imposed for casting into
any
or stream any dye stuffs or other
materials which are not of a deleterious
nature, or which are not in a state
poisonous to fish or other animals
using the waters thereof.
river
Now flax water comes under this 1842
Act and it does so in spite of the fact
that it is not poisonous in itself. Flax
water absorbs oxygen, and if enough
oxygen is taken out of the water the fish
die. We have proved by experiment that
where fish have actually turned over and
looked to be dead in the rivers they will
revive when put into fresh water. Life
comes back to them and they seem to be
none the worse. Nevertheless, the fact
remains that flax water is looked upon as
poisonous and is dealt with as such.
One of the defects of the 1842 Act, as
far as the farmers are concerned, is that
that Act deals with all rivers and waters.
The result has been that in many cases
farmers have been prosecuted for turning
flax water into rivers or lakes where there
were no fish and never had been any fish
or fishing. And when this was done the
prosecutions were brought in exactly the
same way by the old conservators, and
these farmers were constantly brought into
court, dragged before a magistrate, and
prosecuted for something of which they
really had not been guilty.
I need not tell you or the House the
tremendous importance to our war effort
of growing flax. We are practically de-
801 Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill-

13 MAY 1941
Second Reading
pendent on home production for our linen
nills and other great industries, and
therefore it seemed incumbent on the Govemment to bring in some measure of
protection and to see that the farmers who
were good enough to grow flax for the
belefit of the country should not be
attacked on small matters of technique or
law that had very little to do with the
killng of fish. I may tell you we hope to
grov 100,000 acres of flax and the importance of this Bill is shown by the fact
that about 75 per cent. of it will have to
be dam retted in these dams. This Bill
will therefore cover a great number of
Ulster farmers.
I would like to make it clear that this
Bill is not a case of flax v. fish or of fish v.
flax. I is a case of flax and fish. I have
no desire and the Government have no
desire that the rivers should be denuded
of fish, because there is no question or
doubt but that we all agree that fishing
is an excellent thing in itself, brings
a great number of people to this country,
and adds to the amenities of the country.
It also has a certain value. It is flax and
fish. We want to assist both sides,
because if there was only good will between
the farmers and the fisheries it would be
very much better than the state of
squabbling and fighting that has been
going on for the last 35 years.
It is a difficult matter, because two
Commissions were set up and sat two or
three years and were never able to produce any solution to the constant bickering between the farmers and the
fishermen. We hope at any rate that
this Bill I have brought in to-day will
for the moment, and perhaps finally, do
away with the eternal squabble. There
are two most important Clauses in this
Bill. One is that these prosecutions,
instead of being taken as in the past by
policemen or by the servants of the conservators or some individual, must go
through the Attorney-General, and the
Attorney-General may consult the Ministry of Agriculture or the Ministry of
Commerce. That fact ought to do away
largely with what I might call petty
prosecutions.
In the old days the belief of the
farmers was that certain men were
bribed or made money by bringing up
trumpery cases and getting the credit of
bringing the farmers to court. It is also
a good defence for the farmer to say and
prove that he has taken reasonable care,
either by putting in these new dams or
in some other way to see that his water
had not gone into the river. That is one
line of defence. The valuable thing to
the farmer is that he has got two lines
of defence. One is that the prosecution
must go through the Attorney-General,
and therefore we can take it it will not
be frivolous, and the other is if the
Attorney-General permits the prosecution
the farmer still has the right if he comes
before a resident magistrate to satisfy
him on that point. Therefore, he has a
much deeper front than in the old days
when a prosecution was simply brought
by any informer.
We hope and believe that this Bill will
do away with a great deal of the fears
which our farmers have now as to the
dam retting of flax. A measure of this
kind has been brought in in England,
but it is not the same as ours, because
we have our own difficulties in Ulster
and have to deal with them in our own
way. This Bill is particularly for our
people in Ulster.
There is just one other point I would
like to mention, and it is that the Bill
does not in any way do away with a man's
civil rights; that is to say, if a man
suffers injury, and can prove that injury,
by the flax water coming on his property,
he has still his civil rights in court. The
Bill does not in any way do away with
the civil rights that exist at the present
time. The Bill also deals with the
application of fines, and in that respect
is permanent. It merely modernises a
state of affairs which, however necessary
or desirable in 1842, has become out of
date in 1941.
This is not a great Bill. It is not a
Bill that is going to cause any great heat
or excitement. It is not a Bill that any
Minister would get much credit out of,
because, in fact, it is largely an agreed
measure. I hope the House will pass it.
I believe it will be of definite value to
the farmers and also to the war effort.
While it is only down as a war measure,
as all the measures we pass now are, I
have the hope that this Bill may become
permanent, because if it brings goodwill between fishermen and farmers,
which I and every Member desire it
should, then I can never see the Bill

The Minister said something which
I do not accept not if all the experts in
Ireland, England and Scotland supported him, and that is that flax-water is
not poisonous. He went on to explain

absorbed oxygen, and that killed the fish.
That is the same thing. I remember
when I was a boy walking many a time
along a stream that was well stocked with
trout. When the flax-water was let into
it, as it was let in wrongly year after
year, all one had to do was to walk in

The very minute it entered the pools in
this stream where the fish and fry
lodged one saw the fish coming to the
surface. Next they would turn their
bellies up, and then if you waited
for about 20 minutes they would be dead.
If that is not poisonous I would like to
know what is. It does not matter if all
the experts in Ireland and England said
different; that is correct. I daresay if
there was a bigger volume of water at
this particular place the results might
not have been so immediately destructive.
Flax-water is poisonous, and very
poisonous. The Minister said if you lifted

know when the Government intend to
take the Committee Stage of the Bill. I
know enough about flax water to argue
about the damage it does, but not enough
about fishing or how it is carried on.
Supposing the Government did not take
the Committee Stage of the Bill immediately, but instead met these people to see
what arrangement they might be able to
make to satisfy them. The Minister has
told us that fishing clubs are bitterly
opposed to the Bill. In a case of this
kind where a lot of bickering and discontent may be raised could we not hold
over the Committee Stage, meet these
people and argue the matter out, and
give way where you think you can give
way without injuring the interests of the
flax producers. I make that suggestion
to the Minister.
I do not think the Minister will say that
this is a Bill which should be rushed.
There will be no flax retted for a long
time. If the matter is left open and there
is a general discussion on the Bill before
the Committee stage you might be able
to make it very simple. I cannot think
that any people would be so unreasonable
as to press their claims against something
that might affect our war production. I
know some of the fishermen. They are
very reasonable, intelligent, and competent men, and I was wondering if the
Committee stage could be delayed until
you had an interview with the people
who, the Minister says, are opposed to
the Bill. Any I met are opposed to it,
but they seem to be very competent people,
and if the suggestion is adopted it will
help.
Mr. ELLIOTT: While I rise to give
the Bill my support I must confess that if
it had gone a little further I would have
given it more hearty support than I can
in its present form, but believing, as I
do, that half a loaf is better than no bread
I decided to accept the Bill as it stands.
Some people have the idea that those of
us who represent agriculture in this House
are out to protect the farmers at all costs,
no matter what injury we may do to any
other industry. I support this Bill from
two angles. First of all, I think it is a
807 Landlord and Tenant Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Elliott]
Bill brought into being to protect farmers
from injustice, and therefore I give it my
support; and, in the second place, it is a
Bill that is going to help to preserve the
fishing industry and interests, and for
that reason also I give it my support. I
believe the two things ought to be considered. I do not believe any Bill ought
to be introduced into this House that is
going to destroy one or the other of these
interests, and as both these interests are
going to be protected I will support the
measure.
Some people have the idea that all
farmers who grow flax and who dam ret it
do not care what happens to the fish so
long as they get their flax water drained
cff. I want to say that while there may
be some black sheep-and there are very
few flocks in which there are not some
black sheep-the majority of the farmers
do not want to destroy fish in any river
or to destroy the fishing industry in any
shape or form. What we do want to protect the farmers from is petty prosecution
and petty persecution. We want to see
some protection for the man who is doing
his level best to get his flax dam retted
and at the same time is doing his best to
do away with the flax water without
causing any injury to fish. He should not
be hauled before the court and fined for
something he could not prevent.
As far as I am concerned, although I
am an agriculturist myself and represent agricultural interests, I have no
sympathy with any man who wants to
let the flax water drain off his dam and
go into a river to the detriment of the
fishing industry. I do not stand for any
such thing, and I am glad there is not a
clause in the Bill allowing a farmer to do
what he likes with his flax water. I do
think it gives a certain amount of protection to the honest man who wants to
do his best, not only to produce flax and
dam ret it, but to do the least possible
injury-none if he can possibly avoid
doing any-in letting the water out of
his dam.
There are one or two points in the Bill
that I would like amended if the Minister
could see his way. As the present fishery
law stands a bailiff has an inducement to
bring farmers to court by the fact that
he receives a proportion of the fine as
part of his emoluments. I think that is
an iniquitous principle to be included in
any Bill. I do not like it. It still remains to a certain extent by the fact that
the fines will go to the Board of Conservators who will utilise the money to
augment the salaries of their officials.
The inducement is partly there. I would
much rather have seen the fines go
directly to the Crown and not to the
conservators.
When I mentioned this objection some
time ago I was asked what would the
boards of conservators do if they did not
get the fines. All I can say is that if
the boards of conservators have to be
kept in existence by means of fines there
is the more reason why this principle
should be done away with. The boards
of conservators ought to be able to get
their money from some other quarter
rather than from such a contaminated
source.
Another thing I do not like about the
Bill is the fact that it is a war measure.
There is no argument put forward by
the noble Lord in introducing the Bill
which would not equally apply to peace
time as to war time, and if the measure
is good for war time it should also be
good for peace time. He explained that
even though this is a war-time measure,
if it was found to work satisfactorily
there would be no inducement to remove
it from the Statute Book after the war.
These are only small things, but they
mean a great deal. I am sorry my
colleague, the Member for North Derry,
who is president of the Ulster Farmers'
Union, is not here to-day. He 'phoned
me to say that he was unable to be present through illness.
The hon. Member would like me, on
behalf of the Farmers' Union, to say
they are not satisfied that this Bill goes
far enough. They would much rather
have seen it a permanent measure on the
Statute Book. But because they believe,
as I do, that it goes a certain length to
remove injustices from the farmers and
to prevent petty pin-pricking persecu
tions and that it will make it easier for
the farmer who wants to be law-abiding
they are in favour of the Bill. I believe
this Bill will do something to help the
farmer to do what is best not only in his
own interests but in those of the fishing
industry, and for those reasons I will
support it.
809 Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill-

13 MAY 1941
Second Reading
Mr. J. E. BAILEY: As one who
knows most of the difficulties of the
farmers with regard to the retting of flax,
I would like to explain to the Members
of this House some of the difficulties that
are met with. The farmers have always
tried to catch as much water as possible
for this purpose, and that is the reason
that flax dams are made at the lowest
points of the farms. I have no hesitation
in saying that 70 per cent. of the dams
are so situated that it is impossible to
have a catch dam; in fact, in many cases
the catch dam would have to be in a
neighbour's field. We all realise that the
period before the flax is pulled is usually
very dry, and on many occasions farmers
have almost given up hope of getting any
water, or of getting enough water to fill
the dam.
I have known flax to be carted a distance of five miles to be retted. Anyone
who realises the weight of this green flax
when it is newly pulled-and it must be
retted at this stage-will understand some
of the farmers' difficulties. I can honestly
say that 90 per cent. of the farmers have
tried to obey the law, but I also wish to
say
that the law has been carried out in
a most unreasonable way so far as prosecutions by the police are concerned. The
police, I believe, have been obeying the
dictates of their superior officers who, in
a great many cases, are members of
anglers' associations. I would say that
the law has been administered more in
the interest of sport than in the interest
of equity and justice.
While I welcome the small concession
in the present Bill, I hold that it does not
go far enough. It does not give the people
who cannot make catch dams, in fact it
gives nobody, no matter what precautions
may be taken, an assurance that they will
not be prosecuted. They are depending
entirely on a report made to the learned
Attorney-General by some junior official
of the Ministry of Agriculture or the
Ministry of Commerce. It all depends on
the favourable or unfavourable nature of
that report, and, therefore, to my mind.
the junior official sent down to inspect the
flax dams will be judge and jury, and on
him will depend whether the farmer will
be prosecuted or not.
If the farmer is prosecuted-this is a
point which has not been mentioned in
the Bill-the anglers' association concerned may sue the farmer for damages
for the destruction of fish life. They
have sued in the past for as much as £100
in some cases. I am sorry that I have
been unable to find a decision by a learned
judge on the question, simply because the
cases are almost all settled before they
reach court. The reason is that the
farmer has not the money to fight a case
and settles it. I can tell the House that
this point is a nightmare to the farmer.
a
There was a case in County Down during
1940 where a man was prosecuted for
allowing flax water to escape into
river. He was fined, and was then sued
by the Belfast Anglers' Association. He
settled the claim, and he had to make a
public apology to the Belfast Anglers'
Association. I am not going to give the
man's name or address, but I am prepared to give it privately if necessary. I
will read the apology this particular
farmer had to make publicly:-
Gentlemen, I regret that, owing to
inadvertence, flax water from my dam
on the lands above escaped into the
Kilmore River as a result of which fish,
the property of the Belfast Anglers'
Association, were destroyed. The
association having agreed to accept an
abated sum of £10 in settlement of
their damage, I agree to payment of
this sum, and to publication of this
apology.
I think it is most unfair, when farmers
are. doing their duty to supply food for
the nation in the present crisis, that they
should be harassed in this way. I appeal
to the Government to bring in a Bill even
stronger than the one now before this
House, not alone. for the duration of the
war, but as a permanent Statute. The
Ulster Farmers' Union, while they
welcome this Measure, are in favour of
it being made a permanent Act rather
than a war-time. Measure. I again appeal
to the Government to settle this difficult
question of flax water once and for all
time in a more straightforward way than
they are doing in this Bill.
I wonder how many of the Members
of this House have seen flax being taken
out of a dam at the latter end of August
or the beginning of September, when the
men have to stand up to their neck in
water to throw off the stones that are
used to hold the flax down. How many
811 Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. J. E. Bailey]
of you have had the experience of the
Member for North Tyrone and myself
who have done this job. Indeed, I have.
broken the ice before entering the dam

Mr. HENDERSON: I notice there are
a great many vested interests represented
in this House. The Member who has just
sat down would look well in a bathing

If this Bill becomes law the entire
angling associations of Northern Ireland
are going to be wiped out. Those
Members who have spoken in support of
the Bill are speaking from selfish motives,

I do not think the Member for West
Down is a kill-joy, but he certainly speaks
like one,
as did the Member for the
University, who would not give anyone a

I have never in my life been an angler,

an odd trout or salmon for the family.
The working men who are members of

I am not speaking as a fishing or

a fight into which the Minister of Agriculture has been drawn. It can be
termed a trade dispute between the

Minister that there are anglers in his

and other days of the week angling.
While the Member for South Tyrone

to make about the fishermen, but he

The anglers of Northern Ireland are

Lord GLENTORAN: I am sure the

Mr. HENDERSON: The anglers'

Minister has said that this is a war-time

Second Reading
Measure, and I hope it will be repealed

Mr. BROWN: The Minister has told

We have it here that where a person is

flax water offences for the duration of the

During the last war many promises

let down. We hope that will not happen

have made this measure more comprehensive and made it a permanent measure. I

Mr. MAGINESS: The reception which

There have been a number of criticisms

One felt the elephant's side and said it

was like a wall. The second had happened
to come into contact with the beast's tail,

even the

one could call that fair. It pressed

Νο
The hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's spoke of this Bill as one for the
abolition of prosecutions. I have looked
through the Bill again since I heard him
say that, and I cannot understand how
he got that impression from it. He has
either misinterpreted the existing law or
else he has entirely misconceived the
purport and intent of the measure. What
happens now is that a policeman or water
bailiff sees what he thinks is an infringement of this new measure. Perhaps he
thinks an injury has been caused to fish.
At any rate the board of conservators
signify to the Attorney-General that
they intend to prosecute. They serve
notice upon the Ministry of Agriculture
and the Ministry of Commerce of their
intention and ask for consent. The
Ministry of Agriculture-I can only
speak for it, of course-can send out an
official or inspector to examine the site
where the alleged offence took place. He
sees what the farmer has done. He sees
the near proximity of the dam to the
river. He sees all the facts. He reports
these facts to the Attorney-General, but
he does not in any way seek to dictate
to the Attorney-General.
He justs acts in the way Sir Bernard
Spillsbury would act in case of a murder
trial. A corpse is found. The police
inspect the corpse. A man or woman is
poisoned and they consult Sir Bernard.
Spillsbury, who is
is the expert. He
examines and reports to the Attorney-
General or Director of Prosecutions in
England, who very naturally takes that
report into account. But Sir Bernard
does not dictate to the Attorney-General
or say there must be a prosecution or
there must not be. He simply places his
expert knowledge of the facts at the disposal of the Director of Prosecutions.
This is not a case of poisoning people.
It is a case of alleged poisoning of fish.
The inspector whom the Ministry of
Agriculture sends out occupies the position in respect of salmon that Sir Bernard
Spillsbury does in the case of a corpse.
He sends a report to the Attorney-
General and the Attorney-General will
consider that report, but he makes up his
own mind. He may also think it right
to consult the Minister of Commerce.
But surely it is of very great assistance
to the Attorney-General that he should
have this expert survey of the facts and
not be depending upon a village policeman who may not know anything either
of flax water or of fish.
Now, the hon. and learned Member
spoke of catchment dams. If it were possible to have a catchment dam for every
flax dam in the country that might be
a solution. But it has been found by
these Commissions that it would be impossible in the case of almost 70 per cent. to
have catchment dams and therefore to
introduce any such phraseology as the
hon. and learned Member would seek to
introduce into this measure would have
the effect of cutting down the whole purport of the Act. It would give a yardstick by which the amount of safeguarding
the farmer gave the fish could be

measured. We do not want any such
yardstick. Each case must be on its own

Member by which if you put in, as he

of catchment dams or otherwise" it would
mean there would have to be something
in the nature of catchment dams, and that
is not what the Government wants. That
is not possible in 70 per cent. of the cases.
And therefore to do what the hon. and
learned Member suggests would take
away from the whole effect of this
measure.
I do not know that there was anything
else raised by hon. Members with which
I can deal now. There were other points
which will be raised in the Committee
stage, but it does seem as if at least hon.
Members were going to give this measure
their support, even if a cold support at the
moment. But I believe that a trial of
this measure will show that it will be
beneficial not to one section but to every
section of the community, and that the
support which is rather cold to-day will
become warmer and enthusiastic as the
years go on.

The PRIME MINISTER: I have had
the opportunity of consulting my
colleagues as to whether it would be
desirable or not to have a secret sitting or
session, and we have come to the conclusion that it would not be desirable.
After all, we are a democratically elected
House. We have only power to deal with
local matters; we have nothing to do with
'international matters or
even with the
conduct of the war. I feel it would be
very unsettling to our people if we were
to have a secret sitting because they
would think there was something seriously
wrong, something that the Government
was desirous of hiding. Rumours would
be spread about which would not be in
the public interest.
I do not wish to be misunderstood in
this connection. While the Government
think that at the present time it would
not be desirable to have such a session
we live at the same time in times of
change. Something may occur later on
which would justify the Government
changing the view which it definitely
holds at the present time. I would
appeal to hon. Members opposite-I
think it is scarely necessary for me to do
so-to realise how grave is the responsibility of each one of us. None of us, I
am sure, desire to say anything which
would be helpful to the enemy.
In our

cause. I was literally appalled to discover not a score but hundreds of women
and children, most of them with bags of
some kind under their arms, apparently
making for places where they might stay
for the night. That, of course, was in
apprehension of another attack.
With the knowledge that that exists
not merely in one part of the city but,
I understand, throughout every other part
of the city, is the Government going to
allow that position to continue without
making any attempt to deal with it? It
is all right to say, as the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Minister of Labour has
said, that we are going to deal with these
things in due time, but here is a position
that exists to-night. It is all very well
to look upon that situation with
equanimity or even levity so long as the
weather is good, but what is the position
going to be later on if no action is taken
now.
I do not join with the Member for
Shankill in the invitation he gave to the
Prime Minister, but I do say that if
Members want to be impressed by the
seriousness of the situation they should
take it upon themselves to discover the
condition of things that exists. If the
weather becomes worse the effect on the
health and well-being of this community.
will be incalculable. Individual Members
of this House can do nothing; it is a
matter entirely for the Government. It
is a matter, I definitely suggest, that
should have the most urgent attention of
the Government, not in a week's time or
a month's time, but immediately. In
this matter I am not speaking in any
destructive way.
A suggestion has been made that something should be done in the way of
obtaining tents, and that tent encampments should be made in which there
should be proper canteens and sanitary
facilities. No matter what means may
be adopted, I am perfectly convinced that
something must be done immediately;
otherwise the Government will have to
bear a very heavy responsibility. I feel
more deeply on this subject than hon.
Members realise, and if action is not
taken instantaneously the result will be
such as will throw a tremendous amount
of blame on the Government of the
country. One method to deal with the
problem is that I have mentioned, but
the Government may choose their own
means of dealing with it. But something
must be done, and done immediately. I
will not unduly enlarge upon that, except
to urge with all the strength at my command the seriousness of the position,
which should have the immediate attention of the Government.
A good deal has been said with
reference to the A.R.P. services and the
Ministry of Public Security. I am
bound to make this statement this afternoon. During the past three or four
months I have had an opportunity of
coming more intimately into touch with
the minds of my constituents and,
speaking for my own constituency, I am
bound to say that nothing but the most
profound dissatisfaction exists with
regard to the administration of the
Ministry of Public Security. I regret to
have to make that statement. I do not
make it with any desire to cast any
aspersion upon the Minister, for whom I
have the highest regard, but as a Member
of Parliament representing my constituency I feel that if that is the opinion of
my constituents I must give expression to
it. I venture to assert that that opinion
which I have just expressed is an opinion
shared by a large number, if not, indeed,
the majority of the people of this
country.
If that is so-and I submit it is so
then the sooner this House engages
upon something in the nature of a
general public inquiry into the administration of the Ministry of Public Security
the better it will be for all concerned. I
suggest that a private session of this
House would, perhaps, meet the need,
but if the Government is not willing to
adopt that procedure I do suggest that
some method should be found whereby a
proper and urgent inquiry should be
made into the administration of all our
A.R.P. services and the Ministry of
Public Security.
That is all I desire to say at the
moment, but I do press that the two
matters to which I have referred, and
particularly that concerning the conditions under which these women and
children are living at the present moment
will have the most urgent and serious
attention of the Government.
Civil Defence Precautions-
13 MAY 1941
Secret Session
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I just want to assure
the Member for North Down that the
consideration of this whole billeting
question has been occupying the mind of
the Government since the blitz. The hon.
Member will understand that this is not
exactly an easy matter to deal with. It
is not a thing that can be decided in a
moment without taking various matters
into consideration, such as the safety of
the possible camps, sanitation, water
supply, and communications. But I can
tell him, without letting out any secrets,
that the Minister of Home Affairs, the
Minister of Public Security, and myself
discussed the whole of this question only
this morning. That does not mean we
began the discussion this morning, because
we began it some time ago. It is only
right that the House should know that
that problem is receiving the most careful
consideration, and the decision of the
Government is going to be acted upon as
soon as certain matters have been cleared
up, and I hope they will be cleared up in
a few days.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: I desire to
thank the Minister of Commerce for his
explanation, and I have no doubt it will
help to allay public feeling.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF
PUBLIC SECURITY (Mr. Maginess):
Certain remarks have been made about a
degree of uneasiness that exists in the
public mind with regard to the administration of air raid precautions and the
Ministry of Public Security. There is
nothing more calculated to increase that
feeling of uneasiness, and nothing more
calculated to do harm than for persons
like the Member for Shankill to go around
shouting and repeating that nothing has
been done. He knows as well as everybody in this House knows that a great
deal has been done. He knows as well as
anybody the organisation that has been
built up, an organisation that could not
be built up in a week or a month. It has
taken months to build up the organisation
that functioned remarkably well during
one of the biggest raids that have been
made on the British Isles. Yet in spite
of that the hon. Member has the effrontery
to repeat several times in this House that
nothing whatever has been done. That
any hon. Member can make such a statement, which he knows is calculated to
increase public uneasiness where that
uneasiness exists, shows to me that he
lacks almost entirely that sense of
responsibility which should animate every
Member of this House.
It is the easiest thing in the world to
go about saying that nothing has been
done, and to make fantastic suggestions
which he knows very well can never be
carried out. It is more difficult to come
into this House with concrete suggestions,
and to come, to the Ministry and try to
help. Hon. Members have
given
singularly little help to the Ministry of
Public Security. They come here once a
week and say nothing has been done.
They sneer and say, as the hon. Member
stated to-day, that the Minister of Public
Security could have saved hundreds of
lives and hundreds of buildings. They
know perfectly well that had it not been
for the Minister many more hundreds of
lives would have been lost, and many
more buildings ruined.
Do the hon. Members suggest that an
organisation such as A.R.P. grows like
a mushroom during the night? They
know perfectly well that the Minister has
been working day in and day out seven
days a week-he often works far into the
night-building up the organisation.
The organisation has not failed, neither
has the Minister of Public Security. The
Minister does not get any help from the
hon. Members; they simply criticise.
They do not offer any concrete suggestions, but instead go about shouting like
Solomon Eagle in the City of London
during the plague. If instead of doing
that they would help the Minister, then
they could stand up in this House
and criticise. Up to the moment they
have been nothing but a hindrance, and
it is about time they changed their minds
and in the midst of so many and great
dangers which surround them come to the
Minister and ask, "What can we do to
help you?"
Mr. NIXON: Bunkum.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Twenty
minutes after Six o'clock until
Tuesday next, pursuant to
the Resolution of the House
of this day.

Oral Answers to Questions.
COMPENSATION FOR TRADERS?
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Attorney-General whether he can state if
public compensation is available to traders
who suffer loss from inability to carry on
business because of the presence of unexploded bombs in proximity to their shops.
-
The ATTORNEY GENERAL (Mr.
Black): So far as I am aware there is no
provision for the payment of compensation from public funds in the circumstances referred to by the hon. and
learned Member.
REBATE OF LICENCE DUTIES.
2. Mr. CAMBPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state what
rebate of licence duty is available to
licencees for any period during which
their licensed premises are closed to business owing to air raid damage or
destruction.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The provisions of Section 3 of
the Finance Act (Northern Ireland),
1936, would appear to meet the cases of
the type referred to by the hon. Member.
Under Section 3 of that Act, where the
business for the purpose of which the
licence was granted has been temporarily
discontinued by reason of the licensed
premises having been destroyed or
seriously damaged, the licence holder, on
making applicantion in the manner provided by the Section, shall be entitled to
obtain repayment, or, in so far as the
duty has not been paid, remission, of
such part of the duty for the year as
bears to the full amount of that duty the
same proportion as the period during
which the business is not carried on, or
the part of that period falling within the
year, bears to a whole year.
FINANCING THE REOPENING OF
BUSINESSES.
3. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Commerce whether, in view of
the desirability of enabling owners of
factories and businesses, affected by enemy
action, to recommence operations with a
minimum of delay, he is prepared to
utilise such means as may exist under the
Loans Guarantee Act or any similar act,
with the object of temporarily financing
such owners in the reestablishment of their
businesses, thus providing work for their
employees.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply. Under
the provisions of the War Damage Act,
which applies to the United Kingdom as
a whole, compensation is payable by the
War Damage Commission if factory or
business premises are damaged as a result
of enemy action, and immediate advances
up to £800 can be obtained in necessitous
cases, in order to secure new business
premises.
A scheme made under the Act also provides for the insurance of machinery and
business equipment.
In addition, the War Risks Insurance
Act, 1939, provides for the insurance
against and for payment during the war
in respect of damage of stocks carried by
traders or business firms.
Mr. THOMPSON: Would the Minister
inform us as to the source of and where
the information is available?
Mr. BARBOUR: If the hon. Member
will make application to my Ministry they
will be glad to inform him.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the statement about the War Damage Act is it a
fact that businesses carrying £2,000 worth
Oral Answers

of stock and upwards are compelled to
adopt this insurance, and in the event of
one of such premises being destroyed by
enemy action and holding property belonging to other people in for repairs could
the Minister give us any enlightenment as
to the responsibility of the insurance
company and of the firm?
Mr. BARBOUR: I should like notice
of that question.
NOCTURNAL REFUGEES.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Public Security whether his attention
has been called to the fact that large
numbers of people have lately been trekking from Belfast to surrounding rural
districts each evening in order to obtain
refuge from air raids, and travelling back
to their homes at daylight; whether he is
aware that many of these nocturnal
refugees are infants carried or wheeled by
their parents, and that many are infirm
and aged folk; and whether the Government will give immediate consideration to
the provision of shelter for these people
in adjoining rural areas.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The responsibility for
dealing with the problem-
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the right
hon. Gentleman has misheard. The question was addressed to the Minister of
Public Security.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The responsibility for dealing with the
problem to which the hon. and learned
Member refers has now been transferred
to my Department, and in consequence I
am replying to this question.
I understand from the inquiries that
my Department has made that the
numbers with which we have at the
moment to deal are nothing like so great
as those which could have been found in
the districts surrounding Belfast a few
days ago, but we realise that in the event
of another raid and possibly even after
another air-raid warning they would
increase enormously.
Arrangements are already well in hand
and a considerable number of these
refugees were provided for last night. As
time goes on I hope to be able to make
arrangements for progressively larger
numbers. I would assure the hon.
Member that I fully appreciate the situation and that I will spare no effort to take
ail possible steps in the matter.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to that
statement by the Minister that this
branch has been transferred to his
Department, would he give instructions
to the Transport Department to provide
transport accommodation for people who
have to trek miles into the country to

returning to work in the morning, and
would he more particularly give instructions to the Transport Department that
they are not to order buses to travel idle
on the road by the score and refuse to
take these homeless people in or out to
their business?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question
of the hon. Member raises a very great
problem. I have, of course, the greatest
possible sympathy with people so placed,
but he will understand there is a limit
to the transport available. I will
certainly go into the matter very carefully.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the

houses? Is the Minister aware-I was

will he stop it? In the meantime I will
give the Minister an opportunity to make
statement on

AIR-RAID SHELTERS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Public Security whether he
can state if the number of air-raid
shelters in Belfast and other parts of
Northern Ireland are sufficient to meet

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
The following question also stood upon
the Order Paper :-
6. Mr. CAMPBELL: To ask the
Minister of Public Security whether the
Ministry have come to a final determination against the construction of underground air-raid shelters in Belfast and
elsewhere; and, if so, on what grounds
was this conclusion arrived at, and
whether the Ministry have under consideration any further schemes for the
public safety than those already undertaken.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): With
the hon. and learned Member's permission I shall deal with this and the
succeeding question together.
The number of air-raid shelters is
being continually increased, and it cannot, therefore, be said that the amount
of shelter available as yet meets the
requirements of the population.
With regard to underground shelters,
by which I take it the hon. Member
means deep bomb-proof shelters, the test,
so far as my Ministry is concerned, is
whether it is practicable to provide such
shelters so as to give really safe accommodation to a substantial number of
people within a reasonable distance of
their homes. This has not proved a practicable proposal so far, and I see little
prospect of being able to accommodate
any substantial number in this way.
The hon. and learned Member's
questions on the subject of shelter raise
matters which are naturally much in the
public mind at present, and I am anxious
to keep hon. Members as fully informed
as possible with regard to the Government's plans, progress and problems in
this and other aspects of civil defence.
This I am anxious to do when presenting
the Estimates for my Department, and
I would, therefore, ask the hon. Member,
and indeed hon. Members generally, to
await the debate on that occasion for
further discussion and information on
subjects of civil defence. In order that
the debate on the. Estimates may cover
the points which may be raised as
adequately as possible I would be glad if
hon. Members would give me as early and
ample notice as they conveniently can of
any questions within the purview of my
Ministry which they desire considered.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement, has the. right hon.
Gentleman got, or is he trying to get
Anderson shelters or table shelters or
substitutes?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: With regard to
the Anderson shelters, I cannot get them
for they are out of production. In
reference to the table shelters, commonly
known as the Morrison shelters, I am
doing everything possible. to get a large
number of these. I can make no
promises. It is a supply question, but I
am doing everything I can and I have
put up a strong case on the subject.
Mr. NIXON: In the meantime would
the Minister consider the possibility of
getting something resembling them-substitutes like wooden shelters with planks
or something like that, that would protect
people from falling masonry which has
been the cause of 80 per cent. of the
damage to human life?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: It is very hard
to get substitutes in sufficient numbers,
but we are doing all we can in every
direction possible so far as the exigiencies
of the supply position allow.
SUPPLY OF STEEL HELMETS.
7. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether he is
aware that there is a considerable shortage
of steel helmets for those engaged in
various forms of A.R.P. service, and
whether in view of such shortage he is
prepared to recommend the utilisation of
such resources as may exist in Northern
Ireland for the manufacture of these
helmets.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: All local
authorities in Northern Ireland have
already been supplied with more than
sufficient steel helmets to equip the
authorised establishment of their A.R.P.
services. I am, however, aware that, as
many authorities have rightly pursued the
policy of recruiting volunteers in excess of
the authorised establishment, it has not in
many cases been possible to make a personal issue to each individual volunteer.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 MAY 1941
There should, however, be steel helmets
for all persons who are required to undertake duty at any particular time.
In
determining the scale of equipment to be
issued the Ministry has followed the
policy which is laid down in Great
Britain.
At an earlier stage, when the supply
position was a great deal more difficult
than at present, the question of arranging
for local manufacture was considered, but
it was not found practicable.
I may add for the information of the

CONSPICUOUS PUBLIC BUILDINGS
8. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether his
attention has been directed to the conspicuous nature of a number of public
buildings, whether he is prepared to order
the treatment of the exterior of such
buildings so as to render them less conspicuous from the air, and whether such
work can be effected out of the funds of
the National Exchequer.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Representations
have been made to me from various
sources on this subject. Whether or not
treatment is necessary or desirable is a
matter for the experts of the Service
Departments.
Section 39 of the Civil Defence Act,
1939, provides for the payment by the
Exchequer of 50 per cent. of the approved
expenses incurred by factory occupiers or
public utility undertakers who are
required to carry out measures of
camouflage. The camouflage of buildings
other than those in these categories would
not be within the purview of my Department and the question of the cost would
be a matter for the Service Departments
to resolve.
ACCOMMODATION IN COUNTRY
SCHOOLS.
9. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply to this question.
I am aware that in many-perhaps
most-public elementary schools the desk

may mean a shortage of desks. Steps are,

desks transferred from Belfast schools to

needed, and I hope that by this means
the position in the country schools will
soon be materially improved.

Lady aware of the fact that the Cookstown Regional Committee have
have been
pressing for delivery of these desks for

Member must be aware that there are

Mr. NIXON: With regard to the difficulties, is it not a fact that a large number of schools in Belfast are more than
half empty, and would it not be possible

We
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Basil Brooke): I rise to present the
annual Estimates of my Ministry, for the
first time as Minister of Commerce, under
circumstances the difficulty of which will
be appreciated by the House. It has
been the practice in the past to give the
House an account of the activities of the
Ministry during the past year; but I am
sure that hon Members will appreciate
that on grounds of public interest there
would be obvious objections to
embarking on any detailed description of
certain branches of my Ministry's work
at the present juncture. An increasing
amount of work carried out by my
Ministry has been undertaken on behalf
of Imperial Departments, and I propose
to take these services first.
The work for which my Ministry is
responsible in connection with the supply
of raw materials has increased in
volume and importance during the period.
under review. In this work it has been
the policy to endeavour to ensure, as far
as possible, that the control of supplies.
is exercised locally rather than from
Great Britain. This policy is, in my
opinion, best calculated to ensure the expeditious execution of work for which the
Northern Ireland Government is in any
way responsible. As is inevitable the
necessity for diverting our supplies to the
vital requirements of the war renders it
necessary for my Ministry, in the exercise
of local control, to impose a large
measure of restriction on local activities
not directly connected with the war
effort.
The work of my Ministry in connection
with supplies may be roughly divided
into two categories covering building and
non-building materials, respectively. With
regard to building materials, I found it
necessary to arrange for compulsory
powers to be delegated to my Ministry
for the control of bricks and road-making
materials. Should the need arise I shall
not hesitate to use these powers to ensure
that our local resources are utilised to
the greatest advantage in the national
interest. Needless to say, I would much
prefer to achieve our objective through
the voluntary co-operation of the producers concerned, and I am glad to state
that in almost every case this cooperation has SO far been readily
forthcoming.
necessary
Closely connected with the control and
distribution of building materials is the
restriction of new building operations.
In order to ensure that there are
adequate supplies for essential
purposes it, unfortunately, became
to increase the restrictions
on new building operations as from
April 14, and
and our problems in this
sphere have been intensified by the
recent air attacks on Northern Ireland.
In present circumstances it must
necessity be the policy of my Ministry to
prohibit the rebuilding of damaged
premises, except where such premises are
of vital importance to the war effort.
At the same time where damaged buildof
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
20 MAY 1941
ings readily admit of first-aid repair
every effort will be made to provide
sufficient materials to enable this work
to be undertaken.
Amongst the non-building materials
with which my Ministry is concerned, by
far the most important to our community is flax. The effects of the curtailment of imports of flax on our
principal manufacturing industry are
well-known to hon. Members. The efforts
which are being made to increase homeproduced supplies will, I hope,
eventually result in giving more employment in this industry. As hon.
Members are aware, the present position
rules out the possibility of releasing
supplies for the manufacture of goods
for the home market, and makes it
necessary to exercise close control over
releases for export requirements.
CO-
In the interests of the linen industry
my Ministry has undertaken, in
operation with flax control, a scheme for
the control and direction of the linen
export trade. By means of this scheme
we are able to guarantee to the British
Government that new flax released to the
linen industry is not only prevented from
finding its way in the form of manufactured articles on to the home market,
but is directed to those channels of export along which flow, in the reverse
direction, the materials of war required
by this country. By means of this
control we have been able to obtain a fair
share of the supplies of raw material
available, and, while the position leaves
much to be desired, I hope that we shall
be able to provide for our essential
export requirements.
While we cannot hope to obtain the
release of flax for the manufacture of
linen for the home trade, I have
endeavoured to obtain some improvement
in the position of our making-up industry
by the relaxation of certain restrictions
imposed by the Limitation of Supplies
Orders. I am grateful to the President
of the. Board of Trade for his readiness to
meet us on this point as far as concerns
the production of cotton shirts and
uniforms. Under this concession articles
of this kind made up in Northern Ireland
can be sold outside the quota of restrictions imposed by the Limitation of
Supplies Orders, subject to their being
certified by my Ministry. The removal
of statutory restrictions obviously does
not eliminate all the difficulties which
face our manufacturers at the present
time, but I regard this concession as a
recognition of the need for special treatment of Northern Ireland's problems.
Salvage of waste paper and scrap metal
has been carried out in Northern Ireland
by my Ministry on behalf of the Ministry
of Supply. Until December last we relied
for our salvage contribution on the existing collecting services of the local
authorities, supplemented by the efforts.
of voluntary organisations, such as the
Northern Ireland Salvage Committee,
under the chairmanship of the hon.
Member for South Derry, to whom I am
glad to pay a tribute. Much good work
was done, but it became apparent that
salvage was too important a source of
war material to be left entirely to voluntary effort. Accordingly, in December
last a Compulsory Salvage Direction was
served on the larger local authorities in
Northern Ireland-eleven in all comprising about half of our total
population. The Direction requires the
local authority concerned to provide and
maintain a satisfactory salvage service,
but permits the authority to take into
account existing collections by voluntary
or other persons. The councils have, on
the whole, tackled the work with commendable energy and I am glad to say
that, in spite of war-time difficulty in
obtaining equipment, valuable progress
has already been made.
The export drive initiated last year has
been pressed forward with energy, and it
is satisfactory to note that our overseas
trade in linen still holds a high place in
the list of United Kingdom exports. The
scarcity and high price of flax have been
adverse factors, which have resulted in
some contraction in the yardage exported.
A further threat to this important trade.
emerged during the year in the possibility
that the new purchase tax under the
Imperial Finance (No. 2) Act, 1940,
would be regarded by the United States.
revenue authorities as element of
wholesale value for the purpose of the
United States import tariff on linen.
Happily a decision has now been reached
by the United States Treasury that the
United Kingdom purchase tax is to be
disregarded in computing the value for
customs duty of linen entering the United
States.
an
Members will be aware that my
Ministry of Commerce
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir B. Brooke]
Ministry has for some time past been
actively interested in the provision and
equipment of a number of new flax processing factories in Northern Ireland to
help to meet the need for additional
supplies of flax fibre, the necessity for
which has already been recognised in the
measures taken by my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Agriculture to increase
the acreage under flax.
raw
I need not stress the importance of
obtaining adequate supplies of
material for our linen industry from the
point of view of the export trade and as
a means of stimulating employment in our
Province. The purpose of the new
factories is to provide scutching facilities
for flax, which, owing to lack of retting
facilities, many farmers will wish to dispose of in the green state. All arrangements are already in an advanced state,
contracts have been placed and work has
already been started. The Government is
confident that when these new units are
in operation the facilities, taken as
whole, will be adequate to deal with the
entire 1941 crop.
The Estimates themselves do not
include any monetary provision for the
expenditure involved which will be met
through the medium of advances from the
Imperial Department concerned.
The problem to which I have recently
devoted the major portion of my time is
that of bringing our surplus labour back
into productive work. Manufacture for
the export trade can provide some outlet,
but hon. Members will readily realise that
difficulties of transport and raw materials
militate against expansion in that field at
the present time. Industry must, therefore, in the main concentrate on the production of goods vital to the national
effort. If I refrain from describing in
detail the steps being taken to achieve
the end in view, hon. Members will readily
understand my reasons. If, however, any
hon. Member would care to go more fully
into any aspect of this question or to
make suggestions as to how the productive
capacity and the labour resources of our
area could be more adequately utilised I
shall be glad to talk matters over with
him. For the moment, suffice it to say
that while vigorous steps have been
taken towards a concerted effort designed
to secure the utilisation of both our latent
productive capacity and available labour,
much yet remains to be done. This is
receiving my unremitting attention.
I should like to conclude on a personal
note. At the beginning of the war I
appealed to the farmers of Northern Ireland to do not only their share but more
than their share in the war work that lay
before them. Their response was truly
magnificent. The quota of arable land
which should have been ploughed in Northern Ireland was 150,000 acres. Instead, the
farmers put forward all their energies
with the result that they ploughed no less
than 270,000 acres over and above their
requirement. That was a magnificent
effort, and it is useless to say it was easily
done. Many farmers made a very
definite sacrifice. There were many
difficulties to be surmounted. To my mind
if the rest of the United Kingdom had
responded in the same way as the farmers
of Northern Ireland responded the food
position in this country would have been
a great deal easier.
We are fighting in a total war, and I
want now to make the same appeal to the
industrialists and employees in Northern
Ireland as I made to the farmers at the
beginning of the war. I know that each
individual must think for himself and
must look forward to the future. I would
ask the industrialists not to let their
vision of the future prevent their carrying out the urgent war work which is
before them. I would ask them, even
perhaps at inconvenience or loss to themselves, to do nothing which would reduce
the output from their factories, because if
this war is lost there will be no factories
and the work they may be doing will be
for Germany and not for their own
country.
I would ask the workers, too, to look
at this question as part of their contribution to the war effort. I am sure that
the Members read Mr. Bevin's speech the
other day referring to our German visitor,
Rudolf Hess. Mr. Bevin is a great
figure in the trade union world. He said
that Rudolf Hess was one of the people
who got hold of the membership card of
every trade unionist in Germany, and
then those who were trade unionists were
either put to death or sent to concentration camps.
Mr. Bevin knows the efforts
which our workers made in many years
past in order to establish their position.
They are fighting now for that position
and in order to keep the trade union
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
20 MAY 1941
movement going ahead. If we lose this
var all those privileges for which they
have fought and which they have got will
disappear.
I ask the workers of Northern Ireland,
even though there may at times be difficulties, to let those difficulties be settled
rather than to go slow or go on strike.
They will help not only themselves in
their war effort but they will help me in
my effort to get more work for them and
for the industries of this country, because
unless I can show that the output from
the various tools and machines in
Northern Ireland is as good as that in
England I have no case when I go over
to London to fight their battles. There
are difficulties, as hon. Members are quite
aware, in getting work here. Unfortunately the sea lies between us and our
raw material. That means that the raw
material has to be handled twice or three
times, or perhaps four times, while in
England it would be handled only half
that number of times.
Unless I can show that the workers of
Northern Ireland are capable of putting
through a bigger output of war work, I
consider I should be wrong in urging that
the machines should be sent across the
water in the country's interests I must
take the long view. Therefore, I appeal
to them and to the manufacturers to do
all they can; in fact, to do what the
farmers have done in Northern Ireland.
They must do their share and more than
their share in the great work that lies
ahead of us. That is all I have to say.
I do not wish to appear to be preaching,
but I feel this so strongly that I have no
hesitation in making this appeal, feeling
confident that every man in Northern
Ireland, for his country's sake, will make
the biggest effort possible. I beg to move.
Mr. JOHNSTON: It is with the
greatest pleasure that I have heard, and
I am sure the Committee has heard, this
speech from the Minister of Commerce.
It is unfortunate that the report of his
first year should be made in a war year,
and that the efforts of the right hon.
Gentleman should have been divorced
from commerce and peace pursuits to
those of war. The Ministry of Commerce
is not a warlike Ministry. It is a Ministry
of peace, and yet this Estimate is entirely
devoted to war. That is contradictory in
terms.
There is just one point to which I would
like to draw the attention of the Minister
and of the Committee. The right hon.
Gentleman had a tremendous lot of praise
for the farmers and for the amount of
work they have done in ploughing up
extra land in order to provide food for
our people. He said they ploughed much
more than they were required to do and
had done excellently, and yet there was
an innuendo that traders, manufacturers,
and operatives were not doing their share.
I would like to contradict that as far as
my knowledge goes. The industrialists
and workmen are doing their share as far
as they are abie, but their share is limited
to the amount of supplies they can get.
Personally, my own plant is very often.
held up and disorganised for the want
of material. We are supposed to be a
linen manufacturing concern, and yet I
have not 20 per cent. of linen on my looms
to-day. While we are working the rest of
them on cotton we are very often idle and
standing still because the cotton cannot
come from Lancashire. That is not the
industrialists' fault. I would say it was
rather the fault of the Ministry of Commerce in not getting the stuff across a
little better. Therefore, if the Minister
of Commerce says the industrialist is not
doing his best I would say the Ministry of
Commerce are not doing their best in
seeing that these delays do not take place.
I know that the ship does not always get
there and that transport is not all that
it should be. We have to wait until at
length the material comes forward, and
then we start. I believe the Minister to
be quite wrong in asserting or thinking
that the operatives or the employers are
not doing the best they can.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: If the hon.
Member would allow me, I would like to
point out that I did not assert that. I
merely asked them to do the best they
possibly could. I know their difficulties
perfectly well.
Mr. NIXON: This is the first Estimate
the Minister has introduced in his present capacity. He has now the assistance
of a Parliamentary Secretary. I have
found very great energy in the Parliamentary Secretary in regard to his work as
assistant to the Minister. I brought two
things of public interest under his notice
and he dealt with both of them with great

promptitude. He did not say the matter
was being considered and he did not say
He said that
they were taking steps.
steps had been taken, and so they had.
There is no use in coming here and saying,

We
have heard that too often for years and

Then the Minister told us he is going

whether or not it is the Ministry of

I do not know. It is no use putting

The Minister also told us he was taking

What the Minister said about the war

and, as far as I am concerned, I would

not be their fault if the war is not won.
If some of them are not working it is
not their fault, and it is up to the Ministry to see they get transport that will
enable them to go to and from their

Of course, it would not do if there was
not a large increase in the staff of the
Ministry, and a very large increase in
the salaries. Generally speaking, if you
take the Estimates when they are first

does not look very big. But I have been
in this House since 1929, and I know that
this Estimate is not by any means final.
It is merely intended to get us through
to-day. There will be another Estimate
later on, and maybe another one on top

support of my statement about the very

If you look to see where this increase
took place you will find that last year
there was one assistant secretary, and now
there are two. If you turn over to the
column dealing with salaries you will find
that last year the one assistant secretary
got £1,150, and now the. two are getting
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
20 MAY 1941
between them £2,692. If you divide that
by two it works out at £1,300 and something each. That is to say that, not alone
has the number of assistant secretaries
been doubled, but the salary of the existing
assistant secretary and the new assistant
secretary has been increased by a couple
of hundred pounds a year, according to
the Estimate.
When you come to Commerce,
Economic, and Fisheries Branch you find
that last year, 1940-41, there were three
Principals at £2,456, and this year there
are four at £3,401. A thousand a year
is considered no salary at all for a man
here, we are such a very wealthy country,
and yet you have our glorious pilots who
won the first battle of Great Britain last
September, five miles up in the air, the
men we are always praising, shooting
down Germans for two or three pounds
a week. Yet the gentlemen here, who
already get a salary of over £1,000 a
year, receive an increase amounting to
more than one of these gallant fellows gets
altogether. Is it any wonder that things
are going the way they are? No, it is
not.
Then you have the Staff Officers. There
was one in 1940-41, and he got £525.
Now you have four getting £2,255. In
addition you have a new job, a lady Staff
Officer, or, as they put it here, staff
officer, woman, £392. Of junior staff
officers you formerly had three, and that
number has jumped to six. The post of
exhibition officer has been discontinued.
There are no exhibitions now, except that
you might call this an exhibition of
extravagance, making more jobs and
bigger salaries, but you would not want
to show that up. Senior clerks have
increased from three to five. There is a
decrease, from six clerks to two, but you
have fifteen new temporary clerks
appointed.
Every time these Estimates come before
the Committee we see a great increase in
staff and a great increase in salaries. That
goes on all the time, and wherever and
whenever it is going to end I do not know.
I do not want to belittle the Minister at
all. He is putting forth a brave lot of
energy for a start, and he may not be
personally responsible for some of the
matters I have drawn attention to. But
one cannot help comparing this war with
the last war.
In the last war we had no
Ministry of Commerce at all in this
country. We had no assistant secretaries
or staff officers, or even a woman staff
officer, and yet we got on,
shall I say,
better than we are getting on now.
It is no privilege to me to expose these
things. A junior Member of the Government, who certainly does very well in his
own Department-I refer to the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Labour-suggested last week that Parliament should close altogether for the
duration of the war. I do not know
whether that inspiration came from
higher Government sources or not. It
might be very convenient for Ministers
not to have to face this very limited
criticism.

PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF

for the duration of the war. I said it
should close in the meantime. I would
strongly object to closing Parliament for

Mr. NIXON: I cannot say that you
have improved your original statement
very much. If I am talking about the
war and I say we should close Parliament in the meantime I wonder what you
would think I meant. I am not going to
contradict the Parliamentary Secretary
when he says he only meant to close Parliament in the meantime, but I do not
know what interpretation he puts on "in
the meantime." If I am talking about
the war and I say we should close Parliament in the meantime, everyone would
think I meant to close it for the duration
of the war. I am glad to know from what

Parliament is not going to be closed. I

If I waded all through these Estimates

I have already referred to, of people

I have already drawn attention to sufficient to expose what goes on all the time.

my position here as a representative of

Mr. SPEAKER: Before calling upon
hon. Members to ask questions I have
with the greatest regret to report to the
House the death of Mr. McAleer, the
hon. Member for Mid Tyrone. Those
who knew him as long and as well as I
did will have appreciated his quiet and
kindly disposition. I must here add a
personal note, that I myself always
appreciated very much indeed his perfectly correct attitude towards the Chair.
I am sure the whole House will join with
me in extending our sincerest sympathy
to his relatives.

civilian use through the normal trade
channels, but applications are considered.
only from persons who can show that

national interest.

Transport and arrangements have been
made whereby Northern Ireland applications must be transmitted to the Ministry
of Transport through my Ministry.

Mr. BARBOUR: Insurance of commodities under the War Risks Insurance
Act, 1939, is compulsory in the case of

Traders whose stocks are for any reason

business equipment and private chattels

Assistance Board to small traders who are
not insured, and, accordingly, I do not
consider that representations to the

purpose.
Question of Conscription.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME
MINISTER.
Mr. DOWLING (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether he has
any statement to make with regard to the
application of conscription to Northern
Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: I observe
that in the Dail yesterday Mr. De Valera
and representatives of the opposition
parties referred to the question of applying compulsory military service
to
Northern Ireland. In my opinion this
was an unwarrantable interference.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Northern
Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Its constitutional position has been clearly
defined and established by Statute
Therefore, all matters connected with
Northern Ireland are completely outside
the jurisdiction of the Eire Government.
and So they shall remain. (Hon
Members: Hear, hear.)
On behalf of the Government of
Northern Ireland I repudiate the claim
of Mr. De Valera to speak in the name
of the people of this area. We in Ulster
desire that the. relationship between Eire
and ourselves shall be that of friendly
neighbours. But this is only possible if
each Government scrupulously refrains
from intervention in the affairs of the
other. Instead of this Mr. De Valera,
by his attitude towards Northern Ireland,
maintained throughout a long period of
years, has aroused bitterness and
animosity which I personally deplore.
A few days ago Mr. Churchill asked
me to cross to London to confer with him
on the desirability of applying universal
service to Northern Ireland similar to
that in the rest of the United Kingdom.
My colleagues and I have always felt that
conscription is the only fair method of
recruitment for the Forces of the Crown.
It places all classes and creeds on the
same level and each man is told just
where his duty is, whether it is in the
fighting forces of the Crown, in the
workshop making the indispensable.
implements of war, or on the farm producing the necessities of life.
It is obvious that total warfare such
as our Empire is experiencing can only
be met by every citizen playing his or
her part in the defence of home and
country. I have always stood for equality
of treatment throughout the United
Kingdom. When receiving the advantages of our citizenship within the
Kingdom we cannot do otherwise than
accept the liabilities and responsibilities
associated with the position.
man
It must be apparent to everyone that
before our Empire is a gigantic task
which will demand the courage and
sacrifice of us all. I am sure there is no
or woman amongst us who would
listen, for even a moment, to any whisper
of surrender to the forces of evil which
have brought about this deplorable and
appalling war, which is being waged by
our foes with cruelty and severity beyond
words to express and never previously
experienced in the world's history.
All classes suffered from the recent
barbarous air raids; the bombs made no
distinction. We are all in this togetherdistress and tribulation have been the
common lot. Everyone is in the front
line, and surely there is no one so selfish
and depraved that he would be unwilling
to play his part. We must stand together
Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
27 MAY 1941
and work together with all our strength
until victory comes. The fighting forces
want more men. From our industrial
establishments the nation requires still
more output. The defence service is the
duty of the whole community and must
not be left to a public-spirited few.
I have just heard that Mr. Churchill
has announced to-day that the Imperial
Government has decided not to apply conscription to Northern Ireland at present.
This decision will be loyally accepted by
the people of Ulster, I am sure, as having
been taken by those in the best position
to decide what is most likely to further
the Empire's struggle for justice and
freedom.
