Estimates-
Houses of Parliament
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
Now that guineas are being paid I
find that people want to get on these
Committees, apparently to get the
guineas. (Official Report, vol. XXI,
col. 1470.)
If that is what the guineas are for I
object to them. I object to the payment
of those guineas because it puts more
power into the hands of the Chief Whip
and into the hands of one party. Already
41 per cent. of the Unionist Members are
in Government positions. The last committee appointed consisted of 11 members.
and nine of the 11 were Unionists. The
Chief Whip says he is annoyed with them
following him, apparently to get guineas.
It puts power into the hands of the Chief
Whip which should not be there, that is,
if his own statement is correct, and I am
sure it is.
I have been in Parliament since 1929,
and I was induced to go on one committee
for which guineas were paid. I took the
guineas. That was the Transport Committee. I thought when I was going on
that Committee it would be able to do
good, but all our labour was in vain. The
report was shelved by the Government and
the guineas were lost to the taxpayers. I
declined to act on the next committee
when I was asked to become a member. I
am willing to go on any committee provided this provision is deleted. Whatever you are going to give an M.P., be
the same more or less, give it to him. I
do not care if you make it more, I do not
care if you make it less, but I object to
giving it to him on condition that he
accepts two guineas every time he does
certain committee work.
Lest there be any mistake I would point
out that the only committees that this
applies to are Parliamentary Committees
set up by this House. It does not apply
to a departmental committee. When it
does not apply to a departmental committee why should it apply to the other
committee? I know that at present there
are Members sitting on that side, and on
this side, too, who are members of committees for which there are no guineas. I
do not want to be misunderstood. I am
referring only to committees covered by
this minute which I am criticising.
We claim that we are following in the
footsteps of the Imperial Parliament, the
Mother of Parliaments. In this respect
we have departed from the footsteps of
the Imperial Parliament, and departed
for what? For guineas, which are in the
gift of the Chief Whip. I object to that.
The Prime Minister a few moments ago
was extolling our relations with the
Imperial Parliament and our determination to maintain those relations. I
endorse that statement-

I
Mr. NIXON- -but I want to follow

want to follow it all the time, and if the

Firstly, hon. Members will have

formerly borne on the Ministry of Commerce Vote, and it is, therefore, not a new
item but a transfer from one Vote to
another. Hon. Members will also be aware
that since these Estimates were prepared
we have learnt with regret of the death
of the distinguished officer who filled this
post. It is not proposed to replace him.
in the meantime, but rather to make
other arrangements for the carrying on
of the valuable work with which he was

eventual saving under this head which
should permit of the final figures showing
a reduction as compared with last year.
Secondly, the staff of the Press Office
and Regional Office has been increased,
owing to the additional work which has
been thrown upon it. The recovery from
the Ministry of Information of its proportion of the expenditure on the staff
of the office, however, has also been increased. What is actually recovered.
from that Ministry is about threequarters of the salaries of the staff, together with a charge for centralised
services and for accommodation, etc.

I also notice in this Vote travelling,
etc., expenses of the Prime Minister and
of officers on departmental business, £500.
There is a motor-car and the wages of a
motor driver. The £500 covers travelling
expenses. Does it cover the travelling
expenses of the Prime Minister and the
other Cabinet Ministers on the futile excursion which they made to Westminster?
I do not know and I will not say anything about it at the present time. It is
a part of the policy of the Prime Minister
to approach the Prime Minister of the
Imperial Parliament occasionally, and to
make certain representations which he
might consider were the views of the
people he represents. But I would say
that any Member practically on that side
would be in an awkward position and
would have great difficulty in approaching
the Prime Minister of the Imperial Parliament, to wit, Mr. Churchill, because
they could not help thinking and he could
not help thinking of the time they organised to stone him out of the City of
Belfast. I am only using that argument
to show that their influence is bound to
be very slight, having regard to previous
mischievous propensities in that direction.
We come now to the £1,980 for Press
office and Regional Office in the Ministry
of Information. The Press officer gets
£800 per annum. He is supposed to find
out information in Northern Ireland. He
was just here a couple of years as editor
of the "Whig" when he got this job. The
same thing applies to his assistant. A
short time ago I asked whether any
Member or person other than a member
of the Press gallery had a right to make
notes. It shows you how little this officer
has to do. He sits there making notes,
although he will get the whole thing in
Hansard for threepence if he cares. That
is a good example of how these men spend
their time. Talk about conscription. One
of these officers is of military age. What
is he doing here? What is the idea of it
and what is at the back of it? You get
members of the Government to stand upthe Prime Minister said he wanted to
avoid politics while the war is on. The
other night I was reading one of the local
newspapers and it referred to the censoring of speeches made here. Everything
calculated to impair the political efficiency
and sway of the Government is cut out of
the Press. That is why that money is
being spent and for no other purpose.
There are not many here in this House
who have the courage to sit even as a
temporary opposition and they are getting
fewer. More than one Member has left
in despair and in disgust, and sometimes
you would be tempted to do the same.
But there are bigger issues at stake. The
longest night has a morning, and we have
experience of that to-day in a far bigger
issue than anything that can come up
here or anything that is in our power.
We know that and we hope to see an
Estimates-
Cabinet Offices
27 MAY 1941
improvement. The late Prime Minister
said distinctly and pledged himself that if
a second Press officer was appointed an
Ulsterman with a knowledge of Ulster
would receive the appointment. There
were 60 or 70 applications from Ulster
candidates, who were all from time to
time reporters in this House, and all were
weighed in the balance and found wanting. The weighmaster took his own
selection of the people he thought best
qualified to see that the Government and
their supporters got a good Press. That
is the beginning and the middle and the
end of everything here in Northern
Ireland. I am very sorry it should be so
having regard to the very serious position
of affairs outside.

by any chance would you see a reduction.

Reference was made by the last speaker

directors of railway companies? Such a

person, because after all the Prime

The CHAIRMAN: We cannot discuss

Mr. AGNEW: I feel that the salary

us take into consideration that he is also

coincides with his business, during the

he no longer has the confidence of the

If we come even to the question of the

We here, from time, to time at least, are

for the Members of the Opposition.
I feel that if I visited my constituents
and told them that the Cabinet was costing a sum of £12,179 they would be more
than surprised. They could hardly
believe it. When we, look at the so-called
sacrifices made by the Prime Minister we
must also look at the sacrifices made by
the people I represent as far as presentday conditions are concerned. There is a
very great need of levelling up. If the
Prime Minister is worth the salary he
receives I would ask him to take greater

note of those of us who reside outside

Major SINCLAIR: The hon. Member
for Shankill referred to the Prime
Minister's position here as a part-time
job. I think I ought to make it clear to
the Committee that the Prime Minister's
job is not by any means part-time. Not
only does he work during the ordinary
working hours of the day but he is frequently working for the benefit of Northern Ireland far into the night.
Reference was made to the size of the
salary the Prime Minister is receiving.
Not only does that cover certain expenses
of office, but in addition it is halved by
the operation of income-tax. I do not
think the responsibility of leadership
which the Prime Minister bears can be

Reference was also made by the hon.

the Ministry of Information pay about

GOVERNMENT HOSPITALITY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which

Major SINCLAIR: The amount which
is being asked for this year for the grantin-aid to the Government Hospitality
Fund is £350. In addition, there is a
balance in the fund left over from last
year of about £71. As I explained in
introducing the Supplementary Estimate
under this head, the token provision made
last year, together with the balance then
in hand, was found to be inadequate to
meet the hospitality which was extended
to important visitors crossing to Northern
Ireland in order to further the successful
prosecution of the war. Government
hospitality in wartime is required mainly
in connection with such visitors, and I
can assure the Committee that expenditure from the fund will be kept within
the narrowest limits. The total expenditure incurred last year was a little more
than £500 and full details will appear in
due course in the form of a note to the
Appropriation Accounts. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

31st March, 1941, due to the continuance

cannot be postponed indefinitely without

As to channel improvements, the
which the dipper dredger
"Leprechaun" and attendant craft have

were
deleted from the contract because
the material to be removed proving
impossible to dredge with the bucket
ladder dredgers employed by the contractor he claimed that the execution of
the designed work in these reaches necessitated rock removal methods, in payment
for which he was entitled to rock rate
which was approximately 16 times the

As it was considered that these reaches
could be dredged by the Ministry's own
dipper dredger at a cost very much below
contract rates for rock removal, certain
reaches, namely, four areas between Portglenone Bridge and Portna sluices, the
area immediately upstream of Movanagher
Weir, and areas above and below Carnroe
Weir, were omitted from the contract.
The different type of dredging plant
to be employed necessitated different
methods of disposing the dredged material
on the banks, and in order to execute the
work as economically as possible the new
channel to be excavated over these areas
was re-designed.
During the present year some 100,000
cubic yards (bulk computation) have been
dredged and deposited on dump, of which
total approximately 50,000 cubic yards
have been double-handled.
As to fisheries, commercial catches of
both salmon and eels were exceptionally
good during the past season and show
that the drainage works have not caused
any permanent deterioration in the value
of these two fisheries.
In regard to flood alleviation, three
winters have passed since the maximum benefits around Lough Neagh
could be achieved, and in all these three
seasons precipitation has been above the
normal, but in every case results have
been entirely satisfactory as on no
occasion has the level of the lough reached
the commencement of flood level and no
flooding attributable to high water levels
in the lough has occurred.
During the year under review
abnormally low river discharges were
experienced from the middle of May until
the end of September, during which
period discharge seldom exceeded 30,000
c.f.m and for a long time was only
15,000 c.f.m. This spell broke early in
October, and the past winter-though not
abnormally wet-has had periods of
heavy precipitation accompanied by a
rapid thaw following upon a severe
blizzard. The maximum level attained
by the lough is 52ft. 4ins. O.D. on the
21st December last, which is 1ft. 2ins.
below the commencement of flooding.
From daily records and observations it
is calculated that prior to the execution
of the works similar weather conditions
would have resulted in Lough Neagh
exceeding commencement of flood level
from the 12th November to the 9th
January, a consecutive period of 59 days,
and from the 5th February to the 8th
March, a consecutive period of 32 days,
that is, there would have been flooding
around Lough Neagh during 91 days.
The maximum level which Lough
Neagh would have reached is 55ft. O.D.,
when approximately 33,000 acres would
have been under water with a saturated
of approximately 50 per cent.
greater. I beg to move.

INSPECTOR OF MENTAL
INSTITUTIONS.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
name, address, age, place of birth, qualifications, and experience in mental work
of the doctor recently appointed by him.
as Inspector of Mental Institutions, and
at what university he graduated; how
many applications were received for the
position, and whether any of the candidates had longer experience; whether he
can state the names of those placed on
the short list, if any, and whether they
all complied with the terms of the advertisement; whether only one candidate was
accorded an interview, and, if so, why
none of the other applicants was interviewed.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The name of the
doctor whom I propose to appoint to the
vacant medical inspectorship in this
Ministry is Thomas William Harold Weir.
He is at present attached to the Joint
Counties Mental Hospital, Carnarvon,
North Wales, and his age is 32.
place of birth is Armagh. His qualifications are as follows:-
The
The degrees of M.B., B.Ch., B.A.O.,
Queen's University, Belfast, 1931. He
obtained the diploma of Psychological
Medicine (Conjoint Royal College of
Physicians and Surgeons of Ireland,
1932). He also obtained the diploma of
Public Health at Queen's University in
1934, and the degree of M.D. with commendation at Queen's University in 1935.
His experience in mental work is as
follows :
Assistant Medical Officer,
Armagh County Mental Hospital, for
over five years; Assistant Medical Officer,
County Mental Hospital, Melton, Woodbridge, Suffolk, for nearly two years;
-
Deputy Medical Superintendent, Joint
Counties Mental Hospital, Carnarvon,
for nearly three years, the position which
he still holds.
Applications were received from 17
candidates. No candidate considered to
be suitable for the position with qualifications equivalent to those of Doctor
Weir had longer experience in mental
treatment.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
it is not in the public interest to furnish
the information asked for in the last
portion of the question.
Mr. BROWN: The Minister says it is
not in the public interest to give certain
information. Am I not entitled to know
why only one candidate was interviewed?
Will the Minister please tell the House
that, or, if not, will he tell us what the
public interest has got to do with a question of information of this kind? Why
was only one of the applicants interviewed?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have the
responsibility of selecting the best officer
for this position. I have done so, and I
do not think it is necessary for me to go
into details of the method I took to find
out who was most suitable.

a full year, whereas in 1940-41 we only

This is a rough outline of the cost of
carrying on the services which affect the
lives and homes of the working masses in
this area of ours. The question that
naturally arises in the minds of those who
are interested in these services is—are we
getting efficient service? Are the people
being dealt with expeditiously, courteously
and, above all, sympathetically?
I think I can honestly say that the
services rendered in every department of
the Ministry of Labour are given wholeheartedly and unstintingly, and no words.
of mine are adequate enough to express
my appreciation of the work of the
officials especially during the very trying
period we have gone through.
Hon. Members will be familiar with the
legislative measures that have been introduced during the past year, so I need only
remind them of a few of the outstanding
and more important changes. Under the
general scheme of unemployment insurance
the weekly rate of benefit for men and
women was increased by 3s and for young
men and women it was increased by 2s.
At the same time the contribution rate
was increased by 2d, one penny for each
contributing party. The rate of dependants' benefit was increased in respect of
the first two dependent children from 3s
to 4s per week. Under the agricultural
scheme, the maximum weekly amount of
benefit was increased to 41s per week.
The weekly benefit rate was increased by
3s per week for men, and by 2s per week
for women, young men and young women.
The rates of contributions of these classes
were increased by d for each contributing
party. What was known as the continuity rule was altered to permit of the
payment of benefit in cases where the
claimant proved unemployment for two
days in any consecutive six.
I should like also to remind the
Committee that non-manual workers
earning between £250 and £420 per
annum were brought within the scope of
unemployment insurance. It seems rather
curious that, in spite of the publicity
given to this change at the time, it was
found necessary for our inspectors to
make special surveys in order to bring
the requirements of the Act to the notice
of those affected by it. I would specially
remind business and commercial concerns
who have in their employment men with
salaries ranging between £250 and £420,
and who have failed to insure them, that
they are violating the law, and it will be
my duty to take steps to enforce this
requirement.
The. Determination of Needs Act
largely removed causes of complaint
against the household means test by providing that, in assessing the needs of a
person living as a member of a household,
the only resources which will be
aggregated will be those of the applicant,
his wife (or her husband), and his or her
dependants; not, as formerly, the
resources of all members of the. household. These changes will apply, not only
to persons in receipt of unemployment
assistance, but to those drawing supplementary pensions, as will also the exemption of new money put into war savings.
some
These are some of the important
matters I thought it my duty to bring
before the Committee, but there are also
important concessions regarding
rent and an alteration which raises the
basic rate of assistance. from 24s to 26s
per week for man and wife. This came
into operation yesterday, the 2nd of
June, but it will require time to adjust
all the existing allowances to meet the
changed rules.
Everyone will agree that this tendency
to lessen hardship and to better the conditions of living for those on the lowest
rung of the ladder, is an effort on our
part to attack the scourge of poverty
and consequently improve the physical
and mental morale of our people.
this day of Christian civilisation we must
see to it that every applicant receives not
only sympathy but social justice.

Hon. Members will remember that the
contributory pensions scheme was amended
during the year so as to entitle a woman
to a pension at 60 if she is herself insured
or is the wife of an insured man who has
qualified for a pension at sixty-five. The
new provisions came into force on 1st
July, 1940. I am glad to say that 3,300
women became entitled to pensions on
their own insurance, and 2,800 on their
husbands' insurance, making a total of
6,100.
By the same Act supplementary
pensions were introduced. They became
payable as from 3rd August, 1940, to all
old-age pensioners, except blind persons,
and to widows over sixty in receipt of
widows' pensions. They were subject to
the same means test as that applicable
to unemployment assistance, which, as I
have just mentioned, has been amended
recently in their interests also. All male
pensioners over sixty-five and all women
pensioners over sixty are, therefore, entitled to a supplementary pension if they
are in need. Blind persons are excluded,
as they are provided for under the blind
welfare schemes of the various local
authorities. There are, roughly, about
33,000 supplementary pensions in payment.

Though the health benefits will be

many societies at the present are paying

increase, which I hope will be introduced

It is of the utmost importance at the
present time that production should go on
with the least possible interruption due
to trade disputes since every grain of
sand thrown into the machinery of production which is vital to our war effort
is damaging and slows up output. For
the purpose of adjusting such disputes I
made the Conditions of Employment and
National Arbitration Order (Northern
Ireland), 1940, which provided that disputes which could not be quickly settled
by negotiation or arbitration should be
referred for settlement to the National
Arbitration Tribunal, Northern Ireland.
This important body, whose decisions are
binding on all parties to a dispute, consists of a chairman, two other appointed
members, and two members selected from
panels representing employers and workers
respectively.
The country is indebted to three distinguished men, the Right Hon. Mr.
Estimates-

Justice Brown, K.C.; Mr. D. Lindsay

has so often delighted us in this

and appointed members on this tribunal.
without fee or reward of any kind. I
must also express our appreciation of the
equally generous action of some members
of the panels of representatives who returned their fees as a contribution to
the war effort, and my gratitude to the
employers and trade union representatives for their continued help.
The tribunal has so far adjudicated in
forty-eight disputes, affecting directly
over 12,000 people, and I do not think I
am going too far in saying that it commanded public confidence from the outset, and that its decisions have given
general satisfaction, leaving the parties.
concerned with the sense that they have
had a full hearing and an impartial
judgment.
And now I come to the final survey of
the work of our Department, the placing
of men in Great Britain.
Mr. HENDERSON: Now you are
talking.
Mr. GORDON: Throughout the year
there has been a constant demand from
Great Britain for skilled workers, and
men fit for outdoor labouring jobs.
Recently, also, men suitable for light
labouring in indoor factories have been
asked for in large numbers. It is our
privilege to help by meeting this demand
so far as we can and, at the same time,
we endeavour to ensure that the requirements of Northern Ireland, both present
and prospective, are not prejudiced by
the transfer of workers to Great Britain.
I have been much criticised in this
House for doing my duty in this
direction, and tales of hardship amongst
the transferred workers have been quoted
without, I am afraid, much inquiry on
the part of those who circulated them.
Whenever I have been given distinct
particulars of such allegations I have had.
them investigated, and in very few
instances indeed have I found any
substantial basis for the charges made
against me.
:

Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL: I intervene in the discussion because I wish to
introduce a matter which I consider of
material importance on the broad general
question, but may I, first of all, take the
liberty of congratulating the Minister of
Labour on his elaborate and instructive
statement. I should also like to compliment him on the sympathetic manner in
which he deals with the unemployed, the
down-and-outs, and on his courage in
making up his mind to do the right thing
and not allow his department to be
imposed upon.
I desire to bring forward a matter
which I mentioned on a previous occasion
-the question of what steps should be
taken to keep the unemployed fit for work
when it becomes available. After being
three or four years out of employment a
man becomes so feeble, weak, and practically without any muscular system that
when he gets a job involving a certain
amount of exertion he is really unable to
do it. I can sympathise with many men
who have to give up jobs for this reason.
I do not suggest army drill, but for an
hour or two on one, two or three days in
the week he should, under instruction, do
simple exercises which would keep him in
a fit condition. In my view it is the duty
of these men to keep fit; first, because of
their families, and, secondly, because of
their duty to the community.
The other point I want to draw attention to deals with national health insurance. I am aware that in this
matter we follow to
a large extent
the system existing in England, but
there are certain hon. Members who
think that we might with benefit
depart a little from that system. I had
the honour to be at the first representative meeting, held in London under
the chairmanship of Sir Victor Horsley,
to deal with this matter. Sir Victor was
Radical member for one of the London
divisions, and was chief adviser in
reference to the introduction of the
system. The interesting thing about it is
that when a man or woman gets seriously
ill they are dropped like hot cakes and
dumped on to the charitable public by
putting them in voluntary hospitals. The
work is left to the charitable public and
the voluntary staffs of the hospitals. At
first the insurance companies paid a trifle
towards the maintenance of these insured
people while in hospital, but they never
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
3 JUNE 1941
paid anything like what it cost to keep
them. At the present time only some
insurance companies pay anything.
The Royal Victoria Hospital receives
large numbers of these people, but it gets
nothing at all from the insurance
companies who intimated that they could
not do anything and left. The upkeep of
these people was left to the charitable
public, and they get the best medical
attendance and skill as long as they are
in hospital. They do not, however, pay
for it. The hospitals, therefore, reduce the
period of incapacity, and in doing so and
in arriving accurately at a decision as to
the man's treatment in a proper manner,
they are of enormous benefit to the insurance companies in getting them off the
sick roll. Yet the companies do not accept
any financial liability whatever-even an
enormously wealthy company like the
Prudential Insurance Company. Is there
any reason why the Royal Victoria
Hospital or any other hospital should do
the work in this way for these companies?
I know this is not a matter primarily to
be dealt with by the Ministry of Labour.
We can only follow step by step, but
perhaps we could introduce some system
that would be helpful to those across the
water. It was with a view to voicing
these two points that I rose to intervene
now. I feel they are two points of very
vital importance to the community.

On the administrative side I can and

ment. They are no more responsible

to endeavour as far as possible to have
men with a little degree of sympathy and
with a proper understanding of the local
conditions prevailing in a particular
district in which they operate. There are
still many anomalies in existence in so

far as unemployment is concerned. We

Take the question of married women.
Although they might have a splendid
record prior to their marriage they are
held up and disaliowed unless they can

before marriage. In some cases they may
be allowed. Something should be done
for people who have had long periods of
insurability. I notice also-and this has
always been a source of complaint with
me-that there are people in certain
departments of the Ministry who have
other sources of income. I find in the

£100, and a clerical assistant (grade II)
in receipt of £185 though holding another
post. In the inspection and investigating
officers' (pensions) section there is one
officer who is in receipt of a constabulary
pension. If we want to solve the question
of unemployment and give consideration
to the unemployed then no one in receipt
of a pension should be brought into the
service. I have always protested against
that and will continue to do so.
I believe there is room for improvement
in regard to the question of national health.
insurance because we find that the rates
of benefit paid by the various approved
societies are not uniform. The head of a
house who is ill may probably have to
exist on 15s a week or more according to
the society he belongs to, and his dependants suffer. The time has come when
the national health insurance scheme
should be overhauled and put on a proper
basis. We should have a State medical
service and cut out a lot of the anomalies
now in existence. Even the new changes
that may be brought into operation will
not bring added benefits to the extent we
desire. It means that if the head of a
home is ill, and in receipt of sickness
benefit he must in order to supplement
his income apply to the poor-law guardians
for support. There is no other avenue
left open. The Department and Government should give serious consideration to
the problem of national health insurance
and bring the scheme up to a standard
that will improve the conditions in respect
of both claimants and dependants. The
head of a house may be insured for benefit
and medical services. That only applies
to himself. Medical treatment should
apply to every member of his family and
the Government should take cognisance of
this fact and give the matter serious consideration.
We come now to the major problemthe problem of unemployment. We have
been told to-day that there has been a
reduction, but we have not been told the
actual figures. If there is a reduction in
the unemployment figures, I am afraid
it does not apply to my constituency or
the area in which I live. I would like
to see officials of the department going out
and having a proper survey in order to
see what can be done in the way of giving
work to our unemployed. I have always
asked for that. While we have such huge
unemployment in certain areas we cannot
find any prosperity. I come next to the
question of unemployment services and
grants to local authorities. I feel that
every assistance should be given to the
local authorities by way of grants for the
carrying out of schemes of public utility.
There are many local authorities who
require additional financial help, and I
appeal to the Minister to consider
seriously the question of increasing the
grants to local authorities. Many schemes
of public utility could be brought into
force.
I have spoken before on the question.
of sending our unemployed to Britain.
If the Government is really anxious to
bring prosperity to Northern Ireland, the
only way to do so is to endeavour to open
up our industrial life and provide work
at home. The amount of money likely
to be spent on sending our workers out of
this country comes to £44,000, while a
sum of £112,800 is estimated for the
training of unemployed persons. I would
like to know how much of that has been
spent in providing employment and training for workers in Northern Ireland. I
feel there is ample scope in Northern
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
Ireland to develop a scheme of training.
whereby our workers could be trained and
used when required. We cannot expect,

I made a protest here with regard to

say that through the representations made
to
the department concerned. great

possible conditions. That is what we are

he is actually placed in a position of

benefit at all. They would get money
from some source given for employment.
I am glad the hon. Member for South
Armagh raised this important question.
The day is not far distant after the war
when the pensionable age will be about
55. There is not the slightest doubt
about that, although the ex-Minister of
Labour, now the Prime Minister, told
us in this House we could not possibly
give another 5s to old-age pensioners.
Notwithstanding that statement some
of them are getting 14s and 15s a week
or even £1 a week. They will get more.
I hope the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary will bring forward a
scheme some day reducing the age to 55.
So far as we can see it is going to take
something like that to absorb the unemployed.
I myself along with the Ministers in
this Government could find useful employment for at least 8,000 able-bodied
men in Northern Ireland. Something
should be done besides paying out doles.
I will support the Parliamentary Secretary if he does something to reduce the
number of unemployed. The Minister
to-day quoted letters sent to him by
people who apparently were well treated.
I know we get dozens of letters complaining very bitterly about the terrible conditions under which some of them lived
in England during the past two years.
They were in starvation. I am glad to
know that is changed now. In any case
I think there is nothing to be proud of.
We are paying at least £3,000,000 in
public assistance and unemployment
benefit, and until that is stopped I will
always criticise the Minister of Labour.

am sure I share the view, not only of

The sending of workers across
water is undesirable. It may be. necessary at the present moment, but it is

is particularly

Mr. GRANT: I would just like at the
outset to say on behalf of the Ministry
that we appreciate very much the kind
words uttered by Members this afternoon.
This is about the only time during the
course of the year when we get any kind
words and we always look forward to this
particular occasion in connection with our
Estimates. The hon. Member for the
University raised the question of keeping
the unemployed fit. That is a question
that appeals to every Member. Personally I was very much interested in a
scheme for keeping the unemployed fit
that we had in the Ministry. Along with
we
the gentleman who is now Permanent
Secretary of the Ministry I devoted a considerable time in going round different
districts to find suitable places for these
men to get physical training. After a
good deal of difficulty we were able to
persuade the Minister of Finance, who is
now the Prime Minister, to allow us to
provide milk and biscuits for these people
who were training, but hon. Members
will appreciate that when the war broke
out we could not carry on the scheme
because conscription came into force in
England and people naturally thought
there were opportunities for this type of
men to keep physically fit in other
spheres. The scheme had, therefore, to
be dropped during the course of the war.
Another point the hon. Member
raised was the question of national
health insurance. He said that
should sometimes go ahead of Great
Britain. Anyone who has any idea of the
financial position of national health insurance here could never seriously suggest that
we should go ahead of Great Britain. It
is to our advantage to keep up with Great
Britain in connection with this scheme.
While I do appreciate what the hon.
Member and others have said about the
splendid work being done by
voluntary hospitals and I join in the
tribute paid-I am very much afraid the
time is not opportune for anything to be
done in that direction. I have been informed on reliable authority that some
approved societies paid and still pay
grants to hospitals. They did this out
of surplus funds. Now, of course, there
are no surpluses and they are not able to
carry that on. Some societies had to
decide between providing dental treatment to their members or giving grants
to hospitals. I think the majority of
our
the people favoured dental benefits, because there are not the same opportunities
for getting dental treatment as there are
of getting ordinary hospital treatment.
It is very regrettable that that state of
affairs should exist, but the fact remains
that it does exist, and we have to
admit it.
The hon. Member for Woodvale was
certainly very appreciative about the
Ministry in his remarks. He did not
really say anything of a critical nature
except to point out some small increases
from year to year. That point was also
stressed by other hon. Members. I am
perfectly certain that if they were
addressing election meetings in their own
constituencies they would have to face
up to this, that at least £18,000 of the
increase is due to war bonuses for the
lower grade clerical staff in the different
Ministries. I do not think even the
Member for North Down could criticise
that in his own constituency. As far as
I can see everybody at the present time,
except those in higher paid positions, is
getting a war bonus owing to the increased
cost of living. I think that is justifiable. In the other clerical positions
there are the usual annual increments. We are not really responsible
any more than other Members for these
increases. We are bound to say that we
appreciate that the persons receiving them
are justly entitled to them.
I am sorry the hon. Member for South
Armagh has gone. He raised quite a
number of questions. He referred to the
increases in travelling expenses, courts of
referees and umpire. I would point out
to him that we could reduce the amount
of expenditure in connection with these
different courts if he personally would
lay off. There is no man who takes more
interest in calling for these courts and
putting questions to the umpire than the
hon. Member. He claims that as a right.
It is his right and he is justified in
exercising it, but at the same time if he
increases the number of courts that would
normally be held and calls for umpires'
decisions probably more often than the
umpire might be called upon, he should
not object to the bill being paid.
The hon. Member raised the question
of the appointment of chairmen of courts
of referees and said that only people with
sympathetic natures should be appointed.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
3 JUNE 1941
I am afraid he is not in possession of all
the facts in connection with these appointments. I do not think I will be giving
a great deal away when I say that within
the last year we had to remove a person
from that position for the reason that
we thought he was not sympathetic
enough and did not go with an open mind
to his courts. Yet it is amazing the number of people who interested themselves
in this particular gentleman and protested.
against his removal. Up to the moment
the Minister has refused to allow this man
to preside over these courts.
We only
want these courts presided over by people
with open minds, who if they err will do
so on the side of sympathy with those who
are unfortunate enough to have to appear
before them.
I am sorry the Member for South
Armagh is not present when I am dealing
with my next point. I am afraid his
information was lacking on this question.
He dealt with certain people in the Ministry who held dual positions and instanced
the case of the officer in connection with
industrial relations who is in receipt of an
extra £100. I think he tried to leave the
impression on the Committee-rightly
from his own point of view-that this was
an instance of a man occupying two
positions. Anyone who has any experience of industrial relations in connection with the Government of Northern
Ireland will know, and I am sure if hon.
Members opposite in the Labour movement were present they would admit, that
this officer is one of the most capable men
we have in the Civil Service.
Our Ministry and the public at large
Owe
a great deal to the industrial
relations officer. I am not going to
mention his name. He is well known.
Hardly a week passes without our receiving either letters or verbal expressions
from those engaged in industrial disputes,
or the prevention of such disputes,
referring to the capabilities of this officer
and stating how fortunate the Ministry is
to have him. For many years he has
been in receipt of £100 over the salary
paid for the office he occupies, and I think
it quite right that that should be continued.
He is well qualified to fill many higher
offices, but we are very jealous of him in
our Ministry and we think we are fortunate in having him connected with it. I
am sorry the hon. Member for South
Armagh did not understand the position.
He also raised the question of national
health insurance and pointed out that
something would have to be done to
remedy the evils that exist in connection
with it. Now, the Minister in his speech
dealt very fully with the new legislation
brought into the Imperial House. Northern Ireland will be included in that, and
it will have a considerable bearing on the
benefits paid in connection with health
insurance. Personally, I agree in substance with the remarks of the hon.
Member for South Armagh. I always
thought that the health-insured person, if
anything, deserved more sympathetic and
more practical treatment than even the
unemployed person, because when a
person is ill, he really requires more
money to build himself up again than
a man who is ordinarily unemployed.
The hon. Member also threw out a
suggestion that the Minister of Labour
should have a survey of his particular
area, that is, South Armagh. He would
then see that the unemployment problem
had not been reduced very much in that
particular area. That is not a matter for
which the Minister of Labour is to blame.
There is an opportunity of reducing unemployment in South Armagh. I understand that His Majesty's Army is still
open to receive recruits at any time. Our
own Government tried to find work for
them by agreeing to conscription, but a
good many people in South Armagh were
not particularly favourable to it. Therefore the hon. Member cannot blame the
Minister of Labour in this case.
He also raised the question of training.
schemes and said that we should not send
trainees over to Great Britain. This is a
question about which I am very much
concerned. I am very much interested in
it, and while it may seem strange to hon.
Members opposite, I would point out that
I am a great believer in training schemes
in Great Britain. I realise that if we
send our young men to Great Britain and
get them trained in the training centres
there and I have had an opportunity of
seeing them myself there is certainly a
better prospect of those men getting jobs
over there than if we had training centres
in Northern Ireland. It is easy to say
that charity begins at home. We have
had experience in the Ministry of Labour
of training schemes, and hon. Members on
both sides of the Committee will recollect
that when we got some of our trainees
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
into engineering establishments in the
city the apprentices in those particular
establishments, who were far better
qualified workmen than the trainees but
received considerably less wages, went on
strike. And who is to blame them?
They had greater skill and could do better
work than the trainees; yet they were
receiving less pay.
That is one of the problems I could
always foresee would take place if we had
a training scheme in Northern Ireland. I
say without any hesitation that our trade
union movement in Northern Ireland,
taking it all over, is on a far stronger
basis than it is in Great Britain, and
there are not the same opportunities for
trainees to get into the establishments
here as there are in Great Britain. For
that reason, and many others, the
Ministry is certainly strongly in favour of
sending trainees to Great Britain, and so
long as the market there is open to
trainees and the present heads of the
Ministry of Labour are in office we will
send trainees to Great Britain.

matter of fact he stated quite plainly that

in the Ministry. When the Supplementary Estimates were before the Committee

We have very few permanent technical

The particular man referred to, I understand, was brought in because two of his

Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: I should like
to say a few words on the cost of administration.
hon.
Mr. SPEAKER : Does the
Member wish to speak on the Report of
the Resolution regarding Cabinet offices?
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Yes. I should
just like to say a word or two with regard
to the cost of administration. I am rather
appalled to find that the saving effected
through the voluntary offer of the Prime
Minister to do without the allowances for
contingencies of office has been more than
nullified by increases that have been
made, and that there is actually an increase in this Vote of £700 or £800. I
suggest to the Prime Minister and to the
House that this represents a trend which
has got to be very seriously curbed. I
stated in Committee of Supply this afternoon that I was in this House largely
owing to the effects of unemployment.
There is also the very serious issue of the
trend of increases in the cost of general
administration. I desire to point out that
the reduction made by the voluntary act
of the Prime Minister has been more than
wiped out by increases in other directions.
In fact the whole Vote as it stands to-day
is really £700 or £800 more than that of
last year despite the voluntary reduction
made by the Prime Minister. One of the
Members of this House said in May last:
I think all Members of the Committee realise that there is a feeling in
the Province that the cost of governing
a population of a million and a quarter
is too heavy.
More recently another Member, speaking
on the same subject, said:
The cost of the services of this
country has increased enormously and
I am not putting it too high when I
say that we are, in proportion to our
population, the most expensively
governed country in the world.
Mr. SPEAKER: I should explain to
the hon. Member for North Down that on
the Report Stage of the
the Estimates
Members can discuss only the items in the
Estimates. The procedure is that the
whole range of policy can be discussed in
Committee, but when the Votes come to
the Report Stage only the specific items
mentioned in the Estimates can be
debated.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: You will realise
that, being a new Member, I must take
some time before I become fully acquainted
with the procedure. I will content myself
by saying that the present existence of
war conditions does impose a heavy
burden upon the executives of the various
Departments, and in making any charges
with regard to the cost of administration generally I do realise that they
are up against exceptional difficulties;
still, I should like to express the hope
that in the midst of this war effort the
executives of certain Departments will
exercise the most stringent economy.
That is all I want to say.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): In reply to the hon.
Member for North Down I may recall
that in introducing this Vote. I explained
that the Liaison Officer had unfortunately
died since the Estimate was prepared,
and that it was not proposed to replace
him, but to make some other arrangement for carrying on the excellent work
which he did on behalf of the Government. The saving effected through the
Prime Minister's public-spirited action as
shown in the Estimates is for a period of
eight months; the actual saving will
amount to £2,000.

Oral Answers to Questions.
COLLECTION OF KITCHEN
WASTE.
(By
1. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Commerce whether, owing
to persons collecting waste food from
towns, villages and other places in Northern Ireland without having the necessary
equipment to convert it into food suitable
for feeding pigs and poultry, he is prepared to set up a Waste Food Board to
supervise the collection and treatment of
this kitchen waste; whether he is prepared to set up processing plants in
every town and village of reasonable
size, as is being done in England; and
whether he is aware that large accumulations of this food are occurring in
certain towns, thereby causing a grave
menace to the health of the people.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): My Ministry is in
close touch with the Salvage Department of the Ministry of Supply and is
negotiating with that department for the
installation of one or more concentrator
plants in Northern Ireland at centres
where their use would be economic. In
view of the relatively small tonnage of
kitchen waste available in this area, I do
not consider it necessary to set up a
separate Food Waste Board for Northern Ireland.
I have no information to show that
accumulations of kitchen waste in Northern Ireland towns are causing a nuisance.
I have, moreover, been given to under-

stand that a keen demand for pig feed
exists. If, however, any nuisance arises
from such a cause, the local authority has
adequate powers to deal with the matter.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY: Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that a number of
people who are collecting this waste
destroy it?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not
aware of that.
ALLOCATION OF GOVERNMENT
ADVERTISING.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can explain the
allocation of advertising amongst papers
circulating in Fermanagh and Tyrone,
whereby the Nationalist weekly Press representing the vast majority of the people,
receives only a relatively small proportion
to that given to the Government party
organs; whether advertising from the
Department of Agriculture for the four
weeks ending 31st May was "Fermanagh
Times" (Unionist) 93 single column
inches; "Impartial Reporter" (Unionist)
102 inches, and "Fermanagh Herald'
(Nationalist) 18 inches; whether the
Government does not require Nationalists
to "Cut more turf" when it appeals so
extensively to Unionists and so sparsely
to Nationalists, and whether the Minister
asked for any circulation certificate for
the two Unionist papers, and if so, can he
state the details; whether the circulation
of the "Herald" is at least 2 times that
of the "Times," and whether the "Times"
prints many Government pamphlets and
reports without the Government having
asked for tenders.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The question of the distribution of Government advertisements to the
various newspapers in Northern Ireland
has always been one of considerable
difficulty. Some years ago newspaper
representatives were requested to suggest
some system-other than inserting advertisements in
every newspaper-which
would ensure that fair play was given to
everybody, and that no newspaper would
have any reasonable cause for complaint.
This request was not complied with, and
since then the Ministry has endeavoured
to divide the advertisements among as
many newspapers as possible, but obviously
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
10 JUNE 1941
every advertisement from Government
Departments cannot be inserted in every
newspaper in the Province. This would
entail a considerable waste of public
moneys.
The course adopted by the Government
after obtaining advice was to select newspapers with the best circulation. These
were placed on a roster which is kept in
my Ministry, and it is from this roster
that selection is primarily made. It is,
of course, necessary from time to time, to
meet Departmental requirements, to
advertise in other newspapers to ensure
wider publicity. The roster has been
formed in order to secure a fair distribution of advertisements, and if any paper
can prove that it has a circulation higher
than that of another paper in the same
area, the Ministry would feel justified in
giving weight to its representations.
The "Fermanagh Times" holds certain
printing contracts, which were placed
after competitive tenders had been invited.
by advertisement. The "Fermanagh
Herald" did not tender.
I must, however, add as a general
observation, that the political views of the
newspapers concerned do not in any way
affect the allocation of advertisements,
which are placed with the object of getting
the best results.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the right
hon. Gentleman say if the "Impartial
Reporter," one of the three newspapers
named in my question, is a non-union
printing office?
Has the "Fermanagh
Times," another newspaper named in the
question, notified its workers that it has
ceased to be a union office, and are its
workers out in consequence, and is the
"Fermanagh Herald" the third newspaper named, the only paper in County
Fermanagh which observes trade union
conditions in regard to the staff?
Mr. BARBOUR: I am not informed
on that.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the right hon.
Gentleman tell me if the Government
stipulate in advertising contracts for the
"fair wages" clause?
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think that
arises out of the right hon. Gentleman's
reply. I think the hon. and learned
Gentleman would be well advised to put
down another question.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Disappointed as I
am with the reply I will raise this matter
on the adjournment.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask what right
has the hostile Press that the hon. and
learned Member for Central refers to, to
expect patronage from the Government of
Northern Ireland?
LIABILITY FOR GROUND RENT.
3. Mr. DOWLING asked the Attorney-
General whether the Government is in a
position to make a statement as to
whether owners of industrial, commercial, or house property destroyed by
enemy action are responsible for payment of ground rent until such times as
the buildings have been restored after
the war.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): The liability of Owners of
property destroyed by enemy action for
payment of ground rent will depend on
the terms of the contract of tenancy contained in the lease or grant under which
the property is held. Unless, however,
the lease or grant contains provisions of
a very unusual nature, I think it may
be taken that the destruction of the
buildings on a piece of ground will not
in general entitle the owner to suspend
payment of the ground rent.
The hon. Member will be aware that
the English Landlord and Tenant (War
Damage) Act, 1939, contains elaborate
provisions as to the courses which may be
pursued by tenants of property rendered
unfit by reason of war damage, and that
the Minister of Home Affairs has announced in this House the intention of
the Government to introduce legislation
on similar lines during the present
Session.
CHARGES ON BLITZED PROPERTY.
4. Mr. DOWLING asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government will
fix the rate of interest on loans or debentures charged on blitzed property so
that the amount payable will not exceed
the amount to be received from the
Government, viz., 2 per cent. on the
capital value of damage to property
caused by enemy action.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply. The

PRODUCTION OF POTATOES.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
quantities of potatoes produced in each

Lord GLENTORAN: The last season
for which details of the quantities of

for publication is 1938. The figures for

ARMAGH COUNTY COMMITTEE OF
AGRICULTURE.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to the report in the Press
that the Armagh County Committee of
Agriculture at its last meeting discussed
the question of resigning in a body as a
protest against the Ministry's refusal
to make such a very old-established
fair centre as Newtownhamilton a cattle
grading centre; whether similar dissatisfaction exists in many parts of
County Down owing to the fewness of
grading centres and whether a request
from the old-established fair centre of
Hilltown for a grading centre for sheep
on at least two or three days in the whole
year has been repeatedly turned down;
and whether he will take the necessary
steps to remedy these, grievances.
Lord GLENTORAN: I have seen the
report referred to by the hon. Member,
and I am fully aware of the circumstances
in which it has been found impracticable
to accede to the request that Newtownhamilton should be made a centre for the
purchase of animals under the Meat and
Livestock Scheme.
Oral Answers
Sittings of the House
10 JUNE 1941
It will be obvious that the Ministry
would not be right in approving of a
centre if the number of animals likely to
be presented for purchase. there were not
sufficient, having regard to neighbouring
centres, to justify the appointment of
additional officials and the expense of
operating the additional centre..
In the case of Newtownhamilton, it is
to be regretted that the Markets
Committee proceeded with their scheme.
for the erection of a weighbridge despite
letters from the Ministry intimating to
them that the numbers of animals likely
to be presented at Newtownhamilton were
not sufficient to justify its inclusion as a
purchasing centre. This view was
naturally greatly strengthened by the fact
that there were already purchasing
centres at Keady, Markethill, Camlough,
and Crossmaglen, all within some eight.
miles of Newtownhamilton.
As regards Hilltown, as the hon.
Member has been informed, the facilities
available there for the purchase of sheep
are quite inadequate and, furthermore,
the existence of centres at Newry and
Rathfriland precludes justification of
the expense of additional officials for a
centre at Hilltown. Also there would be
serious transport problems to be overcome even if other circumstances
rendered the inclusion of Hilltown a
practicable proposition. I am sure that
the hon. Member will agree that in
present circumstances the unnecessary
employment of road transport is to be
deprecated.
I am not aware of anything in the
nature of general dissatisfaction with
regard to the number of purchasing
centres either in County Down or in the
Province as a whole. The hon. Member
will understand that to set up additional
centres must add greatly to the expense
of administration.
Mr. BROWN: Would the Minister
not agree with me that the fewness of
the centres necessitates increased transport on the part of the farmers, as well
as the waste of their time?
Lord GLENTORAN: No, it largely
depends if the centres are natural
centres for transport where there are
railway stations and other facilities and
where we want the actual animals to go
forward for slaughter.
Personal Explanation by Mr. Grant.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
Labour (Mr. Grant): I have your permission, Mr. Speaker, to make a personal explanation regarding the part of
my speech in this House on Tuesday
last, in which I mentioned the name of
the Very Rev. Dr. Woodburn, the ex-
Moderator of the General Assembly.
Hon. Members will recall that in the
course of my reply to the debate on the
Estimates of the Ministry of Labour I
referred to Dr. Woodburn's valedictory
address as Moderator.
My statement this afternoon must be
non-controversial, and I have no desire,
even if I had the opportunity, to deal
with the points on which Dr. Woodburn
and I hold different opinions. I recognise, however, that in the course of my
reply, which was necessarily made without much time for preparation, I used
certain words which were not justified,
and, standing in the place where I made
my original statement, I wish to take
this, the first available, opportunity, to
express my sincere regret to Dr. Woodburn for any pain I may have caused
him.
I have the highest personal regard for
Dr. Woodburn, who has rendered long
and distinguished service to the Church
to which I myself belong, and I hope this
explanation will be accepted in the spirit
in which it is offered.
I should like to add that I decided upon
the course I have adopted upon my own
responsibility and without regard to outside influences. I think I can claim that
I have always had the courage of my
convictions, which involves not only
standing up for what I believe to be right
but making amends as far as possible if
I have erred. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.).
I thank you for giving me the opportunity to make this personal explanation,
and hon. Members on both sides of the
House for their indulgence.
Sittings of the House.
QUESTION OF SECRET SESSION.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House, at its rising this day,
do adjourn until Tuesday next."-(Lord
Glentoran.)
Sitting of the House-
Secret Session
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. HENDERSON: I rise to protest
against the adjournment of the House
until Tuesday next. Members sitting on
the back benches behind right hon.
Gentlemen and Members on this side have
asked for a secret session to enable them
to discuss matters of vital interest in
connection with the affairs of this
country. There are many things we do
not like to raise in public. For some
reason best known to the Prime Minister
he absolutely refused to allow this House
to sit in secret session to discuss these
matters.
If the Prime Minister of Great Britain,
in the interests of the State, thinks it
necessary to have a secret session, I cannot
understand why our Prime Minister will
not allow us to have one here. There are
many things that could be discussed, and
many things that could be said in the best
interests of the country. I do not wish
to raise any controversial subject, such as
was mentioned by the hon. Member who
has just sat down. It is true to say, at
least I am told on reliable authority, that
messages are now transmitted by telephone via Dublin to Belfast. Imagine
important messages being sent through a
country which is infested with Nazi spies
and where the wires could be tapped. If
that state of affairs exists, it is a serious
matter which should not be tolerated at
all.
I am also given to understand that
even the mails come now to Belfast via
Holyhead and Dublin. It is a serious
matter that important documents for
Northern Ireland should come through
Dublin, the capital of a country which
to-day is in the same position as Italy,
endangering not only the lives of their
own people but the lives of Northern
Ireland men and women. Things are in
such a state in the Free State that the
leaders there are going to drive the people
into starvation unless something is done.
I have the feeling, as more distinguished
men than I am have, that the Battle of
Britain will take place in Southern
Ireland. You know the conditions that
are likely to prevail then. People coming
from the Free State into Northern Ireland
may be asked to show their identity cards,
but they can come in here without any
passport at all. To all intents and purposes it is the same as Italy. Why should
we sit idly by and not protest to the
British Parliament that a country that
is part of the Commonwealth should be
allowed to house Italians and Germans
who are murdering the people of this
country?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
making a speech on the points he has
raised. It is sufficient to mention his
points and not elaborate them.
Mr. HENDERSON: That is one of my
reasons for a secret session. Another
important reason is that thousands of
Northern Ireland people have gone to
England and Scotland to work, and it is
absolutely impossible for most of these
young men and women to get travel
permits to come back even for a holiday
in their own country. Why such restrictions should be placed on Northern
Ireland is more than I can understand. I
think the Prime Minister should get in
touch with the British Parliament in
order to see if travelling facilities cannot
be afforded to loyal citizens or munition
workers who wish to visit their brothers
and sisters on this side. There is a great
deal of dissatisfaction in all parts of
Northern Ireland on this matter.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not wish to
interrupt the hon. Member, but he is
going too far. It is easy for him to refer
to his points. He can mention the
subjects, but to debate them is not in
order.
These are some
Mr. HENDERSON:
minor things. There are many important
matters that Members might be able to
assist the Prime Minister on. There are
other vital matters we do not like to raise
in open House. I appeal to the Prime
Minister to give one day to discuss these
matters.
The PRIME MINISTER: As far as
possible it is my wish to meet the wishes
of hon. Members of this House, but the
hon. Member is in error in saying that I
absolutely refused to give a secret session
when the matter was raised on a former
occasion. He did not inform me that he
intended to raise the question again today; but if he will read what I said on
the former occasion he will see that what
I said was that under the conditions then
existing I did not think it was necessary
or desirable to have a secret session, or
words to that effect. What I say now is

Secret Session

this, if it is thought desirable that there
should be a secret session to deal with
certain specified matters, the Government
will be quite willing to reconsider the
matter.
Mr. NIXON: I am not going to say
very much. I am glad that the Prime
Minister has made the statement he has
made. I do not want to pose as a
lecturer in this House or any other place,
but I want to say this-and I have said

who opens his mouth in a way calculated

Mr. BROWN: I am not concerned

I can assure the Prime Minister that from

Supply in secret session from our particular point of view. I am not going

on both sides-about the operations of
the Area Board of the Ministry of
Supply. It has left us in the position.
that Northern Ireland has not been able
to play its part industrially in the present crisis as we would wish and as it is
able to do.
The Prime Minister says he is willing
to consider the matter, and I can assure
him that as far as I am concerned-and
a number of Members have told me they
share the views of the hon. Member for

be a secret session to discuss A.R.P. and

is equally important that we should investigate that matter so far as we are
concerned. No Ministry is more important at the present time. Although,
strictly speaking, we are not concerned
in the ordinary way we are concerned
by representation. I think the Minister
of Commerce is the representative of
Northern Ireland on that Committee.
am

not finding any fault with the

Mr. JOHNSTON: Perhaps you would

matter, and I am open to correction, any
Member can
spy strangers and
then a vote of the House is taken as to
whether they should call upon strangers
to withdraw. It is not the function of
the Prime Minister to say whether there
is going to be a secret session or not, that
is the function of the House. I am also
rather curious to know how the Members
present are going to satisfy the curiosity
of people who are anxious to know what
has taken place, in a secret session. When
they go outside they cannot say a word
about anything.
Lord GLENTORAN: In reply to the
hon. Member, I may say that I have
taken part in a great number of secret
sessions. Some Members may not be
aware that it is the custom whenever a
secret session is to be held to give notice
of that session so that the Members on
all sides can come prepared for the necessary debate. If someone were just to rise
and move that strangers leave the House,
that would not facilitate hon. Members
or give them the opportunity which they
desired of raising matters in which they
are particularly interested. Therefore, it
has always been the custom to give due
and proper notice that a secret session is
to be held so that hon. Members can come
prepared to deal with the points they
wish to speak upon.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think the
right hon. Gentleman was attempting to
define the question of procedure. The
procedure is as was explained by the hon.
Member for North Armagh-if any
Member wants to get up he can do so;
there is nothing to prevent him. The
motion will go before the House and the
House can vote whichever way it pleases.
It is entirely a matter for the House.
Question put, and agreed.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): With
your permission and that of the Commit-
Estimates-

tee I will address my remarks to the two
Estimates on the Order Paper-
Class V, No. 1 and No. 2. Last
year the net total of the two
Votes of this Estimate was £2,332,042;

an increase over last year of £557. This
is due mainly to the payment of war
bonuses to the junior members of the
staff. As I explained last year, several
of our principal officers are on war service and many others have been lent to
other Government departments. In this
way I feel that the officials of the Ministry
of Education are making a real
contribution to the general war effort.
Notwithstanding the reduction of our
staff during the recent emergency the
officials willingly shouldered very heavy
additional burdens for which they
deserve the greatest credit and the Government's warmest thanks. In spite of
all the difficulties and handicaps inseparable from the times, I am satisfied
that the administration of educational
services in our area continues to be
carried on efficiently and satisfactorily.
Vote 2, for educational services
amounts to £2,398,040, being an increase
of £132,733 on the Estimates for last
year. Most of this increase is due, as
hon. Members will see, to the provision
made under Subhead F2 for £125,000
in respect of payments to education
authorities and school managers for the
provision of air-raid protection in their

are to be found in Subhead A3, where

respect of payments to the Teachers'
Superannuation Fund.
Hon. Members will not expect or wish
me to make a long speech giving a detailed
account of every item in the Estimates.
I shall gladly try to explain any particular
matter arising out of them on which
Members may wish for fuller information.
I am glad to be able to assure the Committee that until very recently education
in our area-elementary, technical and
secondary was proceeding normally and
satisfactorily. There was, of course, a
certain inevitable dislocation within the
last month or so, but I am glad to say
everybody concerned is busy gathering up
the threads again. We are confident that
very shortly we shall be able to say, without any reservations, that we have overcome all difficulties and that we have
again in full operation that system of
education of which we here are all proud.
If I may say so, it is a system which must
be maintained, come what may, if the
children are to be fitted to carry on the
business of life and the business of our
country when this war is over.
Hon. Members are aware that many of
our elementary school childern in Belfast
have been sent to the country, and the
Education Authorities and managers, in
conjunction with the Ministry, are
present engaged in assigning teachers to
schools outside Belfast wherever there has
been a considerable influx of pupils. Hon.
Members will be interested to learn that
the teachers themselves have asked that
those amongst them who were working in
rest centres in the city should remain here
in order that they may be available again,
should unfortunately the occasion arise,
to carry out the same duties that they
performed so efficiently twice within the
past few months. I would like to take
this opportunity of saying that the teaching profession has every reason to be
proud of the devotion to duty and the
self-sacrifice which was shown by teachers
in the city and in the country.
The citizens of Belfast, as well as the
Government, owe a deep debt of gratitude
to the teachers at the rest centres, and
I am grateful to my right hon. and
learned Friend, the Minister of Public
Security, for having publicly acknowledged that debt in such generous words.
The rest centres will continue to be
staffed in the main, by teachers of the
elementary schools. The Belfast Education Authority and His Lordship, the
Roman Catholic Bishop of Down and
Connor, are taking good
that
teachers shall not be assigned to the
country who wish to remain here in order
to carry out important voluntary duties
of civil defence.
care
As might be expected, of course, there
are difficulties which have arisen in the
country districts, principally of accommodation and the supply of desks. These
difficulties are being steadily surmounted,
and we have good reason to be satisfied
with the progress that is being made. Of
course, it would be a great deal easier for
all concerned, and also much better for
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
the evacuated children, if the parents
would allow them to stay evacuated. The
backward and forward flow from city to
country and from country back to city
makes it much more difficult for the
authorities in Belfast as well as in the
country to plan for the education and to
care for the general welfare of the
children. The greatest trouble at present
is in connection with desks. Many were
destroyed in Belfast, and it is impossible
for us to provide every child in the
country with a desk at which he or she
may sit during the whole school day.
There is no harm whatever in a class
standing for certain lessons as was the
custom some years ago; indeed, I think a
child will often obtain more rest and
freedom from fidgets if it stands for a
time after a long period of sitting.
In introducing the Estimates last year
I spoke of the adverse effect of the blackout and difficulties of transport during
the first year of war upon the attendance
at technical schools throughout the
Province. I am glad to say that this fall
in attendance has been checked, and the
figures for the second year of the war have
been well up to peace-time standards.
The technical schools continue to do the
excellent work to which we have been
accustomed for so long that we are apt to
take it for granted. We are essentially
a Ministry of peace, and as such we are
apt to be relegated to a back seat in
time of war; but we like to feel that we,
too, are playing our part to-day, and so
I must mention that the technical schools
have undertaken new responsibilities
arising directly out of the war. They
have trained unemployed for war work;
they have established special classes for
skilled members of the combatant services.
Hon. Members will not wish me to particularise too closely on these points. They
have welcomed into their classrooms
almost 3,000 soldiers anxious to pursue
studies ranging from Spanish to woodwork-which may be of interest and profit
to them when they return to civil life.
The domestic economy teachers of the
technical schools also have helped with
food demonstrations, with the organisation of their schools as feeding centres for
evacuees, and with the jam-preserving
schemes of the Ministry of Food.
Relatively speaking, secondary education
has been little affected during the year,
and as I speak some thousands of boys
and girls throughout the towns of Ulster
are undergoing their first day of examina.
tion for the junior and senior certificate.
During the school year that is now closing
four giris' schools successfully operated
evacuation schools in the country, and I
think that hon. Members will agree with
me that every prudent headmaster and
headmistress in Belfast would be well
advised to endeavour to work out some
scheme of evacuation for at least the
younger pupils so that they may be in a
position to put their plans into operation
with a minimum of trouble should the
occasion arise.
Perhaps I may be allowed here to refer
briefly to the election of scholars yesterday at Trinity College, Dublin, and to
inform hon. Members that out of a total
of 24 foundation and non-foundation
scholars chosen eight had been educated
in our Northern Ireland schools. We are
accustomed to our young men and women
gaining this high academic honour each
year, and I mention the point specially
on this occasion only in order to show
that four out of the eight Ulster students
were educated at schools outside Belfast.
Our country secondary schools are
excellent; they deserve to be congratulated on their success, and I am glad to
have this opportunity of doing so. It is
a splendid record.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is the hon. Lady
referring to the elementary schools?
Mrs. PARKER: No, to secondary
schools. I am glad to say that during
the past six months or so the secondary
and technical schools have taken up with
enthusiasm the scheme launched by the
Air Ministry for the formation of an
Air Training Corps, designed to interest
boys of 16 to 18 years of age in the
highly specialised and technical work of
the Royal Air Force. The Air Ministry
has approved in Ulster the formation of
thirty-six school units-some technical,
some secondary, and some joint units.
In each case the officers are all, or almost
all, teachers in the schools concerned.
Apart altogether from the fact that these
units form a natural recruiting ground
for the Royal Air Force, and apart also
from the fact that the drill and physical
training involved are of direct physical
benefit to the boys taking part, there is
a real educational benefit.

In conclusion, may I say a few words
about education and its relative importance in the scheme of things to-day.
I am asking for a large Vote, it is true,
but it is well worth while viewed as an
insurance premium for the future of the
State and of the individual citizens. We
cannot afford to allow any slackening in
the effort to provide the best education
for Ulster boys and girls. That point
cannot be too strongly emphasised. I
have heard more than once in recent days
persons who formerly were loud in paying lip service to the value of education
saying that these were not the times to
worry about lessons and school work. I
profoundly disagree with that outlook,
and I hope hon. Members will agree with
me that now more than ever before it
is a vital necessity for us to bend all our
energies to ensure that our educational
system operates as nearly as possible with.
peace-time efficiency.
If we do not strive to this end, if we
do not always remember the plain fact
that the young are growing up in times
of unexampled difficulty, and that every
effort must be strained to develop their
character, to teach them the essential
difference between the true and the false,
and to train them to play their proper
part in life, then all our war effort will
be wasted and the sacrifices of our armed
forces will have been in vain. This is
my belief, and, in the hope that it is the
belief of all hon. Members, I beg to move
the adoption of these Estimates.

matter. It may not seem a big thing

put these points forward not in the spirit
of propaganda, but in a spirit of helpfulness for a section of the community
which needs it, and I hope the hon. Lady
will consult the Minister of Agriculture
to see what can be done.

Certain remarks which I wish to make

instruction. It has received a new
importance to-day. People. have appre-
