HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Professor Corkey]
ciated the value of this element in
education in a way they have not done
universally in the past. We have all been
made aware of the fact that the principles of our democracy are the fruit
of our Christianity and are latent in our
Christian religion, and we realise that if
we lose our Christianity our democracy
will have no basis or foundation or ground
on which to stand. The point I wish to
make is that this element in education
is a far more complicated and difficult
undertaking than is realised, and while
certain parts of that education are well
given in all the schools there has been,
I think, a tendency to neglect, perhaps
not even to appreciate the existence of
other factors.
May I take the liberty very briefly of
suggesting some elements which, I
think moral education does contain.
First of all, without an appreciation of
fine things no man is educated. I mean
fine things particularly in character, and
I may say also fine things in nature and
in art. That sort of instruction is not of
the kind that can be given verbally.
Young people get it from example. They
appreciate and learn to value things
more
by example than by instruction. The character of the teacher
is perhaps the most vital fact in the
situation. That is the first factor in a
satisfactory moral education, and without
it there is nothing of any worth.
Further, the precepts of morality were
summed up long ago in a simple form
in the decalogue which we still teach
to the children. We are told to be
cheerful, kind, generous, persevering,
charitable, and so on. These things can
be taught and are taught in connection with
religious instruction very well. In addition, there is the discipline in the school
which helps the children to appreciate
these maxims which are the rules that
enable ordinary people to go through this
life.
In addition to the rules and discipline
there is, I think, in a complete moral
education an element of worship. Life
is a sacred thing. The tasks of life are
God imposed, and unless people learn to
turn aside at times and understand the
presence of God, the obligation of God
upon them, they will not live strenuously
a self-denying, upright, self-sacrificing
life. I may say that element is also
appreciated in our schools. Just the
other day I had the pleasure of attending what is called an inspection of
religious instruction in one of our schools.
The service that was observed on that

the children have brought home to them
a sense of the grandness of life that could
not be brought to them by any other
means.

Member for South Armagh, and by other
hon. Members including the hon.
Member for South Down, to the question
of feeding necessitous children and the
free provision of books. I would like to
point out, as I have already done on
many occasions in this House, that our
policy has been to urge on the education
authorities concerned to do whatever is
necessary, and as much as possible, towards the feeding in the counties of
necessitous children.
The county for which the hon. Member
for South Down spoke, the County
Down, in 1939 provided 185,761 meals
for school children. I wonder if the
hon. Member realises that his county
stands very high on the list of those helping poor children who need these meals,
but it does remain that my Ministry are
most anxious to see an extension of this
assistance given to necessitous school
children. I appreciate that in some
districts, in some regions, in some
counties much greater help could be
given in this direction. And if any
words of mine spoken at this Table can
carry any weight, then I would once
more emphasise that it is of paramount
importance that the school children
throughout the Six Counties should be
helped by the education authorities as
far as is humanly possible in the direction
of feeding.

Supply
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
Two points were raised by the hon.
Member for North Derry with reference
to teachers who were to be assigned to
schools where there were evacuated
children. The procedure, where there
has been an influx of evacuated children,
is that the manager or the education
authority concerned notifies the Ministry and then action is taken with the
evacuating authority.
The other question which he raised was
with regard to the numbers of children in
two-teacher schools. I am not in a position
at the moment to give him an answer,
but with his permission I will communicate with him on the matter. I am in
complete agreement with what was said
by the Member for North Derry throughout the major portion of his speech, and I
would like to thank him and the Member
for the University (Rev. Professor Corkey)
for what they have said. With regard to
the teaching of morals and civics I quite
agree that at this time, above all others,
something is required to show the people
what their moral duty is, and to show
them what their duty to the State is. I
think that if we can, in the course of time,
find some way of making our children
realise that they have a duty not only to
themselves, but to the State also, and to
realise that those duties have a connection
with their duty to God, then I think we
may be able to look forward to the future
with very great confidence, because I am
quite sure that what is taught to our
young people, at any rate up to the age
of 18, is what lays the foundation for the
future of their lives and the future of the
State.
Question put, and agreed to.

Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Offences and prosecutions)
ordered to stand part of the Bill.
CLAUSE 2 (Application of fines).
Question proposed, "That the Clause
stand part of the. Bill."
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Clause 2
lays down that under certain circumstances a fine imposed for an offence
under this Act will go to the fishery
authority of the district. That is a principle with which I cannot agree..
I
cannot think of any other case, though
there may be cases known to my legal
friends, where such a thing is tolerated.
If this Bill becomes law in its present
form it will be. possible to prosecute a
farmer for letting off flax water into a
stream or river. If the case goes against
him and a fine is imposed, according to
Clause 2 of this Bill that fine will go
to the fishery authority of the district.
Thereafter that fishery authority can proceed to bring a civil bill case against that
same farmer for damages.
We had a case in the Crossgar district
of County Down where a farmer was
fined for allowing his flax water to discharge into a stream. Then the Belfast
Anglers' Club brought a civil bill against
him for £60 damages to fish life in the
stream, and in order to keep the case.
from going into court the farmer settled
it by giving £10 for damages and publishing an apology in the Belfast newspapers
and paying the expenses. Surely nobody
should be permitted to recover damages
under civil bill from a farmer and at the
same time be in the position of receiving
the fine imposed by a court upon that
same individual for a criminal offence.
Personally I cannot agree with that, and
I think the whole principle is obnoxious.
If you propose to retain the law as it is
under which these people can sue and
recover damages in the ordinary way,
then this Clause ought to be wiped out
altogether and it should be a matter of
damages pure and simple as between the
parties. If, on the other hand, you are
going to pursue the line set out by
Clause 2 and prosecute a farmer for
allowing flax water to discharge into
rivers and streams and fine him under
certain circumstances then an action for
damages at a civil suit should not lie.
Unless I get some undertaking that one
or other of the horns of the dilemma is
going to be sawn off I cannot support
this Clause as it stands.
Mr. MAGINESS: I think the hon.
Member for North Derry has not appre-
1027 Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Mr. Maginess]
ciated the position under this Bill. The
offence contemplated under the Bill is
entirely different from an action for
damages brought under the civil law.
Under the Bill the offender is probably
prosecuted by a servant of the Board of
Conservators, but if the flax producer is
fined under Clause 2 (a) of the Bill undoubtedly the fine goes to the Board.
Under the law as it exists at the present
time one-third goes to the informer and
two-thirds to the Board of Conservators.
As there was some encouragement under
the existing law for a witness to press a
case if he should in the end get onethird of the fine, the Ministry came to
the conclusion that it would be better to
remove the temptation from him altogether and do away with this one-third
of the fine to the informer and give the
whole sum to the Board.
When the hon. Member says that the
person who gets the fine can bring a
civil action I think he is slightly misinterpreting the position. The Board
of Conservators is a body which has
certain authority over the fisheries in
Northern Ireland, or rather a district of
Northern Ireland, and it is their duty to
see that the fish life in the rivers and
lakes is preserved as far as possible. It
is their duty to see that the law in respect of that fish life is observed, but
they do not necessarily own the fish. As
we know the several fisheries of the lakes
and rivers in Northern Ireland are
owned by different persons.
It is quite true, as the hon. Member
well knows, that the ownership of certain
rivers is in certain hands. It is not in
the hands of the Board of Conservators;
it is not the Board which brings a civil
action, it is the owner of the fish. This
Bill, of course, does not go contrary to
the established principle of British law
whereby a person who by his own act or
negligence damages the goods or property
of another person is liable in an action
for damages to the second party. This
Bill does not purport to interfere with
the civil rights of the individual, but
those individuals are not the same individuals who are taking part in any
prosecution which would be brought
under this Bill or under the old Act
which this Bill amends.
The hon. Member will, I am sure,
realise that if a person owns a fishery he
has an ownership in the fish; he has an
interest in the fish in that fishery, and
he has an interest in seeing that his
property is preserved. If someone else
injures that property he should not be
deprived of his civil rights. If any hon.
Member assaults me and the police prosecute him for that assault it would not
prevent me from bringing a civil action
against him for the damage which I
had suffered at his hands. That is
the same condition of affairs as exists
under this Bill. The Board of Conservators act as a sort of police force
to the fisheries in Northern Ireland, but
they do not own them. They bring the
prosecution, or may bring the prosecution,
but they do not bring the civil action.
The only person who is entitled to bring
a civil action is the owner of the fish.
I do not think the hon. Member need be
under any misapprehension that any
person will get paid twice; first, out of
the prosecution, and, secondly, out of the
civil action. The prosecutor in one and
the plaintiff in the other are entirely
different persons. I think that answers
the point put forward by the hon.
Member.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: It may be as
the Parliamentary Secretary has pointed
out, but the fact remains that for the same
offence the farmer is liable to pay twice.
These conservators may not own the
fisheries-I do not know whether that is
absolutely correct-but the fact remains
that they have a very vital interest in
them. As a board or body they may not
own them, but the members are nearly
all connected with bodies who do own
them. I think the whole principle, however it may be argued in law, is bad from
a moral point of view that an interested
party should recover the fine. In every
case of assault, such as was mentioned by
the Parliamentary Secretary, the fine
should go to the Crown, and not to any
private party. I should be satisfied if the
fine were given to the Crown. Although
the conservators or Fishery Board do not
own the fish they distribute this money.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
CLAUSE 3 (Short title, construction,
citation and duration).
1029 Fisheries (Flax Water) Bill

10 JUNE 1941
Adjournment
Question proposed, "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I wish to say
that whilst I am not going to oppose the
temporary nature of this Bill I think the
last Ciause of all in the Bill is a downright insult to the farming community.
It provides that, as soon as the present
emergency is over, any temporary easement that may have been provided by this
Bill shall be wiped out; in other words
when the community has got what it
needs and can do without them the farmer
and flax producer are no longer required.
Lord GLENTORAN: I should like to
assure my hon. Friend that he is under a
complete misapprehension as to the views.
of the Ministry on this matter. It is true
that this Clause is put into this Measure,
but it is one which is put into practically
every Measure which we have brought in
since the commencement of the war. This
is essentially a war Measure, and I hope
that those who are interested in the
fisheries will pay attention to what I have
to say. We have brought this Bill in in
order that the production of flax may be
increased. I expect I will have difficulty
in another place in getting this Bill
passed. No matter what difficulties arise
we will get over them, because we are
determined to give this easement to the
men producing flax. I did not bring in
this Bill-I stated this when introducing
the Measure-with the idea that it was
a great one or a Bill which would bring
happiness to the farmers or those who own
the fish. I am quite certain I shall get
kicked by both sides. I did not bring it
in for the purpose of creating dissension,
but as a dove of peace. There should be
some give and take between farmers and
those who own the fish. Both are very
valuable to this country.
It is a
I know that the bitterest cases which
have been fought in our local and county
courts are the regular yearly rows between
the fish owners and the farmers.
great pity because both hold great
interests, and as good Ulstermen they
should try to come together and settle this
thing, if possible. I believe that in this
Bill there is the necessary machinery for
making some sort of happy agreement
between the fishery interests and the flax
growers. That is the only reason why I
brought in this Bill. It was far from the
minds of those who drafted the Bill that
there should be any insult to the farmers.
The Measure has been brought in to help
them, and we believe it will be of
assistance to the farmers.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
Title agreed to.

explain the allocation of advertising.
amongst papers circulating in Fermanagh

counties, received only a relatively small
proportion of that given to the Government party organs. The reply the Minister gave was highly unsatisfactory, and

question I put was not answered at all.
In the month of May, last month, the
Department of Agriculture gave to the
two Unionist papers in Fermanagh 195
single column inches of advertisements,
while to their Nationalist competitor in
the same county only 18 inches was given.
In that county the Nationalist population
are in a considerable majority. Yet 92
per cent. of the advertising in the weekly
Press in County Fermanagh went to the
two privileged papers representing a
minority of the population. Eight per
cent. went to the Nationalist paper which

in itself, is higher than the ratio the
Government recognise and accredit to

Was it ever made to the two other

Is the "Fermanagh Herald," the

The company which owns the
"Fermanagh Herald" is known as the
North-West of Ireland Printing and
Publishing Company, Limited. It applied
-and I ask the Minister's attention to
this point-about the beginning of last
year, 1940, to be included in the list of

for the Unionist papers. The opportunity
arises for them. There is no delay. They
get work of this nature. I am told they
get more work than they can handle sometimes without even having to tender for
the work.
One consideration is of importance in
this respect.
In these Six Counties a
newspaper has what I may term a selective
distribution or selective circulation.
Numbers of people in our area read
habitually one daily or one weekly paper
and read nothing else. You will get in
the city of Belfast "News-Letter" men,
"Whig" men, and "Irish News" men.
They read almost traditionally their own
organ: they read no other organ. It is
selective circulation. And in the distribution of Government advertisements the
whole public of the area has to be
approached, and I take it that is your
object. That is the intention-to reach
the whole public of the area. If that is to
be attained the department concerned will,
by omitting one newspaper from its list,
exclude a definite block of readers. The
information you seek to circulate to the
public will never reach a definite section
of that public if you shut out from the
list the organ they are accustomed to read.
The Government advertising is intended.
to reach the whole public, and appeal
through the newspapers of the area.

VACANT BELFAST HOUSES.
any
3. Mr. CLARK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that a
large number of houses in the city of
Belfast which have not suffered
damage in the recent air raids have been
vacated by their tenants, and, if so, what
steps he proposes to take to have these
houses utilised for people who are
homeless.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is a fact that
many houses in Belfast which have not
suffered any damage in air raids have
been vacated by their tenants and some
of these have already been acquired for
the accommodation of homeless people.
If it is necessary or if it is in the public
interest, I shall take steps to utilise all
such houses for this purpose. I do not,
however, consider it would be a satisfactory solution to the problem, nor one
which would commend itself to those who
have been rendered homeless, to rehouse
them in dwellings which have been considered unsafe by their tenants
evacuated by them.
and
It is the aim of my Department to find
accommodation in the more remote
country districts for the women and
children and for the aged and infirm and
to use the billets and empty houses in or
around Belfast for those homeless persons
who are not in the priority classes or who
work in the city.
POTATO CRISPS.
4. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he will
consider the establishing of a potato crisp
factory along with the factories for
making potato flour and meal for cattle
feeding; and whether he is aware that
potato crisps would be a very valuable
asset to the nation's human food supply
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Lord Glentoran): As the hon.
Member is no doubt aware, my Department has already announced that a
number of factories will be set up in
Northern Ireland in the near future for
the manufacture of potato flour for
human consumption and potato meal for
animal consumption. The conversion of
surplus potatoes into these products will
result in a substantial saving of shipping
space and will provide commodities which
at present are not available. The process of manufacturing crisps involves the
use of substantial quantities of cooking
fats, which are already in short supply.
I cannot, therefore, recommend
establishment of such factories.

Lord GLENTORAN: The Ministry of

That simply shows the increase of work

a large number considering that we have
a turnover of £35,000,000 per annum.
Hon. Members will be aware of the fact
that apart from the usual work in the
Ministry we have had to undertake a very
strenuous campaign, and in addition to
this tillage campaign we have also undertaken one of the biggest trading concerns
in the country.
For instance we purchase all the meat,
pigs and cattle, and now we are going also
to purchase eggs which will amount to a
turnover of another £5,000,000. The
reason we have to take over eggs is in order
that there should be a fair distribution to
workers. We have found that there has
been a very powerful black market in the
egg business. People go round and collect
eggs at the farms and the result is that
the workers in the city have not been able
to get a fair share. For that reason the
Ministry of Food is going to take over the
entire distribution of eggs, and we as a
Ministry are acting as agents in the
matter.
I should like to refer to the success of
the tillage campaign. In spite of the bad
spring and the many difficulties farmers
have had to contend with I am glad to
say we have carried out all we contracted
to do. The whole campaign has been
most successful, thanks to the goodwill of
the farmers and the assistance which was
given to my Ministry. I am satisfied
that next year when I call upon them to
make a greater effort than ever they will
respond and we will get all the extra
tillage which the country will require for
food.
Another matter of great difficulty that
my Ministry has had to contend with since
before Christmas is the serious outbreak
of foot-and-mouth disease. I am glad to
say we have succeeded in stamping out
that outbreak. If we have done so it is
only because we have received the greatest
assistance from the farmers of the three
infected counties. I would like to thank
those farmers because I may tell the Committee that it is only by the goodwill of
all
parties that this scourge can be
stamped out. We are under a deep debt
of gratitude to the farmers in those
counties which were affected. We are not
out of the wood yet because while we have
foot-and-mouth disease so near us as it is
on the other side of the Border there is
continual danger of infection being
brought back to this area.
Therefore I would call upon all
farmers to help me to stop smuggling over
the Border. I am satisfied there is no
more reprehensible action a farmer can
do than, for the sake of making a few
pounds, to endanger the whole trade
of Ulster and also endanger our food
supply by carrying on this smuggling
practice. I therefore hope that farmers.
will help me. They are the ones who
can help to stamp this thing out. I do
not think it would be too much to say

put in jail. In fact, that is the only way
it can be satisfactorily dealt with. I am
asking now for the help of everyone connected with the cattle trade and farming
industry to stamp out the practice and
keep the Ulster herds safe from serious
disease.

It is hoped that we will have an ample

ordinary sense, which makes it very difficult for agriculturists to get sufficient
labour at the wages laid down by the
Agricultural Wages Board.

ture ought to take steps to see that men

was only after a great deal of correspondence with the Ministry of Home

man with an agricultural tractor,

If the Ministry are relying on these land

The hon. Member who spoke last
referred to the live-stock policy. He, like

on the other side of the water who control

to turn straw into manure, how can we
go on for ever living on the land? You
want something to put back. You cannot
rely entirely on artificials. If by this
policy cattle are seriously reduced where
is the manure coming from in the spring
to fertilise additional land coming under
the plough? Artificials are in short
supply as everybody knows. If you want
artificial manure you have to order
months in advance. Perhaps the Minister

reduced and present prices are apt to

being fattened at all, just grass fed for

down I would ask the Minister to clear

TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): I am
sure that the Minister has been gratified
by the manner in which his Estimates
have been received. The criticisms most
hon. Members offered were, on the
whole friendly and constructive. The
remaining criticisms, if I may say so, were
extremely ill-informed. We started off
with some pungent remarks by the hon.
Member for Woodvale, and the only thing
which emerged from these remarks was
that he had not listened to the Minister
introducing his Estimates and had not
read the statement which the Ministry
issued some few days ago because he talked
in his speech about people in snug and
well-paid positions not having to make
sacrifices but getting bonuses. As the
Minister explained bonuses were only
issued to the people in receipt of very
small salaries. They did not affect people
who were well paid or were higher-grade
officials. All they did was to compensate
those in receipt of a small weekly wage
according to the rise in the cost of living.
I am sure no Member would protest
against a person in receipt of a small wage
getting an increase according to the cost
of living.
Then in spite of the Minister's protests
the hon. Member declared that we were
responsible for the inspectors under the
Food Control Board. As a matter of
fact when the Minister of Commerce introduced his Estimates the salaries of these
inspectors formed part of those Estimates.
The hon. Member did not mention them
then, but he now seeks to saddle the
Ministry of Agriculture with an inspectorate with which it had nothing to do.
These inspectors under the Ministry of
Food Control have nothing to do with the
Ministry of Agriculture. We have no
responsibility for them, nor can we control
them in any way.
The hon. Member for South Tyrone,
whose criticisms are always received by
the Ministry with the greatest respect,
mentioned that in certain cases payments
had been delayed, but this was due in most
cases, if not in all, to the fact either that
the farmers were late in sending in claims,
or when they did they filled up the forms.
wrongly, and in some cases filled them up
illegibly. Great trouble had to be undertaken in order to find out what the correct
position was. It may seem peculiar to
the hon. Gentleman, who no doubt fills
up every form correctly, to find the
number of strange answers received by
the Ministry in respect of the questionnaire sent out in regard to this £2 per
acre scheme. In some cases there are contradictory statements in the replies. The
top half contradicts the bottom half, and
you have to write to the different persons
making the claim and ask them to clarify
the position. All that takes time.
With regard to the question of tractors
and what farmers can and cannot do with
the 5s licence, I thought that that
position had been made clear when the
Minister of Finance was introducing his
Estimates, but if hon. Members believe
that the farmers in the country are
generally not aware of the true position
I have no doubt the Ministry could inform them by a simple explanation of
what they can and cannot do. As I
understand it myself they can bring
produce from one part of the farm to
another, but they cannot use the tractors
to go to a village or market and bring
produce back to the farm that way.
However, the Ministry in case there is
this doubt about it will make the position
clear.
Another point mentioned by the hon.
Member for South Tyrone and other
Members was the position of labour for
the harvest. This has been exercising
the Ministry for some time. It is
realised that the harvest which should be
very considerably larger than last year
will require a fairly substantial amount
of labour, and the Ministry hope that
when harvest time comes the labour will
be available. We are training land girls
at the moment, and we hope in harvest
time to have 200 of them available for
work. We also hope in other respects
to get labour which will mean that none
of the harvest will be lost when the
autumn comes.
The hon. Member for Shankill spent

whoever stamped a milch cow in Cavan
was not an inspector of this Ministry.
Cavan, in case the hon. Member is not
aware, is not in Northern Ireland but
in Eire. Consequently, no inspector
from the Ministry would stamp either

a cow or mule in County Cavan. The

The hon. Member for South Down
really did not criticise the Ministry at all,
but made an attack upon Scotland and
the men who come from Scotland. This,
of course, is not unusual nowadays. It
is a custom that has grown up largely in
Europe to attack members of other races.
We have Herr Hitler in Germany preventing any Jew from occupying a position in official Germany. He can do that,
I understand, by examining the blood,
but whether the blood of a Scotsman is
different from the blood of a Northern
Ireland man I am not in a position to
state. In any case, the principle of this
Ministry is the principle adopted throughout the British Empire, that the best man
should be given the job irrespective of
where he comes from.
We are not going to discriminate
against Englishmen, Scotsmen or Welshmen, just as England, Scotland and
Wales do not discriminate against
Northern Ireland men. If we are going
to prevent a man getting a job simply
because he lives or has lived in Scotland
and are going to give it to a
man in
Northern Ireland, irrespective of the
ability which each man possesses, then we
may give up entirely the idea of having
a Ministry of which any country might
be proud. This Ministry has officials who
are not second to those of any other
Ministry no matter where you go, and it
is because this principle has been adopted,
that irrespective of his birthplace the man
with the best qualifications receives the
job.
The hon. Member also complained
about a town in South Armagh which
built a weighbridge and then expected to
be a grading centre on that account. I
think the hon. Member was not quite full
enough in his statement. It is true that
the people of that district did build a
weighbridge, but the hon. Member
omitted to tell the House that before
doing so they had asked the Ministry was
there likely to be a grading centre established there, and they were told that there
was not. In spite of that information
they proceeded to build the weighbridge,
and then said: "Now we have the weighbridge built, will you not change your
mind?" These grading centres are established throughout the country on a
certain principle. That principle does
not include the fact that in spite of
warnings the people in that district should
put up a weighbridge. If the fact of
putting up a weighbridge meant that a
grading centre would be immediately
established in the town, we no doubt
would have weighbridges built in every
town and hamlet in the North of Ireland.
Regarding the statement made by the
hon. Member for North Derry-and the
hon. Member for South Tyrone also
referred to it—the Ministry is always glad

mentioned that he would like to discuss

Much valuable information and advice
come from him. He sums up a situation

is one of the assets of this House of which
this Ministry in particular is very proud.
The hon. Member mentioned the
question of manures and the tillage of
poor land. There is no doubt that not
only in Northern Ireland but in every
other country where you go on increasing
the acreage under crop you must face this
problem sooner or later. Naturally
enough, a farmer if he has to plough ten,
fifteen, or twenty acres will plough his
best acres first because that gives him an
immediate return. Consequently, where
you go on increasing year by year the
number of acres that man has to plough
he eventually reaches a stage when he has
to consider the possibility of ploughing
up poorer land.
That again raises the question, which
the hon. Member has mentioned, of farmyard manure and the amount available
and also the question of the various forms
of fertilisers which would be necessary to
transform that poor land into land capable
of good production. Those are all matters

Briefly, I can say that from the time
the scheme comes into operation the eggs
produced in Northern Ireland will be sold
to packing stations only. There they will
be tested and stamped with "M.F.",
meaning Ministry of Food, or with some
other marking. The producer at the
present time can sell to whoever he likes,
and consequently some people get a lot
of eggs while other people get very few,
but now he will have to sell to these packing stations and they in turn will distribute the eggs to the retailers. The
customer who has doubtless registered
with his retailer at the moment will be
able to get his proportion of eggs. In
future, as I have said, the producer will
have one outlet only and that outlet is
the wholesale market. He must no longer
sell to private customers.
I think I have mentioned the subject

Oral Answers to Questions.
CUTTING OF TURF.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has seen the notice
in the Press issued by the Ministry of
Commerce requesting all persons who can
do so to cut as much turf as possible
during the present season; whether he is
aware of the fact that his Ministry is
seriously stultifying the compliance with
this request by the fact that the Ministry
has failed to exercise its powers of making
turbary regulations under the provisions
of the Land Purchase Acts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): Yes, sir, I have seen the notice
to which the hon. Member refers.
The hon. Member would appear to be
under some misapprehension as to the
nature of the functions exercisable by my
Ministry and the extent to which they
are capable of being exercised.
The primary object of regulations
which this Ministry is empowered to make
is not, as the hon. Member seems to
think, to stimulate cutting, but to
preserve the rights of tenant purchasers
to cut turf for consumption on their own
holdings. This power of the Ministry,
however, applies only to turbary on lands
which formed the subject of sale proceedings under the Irish Land Act of 1903
and the later Acts. The area concerned
forms only a small proportion of the
whole, as under existing legislation my
Ministry has no authority to intervene in
respect of turbary where sales took place
under earlier Acts (except to settle
disputes) or of any turbary which is in
the hands of private owners.
I should like to add, however, that I
fully support the request of the Minister
of Commerce in urging those who have
large turbary holdings to cut as much
peat as possible as a special war effort.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether it
is not a fact that repeated applications.
have been made to the Ministry to put
into operation the regulations dealing
with turbary over which they have
control, and will he give. the reason why
these repeated applications were refused.
Mr. BARBOUR: Because we have no
turbary under our control. All we can
do is to make regulations for the protection of those who have turbary.
CONCESSION TO OWNERS OF
TRACTORS.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Finance whether the concessions recently
granted to the owners of agricultural
tractors operating under a 5s licence include the drawing of turf from the bog to
the farm for use on the farm.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
It has always been permissible for
tractors taxed at 5s to be used to draw
supplies of turf required for agricultural
purposes as distinct from fuel to be used
for domestic purposes, and the concession to which the hon. Member refers
does not alter the position.

ERECTION OF FLAX BARNS.

& Sons to tender on or before the 12th
May for the erection of flax barns, but
no tenders were received.
Further invitations to tender for the

had not replied to the earlier invitations,

HARBOURING ENEMY ALIENS.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether any
enemy aliens are employed in the homes
of citizens of Northern Ireland, or are
there as visitors or paying guests, and,
if so, whether he can state the names
and addresses of the persons harbouring
these aliens.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The control of
aliens in Northern Ireland is a Reserved
Service, and I am not, therefore, in a
position to supply the details asked for.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the Minister
have inquiries made from the Imperial
Authorities to find out the number of
gentlemen who have aliens and enemies
of this country in their homes.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
hon. Member might be more precise as
to the information he wants.
Mr. HENDERSON: As a Member of
this House I want to know can the right
hon. Gentleman, who is responsible for
looking after the defence of Northern
Ireland through the Minister of Public
Security, not make representation to the
Imperial authorities to find out the
number of aliens housed in the homes of
so-called patriots in Northern Ireland?
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether any of the
citizens referred to were domiciled in the
Whiteabbey Sanatorium?
INSPECTION OF AGRICULTURAL
TRACTORS.
5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
public service vehicle inspectors in Co.
Tyrone are insisting on the inspection of
agricultural tractors operating under
a 5s licence; whether the inspectors,
although these vehicles are not goods
vehicles, are insisting on putting goods
vehicle plates on them; and whether he
will issue instructions clarifying the
position.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have nothing
to add to the answer which I gave the
hon. Member on this point on the 6th
March last. Tractors of the class
mentioned are goods vehicles within the
meaning of Part III of the Motor
Vehicles and Road Traffic Act (N.I.),
1934, and as such must be licensed and
plated under that enactment.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask for a definition of what is an agricultural tractor and
a goods vehicle?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is another
point, but I think the hon. Member does
not seem to understand that it is just as
necessary for an inspection of these agricultural vehicles and tractors as it is for
any other vehicle.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether it
is
necessary to have a public service
vehicle licence on a tractor drawing turf
from the bog?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly, if it
is on the public road it must have.

AN INTERRUPTED EXAMINATION
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether during the course
of the recent examination for junior
nurses in Northern Ireland the air raid
alarm was sounded; whether during the
Sir DAWSON BATES: If, as is presumed, the question relates to the 6th
May it is a fact that a written part of the
preliminary examination for nurses was in
progress on that day when an air raid
alarm lasting some twenty or thirty
minutes was given shortly after 2 o'clock
in the afternoon.
I have caused inquiries to be made and
I am informed that the course of the
examination was not interrupted, that the
candidates proceeded calmly with their
work, with the exception of about two
who were somewhat perturbed at first,
but who quickly settled to their work
again when they observed the attitude of
the others, that the time allowed for
answering the paper of questions was extended by fifteen minutes, and that all
these candidates-68 in number-passed
in that particular paper of questions.
Further, in the recent preliminary
nurses' examination out of a total of 145
candidates only 18 failed, whereas in the
two preceding examinations the failures
were respectively 33 out of 128, and 30
out of 130; so having regard to these
results I see no reason for making any
special representations on the matter.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's answer and in view of the well
known fact that when the air raid alarm
is sounded this House is adjourned and
the Members and civil servants have to
retire whether they like it or not, is it
fair to keep these young girls working on
examination papers during an alarm and
before the All Clear is sounded, or would
any person of commonsense do any such
a thing?

WAR DUTY ALLOWANCE TO
POLICE.
Mr. GAMBLE (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Public Security
whether he is in a position to make any
statement in regard to the payment of
war duty allowance to sergeants and
constables of the Royal Ulster Constabulary and to the full-time mobilised
sergeants and constables of the Ulster
Special Constabulary; and whether he is
prepared to make a similar allowance to
the sergeants and constables of the
Belfast Harbour Police Force now serving
under the control of the Government.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The question of
war duty allowance to the police force
under Government control was last raised
in this House on the 22nd April immediately following the first heavy air raid on
the North of Ireland. As hon. Members
will recall, I stated in reply to a question
that the conditions which led to the grant
of war duty allowance in Great Britain
did not then fully apply in this country.
Since that date, however, there has been
further heavy raiding in which the police
forces acquitted themselves with distinction, and after a careful survey of the
position the Government feels that conditions of service since the beginning of
May have approximated very closely to
those applying to the police forces in
Great Britain. The Government has
accordingly come to the conclusion that
as from the 1st of May, 1941, war duty
allowance at the rate of 4s per week to
sergeants and 3s per week to constables
(being the rates payable throughout Great
Britain) should be paid to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary and to the full-time
Ulster Special Constabulary. The Government has decided, too, that the sergeants
and constables of the Belfast Harbour
Police Force should benefit by a concession
which will secure to them remuneration
equal to the net pay of members of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary of corresponding rank and service.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the right
hon. Gentleman's anxiety for the police.
forces at the present time is he prepared
to make the payment of this allowance
retrospective to the date to which it
applied in the English forces?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: No. The allowance to the English police forces dated
from the time heavy air raiding began in
Great Britain, I think about September
of last year. I am making it retrospective to what in the opinion of the
Government is the date at which the
conditions here approximated to those
across the water.
Mr. BEATTIE: Has it been the
uneasiness in the police force that has
brought the right hon. Gentleman to his
senses at last?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: No, it has been
anxiety to do by the police force here
what is fair and just and to maintain the
principle which the Government have
acted upon, that the remuneration of the
forces here and in Great Britain should
be on a parity in regard to the conditions
of service.

Oral Answers to Questions.
WHITE ABBEY SANATORIUM.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether officers of his
Ministry made repeated inspections of the
Whiteabbey Sanatorium in recent years;
whether they reported any irregularities;
whether they had power thoroughly to
investigate the supervision and management of the institution and to attend
meetings of the Corporation Committee in
charge; whether they attended such meetings and whether the minutes of this
committee were regularly furnished to the
Ministry; and whether he will authorise
an inquiry with a view to elicit if the
irregularities and disorganisation which.
had disquieted the public could have been
detected or averted by reasonable care on
the part of the Ministry.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Medical inspectors of
my Ministry have made periodical inspections of the Whiteabbey Sanatorium in
recent years, but these inspections could
not possibly have revealed the irregularities disclosed by the recent sworn
inquiry. The object of the inspections is
primarily to ensure that the patients in
the institution are receiving adequate
medical treatment and no evidence was
tendered at the inquiry which would indicate that that was not so. The Ministry's
inspectors have not the same powers and
duties in regard to these institutions as
they possess in regard to poor-law institutions.
Meetings of the committee were attended
by medical inspectors of my Ministry by
special invitation of the Tuberculosis
Committee. In the absence of such invitations, inspectors have no right to
attend the meetings. Minutes of meetings
were, however, furnished regularly to the
Ministry. The hon. and learned Member
will, however, appreciate that the minutes
merely indicate the conclusions arrived at
and do not purport to disclose everything
that takes place at meetings, still less do
they reveal the activities of committee
members outside committee meetings. The
irregularities revealed by the inquiry
could not, therefore, have been discovered
by examination of the minutes, however
meticulous. I do not, therefore, propose
to institute the inquiry suggested in the
last part of the question.
POSITION OF BLIND PERSONS.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
desirability of setting up a Commission of
Inquiry to consider the position of blind
persons, and the failure of county councils
to apply in full the 1938 Act; whether
county councils make provision for dependents of blind persons in accordance
with the 1938 Act, and, if so, the actual
amount paid to such dependents;
whether the position of the blind in Derry
City is in keeping with the terms of the
1938 Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard
to the first part of the question, I would
refer the hon. Member to the reply given
on the 24th June last to the hon. Member for South Down in which it was
pointed out that county councils,
generally, were adopting a more generous
attitude towards blind persons. I do
not, therefore, propose to act as suggested
by the hon. Member.
In assessing the needs of blind persons
county councils take into consideration
the needs of dependents of the blind
persons. I have no statistics available
to show the actual amounts allowed by
county councils in respect of dependents.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the Londonderry Corporation.
has recently given very careful consideration to the question of assistance to
blind persons and a new scheme has been
introduced. This scheme provides for an
estimated expenditure of £1,194 10s in
1941-42 as compared with £908 in the
previous year. I have no reason to suppose that the new scheme will not be
operated in accordance with the terms of
the Blind Persons Act (N.I.), 1938.

may be more unsympathetically dealt

with England. But I have explained to

to induce the local authorities to be a little
bit more generous towards those unfortunate people.

7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime

United Kingdom, and, if so, whether he
can state why merchants in Great Britain
have to obtain an export licence from the
Board of Trade to send their goods to
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
As Northern Ireland is part of the
United Kingdom merchants in Great
Britain are not under any necessity to
obtain an export licence from the Board
of Trade for the shipment of goods from
Great Britain to Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that merchants have
had to comply with that request and
obtain export licences? Will he further
investigate the matter and see why that
is so?
a
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think
probably the hon. Gentleman is under
a misapprehension. The position is that
merchants shipping have to obtain
licence from the Censorship Department.
That is not the Board of Trade. That
is merely a question of protection.

SILAGE FROM GRASS CUTTINGS

9. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he will make
arrangements to have the grass cuttings
of golf links, bowling greens and other
sports grounds made into silage in order
to assist feeding livestock during the
coming winter.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): The question of the
ensilage of grass cuttings has been discussed by my Ministry with golf, bowling
and other sporting clubs. Generally
speaking it would not be practicable or
profitable to adopt the suggestion contained in the hon. Member's question
because of the fact that only a very small
quantity of grass is cut at any one time,
especially on bowling greens or sports
grounds.
I am glad to be able to assure the
House. that all golf courses in Northern
Ireland are contributing towards the
national campaign for increased food production according to their individual
circumstances. Many of them have given
up considerable areas of their courses for
cultivation while others are grazing sheep
throughout the year. Where such grazing
is being carried out the cutting of the
courses has been reduced to a minimum.

CLASS VIII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF PUBLIC SECURITY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
,'That a sum not exceeding £35,151 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending 31st March, 1942, to defray
the salaries and expenses of the Ministry
of Public Security."-(Note-£23,000
has been voted on account.)
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The revised
estimates for my Department reach the
substantial sum of £3,751,488 net. The
original estimates, prepared at the
beginning of the year, have been amended
to reflect the transfer of certain functions
to the Ministry of Home Affairs and
advantage has been taken of the opportunity to enlarge the original figure for
the civil defence services so as to make
provision for a further expansion of some
of the services; for a wider free shelter
policy and to meet the need of further
equipment requirements which recent
experience. has indicated.
Compared with last year's figures the
total sum which I am now asking of the
House shows an increase of £1,362,746
net. This is more than accounted for by
the expenditure, which I contemplate for
civil defence as that Vote (4) in itself
shows an increase of £1,431,330 net. The
difference between these figures is due to
the fact that the other Votes (1, 2 and 3)
taken together show a net reduction of
£68,584.
Since it was established a year ago the
internal organisation of the Ministry has
been modified and altered to meet the
tasks imposed by a critical period and a
changing situation, but its chief functions
are, as before, divisable into two main
categories internal security and civil
defence.
The expansion of its functions necessarily implies an increase of work for
those concerned, and this, combined with
the events of the past few months, has
placed no small strain on the Ministry's
staff. Their hours of work have been long
and arduous, their duties increasingly
strenuous, and I cannot allow the
occasion to pass without acknowledging
gratefully the willing and loyal service.
which they have continued to render.
The security of the Province, for which
my Department is responsible, has been
in the keeping of the constabulary forces.
During the year that is past the public
peace has been well preserved, and I
would take this opportunity of paying
tribute to the officers and men of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary for the great
part they have. played in accomplishing
this result. Their devotion to duty, their
courage and their high standards of
public service have been beyond praise
and have added lustre to an already fine
tradition. Their task has not been easy,
and it has only been by ceaseless vigilance
and energetic action on the part of the
police that the subversive elements have
been kept in check. In recent weeks the
duties of the force have been considerably increased by enemy raiding. During
these, and in the difficult aftermath period
the Inspector-General and those serving
under him rendered a public service of
the highest order and co-operated fully
with the civil defence services in the
strenuous tasks with which they were
faced.
The work of the regular force has had
the consistent and valuable help of the
Class "B" Special Constabulary. A considerable number of this category has
1 JULY 1941
Estimates
Ministry of Public Security 1126
equipped, sufficient in numbers, and,
perhaps most vital of all, in enjoyment
of the confidence and co-operation of the
public at large.
been mobilised for full-time duty in consequence of the
many additional precautions which a state of war entails, and
I think I may say that they have proved
themselves worthy of the force to which
they are attached and well deserving of
our thanks for the part they have played.
For the part-time members of this section.
of the Special Constabulary it has also
been a year of continuous vigilance and
activity. In Belfast they form a valuable police auxiliary and have also done.
excellent fire prevention work. Outside
Belfast they have, in addition to their
usual police duties, spent much time and
energy in military training so that, in
the event of invasion, they may take their
places with the Local Defence Volunteers
under military command to resist and
defeat the enemy.
I have heard many
military officers express their appreciation
of the military value of this force for
purposes of local defence, and at the
request of the military authorities I am
arranging that those of this class-and
they form the bulk of the force-who
would come under military control in case
of invasion, will receive an issue of battle
dress and steel helmets for use in the field.
I now come to the newer section of the
Special Constabulary-the Local Defence.
Volunteers, or, as they are now called, the
Ulster Home Guard. Every effort is
being made to strengthen the organisation
and efficiency of this force and much in
this direction has already been accomplished. Despite the difficulties of winter
conditions, training has been maintained
throughout the year and is progressing
well under military direction and with
much valuable co-operation from the
military forces. Clothing and equipment is well advanced. Issues of battle
dress have been made on a large scale
and every man will shortly be equipped
with a steel helmet. I think I can
assure the House that
that in training,
efficiency and equipment the force can
stand comparison with its counterpart in
Great Britain.
I must turn now to the equally important sphere of civil defence. It has
been called our fourth arm, and rightly
so, for on it depends, in large measure,
the stability and integrity of the home
front in the face of the attacks on the
civil population which Teutonic culture
has added to the trials of war.
To fulfil this purpose the civil defence
services must be well trained, reasonably
Let me say here that the organisation
and development of a system of civil
defence is not the easy task which some
critics appear to think. It is essentially
a practical business dependent upon
practical considerations as well as the
goodwill of the community; and, may I
add that, while exhortation and propaganda have their place, real steady progress demands deeds rather than words,
and an anxiety to solve and not merely
to search for the difficulties which exist.
It is impossible to over-emphasise the
importance of careful training and it has
been the aim of the Department throughout the year to stimulate and encourage
civil defence authorities throughout the
country to hold frequent
hold frequent organised.
exercises. The test of actual raiding has
shown that, in the main, the training
followed has been on sound lines and has
abundantly demonstrated the virtue of
practical exercises. It has also brought
much valuable experience which by schools
of instruction and other means is being
brought home to the various services
affected. From this experience it is not
unnatural that the youngest of the
services the emergency welfare service—
should have had most to learn. The
importance of that service is obvious and
steps continue to be taken to improve the
provision for mitigating the inevitable.
hardship arising from air raids. The
Belfast Civil Defence Authority have increased and are increasing their provision
of rest centres and dividing them into
first line in which immediate comfort can
be given after the raid, and second line
in which the genuinely homeless can be
accommodated, in places more remote
from the target area, for a further night
until the arrangements for their evacuation or billeting can be put in train. The
Ministry of Home Affairs is arranging to
receive them into other centres where they
can be accommodated if necessary while
the detailed registration and allocation.
to houses, billets, etc., is completed. The
emergency feeding arrangements have been
strengthened in conjunction with the
Ministry of Food and ready-cooked meals
can now be prepared and distributed from
kitchens provided by that Ministry.
Restaurants for people who, for one reason
Estimates-
Ministry of Public Security
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. MacDermott]
or another connected with the aftermath
of attack cannot obtain meals at home or
in their former restaurant or canteen, are
being operated and form a standing.
nucleus for the expansion of emergency
feeding when the need arises.
Greatly increased and improved provision has also been made by the establishment of district welfare offices, for the
supply of information and guidance on
the various personal and financial
problems which fall upon people who have
suffered or whose friends or relatives have
suffered in an air-raid. The lessons
learned in Belfast are being applied for
the city of Derry with, of course, considerable modification to allow for the
difference in area and population.
So
far as they are applicable they will also
be applied in the other larger towns, but
the greatest difficulties are naturally
peculiar to the large centres of population.
With the supervision of training is
closely linked the control of operations
during raids, a system which enables the
resources of the different services throughout the country to be marshalled according
to the need of the moment. The importance of mutual assistance cannot be overstressed, but practice here is also essential
if the best results are to be obtained, and
I trust that all responsible authorities will
do their utmost to rehearse their personnel
in this and the other aspects of civil
defence work. In this connection I would
again like to express my appreciation of
the manner in which, during the recent
attacks on Belfast, the services in outside
districts rallied to help those who had had
to bear the brunt of the onslaught. Their
timely assistance and, above all, their
anxiety to get on the spot and engage in
active service were most encouraging.
Parochial interests and obligations were
put out of mind and the one thought of
all was how best to help where help was
most needed.
So far as equipment is concerned, I
am glad to say that the supply position,
though not yet free from an atmosphere
of "priorities," is much easier than it
was earlier in the period under review.
Notwithstanding the difficulties in this
direction personnel and service equipment to the value of over £233,000 was
issued during this period. Much, of
course, remains to be done, but I am
glad to say that steel helmets are now
more readily available, and I hope the
day is not long distant when every
effective A.R.P. and civil defence
worker will have his or her own helmet.
I should add here that large quantities
of the new civilian type steel helmet are
now becoming available and supplies
have already been released to those areas
where the Fire Prevention Order or the
Fire Watcher Order has been applied.
Priority of supply is being given to those
who have liabilities under these Orders.
As additional stocks become available
free issues will be made to supplementary
fire parties organised by local authorities,
and finally it is expected to have supplies
available for sale to the general public.
There has also in recent months been
an improvement in. the supply of that
most important article for fire
fighting, stirrup pumps. In addition
to meeting outstanding demands from
the civil defence services, the Ministry
has issued a substantial number of
pumps to local authorities for sale to the
public at a cost of £1 each, which is a
considerable reduction as compared with
ordinary retail prices.
While on the subject of equipment I
should like to refer to the question of
uniforms for the civil defence services.
Last November it was decided to issue
uniforms to A.R.P. personnel in Great
Britain, and steps were taken by the
Ministry to make a corresponding issue
in Northern Ireland. Supplies of
bluette uniforms, as they are called, are
now being received weekly, and, though
delivery has been slow, I hope a substantial number will soon be provided
for. Similarly, it was decided to issue
waterproof capes for the use of wardens
during inclement weather, and all demands from local authorities for
this type of clothing have been satisfied
by issues. Approval has also recently
been given for the issue of heavy serge
uniforms for rescue and first-aid party
workers and supplies have been ordered,
though in this case some time must
elapse before these uniforms are available. The issue of uniforms to civil
defence workers may not strike hon.
Members as an essential matter. But it
has far more than a mere sartorial importance. It is the outward sign and
Ministry of Public Security 1130
Estimates-
1 JULY 1941
It
recognition of a body which has already
established its own esprit de corps and
its own value to the community.
will be the dress of duty and service, and
I hope it will be the habit of all civil
defence personnel who are entitled to
wear any of His Majesty's decorations
or medals to mount their ribbons
accordingly.
I said a moment ago that the civil
defence service must be sufficient in
numbers. I am glad to say that in some
of the raided districts the A.R.P. personnel strength is now greater than
before the attacks. But the scope of
civil defence is ever widening and we
must have sufficient personnel to man
and to keep manned not only the pumps,
the rescue parties, the casualty services,
the wardens' posts, the gas services, the
messenger service, the welfare services,
the report and control centres, but also
the vital service of fire prevention. So
wide is the field that there is something
that everyone can do to forward civil
defence. For many that something may
be limited to some task in the home, in
the street, or the immediate neighbourhood. But there must be many others
able to help those who are already helping them in the established services. We
owe more than we can tell to the steadfast
voluntary service of thousands, but we
must not kill the willing horse. We
must aid and support him in every way
possible, and the time has come when
all who are fit and free to do so must
help to the best of their ability.
I have also said that the services must
enjoy the confidence and the co-operation
of the whole community. I think I may
claim that they do enjoy to-day-and
deserve the increasing confidence of the
public. But in itself this is not enough.
Indeed, it is sometimes an embarrassment,
for there are those who do not scruple to
pass on their own responsibilities in a
manner which can only be described as
exploiting the willingness to serve of those
who are better citizens than themselves.
Co-operation is needed as well as
fidence. It is coming. But it cannot
come too completely or too soon. If the
members of the public who are not in the
services determine to help those who are
in every way they can they will add
enormously to the usefulness of civil
defence, and in so doing they will certainly help themselves. Just as on the
conmodern field of battle there must be the
fullest understanding and co-operation
between the different arms and, indeed,
the different elements, so it is as between
the civil defence services and those they
serve.
The tide of German aggression has
poured fastest and strongest where there
has been least collaboration. In this
respect what is true of the nations is true
of the individual, for in this war no one
can live to himself with impunity. But
working together with a common purpose
the momentum of our effort must increase
and develop till right is clothed with
might and victory crowns the common
cause.

One member of an A.R.P. service on

the other leg fractured. He was taken

it was decided that his £1 a week would

disabled for any work under A.R.P. he
is cut off. Does the right hon. Gentleman
think that is the sort of treatment that
should be given to voluntary workers?
If he does he is making a great mistake.
A man totally disabled owing to A.R.P.
services in a time of need should be

for at least a very considerable period of
time, or until such time as compensation
is given for the disability suffered. If the
right hon. Gentleman wants the name
and place I am prepared to give them to

As I say, the Belfast Corporation is not
just as black as it is painted. I read on
Saturday that the Corporation is to provide the personnel for a course of
instruction for fire watchers. Fire watching is not an amateur job. No matter
how a man may try to help in the putting
out of incendiaries or towards the
extinction of a fire if he has not had experience and knowledge he only becomes
a danger to himself and those working
with him. I suggest to the right hon.
Gentleman that he should immediately
form in Northern Ireland a paid body to
give fire advice. He may say he has given
wonderful service-I will not dispute that
-but he has not done half what is
required.
He has the "B" Specials that he spoke

L.D.Vs. If fire watching is anyone's
job it is that of a policeman or military
man, not a civilian. The fire watcher's
job requires training. No civilian should.
be asked to do fire watching on any business premises if he has not the necessary
training to know what to do when the call

the present system of voluntary fire
watchers being taken from the ranks of
the employees in a firm. The thing is a

fail to recognise their duty to the firm

I myself am a victim. If I told the

itself in the auxiliary fire
fire service,

gas identification groups, bomb identitification groups, and it has also

case.

coming events. It is a new type of warfare. Hitler has attempted to create discontent and dissatisfaction amongst our
people in every way possible. He is

him in that

I would like to say more, but I do not

I hope that the seriousness of the times

now

performance of duty by the fire-fighters
of all ranks, by the police and by the
general body of voluntary workers. That
fact is one of the bright features of the
last two grim months in Belfast, and I
do feel that if Ministers were living, as
some people are living, in danger zones
they would learn much.
One fact that struck me very vividly
in actual personal experience in the past
two months was looking at the exodus of
vast numbers of the civilian population of
Belfast at nightfall to the surrounding
country areas. It was a very distressing
sight. It has greatly lessened during the
past few weeks. While it did last you
saw an endless procession of young and
old, healthy and invalid, leaving the city
on foot, in carts, or lorries or buses. You
saw parents carrying or wheeling their
children. You saw multitudes of people,
young and old, hurrying along or drifting
along, and as far as one could judge by
appearance, not knowing and not even
caring in many cases where they were
going. They went out into the country
from the city. They slept in gardens or
in fields. They lay down in barns or
haysheds. Some went to the hillsides.
There they remained till day came, and
then at daybreak, if you were on the
scene again, you saw them trekking back
to the city in the early morning hours
haggard and tired and woebegone.
It was a pitiable sight to see children
struggling on outwards in the evening
and inwards in the morning beside their
parents, their guardians and seniors. Of
course the dread was on these refugees
of falling roof, and they fled in bewilderment. They fled in confusion. They
fled in terror to the open spaces of the
country. There at least they felt secure
from anything except a direct blow, and
even the danger in that direction was
minimised by the fact that if implements
of war fell in the country they would
probably sink into the soil, which would
weaken the shattering and devastating
effect that a fall in a crowded city would
have. I felt then, and I feel still, that
no adequate organisation for the supervision of these nocturnal fugitives had
been planned, no co-ordination
measures to cope with concentrations of
these crowds existed. I do not know if
any co-ordination exists even at the present moment or if things still are at a
of
loose end. But if they are, I will suggest
very strongly and seriously that steps
should be taken forthwith if there is to
be a succession of night raids on Belfast
or other urban centres. We all know
that the Prime Minister of the United
Kingdom envisages a war which may last
into the year 1943.
Then another topic that is rather a
grave one with me is the rent that is in
many cases exacted from these distracted
people. You hear of it in different
quarters. You read of it in the Pressof what is hardly Christian decency. The
people in some country areas round the
perimeter of Belfast are really worse
than Shylock in extorting the last penny
from these people who have very little
to spend. That is a deplorable thing in
our boasted civilisation and in the midst
of a vast war. I hope that some drastic
steps will be taken to check that evil.
It is a matter of satisfaction that during
the past two months we have had a
succession of dry, crisp weather. Had
it been a succession of rain, things would
have been very different. The suffering
of these people would have been increased

Oral Answers to Questions.
THIRD PARTY INSURANCE.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Attorney-
General whether he can state if third
party insurance is sound in respect of
giving protection to person and property;
whether the Zurich Assurance Company
is a recognised British company, and
whether their policies covering third
party are in accordance with the Act of
Parliament; whether in the case of
McPherson V. the Zurich Assurance
Company the policy was in order and
covered person and property; whether the
Zurich Assurance Company made
offer of £35 to McPherson up to the
hearing of the claim; what was the cause
of delay in having this claim dealt with
having regard to the fact that the accident took place in May, 1939, whether
the policies issued by the Zurich Company
to motor-car owners empower the company to inspect the said vehicles, whether
the Zurich company inspected the car in
the case of McPherson v. Zurich Company; whether legal costs in such cases
are too high, whether he can state the
actual costs in this claim; whether a poor
man can meet such liabilities as to claims;
and whether it is necessary to amend the
law in relation to third party insurance in
view of the decision given in this case in
favour of the Zurich Company.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply to this question.
I have no reason to assume that insurance against third party risks, arising out
of the driving of motor-cars, is unsound,
but I would like to remind the hon.
Member that such insurance is compulsory only for liability incurred in respect
of the death of, or bodily injury to, any
person. Insurance to cover liability in
respect of damage to property is not compulsory and public opinion has never
required that it should be compulsory.
The assurance company mentioned by
the hon. Member is authorised to transact
motor vehicle insurance business, and I
have no evidence indicating that any of
the policies which it issues do not comply
with the requirements of the law. They
usually give the company the right of
access to vehicles for the purpose of
examining them.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
the legal proceedings to which he refers
were instituted by a member of the public,
and I am not in possession of the facts
of the case; I am, therefore, not in a
position to answer the specific questions
which he asks. The reports of the case
which appeared in the daily papers seem
to indicate the claim was one in respect of
damage to property, and was, therefore,
outside the scope of the enactments
relating to insurance against third-party
risks.

PENSIONS OF
EVACUEES.

are causing hardships; if so, whether he
will make representations to the Board to
give more sympathetic treatment to these
unfortunate victims of war; and whether
he can inform the House as to the
number of supplementary pensions reduced
since April, 1941.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In answer to the hon. Member
I may say that the Assistance Board
informs me that when pensioners have
been evacuated to billets provided at the
public expense, their supplementary
pension must sometimes be reduced, since
it would obviously be improper to use
public funds to pay twice over for their
accommodation. If such a pensioner has
commitments if, for example, he has to
pay for the rent of a house in Belfast-the
reduction is deferred for a reasonable
period (usually about a month) to allow
him time to get rid of these commitments

RENTS CHARGED TO REFUGEES.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
exorbitant rents are now being charged
by farmers and other property owners
throughout Northern Ireland to refugees
from Belfast; and whether he will bring
in legislation to stop profiteering at the
expense of the working class and apply
it retrospectively from April, 1941.
Sir DAWSON BATES: A number of
complaints have been received by my
Ministry in response to the advertisement
which was published in the Press inviting
persons who were being charged exorbitant rents to report the facts to the
Ministry. These complaints are being
considered by the Ministry's legal
advisers with a view to prosecutions being
instituted under the Rent Restriction
Acts if the circumstances warrant such a
course being pursued. If it is found
that the existing law is not adequate to
stop profiteering as regards house rents I
am prepared to introduce legislation which
will, of course, be retrospective.

Contracts for Erection of Flax Barns.
The. MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have your permission, Mr.
Speaker, to give an explanation to the
House, and in particular to the hon.
Member for South Tyrone, regarding a
reply, which I now consider to have been
misleading, to a Parliamentary question
put by him on the 24th June concerning
contracts for the erection of flax barns.
The hon. Member asked me why Messrs.
R. Patton & Sons of Dungannon had not
been invited to tender in connection with
these contracts and I replied that the
firm had been invited on the 3rd May to
tender for the erection of flax barns but
no tenders were received, and so when a
contract for storage sheds was put out to
tender on the 20th May this particular
firm were not invited to tender because
they had not replied to the earlier
invitation.
I have since been informed that the
reason Messrs. Patton & Sons did not
send in a tender on the first occasion was
because they had seen a letter (not
addressed to them) from an architect in
the. Ministry stating that Messrs. Patton
would be given a chance to compete for
the second contract, i.e., the erection of
storage sheds. The branch of the
Ministry concerned with the issue of
invitations to tender unfortunately overlooked the letter in question and assumed
from Messrs. Patton's failure to reply on
the first occasion that they were not
interested in these contracts and, accordingly, did not ask them to put in a tender
for the second contract.
I had not this information before me
when I made my reply in the House and
I have taken this opportunity to give the
full facts of the case in order that the
hon. Member for South Tyrone may be
apprised of the true position.
I regret that Messrs. Patton were not
given an opportunity to tender for the
erection of the storage sheds and I have
taken steps to ensure that in future they
will not be overlooked for any similar
contracts which may have to be placed
by my Ministry in the Dungannon
vicinity.
