CLASS III. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £61,802 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1942, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Home Affairs."-(Note-
£14,000 has been voted on account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: Following the
usual practice I propose, with the permission of the Committee, to make any
remarks that seem to me to be helpful on the Estimate generally in the
course of introducing this Vote. It will
be seen that the net increase in the expenditure set out in the Estimate
amounts to £20,957, and of this amount
£13,746 is accounted for by the salaries
of the evacuation branch which has been
transferred from the Ministry of Public
Security to my Department, together
with the particular section of the new
services with which it dealt and which
my Ministry has now taken over. A
further £3,597 represents the salaries of
a branch that it has been necessary to
set up to deal with refugees, which includes both persons who leave the city
temporarily and those who have been or
may be evacuated as an immediate consequence of a raid, and £5,615 represents
the cost of a supplies branch, the services
of which are required in connection with
billeting arrangements and with hostels.
It will be seen, therefore, that broadly
speaking, the increase in the Estimate is
due to the provision of staff to undertake
new work, and that in so far as this
work, while new to us, is identical with
services formerly supplied by the Ministry of Public Security, the same staff
has, broadly speaking, been engaged
upon it. I think, however, it is right
to refer to the addition of two assistant
secretaries to the headquarters establishment. One of these is engaged exclusively on our new civil defence work.
I think the need for such an appointment is evident, and that I need not say
any more about that. The other
assistant secretaryship became necessary
by reason of war work in connection with
roads and transport. It would not be
difficult to outline in what directions
this work has increased, but I think it
will also be understood that this particular section of the Ministry's road and
transport activities is not one to which
it would be in the public interest to give
any publicity.
With regard to the prison service I am
able to report continued steady progress
as to accommodation, dietary, and
discipline. Provision is made for a tota!
of nine hundred inmates during the year,
and this increase is due mainly to the
number of persons who have had to be
interned under the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act, and the Estimate
reflects generally the increased charges
for food, clothing, etc., which are due
to war conditions. I would like to take
this opportunity of expressing the
Government's appreciation of the work
performed during air raids by the staffs
of the three prisons. I am sorry that I
cannot say very much more than that
about it, but the Committee will, I
think, understand my brevity on the
subject. They showed the greatest
gallantry and efficiency and gave wonder-
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
8 JULY 1941
ful help to the authorities at that particular time. The fact that five
internees recently escaped from custody
in Belfast Prison is engaging my
attention.
The estimate for Malone Training
School and Reformatory and Industrial
Schools does not present any unusual
feature. There is a slight increase in the
probable number of inmates due to war
conditions to which also can be, attributed
the increased total amount. The question
of juvenile delinquency has become more
marked since the war. The number of
young offenders, unfortunately, shows an
upward tendency due to the prevailing
conditions the lack of parental controllaxity in enforcing school attendance
owing to evacuation and to general
restlessness. To remedy this state of
affairs is a matter for the community as
a whole, and without the general cooperation of the public no measures to.
combat this social evil can be successful.
The work done in Malone Training
School in this connection is, I am happy
to say, having very good results, and the
number of trainees who fail to benefit
from their period of training is relatively
small. When we can show that 95 per
cent. of the boys who leave make good
citizens nobody can say the Borstal
system is a failure. I would like to say
a word in regard to the governor and his
staff. That very happy result is due to
the interest, apart from their official
duties, they take in the boys. When one
sees the letters received by the governor
and his wife from these, old boys thanking
them for what they received at the school
one feels that that is the greatest
testimony that can be expressed.
Although not a matter coming strictly
within the purview of the Estimates, I
think the Committee will be glad to learn
that the question of accommodation for
the Petty Sessions Courts at Belfast has
now been settled and arrangements are
actually in train whereby the Old Town
Hall building is being placed at the
disposal of the resident magistrates for
court and office purposes.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Who settled the
question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Though the
hon. and learned Gentleman may differ
from me I claim credit for it.
Mr. BEATTIE: You are entitled to it.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This arrangement will, I trust, finally solve the very
vexed question of the congestion at the.
Petty Sessions courts and will give the
public the facilities to which they are
entitled.
In connection with the work of the
Local Government Division, I feel that
hon. Members will expect me to make
some reference to the recent inquiry
held into the administration of the
Tuberculosis Sanatorium. Hon. Members
are aware that while the action taken
by me as a result of the report furnished
by the inspectors had to be of a very
drastic character the. suggestion has been
quite widely made that even more drastic
and far-reaching steps should be taken.
With regard to this suggestion I can
only say that while it is the policy of my
Department to examine all such possibilities I think we must remember that
our local government system is fashioned
on democratic lines, and it is a prime
essential of any such democratic organisation that public opinion should be relied
upon to demand honesty and efficiency in
public administration. I cannot too
strongly emphasise that ratepayers are
also citizens and that they do not discharge their duties as citizens simply by
paying their rates. I have to say, therefore, quite frankly that I am not in
favour of abolishing popularly elected
bodies save as a last resort, for I consider
that it must always be to some extent a
confession of failure on the part of the
public to live up to their civic duties and
responsibilities when this has to be done.
I deplore the necessity of having been
obliged to appoint Commissioners in this
particular case, but I have no doubt
whatever as to the propriety of that action
in the circumstances, and I have every
confidence that the interests of the ratepayers will not suffer during the time
that the Commissioners may remain in
office.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is that the Belfast
Corporation?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am referring
to the Tuberculosis Committee.
I am
sure the hon. Member does not want the
other thing. Hon. Members will recollect
that very
substantial economies were

As an
Hon. Members are aware that a scale of
diet is provided for each class of inmates.
This scale is, of course, the maximum and
in fact these maximum quantities are not
always needed. For example, when tea
is being made for a very large number of
persons the amount of dry tea per head
required is very much less than is needed
for two or three persons. Consequently
there ought always to be a very considerable saving shown on the maximum issue
of tea. Again patients do not always
require the full amount of meat which
they might eat if they were in better
health, and so on.
In the case of beef and mutton no
saving on the maximum issue at all was
shown for the years 1937-1939, when the
Guardians were in office, but in 1940,
when the Commissioners were in charge, a
saving of 929 lbs. of meat was shown,
which the following year increased to
7,864 lbs. Similarly in the case of cheese
no saving was shown for the years 1937-
1939, and in the two years the Commissioners have been there savings have been
11,582 ozs. and 18,386 ozs.
In the case
of potatoes a saving of 40,131 lbs. was
shown last year as against no savings
under the Guardians' management, even
though the total maximum scale allowance
has been very much reduced. In the
case of bacon there have been savings of
410 and 316 lbs. respectively in the last
two years as against previous nil returns.
I wish to emphasise these figures because
it has been suggested that the Commissioners have saved money at the expense
of the inmates. That is not so.
I do not think there are many other
Local Government matters with which I
should now occupy the time of the House,
but I would like to take this opportunity
of expressing my appreciation of the
assistance we have received from officers
of local authorities in connection with

difficult task. They undertook it without

ordinary duties which are exceptionally

I also wish to express my thanks to
another type of local officer who has been

indeed, though not officially connected
with my Ministry. In this I refer to the
school-teachers, and I cannot speak too

number of matters lately, such as
evacuation.

Ministry of Home Affairs 1182

8 JULY 1941
The only matter remaining for me to
Ideal with is that of evacuation. Hon.
Members will understand that I must of
necessity say very little about this, and
in so far as I say anything at all that I
must deal with it in the most general
terms. I may, however, perhaps say that
when my Ministry took over this service
after the raids we found that owing to
the severity of these raids a very large
number of persons had left Belfast and
gone to the country. The ordinary peacetime evacuation scheme which had been in
operation before the raids took place
could not, of course,
deal with the
situation that arose, and, consequently, no
records were available to indicate the
extent of this post-raid evacuation or the
location of the persons who had gone to
the country in this way. My Ministry
has prepared a scheme designed to provide for this kind of after-raid evacuation,
and we are in the course of completing a
survey of the country as a whole which
will enable us to carry out a very much
needed redistribution of the temporary
residents in the country. The particulars
of this scheme will shortly be made known
to the public and for the moment I think
all I need say is that in principle it is
based on the idea of moving people, in the
first instance, to distribution centres
situated at a relatively short distance
from the target area, and from these
centres they will subsequently be billeted
either in private houses or in hostels.
Hon. Members will be aware of the
many difficulties that have arisen and I
think I may say that we have had due
regard to all these and that we have
devised a system which I hope will take
care of them in so far as it is possible to
do so. We have in mind the desirability
of avoiding as far as possible separating
families of small children, of making
special provision for certain classes of
persons who are not suitable for one
reason or another for billeting in private
households, and we have kept in mind the
fact that if billeting is to be a success
the conditions must be reasonably comfortable for the host as well as the person
billeted. Further, we have not lost sight
of the fact that persons who have spent
all their lives in the city cannot be
deposited in the country and left there
without any provision being made for
their occupation and well-being, and
we are taking steps in this direction.
And that is as much as I feel that
it would be right for me to say in public
on this subject at the moment. I am
afraid it is not a very satisfactory statement of the position, but hon. Members
will, I feel sure, bear with me in the
circumstances, and I might add that if
there is any particular information which
any hon. Member would like to have on
the subject I shall be only too pleased to
let him have it privately. I beg to move.

I was speaking about the inquiry at

Mr. Dunlop did not feel competent to

and he adjourned the inquiry and

General. I stated that I was quite

was written behind the back of Dr.
Walker and withdrawn by the person who
wrote it. That letter was a libel.
Regarding the moral character of Dr.
Walker and the matron, I prefer to take
the evidence of Professor Holmes. I am
quite satisfied with it, and so would any
reasonably-minded individual in the
world to-day. The Attorney-General is
now present, and I should like to know
under what law of evidence is a letter
written about a matter seven or eight
years ago, behind the back of the person
concerned and then withdrawn, acted
upon. In my experience, if a person
withdraws his evidence or goes back on
it before a judge, the judge rules out the
evidence on the spot, on the instant.
Who had a better right to know the
nature of the letter than the person who
wrote it, and withdrew it? He only
wrote it when he thought he would not
have to prove it. But it was acted upon.
There was some gossip at that time evidently, and it was mere gossip, like the
story of Dr. Walker going to the matron's
room, and Professor Holmes had to be
brought on the scene. I am very sorry
that such a thing occurred.
Now we will go on to evacuation, which
is a most important subject. The House
will recollect that after the war broke out
nearly everyone in Northern Ireland who
had a big house sent a letter to the then
Prime Minister placing his house at the
disposal of the authorities for the duration of the war. Every night there was
a list of these big houses published in the
papers. I would like to know where these
people are now and where these big houses
are. We will leave that there. But the
Parliamentary Secretary promised that
there would be legislation to deal with
the people who were charging excessive
rents to evacuees. Perhaps he might
have said "if it was found necessary."
He may have said that. I am not sure.
I understood that there was going to be
immediate legislation. The Ministry of
Home Affairs advertised for people who
had any complaints to send letters to the
Ministry of Home Affairs. The Ministry
also gave instances of what agents could
not do in respect of the letting of houses.
For instance, a house under £13 valuation cannot be let furnished. The
Ministry of Home Affairs went to a good
deal of trouble in that respect, but they
did not get as many replies as they
thought they would get. That was
through no fault of the Ministry, and it
does not prove that excessive rents are not
being charged. First and foremost, a lot
of these people who were evacuated did
not see a paper at all, and second, if they
did see it, about the last thing they would
do in the world is to sit down and write
a letter to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

I am sorry I have had to speak so

It is a pity of the councillors when they
go into these associations. I am referring
to Belfast now, not the country. I will
say this regarding Belfast. Some of the
lowest people in the city have found their
way into these associations. I was vicechairman of one and vice-president of
another. And every time I went to the
association there were women who were
always selling tickets for various things.
I had a shrewd idea of where the money
was going.
They would come and say, "Alderman,
let me introduce you to our new member,
Mr. Brown. He is not working. Can
you get him a job?" I heard nothing
but that, and everyone else has to listen
to the same thing. It puts councillors
and aldermen in a false position and
they have to run away. I do not know
how any man can stick it. You hear
nothing else. The point is that some
councillors and aldermen think these
people have more power than they have,
and they are afraid to defy them. I
listened to that kind of thing for a long
time. One night I got up and announced
that I was going to talk to them. I did
and hoisted the banner of independence.
The minute a person is nominated by
one of these associations the influence of
the party and the Press is thrown in
behind the nomination. Who are these
people? In a constituency
a constituency of about
20,000 voters you have an association
consisting of about 60 ladies-I will call
them ladies to be polite. I do not mean
it-and about ten men. I except a few.
I do not condemn them all. But there
is not anyone who would go to one of the
sixty for advice on any one subject.
There is only one thing before them and
that is to try to have a contest till they
get money out of the candidate. That
is all they are thinking of from one end

elections as they can and to try to get
the candidate and his wife to entertain
them.
I know that does not apply to the
country.

There is a matter on which I have first
hand information and I would like to
say a word or two about the work of the
Ministry in that connection. For a
number of years I have taken an interest
in an organisation which does useful work
for discharged prisoners. For a number
of years the society was in some, difficulties, but thanks to the sympathy and
guidance of the Ministry the organisation
has been reorganised and re-established
with a new agent and a new committee.
The Members of the House will be pleased
to know that the good chairman of the
committee is the Vice-Chancellor of
Queen's University. Men discharged
from prison are in a
very difficult
position. I know that you cannot do very
much for some of them, but there are
always a few who can and ought to be
helped in that critical position in their
lives, and thus the society's agent meets
them at the prison gates and assists them.
I am glad to say that in recent months
the society has been able to pilot a
number of these unfortunate people, into
positions and to guide some of them into
the forces of the Crown where they will
be able to live worthy lives and get a
second chance.
Reference has been made
to the
problem of evacuation and rehousing of

prepared for all emergencies that might

There is just one other thing and that is
to reiterate the suggestion that was made
by the Member for Ballynafeigh. This is
a subject in which I have had an interest
not for a few years but during the greater
part of my life. I would suggest that the
Ministry should keep an eye open on the
results of the new conditions that obtain
in Belfast at the present time owing to
the fact that there is a tremendous circulation of money, and owing to the
further fact that the authorities are very
much preoccupied in other things. On
the day of the so called blitz I visited one
of the areas and I saw the homes of the
people wrecked. People were very miserable. I saw also a fact that stirred my
heart with pity. I do not blame the
people. I saw the public houses crammed
to overflowing. As I say, I do not blame
the people because they had been misled.
They had been befooled, and at the time
of their trouble flew to what they thought
would help them. I did not blame them
and I do not blame them now. I pitied
them.
One other fact I wish to mention in
that connection. Only the other day I
had a complaint made to me by an owner
of property in the city. He said that at
the present time, owing to the new conditions, changed hours, long nights,
plenty of money, and masses of people,
some of the tenants in his houses could
not get sleep until two or three o'clock
in the morning owing to the noise, revelry
and drinking in and around the air-raid
shelters in the locality in which he is
situate. I do not blame the police.
Their hands are full and they are doing
their work well. I suggest to the Ministry that the new situation has been
created by war conditions. I do not think
that liquor is doing so much harm as it
did in the last war owing to Lloyd George,
who made the price of liquor such that
men do not buy so much of it as they
did. At the same time, the situation is
such that I hope the Ministry will keep
an eye on it and see that this aspect of
our national life is improved and that
this burden on our nation is reduced as
much as possible during these terrible
lays. Hitler has dealt with this thing in
a drastic way in his country. I do not
want to develop this line. A new situation
has been created. I do not blame the
police. They are doing their work well,
but perhaps the attention of some of the
authorities would be redirected to the
new situation created. I feel that the
Ministry has a great business on hand. So
far as the greatest part of its work is concerned it is doing its work admirably and
well.

Mr. AGNEW: One is surprised at the
cost of administration of this depart-
One particular section does call
for serious attention and that is our
prison service. The reason of that cost
can be easily explained by the fact that
this democratic Government believes in a
policy of keeping men interned with no
charge preferred against them. I feel,
and a great many outside feel, that if a
person has committed a crime it is the
duty of constituted authority to prove
that that person has committed an offence
and have him brought before the proper
authority to be dealt with. Such is not
the case here. Unfortunately, many
innocent people are at the moment in
prison with no charge preferred against
them. I would like the Minister to deal
with this serious problem, because it has
caused uneasiness and hardship owing to
the fact that the same department who
have interned these people said, "You
are not entitled to any assistance from
the poor-law authorities in order to live."
That is a very inhuman way of dealing
with this problem. The Ministry should
consider the aspects as they find them and
see that justice is done.
As to the important problem of
evacuation, I feel that the Government
has adopted a proper procedure. After
almost two years of war we find that
changes have taken place on the question
of evacuation, which has been handed
back to the original department. Is it a
fact that evacuees or refugees from the
city of Belfast arrived in my area and the
only place of solace they could find was
the workhouse? That is not the proper
way to meet the occasion at all. We were
told by the late Prime Minister quite a
long time ago that everything was in
push-bell order. Now we find the position very acute and there is absolutely no
provision in certain areas. I protested
very strongly to the Commissioner in
Armagh in that respect. The answer he
gave was that the working classes of
Belfast desired to live in working class
areas. That was very misleading. In a
time of emergency it is the duty of the
Ministry of Home Affairs 1208
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Agnew]
Government and the local authority concerned to see that no one is left homeless,
and that the refugees are not sent to the
workhouse. It is an absolute scandal that
in this age of progress and so-called civilisation the workers of Belfast, who
had been displaced from their homes,
could find no other place but the union.
I sincerely hope it will never happen
again, otherwise there will be serious
reaction. I would like to know if
individuals from the privileged class had
been in the same position and reached our
town would they have been sent to the
workhouse. Certainly not, they would
have been found in the best hotels with
most beautiful accommodation. There
was ample room in Armagh for every
refugee in the houses of the privileged
class, but they did not come up to
expectations and do their duty.
The
onus was left practically on the working
classes of Armagh, and houses already
overcrowded owing to present conditions
are worsened. I visited them myself and
was absolutely disgusted. Now is the
time for the department to meet the
situation in a proper spirit and build
houses and provide suitable accommodation. There is ample space near Richhill
and other centres.
There is another matter about which I
am seriously concerned. We find in the
Armagh district an area officer has been
appointed for billeting purposes, and I
would draw the attention of the Ministry
to the fact that he has recently retired
from the police with the very substantial
pension granted to a sergeant while we
have many unemployed walking round.
unable to get a job. Is it the desire of
the Ministry to give good jobs to men who
are pretty well off without them. That
is not fair. We advocate one man one
job, and surely it is not too much to ask
the Ministry to go into this question
because there are plenty of people who
have no pensions capable of doing this
work. It is a scandal in these times to
be handing over such jobs to men with
good pensions from the police. It is an
outrage and should not be tolerated by
any Government department, but I fear
it is encouraged.
I also wish to raise a question with
regard to the poor law. I feel it is time
the whole question of the poor law was
gone into.
The poor law requires very
serious reform. In the various counties
we have county councils, rural councils,
and boards of guardians, and in
opinion there is serious overlapping in the
administration. This could be centralised
inside the county council with various
departments dealing with tuberculosis,
mental patients, and so forth. Local
government is overloaded and overlapping.
It is a mysterious system all through and
one which is very hard to understand.
Take the county councils. The county
council in County Armagh deals with
mental patients, tuberculosis, education,
the infirmary, and interlocked under the
control of the county council is the poorlaw system.
There is also the question of the rural
councils. I think it time that changes
were made.
They will not in any way
take away from democratic principles. I
refer to mental hospitals. I feel that the
Ministry in the no very distant future will
have to go into the question of the staffs
of mental hospitals. Whilst much has
been done for the betterment of the conditions by the various committees throughout Northern Ireland much has yet to be
done. The staffs work very long hours in
carrying out their duties. The Department concerned should at an early date
set up a commission of inquiry, not into
the administration of the institutions, but
as to how they can be improved.
I notice in the Estimates that the
amount laid down for spending in connection with maternity and child welfare is
very small. In my opinion the Ministry
of Home Affairs should increase it considerably because we want to do away
with disease and sickness, and give a
better system of treatment to mothers.
We must start at the right place to see
that proper maternity hospitals are provided on similar lines to those in Great
Britain. There is a great work being
done there, but unfortunately in the provincial areas there is not that accommodation; neither is there suitable room for
clinics for mothers and children.
have advocated that for quite a long
period in our own area, and I hope that

been spent on the medical services in the

Finally, I would ask the Minister in

That council is imposing a rent which, in

paid. I hope the Minister will go into
the various matters raised, because they
deal with the question of human welfare.
Mr. BROWN: I wish to say a few
words with regard to the most sensational
event that has taken place here within
recent times, the suspension of the
Tuberculosis Committee of the Belfast
Corporation. The general view of the
country, so far as I come in contact with
it, is one of amazement that the Government had not the courage to go in and
suppress the Corporation. We had the
housing and many other scandals, and
the people in the country are wondering
how many scandals there will have to be
before the Government are prepared to
put down their foot in this matter. Are
the Belfast Corporation stronger than
the Northern Government? Is that the
position? This House was adjourned a
short time ago so that a certain distinguished visitor should be received
first by the Corporation. I objected to
that then as a slight to this House, and
I will object to it if it is suggested again.
Can the Ministry say quite frankly
that there has been a great improvement
in the administration of the Board of
Guardians since the commissioners were
appointed? The Corporation should be.
abolished at once as an example to the
whole of Northern Ireland. I trust that
even at this late hour the Government
will reconsider their views on this matter
and put in commissioners for a time at
least, because so far as I can discover that
is the view taken generally in the
country.
Another matter on
speak is civil defence.
which I want to

With all due respect to the chairman

In my opinion he both wants to know
about it and does know about it
and about A.R.P. matters in general.
Furthermore, he presides over that

There is no necessity for the hon. Member
for Woodvale or myself getting excited

his duty with energy and ability. This
Committee could accomplish far more if

of the Committee I am not satisfied with

defence in a better way.

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): It would appear
to me that the two main topics that have
interested the Committee to-day on the
review of these Estimates are, first of all,
the question of evacuation in so far as
it concerns this Ministry, and, secondly,
the result of the inquiry into Whiteabbey
Sanatorium, in which there has been,
somewhat to my surprise, a tremendous
amount of interest taken not merely by
Members from the city but by Members
outside the city.
With regard to evacuation, I am sure
it is appreciated by hon. Members that
very unusual circumstances had to be
coped with. Evacuation, when it was
contemplated, as I think you will remember the Minister of Public Security
explained here, was supposed to be a process carried out when there was peace and
quietness in which to carry it out.
Various schemes put forward by that
Ministry and sanctioned by the Government received but a poor response. When
the two serious air raids occurred there
was evacuation on a large scale; in fact,
I think it is not going too far to say that
since Moses was confronted with his evacuation from Egypt there has been
nothing of an equal character. One must
remember that as regards his problem he
had the assistance of the many recorded
miracles, notably in the matter of feeding.
I wish I could give the exact number of
houses destroyed, because if that information were in the minds of Members
they would have more sympathy and a
proper appreciation of the difficulties that
then confronted the Ministry of Public
Security and subsequently the Ministry
of Home Affairs in dealing with these
people. Be assured that there is no feeling of self-complacency about how we
handled or endeavoured to handle this
problem. People went out in large
numbers. They had to be sorted out and
billeted in comfortable surroundings. We
tackled that problem with all the energy
we could.
The hotel mentioned by the hon.
Member for Pottinger will be used, not
as a place of refuge for the well-to-do
class; in fact, I am bound to say that
members of the Government, from the
Prime Minister down, have incurred the
most serious criticism, I will not say
abuse, for taking over that hotel but we
have done it irrespective of that criticism.
The building is going to be used for the
people whose interests the hon. Member
has so much at heart. They will be
sorted out; they will be living there, and
the hon. Member is perfectly at liberty to
go and visit them and see the scheme
when thoroughly organised. To-morrow
we hope to have an interview with a man
who, we trust, will be found capable of
running a hotel on the large scale we have
in mind.
The hon. Member for South Tyrone was
good enough to speak appreciatively of
what we are doing in his county. At the
same time I should like to take the opportunity of expressing my appreciation to
members of local authorities, like the hon.
Member for South Tyrone, and to the local
officials all over the Six Counties with one
exception-I do not propose to give that
county any infamous notoriety, because I
am sure it will do better in the futurefor the great assistance we have received
in dealing with this problem. The hon.
Member for South Tyrone gave some indication of the scheme we have in mindwe hope to establish more than one centre
of that character-with a view to dealing
with people who have had to leave their
homes.
The matter of huts has been mentioned
by the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh.
We are dealing with that problem. As
you have heard from the Minister of
Commerce we felt that his Ministry has,
perhaps, some priority over ours in providing for the skilled craftsmen whose
work is necessary for the sustenance and
maintenance of and increase in our war
effort.

Of course
the Nissen huts can only be considered
as a substitute for proper billets. At the
present time we are having a census taken
in the Six Counties-I trust we get time
to carry it out-to see what billeting
accommodation we have at our disposal.
Hon. Members should remember that this
country has not got a great surplus of
houses.
The hon. Member for Pottinger
alluded to the houses promised at the
beginning of the war. We were supplied
immediately with that list from the
Ministry of Finance, and we found-I
do not think I am giving anything
dangerous away in telling this that a
great number of these houses from the
interval since the outbreak of war had
been requisitioned by members of the
armed forces. When one made inquiries
about a house it was often found it was
pre-empted or ear-marked, or the
various words which describe it. In
many cases these houses were not
available, but not for the reasons
suggested, that the owners were reluctant
to facilitate the Ministry in taking them
over for working people had that been
possible. Although there is quite a
number of these large houses, on investigation it was found that they lacked
sanitary accommodation, water supplies
and so forth, and that they could not
be readily made available for the

survey is completed and the evacuees are

reasonable criticism by hon. Members
with regard to people living under improper conditions will not be made with
any degree of truth.
There is another matter which hon.
Members have raised-exorbitant rents.
Some weeks ago the hon. Member for
Woodvale very properly and accurately
reminded me of the answer I had given
here to inquiries on his part. We did
advertise, and I must confess I was somewhat disappointed with the number of
complaints received. Ten related to
houses which, in fact, cannot be let as
furnished, namely, houses of a valuation
of £13 or under. Two other complaints
were made which prima facie appear to
come within the meshes of the penal
section of the Act. These cases have
been referred to the learned Attorney-
General. They are under investigation.
We are trying to get evidence pieced together for the purpose of a prosecution,
and on the result of that will depend
the view we form as to whether or not
we need further strength. If it is found
that more drastic legislation is necessary
then the Government will not hesitate to
ask the House to give them the necessary
power. It may be well worth considering-I merely throw out the hint for the
consideration of hon. Members-whether
or not a more summary method of dealing with exorbitant rents could not be
designed by the setting up of a tribunal
specially for the occasion where complaints could be made in an informal
manner, and the persons who are bleeding the people at the present time could
be made to disgorge their ill-gotten gains.
Of course legislation of the sort would
be retrospective.
Mr. BEATTIE: You mean a fair rents
court to apportion a fair rent for the
people?
Mr. LOWRY: I would not go so far
as to define it as a fair rent court. It is
rather the refunding of such money as
would be regarded as excessive or an unfair return compared, say, with the first
day of the war, 1939. I also think it a
desirable part of such legislation that they
should also be fined or imprisoned, or
both. So much for that question of
evacuation and the manner we are

Another topic that raised a good deal

on Whiteabbey Sanatorium. I should
like to say with respect to this that the
Ministry is satisfied that the inquiry was
held by the two inspectors appointed for

courage and skill, and that their findings
were fully justified by the evidence given.
before them. I need scarcely remind the

is a gentleman with a good practical

be conscious of this, that the two

with certainty on the facts given in
evidence before them and to draw a correct inference than any persons, even
those persons who have taken the trouble
to wade through the pile of evidence.
These inspectors are the persons in the
position to pronounce with certainty on
the facts given before them. And the
hon. Member should not assume, because

of Belfast.
As to why that letter was so much in
evidence, it was cogent evidence against
the Medical Superintendent of Health
for the city of Belfast, and it was used
as evidence against him and as evidence
against nobody else. For my own part I
am happy to think that the Ministry

fearless, skilled, courteous and

Mr. NIXON: With reference to the
letter written by Dr. Thomson, the
medical superintendent of health for the
city of Belfast, the Parliamentary
Secretary said that that letter was only
used in evidence against Dr. Thomson.
Mr. LOWRY: Yes. The hon.
Member, unless I misunderstood him,
led me to think that he considered the
inspectors had used that letter in forming their conclusions against Dr. Walker
and the matron. That is not so.
Mr. NIXON: The hon. and learned
Member is slightly in error. What I did
say or intended to convey was that the
inspectors used that letter against Dr.
Walker, but not against the matron. At
all events the Parliamentary Secretary
says that that letter was only used against
the writer, Dr. Thomson. I know that
that would be quite in order, but, if it is,
where is the penalty? He was over the
whole of the health services; he was over
Dr. Walker; he wrote that letter. That
letter was libellous. The insinuations in
it were proved to be a lie. That letter
was read on the advice of the Attorney-
General; that letter, according to the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs, was used only against
the writer, which would be undoubtedly
within the law of evidence. But where
is the penalty on the medical superintendent?
Mr. LOWRY: He was severely censured.
Mr. NIXON: Severely censured-a
man who will soon be retiring. That will
not leave him without a cup of tea in the
morning; that will not leave him without
a pension; that will not leave him without his month's salary. I say that on the
statement of the Minister of Home Affairs
and on the findings Dr. Walker and the
matron stand condemned. I would ask
the Parliamentary Secretary if he has
time to look up what the findings against
Dr. Walker, and more particularly against
the matron, are based on. There never
were such findings against anybody, and
I want to tell you here and now that an
injustice has been done.
It is not the first injustice that has been
committed in Northern Ireland. Injustice
in Northern Ireland, I say, is quite a
common thing, and if we had not the
over-riding influence of the great Imperial
Parliament things would be worse. The
Prime Minister is by nature just. I do
not know why he does not assert himself
more than he does. Every injustice done
will come home one day or another. You
may think you
will shake it off, but you
will not. I do not like to mention myself,
but I am here through an injustice. It
never did me any harm. You have never
been able to shake me off, and you never
will. A lot of people-I cannot tell why
-got the idea into their heads that I had
a special spite against the Minister of
Home Affairs for a certain thing that
happened to me some years ago.
I had no special spite against him, and
I have not now, because that was decided
by another person in London, and it was
decided in the presence and in the hearing
of a porter, who is now out of reach, and
cannot be injured. He let me know.
Some people seem to think that a porter
has no ears at all. I heard all about it.
I am here and I am going to be here..
The Minister of Home Affairs was only
obeying the orders he got from London.
Anyhow, I am here, and there is no use
going back on that; it has lasted long
enough. I am one man who has survived it. I myself do not see that I am
failing in any capacity-others may—but
I neither see it nor feel it. I would do
justice though the heavens should fall.
Justice has not been done to this strange
girl who came here from England, who
was doing her best, who was a model of
virtue. If this girl had not submitted
herself for medical examination by Mr.
Holmes nothing in the world would have
cleared her. And all because the medical
superintendent of the institution went
into her room. The way this lady and
gentleman have been treated and maligned
is most disgraceful.

If we on both sides of this House knew
what the people are whispering about us
we might be surprised. I remember that
in Lisburn a man told a reckless story
about a young lady who went to see some
friends. The man he told it to went
straight to her father. The father saw a
lawyer and consulted a K.C., and the
libeller had to pay some hundreds of
pounds for his libel. If anyone who
hears a libellous story did that there
would be less tittle tattle. I remember
a story that a sergeant in Liverpool had
been arrested on the street and had been
handcuffed. When I heard the story I
said: "That is a lie on the face of it;" a
sergeant would not be handcuffed on the
street, even if he were arrested. I came
at the persons who told the story afterwards, and they never even apologised;
they said they heard it.
If people allow themselves to be carried
away by tittle tattle, nobody will be safe.
Then the Medical Superintendent Officer
of Health, Dr. Thomson, is severely
censured; he was condemned on his own
handwriting. He was an enemy of Dr.
Walker's from the very start. Dr.
Walker never could lift up his head with
Dr. Thomson and the Committee on top
because he would not agree to recommend
a certain site and take a bribe and let
some of them get bribes too. That came
out in evidence before the inquiry, and
those over his head knew. Now he is sent
out into the world to look for his living.
So is the matron, who was brought over
here from London, and who was carrying
out her duties most efficiently.
matter of fact, she would not take this

Oral Answers to Questions.
PAYING OFF OF WORKERS.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Public Security whether tradesmen on
certain Government jobs have been paid
off without any explanation being offered;
whether he can state who was responsible
for this action, the Security Police or the
local R.U.C.; whether he can also state
if the Security Police were responsible for
the paying off of workers employed in the
N.A.A.F.I. in Armagh, Enniskillen and
other towns.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): I am
not aware of any instances where a person
employed on a Government of Northern
Ireland contract has been paid off in the
circumstances suggested by the hon.
Member.
As regards contracts in Northern
Ireland undertaken by Departments of
the Imperial Government, the responsibility for engaging or dispensing with the
services of workers for these contracts rests
with the contractors and the Imperial
Departments concerned.
Similarly, with regard to the last part
of the question, the engagement and dismissal of N.A.A.F.I. employees is a
matter for the authorities of that institution.
Mr. AGNEW: Would the Minister tell
us who is the responsible authority for
supplying information for the displacement of men on a job? Is it not the
local R.U.C.?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The responsibility
for terminating a job is the responsibility
of the contractors. The R.U.C. are only
concerned where in the case of contracts
involving a special question of security
they are asked for confidential reports
concerning a member of the personnel. In
that case it is their duty to furnish a confidential report and there their responsibility ends.
Mr. AGNEW: In view of that unsatisfactory reply I desire to give notice that
I will raise the matter on the adjournment.
FOOD FOR THE L.D.V.
2. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether, in
view of the proposed disbursement of the
sum of £3,450 for food to Local Defence
Volunteers engaged in the defence of
Government buildings, he can state. what
facilities are similarly available for Local
Defence Volunteers who are engaged in
prolonged service in connection with the
protection of civilian property or defence.
duties generally.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: It is the policy
of my Department in matters of this
kind, which affect the wellbeing of the
Ulster Home Guard, to follow as closely
as possible the rules which have been laid
down for the Home Guard in Great
Britain. The facilities available, in the
absence of arrangements for the supply
of meals, therefore follow the relevant
Army Council Instruction, which was
issued last year, and which provides that
where extra expense is necessarily
incurred by a volunteer in the performance of his duties he will be eligible
for subsistence allowance, if he desires to
claim it, provided that he is employed on
a continuous period of duty duly
authorised, and in excess of five hours'
duration.

whether the Minister can state the length

in the

ARMAGH UNION INFIRMARY
APPOINTMENT.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
Nurse Chambers, who was recently
appointed superintendent nurse in
Armagh Union Infirmary, had the necessary qualifications in view of the standard
required from the previous occupant of
this post; whether the Armagh Board of
Guardians varied the terms of appointment on this occasion, and why Nurse
Devlin, who had all the necessary qualifications, was not appointed; whether the
Minister is satisfied with the appointment
made by the Armagh Board of Guardians.
in view of the necessity of the superintendent nurse having fever hospital training, and whether inquiries will be made to
ensure that only a qualified superintendent
nurse will be appointed on merit by this
Board of Guardians.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The person appointed
to the position of superintendent nurse at
the Armagh Union Infirmary complied in
all respects with the terms of the advertisement as approved by the Board of
Guardians at their meeting on the 10th
June last and with the qualifications prescribed by the Ministry for such a
position. Accordingly, approval to the
appointment was given by my Department. I am informed that the advertisement prescribed, in error, an age limit for
the position, but that the Board did not
consider themselves bound by this
restriction. It is true that the Board on
this occasion did not prescribe that each
candidate should be registered as a fever
nurse. There was, however, no obligation
on the Board to attach such special qualification to the post.
Mr. AGNEW: Is it a fact that the
superintendent nurse who was appointed
was only a junior nurse and the one who
was defeated was a senior nurse?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, but in any
event the best nurse was appointed.
Mr. AGNEW: In view of the unsatisfactory reply given I will raise the
matter on the adjournment.

WAR DAMAGE COMMISSION.
6. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
he can state if it is the intention
of the Imperial Parliament to form
a regional branch of the War Commission in Northern Ireland for the
purpose of dealing with claims arising as
a result of air raids in Northern Ireland;
whether he is satisfied that, by reason of
the geographical position of Northern
Ireland, such an arrangement will prove
satisfactory and, if not, whether he will
make representations for the appointment
of a local War Damage Commission with
authority to settie such claims without unreasonable and vexatious delay; and
whether he will take steps to ensure that
the services of local professional men, possessing the necessary qualifications will be
employed for the work necessary in connection with such administration.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
A Regional Office for Northern Ireland
of the War Damage Commission was
opened in Belfast on 28th May last and
is situated at 27 Great Victoria Street.
Under an agency arrangement between
the War Damage Commission and the
Ministry of Finance the Regional Office
will, save in exceptional cases, have full
authority to make payments in accordance
with the provisions of Part I of the War
Damage Act, and I am satisfied that this
agency arrangement will result in a settlement of claims with the minimum of
delay.
Arrangements have been made for the
assessment of claims under the Commodities Insurance Scheme and Part II of the
War Damage Act by local assessors and
valuers, and this work is proceeding. In
order to minimise delay as far as possible
it has been arranged that the Ministry of
Finance, as agent of the Board of Trade,
will make payments direct within wide
limits under both schemes. It is proposed
to employ a staff of valuers on a full-time
basis for the assessment of claims under
the Private Chattels Scheme, and these
will be selected from among the local professional men competent to do the work.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement with regard to delay
is the Minister aware that a great many
people who have had damage done to their
property are unable owing to circumstances which the Minister will appreciate
to obtain competent people to make an
estimate of their damage for this Commission, and under the circumstances
would the Minister extend as far as possible the time allowed for putting in these
estimates or claims for damage?
Mr. BARBOUR: I can appreciate the
difficulty that the unfortunate sufferers
from the recent air raid are under. As
to an extension of time I will certainly
give that sympathetic consideration so far
as lies in my power.
I would be glad to
see elasticity in this case. I can assure
the hon. Member it is difficult to deal
with the number of claims in a short time,
and I will take a personal interest to see
that the work is expedited as far as possible.
Mr. NIXON: I am obliged to the
Minister. If I may be allowed to go a
little outside the question I would like to
thank the Minister and to say that I know
cases of people who have not been able
to get any estimates by competent persons
because the latter are engaged on similar
jobs for other people.

to enact. In order, therefore, that a comprehensive measure, may be introduced in
this House containing similar provisions
to those contained in the English Act of
1939 and the amending measure
before the Imperial House, it is necessary

Mid-Week Pay Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. CAMPBELL: This is a Bill to
provide for the weekly wages of weekly
wage earners being paid not later than
Wednesday of each week. It is confined
in a definite way to wage earners who
earn their wages and receive their wages
week by week. It does not purport to go
beyond that limited class. I admit it is
an extremely large class, if limited. The
measure is really experimental and exploratory. Moreover, it is permissive in
that whether it will come into operation
or not in any area will depend upon the
local authority of that area. If the local
authority think the area would be better
without it the measure will not apply
within that area.
The payment of wages on Friday and
Saturday, which are now the usual days,
is very largely a matter of usage and
habit. Workers, and also housewives,
would soon accustom themselves to a
Wednesday pay day. Some firms already,
in fact, do stagger their pay days, and I
understand that in those cases the workers
are quite satisfied with the workability
and desirability of the reform. I am not
asking, as may seem from a cursory glance
at the Bill, for two pay days in the week.
That might be an acceptable measure to
many. The Bill has no such intention
Mid-Week Pay Bill-
Second Reading
15 JULY 1941
and no such scope.
I submit to the House
that the change, which I believe will come
some time sooner or later, if it does not
find acceptance in the House to-day, when
it does come will work for good in ways
which will readily occur to the minds of
hon. Members. For instance, it will
relieve the strain-and it is a very marked
strain under present-day conditions-on
the staffs in the shops on Saturdays and
also on large numbers of distributive
workers whose heaviest day of the whole
week is probably Saturday.
At the present time residents in Belfast,
evacuees and refugees pour into the centre
of the city at week-ends. I do not
know whether hon. Members are familiar
with the conditions on recent Saturday
evenings in Belfast. It is almost impossible for one to thread his way through
the crowded thoroughfares. They are
packed to overflowing, and it is only with.
difficulty that one can walk through the
dense throngs. People flock in from the
country and the centre of the city is in
an overcrowded and congested state.
submit that these mass crowds are a
positive danger to public security in ways
which the House will readily comprehend.
I
In many homes mid-week wages will
probably be spent more wisely and more
judiciously in the middle of the week
than wages spent on a Saturday afternoon. It is an important fact that recently
the question of overcoming the disadvantages arising from the practice of
concentrating pay days at the end of the
week has been raised by Mr. Ernest
Bevin, Minister of Labour and National
Service, with his Joint Consultative
Committee consisting of representatives of
the Trade. Union Congress and the British
Employers' Confederation. Both sides of
the Committee agree that the substitution
of pay days earlier in the week-I ask the
attention of the. House to this-would be
of considerable assistance, not only to the
workpeople concerned but also to those
engaged in transport and distribution.
That was the agreement of a body
eminently representative of the British
workers and the British employers.
You see the trend of their minds. You
see the way they are shaping towards this
reform. A reform of this kind will not
be accomplished in a day, but minds are
shaping in that direction. It was felt by
that representative and comprehensive
committee that the precise arrangements
would need to be. left for settlement
between the interested parties. They
have not turned down the ideas or
rejected the principle underlying the Bill,
but they felt that the precise arrangements would need to be left for settlement between the interested parties in the
light of their particular circumstances.
Both sides of the Committee have recommended their constituents, the Trade
Union Congress on the one hand and the
Employers' Confederation on the other,
to give favourable consideration to the
matter.
There could not be a weightier
expression of opinion than that; there
could not be a more representative
expression of opinion than that two
great bodies, representing two great
divisions of English society, the masters
on the one hand and the men
on the
other, the delegates of the Trade Union
Congress coming face to face with the
delegates of the Employers' Confederation,
and agreeing on this point that it may
be an advantage to consider an earlier
pay day, and then going further still and
agreeing to recommend their respective
constituents to give. favourable consideration to the matter. I hope the Minister
of Labour, who will be dealing with this
matter, will bear that very weighty, very
strong, and most convincing expression of
opinion in mind in his outlook on this
Bill. I have said that if the principle
of the Bill does not find acceptance
to-day, I believe the day will come when
it will find acceptance.
I need not go at length into the
different clauses, which are only five in
number. The first Clause provides that
in a district in which the local authority
put the Act into operation the weekly
wages payable by an employer to a workman shall be paid not later than Wednesday of each week; if necessary they can
be paid on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. Clause 2 provides penalties for
offences against the Act. Clause 3 states
that the provisions of the Act shall extend
to the district of any local authority in
which by an order of the Ministry of
Home Affairs the Act is declared to be
in force. It also provides that the Ministry may, on the application of a local
authority, declare the Act to be in force
in that district, and such order shall be
published as the Ministry shall direct.

The
Mr. BYRNE: I beg to second.
hon. and learned Member for Central
has explained the Bill so fully that I am
left with very little to say. It will be to
the advantage of both the work people
and the employers that there should be
an earlier pay day. The working people
will be given better conditions for spending their money. There will not be the
same rush in the shops, and there will
not be the same difficulty in the procuring of goods. Many of our working
people go to the public market to purchase their butter, eggs and vegetables,
and on Friday or Saturday the market
is over and they have not the advantages
they would otherwise have.
It
It may be said that the Measure will
be an inconvenience to employers.
will mean only a very slight change in
their books. I believe it would be to the
advantage of the general public that this
Bill should be passed to-day. The hon.
and learned Member has said that if the
Government do not accept the Bill there
is no doubt that it will come into operation in a very short time. As I have
said, it will be an advantage to both the
worker and the employer. There is no
compulsion. The local authorities have
power to put it into operation if they so
wish, and if they do not wish to do so
they will be quite free to remain as they
are.
Question proposed: "That the Bill

Mr. ELLIOTT: I cannot see my way
to support the Bill introduced by the hon.
and learned Member for Central. My
first reason is because I have had no
representations made to me from any
quarter that there is any necessity for the
introduction of such a Measure. I must
confess I am rather surprised the hon.
and learned Member should introduce any
measure which has in it an element of
compulsion, because I know very well.
that he abhors that word and its effect
on any person. At the present time
employers, with the concurrence of their
employees, select the pay day. That has
gone on for generations, and I see no
reason why it should be altered.
The suggestion has been put forward
by the hon. and learned Member that if
the wages were paid during the week,
instead of on Friday or Saturday, people
would be able to spend the money to more
advantage. I do not agree with that. I
believe that if the wages were paid on
Wednesday, instead of Friday or Saturday, many people would have a very bare
week-end. The wages would be spent
before the end of the week, and there
would be no money in the home at the
week-end. I come into contact with
many wage earners, and have more employees than the hon. and learned
Member. I know how they spend their
money. It may be that more money
would be spent in a certain way if the
wages were paid in the middle of the
week, but it is questionable if it would
be to the advantage of the wage earners.
The system that has been in operation
for many years, in fact for all time, has
been that employers and employees select
what, in their opinion, is the most suitable day on which the wages should be
paid.
That system has been carried out
with satisfaction to both parties, and I do
not see why a Bill should be introduced
into this House, and accepted, which
would compel any employer to pay wages
on a certain day. We want work for our
people; we do not want any more compulsion than is necessary. At the present
time employers are fettered by too many
restrictions, and if a Bill such as this was
passed it would mean that more inspectors
would be appointed to see that the regulations were carried out. I oppose the Bill.
We should let well enough alone. Let us
carry on and win the war, and let the
employers pay the wages on the day most
suitable to their employees and themselves.
Mr. GORDON: I beg to move to leave

The Bill is too indefinite.
I have given my reasons for objecting
to the Measure. I foresee great difficulties if the proposed change took place.
Our working people have adjusted themselves during a long period of years to a
system of payment on Friday-some firms
pay on Saturday-and this enables our
people to do their business at the long
week-ends.
The hon. and learned Member mentioned the congestion which takes place in
the centre of the city on a Saturday evening, and the difficulty people have in
doing their shopping. I have often seen
the hon. and learned Member endeavouring to board a tram or bus between five or
six o'clock in the evening, and I have

because he was not able to do so. That

which women would be going down to do
their shopping in the centre of the city.
The hon. and learned Member is aware
that shops in the centre of the city remain
open until a late hour on Saturday evening. The owners know this is the day on
which the masses of the people are paid,
and the day on which they do most of
their shopping.
There is another point. Take the case
of a woman who has to stay in the house
all week looking after her children. She
cannot leave to go down town shopping
because her husband is at work, but on
Saturday a kindly, generous husband sits
at home-a kind neighbour may do likewise to look after the children so as to
enable her to get out to do her shopping.
Hon. Members will understand how
money slips through the fingers, and if
pay day was changed to Monday or
Tuesday people would not be in the same
position to do their shopping on Saturday
afternoon as they are with the pay days
as at present.

Mr. AGNEW: The question I have, to
raise is concerned with the Ministry of
Public Security. I have found that on
many occasions I have made an attempt
to get information from the Department
and from other sources as to the displacement of men employed on certain jobs
carried out by contractors in Northern
Ireland under the control of the Imperial
authorities. I have found that quite a
number of men who were working on
this particular job were told that their
services were no longer required. They
were told this at the office of the particular firm by which they were, engaged.
But in order to satisfy themselves these
men went further and asked the local
employment exchange and they were
informed that it was an outside Imperial
authority who were dispensing with their
services.
Now we must realise that this manner
of treating men is unfair. After all if
I myself was employed on a job and discovered at the end of a month or six
weeks that my services were being dispensed with, and when I made further
inquiries from the Labour Exchange I
was told that it was outside Imperial
authorities who practically warned me
off all jobs of such nature in Northern
Ireland, I would like to know who was
the party responsible for doing this
particular work. Here are men who
have not committed any crime discharged
through the agency of the local police.
They are charged with a crime they have
never committed. As a working-class
representative I resent very much such
tactics. If the Minister can explain to
me, in view of some representations and
references which I supplied on behalf of
some men who were paid off that there is
any definite proof that these men had
committed any crime, then I will be
satisfied.
As far as I can recollect the total
number of men affected is about 23. I
have already submitted. a list to the
Minister of 16. That was some time ago,
and up to the present I have received
no information whatsoever as regards
these particular men who were employed
on various jobs throughout Northern
Ireland. They were all in the same boat.
They are victims of suspicion and the reaction of it all is worse, for no matter
what job is being done if it so pleases
the local police they can say so-an-so is
suspect and he is refused the right of
earning his livelihood and providing for
his wife and family. Let me go to the
other section of the question, the
N.A.A.F.I. I have a letter here dated
19th December, 1940, from the District-
Inspector of the Royal Ulster
Ulster Constabulary in Enniskillen concerning the
particular case of a man who was employed in the N.A.A.F.I. for ten years.

I now come to the question of the
appointment of a superintendent nurse in
the Armagh Union Infirmary. On a
previous occasion when an appointment
was made it was absolutely essential for
Nurse Rodgers to hold the qualifications
of superintendent nurse with fever
experience. To my amazement, I discovered that the Armagh Board of
Guardians did not take that into consideration this time. They appointed a
junior nurse to the post of superintendent
in spite of the other applicant having high
qualifications, including fever, and being
senior. According to the terms of the
advertisement in the Press an age limit
was fixed, and we were then informed in
a reply given by the Minister that this
was in error. That being so, the best
thing to do is to give justice to everybody
by re-advertising the position. That
would save the guardians further trouble
and do justice to the applicants.
It is a peculiar state of affairs. Here
we find the local government authority
issuing an advertisement and putting in
an age limit. Now, after the Minister
has sanctioned the appointment we discover the age limit was in error. I feel
there is something wrong, and that the
Minister of Home Affairs should send an
inspector there to get the full facts. I
have been speaking to the senior nurse,
who was an applicant for the job and who
was turned down. There is something
radically wrong with the system of local
government. I do not know how the
Minister approved of an appointment
some years ago which necessitated fever
experience and then allowed the
guardians to change as they pleased and
appoint a nurse who had no fever
experience. In view of the points raised,
I hope the Minister will visit Armagh
and have a talk with the Board of
Guardians. He should ask them to
re-advertise the post stating they had
committed an error as regards the age
limit.

their employment. As I think I made.

Mr. AGNEW: There is no proof.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: That is all the

by the police.
Mr. AGNEW: Then they are infallible?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I am not saying
they are infallible, but I am perfectly
certain of this, that if we were to wait

imperilled than it is. The police are confronted with a difficult task, and I am
satisfied they discharge it to the best of

RENTS OF UNINHABITABLE
HOUSES.
1. Mr. DOWLING (for Rev. Professor
Corkey) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that in a
number of cases where working-class
houses have been bombed and officially
declared to be uninhabitable and vacated
by the tenants, these tenants have been
persuaded by interested parties to continue to pay the full rent on the ground
that otherwise they may not be able at
the end of the war to obtain repossession
of the house, or any other house, at a
rent comparable to the rent they are paying; and what steps the Government
propose to take to prevent these people
being exploited in this way.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
As he indicated in his reply to the hon.
Member for North Down on the 15th
instant, the Bill at present before the
Imperial Parliament
the
amending
Landlord and Tenant Act, 1939, contains amendments to the War Damage
Act, 1941, which this House has no
power to enact, but it is intended to
introduce legislation similar to that
passed by the Imperial Parliament. In
the amending Bill at present before the
Imperial House provision is made
relieving tenants of the class referred to
by the hon. Member from any obligation
to pay rent in respect of premises which
have been rendered unfit by reason of
war damage. It is proposed to introduce
a similar provision in the Bill to be
placed before this House.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: I would like
to ask the Parliamentary Secretary does
he realise the chaotic conditions that are
likely to arise by reason of this extraordinary state of affairs?
Mr. LOWRY: No chaotic conditions
will arise for the Bill will be made retrospective to the day the first pane of glass
was broken.

Bill was passed in 1939 in England and
has not yet been brought forward here?
Is it a further fact if the Government

find time to bring in the amending Bill
when necessary?
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Parliamentary Secretary when he proposes to
place this Bill before the House?
Mr. LOWRY: When Parliament reassembles it will be done first thing.

become worse. It is no answer for the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs to state that the provisions of whatever Bill is introduced here
will be retrospective. Rent is being
extracted from solvent tenants of damaged
premises who are able to pay, and where
property has been destroyed and the
tenants are not solvent, the landlords are
unable to recover, and the opportunity to
disclaim or retain the property is not
available.
The retrospective nature of the Act
will be all the more difficult to enforce on
account of the delay in passing the
measure, because even if this Bill is introduced when the House re-assembles in
September it will be a considerable time
afterwards before the Bill is finally
passed. I solemnly warn the Government
that unless this Bill is passed immediately
on the lines of the Imperial Act, the
chaotic conditions to which I have referred
will get infinitely worse, and this Government will have to face a condition of things
that they will very much regret in the

join with the Member for Woodvale in
advocating that a measure on the lines of

With regard to the delay in introducing the War Damage Bill, I venture to
say I can demonstrate to the House that
it has been a most fortunate circumstance
that this Bill has not yet been introduced. In September, 1939, with a great
variety of other Acts, hasty legislation
on this subject was rushed through the
Imperial Parliament. At that time nobody could visualise the exact circumstances that would arise after there was
a heavy and destructive air raid. A section
was inserted in that Act authorising this
Parliament to pass a similar Bill, which
it otherwise could not have done under
Sections 4 and 5 of the Government of
Ireland Act. The matter was carefully
considered by the Cabinet of Northern
Ireland, and it was decided, wisely in
my judgment, to wait and get the experience that would be available since
the passing of the two Acts in England.
It was found necessary in March, 1941,
to introduce in the Imperial Parliament
a further Bill which has not yet been
finally passed. The reason for the introduction of the new Measure is that under
the legislation that was passed in such a
hasty fashion, without any experience,
decisions have been made by the courts
which in the light of experience have
been shown not to be adequate and not
to cover all the circumstances that could
arise. The Cabinet here wisely decided
to wait and see what was the best thing
to be done in order to have a Bill introduced here which would be comprehensive and would cover every possibility
of hardship, and which at the same time
would see that everything that was fair
and just would be done as between landlord and tenant. Had there been the
same hasty legislation here as there was
in England you would have had this
situation; that under the existing Act of
Parliament rights would have been
established by the decisions of the
courts, and cases of hardship would have
arisen. In the light of the experience
gained in England, and from the legis
lation passed there, we consider we are
now in a position to introduce a Bill
which will cover every conceivable case
of hardship.

Northern Ireland-I will not say on the

The PRIME MINISTER: Certainly,

Mr. NIXON: It is quite possible. If

The Government is too busy.

Oral Answers to Questions.
WAR DAMAGE INSURANCE.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if all
business and commercial premises carrying
£2,000 of stock or over must be insured
under the War Damage Compulsory Insurance Acts; how far this insurance
covers chattels, the property of clients, on
such insured premises for the purpose of
repairs or other legitimate commercial
purposes, and what steps, if any, his
Ministry is taking or will take to enforce
the provisions of these Acts?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right.
hon. Friend to reply.
Provision for the insurance against war
risks of goods for sale is made in the War
Risks Insurance Act, 1939 (Commodities
Insurance Scheme), and that Act and the
Regulations made thereunder provide
that a seller or supplier of goods, other
than goods consisting of food for human.
consumption, must insure his goods under
the Act if the value of the goods is more
than £1,000. In the case of food, insurance is compulsory if the value of the
stock is more than £200. Certain classes
of goods for sale are exempt from compulsory insurance, but are insurable under
the Act on a voluntary basis.
The War Risks Insurance Act, 1939,
does not provide for the insurance by a
person of chattels belonging to customers,
which are on his premises for the purpose
of repair or other commercial purpose.
Such goods may be insured by him under
the Business Scheme provided for in the
War Damage Act, 1941, for the sum
which he would lose if the goods were
destroyed. He is not compelled, however,
to insure them unless
(a) he is under an obligation in the
event of war damage to repair, or
replace them, or to pay damages or
compensation, and
(b) the total value of the goods insurable under the scheme which are
held by him in connection with his
business exceeds £1,000.
So far as the last part of the hon.
Member's question is concerned, the
responsibility for ensuring compliance
with the compulsory provisions of Part II
of the War Damage Act and Part II of
the War Risks Insurance Act rests with
the Board of Trade.
Mr. NIXON: Is it a fact that there is
no protection under the War Damage Act
for a client who has his property with an
insured person for repair or for other
legitimate purpose? Has that person, or
has he not, any protection at all?
Mr. BARBOUR: I believe that depends on such arrangements as the client
may make with the person with whom he
has left goods for repair or for some
treatment. It depends entirely on that.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that a
person who has temporarily removed from
premises that have been destroyed is entitled under the War Damage Act to
make a claim for the amount temporarily
removed, provided the building where
they were removed from has been
destroyed, and would it not be in keeping
with that class of war damage that a
motor car that has been temporarily
removed to a garage for repairs would be
in a similar position, and that the motor
car would be subject to the application
of the War Damage Act?
Mr. BARBOUR: I sympathise with
the hon. Members in the questions put
by them, but it is rather a complicated
matter, and I think it would be better

my very best to give a reply.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the owner puts a
car into a garage at his own risk, and has
any change taken place during the period
of emergency under the War Damage
Act?
Mr. BARBOUR: I understand that
motor cars were covered in a special
clause. They must be insured.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister take
any special steps to make firms prove that
the property alleged to be burned and
belonging to a client who has no remedy,
was in fact burned?
RE-EMPLOYMENT OF ULSTER
VOLUNTEERS.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if and
when representations were made by the
Northern Ireland Government to the
British Government in implementing the
promise given in this House on behalf of
the Government on 18th March last, that
representations would be made to the
Imperial Government with a view to the
introduction of legislation to ensure that
all men in Northern Ireland who voluntarily joined the Army, Navy or Air
Force should be reinstated in the employment they had left, on being discharged
from service, on the same terms and conditions as apply in the case of men conscripted in Great Britain; and whether,
if such representations have been made,
he can state the result.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes. As
promised, representations in the terms of
the Resolution passed by this House on
18th March last have been made by me
to His Majesty's Government in Great
Britain. I also discussed the position
with the Secretary of State during his
visit to Northern Ireland, and I am
aware that the matter is receiving most
careful consideration by the Imperial
Government.
I regret I am not in a position to give
a more definite answer to-day.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Prime Minister whether the Act of
1920 confers powers on the Government
to pass legislation for the citizens of
Northern Ireland on all matters arising
therefrom, and is it a fact that he and
his colleagues have delegated their powers
of legislating for the civil population to
the Secretary of State in Great Britain,
and by whose authority has that delegation taken place?
The PRIME MINISTER: No. We
have not delegated any powers which
were given to us by the Act of 1920, the
Government of Northern Ireland Act, to
any British departments. Certain services were reserved under that Act to be
dealt with by the Imperial Government,
and this is a service which comes under
one of these heads.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is not the Prime
Minister aware that the question refers
to a guarantee by legislation for the employment of these men who join up on
a voluntary basis in His Majesty's
Forces, and is it not a fact that the
Prime Minister has power conferred on
him under the Act of 1920 to pass legislation to give that guarantee without any
representations to the British House of
Commons?
