APPEALS AGAINST BILLETING.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
Defence Regulations provide for the
setting up of tribunals to which aggrieved
persons served with notices for the billeting
of evacuees can appeal; whether it is
a fact that such notices cannot be enforced
in the absence of a tribunal of the kind;
whether such a tribunal has been set up
in Northern Ireland, and, if not, when
such a tribunal will be set up.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I must thank
the hon. Member for the opportunity of
stating the law on the subject of billeting
notices.
Under Article 22 of the Defence
Regulations, any person contravening or
failing to comply with the requirements
of a billeting notice is liable on summary
conviction to a fine not exceeding £50 or
three months imprisonment, or to both
fine and imprisonment.
It is a fact that the Defence Regulations also provide for a complaint being
made by persons aggrieved by the service.
or operation of a billeting notice to
tribunals, and at the foot of each billeting
notice the householders are informed that
such complaints should be made to the
office of the local authority. These tribunals have been provided for Northern
Ireland under an Order made by the
Secretary of State for each local authority
in Northern Ireland.
In answer to the question as to whether
or not a billeting notice can be enforced,
I would refer the hon. Member to the
decision given by the King's Bench
Division in England last year, in which
it was held that once a billeting notice
was served it was alive, and remained
alive until it was removed by revocation,
by the billeting officer or by cancellation
by the Complaints Tribunal. The Defence Regulations, in the opinion of the
Court, in no way provide for the suspension of the operation of the notice
because at some indefinite time the recipient of the notice makes a complaint to
the tribunal; the notice was operative
from the moment when it was served.
This decision makes it very clear that
a billeting notice can be enforced, and
though I am very sorry to think that
there should be citizens in Northern
Ireland so lacking in sense of civic duty
as to require a legal decision for them to
carry out what should be a moral obligation, the Government is determined to
prosecute such citizens with the utmost
rigour of the law.
Mr. WARNOCK: Might I ask the
Minister of Home Affairs how many prosecutions his department has instituted
against people who have refused to receive
evacuees?
Sir DAWSON BATES: One up to the
present, but there will be many more.
Mr. BEATTIE: Has the right hon.
Gentleman got a number of cases from
Newcastle district of refusals, and will
the right hon. Gentleman pursue these
refusals in accordance with the answer
he has given?
Sir DAWSON BATES: All these cases
are being investigated.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the statement that people will be prosecuted in
connection with that offence, did the
Minister see in the Press where a billeting
officer disappeared for a considerable
time and left all the people waiting for
billets, and weeping and wondering
during his absence whether he was ever
going to come back? What will be done
Will he be
to that billeting officer?
prosecuted?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I need hardly
point out that if that is true the gentleman will not occupy the position any
longer. I do not always believe everything that appears in the Press.
Mr. BROWN: Is it correct or incorrect, as stated in a recent case at

could not be enforced in the absence of
tribunals?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That particular case is sub judice. That does not
prevent other cases being taken.

a conviction?
MORRISON STEEL TABLE
SHELTERS.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he will take
steps to have the issue of Morrison indoor
steel table shelters extended to other
areas in Northern Ireland as well as
Belfast and Londonderry; and whether
any progress has been made along the
lines of the suggestion that such shelters
should be manufactured wholly or partially in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): The
supply position at present is such as to
preclude the issue of this type of shelter
to other areas. With regard to the latter
part of the question, the possibility of
making use of manufacturing capacity in
Northern Ireland in making some of the
constituent parts has, at my request, been
represented to the Ministry of Supply.
Meanwhile, if there is any local firm with
the necessary capacity who wishes to participate in the Ministry of Supply programme, my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Commerce will readily afford
it all possible assistance.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman what investigations, if
any, he has made in regard to the suitability of the Morrison shelter for the
homes of Northern Ireland, whether it is
a fact that Morrison shelters require a
concrete foundation floor to be of service
for the purpose for which they were
erected, and whether it is a fact that at
least 60 per cent. of the floors of the
homes of the people of Northern Ireland
are wooden, and in view of that state of
affairs, whether he thinks the Morrison
shelter would be suitable to be placed on
wooden floors?
Mr.
MacDERMOTT: I understand
that the Morrison shelter is not suitable
for every type of house, particularly the
smaller houses with very small rooms,
because it measures 6ft. 6ins. by 4ft. 6ins.
and it is advisable that there should be
a space round three sides of it. With
regard to the suggestion the hon. Member
has made as to requiring a concrete floor,
my understanding of the situation is that
it is not necessary that the shelter should
have a concrete floor, but it is advisable
it should be on the ground floor of the
premises.
Mr. BEATTIE: Pardon me if I have
misrepresented the matter to you. I
understand it is necessary to have the
Morrison shelter placed with at least
something substantial below it, and is he
aware that 60 per cent. of the floors of
dwellings in Northern Ireland are
wooden, and are they suitable for
Morrison shelters?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: It may be that
60 per cent. of the floors are wooden, but
I understand the Morrison shelter can be
used effectively on wooden floors.
Mr. WARNOCK: Is it a fact that 99
per cent. of the floors of houses in the
United Kingdom are wooden?

Death of Senator Long.
The PRIME MINISTER: With your
permission I would like at this stage to
say just a few words, but they will be
words from my heart. We all heard this
morning with very deep regret of the
death of Senator Long. He was one of
the original members of our Senate.
He
was a member of the Government for
many years. He was Deputy Leader of
the Senate, and he acted as Chief Whip
of our upper House. He was known to
all of us as a genial and kindly gentleman, as a good friend, and as a publicspirited citizen. His public work was
very widespread. He was connected with
the County Council of Londonderry for
41 years.
I understand he was chairman
for 21 years. He also was a member of
the Rural Council of Limavady and of
the guardians of that town and district.
He took
wide
a
interest in many
other forms of public work. He
was a most charitable gentleman, and
every good cause brought to his notice
received his willing and kind assistance.
He has passed from our midst, but he has
left behind an inspiring example to us all.
We mourn his loss, we revere his memory,
and with very full hearts we extend to
Mrs. Long and the members of her family
our sincere and heart-felt sympathy.
Mr. BEATTIE: I must pay my tribute
to the passing of one whom I have known
since I became a Member of this House.
He was a very familiar figure both in the
House and in the country, and on my
visits in and around Derry I found the
name of Long was known in every home.
He seemed to be part of the make-up of
the community and one of themselves.
He never acted outside of that ambit. I
never took him to be a politician. I do
not think he was inclined to take politics
as a line of life. My view of the late
Senator was that he took life to have one
object, and that object was to help one
another, and he certainly helped many of
the varied classes in the community in the
area he represented. And in the Senate,
where he was honoured, loved and respected, I believe his presence will be
missed very seriously. I feel that the
spirit he has left behind might be a guide
for others to follow. We have too few
kind-hearted people in our midst to lose
one. He was one of the good, true men
of his time. I am satisfied he has left
very few enemies but has left many
friends, and they will, I am sure, think
of him as time goes on. The loss to the
community and to the Senate will be
nothing to the loss to the widow and
family. He was father in the home. He
was the guiding light in that home. To
him the family looked for guidance, and I
think I can say in all sincerity that
guidance never was cast aside by the
members of his own home. To Mrs.
Long and the surviving members of the
family I wish to express my deepest sympathy in the very serious loss they have
sustained.

(Flax Water) Bill and the Appropriation
Bill without any amendment.

Oral Answers to Questions.
FIXING OF PIG PRICES.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
result of his representations to
Ministry of Food to have fairer prices.
fixed for pigs, in view of the hardship.
that the present uneconomic prices impose
on producers.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): In the
absence of my right hon. Friend, I have
been asked to take this question.
I regret that I am not in a position to
make any statement on the question of pig
prices.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Parliamentary
Secretary tell us when he hopes to be able
to make a statement?
Mr. MAGINESS: No.
Mr. BROWN: Does the Parliamentary
Secretary intend to allow the matter to
lapse?
Mr. MAGINESS: No.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Agriculture whether he has any hope for
the pig producers of Northern Ireland?
ACREAGE UNDER FLAX.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the flax
acreage in the present season, and the
acreage to be aimed at next season.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. As has previously been pointed out
it would be against the public interest to
publish production statistics such as are
asked for in the hon. Member's question.
I am glad to be able to say, however,
that the farmers of Northern Ireland have
responded most magnificently to the
appeal for a greater area under flax this
year. I am also confident that, despite
the very discouraging pulling season, they
will respond equally loyally to whatever
call is made on them in respect of flax for
next season, especially in view of the fact
that the crop is an essential one in the
national interest.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that
reply of the Parliamentary Secretary may
I ask whether he can give us any account
of how many acres have already been
pulled of this year's flax crop?
Mr. MAGINESS: No, sir. It is not in
the public interest.
Mr. BROWN: Is it in the public
interest to allow this flax to go to rack
and ruin?

PRICE OF NORTHERN IRELAND
POTATOES..
3. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the reason for fixing the price of
potatoes grown in Northern Ireland at
45s per ton lower than that for potatoes
grown in Great Britain; whether it is a
fact that it costs just as much to produce
potatoes in Northern Ireland as anywhere
else in the United Kingdom, and whether
these Northern Ireland potatoes are of as
good, and in many cases of superior
quality to those grown in England.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply. Growers' prices for comparable
main crop varieties of potatoes are fixed
for Northern Ireland, after consultation
with growers' and merchants' representatives, mainly in relation to the
growers' prices applicable in the Lancashire area where the bulk of Northern
Ireland potatoes shipped to Great Britain
is sold. This variation is from 20s to 30s
per ton according to area to allow for the
normal costs of transport. This is in
accordance with the practice in Great
Britain where the price payable to
growers varies according to area to take
into account the costs of transport to
recognised markets. In the case of Northern Ireland a subsidy to cover the increased costs of freight due to the war is
at present payable by the Ministry of
Food.
With regard to the second part of the
question, it should be noted that in view
of the lower labour costs in Northern
Ireland the costs of production of
potatoes are not so high as in Great
Britain.
It is, I think, not possible to generalise
in regard to the quality of Northern Ireland potatoes as compared with potatoes
produced in Great Britain.
Will the
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON:
Parliamentary Secretary please inform
the House when he expects this subsidy
he mentions will be paid?
SHORTAGE OF HARVEST LABOUR.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has taken or
proposes to take any steps beyond those
already announced to deal with the
serious shortage of labour in harvesting
this year's greatly increased crops in view
of the fact that the existing arrangements
are proving inadequate, and whether he
will recommend the Government to
extend the 75 per cent. labour grants
for drainage and other land improvements to all work in connection with this
year's increased crops.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply. The
Ministry of Agriculture continues to take
every possible step to secure the labour
necessary for the harvesting of this year's
crops. With the co-operation of the
military authorities soldier assistance has
been forthcoming. It is true that in
certain districts the military position does
not permit of all requests for such assistance being satisfied immediately, but the
military authorities are co-operating
readily in our efforts to get over the
difficulties in these few isolated instances.
Recruiting for the Women's Land Army
in Northern Ireland is being continued,
but with other branches of the war effort
also seeking female workers, it is to be
expected that the demand for female
labour on the land should exceed the
supply. In order to safeguard the
farmers from losing essential workers
through the attraction of emergency
contract work in Northern Ireland at the
present moment, my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Labour, recently made
an Order making it an offence against
the Defence Regulations for an employer
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
2 SEPTEMBER 1941
in an industry other than agriculture to
engage a worker who is normally employed in agriculture. Special attention
has recently been drawn to this Order,
and farmers who lose workers in this way
have been advised to get in touch either
with the manager of their local Employment Exchange or with my Ministry's
County Executive or Area Officers.
The answer to the second part of the
hon. Member's question is in the
negative.

to come from, and is it a fact that he did
not know?

Mr. MAGINESS: That question should

Mr. BEATTIE: Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary has not got the purport of my question. Is it not a fact
that the supply of harvest labour devolves

LAND GIRL STATISTICS.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
number of land girls trained in Northern
Ireland during each successive year respectively, from date of commencement of
present war to the present date; the
number of these girls employed by
ordinary farmers, the period of employment, and the wages paid to such girls.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. It will be recalled that in 1939
and early in 1940 the Ministry, as an experiment, provided two courses of training
in farm work at the Ulster Dairy School,
Cookstown. These courses were attended
by 32 girls. Six of these girls are
employed on their own farms; five are
members of the Women's Land Army in
Northern Ireland, to which reference will
be made later. Two are members of the
Women's Land Army in Great Britain;
one is employed privately as a dairy maid.
Of the remainder several have got married
and a number are known to have engaged
in other forms of national service.
(Laughter.)
In April, 1941, it was apparent that
there would be a demand from farmers in
Northern Ireland for the services of land
girls and it was decided to inaugurate here
a branch of the Women's Land Army.
Twenty-seven girls have taken a course of
eight weeks' training on private farms in
Northern Ireland. Twelve have completed their training and have been
allocated to farms. These girls have
entered their present employment at
various dates since the beginning of
August, and in every case the farmer concerned has undertaken to employ at least
one member of the Women's Land Army
for the duration of the war. The fixed
wages for members of the Women's Land
Army in Northern Ireland are 27s per
week less 15s per week for board and
lodging.
As a result of recent publicity numerous
enquiries have been received. The hon.
Member will, of course, appreciate that
only candidates who are likely to prove
suitable are being accepted for the
Women's Land Army.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Can the Parliamentary
Secretary inform us whether it is possible
to obtain some of these land girls who are
not engaged on other forms of national
service?
Mr. BROWN: Can the Parliamentary
Secretary tell us whether the fact that he
has 12 land girls available for work on

THE COAL SUPPLY.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can make any
statement on the present position and
future prospects of the
coal supply
situation.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The question of coal
supplies for Northern Ireland is one
which continues to receive unremitting
attention. The provision of supplies
both for consumption during the coming
winter and for reserve stocks has been
the subject of negotiation between my
Ministry and the Mines Department.
It is anticipated that the arrangements
made will provide adequate supplies for
public utility undertakings, industrial
undertakings, and institutions, but in so
far as domestic consumers are concerned
it is not improbable that here, as in
other parts of the United Kingdom, a
measure of rationing may prove necessary.
I welcome the opportunity afforded by
the hon. Member's question to impress
upon domestic and other users the need
for effecting all possible economies in coal
consumption.

9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

Board has been in existence; whether the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Electricity
Board has been in existence for a period

During that time electrical
energy has been purchased by the Board
from the Belfast Corporation at cost of
production, as ascertained in accordance
with the provisions of sub-section 3 of
Section 13 of the Electricity (Supply) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1931, and the rules
embodied in the Second Schedule to that
Act.
I am advised that the effect of this
method of calculation is to reduce the
cost of supplies in Belfast by a substantial
sum.

ASSESSORS FOR ASSESSING WAR

12. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The assessors employed on the
assessment of war damage claims in Northern Ireland under the War Risks Insurance Act, 1939 (Commodities Insurance Scheme) and the War Damage
Act, 1941 (Business Scheme) are:-
Messrs. Wm. Montgomery & Son, Messrs.
Walter Hume & Co., Messrs. George
Crawford & Co.
The fees payable to these firms of
assessors are in
accordance with the
following scale which has been approved
by H.M. Treasury:-For claims not
exceeding £50, £1 1s Od; for claims over
£50 up to £150, £2 2s Od; for claims
over £150 up to £250, £3 3s Od; and
for claims over £250:-Principal's time,
£5 5s Od per day of 8 hours; senior
assistant's time, £3 3s Od per day of 8
hours; junior's time, £1 1s Od per day
of 8 hours, plus travelling and out-ofpocket expenses at rates corresponding
to approved scales.
The valuers employed on the assessment of claims under the War Damage
Act (Private Chattels Scheme) are:-
Mr. Fred J. Brice, Mr. W. H. Ferguson,
Mr. A. E. A. Frazer, Mr. James King,
Captain J. D. Nicholl, Captain J. Ross,
Mr. James Walker.
The fees paid to these valuers are at
the rate of £3 3s Od a day for principals
and £1 11s 6d a day for assistants employed by them on the work.
In order to expedite the assessment of
claims under the Private Chattels Scheme
arrangements have now been made by the
Ministry of Finance for the engagement.
of valuers on full-time employment to
assess claims under that scheme.
The hon. Member will no doubt realise
that it would be contrary to the public
interest to publish details of the number
of war damage claims received.

Mr. BEATTIE: I think this Motion
can be rightly challenged. It is not in
keeping with the dignity of this House
or with the duty devolving on each
Member to his constituents and in the
national interests that the opportunities
of the Members to help in the furthering
of the war should be curtailed. It is too
much to ask that we should adjourn until
this day week. I am rather inclined to
think that the Government, or the caucus
of the Government, that is those in paid
positions, are running this part of the
country in accordance with their own likes
and dislikes, and are becoming more of a
serious menace to Parliamentary representation than Hitler ever was. We are
asked to leave the destinies of the people
of Northern Ireland in the hands of this
caucus.
We are only told so much for each
Tuesday when we attend. We had an
example to-day in the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture
who is also, I understand, Parliamentary

I am not going to be subservient to the

House, and I hope I will have an opportunity of doing so not only on one day
a week, but on the three working days on

I say
here and now that Northern Ireland has
failed in its obligation in regard to the

which would be forthcoming from every

her weight. I know from my own experience, from visits, and from personal

in which she would if she were given
the opportunity.
We have now come to the point where
six men rule Northern Ireland. Their
power is also limited as they have become
agents of the power across the water, but
we, as representatives in this House, have
neither art nor part in what is being
done. I say that the reason for the

within the confines of the Cabinet of
Northern Ireland. There there is dictatorship from beginning to end, and dictatorship which does not represent the people
of Northern Ireland. Therefore I make
my strong protest against the curtailment
of the time of this House for the purpose
of accommodating Cabinet Ministers and
allowing them to put into full operation
the dictatorial powers they have been
practising since the war commenced.
I feel we have ample duties to perform
to our people. We have failed in our
obligations to them. What is the use of
preventing this House from sitting tomorrow and on Thursday? Cannot we
consider the question of the destruction
of the property of the people; have we not
got the needs and requirements of agriculture, and all those domestic questions
to settle? They require immediate attention, and we are not paying one solitary
hour's attention to them. I would like
to see the Cabinet of Northern Ireland
being subject to the terrible ordeal
through which some of the people I
represent are going at the present time.
I would like to see some of the right hon.
Gentlemen living in hen-houses or paying
uneconomic rents for lodging accommodation.
It is their duty to come to this House
and get the loyal support of the Members,
and then go ahead with serviceable work
instead of hiding in their buildings. I
do not know what the health of the people
will be in another two months' time, as
the cruel conditions under which they are
allowed to exist are horrible. There is
another thing I want to say, and I say it
not to individual members but to the
Government as a whole. The people will
revolt with the result that instead of
Ulster being a centre of national effort
her attention will be taken up with home
conditions and such matters. Under the
present conditions the Cabinet do not get
a 100 per cent. pull from the working
class of Northern Ireland. They cannot get it. Last week I saw a woman
and a little child looking for accommodation. I went to a house where I knew
ample accommodation was available and
the owner said he would put them up
for a week for 30s. We have to deal
with questions of this kind. We have to
provide homes for the homeless and we
have to do something for the unemployed.
The number of unemployed in Northern
Ireland is too high at the present time,
and the Minister of Labour and his
Parliamentary Secretary are taking no
action in the matter. All the Parliamentary Secretary has done is to take
over another position. I am not denying
his qualifications, but his first duty is to
the Ministry of Labour.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Question put, pursuant to Standing Order
No. 2.
Agricultural Improvement Council.
The following Notice stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Brown:
"That in the opinion of this House
and in view of the fact that an Agricultural Improvement Council has been set
up for England and Wales, a similar
body should be set up for Northern
Ireland on the following basis: -The
Minister of Agriculture; one representative each of the Ulster Farmers'
Union, the Royal Ulster Agricultural
Society and the Ulster Agricultural
Organisation Society; one representative each of the six County Committees
of Agriculture; a representative of
agricultural employees; a representative of consumers; and two Members of
this House not acting in any of the
capacities enumerated."
Mr. BROWN: With your permission,
and the permission of the House, I wish
to amend this Motion to read: "That in
the opinion of this House an Agricultural
Improvement Council should be set up
for Northern Ireland." Reference has
been made to-day to the lack of consultation on the part of the Government with
the Members of this House, and it is
because there is almost complete lack of
consultation between the Government and
the Members of this House that I bring
forward this Motion to-day. I want the
Parliamentary Secretary to accept, on
behalf of the Minister and himself, an
assurance that I bring this Motion forward to help and not to hinder them in
the great task they are engaged in. But
as I said, it is because of the almost
complete lack of consultation between the
Ministry of Agriculture and the Members
of this House that I bring forward this
Motion, and I ask him to approve of it
in this form. Might I ask for order?
Mr. SPEAKER: Is there a seconder
for this Motion?
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: I second the
Motion. I merely want to say this; that
I consulted the Ulster Farmers' Union,
so far as the branch in my own area is
concerned, in regard to their views on the
Motion of the Member for South Down.
They agreed with the Motion that it
would be a good thing to adopt such a
council here in Northern Ireland, but
they did not agree with the original
Motion as to the suggested composition.
I second the Motion.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Landlord and Tenant (War Damage)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In asking
the House to
to give
give a Second Reading to this Bill I think it well before
referring in detail to the provisions of
the Bill to ask hon. Members to recall
to mind the many requests made to the
Government to introduce a Bill defining
the rights and liabilities of landlords
and tenants as a consequence of air raid
damage to property. As I explained at
the time it was not possible to proceed
with legislation in this House until experience had shown whether the
Imperial Act of 1939 covered all the
points that were likely to arise affecting
the relationship of landlord and tenant
where property had been damaged by
enemy action. After the introduction of
the Bill now before the House in April
last, it was found necessary in Great
Britain, in the light of the experience
gained there, to introduce an amending
measure dealing specifically with two important aspects of the matter, namely,
the rights and liabilities of tenants holding under short tenancies where property
had been rendered unfit and the liability
of ground lessees for the payment of
ground rent when the premises comprised
in the lease had been rendered unfit for
habitation.
In the original Act passed by the
Imperial Government, no special provision was made in the case of tenants
holding under short tenancies, nor was
any provision made for the relief from
payment of ground rents. Both these
matters have been dealt with in the
amending Bill which has been passed by
the Imperial House, and the relevant
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattie
provisions have been incorporated in the
Bill now before this House together with
the remaining provisions of the original
Bill which it was not considered necessary
to alter.
I might also point out that the amending Bill passed by the Imperial Parliament also contained certain provisions
amending the War Damage Act of 1941,
and these amendments have also been
introduced into the measure now before
the House. It will be appreciated,
therefore, that the present Bill is a comprehensive one, bringing the law in Northern Ireland on the subject of landlord
and tenant generally into conformity with
that prevailing in Great Britain.
With regard to the provisions of the
Bill, it will be seen that the Bill has been
divided into four parts, and I propose to
endeavour to assist the House in considering the Bill by explaining to the best of
my ability the various parts of the Bill
in turn. Part I of the Bill deals particularly with the obligation of any person to do repairs in relation to land.
Land, as will be seen from the definition
clause, includes buildings. Clause 1
provides that an obligation to repair
under a disposition, that is a document
creating or transferring an interest in
land or a contract collateral thereto shall
be construed as not extending to the imposition of any liability to make good
any war damage occurring to the land
comprised in the disposition. It is also
provided that, apart from the relief
given by the said clause, if it is found
that by reason of war damage it is impracticable or of no substantial advantage
to carry out ordinary repairs, that is
repairs not due to war damage, the
obligation to carry out such repairs shall
be suspended and the consequential provisions set out in the clause shall have
War Damage Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
effect. Clause 2 imposes on a tenant who
is under an obligation to repair the
obligations of notifying a landlord or
mortgagee as the case may
be of any
damage caused to the premises by enemy
action. The necessity for this provision
will be obvious to hon. Members.
Clause 3 modifies Section 26 of the
Settled Land Act, 1889, in so far as it
relates to the application of capital
moneys arising under the Act.
I would draw the attention of hon.
Members specially to Part II of the Bill
and particularly to the provisions of
Clauses 4 and 13 of the Bill. Provision
is made in Clause 4 enabling a tenant of
property rendered unfit by war damage
to serve on his landlord either a notice of
disclaimer or a notice of retention. In
the event of the tenant failing to serve
either of these notices, the landlord may
serve upon the tenant a notice to elect
calling upon the tenant to serve upon him
either a notice of disclaimer or a notice
of retention. The landlord may also on
receipt of a notice of disclaimer serve on
the tenant a notice to avoid disclaimer
requiring the tenant to retain his lease on
terms set out in Clause 11 of the Bill.
As to the effect of the various notices
referred to, it is provided in Clause 8 of
the Bill that if and when a notice of
disclaimer is accepted by the landlord or
is declared to be a valid notice, it amounts
to a surrender of the various interests in
the land with a consequent relief from
the payment of rent including ground
rent. Clause 10 provides that where a
notice of retention is served, the tenant
will be obliged to undertake the repair
of the war damage to render the premises
fit, but he will be relieved of any obligation to pay rent either in whole or in
part while the premises are unfit.
Where a notice to avoid disclaimer is
served by the landlord, Clause 11 provides that on this notice becoming effective the landlord will be responsible for
rendering the premises fit as soon as practicable and the lease will remain alive.
The tenant in this case will be relieved
from liability to pay rent during the
period while the premises are unfit.
Clause 5 of the Bill prescribes the period
within which a notice to elect must be
served and for the serving of a notice to
avoid disclaimer. Its provisions are self
explanatory, and I do not propose to deal
in detail with the provisions of this
Clause.
Provision is made in Clause 6 for the
determination by the court of disputes as
to the unfitness of premises. This Clause
sets out the procedure to be followed by
the parties when such a dispute arises;
while Clause 7 gives the particulars to be
included in a notice of disclaimer. Clauses
8, 10 and 11 of the Bill have already been
referred to by me. Clause 9 empowers
the court to modify the effect of a notice
of disclaimer in certain respects on an
application by an interested party.
Where further war damage occurs to
land after a notice of retention or a notice
to avoid disclaimer has been served, the
court in such case is empowered by Clause
12 to authorise the withdrawal of the
notice. As and from the date on which
the notice is withdrawn, a notice to elect
or a notice of disclaimer shall cease to
have effect and the lease shall have effect
accordingly.
I now come to Clause 13 of the Bill
which, as I have stated, makes special
provision in the case of premises rendered
unfit which are held under short tenancies, that is, weekly, monthly or quarterly
tenancies. Clause 4, to which I have
already referred, does not apply in such
cases and accordingly the question of
serving the various notices does not arise.
Specific provision is made relieving a
tenant of the category mentioned from
any obligation to pay rent in respect of
the tenancy during the period the premises are unfit and unoccupied.
Clause also sets out the circumstances in
which a dwelling-house may be considered
fit and authorises the sanitary authority
to issue certificates of fitness which shall
be final until the contrary is proved.
The
I should also like to draw the attention
of the House to sub-clause (6) of this
Clause, which empowers the court to
terminate tenancies in the circumstances
set out in the Clause. Clauses 14 and 15
deal with multiple leases, that is, a lease
comprising buildings which are used or
adapted for use as two or more separate
tenements, and make special provision
enabling the court to determine whether
the tenant should be allowed to exercise
his right of disclaimer or retention. The
court in such case may make such order
as is provided for in the Clause. The
court is also empowered in the case of a
1359 War Damage Bill-

2 SEPTEMBER 1941
Second Reading
multiple lease to authorise the landlord
to recover possession of the whole of the
and where he would not otherwise be
entitled to do so.
Clause 17 provides for the apportionment of rent where a lease has been
surrendered or where the rent payable
either under a lease or a short tenancy
ceases to be payable.
I now come to Part 3 of the Bill. It
will be seen that this Part of the Bill
contains a number of provisions affecting
the rights of landlords and tenants consequent on the passing of the War
Damage Act, 1941. Under the amending
Bill recently passed by the Imperial
House, the Parliament of Northern
Ireland was empowered to make laws for
purposes similar to the purposes of the
recent amending Act passed in Great
Britain with respect to the War Damage
Commission. The provisions contained in
this Part of the Bill are, therefore,
identical in terms with those recently
passed by the Imperial Parliament.
The only Clause in this part of the Bill
to which I would draw special attention
is Clause 13, which enables a tenant
whose premises have been rendered unfit
by war damage to serve on the landlord
a conditional notice of retention, the effect
of which is dependent on whether the
War Damage Commission decide to make
in respect of the premises a cost of works.
payment, that is, a payment representing
the cost of repairs, or a value payment,
that is, a payment representing the prewar value of the premises. In the event
of a cost of works payment being made
the notice will become absolute; on the
other hand, if a value payment is made
the notice becomes a notice of disclaimer.
I do not think it necessary to refer
specifically to any other Clauses in the
Bill, except to Clause 36, to which I
would specially direct the attention of the
House. It will be seen that this Clause
provides that the Bill shall have effect in
relation to any war damage occurring
since 1st September, 1939, and that in
any case where before the passing of this
Bill land has been rendered unfit by
reason of war damage, then in respect of
the period between the date on which the
war damage occurred and the date of the
passing of this Act the Court may, on
the application of an interested party,
make special modification of the rights
and liabilities of the persons interested in
the land as in the circumstances the Court
thinks fit. It will be seen that the
general effect of the Clause is that if any
person considers that he is in any way
aggrieved by reason of the fact that he
has paid rent in respect of premises which
were unfit for habitation he may apply
to the Court to have his grievance
remedied.
I hope I have made the more important
Clauses in this Bill clear to hon.
Members, but if there is any point on
which further information is required I
shall be glad to deal with it. I beg to
move.

Mr. BEATTIE: Earlier this afternoon

in constant debate. I presume the

It is the duty of those who have

man.
I wish to refer to the exorbitant rents
and the destructive manner of landlords
who are dictating to their tenants how
much rent they will have to pay for their
homes. If the tenants have been away
from their homes for any period from one
week to three months they have to pay
the back rent. If this Bill had safe-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

guarded the tenants in that direction I
would not be charged with over-talking
in this House. I have been talking in

From what I have read of this Bill, I
believe it will be a benefit to some classes
of the community, but it will not be as
great a benefit to the masses as the Bill
which is awaited from the right hon.
Gentleman. If I get a measure extending the operations of the Rent Restriction
Act to all classes of dwellings that are
habitable, I would feel that a good day's
work had been done by the right hon.
Gentleman. But one must not ignore
this Bill because there is nothing in it
that will benefit to any great extent the
class of people one represents. This Bill
is not going to benefit the working classes
to any great degree. I want to be quite
open with the right hon. Gentleman. The
landlord class has very little accommodation in my mental make-up; they have
no space in my cranium for serious consideration.
Perhaps that is due to many causes.
Perhaps it is due to my early environment in which we were compelled to pay
for something we could not afford to pay;
perhaps it is due to the exploitation
which took place when the opportunity
was afforded through there not being an
ample supply of dwelling-houses, and
perhaps it is due to the exploitation of
the poor people who had to leave their
homes when they became uninhabitable,
and who, when they returned after they
had been made habitable, were asked to
pay the back rent before they were
allowed to sleep in them for one night.
That may be the cause of my failure to
recognise responsibilities to all classes of
the community, especially the class which
this Bill benefits.
Mr. GORDON: You mean to say they
pay rent for uninhabitable houses?
Mr. BEATTIE: On Easter Tuesday
and in May of this year certain people

If you promised to pay he would mark

That is the position, and I think it is a

Gentleman and I have the honour to

thing towards relieving that condition of

Non-Party Government
Non-Party Government
2 SEPTEMBER 1941
The position in regard to the harvest is
an extremely serious one. I do not propose to go into any detail at the moment.
I ask the Government to bear in mind
that there is no matter of greater urgency
or greater importance at the moment than
the proper harvesting of our hugely increased crops.
That proper harvesting,
unfortunately, is not taking place. I
would like the Prime Minister to consider
the question of allocating time for this
important notice of Motion. It is a matter
which brooks no delay. It is extremely
serious. It will be a very grave loss to
the State and country if serious steps are
not taken. It is because I want to avoid
this loss that I am pressing the extreme
urgency of this matter. I hope we will
get the Motion dealt with first. I make
no apology for asking that it be dealt with
first.
We have been told by people in Great
Britain that as regards food money has
ceased to matter. That is perfectly true.
This is a much more important matter
than even money. I beg the Prime
Minister to give us an undertaking that
provision will be made to hear the views
of provincial Members on this very important matter. I know the position in the
country from personal experience. Up to
the present the position is not satisfactory.
I hope from the point of winning the
war and saving our farmers from calamitous losses the Cabinet will arrange to
provide an opportunity to discuss this
matter on Tuesday next.

harvesting. On Wednesday the Finance
Bill (Second Reading) will be taken.

AUDITING OF BELFAST CORPORA-
TION ACCOUNTS.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if a
Local Government auditor and staff are
permanently employed in the Belfast City
Hall auditing the Belfast City Council
accounts; whether these officers have office
accommodation there; whether the
Minister has seen in the Press a report
that the so-called "big six" are going to
call in outside experts to assist in their
investigations; and whether these investigations are designed to cover the work
already done by the Government auditors.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer to the
first and second parts of this question is in
the affirmative. With regard to the latter
part of the question, I have seen the Press
report referred to by the hon. Member.
The answer to the last part of the question
is in the negative.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement that the answer to
the first and second parts of the question
is in the affirmative, will the Minister
contradict me if I say that the public
auditor charged with this duty is one of
the most competent and upright men in
the United Kingdom?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I never suggested anything else.
Mr. NIXON: And if he is as he is—
why is there another auditor being
brought from London to supervise his
work?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
hon. Member is under a misapprehension.
As I understand the situation this special
committee feel it right to get an expert
to go into the arrangement and administration of the accounts branch of the
Belfast Corporation.
Mr. NIXON: They cannot audit the
accounts without supervising him.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that the
Belfast Corporation pay to the Government £1,500 a year for the audit department, and is it a fact that the audit
department always found the treasurer's
department in perfect order? Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that this expert if
he is brought here can only examine the
work that has already been accepted by
his department as in order?
Sir DAWSON BATES: All I can say
is that the last investigation did not show
that the treasurer's department was in
perfect order.

EVACUATION AREA OFFICER IN
ARMAGH.
7. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state who
was appointed as area officer in Armagh
to deal with billeting and evacuation ;
whether this man is already in receipt of
a good pension sufficient for his needs;
whether the local employment exchange
was requested to furnish a list of suitable
persons for this job; whether the person
appointed had any service with H.M.
Forces, and whether ex-servicemen were
considered to fill the position; whether
he can state how many people are employed on the work mentioned in Armagh
area, and their names and rates of pay;
whether the appointment of an area officer
meant any reduction in unemployment,
or is it the desire of his department to
give good jobs to pensioners; and whether
he consulted the Minister of Labour
before sanctioning such appointments.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I should like
to explain to the hon. Member the position as regards the persons appointed to
act as area billeting officers in Northern
Ireland.
When my Ministry took over the
administration of the evacuation and
billeting of the priority classes from the
evacuation areas, no information was
available regarding the number of billets
available in the country or of the persons
who had been billeted or who had billeted
themselves in the country after the two
air raids upon Belfast. At that time the
boards of guardians were the reception
authorities, and the clerks of the
guardians were the reception officers with,
in most cases, a voluntary staff of billeting officers to assist them.
It was clearly impossible for these
officers to continue to carry out this work
in addition to their ordinary activities,
and accordingly I decided that billeting
officers should be appointed by the
Ministry in order to obtain as quickly as
possible information with regard to the
billets and the persons billeted.
The local authorities were asked in each
case to submit the names of individuals
in their area who would be suitable for
appointment as billeting officers, and in
most cases they submitted the names of
individuals who had actually been carrying out the work in a paid or voluntary
capacity. Each of these individuals was
interviewed at the Ministry, and if no
individual had been recommended by the
local authority, the Ministry sent down
a billeting officer to that area selected
from other persons who had been
interviewed.

passed by Fermanagh County Council and

Minister will discuss this matter with

ROAD TRANSPORT BOARD
TRAVELLING TICKETS.
10. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Northern Ireland Road Transport
Board have ceased to issue monthly or
weekly season tickets to any adults or
school-children other than existing holders
of such tickets; whether he is aware that
this will impose a great hardship on
people wishing to obtain a season ticket
for the first time, and especially on
parents of children commencing to go to
school and requiring to travel by bus; and
whether he will make representations to
the Board to have the privilege restored,
particularly in the case of school pupils.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that except on certain routes the Northern
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 SEPTEMBER 1941
Ireland Road Transport Board has not
declined to issue monthly or weekly
tickets to adults or school-children who
have not previously had them.
Owing to the altered conditions under
which public transport has had to make
provision for the carrying of greatly increased numbers of workers to and from
their places of employment the Board has
been obliged to withdraw its services from
important routes adjacent to railway lines.
and elsewhere curtail services for the conveyance of less essential travellers in order
that vehicles may be made available to
carry workers in other areas.
Further, it has obtained a number of
omnibuses from outside Northern Ireland,
but has still an insufficient number to
carry all who wish to travel at peak hours.
The Board considers it to be its duty, in
my opinion quite correctly, to give preference to workers, and in order to
accommodate them has been obliged at
such hours to restrict the passengers
carried to those who hold monthly or
weekly tickets. Obviously, therefore, it
cannot issue more monthly or weekly
tickets on any route than the carrying
capacity of the vehicles at those hours.
I fully appreciate the very great inconvenience which this arrangement must
cause to many persons and particularly to
school-children, but I can assure the hon.
Member that there is no alternative as
workers must be carried to and from their
work, and employers and others do not
appear to be able to make any alterations
in working hours, which would allow the
traffic at peak hours to be spread over
longer periods.
I understand that the difficulties experienced in the Newry area are acute
because of the considerable number of
children who travel from long distances
to schools in the town, and I know that
the Board have been giving and will continue to give the situation close attention;
but I regret that it has not been possible
to provide any greater facilities without
at the same time causing greater inconvenience and lessening the national war
effort elsewhere.
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact that the
people excluded from these season tickets
included workers on work of national
importance to which the Minister referred ?
Are we to take it from his reply that
these workers will now get these season
tickets?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
of what my hon. Friend states, but if he
will give me the facts as he has mentioned
I will take it up with the Road Transport
Board.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister take
my word for it that the issue of these
tickets was stopped to everyone including
workers on work of national importance?

(Hon. Members: No, no.)
The PRIME MINISTER: No, in a
serious way.
Mr. BEATTIE: That declaration is a
serious thing. Is it not clear and without
any misunderstanding what Clause 3
really means, that is, sovereign rights for
small nations? The right hon. Gentleman agrees with that. I am glad to hear
it, and I hope after the war north, south,
east and west will be able to live happily
together.
The PRIME MINISTER: I entirely
disagree with the hon. Member's interpretation of Clause 3.
CABINET STAFF.
17. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he has made another
appointment to the Cabinet staff.
The PRIME MINISTER: I assume
that the hon. Member's question refers
to the recent promotion of a principal
officer to the rank of acting assistant
secretary in the offices of the Cabinet.
The official who held this position was
an
assistant secretary, and in June,
1940, took up duties in the Home Office,
London; the post was then filled by an
officer of the rank of principal. Having
regard to the increasing duties and
responsibilities which continue to devolve
on the Cabinet Secretariat owing to the
war and other conditions and the very
efficient services rendered by the officer
in question, I feel that I was fully
justified in agreeing to his promotion on
an acting basis.
Mr. NIXON: When will the Prime
Minister stop making these new appointments? Is he aware that the country
cannot pay for them? Has the refusal
of the Government to set up a special

committee to inquire into expenditure

is

NEW INDUSTRIES IN SOUTH
ARMAGH.
18. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can give consideration to the claims of South Armagh for
establishing new industries, in view of
the present industrial situation in that
area; whether he will appoint a commissioner in Northern Ireland to examine
the possibilities of instituting new industries and relieving the industrial
chaos which prevails; whether the Prime
Minister is aware of the serious industrial situation in South Armagh, and
whether steps will be taken to give some
help to this distressed area.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
As the hon. Member is aware, the
financial facilities which were made
available under the New Industries Act
are not confined to any particular
districts but extend to the whole of the
Province. I would point out, however,
that new industries are not established
by the Government but by private enterprise, with or without assistance from
Government funds. The location of a
new undertaking is, therefore, a matter
which must necessarily be left to the final
decision of those proposing its establishment. As regards the second part of the
question, I strongly disagree with the
hon. Member's description of the industrial conditions in Northern Ireland
as chaotic, and I do not consider that the
appointment of a commissioner is called
for, or that it could in any way further
the object which the hon. Member has in
view. In reply to the last part of the
question I would remind the hon.
Member that employment for unskilled.
workers is available in Great Britain,
and that my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, is ready to facilitate
those willing to offer themselves for work
of national importance in that country.
BELFAST CIVIL DEFENCE
OFFICER.
19. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
amount per month spent on advertising
by Captain C. A. Hayes, Civil Defence
Officer, from the 1st May, 1941, up to
the present time.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Advertisements,
appearing over the name of the Belfast
Civil Defence Officer, are issued pursuant
to the instructions of the Belfast Civil
Defence Authority.
The total amount expended in
advertisement by the authority since the
1st May last is, I am informed, approximately £640. This figure includes
matter covering all aspects of civil
defence such as advice to the public,
training, recruiting, the placing of contracts and so forth whether appearing
over the name of the Civil Defence
Officer, or other authorised officers in the
service of the authority.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the statement as to the large sum of money spent
by this one officer, would I be in order in
asking the Minister is there any competition in connection with the various
secretaries in his Department to see which
will spend the most on advertising!
20. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state if
Captain C. A. Hayes, Civil Defence
Officer, was at his post in Belfast during
the enemy bombing attack in the early
days of May last.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I am informed
that on the occasion of the air raids on
Belfast in the early days of May last,
Captain Hayes, Civil Defence Officer, proceeded to Control Headquarters immediately on the sounding of the
"alert" and remained there on duty
throughout the duration of the raids.
EXAMINATION OF IDENTITY
CARDS.
21. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether the police have
instructions to stop well-known men whom
they can name and know well and demand
the production of their identity cards.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Under the provisions of Regulation 1 (A) (1) of the
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 SEPTEMBER 1941
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Regulations it is an offence for any person aged
14 years and upwards in Northern Ireland not to produce an approved document
of identity on demand to any police
constable in uniform.
Apart altogether from this statutory
requirement, hon. Members will agree
upon the desirability of ensuring that
under war conditions everyone has in his
possession documentary evidence of his
identity, and security reasons connected
with the existence of a land frontier
render the observance of this requirement
specially desirable in Northern Ireland.
I have, therefore, emphasised to the police
the necessity of occasional checks of
documents of identity so that our people
may at all times be conscious of the legal
position, and of the responsibility which
rests upon them to comply with this
simple but very important precaution. As
this process of checking is aimed at securing general compliance with the law
rather than of establishing the identity of
particular persons, the police are instructed to perform this duty in respect
of those who are well known to them as
well as of those who are not.
Mr. NIXON: In consequence of the
Minister's failure to answer the question
I will repeat it. The question is: Have
instructions been given to the police to
stop people well known to be loyal and
bring them to the side of the road to
examine their identity cards while others
are walking past? What would the
Minister himself say or do if a constable
came forward to him and said, "Mr.
MacDermott, come here till I examine
your identity card," while everyone else
is allowed to walk past?
Mr. MacDERMOTT: When the hon.
Member reads the answer, which I do not
think he has heard perfectly, he will see
that his question is answered. So far as
the latter part of the supplementary question is concerned, I have been stopped and
it never occurred to me to resent the fact.
I quite appreciate that one constable cannot stop all the people in the street at the
same time. In this case, I take it, the
hon. Member has been stopped, like
myself and other Members of the House.
Hon. Members should welcome the fact
that the law is not being enforced only in
regard to those not known to the police,
but in regard to all and sundry. There
is no special direction to the police to
single out men who are well known.
Mr. NIXON: That is the whole question.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The question has
been answered. There is a direction, as
I have already said in my reply, that
they are to go through the process of
checking irrespective of whether the
persons they check are well known to them
or not.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's second answer, which does not
improve matters, that answer is calculated
to create the impression that I object to
well-known people being stopped to have
their identity cards examined. I do not.
The question is, are well-known people to
be stopped while others are allowed to
pass?
If a certain man in a high position
drank less whisky there would be more
efficiency.

MILITARY AND HARVESTING
OPERATIONS.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
charges made to farmers in Northern
Ireland for the services of the military
in harvesting operations, by whom the
charges are collected and by whom they
are retained; and whether the soldiers
concerned receive any of the said charges.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply.
Payment for military assistance in
harvesting work is at the rates prescribed
for agricultural workers by the Agricultural Wages (Regulation) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1939. The cost of harvesting
work done by soldiers will be collected by
the Ministry from farmers and will be
transferred to Army funds. The question
of actual payments to military personnel
is one for the War Office and my Ministry
has no official information on this point.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Landlord and Tenant (War Damage)
[Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session, being an Act 'to modify
the rights and liabilities of landlords,
tenants and other persons interested in
land damaged by war,' it is expedient to
provide for the payment out of moneys
provided by Parliament of the remuneration of any assessor summoned by a county
court judge to assist him in any proceedings taken in pursuance of such Act
of the present Session."-(Governor's
recommendation signified-Mr. Barbour.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): The resolution at present before the Committee provides for
the payment out of moneys voted by
Parliament of the assessor who may be
called in by the county court judge in
any cases arising under the Bill where
technical advice or assistance is necessary.
The fees to be paid to the persons called
in as assessors will be fixed in accordance
with Clause 33 (4) of the Bill, that is to
say, they will be at such rate as may be
prescribed by rules of court made with the
consent of the Ministry of Finance.
It
is not possible to give an estimate of the
amount involved, since this will depend
upon such an indeterminable factor as the
number of cases which are submitted to
the county courts, but it is hoped that
the number of such cases will be small in
proportion to the total number of
tenancies covered by the Bill. I beg to
move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I want to try to remove a little weakness in the Ministry of
Finance. In this Bill we are bringing in
assessors. I think it is necessary and
important that the court should have the
assistance of assessors, but a weakness of
the Ministry of Finance in the past has
been to place too high a value on their
labour. We have been reviewing the fees
paid for many years to members of
various committees, and because of the
amounts allowed we view some with
alarm. If these assessors are brought in, I
expect them to be reasonably paid but not
over-paid. I hope the right hon. Gentle.
man will keep the fees in conformity with
reasonable demands and not give five, ten,
fifteen, or even thirty guineas a sitting,
as is being done to-day. We in this part
of the world are making our contribution
toward the national effort. We are promised, after the war, a new social order
and majority rights. Section 3 of the
joint declaration refers to majority rights.
If I am going to sit alongside any man I
am going to see that my services are
valued on the same standard. Too long
have we suffered from an inferiority complex at the hands of the Ministry of
Finance in connection with our services.
I give warning that I shall watch with
interest the fees paid to the assessors who
are to sit with the county court judge to
enable him to come to a proper conclusion, in order that those fees may be
reasonable and not exorbitant, and in
accordance with the value of the work
performed.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.

Mr. BEATTIE: Is there no one going
to get up to give us a sort of Committee
explanation of the various Clauses of this
Bill? I do not wish to dictate to the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Home Affairs-
The CHAIRMAN: The Clauses were
explained by the Minister of Home
Affairs on the Second Reading.
Mr. BEATTIE: While I admit that
under very trying circumstances the right
hon. Gentleman tried to give the House
an outline of this Bill, he dealt only with
the general principles. He did not go
into the details of the various Clauses,
and it is in doing that that the real
value of the right hon. Gentleman and
the Parliamentary Secretary becomes
apparent. They should tell the Members
of the Committee what in their opinion
is the correct meaning of the different
Clauses, and then if we see anything we
do not agree with we can give advice,
and, if necessary, move amendments,
with the object of producing a perfect
piece of legislation. Therefore, I want
either the Minister or his Parliamentary
Secretary to explain to the Committee
the effect of the first Clause dealing with
the relief from obligation to repair in
cases of war damage. A very important
principle is involved, and one under
which we have been suffering in Northern Ireland. How far does this Clause
go, and what obligations, if any, are on
the owners of property damaged by war.
I want a simple, plain explanation of
each Clause so that we will know where
we actually stand.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): As the
Member for Pottinger has himself
indicated, he was the only Member on
the other side of the House who stayed
to hear what the Bill is about when the
Second Reading was moved. We regard
this Bill as being so plain in its meaning
that it would be an insult to the intelligence of not only the Member for
Pottinger but other Members to start to
give a lengthy exposition of the Clauses.
Shortly, what the Clause means is this.
The obligation to repair, whether it is
contained in a written document such as
a lease, or under a tenancy agreement, or
merely exists under the Landlord and
Tenant Act, 1860, has gone, and not
until the Court so orders can any tenant,
or any landlord if he is under an obligation to do the repairs, be compelled to
carry out repairs, and if it is not
just and equitable that those things
should be done, then the obligation
to do them is gone. I suspect that the
hon. Member's interests are mostly with
the tenants in this matter, and once he
knows his constituents are safeguarded I
am sure he will be perfectly happy.
Mr. BEATTIE: I always knew there
was something in the Parliamentary
Secretary, and I am sure every Member
of this Committee will appreciate the
outstanding ability he has shown in his.
answer to my question. I compliment.
him on his reply, and I want to make a
confession, although confessions are not
in my line. It is that I am deeply
interested in that part of this Bill that
affects the interests of tenants, because
I am always on the side of those who are
least able to battle for themselves. I
have been given an assurance that Clauses
13 and 36 give me all the protection and
safeguards that I require for tenants.
At the same time I am so suspiciously
minded that I cannot understand if and
how this first Clause has any bearing on
Clauses 13 and 36. At the moment I
would say it has no bearing on the other
two Clauses. It simply does away with
the bad old things of the past and brings
in new conditions which I hope are an
indication of the new social order that is
to come after the war.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause ordered to stand part of the
Bill.

I will now deal with the point raised
by the hon. Member for Pottinger.
While this Clause and the retrospective
effect of Clause 36 in our judgment meet
the sort of injustices, oppressions and
extortions which have been suggested
from time to time in this House, the
Minister and I are not altogether satisfied
with the matter in this respect. For the
information of the Committee, I may say
that at the present moment a
memorandum, a draft Bill, is being considered
by the Cabinet for the purpose of getting
at extortioners in a more speedy manner
than even going to the county courts.
That will be supplemental and in addition to the provisions made here.
It may be that in practice these things
will be perfectly all right, but I should
think, from the observations of the hon.
Members opposite, that what they particularly desire is a swift summary procedure for dealing with persons alleged
to be extorting rents. For example, a
question was asked by one of the hon.
Members for the University a short time
ago as to whether we were aware that
certain agents or landlords were suggesting to their tenants that if they did
not pay up for their damaged, useless
houses now, they would not get one again.
As to whether that sort of thing is widespread-I have made inquiries—or not I
have no confirmation. We intend to
supplement the present legislation with a
tribunal, the exact form of which I cannot
give at the moment, but there will be
people associated with it who, by taking
a walk out to a house, will know whether
the rent is extortionate or not.
The Committee can rest assured that if
there be landlords and agents who are
extorting this money, then all they are
doing is saving money for these unfortunate tenants. Anything of an extortionate nature will have to be paid back.
I am sure that the Committee, just like
myself, would like somebody to be saving
money for them.
Mr. NIXON: It would be difficult to

When I use the word condemn,” I

but on the second occasion they had to fly

I do not think I will put the Parliamentary Secretary to the trouble of
answering me again, because he has

and with which I am satisfied.

Mr. BEATTIE: I am going to ask the
right hon. Gentleman and his Parliamentary Secretary to accept the statement I am going to make because it
affects the area represented by the right
hon. Gentleman and myself. People
who have been a number of weeks away
from their houses are invited to return,
it being stated that their homes are now

roofs. When they return they find the

window frames are out; in fact, they are
most dangerous houses to live in.
Landlords in the area to which I am
referring are compelling people to pay
rent for damaged houses, the only repair
to which has been the putting of felt on
the roofs. It has been stated that it is
unreasonable to ask an owner to be denied
the right of giving immediate possession
to another tenant, and three months is
inserted in Clause 13 as the time which

the original occupier. It is also stated

point, because you have intimated to the
hon. Member for North Down that you

Mr. LOWRY: Not unreasonable, but
too long.
Mr. BEATTIE: Many people have
left Belfast and at the end of three
months have not realised their home
responsibilities. The Parliamentary Secretary knows very well the state of mind
of people during a period such as we
passed through, and they do not come
back to normal in two weeks, a month
or even two months. I suggest that
three months is a reasonable and a just

months' period. If at the end of that
time the house is declared fit-I mean fit
to be occupied without danger to the
occupants from falling ceilings, falling
bricks or falling mortar-it should be
subject to examination by a responsible
person so that injury may not be caused

The Parliamentary Secretary can take
my word for it that people have returned

If you come along to certain streets with

Belfast Corporation Inquiry.
Mr. DOWLING: I beg to move, "That
in the opinion of this House, in view of
the fact that an inquiry into the administration of the Belfast Corporation is
essential and necessary, and believing that
this can best be carried out by an independent tribunal, if confidence in Corporation
affairs is to be restored and the rights of
the ratepayers safeguarded, the Government should immediately set up such a
tribunal giving it full statutory power to
deal with every aspect and operation of
the Corporation; and that the report of
this tribunal when completed be laid on
the Table of this House."
I make no apology for introducing this
Motion. For several weeks past the
affairs of the Belfast Corporation have
been made a major issue second only in
importance to the war that is going on,
and by the actions of some sections of the
Belfast Press, supported by the Ministry
of Home Affairs, there are 60 members
of the Corporation that have been placed
in a position not to be envied. Speaking
as one with over 20 years' public experience I have never known a body of
men to be so grossly misrepresented or
asked to accept greater insults than those
20 who voted with me on August 6th,
when I moved, along with other matters,
the dissolution of what has come to be
known as the Big Six Committee. If one
ignored these misrepresentations and
insults to these 21 persons, however unfair
and however hurtful, that would no
doubt please some people, but while a
shadow of suspicion hangs over 20 men
who supported me in this matter I should
consider myself unworthy to hold up my
head in this House if I did not come here
to defend them. Besides this, however, I
must obviously take into account how
these proceedings will react on the party
to which I belong-
Mr. NIXON: Ah!
Mr. DOWLING- -and I have no
hesitation in saying that already very
serious damage has been done to the cause
we all have at heart by the unfair attacks
and misrepresentations and the equally
wrong attitude adopted by the Ministry
of Home Affairs, based no doubt on the
attitude presented by the Press, which
takes upon itself the right to shape
public opinion whether that opinion is
right or wrong.

First of all, following a request of the
Tuberculosis Committee endorsed by the
Belfast Corporation, with the approval of
the hon. Member, who has moved the
Motion, the Ministry of Home Affairs
acceded to the request and held a sworn
inquiry into the activities of the Tuberculosis Committee. Hon. Members will
have seen from the Press some of the
evidence that was given during that
inquiry, and they are also aware of the
findings of the tribunal which, if I may
say so, was presided over in a most able
and impartial way by two inspectors, and
I think anybody who was not prejudiced
or interested in the findings could have
come to no other conclusion than that
the decision arrived at by the inspectors
was correct. The Report of the inspectors
contained many recommendations
amongst others, that certain of the
employees should be retired and others
should be censured, and that the committee itself should be dissolved. The
committee was dissolved by the Ministry
of Home Affairs.
The report was sent to the Corporation
for their consideration so as to enable
them to give effect to certain of the
recommendations. The report came before
the Belfast Corporation on the 20th June
last and they unanimously decided to
refer the whole matter to a special committee of six-which some people refer
to as the "Big Six'-with a view of the
latter bringing in any recommendations
to give effect to the report of the
inspectors. The hon. Member for
Windsor, who approved of that course,
must accept part of the responsibility for
appointing this special committee. One
would have thought that at that meeting
of the Corporation he would have raised
some protest against the findings of the
inspectors or made some protest against
the character of the gentlemen the Corporation appointed as the "Big Six"; at
all events, that he would have tried to
assist the Government, who were striving
to do their best to help the Corporation
to put their affairs in order. It is a
remarkable thing, having regard to subsequent events, and to the action taken
by the hon. Member for Windsor, that
he was present at this meeting of the
Corporation and agreed with his fellowmembers of the Corporation to the
appointment of this Committee, and,
therefore, I do find a certain amount of
difficulty in understanding his present
attitude.
The Corporation subsequently met on
the 6th August, 1941, to receive the
report of the special committee, and the
Corporation, by a vote of 21 to 17,
decided to delete certain portions of the
report and refer other portions to the
respective committees, and they also

of six. The hon. Member, who took part
in the setting up of the Committee, subsequently moved to have it dissolved.
Mr. BEATTIE: You are entitled to

Resolved: "That the Question be now

Question put: "That, in the opinion
of this House, in view of the fact that
an inquiry into the administration of the
Belfast Corporation is essential and
necessary, and believing that this can
best be carried out by an independent
tribunal, if confidence in Corporation
affairs is to be restored and the rights of
the ratepayers safeguarded, the Government should immediately set up such a
tribunal giving it full statutory power
to deal with every aspect and operation
of the Corporation and that the report
of this tribunal when completed be laid
on the Table of this House.'

some busybody singled out himself or
some other well-known person for some

Mr. NIXON: That is right.
To ask the Minister of Public Security
whether he can state how it helps the
war effort for the police to stop a loyal
man whom they know well for the
purpose of examining his identity
card. .
That is a perfectly general question,
and I think it was answered by
pointing out, as I did, that the instructions were not limited to stopping
loyal men, but that the instructions were
that there was to be no discrimination
between people known and not known.

the hon. Member's complaint has been

on the
Adjournment, and he is pointing to a

that, so far as instructions go, there is
no ground for thinking that any discrimination has been made against men
simply because they are well known.
would be in accordance with what every
person wants that steps taken to check
the observance of the law should be
taken with respect to all persons, and
that every person should be stopped
whether he is well known or whether he

affect my course of conduct in any way
--in administering the law is that
different people take it different ways.
I have had complaints from well-known.
men that they were not stopped; other
people do not like being stopped.
When an hon. Member-to take the
case quoted by the hon. Member for
Woodvale-or some other well-known
person is stopped and asked to pull into
the side of the road, I do not think he

Adjournment
[Mr. MacDermott]
has any reason for complaint as long as
he is courteously dealt with, and I did
not gather that the hon. Member had
been discourteously dealt with. The
only complaint would be if a person
stopping him limited his attention to
those whom he knew and ignored those
whom he did not. It would assist me

Mr. NIXON: An M.P. is not

a
Mr. MacDERMOTT: It is the duty of
an M.P., as of any other person, to see
that the law is properly administered.
To come to the other general point which
the hon. Member raised, that is the
efficacy of the National Registration
Identity Card, which is one of the
identity documents that have to be
carried in Northern Ireland-there are
alternatives-I want to say that this is
the form of document in use in Great
Britain. It is not a perfect document of
identity; there is no perfect document
of identity that is practicable. I agree,
if one could find an administrative way
of getting over the difficulty of having a
million photographs taken, that a general
system with photographs would be advisable, and it is a matter which I have
under careful consideration at the
moment.
It is not practicable to enact that all
these documents should have photographs, but something has been done in
that direction-I am not going into details
now and I can assure the hon. Member
of this, that the document as it stands
is not a useless document. It has, in
fact, been useful. It has also been
noticed that when people have documents
which they ought not to have their
attempts to alter them have been immediately transparent. I do not think
the hon. Member should bruit it abroad
that these documents are of no use. They
are useful for a number of purposes, including that of security.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
