em-
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether it is a fact that a
late town solicitor of the city of Belfast,
owing to selling land to his employer for
building purposes, was compelled to
retire from his position; whether it is a
fact that a civil servant recently sold a
site to the Ministry of Finance and no
action was taken in this case, and whether
the Minister can state what is the
difference between a town solicitor's conditions of service and those of a civil
servant.
Mr. BARBOUR: The two cases
referred to by the hon. Member are in no
sense comparable. The town solicitor
mentioned is presumably the one who
was severely criticised by Mr. Justice
Megaw's report on the sworn inquiry
into the Belfast Corporation's housing
schemes in 1925. He was found to have
exercised undue influence in the selection
of a site in which he was interested and
to have wrongfully permitted the insertion of certain covenants in the leases of
particular sites. The manner in which
he fulfilled certain of his duties as town
solicitor was also the subject of severe
censure.
The police barracks site at Newtownards, which is the site referred to
by the hon. Member in the second part
of his question, has already received consideration at the hands of the Public
Accounts Committee to whom the Ministry, as the hon. Member is aware, has
given a full report. It would be incorrect to describe this particular transaction as irregular merely because the
owner of the site was employed by the
Ministry of Finance.
There is a clearly defined procedure
governing transactions where civil
servants are involved in their private
capacity. It is that where it is in the
public interest to enter into a transaction
with a member of the Civil Service the
full facts must be made known to the
Treasury Division of the Ministry of
Finance, with a view to the Ministry's
approval being given in advance.
the case referred to by the hon. Member
this procedure was complied with and
the requisite approval was given.

Finance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The purpose of this Bill is to
give legislative effect to the minor taxation changes which I announced in my
Budget speech last April, and to certain
other taxation concessions which follow
similar proposals contained in the British
Finance Act.
Clause 1 amends the existing provisions
relating to the taxation of agricultura!
vehicles. On taking out a 5s licence a
farmer may now use his tractor on the
public road to haul between different
parts of the agricultural land in his
occupation agricultural produce or articles
required for his land. The farmer who
only uses his tractor on the public road
for passing between different parts of his
land and does not exceed a distance of
six miles on the public road in a week
can, of course, continue to have his
tractor or motor lorry exempted from tax
under Clause 4 of the 1937 Finance Act.
Paragraph (b) of Clause 3 is merely
declaratory and is intended to make the
legal position regarding the exemption
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
10 SEPTEMBER 1941
from taxation of A.R.P. trailer pumps
quite clear.
Clause 2 extends to members of the
Merchant Navy the concession in regard
to short term motor vehicle licences
granted last year by my right hon.
Friend to men of the fighting services
home on leave. Hon. Members will
recollect that a licence may be taken out
for a short period on payment of 10s in
the case of a motor car and 2s in respect
of a motor cycle.
Clause 3 exempts from estate duty gifts
to His Majesty's Treasury during the
war. The House will, I am sure, agree
that this is a reasonable concession to
make at the present time to patrioticallyminded persons.
The next Clause, that is Clause 4,
allows to all persons killed by war operations the same death duty relief as is
at present given to members of the fighting services and the Merchant Navy, that
is, exemption from death duties up to a
maximum of £150, provided the total
value of the estate for death duty purposes does not exceed £5,000. This section
also provides that where the same property passes on successive deaths due to
war operations the estate duty payable
on that property at the later death will
be completely remitted and the property
concerned will not be aggregated with any
other property for the purpose of ascertaining the rate of estate duty payable.
The last Clause exempts from death
duties any amount which may be due to
a person by way of a credit in the post
office savings bank under the recent
income tax proposals of the Chancellor
of the Exchequer, provided the death
occurs before the date on which the
amount was actually credited. This date,
as hon. Members will recollect, is to be
fixed as soon as possible after the end of
hostilities.
All of the proposals which I have
enumerated are revenue concessions, and
I am sure that they commend themselves
without exception to hon. Members. I
beg to move, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time."
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Repair of War Damage Bill,
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: This is a very short
Bill. It is designed to bring our legislation into line with that of the Imperial
Government. It amends both the
Housing (Emergency Powers) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1939, and the Essential Buildings and Plant (Repair of War
Damage) Act (Northern Ireland), 1939.
The main purpose of the measure is to
facilitate local authorities in carrying out
necessary and urgent repairs. Previous
legislation required a somewhat cumbersome procedure to be gone through.
1489 Repair of War Damage Bill- 10 SEPTEMBER 1941

Second Reading
First of all, it had to be ascertained from
the owner whether he was in a position
to carry out urgent repairs. Notices had
to be served, and after the expiry of the
notices
more time elapsed before the
repairs were carried out. Further, in
the case of municipal authorities, upon
whom the burden of carrying out urgent
repairs in the first instance nearly always
falls, I think it has been the constant
experience in Belfast that the necessity
and the power to enter on very short
notice was confined to cases where the
public health was going to suffer. The
Bill states that where houses are rendered
unfit, any urgent repairs which appear
expedient for avoiding danger to health
or preventing the deterioration of the
building may be executed by a local
authority without observing all the cumbersome procedure to which I have
alluded.
I think the House will find, on consideration of the measure, that this is a
Bill which will facilitate local authorities in carrying out urgent repairs and
obviate the complaints-I have heard
them made in this House-that there has
been delay in rendering buildings,
especially housing accommodation, wind
and watertight at the earliest possible
moment. This Bill
Bill is designed to
facilitate local authorities, without going
through a roundabout procedure, to start
right away to houses and make them fit
for human habitation as quickly as possible. I beg to move.

GRADING OF CATTLE.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
number of cattle graded at the several
grading centres in Northern Ireland for
the three months ended 31st August,
1941; the numbers graded as A, B and
C, respectively, and the number graded
below Grade C.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): I
have been asked to reply.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
it is not permissible in the national
interest to disclose actual numbers of
animals dealt with under the Meat and
Livestock Scheme. It is possible, however, to give the hon. Member the following information:
Of the cattle graded and purchased
under the Meat and Livestock Scheme at
the purchasing centres in Northern Ireland during the thirteen weeks ended
29th August, 1941, 13 per cent. were
graded A or "Special", 55 per cent. B,
and 32 per cent. C. Cattle are not
graded below Grade C.
It will be within the hon. Member's
knowledge that as from 9th June last
steers, heifers, cow heifers and bulls
estimated to kill out at under 50 per cent.
of their live weight, and cows estimated
to kill out at less than 47 per cent. of
their live weight have been graded and
Grade
C. Immature
purchased in
animals of this type were formerly purchased only on a reject basis. The
Ministry of Food gave to producers a
considerable price incentive to bring forward for purchase such immature animals
in order to secure such increased
slaughterings during the summer months
as would make it easier to feed the remaining stock adequately next winter,
and also to secure a more even flow of
animals during the summer months and
so avoid an autumn glut. It will be
obvious that the price incentive which
resulted in the purchase of considerable
quantities of these animals in Grade C
naturally increased the normal percentage of animals purchased in that
grade. Such increase is, however,
clearly to the benefit of producers.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Might I ask whether
the Parliamentary Secretary is aware of
the fact that grave dissatisfaction exists
among the farming community at the
present time in consequence of the present system of grading?
Mr. MAGINESS: No, sir. I am not
aware that any general dissatisfaction
exists.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I propose raising this
matter on the Motion for the Adjournment.
GROWING OF SOYA BEANS.
5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
any effort has been made by his Department to get soya beans grown in this
area, and, if so, what has been the
result.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply.
Experiments with acclimatised soya
bean seed of four different varieties have
been carried out in Northern Ireland, but
the results were not sufficiently encouraging to justify further trials.
The soya bean requires a long, dry
summer for successful cultivation, and,
as the hon. Member is no doubt aware,
such conditions are not generally prevalent in Northern Ireland.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that
reply of the Parliamentary Secretary,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
16 SEPTEMBER 1941
may I ask whether any attempt has been
made to grow soya beans on the Ministry's own farm, and, if not, will he tell
the reason that has not been done?
Mr. MAGINESS: The experiments
extended over two years. In the first
year four varieties of seed were grown,
but only one of these was considered
worth harvesting, and even that variety
produced little more seed than was
required to sow it. In the following
year only the variety which had been
harvested the previous season was sown.
It was actually sown on a number of
plots each of which received a different
manurial dressing.
None of the plots,
however, produced a crop which was considered worth harvesting.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Further, arising out
of the reply of the Parliamentary Secretary, may I ask whether his Ministry is
prosecuting and developing the growing
of soya beans?
Mr. MAGINESS: That is covered by
the answer.

JUVENILE CRIME IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
10. Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether
there is a serious increase of juvenile crime
in Northern Ireland; whether a Committee
of this House, under the chairmanship of
Sir Robert Lynn, dealt exhaustively with
this subject, and presented an elaborate
report; whether he is now prepared to
introduce legislation bearing on this
subject with a view to putting a check on
this growing evil?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I regret that
there has been an increase in juvenile
crime, attributable to a large extent to
war conditions.
Financial stringency is mainly responsible for the absence of legislation followng the report of the Committee under the
chairmanship of the hon. Member for
North Antrim.
Hon. Members will remember that this
subject was referred to when the estimates
for my Department were presented on the
8th July last, and that it was then
pointed out that the prevailing conditions
were due to the lack of parental control,
laxity in enforcing school attendance
owing to evacuation, and to general restlessness, and that it was stated that the
remedy was a matter for the community
as a whole, and that without the co-operation of the public no measures to combat
this social evil could be successful.
I can assure the hon. Member that the
question of introducing legislation bearing
on this subject has not been overlooked
and that it will be dealt with at the
earliest convenient opportunity.

GRADING OF POTATOES.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the reasons for putting British
Queen and Arran Victor potatoes in the
lowest grade as regards price, when in
fact these potatoes are equal to if not
better than many of the varieties now
placed in a higher grade as regards the
price to be paid to the farmer?
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply.
In fixing growers' prices for Northern
Ireland it is necessary to ensure that the
prices for any variety are such that, after
allowance for the normal transport costs
to Great Britain, the potatoes can be sold.
in competition with comparable varieties.
in that area. The varieties, British
Queen and Arran Victory, are, for reasons
which it is difficult to appreciate, not
as
regarded by the English consumer
being of as high quality as the varieties
placed in higher grades in the existing
Prices Order. The prices for all varieties
are fixed after consultations with the
growers' and merchants' representatives,
who take all the relevant factors, including that of the maintenance of trade with
Great Britain, into consideration.

COST OF FLAX PRODUCTION.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware that the cost of pulling flax is in
many districts Is 6d a stook, and that it
now costs up to 14s a day to spread flax

the same price per stone for his flax as

Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply. The Minister is aware that in
certain cases farmers have paid wages for
the pulling and spreading of flax which
are higher than the general agricultural
level of the country. The wages paid
may have reached the figures stated by
the hon. and gallant Member in certain
isolated cases, but the Ministry is satisfied that the bulk of the crop has been
harvested at much less cost than the
figures mentioned in the question.
The hon. and gallant Member is
doubtless aware that the Agricultural
Sittings of the House

in the year of our Lord 1941.
Yet the Prime Minister feigns indignation because we are not here to listen
to the speech of a Minister who comes

We will read his

people who have been bombed out of
their houses with bombs partly made of
scrap iron sent from Ulster to Germany
by the Prime Minister and his associates,
who also got Ribbentrop over here for
six weeks.

Clogher Valley Railway and Roads Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The necessity
for this Bill arises from the continued
inability of the undertaking to pay its
way without substantial subsidies from
public funds.
Mr. NIXON: They are going out on
you.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not mind.
As hon. Members are aware the Clogher
Valley Railway is a narrow gauge line
which, starting from the G.N. Railway,
at Tynan, runs for 37 miles through an
agricultural district, which has only six
villages, but no towns. It was constructed
under the authority of a Provisional
Order made under the Tramways and
Public Companies (I.) Act, 1883, and
was opened for traffic on the 2nd May,
1887. To enable the promoters to obtain
the capital needed for its construction the
grand juries of the Counties of Fermanagh
and Tyrone guaranteed the payment by
specified baronies of interest at the rate
of five per cent. per annum on the paidup capital, and also the money needed to
1525 Clogher Valley Railway Bill-
16 SEPTEMBER 1941

Second Reading
make good any loss on working and maintenance. When the baronies in question
were required to pay any sums in respect
of the guaranteed dividends, the Government undertook under the Provisional
Order to contribute a sum amounting to
one-half of the sums so paid up to a
maximum of two per cent. on the paid-up
capital. This provision has operated to
the full since the inception of the undertaking.
The railway has never been a financial
success; in fact during the 54 years of
its existence its working expenses have
always exceeded its revenue except on 11
occasions, and it has never, in any year,
earned enough to pay interest on its
capital. It has, therefore, been necessary
from the beginning to rely on
guarantees to keep the line operating.
the
At first the burden imposed by the
guarantees feli most heavily on the ratepayers of the contributing baronies, but
the Local Government Act, passed in the
year 1898, gave them some assistance in
that it provided that where the amount
required to be raised in any area in any
financial year to meet a railway charge
connected with a guarantee exceeded a
sum equal to sixpence in the pound on
the rateable value of the area the Government might pay out of the local Taxation
(I) Account a sum equal to one-half of
that excess. That fund was wound up in
the year 1924, but by an Act passed in
that year the liability of the Exchequer
was continued, but was limited to 90 per
cent. of one-half of the excess.
Later, in the year 1929, the derating
of agricultural land transferred more of
the liability from the ratepayers to the
Government. During the last war the
railway, like other railways, was operated.
under Government control, and, after that
control ceased, a sum of £16,723 was
received from the Imperial Government in
settlement of claims and was used to meet
the loss incurred in working the line, but
that money was exhausted in the year
1925, and in the following year the county
councils of Fermanagh and Tyrone as
successors to the grand juries took over
the railway from its owners under a
section of the Provisional Order which
provided that if the grand juries were
obliged to pay any money for a period of
three years for maintaining and working
the railway all the property of the railway
company relating to it should become the
property of the grand juries. Since that
transfer took place the line has been
owned by the county councils, and has
been operated by a committee of management, the railway company no longer
having any right to control it or interfere in its management.
Prior to the coming of motor vehicles
the railway was not a success, and the
growing competition with which it had to
contend made it certain that it could
never pay its way notwithstanding the
anxiety of many people in the area which
it serves that they should still have its
services. The vehicles of the Northern
Ireland Road Transport Board operate
along the road over which the railway
runs in places, and I am satisfied can
without any difficulty provide all the
facilities which the railway provides.
Consequently there is no longer any
reasonable ground for continuing to
operate the raliway.
As the capital invested in the railway
amounts to £123,310 a sum of £6,166 is
needed each year to pay the interest to
the shareholders. For many years past
the loss on working has been about
£6,000 per annum, and therefore because
of the guarantees the taxpayers and ratepayers have been obliged to subsidise the
railway to the extent of about £12,000
per annum. For the year which ended
on the 31st March, 1940, and which was
a typical year, these subsidies amounted
to £12,981, of which sum the taxpayers
provided £11,696 and the ratepayers
£1,285.
Every possible economy which could
be effected in the working of the railway
has been effected, yet the position has not
improved, and, in fact, very heavy expenditure on repairs would be necessary
both to the line and to the rolling stock
if the railway were to continue to exist.
It has, therefore, been decided that it is
in the interest of the public that the line.
should be closed to traffic, and that it
should be sold for whatever can be
obtained for it as scrap, and the county
councils agree with that decision.
The Bill, the Second Reading of which
I am to move this afternoon, provides
for the railway ceasing to be operated
and the Committee of Management going
out of office. It will authorise the
appointment of a liquidator to wind up
the affairs of the railway; remove the
1527 Clogher Valley Railway Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
rails, sleepers, and, etc., from the public
road leaving the latter in such a state
that it can be made suitable for motor
traffic; give back to the road authorities
the portions of the road along which the
track is laid; make it possible to give
them also any other land which forms
part of the railway and is needed to
improve the road.
The closing down of the railway must,
unfortunately, dispossess the entire staff
employed in operating it, and, as most
of the employees are advanced in years
and not likely to obtain other employment, the Bill makes provision for compensating such of them as have been in
the employment of the undertaking for
not less than two years. It is proposed
that any employee who has had two completed years' service, but not ten years'
service, shall be given a gratuity of 1-12th
of his annual remuneration for each year
of service, and that each employee with
at least ten years' service shall get a
pension calculated at the rate of 1-60th
of his annual remuneration with
maximum of 40-60ths.
a
It is also proposed that the net
proceeds of the winding-up of the undertaking and the sale of its assets shall be
placed in a fund, out of which the compensation to employees shall be payable,
and that should the fund not prove
sufficient at any stage for the purpose it
will be assisted out of moneys provided
by Parliament.
The Government proposes undertaking
the responsibility of providing the money
(£6,156 p.a.) needed for the payment of
interest, and the Tyrone County Council
is prepared to undertake the distribution
of the interest to the shareholders.
Apart from the removal of an unprofitable undertaking and the improvement
of an important thoroughfare the net
result of the passing of the Bill will be
the saving of nearly £1,300 each year
to the ratepayers of the guaranteeing
baronies and the saving in the first year
of at least £1,500 to the taxpayers, and
the latter saving will increase to at least
£2,500 in the following year and will
ultimately reach £5,500 per annum when
the last pension ceases to be payable. I
beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

the public purse, through taxation, have

We were paying dividends to the shareholders of this line. I presume that
some of these have now passed out. I
note that any of the lands of the railway

Mr. NIXON: This is an important
point. The point I take exception to iswho is to be the judge of a death caused
by the operations of war? I find in this
clause :
If, in the case of any death, it is
proved to the satisfaction of the
Ministry of Finance that it is a death.
to which this section applies, the said
Ministry shall give the same relief . . .
That is as far as it is necessary for me
to read. Why should the Ministry be
the supreme judge of whether a death is
caused by enemy action or not? The
Ministry is not qualified to be the judge.
The other day the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs
brought forward a clause extending, and
properly so, the right of appeal in cases
only where property is affected-on representations from elsewhere. Instead of
making representations from elsewhere, I
am going to make representations from
this Table.
The
This is a case where a person is killed
by enemy action, and the friends claim
that his estate should be exempt from
duties, and they make certain representations and give certain proof.
Ministry is going to be the judge. There
is no provision for appeal in that case.
The Ministry who would benefit by the
money is going to be the supreme judge
and jury of what should be paid to themselves. The thing is wrong. It is contrary to the general principles observed in
this House. I supported an amendment
to the War Damage Bill when only property was concerned. It was brought
forward to give the right of appeal to a
person, but in this case there is no right
of appeal from the decision of the
Ministry. The coroner cannot decide it.
It is not going to be left to the county
court judge or anyone at all. I am surprised that any trained lawyer with a
legal mind would allow any such a clause
to go through. The thing is ridiculous.
not
Quite a lot of cases have, unfortunately,
occurred where people have lost their
lives by enemy action. I will not say
the Ministry's decision would be wrong
or biased, but I say they are
competent to give the decision. It is not
their function. The Ministry is one of
the parties. It naturally wants the death
duties, and the friends want to retain
them. The friends say, "The man who
to
owned this estate was killed by enemy
action," and the Ministry say he was
not. The right way to decide that would
be for the friends to appeal against the
Ministry's decision to a competent court.
This is a comparatively new thing. It is
only in war that anything like this could
possibly arise. You are always in the
front line no matter where you are. I
intended to speak on this point on the
Second Reading, but, as I explained, I
was detained outside listening
grievances against the Government. If
you lose your house or your shop you
would try to get the sympathy and support of the Member of Parliament. That
is why I did not raise these two points.
I was most anxious to do so in order to
give the Government an opportunity_of
considering the matter before the Bill
came to the Committee stage. I raise
them now, one about the farmers and the
other, the more important one, where the
life of a person is concerned.
The Ministry take it on themselves to
come to a decision. I wonder they should
take it on themselves to do any such
thing, because there will be dissatisfaction, but if the matter is decided by the
county court judge or some other man
with a legal mind I would be quite satisfied. He would hear both sides. I certainly would not be satisfied about the
Ministry deciding it themselves. Perhaps
the Minister will not give his decision on
the point I raised this evening. That is
all I ask him to do now, not to give his
decision this evening unless he has his
mind made up that everything he brings
in is like the laws of the Medes and
Persians and cannot be altered, unless
there are representations from elsewhere.
"Elsewhere" will not have time to get
into action now. I do not think the
Minister of Finance will yield to
"elsewhere". It is natural that the
Ministry of Home Affairs should yield
to "elsewhere", because they are legally
minded. They yield where "elsewhere"
is legally minded like themselves. In a
particular case "elsewhere" was right
and the Ministry were right in accepting
the representations of "elsewhere". I
am not legally minded, neither is the
Minister of Finance. I appeal to him-
I am not "elsewhere"-not to take it
on himself that his Ministry should
decide how the death was caused if there

Mr. BARBOUR: In the working out
of this Clause the Ministry would always
be guided by the question of fact rather
than opinion. I think the hon. Member
for Woodvale knows that the cause of
death is practically always determined
there. So there is no dubiety on that
point. The concession which is extended
here was first introduced about 1904,
therefore it is not an Act of recent legislation. I understand that no difficulties
of the kind the hon. Member has alluded
to have been experienced in the carrying
out of the Act.
Mr. NIXON: I may reply to the
Minister by saying that he is under an
illusion if he says that questions of fact
are decided in this country by a Ministry, no matter how superior that Ministry may be. Questions of fact are
decided by a jury who have no interest
in it one way or another. Questions
of fact are not decided by parties to the
dispute, and in this particular case the
Ministry would be one of the parties to
the dispute. A question of fact is
decided by a jury under the guidance of
a judge. There might be a question
of law in it. Very often a question of
law would arise which the Minister or
I would not see, and the judge is there
to guide the jury on questions of fact
and to tell them what the law is.
The Ministry deem itself competent to
decide anything evidently. There can be
no argument put forward against what I
have suggested unless the reason is that
it comes from me. That is all the argument against it. I am sure if I knew
the minds of all the Members listening
I would see that they can see no reason
and no argument against referring a
matter like this, if the parties concerned wish it, on appeal to a competent
court. One party to the dispute is not
competent to decide it. The Ministry of
Home Affairs with the consent of the
Minister took all power out of the hands
of the magistrates, because they did not
know the law and some other things we
will not mention here, but the Minister
of Finance is going to take into his own
hands more power than the magistrates
ever had.
Why he would not leave it over and
consult the Attorney-General is a thing
I cannot understand. He could consult
some of the legal men on his own side.
Some front benchers here
are front
benchers in the courts. There is no use
appealing to the Minister when he turns
down such a reasonable and sensible
request as I make, if I may say so myself.
Let the question be decided by a competent court, not by the Ministry. The
Ministry stand to get the money if
they decide against the suggestion that
the death has been caused by enemy
action. There might be some cases on
the borderline. It is very easy for
borderline cases to occur. Anyone who
exercises his imagination can understand
cases on the borderline.
I do not suppose there is any use in
my appealing to the Minister. I have
done my best. I often try to save the
Government from their folly. I could
give any number of illustrations. I saw
by the papers that the Prime Minister
was down examining huts for homeless
people. When the Government brought
in an Act of Parliament making it
illegal for anyone to build a hut I tried
to stop them, but I might as well have
been idle. That is only one illustration.
I am trying to help the Government now.
Many a time I tried to help them, but I
was always turned down. There are no
brains anywhere but over there.
Mr. BEATTIE: This Clause seems to
me to be legislation by reference as it
refers to a number of principal Acts.
After that semi-Cabinet conference for
the purpose of replying to the Member
for Woodvale I will proceed. One tick
more by the clock and the Bill must be
sheived for at least another week. Are
you listening? I think you had better
take the views of the back benchers on
the opinions expressed by the hon.
Member for Woodvale-
It being half-past Six of the Clock, the

put, pursuant to the Standing Order.
Progress reported; Committee to sit

Motion made, and Question proposed,

(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I want to raise this
question of public air-raid shelters in the
Pottinger Division of the Parliamentary
Borough of East Belfast. I asked a
question on the subject last Tuesday, and
the Minister of Public Security, in his
reply, stated:
I am informed that six public shelters
have already been erected to serve the
needs of the locality to which the hon.
Member refers.
I referred to a certain area in the
Pottinger Division, and I said there were
no public air-raid shelters in that denselypopulated area. When the right hon.
Gentleman made his reply I wondered if
I had missed seeing any of the avenues,
parks or roads which comprise the area
mentioned. Accordingly I personally
went round them, and I have yet to find
one public air-raid shelter in the area
referred to, although you stated there
were six. I asked you last week if you
would come and show me where they are,
and if you will tell me now where they
are I shall be pleased to visit them. In
the area I have mentioned there are no
public air-raid shelters. It is true to say
that in Summerhill they are erecting a
few communal air-raid shelters, but from
the little avenue beside the picture house
to Dundonald boundary post there is not
a public air-raid shelter for the convenience of the people who visit that
district.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY: The hon. Member has
made it quite clear that he is referring to
public air-raid shelters and not to the
communal type of shelter, some of which
have been installed at Summerhill, and
also at several other sites in the area.
These public shelters, as the hon.
Member appreciates
from what he
said last Tuesday, were intended
primarily for the passing or travelling
public. As he put it last Tuesday, there
is not one public shelter for visitors and
others who go into the streets in the area
which he defined. That was, as I understood it, that part of Pottinger Ward
running from Kirkpatrick Memorial
Church along the Upper Newtownards
Road outwards to the boundary post.
The hon. Member will find one public
shelter immediately to the East of the
Kirkpatrick Memorial Church.
Mr. BEATTIE: The reason I mentioned the Kirkpatrick Memorial Church
was because I was not aware of the name
of the avenue beside the picture house,
but it is next door to the church.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I do not know
the name of it either, but he will find
serving the main roads, which were the

public shelter to the immediate east of
the church. He will then find two others

That makes three. He will then find in
Eastleigh Drive two further shelters.
Mr. BEATTIE: Eastleigh Drive is not
in Pottinger Ward; it is in Victoria.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: There is another
shelter in Ormiston Park.
Mr. BEATTIE: Victoria again.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Those shelters

When the hon. Member said last Tuesday
that no shelters had been provided at all,

that dividing line will not be observed by

It is right to say that for the people
frequenting that highway there are six
public shelters. It is true that only three
are in the electoral area the hon. Member

This case was an instance of a direct

"I do not know whether the hon.

The right hon. Gentleman admitted
that a number of these shelters are being
reconstructed. It is a very important
thing to reconstruct them when you find
they are not all right. The original
shelters were certainly not all right, but
there is a great improvement now. It
is not necessary to be offensive to a person
who pointed out that these shelters were
not all right before anybody was killed.
On behalf of the people I represent I
have a right to complain about the
shelters. Thousands of pounds are being
spent in reconstructing shelters which
were not built right in the first instance.
There was not enough cement used in the
walls to keep them together. The walls
were not reinforced in any way, and a
large cement slab was put on top of these
walls. That is what did the damage in
Percy Street. When the walls collapsed
the slab came down and the people were
trapped.
The experts who approved and passed
these shelters should not be retained in
their present positions at all. In the last
war we got on well because wherever there
were failures there were vacancies. At
that time we had Mr. Lloyd George at
the head of affairs. There are no
vacancies now, although there are failures.
I know the Northern Government has no
jurisdiction in reference to what happens
elsewhere, but there have been failures
here in regard to shelters and in other
directions. Look at the state of the city
after two raids! There is nothing like it
in Europe to-day. There was an
Auxiliary Fire Service which was taken
over by the Ministry, but there seemed
to be no organisation. I am not suggesting that the men did not do their best.
There did not seem to be any specific
districts; they were going here, there and
everywhere.
We got over that by getting rid of the
chief of the fire brigade. That was one
vacancy, but it is the only one I heard
about. I do not know anything about the
merits of the case. I knew the man and
liked him personally. Although I voted
against his getting the appointment when
he got the job I backed him up. I do
not know what happened, but I do know
there were no arrangements for dealing
with the emergency. I know the things I
advocated were missing when they were
wanted. We had not the ladders, the
ropes or the picks.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 23rd September, 1941.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
STOPPAGE OF BILLETING
ALLOWANCES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
a billeting officer in the Newtownards
area is withholding from evacuees in that
area their billeting allowance and
threatening them with complete stoppage;
whether he can state what authority, if
any, this gentleman has for acting in this
manner towards those people who are
compelled to live away from their own
home; and whether he will take immediate steps to have the matter
investigated.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that in
the Newtownards area, as in other reception areas in Northern Ireland, the
billeting officers have stopped payment of
the billeting allowance in a number of
cases where, for one reason or another,
the evacuees are no longer entitled to be
billeted at Government expense. The
majority of these cases fall into one of
three classes, namely (1) where the
father has joined his wife and children
in their billet; (2) where evacuated persons have given up their house in Belfast
and have, in effect, become residents in
the reception area; and (3) where homeless persons, not in the priority classes,
had been wrongly billeted in a reception
area instead of being billeted tempporarily in the city or its immediate
vicinity.
In investigating the cases in their areas
and in stopping payments where irregularities are found to exist, the billeting
officers are acting under the authority of
this Ministry whose policy in this matter
is guided by principles laid down by the
Ministry of Health.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is it not a fact
that this billeting officer, Mr. Stewart,
refused to pay the billeting allowance to
the lady concerned from April till
August of this year, and is it not a fact
that the reason why her husband went
down to the billet to stop for a month
was the state of his health? In view of
that position will the right hon. Gentleman see that this lady's billeting
allowance is paid from April right to the
date on which the husband made his first
visit in August?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon.
Member will furnish me with details such
as he has given now I will go into the
matter further.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman inform the House why Mr.
Stewart suggested that this lady and her
children should take other billets which
he would provide?
Mr. SPEAKER: Of course the hon.
Member now is dealing with a specific case
not mentioned in the original question
and he should put down another question.

applications received from serving members of the Belfast Fire Brigade.

of
existing very unsatisfactory state

Sir DAWSON BATES: I propose to
answer this and a similar question by
the Member for South Down together.
I am aware that recent reports received
regarding the purity of the Castlewellan
water supply have not been satisfactory.
The Downpatrick Rural District Council
have been giving the matter their earnest
attention, and measures have already been
taken by the council since these reports
were received for improving the purity
of the supply. Further measures, including the laying of a special pipe line
in the town, are being prepared.
I am not aware that the people of
Castlewellan have to obtain water by
lorry from a distance outside the town.
The council raised a loan of £3,000
in June, 1940, for the purpose of improving the water supply and over £2,000 of
this has been expended up to date.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question I should point out
that the reservoir in question is not
derelict. It will be put into use as soon
as circumstances permit. It is not proposed to incur further expenditure on
excavation of the lake in Castlewellan
Demesne.

7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

and Thomas H. Annett, of 63 Willowfield Drive, Belfast, who were registered
under the Ministry's scheme, on the 19th

billets at Tunney Hill, Cunningstown,
Bailieboro', County Cavan, and that
vouchers were then issued to bring them
back, on the 18th July, to billeting
accommodation in Northern Ireland;
whether, in view of the responsibility
for the billeting of these children in Eire
resting with the Minister, he will order

expenses from the 19th April to the 18th
July, 1941, as chargeable to his evacuation scheme account, owing to his Ministry being solely responsible for the
children being evacuated outside Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Neither these,
nor any other persons, were billeted by
the Ministry in Eire. During the period
immediately following the raids some
persons who sought them were given
travel vouchers to Eire, and subsequently
warrants for the return journey, but the
Ministry has neither authority nor means
for billeting in Eire, and consequently
there can be no question of paying billeting charges in Eire.
I understand that the warrants were
issued in the belief that the children's
family had been rendered homeless, but
this was not the case, and they should
not, in fact, have been given travel
warrants. The Ministry is not, however,
disposed to raise any question about the
honouring of these warrants having re-

BONUS TO TEACHERS.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that the
Burnham Committee, in view of the
award of a second War Bonus to the
Civil Service, has recommended the award
of a further bonus to English teachers;
and in the event of this bonus being
granted by the British Government,
whether he will, in pursuance of the
step-by-step policy adopted in Northern
Ireland, grant a similar bonus to teachers
in this area; and whether he will consider the advisability of granting a bonus
to retired teachers, many of whom are in
very straitened circumstances owing to
the increased cost of living and the very
inadequate pensions they are receiving?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): Yes, sir. I am aware from
reports in the Press that the Burnham
Committee has recommended the award
of a further bonus to English teachers.
If and when such award is made, sympathetic consideration will be given to the
award of a further bonus to teachers in
Northern Ireland, and the teachers'
organisations will be given an opportunity of making suggestions in the
matter. As far as the last part of the
hon. Member's question is concerned, I
am not prepared to consider granting a
bonus to pensioners to meet the increased
cost of living in advance of a similar step
by the United Kingdom Government. If
such a bonus should be given in Great
Britain, favourable consideration will be
given to its introduction into Northern
Ireland, with effect from the same date.

HUTS FOR HOMELESS FAMILIES.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state where
families who have been bombed out of
their homes in Belfast can make application for one of the huts which the
Prime Minister stated "were being erected
in almost every direction in the city for
their accommodation," and whether he
can give the cubic feet of space allowed
to each member of the family; whether
any special arrangements are provided in
these huts for infants and expectant
mothers and, generally, the qualifications
of applicants and conditions of letting.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My right hon.
Friend has asked me to reply. The huts
mentioned in the statement to which the
hon. Member refers are being erected on
the outskirts of the city to provide
accommodation for those who have to
leave their homes as a result of enemy
aerial activity, but this accommodation is
intended only to serve as a temporary
provision for a few nights. Persons who
are rendered homeless are billeted either
with householders in reception areas or in
hostels.
Huts are also being erected in the
neighbourhood of the city for essential
industrial workers whose families have
been evacuated.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
these huts are not being built at all as
homes for the families that are bombed
out?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I was referring
to the huts around the perimeter of the
city. We are erecting these huts in
order to prevent people sleeping in the
ditches when they choose to leave the
city.
TRANSPORT FACILITIES FOR
WORKERS.
12. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he will take steps to
provide reasonably proper transport for
workers travelling by rail and bus to and
from their work in Belfast; whether the
Minister is aware of the overcrowding on
trains operating around Belfast, particularly on the G.N.R. routes; whether he
will abolish 1st and 2nd class on trains
operating at peak hours as has been done
elsewhere.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
My Department has kept in the closest
touch with this matter, and I am satisfied
that, under very trying circumstances, the
transport undertakings are using their
resources of rolling-stock to the maximum
capacity.
There is, unfortunately, a shortage of
transport, caused, on the one hand, by
the greatly increased number of passengers
resulting from war conditions, and, on the
other, by the difficulty of augmenting, or
even maintaining, the amount of rollingstock available. Every effort is being
made by the Transport Board and the
railway companies to increase their available stock, and the Ministry is giving
them all possible assistance in this direction; but the hon. Member will, I am
sure, realise that it is impossible to procure anything approaching the normal
supplies of new vehicles, and that it is
becoming increasingly difficult to obtain
the materials necessary to maintain the
existing rolling-stock.
The closest attention has been, and is
being, given by all concerned to catering
Oral Answers
Oral Answers

for the transport of workmen engaged on
essential works to and from their places
of employment.
I am aware that after the air raids
there was a very considerable amount of
unavoidable overcrowding on the railway
trains, but I have had recent enquiries
made, and I am assured by the railway
companies that, with few exceptions,
workers travelling, even at the peak
periods, are able to obtain seats.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I understand that first and
second-class travel has been abolished in
the suburban areas of London, but,
under present conditions, I do not feel
that anything would be gained by
abolishing it on the trains here.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister take

and abolish first and second-class

Sir DAWSON BATES: From what I

THE DRAINAGE COMMISSION.
15. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether the Drainage Commission appointed by the Government on
the recommendation of the Select Committee on Unemployment in their Second
Interim Report adopted by the Government and the House on 29th April last,
has yet presented the Interim Report
which he stated in the House on 1st July
would be presented shortly; whether he
can state how many meetings the Commission has held since its appointment,
and the date of its appointment; how
many schemes they have examined and
passed, and how matters stand at present
in regard to these schemes; and whether
the work of the Commission will be ex-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Brown]
into
pedited in view of the great and urgent

Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Interim Report of the Drainage
Commission has been submitted. Since
the date of its appointment, May 21st,
the Commission has held five meetings;
the sixth meeting will be held to-morrow,
24th September.
The Commission has before it ten
schemes, which between 1930 and 1938
were prepared by the Government
engineers at the request of the county
councils, and has also had under consideration some rivers for which no
scheme has been prepared. It has not
as yet proceeded to a recommendation in
respect of any specific scheme, as it was
first necessary to determine what degree
of State assistance was desirable in order
to ensure the success of a war-time
drainage programme. The Government
has approved the main recommendations
of the Interim Report, and, pending the
completion of financial consultations
with the Imperial Treasury, the Commission is at present engaged in considering the broad principles which should.
govern a drainage programme generally.
The Commission anticipates that in the
immedate future the way will be cleared
for a detailed examination of individual
schemes, and that it will shortly be in a
position, in a further report, to say what
schemes should be undertaken during the
period of the war and how such schemes
should be administered.
The Commission has been represented
at conferences with the English Ministry
of Agriculture and the Imperial
Treasury, and has had occasion to consult the county councils, in their capacity
as drainage authority for each county,
with a view to obtaining essential data.
Although these very necessary consultations have taken some considerable time
I am satisfied that the Commission, in so
far as a war-time drainage programme is
concerned, will soon be in a position to
make some valauable suggestions.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask is it the
intention to hand copies of the report of
the Drainage Commission to Members of

R.U.C. PROMOTIONS.
17. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Public Security whether his attention has been called to the fact that, of
some twenty promotions to the rank of
head constable in the Royal
Royal Ulster
Constabulary since 1938, only two have
been given to Catholics, and that other
Oral Answers
Finance Bill

Catholics of proved service and qualified

Mr. MacDERMOTT: The figures given
by the hon. and learned Member are
substantially correct. Of the promotions
to the rank of head constable since 1938
eleven were made as the result of a technical examination held under the then
current promotion regulations. Of these,
one was a Roman Catholic. Nine were
made as a result of the findings of a
selection board constituted for the purpose under the promotion regulations, as
revised for the duration of the present
emergency. Of these, one was a Roman
Catholic.
There is no question of "giving" promotion to Roman Catholics or Protestants, as such. Promotions in the
force are made on merit, and a candidate's religion does not in any way affect
the choice.
With regard to the last part of the
question, no doubt there are Roman
Catholics, just as there are Protestants,
in the force who are qualified by service
and otherwise eligible for promotion, but
the duty of a selection board is to prepare a ranking list of the qualified
candidates so that the most suitable may
first be selected for the higher rank.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Will the Minister
give his personal attention to this matter
and take steps to rectify the disparity so
glaring and so contrary to the public
interest?

Mr. MacDERMOTT: In answer to the

is the hon. Member himself who has raised

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): This provision in this Schedule
is intended to assist agriculturists. If a
person has an agricultural tractor and he
does not bring it out on to the road at
all, but uses it only on his own farm or
takes it through a hedge to his neighbour's farm, he is not entitled to pay
these duties. If he takes his agricultural
tractor out on the road he is liable to the
ordinary duty, but if he uses it for
certain limited distinctly agricultural
purposes he gets off with paying 5s.
The purposes for which he can use it,
and get off with paying 5s, are set out in
the Schedule. The particular purposes
for which he may use it and get off with
paying 5s are for pulling about agricultural implements such as a thresher.
He can do that on the road whether he is
going to his own or his neighbour's farm.
If the tractor is used only for taking
about its own appliances, a living van, a
water-cart, or something of that nature,
then the owner has to pay 5s duty. One
other purpose for which he can use it
and pay 5s duty is in connection with his
own land-taking out something to his
own land which is needed on the land.
If he uses it for taking out manure for
the purpose of manuring his own fields
he can take it out on the road and pay
a duty of 5s. If he uses it for bringing
in agricultural produce from his own
lands he can use it on the road by paying
a duty of 5s.
With regard to matters of that type it
must be used for drawing agricultural
produce or articles required for agricultural land which he occupies. I do
not think turf is agricultural produce.
It might conceivably be if, say, a farmer

I should have to pay the duty at the
ordinary rate. If a farmer believes he is
bringing in turf for some purpose which
is an agricultural purpose it is open to
him to contend the matter with the people
who seek to charge him the full rate,
and convince them he is only entitled to
pay 5s.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): The first part of this
Money Resolution relates to Section 8
of the Bill and makes provision for payments out of public funds required (a)
to meet claims for compensation to
former employees of the company which
may arise in the interval before the
Compensation Fund receives the proceeds
from the sale of the railway, and (b) to
meet any deficiency in the Fund itself,
It is estimated that in the first year of
the railway's discontinuance compensation will amount to about £4,000, but
this sum will, of course, diminish as time
goes one. The amount available in the
Compensation Fund for setting against
this liability cannot be calculated with
any certainty since from the realisation
of the scrap value there will require to
be deducted, in the first instance, the cost
of pulling up the railway line and certain
liabilities of the undertaking itself; it is
not, however, anticipated that the net
proceeds accruing to the Fund will more
than partially offset the liability in the
form of compensation.
The second part of the Money Resolution provides for the payment in full by
the Exchequer of the amount required.
to meet the County Council's liability in
respect of their guarantee of the 5 per
cent. dividend on paid up capital.
My right hon. Friend in his Second
Reading speech has given hon. Members
an outline of the history behind the
Government's commitments in the
Clogher Valley Railway. The Committee.
knows how, as time went on, the ratepayers' liability became more and more
the Government's. The result of these
successive transfers to the taxpayer of
the local authorities' financial responsibility in connection with the undertaking
can be illustrated by reference to the
1940 position.
The amount of the guaranteed dividend
in round figures in that year was £6,200;
the working losses came to £6,800. Of
this total of £13,000 the county councils
met £1,300 and the Government the remaining £11,700. The closing down of
the railway and the consequent elimination of working losses means, therefore,
with the Government meeting the full
5 per cent. dividend, a saving of £5,500
to the Exchequer and £1,300 to the ratepayers. Against the Government saving
of £5,500 must, however, be set the
amount required under Part I of this
Resolution to meet any deficiency in the
El
1603 Clogher Valley Railway Bill

Housing Conditions
[Major Sinclair]
Compensation Fund. Since compensation
to employees will not exceed £4,000 a
year the very least saving to the Government will be £1,500 in the first year, and
this amount will, of course, increase as
compensation payments dwindle and will
ultimately reach £5,500 a year when all
pensions cease; these savings are, of
course, minimum figures since they ignore
the amount to be paid into the Compensation Fund from the scrap proceeds
of the undertaking it is expected that
this amount though not sufficient to
liquidate the whole of the
whole of the pension
liability will nevertheless be substantial,
and to this extent, therefore, the savings
I have mentioned will be increased.
Most of the points raised in the debate
on the Second Reading have already been
replied to by my hon. Friend the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, but there is one which
perhaps requires some clarification. It
was raised by the Member for South
Tyrone and refers to section 9, sub-section
(4). In his speech the hon. Member
made reference to the guarantee of the
dividend on the railway stock. The position is that the guarantee itself remains
unaffected by this Bill, and is still the
liability of the original guaranteeing areas
in Tyrone and Fermanagh. The undertaking of the Government is limited to
that stated in section 9, sub-section (2)—
that is, to make good to the Tyrone
County Council such sums as may be
required to meet this guarantee. This
should make clear the meaning of subsection (4), which merely defines the limitation of the Government's undertaking.
The
Hon. Members may ask why it is
necessary for the Government to ensure
to the holders of Clogher Valley stock a
dividend of 5 per cent. I may say that
this matter was gone into very carefully
and legal advice was taken on it.
legal position is very difficult and turns
on whether the courts would consider that
the guarantee originally given by the
Baronies in respect of the 5 per cent.
dividend on paid up capital continues to
attach to the subscribed capital even
when the railway has been closed down.
The Government does not at the moment
propose to test the point in the courts.
On the point raised by the hon.
Member for North Armagh, the Committee will be interested to learn that the
Ministry of Finance has for some years
past been willing to purchase all the
Clogher Valley Railway shares coming on
the market, at a price not exceeding
£8 10s per £10 share, and up to the
present has bought 2,968 shares out of a
total of 12,351 shares; the Ministry's
offer is still open, and I think it will be
admitted that it is, in the circumstances,
one which is fair and reasonable.
Since the Government is a considerable
shareholder in the company, hon.
Members will understand that a substantial part of the money paid out of the
Exchequer under the second part of the
Resolution will accrue to public funds.
I beg to move.

would be tolerated only by the people of
Northern Ireland. If there is one community in the British Empire who are
inactive so far as fighting for their rights.
are concerned it is the people of Northern Ireland. Every street in Ballymacarrett is practically the same with
the exception of a few which have sixfeet entries and some with nine-feet
passages. We all sincerely regret the
terrible things that took place in Oldpark. I often wonder why the Member
for Oldpark never raises his voice in protest against the conditions in his area.
I have always raised mine about the conditions in Shankill. The conditions
under which the people in Everton and
other streets and in the Marrowbone

those people not painted and papered
their houses they would have tumbled

It is true to say that the Minister of
Public Security at the present time is
building huts. There is a danger when
this war is over of those huts becoming
the homes of the people, and to avoid
this the Government should set up a

some 40,000 homeless in Northern Ireland, and there will be anything from
another 5,000 to 10,000 young people
who are marrying now or will marry when
the war is over. Every one of these
people will be looking for a home. The
Government solution is to allow this
question to be dealt with by the British
Government. That is entirely wrong.
I want to see the Government of Northern Ireland looking after their own
people. It would be in the best interests
of the people of Northern Ireland if the
Government set up this select committee.
Hon. Members know that I have never
been very keen on select committees, but
if there ever was anything that would
justify the setting up of one it is the

has only to go to the areas in which
evacuees
are living. The conditions
under which these men and women, who
stood the test of two or three air raids,
are living are disgraceful.
it

the Members of the Government
should make them resign their
very important jobs. They should get

nothing done if it is left in the hands of

Northern Ireland. Colonies for the working people will have to be built on the
fringe of the city. They must be houses

never tolerate the building of a home

Housing Conditions
You have only to visit Belfast to realise
the number of people who are homeless.
I know the figures, and I am trying to
keep them as low as possible. In addition to the houses destroyed by Hitler
there are 5,000 in Ulster which should
be condemned. I want to see something
done. Nothing will be done. We will
have the same chaos after this war as we
had after the Great War. Immediately
the war is over, one of the great evils
which will confront this Government is
that of unemployment. Employment will
have to be found for tens of thousands of
men and women. I am sure the Minister
of Labour spends many sleepless nights.
planning what will be done.
Mr. HENDERSON: If I staged this
show I would get more than the music
halls in Belfast. The people would all
come to see the antiquated men who are
running this country into bankruptcy.
I want to tell the hon. and learned
Member, who may occupy a higher position some day, what will happen if
something is not done. Does he know
what Keir Hardie said when the Minister
of Labour spoke with Willie Walker on
the Labour platform? I am knocking
about the working-class people-shipyard
workers, foundry workers, and air-craft
workers-and I know them. Here is
what Keir Hardie said. He said: "When
Belfast turns red it will be redder than
the Clyde.' We do not want that. Even
the hon. Member for Pottinger does not
want to see it as red as that.
,,
Mr. BEATTIE: A member of a trade
union said that.
Mr. HENDERSON: I do not care who
said it. When the Government returned
by the people do nothing it makes the
people dissatisfied. They will be more
dissatisfied after the war if they come
home to the conditions that prevailed
after the last war. There has been
nothing in Northern Ireland but poverty,
destitution and starvation since the last
war. We want to avoid that. When
these men come home-many of them will
have married or will then marry-they
will want homes to go to. No Member
on this side of the House wants to sit
on the select committee that will
deal with this question of housing.
The Government can put on whoever
they like so long as they deal with
the problem. There are many men
in this House who could deal with it
without waiting to see what the War
Damage Commission are going to do in
England.
The whole of Ulster to-day is gasping
for new homes. If the Prime Minister
had been here, I would have told him
that I had the pleasure of being in
Comber. People are now living in shacks
that have been up for the past 90 years.
Surely, then, is it not time the Government set up a select committee to deal
with the problem. There are 40,000 or
50,000 people homeless at present. We
hope nothing more will happen, but we
might have another 80,000 people in
Northern Ireland looking for homes.
Then there is the question of town
planning. Some years ago this Government passed a measure known as the
Town Planning Act. Ten years ago I
asked the Corporation to do something in
the matter of town planning, and then I
appealed to the Minister, and this Bill
was brought in and passed. Nothing has
been done in the matter, and there is no
country in the world which is so backward in regard to town planning.
Mr. NIXON : There is political
planning.
Mr. HENDERSON: I know the root
of the evil. We have an inactive Government, and the back benchers very seldom
voice their opinions on any matter. Even
a fool sometimes can learn.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I have learned that
from you.
Mr. HENDERSON: You did not
know much until you met me.
In no
other country in the world are things so
awful as they are in Northern Ireland.
There were only about four sanitary
conveniences in Belfast, but as soon as
I took up the hobby ten or eleven were
erected. The people used to have to run
up back passages and break the law. I
got a stop put to that. They can now
perform the laws of nature in Belfast as
they do in London. If I had my way I
would have 134 conveniences in the
City. Let us look at the sanitary conditions outside Belfast. Could you go
to any country where things are in such
a shocking state? You could not unless
you went to Coagh. The Prime Minister
represents Comber in this House. He

has lived there for a generation. He has

He is well paid for his job, but what

same bucket with the stick across it as
existed in the time of Adam and Eve.
This is not a matter to laugh at; it is
too horrible for that.
Millisle is represented by Mr. Speaker.
I love Millisle, Bangor and every other
part of Ulster. The conditions in Millisle
are shocking, while the conditions in
Comber would make a darky blush. I
believe that when a bath is being transported through Comber the people gaze
at it with idle curiosity. Why? Because
it is only the rich who can afford to have
a bath there. How many water closets
are there in Comber? Has any attempt
been made to provide Millisle, Newtownards and other places with a proper water
supply? No. The same old system of
sanitation exists in these places as existed
in the middle ages, in the time of the
cave men, and even before that, in the
ice age.
When did you hear the Minister
of Labour taiking about the horrible conditions which exist in Co. Antrim in
regard to housing and sanitation ? Is
there any necessity for these conditions to
exist in this civilised age, and when I say
civilised age I leave Hitler out of it.
An agricultural labourer living in any
of the small towns in Ulster has to carry
water needed for household purposes anything up to 800 or 900 yards. This water
is brought in buckets. For washing purposes he has to depend upon an old barrel
with which the landlord provides him to
catch rain water. People living under
these conditions can never have a bath.
They may have a very small vessel in
which they try to wash themselves, but I
say that each house should be fitted with
a bath and proper sanitary accommodation. Right hon. Gentlemen opposite have
beautiful baths and beautiful basins. We
do not want such luxuries; we only want
plain baths, plain basins, and an ordinary
lavatory with a decent seat on it.
I often wonder how right hon. Gentlemen take their friends to certain parts of
the Province at election times, and then
tell the people what they are going to do
for them. We know it is impossible to
get anything done at the present moment
because everybody is engaged on war
work. However, we want you to have

started immediately the war is over.
Take the Silent Valley. There is also the
Annalong Valley. I know all about it.
The Silent Valley and the Annalong
Valley could supply every village and
every town in Northern Ireland with
pure
water. If
you do not wish
the Belfast Water Commissioners to carry

It is the duty of the Government to supply the people with pure
water. Everything that is needed so far

Antrim! In most houses all they have
is a bucket in which to fetch water from
long distances. Plans should be prepared
at once to have this evil remedied.
pure water supply should be provided to

I want you to draw up plans for
housing the people. I dread the approach

The huts are all right in a way, but

not be housed in proper homes. How
in the name of God people live in some

In many cases the roofs are only covered

felt has been put so that God's sunlight

until the end of the war unless something is done for them. The Minister of
Public Security will not allow them to

That would please me. But that is not

The Minister of Finance is there, and I

whose husband the Minister often met
when he was alive. She had a combined
shop and dwelling-house, and everything
she had was burned. She went to live at
Newtownbreda. She has got a house,
but she has not got the money to furnish

me a letter, dated the 10th of this month,
and I sent it, with a letter of my own, to
Great Victoria Street. I got no acknowledgement whatever. I went to Newtownbreda the other day to see her, and I
found that she, too, had had no acknowledgement. I got her to send me another
letter, and I had no acknowledgement.
I interfered in that matter as an M.P.
representing that widow. It may be due
to an oversight, but I should have got an
acknowledgment by return, and she
should have got forthwith a grant sufficient to buy furniture for her house.
The people with whom she is are good to
her, but she is not happy. That is not
the fault of the people, nor is it her own

own little houses. I do not know who is
at fault, but if I had received an acknowledgment it would have saved me the
trouble of going from Whitehead to
Newtownbreda.
What I really intended to do was to

Financial Secretary of the Ministry of
Finance to-day. I had troubled him

I take advantage of this occasion to

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Finance Bill.
As amended, considered.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read the Third time." (Mr.
Barbour.)
Mr. BROWN: I would like to make
another appeal to the Minister regarding
what I consider a very serious anomaly
in this Bill. I refer to the part of the
Bill which restricts the use of the 5s
licence and prevents farmers using it in
connection with domestic requirements.
I think it is the duty of the Government
Finance Bill-
Third Reading
30 SEPTEMBER 1941
to remove this anomaly from the Bill and
make it possible for farmers to use the
licence in connection with their domestic
requirements. The present position is
utterly impossible. The position here is
that farmers can use the licence in connection with their stock but not in connection with their domestic requirements.
I submit that the domestic requirements
of farmers should come under the term
agricultural purposes. I cannot see how
the Government or any other authority
can possibly define matters as they
stand in this Bill. Let me give an
illustration. If a farmer uses turf to
boil a pot of potatoes to feed his employees that would not be allowed under
the Act, but if the same pot was used for
feeding his stock that would be allowed.
I cannot see how the Government can
split up that pot and say which section
comes under the Act and which does not.
The position is utterly grotesque and
ridiculous, and we should not "pass the
buck" to somebody else to state what
agricultural purposes are. The Attorney-
General has not defined them, and in a
court of law it could be stated that in Parliament neither the Government nor the
Members knew what agricultural purposes were. The only object this Bill
will achieve will be to create more crops
of litigation. I hope, therefore, the
Minister will, even at this eleventh hour,
reconsider this matter and make this concession to the farmers by including
domestic requirements. As the matter
stands at present it is simply makebelieve, and I hope that in the first place
we will have a clear definition of what
agricultural purposes are, and, in the
second, that those agricultural purposes
will be said to include the farmer's own
domestic requirements. If these distinctions are allowed to continue they will
make the measure utterly worthless to the
agricultural community whom it is
intended to benefit.
Mr. HENDERSON: I
regret that
there are not more Members on the other
side of the House to support the hon.
Member. It is monstrous that during
the war the Minister has not rectified
this very serious matter of the farmers
not being allowed to utilise their tractors
for the drawing of turf from one part of
the farm to another. In view of the
national emergency there will be a great
hardship. Many of the farmers burn
coal now, and they may not be able to
secure a supply for the winter months.
Up to the present the Minister of Agriculture has started no campaign for the
cutting of turf. The farmers may be
called upon to save the serious situation
that may arise in the event of a ceal
shortage in Northern Ireland, and there
is going to be a coal shortage.
The Government are sleeping so far as
a coal shortage is concerned. They have
no stocks in. They know nothing about
it. They are only bluffing the people.
When the coal shortage comes the first
cry will be to the farmers to cut more
turf, but it will be impossible to cut and
dry it during the winter. This Bill is an
injustice to the farmers of Northern
Ireland, and in view of that fact I will
be reluctantly compelled to divide the
House on this important question. I
have always had a great admiration for
the Minister of Finance, but it is
ridiculous to think that a farmer with
potatoes in a field he has reclaimed can
bring them in with his tractor, but cannot
bring in turf from the other part. Only
a lot of idiots would allow that to be put
into a Bill. I will divide the House on
this question of the farmer being denied
the right to bring in his turf with a
tractor.
Mr. BEATTIE: I thought the right
hon. Gentleman was going to clarify this
measure on the Third Reading is it is
important and necessary that there should

Order for Second Reading read.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): This is a very
short Bill, introduced for a specific purpose. On the outbreak of war a
Chartered and Other Bodies (Temporary
Provisions) Act was passed, but
experience has shown that it did not cover
all the bodies needing assistance during a
time of war. In order that they may
transact their business with greater convenience this Bill empowers alterations to
be made in the constitution by the
making of an Order in Council on the
request of a particular body for a particular purpose.
The Second Clause of the Bill brings
within the scope of our legislation certain
bodies previously outside the measure.
In the original Act there were not included bodies which operated outside the
Six Counties. For example, a body
might be operated partly within the Six
Counties and partly without. At that
time it was thought that the matter was
sufficiently covered by the Imperial
Statute, but experience has shown that to
get an Order in Council under the
Imperial legislation takes a longer time.
than the introduction of an Act of Parliament. That being so, experience has
shown that we ought to have wider powers
with regard to this matter in order that
certain chartered and other bodies may
be facilitated without delay.

Increase of Juvenile Crime.
Lieutenant-Colonel MITCHELL: I beg
to move:
"That in the opinion of this House,
the progressive increase of juvenile
crime has become so serious as to
demand the immediate attention of the
Government."
I hold in my hand one of the most
exhaustive and informative Reports that
have been submitted to this House during
the time I have been a Member. It is
entitled, "The Protection and Welfare of
the Young, and the Treatment of Young
Offenders." It was handed in on 11th
October, 1937, after this problem of
juvenile crime had been most carefully
studied by a committee consisting of
Members of this House and prominent
social welfare workers in Northern Ireland for two years. Notwithstanding
that Report, juvenile crime in Northern
Ireland has apparently been steadily on
the increase. Our judges and magistrates
are constantly speaking on this subject
and denouncing the trend of juvenile
crime. I could not myself improve on
this Report, and I put down my Motion
because I want to try to accelerate some
action on the part of the Government. I
do not know that anything better than
this Report could be produced. It deals
with reformatories, juvenile courts and all
the other systems of treatment and
punishment. I have been educated with
the idea that prevention is better than
cure, and, therefore, I am most anxious
to get at the base of this trouble. I do
not know whether everyone else takes the
same view, but during my lifetime I
think one of the greatest influences for
good amongst the youth of the country
has been the Boy Scout movement, accompanied, as it soon was, by the Girl Guide
movement.
Education consists of a great deal more
than teaching a boy that twice five makes
ten, and teaching him how to read and
write. The whole object of education is
to make him a useful citizen, and to train
him to be a useful citizen of the State in
which he lives. I want to suggest that in
every school under the control of or
receiving money from the Government
there should be some organisation
-call it Boy Scouts or Girl Guides
or whatever you like, the name
does not matter-which to a certain
extent would be responsible for
making the boys educate themselves.
I know of nothing that influences the life
of a boy more than another boy, and
that is where the Boy Scout movement
has proved so valuable. They had their
own leaders and they controlled themselves. That, also, is where the
secondary school comes out so well, because they have their prefects, and the
prefects and the senior boys look after
the younger boys. When a boy goes to
a boarding school his character almost
from that date depends upon three things.
-firstly, his favourite pal; secondly, his
favourite master; and thirdly,
mother's letters.
his

a talk with a gentleman who for years
