Ministry through the Grants Committee,
which was formed under the Physical
Training and Recreation Act, is assisting
in every possible way existing organisa
tions, such as Boy Scouts, Girl Guides
and Boys' Brigade with equipment and
money for the hiring of halls and so
forth. I think that answers some of the
suggestions made by the Member for the
University. We have assisted the setting
up of clubs not only in Belfast, although
principally in Belfast, but in many towns
throughout the Province. We have
assisted generally the organised concerns,
apart from the separate clubs, in the
purchase of equipment and repairs. I am
not saying that a great deal more cannot
be done or that a great deal more should
not be done. I hope to see greater help
being given from all directions to these
movements in the near future.
It is not so easy as the Member for the
University suggested, to set up more scout
troops and find suitable leaders. One of
the difficulties from which all youth
organisations are suffering is the difficulty
of finding suitable leaders. It is far
better to have no leader at all than to get
the wrong type of leader. I think some
will be trained. I hope more will be
forthcoming and the more publicity that
is given to this matter the better it will
be in that direction. I know that there
is a great deal of difficulty in getting
room. Every organisation realises and
understands that difficulty at the moment.
It is almost impossible to get a room in
Belfast or in the country for the purpose
of having nursing classes or any of the
other activities connected with the war.
We made representations which would
ensure that some of the schools, at any
rate, in Belfast would be available for the
purpose, and certainly a great many are
being used in other directions for instance, for the Home Guard. This question of accommodation is a very difficult
one, indeed.
I do think it is not quite fair to suggest
that the Ministry of Education is not
doing everything it can to assist in this
great work of prevention of crime and of
helping the young. The question was raised
of the teaching of religion in the secondary schools as a possible way of preventing indiscipline. All I can say is that
this would be entirely a matter for the
governing bodies of the secondary schools.
The Ministry of Education could not give
any undertaking on this point.

If I may speak in my private capacity
for a moment, I really think that it is
absolutely essential that something should
be done. We have the assurance to-day
that something will be done to
implement that Report. As one of the
members of the Committee, I may say
it was an excellent Report. I am fully
aware of the fact that there is a considerable financial stringency and the war
is increasing this very greatly. Yet
there were certain matters in that Report
for the treatment of crime which I hope
will now be explored a little furtherthe personnel of the juvenile courts, the
question of more probation officers, and
what I may call after care treatment.
With regard to the prevention of
crime, with which I am dealing at the
moment, all I can say is that we want
in this matter the co-operation of every
citizen. It is their duty. Parents,
churches and public generally must cooperate with the Government.
If they
do we shall be able to help perhaps to
reduce the indiscipline of youth in this
part of the world to a considerable degree. I would be a very proud woman,
connected as I am with the Ministry, if
I were able to stand at this Table to point
to a very great lowering in the figures
which are repeatedly quoted by His
Majesty's judges in this Province. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. BROWN: I addressed a question
to-day to the Minister of Agriculture
asking him
whether he is aware that a number of
linen firms in Northern Ireland are
being held up from issuing export
trade price lists awaiting an announcement from the Government as to the
amount that is to be allowed farmers,
who have produced flax this season,
over and above the present fixed prices
for flax to cover the heavy increase in
the costs of production, and whether
his Ministry can now make an
announcement on this matter setting
out approximately what such allowances will be so that linen firms can
make provision accordingly and proceed
with the issue of their price lists.
The reply of the Parliamentary
Secretary was:—
The answer to the hon. Member's
question is in the negative.
That rather suggests I was merely
amusing myself by bringing forward this
question. I suggest this is a serious
matter. I intend to give the names of
firms who have drawn my attention to
this matter, and, having given these
names to the Ministry, I am going to
ask the Minister for a reply. My attention was called to this matter by Mr.
R. H. Stephens Richardson, D.L., of the
firm of Richardson, Sons & Owden, and
chairman of the Bessbrook Spinning Company, two well-known firms. We were told
that the Ministry got no complaint from
Mr. Richardson about this matter. It
is permissible for any member of the
public to go to any Member of Parliament and make any complaint he wishes.
He is as entitled to do it that way as
to write direct to the Ministry of
Agriculture.
We know that when the Ministry of
Agriculture were written to about various
matters in the past there was not much
response, but I have not time to go into
that this evening. I hope the case will
not be made that Mr. Richardson had not
as good a right to come to me as he had
to go to the Minister of Agriculture. We
are not in Hitlerite Germany yet when
we must go on our hands and knees to
any Minister. Any member of the public
can come to a Member of this House, and
I hope the case will not be made that
because a direct complaint was not made
by this gentleman to the Ministry I am
not entitled to raise the matter. I have
been denied information, and I now
demand information.
I did not bring this question forward
to amuse myself. The Ministry's officials
may have time to amuse themselves. I
have not; I have too much to do. I
hope the Parliamentary Secretary will
promise now to look into the whole
matter. I do not want anything I have
said to be taken as criticism of either the
Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary.
I have found them both personally willing
to listen to anything I put before them.
I am criticising the unfortunate system

matter.

Mr. MAGINESS: The second part was,
could the Ministry now make
announcement on the matter, and the
answer was equally in the negative. As
the hon. Member will appreciate, the
Ministry of Agriculture never has fixed
and never does fix the price of flax. That
is not a matter for the Ministry of Agriculture at all; it is a matter for the
Ministry of Supply, and, consequently,
until the Ministry of Supply fix the price
of flax or make any change in it, the
Ministry of Agriculture could make no
announcement which would be of information to anyone.
It is true that the
Ministry of Supply may take into consideration the costs of the flax harvest,
but the flax harvest has only just been
completed and the Ministry of Agricul
ture could not appreciate what increased
cost had taken place until they got
reports from the various parts of the
country as to what, if anything, that
increase had been.
It was only last week that the Farmers'
Union were in a position to place those
figures before the Ministry. I am not
suggesting for a moment that anyone
could have placed those figures before the
Ministry before last week because the
harvest was only completed then. It is a
fact that at the first available opportunity
the Farmers' Union did give us those
figures. I am surprised the hon. Member
was not aware of the position. Surely he
must be aware that before you can make
any representation you must know what
the actual increase, if any, has been.
Nobody can tell what that increase has
been until the crop has been harvested.
Now that the Farmers' Union has placed
that information before the Ministry, the
Ministry will be in a position to appreciate the entire situation, and will be
able to pass on that appreciation to the
Ministry of Supply. What the Ministry
of Supply may do is a matter for the
Ministry of Supply.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BANN FLOODING IN CO. DOWN.
1. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that from the month of October
until the spring the River Bann overflows
its banks in the townlands of Teirkelly
and Drumdrinagh, thereby flooding the
roadway for a distance of 120 yards, and
whether he is aware that this roadway
becomes completely impassable to pedestrians and vehicles alike, even the bank
which serves as a footpath as well as the
foot bridge being completely covered;
whether he is aware that this road is
used by commercial vehicles of all kinds,
and that for many people it is the nearest
way to Rathfriland, Ballyroney Station.
and to the telephone, and that it is used
by a great many children attending
school; whether this is not a great inconvenience to the residents of this
district and is very dangerous; whether
a boat has to be kept near this place and
has to be used on many occasions and lives
are known to have been saved by its use;
and whether he will bring pressure to bear
on the Down County Council to have this
road made safe for traffic all the year
round.
The MINISTER of HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am informed by
the Down County Council that the facts
as stated by the hon. Member are substantially correct.
With regard to the last part of the
question, in so far as the conditions
might be remedied by any action taken
by the Down County Council as drainage
authority, I am not prepared to bring
pressure upon the County Council to
undertake any major drainage scheme.
pending the reception of the report of
the Drainage Commission.
I am informed that an immediate
solution of this problem might be
effected by raising the level of the road
for a distance of about 120 yards. The
hon. Member is aware that this is a
matter which, of course, should be
initiated by the Banbridge Rural District
Council of which he is a member.
DRAINAGE COMMISSION'S
REPORT.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether the Interim Report presented by the Drainage Commission
appointed on the recommendation of the
Select Committee on Unemployment will
be made available to members of the
House, and, if so, when.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I am informed that the
Drainage Commission hopes to be in a
position to present a second Interim
Report in a fortnight or three weeks; if
it is thought desirable at that time both
reports may be published together, but
I must point out that as they are interim
reports only, their recommendations will
naturally be subject to those contained
in the Final Report of the Commission
to be presented when its deliberations
have been completed.
TILLAGE REQUIREMENTS
IN 1942.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state
when he will be in a position to outline
the tillage requirements for-1942.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTER OF
AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): I
have been asked to reply.
The Tillage Order for 1941-42 was
issued on October 1st. Briefly, it requires every farmer to have not less than
40 per cent. of his arable land ploughed
and under crops other than hay.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Oral Answers
SUBSIDY FOR POTATO GROWERS.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if
Northern Ireland potato growers will
receive the £10 per acre subsidy promised
to potato growers in Great Britain, and,
if so, whether the subsidy will be paid
under exactly the same conditions.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. The subsidy of £10 per acre will
be paid to potato growers in Northern
Ireland under the same general conditions
as will apply in Great Britain. Certain
minor modifications may be necessary to
meet local conditions.
An announcement regarding the acreage payment scheme appears in to-day's
Press.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of that
reply may I ask whether it is a fact that
the £10 subsidy will be paid to potato
growers even if they use the potatoes for
stock-feeding purposes?
Mr. MAGINESS: Yes. The £10
subsidy is paid irrespective of what the
potatoes are used for. Of course the hon.
Member will remember that in order to
feed the potatoes to stock a licence from
the Ministry is necessary.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Parliamentary
Secretary tell the House why there was
such delay in making this announcement
in Northern Ireland as compared with
Great Britain, where it was made some
considerable time ago?
RESTRICTIONS ON WHEAT
GROWERS.
5. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if it
is a fact that wheat growers in Northern
Ireland are not to be allowed to use their
own wheat for feeding purposes, and if
this is so, whether they will receive
coupons enabling them to purchase a
certain quantity of cereals for each cwt.
of wheat sold, and if not, whether this
will put wheat growers in Northern
Ireland at a disadvantage as compared
with wheat growers in Great Britain.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. Under the Home-Grown Wheat
(Control and Prices) Order, 1941, wheat
fit for milling may only be sold for the
manufacture of flour or meal for human
consumption, or for seed.
Wheat growers will receive coupons
enabling them to purchase cereal feeding
stuffs on the same basis as will apply in
Great Britain.
USE OF NON-MILLABLE WHEAT.
6. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether farmers who have
grown wheat which has been classed as
non-millable will be allowed to use same
for the feeding of their own livestock,
and whether wheat which has been classed
as non-millable and grown by farmers who
do not require same for feeding purposes
will be made available to other farmers
for feeding purposes.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. The answer to the first part of
the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative. Growers of wheat which has
been certified to be of non-millable
quality may sell it to approved buyers.
who in turn may dispose of it for feeding
purposes. Direct farmer to farmer sales
are not permitted by the Order, which
has been made by the Minister of Food,
and which applies throughout the United
Kingdom.
PRICE OF FLAX.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether his Ministry has
made representations to the Ministry of
Supply to secure an increase in the price
of flax to meet the heavy increase in the
costs of production in the current season;
and if so, whether he can state the result
of these representations.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. I have nothing to add at this
stage to the reply I have already given
to the hon. Member's previous question
and the statement I made when he raised
the matter on the Adjournment of the
House on Tuesday last.
Mr. BROWN: I beg to give notice that
I will raise this matter on the Adjournment.
POTATO PRICES.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has taken any
Amendment of Standing Orders 1702
Oral Answers
7 OCTOBER 1941
steps to have Northern Ireland potato
prices increased to the same basis as exists
for potatoes produced in Great Britain;
and if so, whether he can state the result
of such representations.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply. The question put by the hon.
Member discloses a lack of knowledge of
the existing situation, and I would refer
him to my reply to a somewhat similar
question by the hon, and gallant Member
for East Down on 16th September, in
which I pointed out that it is essential to
fix Northern Ireland growers' prices for
potatoes at such rates as will enable them
to be marketed in Great Britain in competition with potatoes produced in that
area. There are, in fact, no general
prices which apply to England, Scotland
and Wales, as, for the purpose of price
fixing, Great Britain is divided into eight
areas in respect of which there is a wide
variation in price according to area and
distance from the normal markets. In
the case of Northern Ireland the difference
between the pre-war and present freights
is borne by the Ministry of Food.
In view of these facts, the Ministry of
Agriculture is not prepared to make representations on the lines suggested by the
hon. Member.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask is it a fact
that prices for potatoes in quite a
number of cases are considerably lower
than those ruling in Great Britain, and
will he undertake to have that grievance
of Northern Ireland farmers remedied?
Mr. MAGINESS: No, sir. To make
it clear to the hon. Gentleman, if it is a
question of potatoes grown within three
miles from Birmingham it costs very
little to bring them to the Birmingham
market. But potatoes grown in Northern Ireland cost a considerable amount
to bring them to that market. It is for
that difference of freight only that there
is a difference in price between potatoes
grown in Northern Ireland and those
grown in other places in Great Britain.
Mr. BROWN: Will the hon. Gentleman then tell us why beef prices are the
same in Birmingham as in Northern
Ireland? Does that not display as great
a lack of knowledge on his part as on my
part?

Member for South Tyrone.

times of sitting should be altered I felt
that the Government would be quite
willing to meet the views of hon. Members. I also added that I would ask the

Members in connection with the matter.
That I understand has been done. Hon.
Members generally have expressed their
desire that a change should be made as
set out in the Notice of Motion. I may
point out further that this Motion is
necessary in order that Standing Orders
may be changed so as to arrange for the
hours set out in the Motion itself. I
beg to move: —
"That in paragraph (i) of Standing
Order No. 1, Sittings of the House,
for the words "three o'clock" there
shall be substituted the words "two
o'clock" and that, accordingly, in any
other provision of the Standing Orders.
relative to Public Business, reference

hour earlier than that particular time,
provided that in paragraph (3) of
Standing Order No. 8, the reference to
half-past three o'clock shall be construed as a reference to a quarter
before three o'clock."

National Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The National Health Insurance,
Contributory Pensions and Workmen's
Compensation Act, 1941, which was passed
7 OCTOBER 1941
Health and Pensions Bill

Second Reading
tions so as to meet war conditions as they
arise. It is expressly provided that this
power will not enable any alteration to
be made in the rates of benefits or contributions. It will, however, enable prorecently at Westminster, has been circulated along with the Bill for the information of Members. Hon. Members will
observe that Section 11 of the Act provides for the extension of its provisions to
Northern Ireland on the passing of the
necessary Act by this Parliament. This
is the usual procedure in the case of
measures affecting the national health and
pensions schemes since health insurance
is established on a United Kingdom basis.
and the pensions scheme is closely interlocked with it.
SO
A Committee has been appointed in
Great Britain under the chairmanship of
Sir William Beveridge to examine the
national insurance schemes in detail,
as to enable the whole position to be
reviewed after the war. In the meantime amendments in the provisions of the
schemes are being restricted to the aspects
which are most pressing.
I am aware that the proposals are
infinitely short of the persistent demands.
made by those who feel that in times of
sickness a greater provision should be
made from the funds of the insurance
societies to meet the abnormal circumstances which arise during that period. I
trust that a more comprehensive scheme
may be introduced after the war so that
health insurance may be placed in a position comparable with unemployment insurance. This Bili is not a step forward,
but an improvement on the position that
exists at present.
The proposals in the Bill provide, in
the first place, for an increase of 3s a week
in the rates of sickness and disablement
benefit. To meet the cost of this, it is
necessary to increase the contribution by
2d a
week-1d being payable by the
employer and 1d by the worker and to
make certain other financial adjustments
in the scheme which, when account is
taken of the increased State grant, will
enable the cost to be met.
In the second place the scheme is
widened to admit non-manual workers
whose salary does not exceed £420 a year,
thus bringing the health and pensions
schemes into line with the unemployment
insurance scheme. Hon. Members will be
aware that manual workers are insured no
matter what their earnings may be.
In the third place it is proposed to take
power to amend the scheme by Regulavision to be made for the case of the
ships' crews who have been captured by
the enemy and who would go out of insurance if the present law requiring them
to show that they were available for work
remained in force, and there might be
many similar provisions necessary as time
proceeds.
There are a number of other points, of
which the most important is probably
that which provides for the setting aside.
of an additional ls 6d a year to meet the
increased cost of medical benefit.
It is proposed that the new provisions
will come into operation on the 5th
January next, with the exception of those
enabling the scheme to be modified by
Regulations. These Regulations may be
made as soon as the Bill becomes law, and
as they will be dealing with a number of
hard cases, I should like to be in a position to have them made as soon as
possible, and I ask the House to accept
this Bill, not as a final contribution, but
as an indication that at this difficult
period in the history of our country we
are anxious to enlarge and improve the
health and pension position of those
within the scheme and those who, by this
Bill, will be enabled to become insured
contributors. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

can get. This question was brought up

this particular occasion because it is a
glaring injustice. The facts are not in
dispute, though I know they come as a
surprise to many Members of the House.
To emphasise it, I will re-state the point
without repeating myself if I can. A
person, before he knows very much about
the various companies, joins one that does
not allow dental treatment. Then, as
most people do, he begins to be troubled
with his teeth. Dental treatment is now
looked upon as something very important
by the medical profession. A person may
not be in receipt of very much wages or
salary, and when he applies to the Prudential, that company will say they
cannot take him over until the company
he is with releases him. The result is
that he is deprived of treatment, and in
some cases such persons may have to pay
away one-third of their wages on dental
treatment. The Government have power .
to correct that, and they can do so by
compelling all companies either to give
dental treatment or to surrender an insured person if that person wants to be
surrendered.
There is another thing. I am not sure
whether it is in order or not to raise it
on this Bill, but if it is not in order Mr.
Speaker will rule me out. I do not know
that I should have given him notice, but
I think he would be on the alert anyway.
There are a great many insured people,
particularly women, at the present time,
and according to the gigantic advertisements in the Press on the part of the
Ministry of Labour they want those
people to go across the water for training
they should get at home. By sending
them across the water you risk their
health. I do not object to their going
across the water if they want to go, but
to send them across has a big bearing on
their health and, therefore, on their insurance. That training should be provided by the Government in Northern
Ireland. I am all out for everyone, old
and young, who is able to do anything
being put to something to help the war
effort.
Mr. GORDON: Hear, hear.
Mr. NIXON: I was always that. This
has a bearing on their health, it has a
bearing on their insurance, and it has a
bearing on our very existence, which is
the most important thing, strictly speaking, to everyone of us here. The
Government should have foreseen this
and have had training centres in Northern Ireland. It is well known that a
great many people who went across the
water to be trained are back again, and
that some of them are out of industry
altogether. The Government had over
two years to look into that and they did
nothing but insert these gigantic
advertisements. Why they did nothing
I cannot tell. It is part of the same old
complaint.
I have a complaint against the Government, and it is a most serious one. I want
them to take some specific action in regard
to insurance. There is no use sitting
there and telling me what they do across
the water, because you only do what
they do across the water when it suits
you. Everything you tell us they do
across the water is not just something
that I could accept, seeing I know a little
about what they do there myself. There
are various items I could not accept, but
I hope to raise them here some time. I
want you to do something about this
glaring injustice. No matter whether
you have to go across the water or not
it is time there was something done. It
is also time there were some training
centres in Northern Ireland.
Mr. BEATTIE: I take the opportunity once again of trying to convert
the Government to the opinions I have
expressed for the last eighteen years in
this House. Since the inception of the
Unemployment and National Health
Insurance Acts I have been an opponent
of the way in which the administration of
national health insurance has been carried
out.
1 can now say why a separation
took place when these two very important measures were introduced into
the British House of Commons. At that
time the big combines had a powerful
1709 Health and Pensions Bill—

7 OCTOBER 1941
Second Reading
influence in that House. They were in
a position to claim that they were in
touch with
with the working-class people
throughout the country, and also with
the needs and requirements of that class
of the community.
The combination of those vested
interests was able to assure Mr. Lloyd
George that they were at that time the
best medium through which that part of
the social service known as national
health insurance could be administered.
Thus a division was made in the two
social services. We are continuing that
division. Now, there was only one thing
that could be a guide to any person in
regulating his attitude to that division,
and that was time. Time has been my
guide, and I know to-day that under the
Unemployment Insurance Acts men and
women, boys and girls, get equal rights
independent of whether they are in poor,
medium, or good health. In national
health insurance no such regulating
factor operates. If you get into an
approved society with a high standard of
health you are going to be in a fortunate
position, because the high standard of
health shown in that society allows them
to accumulate funds to such an extent
that they are able to provide additional
benefits under the Act. A number of
these high standard societies have a
higher rate of benefit and have given
additional benefits.
I do not grumble because they have
progressed in that direction. The evil I
see existing, and this is my grumble, is
that not all approved societies can boast
of having a high standard of health.
Unfortunately, the class of worker for
whom we are trying to provide this particular law is the class of person whose
health has never been of a very high
standard, owing to the class of industry
which he or she has been compelled to
follow. That being so, they formed
themselves into an organisation known as
the Textile Operatives' Approved Section.
They found that the health demands of
their members were higher than, say, the
demands of those in the Prudential, and
the result was that the demands were of
such a nature that benefits could not be
increased or additional benefits conceded.
Therefore, the working class approved
societies were compelled to pay the
minimum sickness benefits. It was not
because they were not willing to pay the
maximum, they were compelled to pay
the minimum to keep their ratio per
member in accordance with the law.
But that was not the most severe blow
to them. In other approved societies
there was dental and optical treatment
and additional benefits, while their
members were called upon to pay equal
contributions but could not be provided
with those extra benefits. That is only
an example, and it is not an isolated
example. That operates where good lives.
are separated from bad lives. When I
found that operating, I said that if I
lived long enough and was in a position
to try to remedy the wrong done in 1912,
I would try to right that wrong. In
unemployment insurance the contributors.
pay the same rates and get the same
results. All people pay the same rates
in connection with national health
insurance, but all do not receive the same
benefits or the same additional benefits.
The people who get the least are those
who require the most. The right hon.
Gentleman and his Parliamentary Secretary know full well that this is not a new
point I am raising. I do not wish them
to think I am criticising them. I am
not; I am expressing opinions which I
have always expressed, and will continue
to express until national health insurance is re-organised on the same lines
as unemployment insurance.
By this Bill, people earning up to £420
per year are brought in. The type of life
represented by a person receiving £420
per annum is a good one, but the poorer
organisation will not get the benefit of
it. The organisations which pay higher
rates of benefit will get that life. The
poorer organisation will only get the lives
of those engaged in industry, lives which
take a turn for the worse at a certain
period. I am sorry that the industrial
workers and the black-coated workers now
to be embodied in this scheme will not be
combined on the policy "all for each and
each for all." If that were done, each
and every one would receive the same rate
of benefit. I am sorry this Bill does not
allow for that. However, I take it from
what the right hon. Gentleman has stated
that he is hopeful that when the war is
over some reorganisation will take place.
From the experience I have gained by
coming into contact with different people
I am satisfied that there will be a change.
The hon. Member for Woodvale stated a
Health and Pensions Bill-

few days ago that when the war is over

Mr. NIXON: So we will.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am satisfied from

I wish to put one or two points to the
right hon. Gentleman. Why did he not
give this concession when he had the
opportunity? Spinsters get pensions at
60, but married women have to wait
another five years.
Mr. GORDON: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: Oh, yes, spinsters are
allowed to draw the pension at 60, but
the wife of an insured contributor must
wait until her husband qualifies for his
pension.
Mr. GORDON: That is right.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is a sorry spectacle. I think we all approve of marriage;
at least we ought to. Marriage is a
sacred thing. Why, then, do we penalise
a woman who marries? If she remained
single she would draw her pension at 60
years of age. If the right hon. Gentleman
assures me that this matter will be
remedied, then from that angle of national
health insurance I have nothing further
to say. However, I am rather doubtful
about the right hon. Gentleman. I have
been looking to the Government to remedy
this matter since the introduction of the
scheme. The Prime Minister will
remember that in my maiden speech I
advocated reducing the age at which
people could receive their pension to 60.
I think the Deputy Speaker supported me,
but he was not inclined to go into the
Lobby with me. I feel the time is ripe
when we should take another step
forward. If you cannot bring men in at
60, at any rate bring in their wives so
that all women may be placed on an
equal footing. It would not take very
much money to do so.
When you take the number of married
women between the age of 60 and 65 years
the cost to the State would be very little
compared to the spending power of the
nation to-day. If that were done it would
enhance the income of the home by 10s
per week. If you gave 10s per week to
the wife at 60 it would be of double value
to the home; it would be as good as £1.
That is the time when the husband is
declining some people may not think so
-and his earning power is reduced. I
am now referring to a man engaged in
industry; one who has to do heavy manual
labour. I claim that our fund is capable
of meeting the financial obligations of
such a scheme. If the right hon. Gentleman assures me that he will give pensions
to all women at the age of 60 he will be
doing a great service to the women of this
country and, at the same time, will be
giving a lead to governments in other
parts of the world.
The Minister certainly set out an increase of 3s. An increase of 3s to a
labouring man would seem a fortune, but
an increase of that amount to right hon.
Gentlemen sitting on the Front Bench
would be absolutely useless. They would
not know they had received an increase
at all. It would be all right from the
point of view of people drawing 18s to
£1, because it would mean they would get
23s, plus the additions. To women drawing a low rate of sickness benefit 3s is of
no use at all. It is when persons are ill
that they require most attention. Many
of these people have large families-they
are the class in the community who have
the largest families-and they are in a
sorry plight when sickness comes. How
are we going to remedy the position in
regard to national health insurance from
the sickness point of view? Is the right
hon. Gentleman prepared to tell me that
he will consider the advisability of giving
supplementary allowances to each member
of the family dependent upon the breadwinner who is laid aside through illness!
If he does so I shall certainly be grateful
to him.
When the husband is ill the wife and
family do not get any allowance. Where
a husband is unemployed the wife and
children receive dependents benefit.
Which position would the right hon.

Gentleman say was the worst from the

This was a very important social

Liberal Party who introduced old-age
pensions.

There is nothing like it in any part of the

to homes where the breadwinner is sick

I know he would like to see

Northern Ireland.
You have only a short time to do it in
because whether the war is over or not

are going to do it for you. I would like

of State control and bring happiness and

Shortage of Labour for Agriculture.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I beg to
move:
"That in the opinion of this House
the Government should take immediate
steps to ensure a fair and reasonable.
share of labour for agriculture in
general, and particularly in connection
with the forthcoming tillage operations."
This Motion has been on the Order
Paper for a considerable time, and it has
got into the minds of some Members that
it has gone out of date. I do not agree
with that idea. I have been through the
country within the last few days and I
think there is a very considerable amount
of this year's harvest to be gathered in.
In some districts I should say there is
fully a half, and to a very large extent
we owe it to the kindness of Providence,
more than to any other cause, that so
much of the present harvest has been
gathered. We have been given one of the
best harvests that perhaps any of us can
remember.
The Motion I have proposed deals in a
more general way with the whole farming
situation than merely by reference to the
present harvest. In regard to the present
year's work on the farm, harvest and
other operations, I take off my hat to the
loyalty of the Ulster farmers. I know
that comparisons are odious, but from my
own observation and knowledge I know of
no other class in the community that has
risen to the occasion of this national emergency better than the farmers. We can
see as one goes about the countryside the
smaller working farmers, some of them
one man; some with only a boy, working
every night until it is dark and until they
can see no longer. There is no question
of overtime with them. I could give you
any number of illustrations where farmers
with not more than 100 acres have farmed
that amount in the last season with one
I pay that tribute to these men.
No doubt there are some black sheep
amongst them as you find them in every
class. Speaking of them as a whole I
think the nation owes them a very great
debt for the effort they have put forth
this year.
man.

attracted there by the higher wages payable for those kinds of work. They are,
I readily admit, very important kinds of
work, but I submit no more important
than the work on the farms at the present time. Why the man who is really
a farm worker, once he has been attracted
from the farm to one of these other kinds
of national work, should be paid on a
different basis or should work under
different conditions from what held when
he was working on the farm, is something
I am yet unable to understand.
My grievance is not so much with the
rate of wages paid for these other kinds
of national work as with the fact that
the men so engaged and employed are not
giving to the nation a proper return in
work for the wages that are being paid
to them. I know of men who left farms
not far from where I live, and who went
and joined other national work. They
have told me themselves that time and
again they were ashamed when it came
to the week's end and they received their
pay and looked at the work they had done
for the pay they received. I am quite
satisfied in my own mind that in a great

on a. very

To a
certain extent that has arisen from adventitious and fortuitous circumstances over
which the Ministry of Agriculture had no

made demands upon labour, and, in

Agriculture stood idly by and did

The real root of the trouble is that
referred to, partly, I think, by accident,
by the hon. Member for Pottinger, that
is, that the wages paid in agriculture at
the present time cannot be compared with
the wages paid in other industries. That
is not the fault of the farmers. It is the
fault of circumstances over which
this Ministry has no control, but so
long as you have on one side a
farming industry being only able
to pay a certain wage to its workers, and
on the other side industries able to pay
a much bigger wage you will have a continual and never-ending drift from agriculture to those other industries unless
some steps are taken to stop that drift.
The Ministry have at the present time
taken the initial step, the Restriction of
Engagments Order passed.
So much for the present. As regards
the future, we cannot speak with any
certainty. We do not know whether
there will be military labour for next
year's harvest or not. We cannot make
plans based on the supposition that
military labour will be available next
year. Our plans must be based on the
assumption that military labour may not
be available. We must base our plans
not on the most optimistic outlook but
on the most pessimistic outlook, and,
therefore, although we hope that there
will be military labour available, our
plans must be based on the assumption
that for the work of the harvest next year
we may not have the assistance of our
military friends.

from industrial labour in that it is not

There are other seasons of the year when

which may be introduced into Scotland

Mr. MAGINESS: The order has not

doubtless be considered with the greatest
possible interest by us all. That order
does not make employment in agriculture
continuous. We have the two interests
involved, and, believe me, I am
am not
without sympathy for both those interests.
We have the farm worker and we have
the farmer. The farm worker who
remains on the land sees other people
doing perhaps less skilful or less tiring
work and getting wages much more than
he is getting. One has the greatest sympathy for a man in his position when
he is asked to remain on the land in the
service of agriculture, and the service of
agriculture at the present time is the
service of the State.
On the other hand, I do not for one
moment suggest, and I do not think
anybody would suggest, that the farmer
wants to pay his labourers a small wage.
He does not, but he has certain returns
from his farm produce, and out of those
returns must come the wages of his
workers. He says, "I am anxious to
pay you all I can, but out of the profit
I get I cannot pay you more than I am
doing at the moment." So you have
the two sides, not perhaps adverse to
each other, not perhaps conflicting, but
interests pulling in slightly different
directions, and with each of those
interests the Ministry have the greatest
possible sympathy.
This difficulty of relative wages is not
confined to Northern Ireland. From what
some hon. Members have said one would
have thought that it was a peculiar
problem of our own. It is not. One has only
to read the farming journals published in
England and Scotland, to study recent
debates in the Imperial House of
Commons, and to read the reports of
various Farmers' Union branches in
Great Britain to realise that the problem
is at present even more difficult in Great
Britain than it is in Northern Ireland.
The root of the evil lies deep. The
problem lies at the base of the economic
structure of the farming industry, but
all that we can do at the present time is
to alleviate as far as possible the
difficulties which have been encountered.
The Ministry have for the past number
of weeks been considering this very
problem. The plans which are in process.
of being made are not yet complete, and
hon. Members will appreciate the fact
that until they are complete it is not
reasonable to expect me to give any
synopsis of what they contain. However,
I believe that when the plans are
complete they will be sufficient to deal
with the situation which exists at present and which will exist next year.
I should like to express my appreciation of the manner in which this Motion
was proposed. It was proposed in that
reasonable manner one expects from the

appreciate the points raised by the hon.
Member. Realising that these facts exist
the Ministry are striving, as far as they

of the Ministry will be sufficient to meet
whatever happens in the future.

The farming community have been

Flax and potato prices must be revised,

Mr. HENDERSON: I gave the Prime
Minister notice that I would raise on the
Motion for the Adjournment the very
important question of having another
Secret Session. There are important
matters that Members on this side of the
House cannot divulge openly concerning
the well-being of the entire population of
Northern Ireland. I feel that many injustices are being perpetrated at the present time, and that there are many things
affecting the public that ought to be taken
into account. That can only be done if
the House sits in secret. The Prime
Minister has, very rightly, arranged that
this House should sit from two o'clock
until six o'clock on only one day of the
week. There cannot be any excuse of
overwork for not granting a Secret
Session.
I think a Secret Session would perform very useful service at the present
time. There are many things I should
like to raise, but I do not want to raise
them in public. The fact of the matter
is that these questions are of such a
serious nature that it would not be in the
interests of the country for Members to
raise them in the open House at the present time; but, if the Prime Minister
refuses to give a Secret Session, I shall
have no alternative but to raise them in
the House, and then the responsibility
will rest upon the Prime Minister's
shoulders. I appeal to
the Prime
Minister to give the Members of the
House an opportunity to speak freely
and openly, and to let us have another
Secret Session. The last one did good.
A big lot may not have come out of it,
but at least it did some good. Members
were able to air grievances and to raise
matters of great public importance.
I should like to speak freely on civil
defence, and I cannot do so unless the
House is sitting in secret. I want to be
quite frank. I have a great regard for
the Minister of Public Security, who is
an hon. and learned Member of this
House; but there is a good lot to be done
that has not been done up to the present
time, and I think the only way we can
get at these questions properly is to have
a Secret Session. A Secret Session will
enable me to do what I think is right in
the interests of the people of Northern
Ireland. I am surprised at some of the
things that are taking place. If the
Prime Minister, acting in conjunction
with the Minister of Public Security, will
let me know that he agrees to have a
Secret Session I will sit down, but I want
to know definitely whether or not he is
willing to agree to a Secret Session. If
the Prime Minister does not agree, he
will compel me as a Member of this House
to raise openly matters that, in my
opinion, might be more or less useful to
the enemy.
The hon. Member for South Derry need
not laugh. Her friends, who own the
newspapers in Northern Ireland, have
been more useful to the enemy than Lord
Haw-Haw by the photographs and letterpress they publish. Some of the hon.
Lady's friends have made statements that
had been better left unsaid. If the Prime
Minister will not grant a Secret Session I
will have no alternative but to speak
openly in order to get justice for the
people I represent. Is there anything in
that statement to cause merriment on the
part of the hon. Lady? The hon. Member
knows that some things have been published about Derry that would not do
Derry any good. I do not know what the
Minister of Public Security is doing in
allowing to be printed some of the things
that I have read. Then he talks about
things that are being done in the country
by other people. I ask the Prime Minister
to let us have an opportunity of debating
in secret some of the vital matters concerning the well-being of the entire
population and the cause of bringing
about the destruction of Hitlerism.

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
pay and allowances of the Special Constabulary mobilised for full-time duty,
including those at the Harbour property,

duty.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): Information as to the pay, supplementary
allowance and war duty allowance of

and (c) the Ulster Special Constabulary

Ulster Constabulary which has been

receives the same allowances as would be
payable to a member of the Royal Ulster

the mobilised Special Constable is provided for under National Health Insurance arrangements.

AREA OFFICER IN ARMAGH.
8. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
many ex-servicemen were interviewed for
the post of area officer in Armagh in connection with evacuation; whether the
person appointed had a long record of
work in connection with evacuation, or
was it on account of his retirement from
the Royal Ulster Constabulary; how many
ex-servicemen are actually engaged on
evacuation work in Armagh area, if any,
and the number employed as permanent
and as temporary.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I regret that it is
impossible to give a direct reply to the
first part of the hon. Member's question;
applications were invited, by advertisement, for the Province as a whole, and a
very large number of applications were
received. These were examined and then
about 70 persons were interviewed, after
which the persons whom it was decided to
apppoint were allocated to the different
districts.
One of the persons appointed as billeting officer for the Armagh area was an
ex-member of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and had been employed as billeting
officer previously in the Armagh Union
by the clerk of the local authority while
the service was being administered by
these officers, and it was having regard to
his special experience and suitability that
he was appointed. I
may say that a
R.U.C. pensioner loses his pension for the
time being while employed at other work.
Six officers have been appointed by my
Department to act in the Armagh area,
which includes Armagh, Banbridge and
Dungannon Unions, and of these six
officers three are women. The three men
are not ex-servicemen. I might add that
all these posts are terminable either on a
month's or a week's notice, and I can assure
the hon. Member that other things being
equal, preference has been given to exservicemen.

VOLUNTARY AGRICULTURAL
COMMITTEE OF M.P.'s.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if it was
with the approval of the Government
that the members of the voluntary Agricultural Committee, consisting of Members of Parliament representing provincial
constituencies, was not consulted at any
time by the Ministry of Agriculture regarding the serious situation that arose
in connection with the shortage of labour
for agriculture; whether he is aware that
since November, 1940, when this Committee was set up and was consulted
about feeding stuffs rationing it has only
been consulted once by the Ministry of
Agriculture and only on one subject, the
Flax Water Bill; and whether, in view
of the way the Committee is being treated
by the Ministry, the Government will
take steps to ensure regular consultations
between the Ministry and the Committee
in future.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
The extent to which the Minister of
Agriculture consults private Members or
their Committees regarding the policy of
his Department is a matter which must
necessarily remain entirely within the
Minister's discretion. I would remind
the hon. Member that the custom at
Westminster is that Committees of
private Members are not consulted
directly by Ministers, but if any such
Committee desires information on any
particular subject the responsible Minister
or his Parliamentary Secretary is invited
to meet them. In this House, I am glad
to say, individual Members of the Agricultural Committee maintain close touch
with the Ministry of Agriculture.
Whether they do so as individuals or as
a Committee is, of course, a matter for
themselves.

The operation of the income basis

It also involves

WOMEN WORKERS FOR GREAT
BRITAIN.
16. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether it is a fact that he is
compelling young girls of 21 years of age
and women up to the age of 55 to take
work in Great Britain; whether a refusal
of this work means a disallowance of
benefit; whether it is a fact that the work
offered is not suitable when compared with
the normal occupation of these women
workers; and whether he will issue instructions that work in England should be
accepted on a voluntary basis.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In answer to the hon. Member
I may say that war work in Great Britain
is at present being offered to unmarried
women between the ages of 21 and 45 with
the possibility of benefit being disallowed
if the work is refused.
Whether it is actually disallowed or not
depends largely upon the suitability of
the work for the person to whom it is
offered; and, in considering this point, the
officers of my Ministry have regard to all
the circumstances of the particular case
that are within their knowledge. If the
person contends that the work is not suitable there is always a right of appeal to
the court of referees.
I should, however, add that
Northern Ireland umpire has held on a
number of occasions that work is not unsuitable for people here merely because it
is in Great Britain, and the Imperial
umpire has similarly held that work is not
unsuitable for people in Great Britain
merely because it is in Northern Ireland.
In view of the extremely urgent demand
that now exists for women for war work
in Great Britain, I am not prepared to
issue directions that such work should be
offered on a purely voluntary basis.

19. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has received.
any representation from the Ulster
Farmers' Union regarding the claim of

flax to cover the substantial increase in

of the voluntary Agricultural Committee of Members of Parliament representing the various rural districts in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply.
The answer to the first two parts of
the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative. I informed the House on
30th September that such representations
had been received. The decision of the
Ministry of Supply with regard to prices
for 1941 has already been announced in
the Imperial Parliament. With regard
to the last part of the hon. Member's
question, prices for agricultural produce
are a matter for the Imperial Government, and since the outbreak of war
machinery has been in operation whereby
the views and representations of the
Farmers' Unions in England, Scotland
and Northern Ireland are taken into consideration by the Departments concerned
before decisions are arrived at.
Such matters are not discussed by
Imperial Departments with Members of
Parliament before a public announcement
is made, and it must be obvious to the
hon. Member that the Minister is not in
a position to do as he suggests.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Parliamentary
Secretary tell us why his Ministry
should accept the ridiculously small
increase of ls per stone? Will he now
reconsider the matter and press for a
fairer and more reasonable increase?

COLLECTION OF EGGS FROM
PRODUCER.
22. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware that in some districts eggs are only
collected from the producers fortnightly;
whether this is followed by additional
delay at the grading station, and, as a
result, eggs are being placed on the market
for retail sale, which are three or four
weeks old, and whether he will take steps
to ensure that this condition of affairs is
remedied without delay.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to
reply. It is not correct to state that in
some districts eggs are only collected fortnightly, nor am I aware of any undue
delay in the collection of eggs from producers. There has been no general curtailment of collection services, although
individual collectors may have found it
necessary to rearrange their rounds in
order to economise in the use of petrol.
If any specific case of delay in collection
is brought to my notice I shall be glad to
have it investigated.
There has been no additional delay of
any kind in the handling of eggs by packing stations. The packing station is still
under an obligation to dispose of eggs
within 48 hours of testing, and I am
quite confident that in Northern Ireland
there has been no falling off in quality
since the introduction of control.
It is not correct to say that eggs three
or four weeks old are placed on the market
for retail. As I have already explained
to the hon. Member, eggs must leave our
packing station for shipment to Great
Britain or for our retail market within
48 hours of testing.

the Parliamentary Secretary that in my
own district, for which I can speak-

24. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether representations have been made to him in

the stocktakers, Messrs. John Wilson &

against the stocktakers appear to have

whether he is prepared, in such circumstances, to have the matter reviewed with

Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact
that representations were made in a letter
from Messrs. John Wilson & Son
addressed to myself. With regard to the
latter part of the question, the Inspectors'
findings in this matter, with which the
Ministry had no hesitation in concurring,
were based on the sworn testimony of
witnesses given at the inquiry, at
which Messrs. Wilson were represented by counsel. I cannot, therefore,
for one moment accept the

Mr. GORDON: It has been thought

1781 Workmen's Compensation Bill
Health and Pensions [Money] 1782
14 OCTOBER 1941
compensation scheme should be the same
as it is already for unemployment insurance and as is proposed in the Bill
now before the House for national
health insurance and contributory pensions. This Bill, therefore, proposes to
raise the existing remuneration limit for

similar change has been made in Great

Kingdom.
Α
The Bill proposes a further amendment, one of minor practical importance
so far as Northern Ireland is concerned.
This deals with the application of the
Workmen's Compensation Acts to a person, such as a taxi driver, who is not an
employee in the full sense but who plies.
for hire with a vehicle, the use of which
is obtained under a contract of bailment
from some other person or firm owning
the vehicle. The law says that in such
circumstances the owner is to be regarded
as the employer and the taxi driver as a
worker entitled to compensation in the
event of an accident.
But on account of the wording of the
existing section the driver's title to compensation depends on ownership of the
vehicle by the person or firm concerned.
If the firm happened to be buying the
taxi under the hire-purchase system and
had not yet actually become the legal
owner the driver would not be entitled
to compensation. The amendment.
solely for the purpose of remedying this
technical difficulty, and it follows an
amendment already carried out in Great
Britain by a separate Act passed there
in 1938. I beg to move.

Major SINCLAIR: The financial
implications of the Bill which are covered
by this Money Resolution relate to both
the health and pensions insurance schemes.
Briefly, they are as follows:-
The rates of sickness and disablement
benefit are to be increased by 3s per week
and the rates of contributions by 2d per
week, of which 1d will be payable by the
employed person and 1d by the employer.
Hon. Members are aware that in addition to the contributions of employers and
employees the National Health Insurance.
Fund, from which benefits are paid,
1783 Health and Pensions [Money]-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Major Sinclair]
receives from the State a yearly grant
based on fixed proportions of the yield of
those contributions. It is estimated that,
in respect of persons who are already insured for national health insurance purposes, the State will in a full year be
required to increase its grant to the fund
by £30,000 because of the changes I have
mentioned. The bringing into compulsory
health and pensions insurance of nonmanual workers, whose yearly incomes exceed £250, the existing remuneration
limit, but do not exceed £420, will, it is
estimated, add a further £1,000 a year to
this State grant.
The extension of the insurance field will
also necessitate additional provision for
the payment of pensions, though no substantial expenditure in this respect will
arise for some time. It is estimated that
the Exchequer liability to the Pensions
Account (out of which contributory pensions are paid to persons before they reach
the age of 70) has been increased by the
equivalent of a capital sum of approximately £160,000 though it is not proposed
for the present to increase the annual
Exchequer grant to that account.
The cost of all over-70 pensions is
borne by the State. Persons who before
reaching 70 have been in receipt of contributory pensions become entitled, on
attaining that age, to pensions under the
Old Age Pensions Act without being
required to fulfil the means, residence or
nationality conditions laid down in that
Act, so that additional provision for the
payment of such pensions to these new
entrants will eventually arise. No extra
expenditure under this head will be
required for the first five years, and it is
expected that for some time afterwards
the additional cost will be small, rising to
about £15,000 a year in 30 years' time.
It is anticipated that for the present
financial year the additional charge on the
Exchequer arising out of this Bill will
amount to about £8,000, representing the
increases, to which I have referred, in the
State grant to the National Health Insurance Fund. I beg to move.

Mr. NIXON: This is a rather old
subject in this House. It has been going
on since the Parliament of Northern
Ireland was set up. The Motion which I
beg to move, states:
"That in order to raise the status of
the Government of Northern Ireland to
the level of other Governments and
democracies, it is essential that Cabinet
Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries forthwith resign, or cease to hold
directorships in public companies."
It has always been laid down by members of the Government that their policy
is to march step by step with the
Imperial Government, but that policy is
only followed when it suits the Government, because it is well known that in
the Imperial Parliament or any other
Parliament in the British Commonwealth
of Nations, no member of the Government
is allowed to be the director of a public
company, and neither is his wife. As a
matter of fact, I recollect a Cabinet
Minister resigned voluntarily because his
wife was a director of a public company
and she did not wish to give it up.
Never was there a time when it was more
essential to put everything on a proper
basis. This is no political Motion so far
as I am concerned, because I am wise
enough to realise that the person who is
playing in politics at the present time is
a very foolish man indeed. Whether he
will get in or not get in if we had an
election is of no consequence.
After that
things will come all right. I believe
myself that after a lot of suffering they
will come all right. I know that you have
turned me down over and over again.
The other day I was reading in the paper
that the Imperial Government are going
to take over all scrap and railings in the
United Kingdom to turn them into guns
and tanks. Years before the war broke
out I told you, standing here, that I
would take the gates in Stormont Estate
and turn them into guns. I was laughed
at by some Members on that side-not all.
I only mention that to show you that I
have some vision. I have in this pocket
a letter, which I can show and did show
to some members of the Government, from
the last Minister of Information, Mr.
Duff Cooper. I wrote to him on the 28th
June, 1940, asking him to restrain the
B.B.C. from antagonising Russia and to
pursue a policy of trying to get Russia
on our side. He did see my view. Russia
was mentioned to-day. I congratulate
the Russians on their gallant fight. I am
proud that the Russian people are our
allies. Everyone I meet is proud, except
one English lady, and she did not know
what she was talking about-as usual.
An argument has been put forward from
that side over and over again that owing
to the small size of Ulster if you
debarred Ministers from holding directorships in public companies you would not
get suitable men public-spirited enough
to resign their directorships when they
become Cabinet Ministers. In other
words, they would stick to their directorships and reject the offer of Cabinet rank.
I say that is a libel on the patriotic people
of Ulster. There may be such men, and
if there are we are far better off without
them. Furthermore, we have Cabinet
Ministers who are not directors of public
companies, and without trying to be
invidious I would say that if there was a
vote or plebiscite taken to-morrow on the
efficiency of Ministers who are directors
of public companies, as compared with
Ministers who are not directors of public
companies, the vote would be for the
Ministers who are not directors, because
they are more efficient than the Ministers
who are. For over twenty years Ministers held on to directorships of these
companies in defiance of all law in the
civilised world. The only instance comparable with Ministers holding on to
directorships is the ex-Shah of Persia. He
held on to everything.
Mr. HENDERSON: But they chased
him.
Mr. NIXON: He did that for his own
pocket. That is the only comparable instance I know of. I will say this that
some Ministers do not seem in the slightest
to appreciate the delicate position. They
are as happy, as self-confident and as
complacent as the gentleman who thought
he could beat the Germans with his
umbrella. Furthermore, I will say and
I will prove it that the very fact of
Ministers themselves being guilty of this
highly irregular policy weakens and almost
renders their war effort abortive.

meet the liabilities
and debts of the Transport Board, and

Undoubtedly it was too much. The
Minister who suggested that was not too

their money for very much less. That is
an example of how a Minister gets himself tied up by launching on a career
and on a course that is wrong.

Another example was the Derating

They gained by that Bill. I said I had

stated that that Bill was forced on them

false, because the Imperial Government
had no power to force that Bill on them.
That Bill was an injustice. It was promoted by the Government who were
directors of manufacturing premises to
close the gap in the revenue at the ex-

I say that a Minister who is a director of
an industrial concern is not competent to
interfere in trade disputes, because the
people in his firm, although they may not
be on strike, are directly or indirectly
concerned with every trade dispute
between trade unions and employers. I
know the present Minister of Labour is
not a director of any company, and he is
just as good as the Ministers who are.
A Cabinet composed of directors of industrial concerns are not competent to
adjudicate in a trade dispute. No matter
how fair or honest they try to be, there
is always a suspicion that they are trying
to down the workers or the trade unions
because they themselves are directors of
companies that employ workers. You
cannot get away from that suspicion, and
that suspicion runs through the mind of
every worker.
I must say that personally the Prime
Minister would not be unfair. I do not
believe he could be unfair if he would.
It is not born in him to be unfair. The
Prime Minister got himself into a wrong
position at first. He is only carrying on
what he found here. I know that, too.
The Prime Minister did not start it,
although he held on to his directorships

I never heard him arguing-maybe I was
not here that he should hold on to the

The very fact that he resigned all directorships outside that proved that the Prime
Minister knew that the position was
wrong.
What am I asking? I am asking the
other Ministers to do the same thing. I

We know that Sir Stafford Cripps or Mr.
Churchill would not have got four votes
in the Imperial Parliament one month

Therefore, I do not mind
about the votes.
I do not know what answer the Prime

feel that it is not in the public interest

public do not accept that as right in

Which Amendment was: To leave

Britain."

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Road Transport Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In moving the
Second Reading of this Bill I would point
out that it introduces no new principle.
Its object is merely to make good a defect
in existing legislation and to make effective a principle to which Parliament has
already agreed.
As hon. Members are aware, the carriage of merchandise for hire or reward
can be undertaken in Belfast and
Londonderry only by the Belfast Corporation, the Northern Ireland Road Transport Board and local carriers licensed by
the Ministry of Home Affairs. The
Belfast Corporation do not, in fact, carry
on their tramways any goods other than
passengers' luggage, although they have
had a statutory right to do so for many
years.
Section 16, sub-section (5) of the Road
and Railway Transport Act provides that
the wages paid to and conditions of
employment imposed on employees of
licensed carriers shall not be less favourable than under contracts in which the
fair wages clause operates. The Act
provides that any person who uses a road
vehicle in contravention of Section
shall be liable. on summary conviction to
a fine not exceeding £100, but it has been
held by the Recorder that the penalty
prescribed in the Section does not apply
to the failure to pay fair wages.
That
is the reason for introducing this
Measure.

It was clearly the intention of Parliament that all local carriers should be
required to pay the same rate of wages
and that employers imposing worse conditions and paying small wages should
not be permitted to compete with those
paying recognised wages, and that the
penalty mentioned should apply.
Experience has shown that while a considerable number of local carriers pay
fair wages, others do not, and it has also
shown that it is very difficult to detect
breaches of the law in this respect. It is
grossly unfair that carriers who operate
their undertakings by using cheap labour
and imposing unfair conditions of employment should be allowed to injure the
business of carriers who pay recognised
rates of wages and impose fair conditions
of employment. This Bill is, therefore,
designed to give effect to the intention of
Parliament and to ensure that the penalty
provided by the Act of 1935 is enforceable. The machinery provided in the
Schedule to the Bill for giving effect to
the proposal is similar to that which
obtains in similar cases for ensuring that
sufficient information be obtained to
enable a prosecution to be taken with
success. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

That night at nine o'clock the hawker

SCHEDULE (Provisions for the enforcement of the Act).
*
1. On the conviction of an employer
under this Act for failing to pay the
recognised wages to a worker, the court
may by the conviction adjudge the
employer convicted to pay, in addition
to any fine, such sum as appears to the
court to be due to the worker on
account of the said wages; but the
power to order the payment of wages
under this provision shall not be in
derogation of any right of the worker
to recover wages by
by any other
proceedings.
2. Where an employer has been convicted under this Act for failing to pay
the recognised wages to any worker,
then, if notice of intention so to do has
been served with the summons, warrant
or complaint, evidence may be given of
any failure on the part of the employer
to pay the recognised wages to that
worker at any time during the six
months immediately preceding the date
on which the information was laid or
the complaint was served, and on proof
of the failure the court may order the
employer to pay such sum as is found
by the court to represent the difference
between the amount which, having
regard to the provisions of this Act,
ought properly to have been paid to
the worker by way of wages during
those six months, and the amount
actually so paid.

COMPENSATION FOR AIR-RAIDED
FAMILIES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House, do now adjourn.'
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I wish to raise
a matter about which I gave notice to the
Minister of Labour. It is a matter of
vital importance affecting the interests of
many people in Northern Ireland.
It
relates to the question of children whose
parents were killed during the recent air
raid. There is one case of a father who
died, but the mother was later killed in
the blitz, leaving three little orphans who
will not receive anything until they are
15 years of age. One other daughter who
kept the house for them is in receipt of
15s a week as her husband was killed, but
she gets nothing for the other three
children. That is only one case. There
are many others. There is the case of a
man who was earning 55s a week. He
had not worked for more than three years
in the past 20 years. He had an only
boy, who was the jewel of his parents,
and who got killed. The parents of that
boy are going to get nothing. In the
death of that boy everything they had
in life was gone. That is only one of
dozens of cases in Belfast. It would not
be fair to ask the. Minister of Labour to
give me an answer now, but I would ask
him and the Prime Minister to take an
interest in this matter. Anyone, whether
rich or poor, who had a son or daughter
killed during the air raid should be compensated.
Mr. SPEAKER: Naturally everybody

Mr. PEATTIE: Under the same conditions. One woman who came to me went

affairs of individuals. We abolished the

She handed it over to a gentleman for

Board. I
say that has got to stop. These

the people of any country should be maintained in. If the Minister knew one half
the things that are happening under this

but I have yet to find one thing the Board

There is one case in my own division.

of the city.
The Prime Minister is wrong when he

Oral Answers to Questions.
USE OF NORTHERN IRELAND
WATERWAYS.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether it would be in the
national interest to encourage the use of
the waterways in Northern Ireland for
the conveyance of sand and coal, thereby
releasing many lorries at present used for
this purpose for more urgent national
requirements, and whether a great saving
in the use of petrol could be made if the
Ministry got the coal and sand merchants
to co-operate and make more use of the
waterways.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF COM-
MERCE (Sir Wilson Hungerford): I
have been asked to reply. I agree that
in the national interest our inland waterways might be used more extensively for
the transport of coal and sand and the
Minister has caused representations to
that end to be made from time to time to
bodies and persons concerned with such
traffic. There are signs of improvement,
but I cannot hold out much hope of a
large scale diversion of traffic from the
roads to the canals for, apart from other
considerations, not many barges are now
available.
INSURANCE OF UNSCUTCHED
FLAX.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he can state the
rate of fire insurance paid by the Ministry
of Supply on unscutched flax in Great
Britain.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I
have been asked to reply. For obvious
reasons I am unable to furnish information regarding an Imperial Department's
commitments to which the Ministry of
Commerce is not a party.
STORAGE OF FLOUR.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether, in view of the fact
that flour is not rationed, he can state
what would be a reasonable quantity of
flour which a farmer occupying up to a
hundred acres of land, and employing at
times about a dozen workmen, and living
in a district subject to isolation in snow
storms, could keep in stock for the requirements of himself, his wife and family
and his workers; whether it is advisable
to keep such a quantity in store, and
whether the authorities did, in fact, so
advise the public some time ago.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I
have been asked to reply. The responsibility for the control and distribution of
flour throughout the United Kingdom
rests with the Ministry of Food. I am
not aware that the Ministry of Food has
established any
definite criterion of the
kind which the hon. Member has in mind.
DISTRIBUTION OF COAL.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can now give the
House an assurance that steps have been
taken, or will be taken forthwith, to
ensure that all coal coming into Northern
Treiand will be equitably distributed
amongst all coal-importing firms and consumers, and that provision will be made
for fair and reasonable supplies of petrol
and transport facilities generally for its
haulage.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I
have been asked to reply. I can assure
the hon. Member that the Ministry is
using its best endeavours to ensure the
equitable distribution of supplies of coal
throughout Northern Ireland.
The supply of petrol to coal merchants
is not a matter for my Ministry. The
subject has, however, been included in
general discussions which are taking place
regarding the carriage and distribution of
coal.
