21 OCTOBER 1941
MALNUTRITION OF SCHOOL
CHILDREN.
5. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education whether she can
give any information as to the School
Medical Officers' report issued by Dr.
Reid to County Armagh Educational
Committee as to malnutrition amongst
children attending schools; whether, in
view of the refusal of this Committee to
provide meals for children suffering from
malnutrition, she will impress on the
Committee the necessity of doing so in
view of their own Medical Officer's
report; whether the Parliamentary Secretary can state the number of educational
committees in Northern Ireland who are
providing meals for children attending
schools.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): I am aware
that following the report of Dr. Reid,.
School Medical Officer, the County
Armagh Regional Education Committee.
in the early part of this year appointed
a sub-committee with a view to preparing
a feasible scheme to relieve malnutrition
amongst the children attending public
elementary schools in County Armagh.
A scheme was duly submitted to the
Regional Education Committee and
adopted. It was then decided that the
sub-committee should meet again and
formulate full details of the working of
their suggested scheme, and that the detailed scheme should be submitted to the
County Council and to my Ministry.
No detailed scheme has yet been submitted, and I now understand that at a
recent meeting of the Regional Education
Committee it was decided, in view of the
large demands which the Committee must
meet under the War Damage Act, and
which were unforeseen when the financial
scheme for the year was formulated, to
postpone operation of the scheme for the
present. In these circumstances, I propose to ask the Committee to give the
matter further consideration.
In the year ended 31st March, 1941,
four committees provided meals for
school children, in addition one Committee gave financial assistance to a
voluntary agency, one Committee provided equipment for a voluntary agency
supplying cocoa, tea, soup and rice to
children, while one Committee distributed
cod-liver oil to 1,000 children.
HELP FOR BLIND PERSONS.
6. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he will make representations to
the Armagh County Council as to the
need of granting greater financial help to
blind persons during the coming year,
and to grant dependants' allowance to
blind persons in accordance with the 1938
Act; whether, in view of the Minister's
many appeals to county councils concerning the welfare of the blind, he will take
drastic action if the councils (including
Armagh) do not deal justly with the
blind; whether he can state the number
of circulars sent to county councils on
this question of blind persons; whether
he is satisfied with the response to his
appeals, and, if not, what action does he
propose to take; and whether he will set
up a commission to go into the question
of the welfare and maintenance of the
blind on similar terms to that operating
in Great Britain.
The following question also stood on
the Order Paper:-
9. Mr. JOHN BAILEY-To ask the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
is aware that extreme hardships exist
among the blind persons of Northern
Ireland owing to the fact that the
County Councils are not giving them
an adequate allowance to their 10s
pensions; and whether he will immediately press the County Councils to
grant supplementary allowances equal
to other pensioners of the same age who
are not blind.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I propose to answer
this question and a somewhat similar
question by the hon. Member for West
Down together.
I do not consider it necessary to make
any further representations to the
Armagh County Council on the matter,
as I am satisfied that the Council appreciates the need for giving greater financial
help to blind persons. The expenditure
of the Council during the year 1939-40
for this purpose was £678. This was increased to £1,211 in the year 1940-41,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
and they propose to spend no less than
£2,900 during the current financial year.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
each case of a blind person is dealt with
on its merits by the County Council concerned, and that without an investigation
into each case it is obviously impossible
for me to say generally whether the
County Council is dealing justly or otherwise with the blind, or whether general
hardship exists.
Since October, 1939, my department
has issued three circulars to County
Councils on this subject, and I am satisfied that the appeals have been sympathetically received and that there has been
a reasonably good response. The estimated expenditure by County Councils
for the current year is £5,000 more than
last year's expenditure and £11,000 more
than that of the previous year. In the
circumstances, I do not consider any good
purpose would be served by setting up a
Commission to go into the question, or of
making further representations at the
moment to County Councils on the
subject.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman, on his own

persons of
Northern Ireland are living on the
poverty basis, is he satisfied in his own

our community, and whether he is aware
of the scheme for helping the blind that
is operating in Great Britain as against
Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think if the
hon. Member goes into the matter further
he will find that our scheme is exactly
similar to that in Great Britain. If he
can show me that it is different I will
be glad to consider it further.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the administration
is not the same, and is it not a fact that
the rates applicable by the county council
are also different-less than those received
in England by about 25 to 30 per cent.?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. I am
not aware, but if the hon. Member will
point out to me any case, it might be some
help to me in making representations to
the local authorities.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not consider the time has come
to transfer this responsibility from the
county council to the Government?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course, the
hon. and learned Member will fully
appreciate that the persons interested as
ratepayers say one thing and another person interested as a taxpayer says another.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask which
party the right hon. Gentleman is interested in?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I want to do
the best for the blind persons.
COUNTY ARMAGH MENTAL
HOSPITAL.
7. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he will consult with the Management Committee of County Armagh
Mental Hospital concerning the hours
worked by nursing and domestic staffs;
whether the long hours worked by this
staff augurs weli for their efficiency and
fitness to carry out their duties; whether
the staff of the institution are entitled to
be members of a recognised trade union
and if such membership, which promotes
the welfare of the staff, is likely to cause
uneasiness or inefficiency; whether the
staff of the institution commit any offence
against the regulations by speaking to a
member of the Management Committee:
whether the remarks made by the R.M.S.
concerning this matter at a meeting held
on 13-10-41 was in the best interests of
the staff or the committee; whether the
Minister will consider the advisability of
setting up a Commission to inquire into
the administration, conditions of employment, hours, wages, etc., of all mental
hospitals in Northern Ireland, particularly in the provincial areas.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This question
is primarily one for the Committee of
Management of the Mental Hospital, and
as the hon. Member is also a member of
that committee he is in a position to have
the matter dealt with in its proper place.
I am not prepared to set up a Commission
of inquiry.
MATERNITY AND CHILD
WELFARE SCHEMES.
8. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Agnew)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
21 OCTOBER 1941
whether he will consider the giving of
higher grants to local authorities for promoting schemes of maternity and child
welfare; whether the maternity and child
welfare scheme now operated works in
conjunction with the school medical
service; and whether sufficient accommodation is provided in provincial
hospitals and infirmaries to cope with the
needs of working-class mothers for
maternity treatment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is, no doubt, aware, the Ministry
in general recoups 50 per cent. of the
expenditure by local authorities on maternity and child welfare schemes. No representations from iocal authorities for
increased grants have been received by
my Department, and I have, therefore,
no reason to believe that the present rate
of recoupment is regarded as unsatisfactory. I do not, therefore, propose to
consider increasing this scale.
With regard to the second part of the
question the reply is in the negative.
School medical services are operated by
entirely different authorities, namely, the
Regional Education Committees.
As regards the last part of the question
existing accommodation has, generally
speaking, proved adequate, but in areas
where this is not so, steps have already
been taken to provide additional accommodation at Government expense. It is
hoped that this additional accommodation
will be available within the next few
weeks.
DISPUTE IN MACKIE'S FOUNDRY.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): On receipt of the notification
of this dispute from the trade unions concerned, the chief industrial officer wrote
advising them that, under the established
procedure in the industry and in accordance with the provisions of the Conditions
of Employment and National Arbitration
Order, they should apply to the firm for
a works conference to deal with the
matter. Copies of the correspondence
were sent simultaneously to the firm and
to the secretary of the Employers'
Association for their information. Until
the machinery of negotiation has failed
to produce a settlement, it would not be
appropriate for my Ministry to intervene.
further.
I am sure my hon. Friend realises that
no matter how fair and helpful we may
wish to be, irregular action by one or
other of the parties in dispute makes it
extremely difficult not only for me and
my officials, but also for the trade union
representatives and the employers themselves, to secure a prompt adjustment in
these matters.

Mr. GORDON: If Messrs. Mackie
have been guilty of a violation of the

Arbitration Order I will certainly take

Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the unsatisfactory reply to both question and

ranging from 41s to 50s per week to women

GROWING OF SUGAR BEET.
19. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware that the Ministry of Agriculture in
England aims at growing 405,000 acres of
sugar beet during the year of 1942, and
that the farmers in Northern Ireland are
very dissatisfied at not having a factory
for the manufacture of sugar beet here;
whether he is aware that the farmers of
Northern Ireland are anxious to grow
sugar beet not alone for sugar, but for
the pulp which makes excellent cattle
feed and enriches the land on which it
grows; and whether, owing to the
shortage of farm yard manure, something
of this nature is necessary in the present
forced rotation of cropping to keep the
land productive.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply.
I am aware that a relatively small increase in the acreage under sugar beet in
Great Britain is being aimed at for 1942.
No evidence is available to show that
farmers in Northern Ireland are anxious
to grow sugar beet, and, from the information before me, I think they are wise
in this. The value of sugar beet pulp as
a feeding stuff is fully recognised. In
existing circumstances in Northern Ireland, and particularly on those farms
where there is a shortage of farm yard
manure, the Ministry is satisfied that it
is in the interests of both the nation and
the farmers that potatoes should be
grown instead of sugar beet.
As the hon. Member will appreciate,
it is difficult to deal adequately with this
subject by means of question and answer.
If, however, the hon. Member so desires,
I shall be glad to discuss the matter with
him and to make available all the information at the Ministry's disposal.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): This Bill proposes to extend for
a further year the operations of the
various Acts mentioned in the Schedule.
The Schedule is a short one, and the Acts
mentioned are three in number. They
are the same three Acts that were contained in the Schedule of the Expiring
Laws Continuance Act passed last year.
The first is the Harbours, Docks and
Piers (Temporary Increase of Charges)
Act, 1920. That, as hon. Members are
aware, is an Act which provides that
application may be made to a Government department for liberty to vary
harbour charges to meet increased cost,
and, of course, Members are also aware
that in regard to public harbour undertakings provision is made that it shall
merely cover increased cost and not
enable any profit to be made.
Such a
provision enables application to be made
in a Government department in lieu of
the necessity of coming to the House for
a printed Act.
The next Act contained in the Schedule
is the Local Government (Emergency
Powers) Act, 1921. This, as hon. Members will recollect, is the Act which, in
case of the failure of a local authority to
perform its statutory duty, confers on
the Minister of Home Affairs power to
appoint an administrator to carry on the
duties, and it is desired by the Government that that power should be continued
for another year.
The third Act mentioned in the
Schedule is the Local Authorities and
Jurors Books (Temporary Provisions)
Act, 1940. That is the Act passed last
year which provided that no local elections were to be held for the space of a
year, the idea being that local elections
could not properly and satisfactorily be
held under war conditions.
The war is,
unfortunately, still with us, and it is
proposed to continue the operation of
that Act for another year. The Act
applies not only to elections for local
authorities, but to the provision of jurors
books, which were also postponed for a
year.
a
Mr. NIXON: As regards the Act with
reference to Local Government elections,
the Attorney-General did not say they
were the same as Parliamentary elections.
There is a difference. In Great Britain
Parliamentary elections, that is general.
elections, have been postponed and very
properly so. That question does not
arise here. Local Government vacancies
are now filled by co-option, and the right
to have by-elections is withdrawn from
county and city councils. That is
direct stroke at democracy, and it is an
encouragement to councils not doing what
is right to continue in that way. As
everybody knows we had trouble in the
Belfast City Council, and a couple of
members resigned because of it. Their
seats were filled by co-option, and the
people were not allowed to signify their
disgust or otherwise at a municipal
election. It seems that a member of a
municipal body can do what he likes.
If he survives there will be no election,
and no one will have a right to dispute
whatever the Corporation may do. The
nominations are made by the Unionist
Association, which consists of about
twenty or thirty people. They select the
candidate, send forward his name, and
he is duly co-opted.
I am not suggesting that the Corporation would reject a person nominated by
any other body. If a Nationalist seat
becomes vacant I know they would accept
a nomination from that party, and if an
Independent seat became vacant they
would accept a person nominated by that
body. I know they have done that. I
have no complaint against the Corporation. The
person nominated by the
association concerned is co-opted. I
object to that principle. Any person
who wishes to challenge the whole thing
should, if he is willing to pay for it, be
allowed to get nominated, stand and contest the seat. Nothing shakes the Corporation or a Parliament so much as an
Expiring Laws Bill

in reference to a free election when a
occasional by-election; it is a safety valve.
When it is known that there is going to
be no by-election the most unpopular and
useless man may be put forward by the
association concerned and he will get in,
seeing that the Corporation, like other
bodies, have an overwhelming Unionist

only suits one party. If the people had

I have no objection to the Bill apart

The Amendment raises a matter of very

resident in Belfast and the employer is

is to be performed, say, partly in Belfast

now if the workman is injured while performing his work in Belfast he is entitled
to the benefits of the Workmen's Compensation Acts, and if he has the misfortune
to be killed by an accident arising out of
and in the course of his employment his

Suppose, though, the injuries are sustained in Dublin, where he is working
under the same employer and under the
same contract of service, he is not entitled
to one penny piece, and if he should
happen to be killed his dependants are
not entitled to one penny of compensation.
The position is
is exemplified more
strongly in this way. Take the case of

are separated by a very short distancea question of a few hundred yards.
Strabane workman employed by a Strabane employer under a contract made in
Strabane will, if injured, enjoy the

his dependants will benefit. If under

to go across into Lifford and is injured

The same thing would apply in the case
A
Take the case of a Great Northern
Railway servant who entered the service

If the contract is made here, if the workman is one of our own workmen, and the
employer is one of our own employers,
why should it make the least difference if
the accident happens in Strabane or
Lifford, Belfast or Dublin, or Newry or
Dundalk?
The workmen of Northern Ireland, I
believe, are quite unaware of the predicament in which they stand in this.matter.
I believe the general body of workers
would be startled if they realised that by
entering into a contract in Belfast, to be
performed partly in Northern Ireland
and partly in the rest of Ireland, as far
as the work to be done in the rest of
Ireland is concerned, by making that contract, they would have contracted themselves out of the benefits of the Act. Not
only that, but I believe the ordinary
worker, when he makes these contracts
in Northern Ireland, is convinced in his
own mind that he is taking with him, no

Ireland, the benefits of the Act. In my

state of mind is that if he goes to Louth,
Meath, Kildare, or Donegal, any of the

outside the Six Counties the benefits he
enjoys within the Six Counties under the
Workmen's Compensation Acts.
I believe that if he realised he was
divesting himself of these vital and
important rights to himself and his
dependants, he would not leave Northern
Ireland at all under a contract of service
of that kind. I believe he would hesitate, indeed absolutely refuse, to go.
The position of the man in the rest of
Ireland is altogether different, and
different to the advantage of the workman. If a citizen of Eire happens to be
injured in Northern Ireland he secures

Prices and Grading of Flax.
Mr. BROWN: I beg to move, "That
in the opinion of this House the Government should at once make the strongest
possible representations to the Ministry
of Supply to secure an increase in the
prices of flax more in keeping with the
substantial increase in the costs of production this season than the inadequate
advance of 1s per stone already announced
and also to secure a more satisfactory
method of grading flax."
I make no apology for bringing this
Motion before the House because, as I
will show, it is a matter of the very greatest
and most widespread concern. We have
to remember that before the war a sum
of roughly £4,000,000 was sent to foreign
countries for flax that could and should
have been grown in Northern Ireland.
That alone will give the House some idea
of the importance of this matter, and it
affects not only the farmer, but our other
staple industry, the linen trade. I am
particularly interested in my constituency
in the production of flax, and that is one
of the reasons why I am pressing it today. In the town of Newry, the principal town in my constituency, we had
four linen mills, including Dromalane.
Now we have none at all. The machinery
of two of them was broken up with sledge
hammers and sold for scrap. We have
only one remaining spinning mill in
Newry, and that has been closed down
for some time, and we have there a state
of unemployment and a state of distress
prevailing which exists in no other part
of Northern Ireland.
The Government cannot and must not
shirk the responsibility for that deplorable state of affairs, because the conditions we have in Newry are due to
neglect on the part of the Government
to get flax grown in Northern Ireland.
I lay entirely and absolutely at the door
of the Government the blame for the
depression that exists in Newry to-daythe fact that not one single branch of the
industry is operating in that town where
there used to be four mills. I raised this
matter at question time to-day, and I am
sorry to say I am not satisfied with the
reply of the Prime Minister. Quite
candidly I am not. The Prime Minister
said it is primarily a matter for the company concerned. I think it is also a
matter for the Government to see to the
welfare of every part of their territory,
including South Down.
I suggest that the Ministry of Supply
are the purchasers of every piece of flax
produced, but it is open to this Government to recommend the Ministry of
Supply to make a condition of allocation,
if you like, that this industry in Newry
will be reopened, and that we will be
given fair play. It is not fair. We have
industry throbbing in many other places,
and work provided for the workers at
home. But in Newry we are not getting
justice or fair play.

the administration of his Department
failed. The first thing I should like to

Dispute in Mackie's Foundry 1944

draw his attention to is this, that yesterday his Department had 63 workmen
before the court under the Defence of the
Realm Regulations relating to production. I think if he examines the
Regulations he can come to no other
conclusion than that Mr. Tom Mackie, or
Mr. Dan Mackie, is a person who has
retarded production. Why do I say
so?
Because these gentlemen gave an
undertaking that there would be no
reduction in the price unless there was an
alteration in the tooling of the machines.
The boys were told that the sky was the
limit; in other words they could earn as
much as they could possibly earn within
the recognised working hours. That was
to say, they could earn £10 a week if
they wished, and the firm would take no
exception to their earning power provided that they gave production.
Production is an all-important factor
at the present time. Therefore in giving
that assurance to the workmen concerned
he was doing only what other good
employers are doing-trying to give the
production necessary for the successful
prosecution of the war. How long did
that assurance last? After five or six
months had elapsed the shop foreman
notified the men that there would be a

tray of 24 shells. That is to say that the
tray held 24 shells and they were getting
11d per tray and they could earn as much
as they liked on that price until their
earning power reached the sky. But this
employer gave an intimation and the men
protested against the reduction in price.
from 11d to 7d per tray of 24 shells, that

In a few weeks' time a larger pulley

place between workmen and employers
10 days' notice must be given. Therefore
Mackie's is liable under the Defence of

agreement, which has been the cause of
the lock-out in this firm. The men

Dispute in Mackie's Foundry 1946

going out at dinner time they are told
they are dismissed. What classification
would the men be considered to belong to
who were on the street in those circumstances? They cannot be strikers. They
can only be classified as aggrieved workmen. The employer changed the conditions, and refused to meet the men to
discuss the matter. Therefore, I think
that justifies the right hon. Gentleman in
bringing the case against Mackie's under
the law which he has been using up to
yesterday against the workmen.
Here is the point.
About fifteen
minutes after the men left the shop where
they were working the management introduced female labour from other departments of the firm. Previous to this dispute the firm put this department on short.
time, which was a loss of 4 hours in the
24 hours of both shifts, for about two
weeks. Now we have got the substance
of what the firm was at. They wanted
a change in the type of labour employed
on the making of these shells, but they
had not the courage to tell the men that
they believed that female labour was
suitable for the material in the making
of the shells. They concocted the dispute, and when the workmen were going
out, told them they were dismissed. They
then replaced these men in fifteen minutes
with female labour, at reduced rates of
wages. The Minister should have
examined that position. That is the
origin of the attack Mackie's made on
these men, who were anxious to remain at
work and produce to the limit of their
ability until such times as the stock would
reach sky high. They were prohibited
from producing, from negotiating, and
using the machinery under which all disputes are expected to be settled. They
were thrown on the streets as dismissed
employees.
The reason the firm gave for the dismissal and stoppage was that they had a
big stock of shells. Imagine having shells
in stock at the present time, when they
are all wanted in the fight for freedom
and democracy. The Minister of Production wants all the shells he can get,
and no firm has the right to put them in
stock and retain them for some future
date. They are required now. The men
said to me: "Surely in a life and death
struggle as we find ourselves in to-day,
could we have too many shells." The
men and boys of this department are
anxious to get back to their work to pull
their weight, as they have always done.
Messrs. Mackie have violated all the conditions laid down for negotiating disputes.
They refused to meet the men; they
refused to give consideration to the representations they made, and they refused
to allow them to return to work. The
origin of the dispute must be the responsibility of Messrs. Mackie, who wished to
displace male labour and bring in female
labour because the material which the
machines were working was suitable for
female labour.
I ask the right hon. Gentleman to do
justice to every class in the community.
As I have already told him, he put 63
men into the police court. Those men
had never seen the inside of a police
court before, and they have been made
to bear the penalty of the law because of
the conditions imposed upon them and
in regard to which they had no outlet
for their views. The employers to-day
are greatly at fault in the majority of
disputes taking place in our city, but I
have failed to find one employer before
the court to give an account of his responsibility in these trying days through
which we are passing. But we can have
63 of these men brought to the court and
fined. I am not going into the merits of
the bringing of the men to court of the
imposition of the fines, but if it is good
for the right hon. Gentleman to bring
the men to the court to make them
realise their responsibility, then I say he
must also bring all those defaulting employers before the court. Some 75 per
cent. of the disputes which have occurred
have been wholly the responsibility of
the employers.
When I was working at the Queen's
Island, or when the Parliamentary Secretary was there, the things that are now the

The management at all times sat down

REMAND HOME FOR YOUNG
GIRLS.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
he has received representations from the
Ulster Girl Guide Commissioners as to the
urgent necessity of providing a remand
home for juvenile girls in Northern
Ireland, and if so, what action the Government proposes to take in this matter.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The representations referred to have
been received. With regard to the last
part of the question the Departmental
Committee, which was appointed to
inquire into the possibility of putting into
immediate operation the recommendations
of the Sir Robert Lynn Committee, has
not yet reported, and he is not, therefore,
in a position to make any statement at
present.
For the hon. Member's information I
might add a search has commenced to
obtain premises.
MEDICAL ATTENTION FOR
EVACUEES.
2. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what arrangements were made for
the medical attention of evacuees in rural
districts.
Mr. LOWRY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The arrangements which were made by
the Government for the medical attention
of members of the population evacuated
under the Government scheme related
solely to unaccompanied children. In this
case arrangements were made whereby
the householder was enabled to obtain
from the doctor norminated by him or
her, free medical attention and medicine,
etc., for the children.
Following the movement of the population to safety areas further arrangements were made by this Department for
the provision of medical services to include
all persons transferred who are not in a
position to pay for medical treatment.
These arrangements provide for an extension of health and welfare services in
reception areas to such persons. They
include domiciliary treatment through
dispensary medical service, provision for
the extension of nursing services, the
admission of patients to hospitals included in the emergency hospital scheme
and the application to evacuees of facilities available for ordinary residents in
respect of infectious disease, maternity
and child welfare and tuberculosis. By
arrangement with the Ministry of Education, school medical services are extended
to evacuated school-children.
As the hon. Member is aware additional hospital and nursing accommodation is being provided throughout the
Province where the need is most urgent,
and it is hoped that this additional
accommodation will be available at an
early date.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY: Arising out of the

ALLOWANCES OF WIDOWS OF
R.I.C. MEMBERS.
10. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he can state
if the widows of members of the old
R.I.C. are to benefit from the increase in
widows' allowances as announced in the
Imperial Parliament some time ago.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I regret that for
two reasons I am not in a position to give
the hon. Member a definite reply to his
question. In the first place any matter
affecting the pensions of Royal Irish
Constabulary widows and dependants, is
one for the Imperial Government and not
for the Government of Northern Ireland.
In the second place, so far as I am aware,
no increase in the pensions of police
widows has, as yet, been announced in
the Imperial Parliament. The position
is that a Departmental Committee under
the chairmanship of Lord Snell has had
the problem under consideration, and that
its report which has recently been published has been the subject of questions
in the Imperial House of Commons. This
report recommends certain increases in
the pensions of police widows, but the
proposals do not take into account the
position of widows whose pensions derive
from their husbands Royal Irish Constabulary service.
FIRE WATCHING .OF BUSINESS
PREMISES.
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he is aware
of the serious danger to those premises
where huge sums of money are paid for
fire watching and also to those business
premises where the employees are giving
their services voluntarily, owing to the
fact that adjoining vacant premises are
not fire-watched, and whether, in view
of this grave menace he will make an
order that all vacant premises must be
fire-watched.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: I am aware of
the danger to which the hon. Member
refers.
Fire prevention in respect of vacant
premises and of premises which are not
occupied for business purposes falls to be
dealt with under Regulation 27b of the
General Defence Regulations.
I have already given a direction under
this Regulation to the civil defence
authorities in the county boroughs concerned to make fire prevention arrangements for premises of this description.

already done much towards discharging

If

Mr. MacDERMOTT: The position of

I quite appreciate the difficulty which

CIVIL SERVICE FIRE WATCHING
SCHEME.
12. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether any firewatching scheme was submitted to the
employees of the Northern Ireland Civil
Service in the respective departments
where they are employed; whether it is
a fact that before any scheme or schemes
can be submitted to the Civil Defence
Authorities, it is the duty of the employers to hold a meeting and have
common agreement on the scheme to be
approved of; whether it is a fact that in
Great Britain they receive a copy of the
agreed scheme before it is put into
operation; and whether he will see that
this procedure is carried out in the Civil
Service of Northern Ireland.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: The Fire Prevention (Business Premises) (Northern
Ireland) Order, 1941, does not apply to
premises occupied by Government departments, but the Government has decided
that certain premises in Government
occupation should be covered by fireprevention arrangements on lines similar
to those which the Order lays down for
business premises.
The general scheme which was formulated by the Ministry of Finance provided that the details of the arrangements proposed by the various departments should be brought to the notice of
each individual member of the staff concerned, who was thus given an opportunity of making representations. I have
no reason to doubt that members of the
Civil Service required to carry out fire
prevention duties at the various Government offices were made aware of the
arrangements to be adopted before they
became operative.
So far as I am aware, therefore, the
action taken by the various departments
has followed closely the obligations of
occupiers under the Order and the spirit
of its consultative provisions has been
duly observed.
In view of the terms of the hon. Member's question, however, I ought to point
out that neither here nor in Great Britain

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE

The information concerning grants and

COMING TILLAGE CAMPAIGN.
15. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the statement made to the House on 7th instant,
that "the plans we are on at the moment
will be such that the farming community.
in Northern Ireland need not fear to go
on with the coming tillage campaign,'
the Government will take steps to ensure
the immediate production of these plans
in whole or in part for the purpose of
saving the large portion of the present
harvest that is still threatened with ruin;
and whether, in view of the fact that the
Government did not implement the
promise made on their behalf in the spring
time, to have flying squads of labour
organised and available he can state what
steps, if any, the Government will take
to compensate farmers who will sustain
heavy losses on account of the shortage of
labour in complying with compulsory
tillage requirements.
Lord GLENTORAN: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply. The
first part of the hon. Member's question
refers to arrangements to deal with next
year's harvest, and the rest of the question
does not, therefore, really arise. The hon.
Member must be aware that the military
provided flying squads of labour during
the whole of the present harvest season.
The Ministry's records to date show that
over 15,000 farmers availed themselves of
the flying squads of military labour,
arrangements for which were made by the
Ministry and the military authorities.
The hon. Member must also be aware of
the very valuable nature of this military
assistance and of the farmers' expression
of appreciation of their help, as well as of
the fact that even unlimited supplies of
labour cannot control harvest weather.
Mr. BROWN: In view of the fact that
we were told almost a month ago in this
House that plans were under consideration
in connection with the tillage campaign,
are we not entitled to demand the immediate production of some of the plans, in
whole or in part, in order to save the
balance of the harvest which is now faced
with ruin?
SUPPLIES OF OATS TO
MERCHANTS.
16. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the tonnage of oats per year which
a merchant in Northern Ireland must
handle in order to be able to obtain a
licence under the latest regulations.
Lord GLENTORAN: Following consultations with trade associations concerned, it has been decided that
merchants, in order to qualify for an
approved buyer's licence, must be able to
show that they purchased direct from
growers in the three years prior to the
outbreak of war approximately 50 tons
of oats per annum. Exceptions to this
rule are, however, made where it appears
to the Ministry that the number of
approved buyers in any district is not
sufficient to meet local needs.
It should be understood that, provided
a merchant holds a licence under the
Feeding Stuffs Control Order, he is permitted to trade in oats although he is not
allowed to purchase direct from growers.
The hon. Member will, no doubt,
understand that these restrictions have
become necessary as a
result of the
flagrant disregard of the Maximum Prices
Order last season before the administration was taken over by my Department
on behalf of the Ministry of Food.

18. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the

Lord GLENTORAN: I am glad to be
afforded this opportunity again to make the
position clear regarding claims for potato
acreage payments. The first qualification
is that every claimant must have at least
one acre of agricultural land. Provided

acre. This is the minimum area
which an acreage payment will be made.

necessary for a person to have one acre
actually under potatoes as appears to be
the impression in some districts.

PRICES OF COWS FOR DAIRY
USE.
22. Mr. T. BAILIE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
wide disparity between the prices of cows
bought for dairy use and the prices
obtained upon resale to the Ministry;
whether the prices realised average about
half the purchase price, and whether in
consequence of the inability of dairy producers to bear this serious loss he will
consider the advisability of having the
prices paid by the Ministry increased in
order to prevent the producers in many
cases giving up business.
Lord GLENTORAN: I think it is desirable to make it clear that my Ministry
only buys on behalf of the Ministry of
Food fat cows for immediate slaughter.
These fat cows are purchased at a price
which is uniform throughout the United
Kingdom and which was fixed after discussion with the English, Scottish and
Northern Ireland Farmers' Unions. The
price of dairy cows is not controlled in
any way whatever, and is therefore a
direct reflection of what the farmers consider them to be worth in view of the
price the Government is paying for milk.
I am, of course, aware that the difference
between the price of a dairy cow and a
fat cow for slaughter has been widening,
but, as I have indicated, that is a matter
within the farmers' control, and I am
sure the hon. Member would not suggest
that the price of dairy cows should be
brought down by reducing the price of
milk.
PRICES OF SEED POTATOES.
23. Mr. T. BAILIE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to the prices payable to
growers of seed potatoes as compared with
the maximum prices laid down for their
resale; whether it is true that the
original price is in some instances nearly
quadrupled, and whether he will take
steps to have these prices more closely
related so as to give a fairer price to the
grower and afford a more reasonable price
to the buyer.
Lord GLENTORAN: The hon. Member is, I think, under some misapprehension in regard to the prices which
have been prescribed by the Ministry of
Food for the retail sale of seed potatoes
in the United Kingdom. These are
maximum prices for delivery carriage
paid to any planter in the United
Kingdom and are not fixed prices.
Written Answers
Written Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lord Glentoran]
In accordance with the terms of the
Potato Control Orders a merchant who
buys seed potatoes from a grower is required to pay the grower a prescribed
price according to variety and district.
He may not resell this seed to planters
at a price which exceeds the price paid
to the grower together with (a) the
actual transport charges and costs of
bags, etc., and (b) a maximum prescribed
permitted addition to cover the
merchant's expenses and to allow a
margin for profit.
As the distances for transport in Northern Ireland are comparatively short,
the transport costs are not excessive. I
feel certain, accordingly, that there can
be few cases, if any, in this area where
the merchant can justify charging a
planter the maximum retail prices which
have been prescribed for the United
Kingdom. If details of any attempted
overcharge for seed potatoes in Northern
Ireland are supplied to my Ministry, I
shall have immediate action taken.

CO-OPERATION IN AIRCRAFT
PRODUCTION.
24. Mr. T. BAILIE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether his Ministry has
been appointed to represent the Ministry of Production in respect of aircraft
production in Northern Ireland, and, if
so, whether he can take steps to encourage the formation of a joint committee of representatives of the management and reperesentatives of the workers
in order that the fullest co-operation
may exist in the war effort.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Yes, sir. As announced some time ago, my Ministry is
recognised by the various Production
Departments at Westminster-including
the Ministry of Aircraft Production-as
the Department concerned with war production in this area. To assist me in
dealing with production questions I have
set up a Production Committee, attached
to my Ministry, consisting of representatives of employers and labour.
I
am also happy to say that a joint committee of representatives of the employers
and employees has been established in
the aircraft production firm to which, I
assume, the hon. Member refers.
PRESENT POSITION OF FIRE
WATCHING.
25. Mr. T. BAILIE asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he is satisfied
with the present position in regard to fire
watching; whether he proposes to revise
the orders at present in force or introduce
legislation in order to secure a more equitable distribution of this responsibility.
Mr. MacDERMOTT: Fire prevention
is too vital a matter to justify any feeling
of satisfaction until the position is not
merely good, but beyond improvement.
The present arrangements have not yet
reached that pitch of perfection, but I
think I may say that there has been a
steady improvement and a growing
realisation of the importance of the
subject and of the responsibilities which
it involves.
With regard to the latter part of the
hon. Member's question, much has been
accomplished under the Order at present
in force which relates to fire prevention
on business premises. Experience has,
however, revealed certain weaknesses and
omissions in it, and I propose at an early
date to make a new Order which will aim
at rectifying these and which will, I hope,
make for a more equitable distribution of
the responsibilities involved.

Mr. GORDON: I have already intimated to the hon. Member that on
receiving information that a dispute is
likely to take place we take immediate
action. We cannot force men to work if
they go on strike, and we cannot make a
firm hold men whom they dismiss. The
hon. Member does not seem to be aware
of the difficulties with which the Ministry
are faced in a matter of this kind. We
are anxious that the men should remain
at work; we are anxious that employers
should retain men in their employment,
and we are anxious to see good feeling
existing between workers and employers
so that both may be enabled to play their
part in carrying out work of national
importance.

Minister to make sure of his information
before passing it on to this House. I am

arrangements have been made for Messrs.

Mr. NIXON: The Minister has
frequently used the words "immediate
action". Do the words "immediate
action" mean that a strike is to be

that what the right hon. Gentleman
means by the words "immediate action"?
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Member is
under a misapprehension. Immediately
a strike is notified to my Department,
the Ministry find out from the trades
concerned if there is any negotiating
machinery available. If there is they
ask the trade union to bring it into operation. The trade union representatives
insist on this being done. If the
negotiating machinery fails in its mission
then the matter is referred to the
arbitration tribunal. The hon. Member
may rest assured that we allow no time
to be wasted in a matter of this kind.
A strike is an exceedingly difficult thing,
and it is very delicate ground upon
which we have to tread. It is our desire
not to do anything which will infringe
on the rights of the workers or employers
or impair the workers or employers
organisations in regard to bringing
strikes to an end.

Members to pass from this question now.

Mr. BEATTIE: I think the House
should be very sympathetic to
Speaker in the difficult task he has to
perform in the way of getting through an
enormous amount of business in the few
hours that this House meets each Tuesday.
I feel that there is too much of a cramped
style in our way of doing the business of
the House. We are not concentrating as
we should on the subjects which this
House has got to review. It is nearly
time that the Government realised that
there is urgent and important business
for this House to do. There are, at the
moment, many urgent and important
matters on which I should like the House
to have an opportunity of expressing its
thoughts. I can never find time to have
those matters fully discussed.
The Prime Minister and everyone else
knows that our ambition is to win this
war. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It
is political suicide for the Government to
allow the tragic position of our war effort
to continue. The Government are responsible for this, because this House meets
only one day in the week. It is a physical
impossibility for this Parliament to do the
work necessary to be done in the short
time at its disposal. I am going to move
that we restore the status quo. The old
arrangement provided ample time for the
discussion of matters of public interest
and importance. For 15 years we were
able to carry on, and no Member of the
House was hindered in having a full discussion on any questions in which he was
deeply interested. That was in peace
time. How much more necessary it is
that we should have every hour of Parliamentary time during the war.
We were told by the Government that
the less time spent in talking in this
House the better in the national interest.
I hold that the more talking we can do
in this House the better it will be in the
national interest. If the time had been
at our disposal in this House, certain
conditions that are now operating in the
city of Belfast, and that were referred to
in the public Press on Thursday last,
would not now exist with detrimental
results to the national cause. As the
Prime Minister knows, I attended several
meetings of industrial workers. I know
of the internal disturbances that are

taking place, and I know that in Northern
Ireland we have not got a representative

The Minister of Commerce is agent for

nothing to do with the Ministry of

I was talking to a representative of the
Ministry of Aircraft Production in
Belfast last week-end. He happened to

days of the last war, when we often met.
He gave me inside information that
startled and surprised me. The sooner
we have a representative of the Ministry
of Aircraft Production in Northern Ireland the better it will be in the national
interest. We want to get these things
put forward, and for that purpose we
must have the time of this House, for
we cannot put them forward outside.
To-day there are three Motions on the
Paper, one in the names of the hon.
Member for Woodvale and myself,
another in the name of the hon. Member
for South Down, and a third in the names
of the hon. Member for South Armagh
and myself. It is going to take three

Motions.
I feel that we are not doing all we
could do in this year of 1941, and the
sooner we realise that and get down to
real business the better, so that we can
all pull together and work together for
the common cause. The Government
have got to drop their political basis of
operations.
The Prime Minister may
think he can carry on. He has declared
that there will never be anything but a
Unionist Government as long as he is
Prime Minister. But the Prime Minister
was not patriotic when he made that
statement. I want the time of this House
for the discussion of matters of vital
importance. Every Tuesday I am outvoted by numbers on the question of the
extension of Parliamentary time. The
law which allows me that time was broken
by the late Prime Minister, because he
had those Members behind him.
I do not want to say anything in opposition to this Motion that would be likely
to convey an intimation to any quarter of
the world that we are not doing all that
we were given to do. That would not be
fair. We are doing all we have been
given to do, but we could do more. We
could double what we are doing. I am
going to ask why we are not getting a
hundred per cent, more to do, and I am
going to try to make my voice heard in
strong protest against the existing state
of affairs. No one has a right to sit on
a high horse and refuse to take cognisance
of what is happening elsewhere. What is
happening elsewhere may happen here
We are engaged in a world
conflict, and if we are going to be in it,
let us be in it a hundred per cent. and
let no man stand in the way.

Russia has stood up to the onslaught

months. We know what happened to
other nations.

Mr. AGNEW I beg to move:—
That this House views with alarm
the serious plight of many unemployed
workers who have had long industrial
records being cast aside and deprived
of all means of existence and disallowed
as "Not Normally Insured" by the
Assistance Board, and that in the
opinion of this House the Government
does not fully realise the gravity of the
situation whereby workers who have
served industry faithfully are placed
in a position of insecurity, their only
alternative being to enter the Workhouse; and this House calls upon the
Government to make immediate provision for such cases who in most
instances, owing to age, can be classified
as "Unemployable", and to make full
inquiries into this serious situation in
order that the dangers of poverty may
be removed, in view of the fact that
many workers, through depression in
industry and unemployment, have lost
all benefit rights under National Health
and Pensions, and consequently do not
qualify for pension when reaching
pensionable age, and are thus unprovided for.
I place this Motion before the House
with full knowledge of the actual situation in Northern Ireland. It deals with
our
unemployed workers. I wish to
convey that this in itself is not a political
question but a question of fact. Workers
with long industrial records are treated
by the Assistance Board in a way which
is dangerous to their well-being. Also
the Board is not having due regard to
the fact of the long service given to industry by those workers. I feel that the
Assistance Board by making disallowances under the not normally employed
condition is not looking at this aspect in
a sympathetic way. It is all very well
for the Board to issue instructions to
area offices to disallow men and women
who have reached a certain age as not
being not normally employed although
they have served industry faithfully. I
would like to know why this has been
instituted at the approach of winter. Is

it the desire of the Assistance Board to

that the disallowances which they make

should like to have some information on

I will quote a case which

is made Minister of Public Security, but
still it is rather unfortunate that these
appointments should take place at this
time. The times are too serious. The
proper thing for the former Minister of
Public Security to have done was to say
to the Prime Minister, "I refuse to take
any other office. I am going to remain
Minister of Public Security and look after
the interests of the million and a quarter
people of Northern Ireland." The Government have done a wrong thing in
transferring the Minister of Public
Security to another position, which is
going to bring him some return some day.
We all know that, but I am not concerned
with the return.
What I am concerned about is the new
man who is going into one of the most
important jobs that could be filled in any
country. The Member for Duncairn has
not a grasp of things. It will take him a
considerable time to pick up the threads,
the same as the ex-Minister of Public
Security. It would be incorrect to say
anything else, and I feel sorry that the
Prime Minister has transferred the present Minister in view of the serious
situation that exists. If anything should
happen owing to the change the responsibility must rest on the shoulders of the
Prime Minister. I really thought that
the present Minister of Public Security
was a bigger man than he is. If I had
been in his place I would have seen this
thing through. I would have said to the
Prime Minister, "Much as I treasure the
Attorney-Generalship, which will enable.
me to gain greater laurels I refuse to
take it until the war is over, and then if
the right hon. Gentleman wishes me to
take the same position I will be delighted
to take it." Had he done that he might
have been a Carson of Duncairn.
The PRIME MINISTER: The responsibility for choosing my colleagues in the
Government rests upon me as it rests upon
every other Prime Minister so far as I
know. I am very gratified to find to-day
that there is general approval in this
House of the changes that I have been

1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if
Section 58 of the Defence Regulations is
applicable to employers as well as employees; and whether he can state the
number of employers who have been
brought before the courts under this
section by the Ministry.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Black): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply to this question.
With regard to the first part of the
hon. Member's question, I think the
question is directed to Regulation 58 AA
of the Defence Regulations. Regulation
58 AA is a regulation which enables the
Ministry of Labour to make Orders for
the purpose of endeavouring to prevent
strikes and lock-outs. It applies to employers as well as to employees. With
regard to the second part of the hon.
Member's question, the Ministry of
Labour, under the powers conferred by
Regulation 58 AA, have made an Order
called the Conditions of Employment
and National Arbitration Order (Northern Ireland), 1940. Article 4 of that
Order provides that an employer shall
not declare or take part in a lock-out,
and a worker shall not take part in a
strike in connection with any trade dispute unless the dispute has been reported
to the Ministry and twenty-one days have
elapsed since the date of the report and
the dispute has not during that time.
been referred by the Ministry for settlement. No prosecutions have yet been
instituted against employers for offences
against this Article.

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. MacDermott): The
personnel of the "A" Class Special Constabulary, a whole-time force,
were,

employment, entitled to bounty in lieu

service provided for the payment of
bounty in lieu of pension to Class "B"
personnel mobilised for temporary fulltime duty.

ULSTER'S WAR EFFORT.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he will consider the
advisability of setting up a Parliamentary
Select Committee to devise ways and
means to increase Ulster's war effort.
The PRIME MINISTER: I feel it is
unnecessary to incur needless expense in
setting up a Select Committee of the
House to consider ways and means of increasing Ulster's war effort. The matter
has received and will continue to have
the constant attention of our Government
in association with the British Government. Should any hon. Member, however, desire to make any suggestions on
the matter they will be welcomed.
Mr. NIXON : How can the Prime
Minister say things are satisfactory when
the men engaged in the principal workshops in Northern Ireland at a public
meeting stated and proved that they
could do 100 per cent. more work if
they were allowed, and will the Prime
Minister, who is the head of everything
in Northern Ireland, tell the House
where is the dead hand this time that is
retarding our war effort?
The PRIME MINISTER: I know of
no dead hand, and I feel that our war
effort is creditable.
Mr. NIXON: Will you contradict the
thousands of men who are there and
made that statement, and who are not
satisfied and want to do more with their
own sweat for the war effort?
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
I was in personal touch with the
Imperial representative in the city of
Belfast who was horrified and shocked at
the condition of the war output in Northern Ireland?
The PRIME MINISTER: I have said
I would be very glad if hon. Members
would make helpful suggestions.

AGRICULTURAL CO-OPERATION
IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he has received a Resolution from the Ulster
Ulster Agricultural
Organisation Society asking him to state
whether the Government, under his
leadership, has reversed the policy of
support and encouragement to agricultural co-operation in Northern Ireland; whether this society has, amongst
other agricultural societies, been receiving
grants from the Government since 1921,
amounting in the year 1939-40 to £650,
in the year 1940-41 to £650, and in the
year 1941-42 to £300; whether, in view
of the valuable work carried on by this
society for the benefit of Northern Ireland's greatest industry, the Government
will restore the yearly grant of £650 to
the society.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
I have received a copy of the Resolution mentioned in the hon. Member's
question. There has been no change in
the policy of the Government which
appreciates the services rendered to the
agricultural community by the Ulster
Agricultural Organisation Society. The
need for strict economy during the war,
however, has compelled my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, to
examine very carefully the position with
regard to this and similar grants with a
view to effecting every possible saving.
Circumstances at the moment show little
justification for the continuance of the
grant, but my right hon. Friend has
already assured me should the society be
able to show that any change of circumstances justifies the restoration of a grant
the matter will be reconsidered between
the two Departments. In the meantime I am keeping in close touch with the
hon. Member for North Tyrone who is
chairman of the society.

9. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether representations have been made to him asking
for permission to manufacture calf meal
in Northern Ireland; whether English
firms manufacture this meal and ship it

North of Ireland manufacturers who are
prepared to manufacture this product.
should be debarred from manufacturing
and supplying the North of Ireland
traders, who have a considerable demand
for calf meal.
com-
Lord GLENTORAN: The arrangement
made with both the Northern Ireland and
cross-Channel associations representing
firms manufacturing compounds is that
the only classes of compounds which may
be sold in Northern Ireland are
pounds for dairy cows, pigs and poultry.
I have not since received from either of
these associations or from the Consultative Committee, which was set up by my
Ministry and on which these associations
are represented, any suggestion that calf
meal should be added to the list.
Having regard to the very limited
supplies of imported feeding stuffs, it has
been found necessary to arrange that the
total quantity available for cows should
be utilised for feeding cows producing
graded milk for human consumption.
Provision could be made for calves only
by reducing the quantities of imported
feeding stuffs at present allocated to other
classes of livestock. In present circumstances I think this would be most
undesirable.

Member is no doubt aware, the need for
economy during the war made it necessary
for my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, to insist that this and similar

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Liabilities (War-Time Adjustment)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The measure to which
I invite the attention of the House this
afternoon is intended to provide a method
of relief for persons who are in serious
financial difficulties owing to war circumstances. It was inevitable that the war
would bring about serious dislocation of
trade and commerce. For no fault of
their own, but entirely on account of war
circumstances, business concerns may find
themselves on the brink of insolvency if
they are not, in fact, insolvent.
measure of protection for debtors is
already provided by the Courts
(Emergency Powers) Acts which ensure
that before a creditor can proceed to enforce his rights by execution or other
remedy he must obtain the leave of the
A
2039 Liabilities (War-Time) Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Sir B. Brooke]
Court. The Court can refuse leave if
satisfied that the inability to pay is due
to war circumstances. The full amount
of the indebtedness remains, however,
and may be accumulating.
Consequently, it has been found that
something more than the operation of the
ordinary law under the Bankruptcy Acts,
as qualified in practice by the Courts.
(Emergency Powers) Acts, is required for
the adjustment of indebtedness due to
the exceptional conditions brought about
by the war. This is provided in the Bill
which I am submitting to the House today, and it will, I hope, be of service in
saving some debtors from bankruptcy and
from the loss of their business without
involving the Government in any
penditure beyond the cost of administration.
ex-
I should emphasise that the Bill is not
intended in relief of ordinary debtors,
but only of debtors whose position is due
to war circumstances. There may be
many unfortunate cases of this character,
as, for example, the loss of visitors to
seaside resorts, or the loss of custom
suffered by shopkeepers due to war
damage and the evacuation of their
customers. Under Clause 1 of the Bill
the debtor will be entitled to ask an
officer, who is to be appointed by the
court under the title "Liabilities Adjustment Officer," for advice and assistance
in enabling him to arrive at an equitable
and reasonable scheme of arrangement
with his creditors. Schemes of arrange-.
ment of this character will have special
regard to the desirability of enabling the
debtor to preserve his business or to recover it when circumstances permit.
If a
The Liabilities Adjustment Officer will
give his services in any case where he
considers that they may be of use.
scheme of arrangement is effected through
his services and obtains the assent of the
debtor and all the creditors, he must
approve the scheme and it will become
binding on the creditors. If the agreement of all the creditors is not secured,
but if the majority in number and value.
agree, the Liabilities Adjustment Officer
may approve the scheme subject to the
conditions stated in the
the proviso to
Clause 1, sub-clause (2) of the Bill, which
forbids approval except in a case in which
the court would have jurisdiction to make
a liabilities adjustment order. A dissentient creditor will, however, have the
right to appeal to the court, against the
approval of the scheme of arrangement
carried by a majority of creditors, on the
grounds that it contravenes the provisions of the Act, or that it is inequitable or unreasonable, and the court
will have power to vary or revoke the
scheme.
The appointment of the Liabilities
Adjustment Officer or officers will fall to
be made by the Lord Chief Justice of
Northern Ireland, and for all the purposes of the Bill the court is the High
Court of Justice in Northern Ireland.
It is to be hoped that the services of
the liabilities adjustment officers will
be of great assistance to debtors and
creditors in coming to mutually satisfactory arrangements without direct recourse to the Law Courts. The bringing
of the parties together to discuss their
difficulties will, I am confident, be of
great service, and I am fully confident
that this extension of what I may call
extra-mural law administration will amply
justify itself. If, however, the parties do
not wish to use the services of the liabilities adjustment officer, or if he fails to
secure agreement, direct application may
be made to the High Court. The circumstances in which this direct application may be made are set out in Clause 3
of the Bill.
If the court is satisfied by the application that a prima facie case exists, a
"protection order" may be made to safeguard the debtor and his property from
certain proceedings, and the court may
give directions as to the management and
disposal of the debtor's property, including his business, if any. When satisfied
as to the merits of the case in general,
the court will make a "liabilities adjustment order." This order will make provision for the payment of debts either in
full or in part, and may provide or allow
for the realisation of the debtor's property for the maintenance of the debtor
and his family, and for the retention of premises used as the home of the debtor, and
furniture, bedding, clothing and tools of
his trade. The provisions in this behalf
are contained in Clause 4 of the Bill, and
in Clause 5 the court is empowered to
make provision in its order for the disclaimer of property and rescission of
contracts, and Clauses 4 to 13 deal with
other matters of court powers and con-
2041 Liabilities (War-Time) Bill- 4 NOVEMBER 1941

Second Reading
trol. I should mention that special provision is made in the Bill that nothing
done or suffered by any person under the
Act, when it becomes an Act, will be
deemed to be an act of bankruptcy.
So far I have spoken of debtors as
persons, but Clause 14 brings in partnerships and Clause 15 brings in private
companies whose principal object is to
carry on a business for profit, and whose
object in making the application is to
enable the company to carry on or recover
that business. Provision is made in the
Bill for rules to be made by the Lord
Chief Justice regarding matters of procedure and the fixing of fees payable
under the Bill. Exemption will be given
from Stamp Duties, apart from such fees.
To sum up, the whole scheme of the Bill
is to provide a means of accommodation
as between debtors and creditors, as far
as that may be possible without recourse
to proceedings in bankruptcy. This Bill
follows fairly closely the provisions of
Part 1 of the Imperial measure of this
year bearing the same title. I beg to
move.

of Home Affairs we have a great man,
but so far as housing is concerned it is a
different matter. The attitude of the
Government is shown by the appointment
of an agricultural Member to the position
of Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Labour. I was terribly disappointed in regard to that appointment,
but I expect I will have an opportunity
at a later date of referring to the matter.
It goes to show that the Government of
this country are not fit to deal with
problems affecting the well-being of the
people. If the Cabinet contained men
with brains they would never have
thought of appointing an expert in pigs
to look after such an important department as Labour. That is a sample of
the blunders committed by the Government.
There never was a time when the
question of housing should be dealt.
with more expeditiously than the present.
I can assure the hon. and learned Member
that for over 24 years I have, as a member
of the Corporation, done my utmost to
try to house the people of Belfast in a
decent way. Why? Because I was
brought up in a house which was built
70 or 80 years ago. I know what it is to
live and sleep in a small back room. Even
the three and a half millions spent by
this Government on housing is nothing to
boast about. Look at the sheds built by
tinkers and tailors. There was an army
of these people. Even civil servants built
houses which should never have been
allowed to be erected. I contend that
every house should have a nine-inch wall,
and that that nine-inch wall should
extend to the roof.
You had a sample of what took place.
in recent air raids on the city-rows of
those jerry-built houses were burned out.
People were charged high rents for these
jerry-built houses. I admit that other
people were responsible as well as the
Government for allowing the plans to be
passed. I would not have passed the
plans. Some of these houses were built

I realise the conditions prevailing, conditions which would only be equalled in

I am

I do not wish to do that; I want, constitutionally, to bring the wrath of the
electors of the country down on the

When a Member moves a Motion in

The hon. and learned Member should pay

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: There is no
doubt that everybody is fully agreed that
the housing problem does require consideration now, especially in view of the
problems caused by air raids. I am sure
the whole House is agreed that this
problem requires tackling, but there
appears to be a difference of opinion as to
how this should be done. To my mind
the Motion of the hon. Member for
Shankill is not the best way of dealing
with it. The Amendment put forward by
the hon. Member for the University (Rev.
Professor Corkey) has created the impression among the ordinary men that this is
a delaying Motion. The Government are
in touch with the Imperial Committee,
which is considering rehousing and town
planning problems in England; but the
Imperial Government are not responsible
for the rehousing and town planning of
Northern Ireland. That responsibility
rests with this House, through the Government now in power.
to
There is in existence a committee consisting of the Prime Minister and two
Parliamentary Secretaries, but they have
no experience of architecture, town planning, or engineering. The Members of
that committee have no experience of these
matters, more than any other Members
of this House. Farming Members of this
House, who were very much exercised in
their minds over the matter, brought forward a Motion stating that the Drainage
Acts had become a dead letter. The
Government immediately accepted the
Motion, and agreed to set up a committee
investigate the matter. Here the
Government have not taken that step.
They have instead set up a small committee of two Parliamentary Secretaries
and the Prime Minister. They are all
very busy men, especially the Prime
Minister, and I fail to see how they could
devote the time, even if they had the
knowledge, to deal with this matter. No
doubt the committee set up by the
Imperial Government will give us most
excellent advice, but the problem is a
Northern Ireland problem-it is not a
problem of the Imperial Government'sand we have our own Housing Acts.
The policy adopted in Great Britain
may not be in the least applicable to the
conditions that prevail here.
The impression has been created that
the Amendment proposed by the hon.
Member for the University is one for
delaying action. I am sure the hon.
Gentleman did not intend to create that
impression, but I know that that is a
fact. For that reason I do not intend to
support the Amendment. I hold that a

problem, is the best way to deal with this
matter. The air raids and evacuation
problem have brought to light a condi-

tion of affairs which very few people

Might I say quite frankly that I

of similar committees. In one case-I will
go back to 1937, two years before the war
broke out I was chairman of a committee. That committee made recommendations, and I will tell the House what
they were. One was to recommend a
naval base at Derry, and that similar
measures should be taken to establish an
aircraft factory at Derry. I was also
chairman of another committee which
made a recommendation, again before the
war. I do not intend to refer to it, but
the late Minister of Commerce knows
about it. It was put into a pigeon-hole,
and lay there until the present Minister
of Commerce, the ex-Minister of Agriculture, pulled it out covered with dust, and
it is now being acted upon. I have
inside knowledge of committees set up by
the Government with Parliamentary
Secretaries, and in the cases in which I
was chairman the reports never saw the
light of day. Therefore, it would be far
better to have a committee with Parliamentary members-experts could give
evidence to guide them-than to have a
small committee of persons who are not
experts, who are busy men and have
not the time to deal with this important
matter. I am not going to support the
Amendment now before the House.
Mr. AGNEW: The problem of housing
is one that should be tackled not just
immediately after the war, but at the

20,000 people were actually lying along

here we find an Amendment which actually agrees in delaying action by the

a problem. We are also told that a small
committee has been set up to deal with
this problem, but I feel that a Select
Committee of this House is the only committee that could get down to the real
issues so far as housing is concerned. It
is an immense job. If I might refer to
my own constituency, and start with the
little village of Newtownhamilton, in the
urban district of Keady, where the most
antiquated system of sanitation is in
operation and the types of houses are a
scandal to any authority, even to the
local authority in charge. In order to
get a proper survey, vested interests and
the rights of landlords should not be
taken into consideration.
Let us take the city of Armagh, the
Primatial City. There again we find in
accordance with information supplied
that almost 400 houses are practically
condemned. I feel that if a small
departmental committee is set up, such
as it is, how is it going to read into the
problem the conditions which prevail at
Armagh in view of the fact that the local
organisation to which
to which I belong has
supplied already to the Ministry some
years ago definite proof of the actual
conditions, and also to Mr. Hanna, the

Unfortunately we find to-day a state of
affairs in existence which calls for an

let us look at the progress in so far as

been in Scotland within the last few
years is amazed at the thousands of
houses that have been built. But no
action has been taken by this Government. This Government may tell us a
Housing Act was passed, but that Act is
held up to-day.
In order to get at the root of the evil
I feel instead of the amendment the

and the old slums which prevail shall be

findings of another committee. Let us

The PRIME MINISTER: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: That, in effect, is

welfare of the people of this country?
