Housing Conditions
Housing Conditions
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
were passed for the rehousing of the
people. There was the garden city
scheme, there was the Wheatley scheme,
and I believe there was a scheme brought
forward by the Liberal party.
The Government of Northern Ireland
did not adopt one of those schemes.
There was too much of the socialistic mark
on them for the Government of Northern
Ireland. The Government of Northern
Ireland created a housing scheme that
brought out a class of get-rich people.
They were given subsidies of £140 where
the valuation was so much. Those were
not houses for the working classes. When
the working classes came forward, 550
superficial feet was the area this Government thought was sufficiently good for
them. Now they are going to have to
wait until after the war.
The PRIME MINISTER: No wonder
you are laughing.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not laughing.
This question is too serious.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am always
glad to see you laughing.
Mr. BEATTIE: If I am asked to do a
job, I generally do it well. I was asked
to demand the immediate attention of the
Government to the need for the rehousing
of the people. We want over 20,000
homes rebuilt in a small area in which I
can move about freely without escort.
We cannot wait. We are not going to
have family life broken up because of the
apathy of the Government and because of
its failure to meet existing needs. We
can see around us every day the erection
of many and varied classes of buildings.
I can see business premises and other premises being rebuilt, but I have yet to find
out where any effort has been made by
the Government to rebuild the dwellings
of the people, and to bring them nearer
to one another than they have been for a
long time.
One of the right hon. Gentlemen
opposite has put into operation an evacuation scheme. He believes that that
evacuation scheme is going to take the
place of a scheme for rehousing the people.
He knows that the people will not accept
that evacuation scheme. We cannot have
in Northern Ireland this separation of
family life. We must have the family
brought together again at the earliest.
possible date. The right hon. Gentleman
has provided hostel accommodation, with
the object of bringing men back from their
wives and families in the country. He
erected those houses-and I must say I
agree with him-for emergency conditions; but he found the men would not go
to the hostels; they would not leave their
wives and children. If they could get
into their homes they would come back.
The right hon. Gentleman has put into
force an Order compelling men to leave
their wives and families in the country
owing to the priority and non-priority
billeting allowances. If a husband now
goes to the country to live with his wife
and family in a billet, the man's presence
in the billet stops the billeting allowance
of the whole family. Therefore, the man
is going to be compelled to live away from
his wife and family and to take accommodation in the hostels provided by the
Minister of Labour. We are not accepting that as a solution of the problem confronting us at the present time. We are
grateful for the Minister of Labour's
hospitality in times of emergency; we are
grateful for the evacuation scheme that
provided temporary homes; but we are
not accepting either as a solution of the
problem of restoring us to our homes at
the earliest possible moment.
I say here and now that the sooner the
Government realise what the people want
the better. The national cause is being
affected in our area because of the scattering of the family, and each and every
Member of the Government knows it. If
a man is travelling for two or three hours
night and morning, and is, say, fourteen.
hours away, do you think he does not
suffer from industrial fatigue? Lord
Henry Bentinck, in his Survey of Industrial Fatigue, proves that the fatigue
caused by travelling is more severe on
certain types of people than manual
labour. I say that the national cause is
being affected by your compelling these
people to live outside the area in which
they are employed, and that the sooner
they are restored to their former position
the sooner will be abolished the complaints that we listened to last Thursday
in the Grosvenor Hall from munition
workers and aircraft workers and shipbuilding workers that Ulster is not pulling her weight.
Housing Conditions
Housing Conditions

When I spoke in that hall that night,
I promised them that if they could assure
me that they would give another hundred
per cent. of output I would take ways
and means to compel this Government to
see that the opportunity was given to
them to provide the necessary material
for the fulfilment of our obligations to
our Allies in Russia and to Democracy
as a whole.
The Prime Minister is not
going to give us that opportunity, because he refuses to recognise the first
essential, that a man cannot be at his
best when living away from home out
of the city and away from his wife and
family. I tell the Government that in
the near future they will hear more about
the Amendment they have carried to this
Motion. I will not be silent while I
know there are people living in henhouses, in pig styes, and in dilapidated.
buildings which at one time I would
hardly have gone into.
The Prime Minister knows all about
this, because in the main street of the
town to which he belongs I was offered
billeting accommodation for my family
at an exorbitant rent, and after inspecting the premises I said I would not house
a pig in them. The exorbitant rent I
was asked I once before reported to this
House. The accommodation some of
these people have got in the town of
Comber, and for which they are being
charged high rents, is scandalous and
outrageous and should not be allowed to
exist. I am
much
wondering how
interest the Government has in these
people who are now profiteering from the
homeless state of the people of Belfast.
Large numbers of farmers have a steady
income every week. All their outhouses,
barns, and dilapidated buildings that
usually shelter goats, cattle, and horses
are being used to house people. I wonder
how much interest the Government has
in the owners of that class of building.
They are certainly showing more interest
in their direction than in the direction
of those who have had to sleep in these
places for so many months. The people
stand for justice for all, but I warn the
Government that they will not stand for
the injustice that has been perpetrated on
them since they became homeless.
If we had an election to-morrow 1
know we would have many more North
Downs, and if we get an opportunity in
the near future I think we will be able
to have a repetition of the North Down
result. I believe that if the people in
75 per cent. of our industrial areas had
an opportunity to express their thoughts
through the medium of the ballot box a
very large percentage of the industrial
representatives on the Government side
of the House would disappear from this
House. This is not a question of
political propaganda; it is a question of
hardship on those people who never by
word or deed did anything to bring about
that hardship, which has been brought
about by the apathy of the Government.
I say here fearlessly that anything the
people have suffered is because the Prime
Minister and his colleagues made it possible for these things to happen. Many
times I read speeches made by right hon.
Gentlemen on the Government side of the
House. I knew at the time that those
speeches were not going to be much of a
safeguard for us, and if I could have
found ways and means to closure these
gentlemen I would certainly have done
it. If those who made those speeches
would read them to-day in the light of
the subsequent enemy action they would
be very sorry individuals. I appeal now
to those who are, at any rate, partly
responsible to come forward and give
their support to the rehousing of these.
people, whose homes have been destroyed
as a result of enemy action.
I do not care if there were forty, fifty,
or sixty thousand houses built long ago.
Had it not been for the loss of life I
would have been congratulating some of
these people on losing their little bits of
sticks and bricks and mortar in which
they were accommodated because I would
have expected we would have had a new
housing scheme with houses containing
all modern conveniences But I now find
that although a lot of the old hovels and
shacks are being wiped out we are not
going to have implemented the promise
that was made by the Government that
the people of Ulster would have the same
consideration as the people of Great
Britain in regard to rehousing. I wonder
if they are not carrying out any rehousing scheme in Great Britain. I was
recently speaking to a lady who told me
they were. I asked her what she had
found here, and she replied, “I have not
found anything like the things I have
found across the Channel, because the
social needs and requirements of the
people across the Channel are being at-

That has been the failure of the Government in the past.
Resolved, "That the question be now
put." (Lord Glentoran.)
Resolved, "That this House, realising
the importance of taking all possible steps
in order that it may be in a position to
deal with the housing and town planning
problem under war and post-war conditions, is of the opinion that the Government should ensure, that the closest contact is maintained with the Imperial
authorities and the panel of experts at
present exploring the matter in Great
Britain with a view to securing that Northern Ireland may share in the benefits
of any policy, financial or otherwise,
adopted in Great Britain."

AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): An
additional provision of £57,495 is required to meet the cost of agricultural
services this year, arising chiefly out of
the various activities of the Ministry
directed towards increasing food production. The first item is the Women's
Land Army which was instituted
as partial solution to the labour

handicaps a small but gallant band

and are doing yeoman service. And in
passing I would like to pay tribute to

which rendered such valuable assistance
in this year's harvesting operations.

very prominently to the forefront. In
order to make the various processes and
advantages as widely known as possible
2093 Supplementary Estimates-

Agricultural Services
the Ministry has arranged for the production of a film on the subject depicting suitable methods of making silage.
It is hoped that this film will be seen by
as many farmers as possible.
Hon. Members were, I am sure, relieved when the outbreak of foot-andmouth disease in Co. Londonderry was
finally brought under control. It
proved a costly struggle and the additional sum asked for is needed to discharge the outstanding liabilities to the
General Cattle Diseases Fund in this
connection. I would like to thank all
those who worked so unremittingly in
the fight against this scourage.
The Ministry, following the lead given
by the Imperial Government, introduced
a scheme for encouraging the growth of
allotments under which a deficiency grant
up to £2 per acre was payable in respect
of all new land taken over, and the results have been very gratifying. The
original intention was to recover the cost
of these grants from the Imperial
Department concerned, but as the local
scheme differed in some respects from the
Imperial Scheme
on account of local
conditions, it was ultimately decided
that it would be more appropriate to
meet the charge out of our own vote.
The need for mechanisation of farming to cope with the additional work involved through the increased tillage
operations has continuously engaged the
attention of my Ministry, and every
effort is being made to ensure that ample
supplies of agricultural machinery and
implements are available. Since the
original estimate was presented to the
House it has been found possible to
secure a much greater allocation of
supplies than was contemplated. It is,
therefore, necessary to increase the provision for credit facilities under the
Ministry's Hire-Purchase Scheme. This
scheme has proved of great service, and
since the outbreak of the war 772
tractors and 1,000 tractor-ploughs and
other implements of a total value of some
£241,700 have been purchased under the
scheme alone. The number of tractors
and tractor-ploughs in Northern Ireland
is now five times what it was at the outbreak of the war.

CLASS VIII. No. 4.
CIVIL DEFENCE SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £2,000,000 be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending the 31st March, 1942, to defray the
charges that will come in course of payment for Civil Defence Services including
grants to Local Authorities.”
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
PUBLIC SECURITY (Mr. Maginess):
My right hon. Friend has had to go to
England on urgent public business, and
he has asked me to move this Vote.
When the Minister of Public Security
presented to the Committee the main
Estimate for these services in the early
part of the current financial year, he
asked for a net provision of approximately £2,300,000. Our revised Estimate of the cost of the services for the
current year in the light of such information as we now have before us and of
the probable requirements of the situation
is approximately £4,300,000. I am,
therefore, asking the Committee to vote
an additional provision of £2,000,000.
When the main Estimate was presented
there was a departure from orthodox
Estimates practice in that the sums
which it was proposed to devote to the
various services grouped under the
heading of "Civil Defence" were not
shown in detail. This conforms to
practice in the Imperial House of
Commons in relation to emergency war
services. The decision was taken not
with any desire or intention to keep the
House in the dark with regard either to
our policy or to our expenditure on civil
defence services, but solely with the
object of securing that the enemy might
not obtain in the neatly collated form of
a State document official information
2119 Supplementary Estimates--

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Civil Defence Services
[Mr. Maginess]
with regard to our civil defence plans,
which might be of use to him in his prosecution of the war against us.
I ought, however, to make it clear to
the Committee that, when the time
comes, the Department will account for
the sums which the Committee has voted
for these services in just as full detail as
if the form in which the Estimate was
presented to Parliament were the form
to which the Committee, by long usage,
has become accustomed. The accounts
will be audited in the usual way by the
Comptroller and Auditor-General; the
Public Accounts Committee will be
given full information of the detailed expenditure; in short, the usual procedure
will be followed.
I am able to give the Committee
certain information on broad general
lines as to how the amount of the supplementary provision of £2,000,000 now
asked for is made up. More than half
is being devoted towards the cost of the
air-raid shelter programme in Northern
Ireland. An improvement in the supply
position has enabled us to embark on an
acceleration of the programme for construction of shelters in areas outside the
County Boroughs of Belfast and Londonderry. The rising cost of materials has
added to the estimated cost of the
original programme, and in the light of
experience we have considered it desirable
to strengthen, and in some cases replace,
shelters that had already been
structed. A sum has also been included
for the equipment of shelters with certain
essential amenities for those who use
them.
con-
Of the remainder of the additional provision asked for a substantial figure is
devoted towards the cost of demolition of
buildings and clearance of debris within
the County Borough of Belfast to meet
the situation which arose after the two
serious air raids in April and May. But
the cost of the altered arrangements that
will be brought about by new fire prevention services accounts for the bulk of the
remainder.
It is intended shortly to make a new
Order under the. Defence Regulations
dealing with this whole question of fire
prevention, so far as it concerns business
premises. It is proposed to place upon
the occupier the obligation to pay the fire
prevention personnel actually required to
be on duty subsistence allowances and
additional travelling expenses directly
arising out of fire prevention duties, and
also to provide certain amenities by way
of sleeping accommodation and otherwise.
The amounts of subsistence allowance to be
paid by the occupier will be laid down in
the Order as follows:-3s for a tour of
duty not exceeding 12 hours; 4s 6d for a
tour of duty exceeding 12 hours but not
exceeding 18 hours, and 6s for a tour of
duty exceeding 18 hours but not exceeding
24 hours. These are the rates which have
been fixed in respect of similar duties
under the fire prevention scheme in Great
Britain, after negotiations between the
Government and representatives of the
Trade Union Congress. The Minister has
been in consultation with representatives
of labour in Northern Ireland, who have
expressed their concurrence with the
arrangements which are being made.
It has been decided in Great Britain
that the cost of subsistence allowances
reasonably incurred by occupiers will be
made good to them by the Exchequer,
and I am able to announce that the
Government of Northern Ireland has
decided to do the same as respects the
cost of subsistence allowances in Northern
Ireland. The arrangements will come
into effect from a date some weeks ahead,
which will be the date of operation of the
new Fire Prevention Order. I beg to
move.

easily appreciated by the ordinary layman. The hon. Member will remember
that there was an attempt made to pass

I am sure the hon. Member will appreciate that in making an Order about firewatching or fire prevention one has to
guard against so many possibilities that
it is a practical impossibility to make it
very short or very terse. We do the best
we can, but it is beyond the power of
man to frame an Order that would go into
small compass and yet cover all the points
that were raised. I quite admit that the
hon. Member's play on the words "voluntary" and "compulsory" was quite
justified, because it rather suggests that,
in fact, the voluntary scheme is compulsory and the compulsory scheme is voluntary. I think that is what the hon.
Member meant, but he will appreciate
that where there is-as, of course, there
is a duty upon the owner of the premises
to have it properly fire-watched, he can
say to his employees, "Do not you bother
about this. I will bring in twelve men of
my own, or whatever the required
number is, "and I will have this place
fire-watched."
That is, after all, a voluntary offer
upon his part; that is to say, he went outside the framework of the Order, which
he was permitted to do, and brought in
outsiders. That was a voluntary act on
his part, and that, of course, entitles it
to be called a voluntary scheme. Whereas
a scheme within the framework of the
Order, that is, in which the owner of the
premises had to do it, would be known
as a compulsory scheme, although, in
fact, the assistance and the fire-watching
of the personnel might well be voluntary
on their part.
I am afraid the hon. Member, if I took
him up correctly, was under the impression that civil servants do not do firewatching, but I think I can assure the
hon. Member that civil servants are like
other employees; that is, they have to do
their turn of fire-watching just the same
as everybody else.

DEATH OF MR. JAMES KELTERS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Lord Glentoran.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I desire to raise a
question of which I gave private notice to
the Minister of Labour. Inadvertently it
was overlooked at question time, but I
will put the question to him now. It is,
whether he is aware that James Kelters,
24 Linden Street, Belfast, was compelled
to proceed to Birmingham on last Thursday night to take up employment, after
protesting that he was unfit to travel; is
he aware that this man was examined by
a Government doctor and declared fit;
whether he is aware that Mrs. Kelters received a telegram on Monday, the 3rd,
from the master of Birmingham Infirmary,
stating "Regret that James Kelters died
at Birmingham Infirmary on Monday,
3rd"; what action is the Minister prepared to take with the medical officer,
whose incompetence has been responsible
for creating such great hardship on the
family of deceased; whether he will have
said gentleman immediately removed from
Death of Mr. J. Kelters
Death of Mr. J. Kelters
5 NOVEMBER 1941
the panel of medical referees, so as to save
many others from the tragedy that has
befallen James Kelters; and is he prepared to meet the costs of the return of
the corpse and of expenses attached
thereto, and compensate Mrs. Kelters for
the loss of the head of the household.
I know the tragic circumstances that
surrounded other cases of a similar kind,
including the case of a boy who lost his
life through being deported to Great
Britain to work which was injurious to
his health. This is the third case that I
have brought before this House. Here is
a man who was compelled by the doctor to
cross to Birmingham last Thursday night
against the family wishes because of his
ill-health. He was certified by his own
doctor as being fit only for light work,
but nevertheless the labour exchange submitted him to a representative of the
Birmingham firm for work, and the
Birmingham firm, I understand, sent him
to a doctor who certified him as fit to
travel to England to take up this work. I
think it has now been proved that the
doctor who certified him as fit to travel
was wrong, and that he is not fit to
certify workmen who refuse to go to work
in Great Britain.
The death of this man has brought
great hardship on the family, and I want
to know if the right hon. Gentleman is
prepared to pay the full cost of the
return of the corpse so that he may at
least be buried in his own burial ground.
Is he also prepared to pay the additional
cost that will have to be incurred by the
family of this man, and will he consider
granting compensation to the widow in
the tragic circumstances of the loss of her
dear husband. I want to refrain from
saying anything against medical officers.
At times we all appreciate their services,
but I do think that the system of examination as carried out at present is wrong.
I have known of cases sent to the medical
officer to certify whether or not they were
fit to travel, and all he did was to look at
their eyes and ask them to put out their
tongue. I think that when a family
doctor has given a certificate to say that
Tom or Dick or John or Mary or Jane
is unfit to travel to England it should be
accepted, because he knows the family
history and is therefore the best judge.
The Government doctor has never
attended them in their life before, and
for him to certify them may endanger
their health and their life. If the advice
of the family doctor had been taken in
this case, this man might have been living
to-day. But he was compelled to cross the
water last Thursday night, when the poor
man was not fit to travel. The circumstances are as I have mentioned in the
question. The widow got a telegram
which said: "Birmingham. Mrs. Kelters,
24 Lindon Street, Belfast. Regret James
Kelters died at Birmingham Infirmary on
Monday, 3rd. Will you please wire reply.
Master of Birmingham Infirmary."

whole thing is a tragedy, and one that

Question, "That this House do now

REPLY FROM MR. EDEN.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to inform the
House that I have heard from Mr. Eden,
Foreign Secretary, in reply to the letter I
wrote at the request of the House:
I write to thank you very much for
your letter of October 28th, in which
you were so good as to forward to me,
at the request of the Northern Ireland
House of Commons, a resolution of congratulations to the Soviet Union.
I shall have great pleasure in passing
on the text of the resolution to the
Soviet Ambassador, for transmission to
his Government.
Yours sincerely,
Anthony Eden.

vacancy for a junior assistant mistress

WELSH COAL FOR NORTHERN
IRELAND.
3. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Commerce whether it is a fact
that in future Welsh coal is to be imported
in increased quantities into Northern
Ireland; whether he is aware of a feeling
of apprehension that this kind of coal
will be unsuitable for householders in
Northern Ireland, and whether he will
make representations to the Minister of
Mines regarding this matter.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Basil Brooke): I am glad of the opportunity afforded by the hon. Member's
question to inform the House generally of
the position with regard to the importation into Northern Ireland of coal from
South Wales.
For reasons directly connected with the
prosecution of the war effort, it has been
necessary for the Minister for Mines to
arrange for the discontinuance of supplies
of coal to Northern Ireland from the
Lancashire and Midland districts of
England, and to substitute therefor coal
from South Wales. When I learned of
the decision of the Mines Department to
discontinue supplies of coal from certain
English coalfields I saw the Minister for
Mines and discussed with him and his
advisers the whole question of supplies for
Northern Ireland. As a result of these
discussions I am satisfied that the action
taken is unavoidable at the present juncture, and that Northern Ireland is not
being asked to use coal which is not also
being used in certain English districts into.
which South Wales coal has never previously been imported.
I am aware that some apprehension may
exist regarding the suitability of Welsh
coal for domestic use in Northern Ireland
and, following representations to the
Minister for Mines on this aspect of the
question, arrangements were made for a
member of the South Wales Coal Control
Board to visit Northern Ireland. This
gentleman, who was accompanied by
experts in the use of South Wales coal,
recently spent a week in Northern Ireland
and following the discussions which he and
colleagues had with coal importers,
merchants and a number of industrial coal
users, I understand that difficulties originally foreseen in the use of this coal for
domestic and industrial purposes are likely
to be overcome.
Mr. THOMPSON: Is it a fact that
many factories in Northern Ireland as a
result of having to use this coal will have
to close down altogether, unless they have
a very special apparatus to burn this coal?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am not aware
of that.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY: Is the Minister
aware that there are a large number of
Dobey stokers fitted to power plants and
that this coal cannot be used in these
stokers?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I do realise
that there are certain difficulties connected
with the burning of this coal and that is
the reason why the Minister of Mines at
my request sent over experts to look into
this question with the industrialists.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: May I ask is
there any other district apart from
Northern Ireland where it is contemplated
that no coal but Welsh coal will be available.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: There will be
other coal in addition to Welsh coal in
Northern Ireland. The same position
does exist in other districts in England.
Mr. THOMPSON: Will the right hon.
Gentleman please see that when this
gentleman comes across he will interview
a number of factory owners at the same
time, so that they may put their views
before him?
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the right
hon. Gentleman say whether any notification was sent by this Ministry to let the
Government know that this was taking
place and whether he can state if there is
a stock of English coal in Northern Ireland?

difficult harvest season, whereby my Ministry is

fact that a great deal of the harvest is lost

BILLETING ALLOWANCES.
Mr. BEATTIE (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether it is a fact that billeting allowance to all homeless people has been
stopped for the weeks ending the 1st and
8th November; whether due notice of this
stoppage was given through the Post
Office, and whether the Minister can state
is the stoppage due to his Department
requiring certain information, and would
it not have been more charitable for the
Minister to send out a questionnaire with
the questions he desired answered and, in
the meantime, continue paying the allowances as heretofore. Are the questions
(1) Your wages (net) including overtime.
at present and prior to billeting; (2) If
you are prepared to pay the full amount
of billeting fees, state "Yes"; (3) If you
are prepared to offer the full amount or
weekly payments state the amounts? Will
the Minister give immediate instructions
for the continuation of payment or is he
prepared to offer suitable homes to these
unfortunate people?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The payment
of billeting allowances in respect of homeless people is intended to be a purely temporary measure operating only until their
house has been repaired, and they are able
to return home, or they obtain accommodation of their own, or make their own
financial arrangements with their hosts.
Billeting notices in respect of homeless
persons are, therefore, issued only for an
initial period of two weeks in the first
instance.
There may be circumstances in which
the re-issue of a billeting notice may be
justified, but when a homeless person
continues to be billeted after the initial
period of two weeks it is obvious that
inquiries must be instituted to ascertain
whether or not the billeting allowance
should continue and whether recovery of
the allowance in whole or in part from
the persons billeted should be effected.
The hon. Member will appreciate that if
the billeted person's liability in respect of
the original home has ceased or diminished
and additional expenditure has not been
incurred by living in the new surroundings, the question of recovery of the billeting allowance must necessarily arise.
Oral Answers
Ministries Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
After the air raids on Belfast a very
substantial number of billeting notices
were issued in respect of homeless people,
and in view of the circumstances obtaining
at the time the validity of these notices
was not confined to two weeks. The
Ministry, however, is now taking steps to
review all billeting notices, and the questionnaire to which the hon. Member refers
must be furnished by all persons who consider that a further extension of the billeting allowances should be made in their
case.
Each case will be considered on its
merits as rapidly and sympathetically as
possible. In any case in which a billeting
allowance is discontinued, payment will
cease as from the date of the decision by
the Ministry's officers and a final payment
will be made to cover the period between
the date on which payment was stopped
by the post office and the date of the
Ministry's decision.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to ask the right
hon. Gentleman did he duly notify the

will be granted? Is it a fact that the

Sir DAWSON BATES: The conditions
here are exactly the same as in Great
Britain. The hon. Member will see from

for purposes connected with the matters

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): The number of liability
adjustment offices and the number of staff
to be appointed will necessarily be determined by the number of cases arising for
adjustment and settlement under this Bill,
and it is accordingly not possible to say
how much money will be expended from
public funds, but it is not expected the
amount will be large. For the information of the Committee I may say that
under the similar Measure in Great
Britain the number of cases brought under
this machinery have been surprisingly
small, indeed. I hope that in Northern
Ireland we may be equally fortunate. I
beg to move.

Another matter to which the hon.
Member for South Down referred
whether it would be easy and convenient
to have a jurisdiction up to £50 available in the county courts. Of course,
proceedings under this Bill will not be
ordinary suits. When one is suing for
a debt one can say at once whether the
sum sued for is over or under £50. Anyone who has had experience of bankruptcy or arrangement matters knows that
one of the difficulties to be overcome is
to know exactly what is the sum involved,
to ascertain the creditors, and to find out
whether the amount in question can be
proved or not.
A further point which, I think, the
hon. Member has overlooked is that in
the county courts in Northern Ireland at
present, with the exception of the
Recorder's Court in Belfast, there is no
bankruptcy jurisdiction at all. The jurisdiction in the Belfast Court has not been
exercised, I think, since 1921. To provide a
county court with jurisdiction would mean
establishing staffs in every county court
in Northern Ireland. It is also advisable,
I think, that there should be in this Bill
uniformity of procedure, particularly
having regard to the special provisions
for adjustment by adjustment officers;
uniformity of procedure which could be
accomplished much more easily were the
proceedings taken in a court which is at
present equipped to deal with such
matters.
Another matter which arises is that in
the county court one sues in the place
where the defendant resides, but in a case
under this Bill one might be dealing with
many creditors as well as with many
debtors, and what might be convenient
for one might be inconvenient for others.
On the whole balance of the argument, I
am satisfied that not only would the Act
be more complicated, but would be less
useful if the county courts were accorded
jurisdiction in addition to the high court.

printed, but not sent out, two Estimates
appeared. The Estimate of the Minister
of Home Affairs is recorded in the Journal
as having been passed by this House last
Tuesday. The Estimate of the Minister
of Public Security, which was passed,
appears in the Records as not having been
passed. What is the position in regard
to the Estimate of the Ministry of Public
Security, seeing it appeared in the Records
of the House as not having been passed by
the House? This is the first point on
which I should like a ruling from you.
Mr. SPEAKER: In this case, through
an error on the part of the Clerk, or a
typist's error, a Vote was recorded as
having been passed, when it was not considered. As a matter of fact, the headings
of the two Estimates were somewhat
similar. The mistake was detected by the
Clerk, who took the necessary steps in
time, and the Votes and Proceedings containing the error were not circulated.
Therefore no question arises at all in this
matter.

Eire Workers-

11 NOVEMBER 1941
EIRE WORKERS IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
Mr. HENDERSON : I gave
the
Minister of Labour notice some time ago
that I wished to raise on the Motion for
the Adjournment the question of his
bringing people from over the Border
into Northern Ireland. I am told on
reliable authority that there is a gentleman in Derry acting as liaison officer in
the importation of labour from the Free
State. Is that true or is it not? Instructions were given to this gentleman
to bring people over the Border. I cannot understand the mentality of the
Minister of Labour or of the Government. Not so long ago the Border was
in danger. From whom? From the
very men and women you are bringing
over the Border now. Have you changed
your policy? Will the Minister of
Labour tell the House how it comes that
male and female labour can come into
Northern Ireland from over the Border
-I am speaking of unskilled labour-at
a time when there are thousands of unemployed male and female workers in
Northern Ireland?
There are thousands of adults, both
men and women, idle in Northern Ireland, and only the other day a Shankill
Road man, who had been out of work
for four years, came to me to see if I
could get him a job. Yet the Unionist
Government of this country are aiding
and abetting people to come from
Southern Ireland to the detriment of the
Ulster workers. Where is your loyalty
now? The Minister of Labour cannot
dispute the fact that in the courts the
other day certain persons were fined for
coming into Northern Ireland without an
identity card or any other form of permit,
and the magistrate fined them 40s. What
was the Minister of Public Security and
his officials doing to allow these people
to come into Northern Ireland? Would
it not be a startling thing if the German
Consul in Dublin came to Belfast and
got some technical job in one of our
factories? I feel very strongly on this
matter. I have nothing to say about
people who come from Southern Ireland
so long as they come in through the
Ministry of Labour to assist the Ulster
people at this particular time, but I
strongly protest against anyone being
brought from any part of the world to
take work from the Ulster people.
were
Think what the workers of this
Province have come through during the
past 23 years owing to the pure neglect
of the Government, and now, when there
is a war, people are allowed to come
into Northern Ireland from other places
and get employment to the detriment of
the workless people of Ulster. Something is seriously wrong, and I hope the
Minister of Labour will explain his
policy on this question. If I
Minister of Labour I would see that every
male and female worker in Ulster was
employed before I brought in people from
outside. If there was a surplus of work
then I would bring in people from outside provided they were loyal citizens. It
is a strange policy the Minister of Labour
has adopted. Only a short time ago he
was packing loyal men and women from
Ulster off like cattle to England and
other places across the water, and allowing them to drift anywhere.
What about recalling these people?
Many of the married men in England are
anxious to get home again to their wives
and families, but they are not allowed to
do so.
If there is war work here for them
to do the Minister of Commerce should
have enough influence to have them freed
from their work in England and returned
to Belfast. The policy of this Government has always been to shout, "Mind
the border. It is in danger of invasion
from the Free State." Yet the loyalists
of Northern Ireland are allowed to starve
while the Government brings in people
from across the border to work here. I
was told that the Ministry of Labour had
engaged a Mr. McGlinchey, in Derry, to
bring unskilled workers into Northern
Ireland from the Free State. Why this
sudden change of policy? This is a matter
that is causing grave concern in Northern
Ireland. You hear it being talked about
everywhere. Only the other day a man
from the Grosvenor Road asked me if I
could get him employment. I told him to
go to his own representative and get a
nomination card for employment with the
Corporation. He replied, "Are there not
hundreds of men from the Free State
working in Belfast on the demolition of
buildings and the clearance of sites? Why
should I have to go to my representative
for a nomination card?" I told him that
was the policy here.
Every unemployed person in Northern
Ireland should go to the Ministry of

Mr. HENDERSON: Then is the

Mr. GORDON: I will come with you.
Mr. HENDERSON: I am delighted.
If the right hon. Gentleman reads the
papers he will find girls have come in
from the South of Ireland without even
identity cards and have got employment
for three or four weeks before they were
caught. Could not these girls-I am not
saying they were-have been sent by the

Why are they kept prisoners while

Minister tell me why the Government
changed their policy? I feel I would not
be doing my duty if I did not draw attention to this. Even the Minister of Agriculture stated in this House it did not
matter whether they had a Southern
brogue, a Scotch brogue, or an English
brogue.
I love the Welsh people, the English
people, the Irish Free State people and
the people of Northern Ireland. I love
everybody, whether black or white, in the
world. I even love the Prime Minister,
though he may not think it. The bird
sitting on the nest does not feed the birds
in the other nests. She feeds her own
brood first. That is what I want. Ulster

you get your house in order I will be the
first to compliment you. On behalf of
the Loyalists who are running about idle
and coming through hard times, I protest
against the changed policy of this once
Unionist Government in importing labour
to the detriment of those living here.

12 NOVEMBER 1941
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 12th November, 1941.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
HEALTH OF INTERNEES.
Mr. CAMPBELL (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs if he
is aware of the deep uneasiness among
the relatives of a number of internees in
Belfast Prison regarding the health and
clothing of these men; whether the question of the health of several of them has
become acute, and whether any of them
are victims of tuberculosis.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): If there is any deep
uneasiness among the relatives of the
internees now in Belfast Prison regarding the health and clothing of these men
I can assure the hon. and learned Member that there is no occasion for it. The
general health of these men is good, and
apart from minor ailments such as
common colds, etc., there is no cause for
any anxiety. I am glad to say that there is
no case of active tuberculosis among the
internees in the prison at the present
time.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Might I ask if in
case any of these men contracted serious
ill-health would the Minister allow the
men's own medical doctor to see them?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think that
is rather a reflection on our own doctor
who is one of the best medical men in
Belfast. Of course, in a serious case
where they might require a specialist I
am sure there would be no objection.
Own
Mr. CAMPBELL: The man's
doctor, who is familiar with his patient's
ailments, very often is able to give great
assistance to the official in charge. There
is no reflection on him.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Very often
his own doctor is wrong.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman define the protection and safeguards for internees in Crumlin Road,
and will he state whether the board of
visitors or visiting justices have the
power or right to go into the part of the
prison where the internees are living and
examine them or receive any complaints
in regard to their welfare, food,
other matters?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.

CLASS III. No. 6.
CIVIL DEFENCE (HEALTH)
SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £156,000 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1942, to defray the charge that
will come in course of payment for Civil
Defence (Health) Services."
Sir DAWSON BATES: As hon.
Members will have seen from the Estimates, a sum of £156,000 is required for
services administered by my Department.
This sum is made up of two sums of
£100,000 and £56,000 respectively, the
former figure representing the estimated
cost up to the 31st March next of the
carrying out of a scheme for augmenting
existing hospital accommodation throughout the Province, and the latter representing the estimated cost of erecting and
equipping huts on the outskirts of the city
of Belfast for what are known as
"ditchers" or "ins-and-outers."
Civil Defence (Health) Services 2228
Supplementary Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The scheme of expansion provides for
the erection of hospital huts, for their
equipment and for the laying on of water
and sewerage arrangements. In order to
complete the scheme upon which my
Department has embarked, a further
£100,000 will be required, the completed
scheme providing for the erection of 50
complete hospital huts representing
accommodation for approximately 2,500
patients.
It is, I suggest, hardly necessary for me
to give the House the reasons which have
compelled my Department to undertake
this scheme. Hon. Members are aware
that as the result of air-raids on the city
of Belfast in April and May last, a considerable part of the normal population of
Belfast has moved into safer areas in the
country. This increased population in the
country has called for the expansion of all
existing public health services, not least of
which is the provision of extra hospital
accommodation. When the need for this
additional hospital accommodation became obvious my Department at once got
in touch with the appropriate Department in Whitehall with a view to ascertaining if hospital hutments similar to
those in use in military hospitals could
be made available to the Government of
Northern Ireland. I might say at once
that my Department was facilitated in
every possible way in this matter, and
hospital hutments were placed at its disposal in accordance with the demands
made upon the Imperial authorities. Up
to the present 29 complete hospital hutments have been delivered, representing
accommodation for approximately 1,500
patients. It is proposed to erect the huts
in the grounds of existing provincial
hospitals, and it is hardly necessary for
me to state that the Government has been
assisted in every possible way in the carrying out of this programme by the local
authorities and other bodies responsible
for hospital administration in
Province.
the
In the first place it is proposed to provide additional hospital accommodation in
the areas where the greatest increase in
population has taken place, and, consequently, where the demand for additional hospital accommodation is most
acute. Steps have been taken for the
immediate erection of the hospital huts in
a number of these areas. With regard
to the details of the figure of £100,000
which is included in this supplementary
estimate, this figure, as I have already
indicated, represents expenditure which
my Department estimate will be incurred
up to the 31st March next and will provide for the erection of 25 complete
hospital units costing roughly £4,000
each. The cost of each unit is made up
as follows:-The actual hut and the necessary equipment to be installed therein will
cost approximately £2,000, while a further
sum of £2,000 will be required to erect
the hut, install the equipment therein and
to provide essential services, such as
water and sewerage therefor. It will be
appreciated, however, that the cost of
each hospital unit will vary according to
the nature of the site on which the hutment is erected and the proximity of
water and sewerage facilities.
My Department in deciding on the
number of huts required to meet the
additional demands placed on existing
hospital accommodation in the Province
have been guided by the best medical
advice and, while it is hoped that the
additional accommodation will not be
taxed to the utmost, it is felt that it is
better to provide a generous margin of
accommodation in order to be in a position
to deal with any emergency which may
arise in the future.
For the information of the House, I
may add that the additional accommodation which is being provided will be available not only for the increased civil population in the various provincial areas, but
will also be available for those members of
the services who require medical or
surgical treatment and who cannot be
accommodated in existing service hospi
tals.
The total cost of this scheme will,
of course, be recoupable to the Northern
Ireland Government by the Imperial
Treasury.
So much for additional hospital accommodation. I now come to the second item
for which this additional estimate is
required, namely, £56,000, to cover the
cost of the erection and equipment of huts
on the outskirts of Belfast for those people
who, though not homeless, will not sleep
in their houses, and go out each night to
seek shelter in the safer quarters, returning to their own houses in the morning.
The Government has given the question
of making provision for these people very
careful consideration, and has had to face

not have been rendered uninhabitable,

may
the construction of these shelters
naturally takes time, and the Government felt that if it could not provide
adequate protection for the people in the
streets or houses in which they lived, it
would have to provide alternative accommodation for them in a safer area. I
am glad to say that the Ministry of

to provide this

I should like to make it very clear,
however, that the Government by its
policy of erecting these huts is not
weakening at all in its determination
that houses in the city should not be
left unprotected and at the mercy of the
incendiary bomb. The huts, which are
being erected, will only be available for
those people who live in the more
dangerous parts of the city, and applications to use them will be carefully
scrutinised by the billeting officers before
a permit is issued. It is still the wish
of the Government that as many of the
priority classes as possible should be
evacuated to the rural districts, and I
hope that parents will, at any rate, allow
their children to be evacuated to areas
where they are less likely to have to
undergo the dangers and horrors of
bombing.
The huts are being erected at ten sites
close to the end of the tram lines on the
various outlets from the city. One
hundred and fifty-seven huts are being
erected on these ten sites, of which 110
are already erected, and the remainder
in course of erection. In addition to this
157, 143 huts have been provided by the
Government to the Belfast Civil Defence
Authority for erection as additional
a
I should just like to point out in conclusion that these huts for the ins-andouters are in addition to and completely
outside the official evacuation scheme
which has been prepared by my Ministry,
and which will go into operation after
any future air raid. Each site for the
huts will be under the control of
marshal, who will be responsible for the
control and supervision of the refugees
making use of the huts. The majority
of the huts in each group will be set
aside for regulars," although casual
visitors will not be turned away if there
is accommodation, but if they wish to
have accommodation for more than one
night they will have to obtain a permit
from the nearest billeting officer. I am
quite sure that the Committee will support the Government in making a provision of this kind. I beg to move.

AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): It would not be
natural if I did not admit that the
Minister is very gratified at the very
favourable reception which this Estimate
has received in the Committee. The sum
of £100,000 for emergency hospital
services has received general commendation, and equally so the provision of huts
for people called "Ditchers" or "In and
Outers.' Several hon. Members have
sought information on a number of points,
and I shall do my best to supply it. The
Member for Pottinger emphasised a
matter about which we are in agreement,
namely, the desirability of the restoration
of family life as much as possible. It
must be remembered that the "Ditcher"
huts are not suitable and were not
intended for family life. For the object
the hon. Member has in view, some of
the very large camps were started, and
that object has been kept clearly before
our minds, and an endeavour will be
made to meet the suggestion of the hon.
Member in that direction. A notable
instance of that is the very large undertaking we have in the neighbourhood of
the city of Londonderry.
12 NOVEMBER 1941 Civil Defence (Health) Services 2242
Supplementary Estimates-
The Member for Pottinger also expressed a natural anxiety about the
supervision of the huts for "Ditchers"
immediately around the city of Belfast.
It is our intention to have every one of
these huts under the supervision of
marshals of both sexes. They will not
be in any way under the control of those
who are responsible for billeting money.
If any abuse has taken place in connection with the payment of public money
it will be their duty to report it. The
marshals will look after the cleanliness of
the huts and see that everything is done
for the health and comfort of the people
as far as can reasonably be done in such
circumstances.
A matter to which the hon. Member for
Pottinger and also the hon. Member for
North Down drew attention was the possibility of utilising these hospital huts for
the relief of congestion in the Belfast city
hospitals. I am sorry to say that that
would be completely against the law. We
cannot use the evacuation scheme for the
purpose of relieving a long-standing
congestion.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. and learned Member. You
must remember that at the moment there
are blitzed victims in the Ballymena
hospital. I have a friend in that hospital
since the last blitz. There are victims of
the blitz in the Royal Victoria Hospital
and the Infirmary. Other hospitals have
a certain percentage of blitz victims. If
you could get these people into the
hospitals you are erecting it would ease
the situation.
Mr. LOWRY: The hon. Member having
amplified the matter and explained exactly
what he meant I can say that these people
will come within the scheme and the
hospitals can be used when the occasion
arises. I rather gathered-perhaps I did
him an injustice-from the hon. Member
for North Down that there was a long
waiting list of some 900 in connection with
the Royal Victoria Hospital, and that it
was for the purpose of relieving this congestion he suggested that the huts might
be used. These hospitals cannot be used
for non-blitz victims. We could not use
the huts erected in the neighbourhood of
Newtownards for that purpose.
As has already been explained by the
Minister we are merely agents for the
Ministry of Health, and in honour and
decency as agents-I am sure the hon.
Member for North Down will agree with
me in this-we must play the game fairly
and squarely. Of course there are other
things for which provision has been made.
-maternity requirements. We will assist
in the way hon. Members have in their

value.

It may well be that in the process of

it will be set right with the utmost
promptitude. There is no desire to
press those who find themselves

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 18th November, 1941.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Ministry of Finance:

Oral Answers to Questions.
SHORTAGE OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOUR.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has set up a Committee to advise him on the best means of
finding a solution to the problem of the
shortage of labour for agriculture, and
whether he can state the names and qualifications of the members of this Committee.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): No, sir, I have not set
up any such Committee. Plans for dealing with this problem are being worked
out by a sub-committee of the Cabinet in
collaboration with the departments concerned.
PRICE OF FLAX.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether, in the event of no
decision having yet been reached in the
matter of increased prices of flax, he will
transmit to the Ministry of Supply a copy
of the statement in the linen industry
review in the "Belfast News-Letter" of
7th instant, stating that "there are many
difficulties to be faced, one of which is the
delay in the settlement of the official
prices to be paid by the Government to
farmers for their 1941 flax crop, and the
consequent inability of spinners to estimate corresponding yarn quotations";
and whether, in the event of a result having been reached in the matter he can
state whether his Ministry approves of
such result.
"
Lord GLENTORAN: The hon. Member
will have seen the statement which I
released to the Press yesterday and will
appreciate that I have nothing to add to
it at this stage.
Mr. BROWN: Might I ask the noble
Lord whether there will be any increase
to those who have sold or will sell flax as
green straw?
Lord GLENTORAN: At the moment
that matter is under consideration.
PLOUGHING UP OF NEW GRASS.
3. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state if it is a fact that his Ministry are
going to compel farmers to plough up new
grass sown down in 1941, and whether he
is aware that a great many farmers
responded to the call for more tillage in
1940-41 and ploughed up their entire
farms and have sown them down in new
grass in the expectation that this would
count as tillage crop in 1942; and whether
he will consider making such exception
to the order as will afford relief to those
farmers named above and thereby save
this valuable crop.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am not aware
that many farmers have in 1940 and 1941
ploughed up their entire holdings and
have sown them down in the expectation
that first year's grass or hay would be
recognised as cultivation in 1942. On the
contrary I am satisfied that the number
of such farmers is very limited, indeed.
In any instance where all the arable land
on a holding was laid down to grass in
1941, the Ministry is prepared to consider
the case on its merits having regard to
all the circumstances.
In view of the necessity for increasing
the area under primary food crops the
hon. Member will appreciate that the
method outlined in his question is not one
to which my Ministry could lend any
encouragement.
INTERIM PAYMENTS FOR FLAX.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether any promise was
given by his Ministry or by anybody acting with their knowledge and approval
that growers of flax would be given
advance of interim payments at various
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
18 NOVEMBER 1941
had
stages, such as when the crop
brairded, etc.; whether this promise was
carried out, and, if so, in how many
cases and by whom; and, if not, whether
he can state why it was not carried out;
whether the Ministry received any applications in connection with the matter,
and how same were dealt with; and
whether he can state how many flaxgrowers this season will have to wait
until next year for their money and why
they will have to do so.
Lord GLENTORAN: The scheme for
interim payments at brairding and at
harvest is part of the contract between
the green fibre processing firms and the
farmers who supply flax as green straw
to them, and is not, therefore, a matter
with which this Ministry is concerned.
In the early part of the year it was
clear that a fairly large number of
farmers were reluctant to grow flax for
such factories until they were certain of
a factory being established within
marketing distance of their farms. Moreover, there was considerable delay in the
green fibre processors and the Ministry of
Supply coming to terms. In order that
such delay should not reduce the acreage
sown to flax, I issued an appeal to
farmers not to delay a decision until they
knew for certain about the erection of
the factories, and I assured them on behalf of the Government that a market
would be found for those who could not
ret and grew green flax straw for sale.
Accordingly, by means of Press
advertisements, I invited all farmers who
were unable to ret their flax and must
sell as green straw, and who had not
made a contract with a green processing
firm, to send the Ministry the necessary
particulars by the end of June.
In response 657 farmers asked the Ministry to
make arrangements for the disposal of
their flax as green straw, and the Ministry has arranged for 522 of them to be
linked with their appropriate processing
firm as if they had contracted in the first
instance they will, therefore, receive
the interim payment referred to by the
hon. Member.
With regard to the balance of 135, it is
hoped that they will be dealt with.
similarly within a short time. In any
cases of hardship the Ministry has made
the advance payments. I would like to add
that the green fibre processing firms have
been very helpful. They have done and
are doing their utmost to absorb the
crops for these people as quickly as
possible. The situation was somewhat
complicated by the fact that certain
farmers refrained from letting the Ministry know which way they were going to
market their crop until they got into
difficulties.
Mr. BROWN: Might I ask the noble
Lord if it is a fact that a number of
people who grew flax to sell as green
straw have recently written to the Ministry stating they cannot get a buyer for
it, and will the Minister give an
assurance that his Ministry will take
steps to see there are buyers for all flax
produced and sold as green straw?
Lord GLENTORAN: That was clearly
answered in the reply to the question.
Of course, the Ministry will carry out
all undertakings made.
IMMUNISATION AGAINST
DIPHTHERIA.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of the fact
that the General Council of Municipal
Authorities in Northern Ireland some
years ago urged his Ministry to introduce
for the whole of Northern Ireland a
scheme for the immunisation by medical
practitioners of children against diphtheria, whereby the Ministry would supply
the serum and bear the cost of the fees of
the doctors, he will now proceed with this
scheme and make its immediate operation
and enforcement compulsory on all local
authorities in order to combat the present
serious position in this matter.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A scheme for
immunisation against diphtheria was introduced by my Department as far back as
the year 1936 and since then my Ministry
has been pressing upon local authorities
by circular letter and by personal visits of
its medical inspectors the importance of
adopting such measures. To encourage
such schemes my Ministry has agreed with
effect from November, 1940, to recoup
local authorities the expenditure incurred
on the necessary immunising material and
has approved a scale of fees payable by
local authorities to medical officers for
their services in this respect. My Depart-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
ment does not, however, reimburse the
local authority for the amount of these
fees.
I am glad to be able to say that since
the scheme was introduced, 47 out of 67
local authorities have undertaken schemes
in their respective areas. I have no power
to compel local authorities to undertake
and enforce schemes of the nature referred
to, nor is it my intention to ask for these
statutory powers.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister consider the advisability of having this scheme
extended so as to enable immunisation to
be carried out by all medical practitioners
under this scheme instead of by medical
officers of health only?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot really
undertake to direct ordinary medical men
what they should do to their patients.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister tell
me that it is open for all medical practitioners to carry out immunisation within the framework of this scheme?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The ordinary
medical man attending to patients knows
exactly what he should do and will carry
it out I have no doubt.
DRAINAGE COMMISSION'S REPORT
6. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the severe
damage and loss of crops in low lying
districts in Northern Ireland by flooding,
he will state when the Report of the
Drainage Commission will be published.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
I am glad to be able to inform the hon.
Member that the first and second interim
Reports of the Drainage Commission will
be published shortly as a Command Paper
and that they are, in fact, at present in
the hands of the printers.
FIRE WATCHING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
7. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether he
can state (a) the number of Acts and
Orders which have been passed and put
into force since the outbreak of war relating to fire-watching in Northern
Ireland; (b) the number of these measures
which are still in force; (c) which Act or
Order gives details as to the personnel
required for fire-watching in various
classes of commercial and industrial concerns; (d) in what particular Act or Order
are the terms of compensation set out for
civil defence injury in Northern Ireland
in relation to fire-watchers; (e) in what
particular Act or Order are the terms of
compensation contained in the Imperial
S.R.O. No. 226 transmitted to Northern
Ireland; (f) whether he is prepared to
undertake that the terms of the new
English Fire-watching Order whereby
supplementary compensation up to a
maximum of 70s per week for men and
47s per week for women will be adopted
in Northern Ireland in order that firewatchers will be placed upon an equality
with Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant) (who was
received with cheers): As this question
contains a number of details the answer
will necessarily be longer than usual, but
I would assure the House I am not going
to establish a precedent in this respect.
In answer to (a): No Acts have been
passed relating to fire-watching or fire
prevention. Various powers have, however, been conferred on my Ministry by
the Defence Regulations. Under these,
first, three Orders have so far been made
dealing with fire protection in business
premises; secondly, one Order has been
made conferring powers, which have not
yet been exercised, enabling the compulsory enrolment of persons for fire preven
tion duties generally, and, thirdly, my
Ministry has given a direction to the civil
defence authorities of Belfast and Londonderry requiring them to make adequate
fire prevention arrangements at all premises and places in their areas which are
not covered by the Orders relating to
business premises.
In answer to (b): For the cities of
Belfast and Londonderry, and in the case
of certain particular premises outside
those cities, the law with regard to fire
prevention in business premises is to be
found in the Fire Prevention (Business
Premises) (Northern Ireland) (No. 2)
Order S.R. & O. No. 188 of 1941recently issued, which, with effect from
Sittings of the House
Sittings of the House
18 NOVEMBER 1941
the 1st December, 1941, will supersede
al! Orders previously in force in those
areas. For the boroughs of Bangor,
Larne, and Newtownards, and the Urban
District of Lisburn, the law with regard
to fire protection in business premises is
to be found in the Fire Watchers Order
(Northern Ireland), 1941-S.R. & O.
No. 8 of 1941. No other business
premises in Northern Ireland, outside
those I have mentioned, are so far
affected.
In answer to (c): Under the Fire Prevention (Business Premises) Order, which,
as I have mentioned, applies in the cities
of Belfast and Londonderry, no rigid
scale of personnel is prescribed. The
Order requires that the arrangements
made must be adequate, and the requirements must vary according to the
nature and characteristics of the premises
concerned. They will be settled by the
appropriate authority for each particular
set of premises in relation to the
circumstances.
Under the Fire Watchers Order,
which, as I have previously mentioned,
applies to the boroughs of Bangor,
Larne, and Newtownards and to the
Urban District of Lisburn, the detailed
arrangements to be made are specified in
the Order itself.
In answer to (d) and (e): The terms
of compensation for fire-prevention personnel are contained in the Personal
Injuries (Civilians) Scheme (S.R. & O.
No. 226 of 1941) made by the Minister
of Pensions and applicable to the whole
of the United Kingdom. Paragraph 18
of the Schedule to that scheme indicates
the necessary adaptations to be made in
its application to Northern Ireland.
With regard to (f), the answer is in
the affirmative, though I should perhaps
point out that the supplementary allowances referred to will be given ex gratia
both in Northern Ireland and in Great
Britain. The hon. Member is mistaken
in thinking that any provision for their
payment is contained in the Great
Britain Fire Prevention Order.

Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House, at its rising this day,
do adjourn until Tuesday next."-(Lord
Glentoran.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I want to make a
strong protest against this adjournment
on the following grounds. We on this
side were promised that a Bill would be
introduced at the earliest possible date
regulating the payment of rents to those
people who suffered through recent enemy
action. I understood that we would
have had this Bill actually for its Second
Reading to-day. I find that is not so.
If this matter was not urgent I would
not be calling upon the House to continue its deliberations. I do feel that
this is a very urgent matter and one that
the Government have not given the sympathetic consideration which it deserves.
It is only a two-Clause Bill. I could
draft it inside half an hour. What we
want.is to see that no rents are payable
while the houses are uninhabitable, and
that no houses will be given away without the tenants thereof being acquainted
by the landlords. These tenants are at
the moment being charged rents on
homes that cannot be lived in, and people
are risking their lives going into some
of these houses. They cannot afford to
pay two rents. If any Member of the
House came along with me he would see
the danger that these people are in by
living in the houses. I agree that it is
humanly impossible to get all the homes
made habitable at once. There is work
going on, but it is going on very slowly.
In my opinion it is a case of the more
hands the less work. I have been in
three streets this week, one of which is
represented by the Minister of Home
Affairs, and the people are clamouring
to get back because of their economic
circumstances.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
now raising some other questions which
have no relation to the resolution before
the House.
Mr. BEATTIE: I was trying to show
how important and necessary it is that
this Bill we were promised should be
brought in. Perhaps I have delayed the
House at a little more length than I
intended. I would like the House to
realise that it is not through sheer opposition I am speaking on this Motion. It is
because of the hardship that is being
imposed on these people. I am not suggesting for a moment-I hope I am notthat there is no sympathy from the
Government side, but I must say there
has been delay, which is creating grave

I think I had better explain why there

Committee. The Parliament of Northern
Ireland is precluded by the Government
of Ireland Act from passing laws in
respect of the following matters, amongst
others (1) Matters arising from a state
of war (Section 4 (1) (2) of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920); (2) the
Navy, the Army, the Air Force, the
Territorial Force, or any other naval,

the Realm, or any other naval, military
or air force matter, including any pensions and allowances payable to persons

widows or dependants (Section 4 (1) (3)
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920).
:
The "protection of the interests" of
Northern Ireland men and women serving
with the forces or engaged in Civil
Defence is, therefore, reserved for the
United Kingdom Parliament. Provision
has been made by that Parliament for the
grant of compensation for injury, and
pensions in appropriate cases, not only
for members of His Majesty's forces and
for those engaged in Civil Defence, but
for all gainfully occupied civilians who
sustain war injuries, and for certain other
classes. All these schemes are administered by the Ministry of Pensions.
I think I told the hon. Gentleman,
who raised a matter of this kind a few
weeks ago, that the Parliamentary Secretary and several members of a Committee who were operating the scheme in
Great Britain called to see me. They
asked me to get the people who have
been injured to make claims for compensation and to get those who had
suffered severe injuries to make claims
for pensions. They were keen and
anxious that everything possible should
be done in order to tide the people over
a difficult period and then ultimately
grant them a pension.
