the ignorance of the individual concerned. He does not know where to go
or to whom to apply. Consequently, he
suffers as a result of his lack of knowledge. The hon. Gentleman told me
that hundreds had been injured and had
received no compensation of any kind.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would I have
been wrong if I had said thousands?
Mr. GORDON: I am doubtful. All
I can say, in conclusion, is this. I was
wondering whether the hon. Member's
indignation was simulated or righteous
indignation on behalf of the people, but
if he has any cases and gives me the
names of the people who, he feels, have
been unjustly dealt with and are
entitled to compensation I will do my
utmost to see that they receive what they
are entitled to.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am going to support this Motion, because I believe that
if it does not do any good it will not do
any harm. I want, first and foremost,
to set out the argument put forward by
the hon. Member for Shankill. He complained bitterly against the administration of the needs and requirements of
the people of Northern Ireland by people
in England, and I fully agree with him,
because we in Northern Ireland are
competent to deal with all matters
appertaining to the lives of our citizens
either in war or in distress brought about
by enemy action.
Mr. GORDON: We are not allowed.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is the fault I
have had to find with the Government
of Northern Ireland since its inception,
and I am glad to know the Minister has
come to share that view with me.
Mr. GORDON: I do not think he has.
Mr. BEATTIE: After the last war we
had a Pensions Committee established.
They got all the cases before them, but I
must say that their recommendations
were not always carried out. Many of the
cases went to the Tribunal. If I spoke in
I
hundreds I would be very modest.
appeared at the Tribunal very often, and
put up cases for the applicants, but I
found that owing to the guidance given
to the medical boards they were compelled
to accept a line of thought which was in
nine cases out of ten loaded against the
applicant. The rate of pensions allowed
to those who succeeded was far too low
for the disability they received and the
extent of the curtailment of their earning
power in the occupation or profession in
which they were engaged prior to enlistment.
The Member for Shankill, I presume,
has seen for himself in his lifetime similar
happenings, and that being so he has
thought it worth while to suggest a remedy
so that the old bad system that operated
after the last war will not operate after
this war. He wants it done by means of
a united effort by the people of Northern
Ireland, free and unfettered from any
interference by people across the water. I
know the right hon. Gentleman will say
that the paymaster has the right to call
the tune, as he will have to pay, and
that he will demand the right to set up
the machinery. I say that position
should be altered, and if the Government
of Ireland Act prohibits you managing
the affairs of your own household it is
time that the Act was amended to give
you full power to look after all services
appertaining to the life and well-being
of the community for which this Parliament was set up to legislate. I believe
that Section 314 was deliberately designed
by the British Government to keep a hold
on this part of the world.
Mr. GORDON: It is useful at the
present time.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is not useful if it is
retarding your legislating for the benefit
of the people of this area. We are not
getting anything from England that we
are not giving back two-fold. We have
given our man power and our woman
power.
The PRIME MINISTER: And we are
getting the benefit of theirs.
Mr. BEATTIE: We are trying to give
100 per cent. of our industrial power, and
surely that should go to the credit of the
people of Northern Ireland. If we are
Select Committee-
18 NOVEMBER 1941 Compensation and Pensions
able to do that we should be able to look
after our members of the Navy, Army,
Air Force and civil defence victims. I
have no fault to find with the Minister
quoting the scales of allowances that have
been laid down. I have dealt with large
numbers of claims since this war began,
and I have found that those scales operate
for only a very short period. One case
that I have returned to the Ministry of
Pensions is that in which an allowance of
35s a week was being paid to a boilermaker who was disabled by enemy action.
During the period he was in hospital
he got 35s a week, but three weeks after
he came out of hospital he received a notice
from the Ministry of Pensions stating that
the Ministry had now decided to grant
him a pension of 17s a week. That award
was made on a temporary basis only,
because there are no pensions of a permanent character made during the war.
I looked at the man and said, "Your
disability at the moment is equal to more
than 17s a week." His disability was
total from his gainful employment as a
boilermaker, and yet his allowance of 35s
a week was reduced to a temporary pension of 17s a week. Was that not a mean
way to reduce his allowance? That temporary pension is subject to review at the
end of every three months, and at the
end of twelve months, if the pension is
ever made permanent, it will amount to
8s 3d a week. His income was cut by
one half at the very time when he most
required the full allowance. My contention is that the full allowance of 35s
a week should be paid during the whole
period of total disability, and that there
should be no difference between the
allowance and the temporary pension.
That is the hardship.
Coming to Civil Defence, you know
that the victims of the blitz did not
receive 35s a week whether they were in
hospital or not. In the Order setting out
what a man, woman, or boy may receive
there are limits set. After thirteen weeks
they are subject to very drastic reductions in the amounts. That being so,
I think the Member for Shankill is
justified in asking for a Select Committee
to be set up to consider this whole question. We have plenty of material at our
disposal from which to put forward
recommendations to that all powerful
body sitting in London which deals with
claims from members of the Navy, Army,
Air Force, Civil Defence, and victims of
enemy action. Surely it would not be a
loss of time to talk these matters over
with that Committee, and I think that is
the purport of the Motion moved by the
Member for Shankill.
I have come in contact with cases of
widows who have lost their husbands, and
one, two, three and four members of the
family. I wonder what compensation, if
any, would meet the loss sustained by such
a widow. Would it surprise you to know
that in one particular case the earning
power of one unit of the family who was lost
exceeded the allowance that that widow
received for the loss of her husband and
four earning members of her family.
Therefore, she is burdened for the rest
of her life with a restricted income
hardly sufficient to keep the household
in decency and comfort, due to no fault
of her own. She is left in that sorry
plight to bring the younger members of
the family through this life and to try
to give them the education they would
have received if the father and the other
earning members of the family had not
been lost. This question of compensation and allowances for those who are
killed and injured in the Civil Defence
Services is one which this Government
could very well deal with.
I was told the other day that I was
poking my nose into A.R.P. The reason
I went officially into A.R.P. was because
of the danger I risked in air raids. When
I had risked that danger on three
occasions I discovered that if anything
did happen to me those I had left at
home would have been left high and dry
without any right to claim compensation.
Therefore, I was advised to sit for
the prescribed examination and enroll
officially in A.R.P. When help is required outside I am there, especially in
my own division, and so I officially enrolled on the representations of those
who thought I had failed to realise my
responsibilities to my own family. I say
that that enrollment does not record the
true date when I first took an interest
in A.R.P., and to say that it does is an
unfair and unfounded charge to make in
this House.
Mr. GORDON: I would like to assure
the hon. Member that I have never made
a charge of that kind against the hon.
Member, and I would not like him to be

The idea of the hon. Member for Shankill

for extending this matter. Section 314
of the Government of Ireland Act limits

If I could get you to follow me into the

Mr. GORDON: The mover of the
Motion would not agree to that.
Mr. HENDERSON: Yes.
Mr. BEATTIE: He wants Ulstermen
to deal with the pensions allotted to
defence casualties. I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. Member. The Committee could make recommendations to be
confirmed by the authorities in London.
That is the view he expressed. I know if
I asked for a repeal of Section 314 I
should be left isolated. In 1926 when
the right hon. Gentleman was Parliamentary Secretary to the then Minister of
Labour, our present Prime Minister, we
opposed the opting out of this part of the
world. We wanted to opt in and voted
for it. I think we can now justly claim
that we were right and the Government
was wrong.
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Member for
Shankill would not agree to that.
Mr. BEATTIE: He has guided me, and
you are not going to shake me. The hon.
Member for Shankill knows his own mind.
He has put his case forward, and knows
what he wants. He is trying to get what
he wants, but, unfortunately for him, he
did not get a full House. Sufficient
interest was not taken in this question.
In a few weeks' time hon. Members will
be on the hustings and pour out eulogies.
on the Government. I am hoping to see
the Government candidate defeated again.
Any little I can do towards that end will
be done. I am satisfied that if this question were put to the electors in its true
perspective the people of Willowfield,
Shankill and Ballymacarrett would vote.
for it every time. That being so I wish
to give my whole-hearted support to the
Motion so ably moved by the hon. Member
for Shankill.
Question put, "That, in the opinion of
this House, a Select Committee should be
set up immediately to make recommendations with regard to the protection of the
interests of those Northern Ireland men
and women serving with His Majesty's
forces, and those serving in the civil
defence forces in Northern Ireland,
especially with regard to compensation for
injury and pensions in cases where death
has resulted from enemy action."
The House divided: Ayes, 2; Noes, 15.

ELECTRICITY BOARD.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if Mr.
Ferguson occupies the position of Chief
Administrative Officer to the Electricity
Board and is at the same time a member
of the Board; whether he considers it
desirable that a servant of the Board
should also be a member of the Board;
and whether he can state details of the
salary and other emoluments payable to
Mr. Ferguson in respect of these two
positions and to what extent the Board.
is responsible to the Ministry of
Commerce.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The answer to the
first part of the question is in the
affirmative. As I informed the Hon.
Member on the 2nd September the
question of the terms of Mr. Ferguson's
appointment as an officer of the Board
is a matter for the Electricity Board
which is responsible for its own staffing
arrangements. The responsibilities of the
Board to my Ministry are limited to
compliance with the requirements of the
Electricity (Supply) Acts (Northern
Ireland), 1882 to 1936.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's statement to the effect that the
responsibilities of the Board to his Ministry are only limited, does he mean that
when this House gives him authority to
set up a board that board can do what
it likes?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: It is the
appointment of the staff as I explained
in answer to the question.
Mr. NIXON: Did not the Minister
or his predecessor actually refuse information on the ground that it was a board
of business men and could not be interfered with? The thing has gone too far.

MILLISLE-BELFAST BUSES.
3: Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
make representations to the Northern
Ireland Road Transport Board to provide
buses direct to Belfast at 6-30 a.m. for
workers living in Ballywhiskin and
Millisle.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I understand that a
train leaves Donaghadee every morning
for Belfast at 6-30 a.m. and that an
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
25 NOVEMBER 1941
omnibus leaves Millisle at 6-10 a.m. to
enable passengers from the Millisle area
to travel by that train. I fully appreciate the desire of passengers to have a
direct service which will not only give
them more time at home, but will also
obviate the necessity for transferring
from an omnibus to a train, but from
inquiries which I have made I am satisfied that it would not be possible for the
Transport Board to accede to the request
made by the hon. Member.
As the hon Member is aware, it has
been necessary to withdraw omnibus services from roads adjacent to railway lines
to permit of services being provided for
workers who now live in districts which
have no railways, and, consequently, it
would not be possible to obtain a vehicle
for the purpose without causing serious
inconvenience to the public. Further, if
it were possible to find an omnibus at that
time of the day to run direct to Belfast,
one vehicle would not be sufficient to provide facilities for the people between
Millisle and Belfast, who would consider
that they had an equal right to travel by
road. In the circumstances, I am not
prepared to make representations to the
Transport Board in the matter.
Mr HENDERSON: Arising out of
that reply will the right hon. Gentleman
state whether facilities will be given to
the people of Ballywhiskin, two miles from
Millisle, who are war workers, and is it a
fact that it takes on the double journey
almost 3 hours of these workers' time
after standing 12 hours in the shipyard?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have tried in
my answer to explain the difficulties of
the whole matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
will the right hon. Gentleman make representations to the Board that the departure of the Millisle bus should be changed
to depart from Ballywhiskin instead of
from Millisle.
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a
serious matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman understand what I am asking.
It is that the bus should start two miles
further along the road to accommodate
those workers who live in Ballywhiskin.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am quite
prepared to take the matter up with the
Transport Board in regard to that particular point.
WHITEABBEY SANATORIUM
REPORT.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs what steps his Ministry
has taken to implement the Whiteabbey
Sanatorium Report and the resolutions of
the Belfast Corporation relating thereto.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The action to
be taken by my Department as a result
of the findings of the Ministry in connection with the sworn inquiry held at
Whiteabbey, and the resolutions of the
Belfast Corporation thereon, is at present
under consideration, consequent on the
examination of the Second Interim Report
of the Special Committee of the Belfast
Corporation. I am, however, not prepared to make any public pronouncement
on the subject as the further reports of
the Special Committee have not yet been.
considered by the Corporation.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is the Minister not
long behind scheduled time for taking
action in this matter. Has he again
missed the bus?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think
I have missed the bus. The hon. and
learned Member may have.
IMPORTED AND EXPORTED
WORKERS.
6. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state
the number of workers, skilled and unskilled, male and female, who have come
to Northern Ireland and who are now
employed in Northern Ireland, and
whether he can state the numbers of
skilled and unskilled workers, male and
female, who were sent to Great Britain
from Northern Ireland since the beginning of, and before, the war.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In answer to the hon. Member,
I may say that it is not possible for my
Department to state the number of
workers who have come to Northern
Ireland, because many of them hold
employment books and go straight to work
without passing through our employment
exchanges.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
Statistics of the number of workers sent
to Great Britain have been kept only
since February, 1940. Since that date,
27,629 persons from Northern Ireland
have been placed in employment in Great
Britain. A considerable number of these
returned home on completion of the work
for which they were engaged, but it
would not be in the public interest to give
any more detailed information.

when

It should be the endeavour of every

done this year must call for considerable
extra labour, and I would strongly urge
any farmer who thinks he cannot keep

scheme, under which grants are made up

as drainage, the clearing of sheughs, the

I would further warn our farmers that

Ireland of adequate supplies to meet all
our requirements provided the total quantity can be imported during the coming

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Excessive Rents (Prevention) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the House
is aware, the position of tenants whose
houses have been damaged by enemy air
raids, so far as the question of rent payable by these tenants is concerned, has
already been dealt with by the passing of
the Landlord and Tenant (War Damage)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1941. Under
that Act, tenants of houses let on a short
tenancy are not liable for rent of a house
damaged by enemy action, so long as the
house is unfit and is unoccupied. If the
house is occupied during the period of
unfitness, a rent as may be agreed between
the tenant and the landlord is payable,
or in default of agreement the court may
fix the rent. At the last sitting of the
House there was a misunderstanding on
the part of certain Members, who forgot
the existence of this Act of 1941 to which
I have referred.
The object of the Bill now before the
House is to deal with the problem of
profiteering in rents at the expense of
persons who have been compelled to leave
their homes since 1st April, 1941, on
account of damage by air raids. It is
proposed to set up Tribunals consisting
of three members, of whom one, the
chairman, shall be a resident magistrate,
or a practising barrister-at-law or solicitor, of not less than six years' standing.
These Tribunals will deal with cases
brought before them by persons who consider themselves aggrieved by reason of
the amount of rent charged to them.
It has been found that existing legislation relating to rent restriction is
insufficient to deal with the problem.
One reason for this is that under the
Rent Restrictions Code where a house is
let for the first time after 1st September,
1939, the rent obtainable becomes the
"standard rent" within the meaning of
the Acts no matter how exorbitant that
rent may be. A number of cases have
come to the knowledge of my Ministry
where houses let for the first time since
1st April, 1941, that is, after the air
raids, have been let at rents far in excess
of what the landlord would normally be
entitled to receive. At present the tenant
has no redress in these cases. Furthermore, existing Acts do not cover the type
of accommodation which, in many cases,
is being provided, for example, in barns
or temporary dwellings of various kinds,
including, as my hon. Friend says, hen
houses.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hen houses and goat
houses.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not know
the difference between a hen house and a
goat house. The present Bill has been
framed so as to cover lettings of any kind
of housing accommodation, whether furnished or unfurnished.
The Tribunal will not deal with cases
which come within the Rent Restrictions
Acts unless the letting took place for the
first time after 1st April, 1941. When
the Tribunal has investigated the circumstances in any particular case and has
found that the rent payable by the tenant
is not fair and reasonable it will fix the
rent which, in its opinion, is fair and
reasonable, and will issue its certificate
accordingly. This rent will, thereupon, be
deened to be the rent payable under the
tenancy agreement entered into between
the landlord and the tenant. The landlord will be compelled to repay to the
tenant within one month any sum paid in
excess of the rent which the Tribunal
determines to be fair and reasonable, but
not exceeding the excess amount over a
period of 12 months. If the landlord
Excessive Rents Bill-
Second Reading
25 NOVEMBER 1941
fails to make repayment within one month
he will be liable to a fine not exceeding
£100. Quite apart from this penalty a
tenant will be able to recover from the
landlord at any time within 12 months
from the date of payment any sum paid
in excess of the rent which the Tribunal
determines to be fair and reasonable, but
not exceeding the excess for a period of
12 months. The tenant, if he so desires,
will be able to deduct from any future
rent payable by him any excess amount
over the rent which the Tribunal has
determined to be fair and reasonable.
It is hoped that aggrieved persons will
not hesitate to bring their cases before
the Tribunals. It is a cheap and easy
method of approach to a court. Unless
they are prepared to do so it is difficult to
see what else the Government can do to
deal with this problem of profiteering by
persons who are prepared to obtain money
at the expense of people who have been
unfortunate enough to lose their homes
owing to enemy action. I beg to move,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Question proposed.
Mr. NIXON: I had not an opportunity
of speaking privately to the Minister of
Home Affairs about this Bill, but I spoke
to the Prime Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and I understood that suggestions would be favourably received.
Therefore, in order to widen the scope of
the debate on this Bill I am going to
move its rejection, but I do not think it
will be necessary to press it if I get from
the Minister the encouragement I got
from the Prime Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary. I did not intentionally pass over the Minister. I had not an
opportunity of speaking to him.
There is nothing wrong with the principle of the Bill. The object of the
Measure is to control rents charged to
people evacuated. As the Minister
stated, the Bill cannot apply to houses
already controlled. That is settled
by another Act. But this is a very disappointing Bill, and in practice will work
out a very disappointing Act unless it
is amended in some way. The Amendment must come from the Government.
There is no use in my putting down an
amendment, because it would not be
passed unless the Government were
sympathetic towards it. If the Government are sympathetic towards the matter
then they should bring in an amendment.
If that were done perhaps there would
be no division. One would think that
such a Bill would be brought in in such
a way as to satisfy everyone. It has not,
but there is still time to make alterations
which will make the Bill acceptable.
The first defect in the Measure is the
fact that there is no appeal from the
decision of the Tribunal. The Tribunal
may consist of a resident magistrate, a
barrister, a solicitor, and two other
people. It will make its own rules and
regulations; in fact, may do what it
likes, and there is no right of appeal.
I think I am right in saying that where
there was a difference of opinion on any
matter it would be decided by the votes
of the majority. I object, first and foremost, to the right of appeal being withdrawn, and I also object to the fact that
there is no basis laid down by which the
Tribunal may fix rents. Rents will be
fixed by the members according to their
state of mind. The members may err
on one side or another, but I am not
going to say on which side they will err.
There will be no rule to guide them, and
there will be no appeal from their decision. What rule would you lay down
to guide them? This is what one would
call constructive criticism. I suggest
that rents should bear a relation to the
valuation, so much a week for every £
of valuation. I am not going to work it
out, although it would be easy to do so.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps the
hon. Member will tell us what he would
do in the case of a hen-house let as a
dwelling-house-a hen-house which was

his costs of production, interest on his
investment in the land, and reward for
his work. His costs of production
allowed should be such that would
enable him to pay wages to his workers
on a level of parity with any other
industry.

I do not wish to weary the House. I
have wearied it enough already, I am
afraid. I wish to finish as I began by
saying that the matter of the restoration
of agriculture to its rightful place is too
big a matter either for the Farmers'
Union of Great Britain or Northern
Ireland, or the Government or both acting
together; it is a matter on which we must
bring the whole public along with us. It
is important that this House, by a Motion
moved and seconded by Members who
have no financial interest in farming,
should say that agriculture will have its
rightful place in the scheme of things in
general. Although I am a farmer's son I
have no financial interest in farming at
the present time. I love the land, and
that is my only excuse for bringing this
Motion forward.
I will conclude with the words of
Professor C. E. M. Joad. He says:
People are coming increasingly to
realise the dangers inherent in a purely
urban community dependent for its
maintenance on food from abroad.
This means not only a new consciousness of the importance of the countryside and a determination that our farming shall not be allowed to lapse into
its pre-war neglect, but a change in
values. It is not only that the country
feeds the body; it enriches the spirit.
"It is only since I started going every
week-end into the country to visit the

progress. Perhaps if they had the

have not got all the way in that matter

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I say we

again.
That is the position at the moment.
Does the hon. Member suggest that our
Government should immediately in face
of these circumstances proceed to try to
get an increase in price for the same commodities regardless of whether the English
and Scottish producers ever get that increase at all. We get the same price for
fat cattle. We get the same price for
oats.
We get the same price for wheat,
the same price for poultry and the same
price, practically speaking, for eggs. I
admit there are one or two commodities,
such as store cattle, that we are not on an
absolute parity with the Great Britain
producer. But I say we have considerably narrowed the margin. The whole
position hangs together, and whatever increase is given in prices to meet the increase in wages we here in Northern
Ireland stand to share in these increases
under the present arrangement. I submit that is not a position in which our
Government could interfere.
In addition to that I would point out
that there is well recognised machinery in
existence to deal with these matters.
There is what is known as the coordinating committee, consisting of four
representatives of the National Farmers'
Union of England, the Scottish Farmers'
Union, the Chamber of Agriculture and
the Ulster Farmers' Union.
The coordinating committee meets alternately in
England, London usually, in Edinburgh
and in Belfast. And the Ulster Farmers'
Union is in constant contact with the
representatives of these other two unions.
As a matter of fact the deputy chairman
is over in London this week.
I appreciate what the mover of the Motion said
in the way of praising the Minister of

I, perhaps, know even rather more of

lines than the hon. Member possibly can
know.
I think our Ministry of Agriculture
appreciates the gigantic task that is set
to our farmers in Northern Ireland. I
think it does appreciate and realise that

the whole farming community of Northern
Ireland, has a right to be compensated on

other sections of the community who perform comparable tasks. But I do believe
-at least I hope it is the case that the
Ministry of Agriculture realises that

given a say in their Own business.
They must be allowed to put forward in

sugar beet. Of that we never got one

to provide against their having to go

Here is one new industry which would

Lord GLENTORAN: I only rise to
reply to one or two points made by the
hon. Member for South Down which, in
my opinion, if allowed to pass would have
a serious effect on our productive capacity
here in Ulster. He made one statement
which he should either prove or withdraw.
He said that he has definite knowledge
that our grading is wrong; in fact,
corrupt. If he has that definite knowledge I
say it is a shame, almost a crime,
that he should have kept that knowledge
from me and allowed poor men to suffer
under that injustice without raising his
voice in this House. He should have
come to me, as Minister of Agriculture,
and said, "I have the proof here. Here
it is, act." If he had done so he knows
quite well I would have acted, and I
challenge him now to bring forward his
proof.
What are the real facts in regard to
grading? A beast is graded and paid for
by the cwt. on the exact amount of beef
produced after death; that is to say, it is
graded at the live weight, and when it is
killed the actual weight of the beast must
be in comparison with the money that has
been paid for it when alive. We have
gone into this matter again and again,
and particularly so when charges were
made originally. It has been found to
be an absolutely accurate system, and
there is no difference between the price
paid for the beast live weight and what it
fetched when killed. Can you do better
than that? We are told that we do not
get the same result here as they do in
England. What more can one do than be
exactly correct.
The hon. Member or someone else might
well say that a grader who was hard on
the people would be a person who would
be commended by me, or it might be said
that a grader who is light on the people
might be commended by me. In both cases
the suggestion would be wrong because I
would not commend any man who was inaccurate. It is just as big a crime to give
too litle as too much: what you have to
give is exactly what the bullock is worth;
what the beef cuts out to. Therefore if
the hon. Member made his statement in
all seriousness he should have come with
the proof to me long ago. It is not yet
too late to come with the proof.
The question of grading has been a
moot point. I fought it with my hon.
Friend opposite at the beginning, because
we had to start afresh, and it was a very
difficult matter to get going. The scheme
is now in absolute working order, and has
attained accuracy.
I must remind the
House that owing to the way we carry out
the grading we can give far more stations
than they do in England. We have
three, four or five stations for every one
in England; in Ulster, I think, we have
70 grading stations which brings the
grading to the farmers' doors. In
England they do not attempt to do that.
I regret the statement which the hon.
Member made against my Ministry-a
statement which is nothing short
of a charge of dishonesty. If he
not prepared to prove it then
it is a serious matter for the hon.
Member, because in a time of war such a
statement must have a bad effect on the
farmers and those who are so splendidly
producing food for the nation.
is
Another statement made by the hon.
Member was also inaccurate. It was a
half truth, which is worse than a whole
lie. He said that the people in England got 45s per ton more for potatoes
than was paid in Ulster. That is not a
fact. The people in England are dealt
with in areas in exactly the same way as
we are dealt with. These areas vary
according to the amount of transport
available and the cost of bringing the
potatoes to the centres where they are
wanted. I am glad to say both from my
own knowledge and what I have been
told by potato growers-in fact, by

constituency-that the farmers are very
pleased with the prices obtained for
potatoes this year. The £10 subsidy per
acre has, as far as I have heard, pleased
the people immensely.
The other matter is not one I need get
heated about. I do get hot when people
make statements which cannot be proved
but which can be very harmful. I will now
deal with this matter-sugar beet. It
Prices and Conditions
Agriculture-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lord Glentoran]
is not a question I need get hot about,
because whether the farmers in Ulster
care to grow sugar beet or potatoes is
largely a matter for themselves. If a
group of farmers waited upon me and
said they were willing to promise their
land for so many years in order to support a factory I should take steps to get
a factory erected in the same way as the
potato factories. But there are one or
two things to remember about sugar beet.
First of all, it takes in or about 10,000
acres of sugar beet to keep a factory
going, and you would require to get a
guarantee that this amount would be
grown. Sugar beet is very difficult to
handle. Big fields are required. It is
not such a simple proposition as some
hon. Members might think. I know
something about the matter, because I
have been in some of the factories time
and again. I have a farm close to where
sugar beet is grown, but I never
touch it..
The other thing against the growing of
sugar beet here is our Ulster climate.
If you want anything like a decent sugar
content you must have sun. The reason
they grow it in certain parts of England,
particularly Norfolk and Suffolk, is because they have sun and they get a good
content of sugar. It is all right over in
England, but no farmers have come to
me and said, "We will give our land
for sugar beet; we will give up potatoes
and other things, and we will take up
this Continental growing of sugar beet."
If such a demand is made I will be glad
to assist the project; that is, if I am
satisfied it is a right project.
I have now dealt with the three
matters which were raised. I should
like the House to understand that farming is now a most difficult and scientific
pursuit. The costing of farming is a
matter of extreme difficulty. When hon.
Members get up and say they want the
price of something to be this or that
figure I can give an answer. I should
not like the House to think I do so because I like the look of the hon. Member or his personality. When I can reply
to the questions put to me it means that
my Department has been working for
weeks and weeks and have come to an
agreement with the people on the other
side as to what we can give. Before I
move in any of these matters I invariably
consult the Ulster Farmers' Union War
Committee.
I should like to take this opportunity
of letting the House know the names of
its members, because they have given
unstinted service to the country and to
the farmers. With the permission of the
House I will read out their names. There
is, of course, the Rev. Robert Moore, who
represents North Derry. He is chairman.
Then we have Mr. Ewart, Gannaway,
Millisle. He is well-known in that end
of County Down. Then also for County
Down we have Mr. J. McCune, Ballybeen,
Comber. For North Antrim we have Mr.
W. Pinkerton, Dunaveryney, Ballymoney; he is a very well-known gentleman. Mr. A. McConnell, Molestone,
Doagh, represents South Antrim; Mr. J.
Stirling, Ross Kells, Ballymena, represents Mid-Antrim. Mr. J. Colhoun,
Mullagherena, Omagh, represents County
Tyrone; while South Down and South
Armagh are represented by Mr. C. Magee,
Carnmeen, Newry. I doubt if you could
get a better committee in the world.
They all know their job; they are practical farmers, and I am sure the House
will forgive me if I follow the advice
these experienced gentlemen give me and
not the advice of people who have not
got that experience.

Mr. GORDON: Some weeks have
elapsed since this Motion was brought
before the House, and consequently many
of the Members may have forgotten the
points that were raised and the charges
that were made against the Government on
that occasion. I have carefully examined
the speeches, as they appeared in Hansard, made by the hon. Gentleman who
sits opposite, and by other hon. Members
who spoke on the Opposition benches. I
was anxious to give a considered reply to
those statements concerning health insured
members who had lost their title to
benefit. I think that was probably the
most important point raised by the hon.
Gentleman who represents South Armagh,
but when the debate concluded on the
28th October I was dealing with an interjection by the hon. Member for Shankill,
who asked how could an engineer
keep two homes, one in the North
of Ireland,
and the other in Great
Britain, on his wages. Evidently it
had been talked about in certain circles
that the person, who had dependants
and responsibilities, transferred to Great
Britain did not receive the allowances
that those who would be transferred from
Great Britain would receive here.
It had become, as it were, living politics,
and every person was talking about the
injustice that was being done to the men
persons.
In the motion the loss of title to health
and pension rights was emphasised by
both the mover and seconder. I am glad
this matter has been raised so that I may
be able to clear away a misunderstanding.
I will endeavour to explain very briefly
to the House how the rights of a person
under the health and pensions scheme are
maintained when he is unemployed. When
a person enters insurable employment,
even if only for one week, he becomes
entitled on ceasing work to a free period
of insurance lasting for at least 18 months
and possibly two years. If at the end of
that period he is incapable of work owing
to sickness, his free period is extended for
a further six months. Furthermore, if
during his free period, he manages to
obtain eight weeks of insurable employment during any two consecutive half
years, his insurance will be continued by
a fresh period of free insurance from the
date on which that employment ceased.
Of course hon. Members will say, "Yes,
you are dealing with persons who are
entering insurance for the first time, the
majority of whom are young people who
can keep their insurance rights alive by
eight weeks' employment every year." The
mover and seconder of the Motion laid
greater stress on the fate of persons with
a long industrial career who, they felt,
should have not only safer rights in industrial insurance, but should receive
some recompense from the industry they
had helped to create or build up.
In cases such as these the conditions
and terms are much easier to conform to.
When a person has been continuously insured for at least 10 years, his free insurance will be continued indefinitely if,
when not employed, he was either
incapable of work through sickness or was
Unemployed Workers-
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
available for work, but unable to obtain
it. The hon. Member for South Armagh
seems surprised at that statement, and I
will repeat it. When a person has been
continuously insured for at least 10 years
his free insurance will be continued indefinitely if, when not employed, he was
either incapable of work through sickness
or was available for work, but unable to
obtain it.
The method of proof in either case is
very simple. If unemployment is due to
sickness, certificates of incapacity will be
issued free by his medical doctor. If it
is due to his inability to obtain employment, the proof is demonstrated by registration at an employment exchange and
by having his card franked. These weeks
of unemployment due to sickness or inability to obtain work all count towards
the number of contributions required for
the grant of a pension. I think these
conditions are fair conditions, and not
by any means impossible conditions to
conform to.
Having regard to the many opportunities for employment that are now open to
men and women, it will be obvious that
any person who really wishes to obtain
work should have very little difficulty in
retaining his title to health insurance
benefit or pension.
At this stage I should remind hon.
Members who took part in the debate
that, apart from private charity, whenever money is paid there are always conditions laid down for paying it, and
wherever there are conditions there will
always be found people who do not
satisfy them. This applies to trade
unions and insurance companies just as
much as to unemployment benefit or
assistance or public assistance. In the
case of the Assistance Board, the conditions are prescribed by Acts passed by
this Parliament. One condition is that
the person must be in need; another is
that he must show that he has a normal
Occupation insurable under the Contributory Pensions Acts; another is that he
must be capable of and available for
work.

A BELFAST CORPORATION
SLOGAN.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he is
aware that the following slogan is painted
on the Belfast Corporation Cleansing
Department lorries "Burn your refuse
and save the rates'; whether he considers
this slogan in keeping with the efforts
made by cities in Great Britain to
salvage all waste material.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I am grateful to the
hon. and gallant Member for bringing
this matter to my notice. When the
salvage campaign began, my Ministry
advised the Belfast Corporation that the
slogan, "Burn your refuse and save the
rates, should be removed from public
cleansing vehicles. This was done by
covering the slogan with salvage posters,
some of which have recently become
detached owing to weather conditions.
The Corporation have promised to
remedy the matter immediately.
CONTROL OF ELECTRICITY
PRODUCTION.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he is in
a position to make a statement as to the
Government's policy with regard to
unified control of the production of
electricity in Northern Ireland, and
whether it is the considered opinion of
the Ministry of Supply that this is
essential in the interests of war production.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: If the hon.
and gallant Member will be good enough
to put down his question again on this
day week, I anticipate then to be in a
position to make a statement.
NORTHERN IRELAND'S FANCY
LINEN TRADE.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether his attention has been
drawn to the article in the "Northern
Whig," of 21st November last, stating
that Northern Ireland's fancy linen
trade is faced with extinction, and
whether he can give the House an
assurance that his Ministry has taken or
will take steps to prevent such an unfortunate development and a further
increase in the total unemployed in Northern Ireland.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am aware
that the Board of Trade have prohibited
the manufacture of certain luxury articles
which include products of the Northern
Ireland fancy linen trade. This prohibition arises from the necessity for
conserving raw material for more essential
purposes, and on the information available I am unable to hold out hope that
the ban on the production of nonessential articles will be rescinded.
If, however, the trade hold stocks of
cloth which can be proved to be unsuitable for any other purpose, I am hopeful of arranging for such cloth to be
manufactured into the articles for which
it was woven. I have also offered to
assist the trade in obtaining raw material
and other facilities for the diversion of
their production capacity to more
essential articles.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask will the
Minister continue to give this matter
special attention in view of the fact that
the last official return issued by the
Ministry of Labour shows an increase in
the number of unemployed in Northern
Oral Answers

Ireland so as to prevent a further increase in the number of the workless?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, sir.
PRODUCTION OF PEAT FUEL.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether, in view of the statement made by the Minister of Mines in
the British Parliament on 26th November
last, that the Committee there which reported against any large-scale development in the production of peat as fuel
and as a potential source of petrol supply,
has been asked to reconsider the subject
in the light of the present coal situation,
he will appoint a similar Committee to
make investigation along these lines in
regard to Northern Ireland's peat
resources.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have already
been in communication with representatives of the coal trade, and also with
owners of peat bogs, with a view to the
greater utilisation of peat as fuel during
the present emergency. There are many
difficulties in the way including questions
relating to transport and price. I do not
consider that any
useful purpose would
be served by setting up a separate Committee for Northern Ireland, but I hope
to keep in touch with the deliberations of
the body to which the hon. Member
refers.

CONDITION OF RICHHILL CASTLE.
6. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether Richhill Castle is in good
condition and suitable for habitation; and
if not in good condition, who is to blame;
whether he will consider handing it over
to the Salvage Department for the collection of scrap; and whether it is used at
the present time for any useful purpose.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
Richhill Castle, which was derelict in
parts when bought by the Government in
1926, is about three hundred years old
and, consequently, is not in good condition
or fit for habitation. It is used at present for the storage of potatoes and seed
for which it would be difficult to find
alternative storage facilities in the farm
buildings. I am advised that the building is not required as a scrap collection
centre. I may add that the Government
has had under consideration from time to
time the question of making a more effective use of the castle, but in view of the
expense which would be necessary before
the building could be restored to a safe
condition it has not so far been possible to
use it for other than storage purposes.

A.R.P. in ARMAGH.
13. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister

with the protection given to the civilian

more shelters; whether he considers that
the present shelters are adequate for the
needs of the population, and that working
class areas are amply provided for.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): The question
of the adequacy of the air-raid shelter
accommodation provided in provincial
towns in Northern Ireland is constantly
before my Ministry, and steps are taken
as opportunity offers to increase and
improve it. In allocating the available

must, of course, be given to those areas

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
PRIVATE LORRY-OWNER'S
SUPPLY OF PETROL.
14. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that when a private lorry-owner's
monthly supply of petrol is exhausted he
can turn his lorry over to the Transport
Board, who will then supply him with
petrol to haul his own goods and charge
him 10 per cent. on the transport costs of
such goods, although all the Board does is
to supply him with coupons; whether he
can get an unlimited supply of petrol in
this way; whether this practice is illegal,
and whether he will put a stop to it and
in future give a more equal distribution
of petrol.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. Member is
under a complete misapprehension.
No
practice such as is suggested in the question exists.
The Transport Board has two classes
of hiring arrangements
arrangements with lorry-
Owners:-
(1) Where lorries are hired full-time,
and
(2) Where lorries are hired for specific
journeys.
In the first type of case the owner must
surrender to the petroleum officer the
basic and supplementary ration in respect
of his vehicle, and in place thereof he is
supplied with coupons sufficient for the
mileage covered while the vehicle is being
used by the Board on work of national
importance.
In some cases the vehicles are based on
depots at a distance from the owner's
home town; in others, they are based at
the depot in the owner's home town. This
depends on the nature of the work for
which they are hired.
The vehicles are entirely at the disposal
of the Board and under their orders and
control.
Where the owners have goods to be
carried, which previous to the hiring had
kept the vehicles partially employed, and
invariably involved much one-way running, the Board undertake the carriage.
of the goods, which may be conveyed in
the Board's own lorries, the owner's lorry
or the lorry of another hirer, according
to the exigencies of the moment.
The second type of hiring relates to the
case where the owner has carried his own
goods in one direction, and the Board
supplies the load for the return journey.
This sort of hiring is of a spasmodic and
occasional nature, and the owner receives
coupons in respect of the extra petrol
used by reason of the vehicle being run
full instead of empty. The goods carried
do not belong to the lorry owner, but to
other people.
The hon. Member will see that the
whole scheme is conceived with a threefold
object, namely:-(a) to increase the
vehicle resources available for public work,
and so help to overcome the present
shortage of transport; (b) to reduce light
running of vehicles, and (c) to conserve
the use of petrol.
He will, no doubt, also observe that the
scheme, which has been developed in
Northern Ireland over a period of twelve
months, is in essentials similar to that now
being put in force in Great Britain by the
Minister of War Transport.
It is entirely in the national interest.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY: If I can prove
the statements set out in the question will
the Minister prosecute the Board?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend will talk to me afterwards we can
go into the matter.

hoped that as a result the Council will

PERMITS FOR OBTAINING NATIVE
TIMBER.
20. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he will
make representations to the Ministry of
Supply for the issue of permits for
obtaining native timber for the purpose
of the erection of green-houses for the

Lord GLENTORAN: I ought to make
it clear that, although the Timber
Control Department of the Ministry of
Supply is the controlling authority in
Northern Ireland, the release of timber
for agricultural purposes is made on the
recommendation of my Ministry, on the
basis of a quarterly allocation which is
set aside for these purposes.
Home-grown timber in Northern Ireland is in exceedingly short supply.
Every effort is being made to induce
sl

[Lord Glentoran]
owners of standing timber to cut suitable
trees, but even when we have exploited
our resources to the full sufficient timber
will not be available for all the more
urgent requirements of industry and
agriculture.
My Ministry's allocation is, and will
continue to be, strictly limited. From it
have to be met the demands of farmers
for reconstruction or repair of farm
buildings, of implement and machinery
manufacturers, food processors, creameries,
abattoirs, and a multiplicity of enterprises related to agriculture and food.
production.
If the supply position were to improve
I would be glad to secure the release of
timber for the erection of glass-houses.
At present, however, there are many
more pressing claims on our allocation.
From the outbreak of hostilities until
the spring of this year the supply
position was such that I found it
possible to release timber to any applicant
for a licence who could be relied upon to
make proper use of it. During that period
hundreds of glass-houses were erected
throughout Northern Ireland. Recently
the demands for more urgent purposes
have increased, and as far as glasshouses are concerned, I regret that I have
had to confine releases of timber to bona
fide market gardeners and to exclude the
claims of the small private grower.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Excessive Rents (Prevention) Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
CLAUSE 1 (Fixing of fair rents and
recovery of excess payments).
(1) Subject to the provisions of this
sub-section, where a dwelling-house has
been let after the first day of April,
nineteen hundred and forty-one, to a
person who has been obliged to leave
any housing accommodation which he
occupied at any time prior to such
letting owing to such accommodation
having been rendered unfit for housing
purposes as the result of enemy action,
and such person (in this section referred to as "the tenant") is aggrieved
by reason of the amount of the rent
which he is paying or has contracted to
pay in respect of the dwelling-house to
the person from whom he has taken it
(in this section referred to as "the
landlord"), the tenant may apply to
the Rents Tribunal constituted under
this Act (in this Act referred to as
"the tribunal'), in accordance with
rules made by the tribunal under the
Schedule to this Act, to determine
whether the rent payable by the tenant
is fair and reasonable having regard to
all the circumstances of the case; and
the tribunal, after giving to all persons
who appear to it to be interested an
opportunity of being heard, shall determine the question:
Provided that this sub-section shall
not apply in any case where the dwellinghouse is one to which the Rent
Restrictions Acts apply and the standard rent of the dwelling-house is, for

(2) If the tribunal determines that

to be such a certificate as aforesaid and
to be signed by a member of the
tribunal shall, without further proof,
be deemed to be a certificate duly issued

the tenant may recover from the landlord, at any time within twelve months

Rev. Professor CORKEY: My statement will be very brief, as I have said
most of what I think I want to say on
this matter. It does not seem to me to

It is generally assumed that whenever a

Committee

[Rev. Professor Corkey]
fixing of prices for various kinds of goods

A short time ago an Act was passed in

was no suggestion in that Measure that
sums which the moneylenders had received
prior to its passing at a greater rent of
interest should be refunded. To take a
more interesting illustration.
When I
was a boy I heard a good deal about the
Gladstone Land Acts and the setting up

Would you think it reasonable that the

Parliament passing a definite law of this
kind.
! That is the only motive I have in bringing forward this Amendment. It seems

CLAUSE 2 (Constitution and procedure of the Rents Tribunal).
(1) The tribunal shall consist of
three members, of whom one, who shall
be the chairman, shall be a resident
magistrate, a barrister-at-law of not
less than six years' standing practising
in Northern Ireland, or a practising
Excessive Rents Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
solicitor of the Supreme Court of
Judicature in Northern Ireland of not
less than six years' standing.
(2) The members of the tribunal
shall hold office for such term as may
be determined at the time of appointment and then retire, but a retiring
member shall be eligible for re-appointment.
(3) The members of the tribunal shall
be appointed by the Governor of
Northern Ireland, and in the event of
any vacancy occurring among the
members for the time being by death,
resignation or otherwise, before the
expiration of their term of office, the
said Governor may appoint a person to
fill the vacancy.
(4) If any member of the tribunal
becomes, by reason of illness or other
infirmity, temporarily incapable of performing the duties of his office, the
Governor of Northern Ireland may
appoint some other fit person to discharge his duties for any period not
exceeding six months at one time, and
the person so appointed shall, during
that period, have the same powers as
the member in whose place he is
appointed. A person appointed under
this sub-section to act in place of the
chairman of the tribunal shall be a
person qualified under sub-section (1)
of this section.
(5) The provisions set out in the
Schedule to this Act shall have effect
for the purpose of the exercise and performance by the tribunal of its powers
and duties under this Act.
(6) The decision of the tribunal shall
be final and not subject to appeal to
any court.

It was originally intended that there

into the matter further we have come to

It will probably be found more convenient to hold

to have several tribunals in existence

cases or make the tenants in the different
counties come to Belfast.

Will there be one' for Belfast or more

It is impossible to see how a question of

Act. It deals with the amount of rent
received by the landlord, and whether

It is a very simple issue of fact.

The Parliamentary Secretary says it is
most unwise and ill-advised in a tribunal
of this kind to have men representing
different interests. That would revolutionise the whole system of proceeding in
these matters in Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Take the Unemployment
Assistance Act. I am sorry there is no
representative of the Ministry of Labour
here at the moment. There you have
tribunals seeking to adjust differences between employers and workmen, and you
find assisting the chairman a layman who
undoubtedly is there on behalf of the
employers and confronting him a layman
on behalf of the workmen. They represent interests, and they do not do it in
secret. They are there to fight their own
battles-one to fight the employers'
battle and the other to fight the workmen's battle, the chairman trying to hold
the scales between them.
If we are to go by the Parliamentary
Secretary's dictum here to-day that is a
wholly wrong, and unjust, and irregular
proceeding. I stand amazed at that.

Take an ordinary arbitration, with which
the Parliamentary Secretary is familiar
as the result of many years' work. The
chairman may be a lawyer, but the other
members are lay persons-one nominated
by one party to the contest and the other
nominated on behalf of the other party
to the contest. In this matter it behoves
the Government to walk very warily and
wisely. They should recognise the
principle in this Amendment. It is not
a wrecking Amendment; it is a constructive Amendment. It aims at securing the same amount of representation
for both parties concerned in the struggle

The hon. and learned Member for St.
Anne's stated that we were being asked
to approve of money which had already
been spent. There are Estimates in this
Bill about which this House was never
consulted. There is money here that has
already been spent, and about which this.
House at no time whatever was consulted
in any shape or form. I say that is
wrong.
In regard to any money proposed to be
spent there should be Estimates placed
before this House, and the Members
should have an opportunity of expressing
some opinion with regard to it. Here we
are asked to approve of an Estimate for
money that has already been spent. It
is very difficult for us to object when the
money has been spent. I suggest that
the House should act on the principle that
all Estimates should come before the
House and that the House should have
some say in the matter before the expenditure has taken place. It is too late to
present the Estimates when the money has
been specifically and definitely spent. In
those circumstances we have no time to
put a brake on extravagance. The
Government should see to it in future
that the Estimates are presented before
the money is spent, and that we are not
asked to pass Estimates for money that
has already been expended.
In connection with this matter I would
draw the attention of the House to a very
important development at Westminster,
and I would ask that it should be followed here. The Prime Minister, Mr.
Churchill, foreshadowed certain legislation, but before he brought in that legislation, he and a number of other Cabinet
Ministers put down a Notice of Motion.

Mr. CAMPBELL: I intended
raise last Tuesday evening a question
of administration connected with the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and I propose,
in brief terms, to do so now, not having
had an opportunity earlier. It concerns
the position of internees in Belfast Prison.
According to a statement made by the
Minister of Home Affairs on recent
occasion he cannot sanction the visit of
an ordinary doctor, who attended any
sick person during his pre-imprisonment
period, to attend him during his period.
of internment. That position does not
prevail in England. Internees in England, even in time of war, can in sicka
ness have visits from their own doctors.
The English Home Secretary tolerates
that, but the Minister of Home Affairs
does not see his way to apply that
position here under his jurisdiction. He
said that in England they had not the
same difficulties as had been experienced
here during the past twenty years. You
would think that that statement hardly
carries conviction. The right hon.
Gentleman did say that an eminent
specialist whose services might be useful.
to an unfortunate internee that was
stricken by illness might have the right of
access.
There would be no question of a reflection on the prison doctor in allowing
an ordinary doctor to visit a patient. I
think it would be agreed by most Members of this House that a man who has
been in attendance on a patient, say, for
years might be of very great assistance to
a prison doctor in the event of the illness
of the patient in prison. He would know
the history and the idiosyncrasies of the
patient, matters that would come before
the prison doctor only in a cursory way.
I think the differentiation between the
system here and the system prevailing in
England is not a reasonable differentiation. In fact, some people are not over
ready to accept Ministerial statements
with regard to the conditions under
which these men are held.
I was very much struck here to-day by
the statement made by the hon. Member for Woodvale that a member of the
Advisory Committee which assists the
Minister is chairman of an important
Unionist Association in the city of
Belfast. The hon. Member for Woodvale described that as a scandal. I could
not use stronger language than he used
with regard to it. It does strike one as
remarkable that in a tribunal of three,
dealing with the detention or release of
these men, one of the three should be
prominently attached to the political
organisation which is whole-heartedly in
the service and at the disposal of the
Government. He added that the gentleman referred to was a brother-in-law of
a Member of this House, who is a strong
supporter of the Government.
One of these internees left prison some
time ago to sink into his grave. None
of these men has stood convicted of any
offence; not a few of them are believed to
be absolutely innocent of any illegal
Treatment of Internees
Treatment of Internees
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
associations. Their inoffensive character
and unblemished record have not saved
them from being denounced in undisclosed quarters and couped up in prison.
Anyone who has read the reports of the
Parliamentary Debates at Westminster
knows that there has been increasing
restiveness among Conservative, Liberal
and Labour Members because of the detention of certain persons by the Home
Secretary as a war emergency measure
under the Defence of the Realm Regulations. Here that power is part of the
permanent law of the area. The Minister
can accept or reject the advice of the
Advisory Committee. He is the ultimate
arbiter of the liberty of the citizen.
Against his rule no appeal lies to any
quarter; no court has jurisdiction
intervene.
to
man
An innocent man could be kept in jail
-I do not say the right hon. Gentleman
would do that-but an innocent
could be kept in jail on the sole fiat of
the right hon. Gentleman. He may not
have reasonable cause, but he need not
satisfy any court authority or any body
that he has cause. He
can snap his
fingers at any authority; he is in the
position of an absolute dictator. That is
a very heavy responsibility; it is almost
too heavy for any man to bear without
a probability of mistakes arising, of
erroneous information being acted upon,
and of injustices occurring from time to
time. I think it is an evil system which
puts any man under lock and key at the
word of any Minister induced to act by
possibly unreliable informants.
People used to think that a citizen was
deemed to be innocent until he was found
guilty. These men have neither been
accused nor found guilty, and must be
presumed to be innocent; there is no
conviction against them. Nothing could
be more obnoxious to feelings of justice
than the imprisonment of an innocent
man. I am sure every Member of the
House would feel strongly against anything of that kind. A more grievous
wrong could not be inflicted. Very often
it happens, I fear, that the wrong is not
done alone to the persons interned, but
to the families whose breadwinners they
are. I have heard of men who were in
more or less regular employment being
shut up without the least scintilla of
warning or information. In four cases
there were 36 persons, mostly young
children, dependent upon them, and left
in abject poverty without their support.
I understand that these men object to
wearing prison raiment worn by men
who have been convicted or are under
remand. I can understand that feeling.
They have refused to wear the garb
of men who are, or may be, malefactors.
Most of these men are poor.
In many
cases their dependants have no means to
replace their threadbare tattered raiment
by clothing to protect them against the
rigours of winter weather. I think the
responsibility rests upon the Ministry—a
heavy responsibility-to provide necessary
raiment different from the prison garb.
Humane custom dictates this course.
Besides it would be some security against
grave illness befalling a man whose health
had been weakened and run down by the
severe privations of prison life.
I understand the Minister's reply to be
that if they do not accept prison garb in
place of their worn-out clothing they
would get no other clothing from the
authorities. They must lump it or leave
it. I think that is unreasonable. I
think it is harsh and I think the harshness is obvious. The self-respect of these
men should not be unnecessarily hurt.
The Minister was kind enough to extend
to me an invitation to visit the prison,
but I feel a visit would be futile, hedged
round, as it would be, by the unsympathetic restrictions which would be enforced
on an occasion of that kind.
Mr. NIXON: It is my duty to bring a
serious matter before the House and I
want to say, at the outset, that I am
sincerely sorry for the new Minister of
Public Security, because I will be
surprised if what I bring before the
House has his approval. I would be more
than surprised if it has his approval. He
has a difficult task, and one of his greatest
difficulties-it is the greatest difficulty of
any Minister here or in England at
the present time is to prevent some selfconceited and generally incompetent
official from ruling.
The matter of complaint is this, which
appears in the Press to-day, emphasised, I
may say, in banner headlines:
"Belfast Warned. You will get
another Blitz. Lieutenant-Colonel C. S.
2413 Speech by Colonel Davies
Speech by Colonel Davies
2 DECEMBER 1941

... Davies, senior A.R.P. inspector of the
Ministry of Public Security, speaking
at a meeting to organise home fire
guards in St. Kevin's Hall last night,
said: You will get another Blitz. Do
not think you will not. German aeroplanes have been circling round up and
down the coast. I know what I am
talking about.”
That speech was preceded by a big
advertisement—almost as big as that-in
the Press that this great man, Colonel
Davies, was going to speak, and he did
speak, and that is what he said. That
speech has caused grave public apprehension in the city of Belfast. Now we are
here as M.P.s mixing with the public
every day. We are asked questions about
air raids twenty times a day and perhaps
oftener. We say, "We hope there will
be none. The Germans are busy enough
at the present time." Every M.P. on
each side of the House, as far as I have
heard, has had the discretion to try to
raise public moral instead of lowering it.
I think they all have done that. I have
heard of no one who did not. But here
is a gentleman advertising his speech and
his great meeting. First and foremost
he never should have been allowed to
advertise it at all, because if he has a
statement to make and advice to give to
his own A.R.P. he could order the men
to assemble in a hall and give it to them
behind closed doors. He has no right to
advertise himself as such a great speaker.
If there is a public speech to be made or
any speech like that the Minister is the
man
to make it or his Parliamentary
Secretary.
I would like to know how Colonel
Davies knows all this. Is he in touch
with Field Marshal Goering? It is the
only way he could know it, because I
venture to say he is the only man who
does know. It has been left to him.
And as regards German aeroplanes
circling round, sure we know that ourselves. They are searching round England every day. There was an announcement from the Minister of Public
Security that they were over here the
other day, a very proper announcement
and well worded. No one could take
exception to it. If any person got up
and made the statement I have quoted in
public, if he was not a public official what
would happen? He would be prosecuted
if he would not be interned. But Colonel
Davies knows all about it. I met a man
to-day who has a delicate wife and eight
children in an area that got a big
walloping during the last blitz. He has
been invited by the Minister of Labour
to go across the water for a job, and then
an official who says he knows what he is
talking about tells him that when he is
away, or words to that effect, his wife
and eight small children are going to
get it.
I am not attacking the Minister. I do
not believe in my heart he would be a
party to any such thing. It is the one
thing I was afraid of, that some of these
fellows would get him into trouble. If
there is a public speech to be made the
Minister is the man to make it. These
officials have no right to do so. As I
say, I do not hold the new Minister responsible, but the waste of money in his
Department is amazing. In nearly every
paper every day this great speech was
advertised.' The advertisements about
the election were nothing to it. There
was no need to draw a crowd. Whatever lecture he wanted to give his own
men Colonel Davies could have given
behind closed doors. But he must tell
us publicly what is going to happen and
he presumes to know all about it.
Many people are taking the notion,
and it is getting widespread, of clearing
out of town at night the way they did
some months ago. This thing is now
widespread. I have been spoken to and
rung up here and approached several
times to-day already. I am trying to
get this indiscretion stopped once for all.
I do not want to say more, but the
Minister first and foremost must watch
these people who are advertising themselves. He should not allow them to
issue these nonsensical advertisements.
The public have enough to pay. Let a
watch be kept on all unnecessary
penditure of public money. There is
quite a lot of it. I privately gave the
Minister some information on that point
to-day. The reason I gave it is because
I believe he will attend to the matter.

away

I only mention those things to show

Mr. HENDERSON: I would like to
support the last speaker in this matter.
I hold the Minister partly responsible. He

They went helter skelter to all parts of

At the present time everyone of us is

if this Colonel Davies and people like him

It is a serious matter, and I
night.
contend that the Minister should see that

The Minister cannot be charged with

the looseness of statements made and to

Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like
to say a few words in answer to the speech
made by the hon. and learned Member
for Central in regard to the treatment by
the Government of the internees in our
midst. Personally I am rather surprised
that the hon. and learned Member has
raised this question at all. He has
endeavoured to show that the Government
in their treatment of the internees are
both inhuman and unfair. That accusation is absolutely unjust. I would personally be very sorry if through any act of
mine one person should be detained in
jail or in confinement a moment longer
than I thought necessary in the interests
of the State and the preservation of the
peace.
The hon. and learned Member has contrasted our supposed treatment of the
internees with that meted out to the
internees in England. It is not for me
to make any
comment on how the
internees are treated there. That is a
matter entirely for the British Government. But I am prepared to defend anything that we do. One point on which he
laid special stress was that we do not
allow individual internees to have their
own doctors. I think that on reconsideration he will see that that would be
impracticable. I have already told him
that we have one of the best medical men
in Belfast in attendance on these
individuals. I am quite prepared, and I
am sure he would be quite prepared, to
call in a consultant if it became necessary. As regards their food, I venture to
say that it is better in many ways than
individuals outside the jail get. Then as
to their clothes they are allowed to wear
their own clothes, but if they do not
choose to provide their own clothes the
Government are prepared to provide
clothing for them.
I would not suggest for one moment
that the hon. and learned Gentleman has
any sympathy with these people, I would
not accuse him of that, but-and this is
difficult to put into words when one has
been through all that has happened during the last 20 years and seen the terrible
outrages that have been committed, lives
lost and millions of money gone up in
smoke I have never heard the hon. and
learned Member raise his voice in protest
against these men's actions. He knows
very well that peace was restored after a
very anxious period and after all these
losses only when we had gone in for the
procedure known as internment under the
Civil Authorities Act. It took time, but
eventually peace was restored. Without
the operation of that Act I am not prepared to say what might have happened.
Now we have got peace in our midst for
the time being except for spasmodic outbreaks, but we have the German enemy
hammering at our door. Are we prepared to allow these men, these fifth
columnists, to walk out and, if the
Germans came here, join in and help our
enemies? We are not. My duty is a
very responsible one. It has been
entrusted to me by this House. It is to
try to maintain peace and order in this
community, and if I did not do so I
believe I would be failing in my duty
after the experience of the past and with
the knowledge I have. After all one of
the most deadly weapons used here is the
weapon of intimidation.
That weapon
does not exist in England, but when used
to any extent over here it renders justice
impossible.
My duty is perfectly clear. The House
entrusted me with this power and I intend
to act. I repeat to the hon. and
learned Gentleman that if he wishes I
am prepared to allow him to come up
and visit any persons he wishes in the
jail. He can see them himself and he
can cross-examine them. I do not know
that he himself would be very welcome,
because, as I have said before, there is
no one who has less sympathy for the
I.R.A. than the hon. and learned Member who gets up here and pleads on their
behalf.
