Speech by Colonel Davies 2420
HOUSE OF COMMONS
. Mr. GRANT: The question raised by
the hon. Member for Woodvale this afternoon certainly has given me some foodfor thought. I would like to point out
in the first instance that this was a public
meeting for recruiting purposes, and the
only way we can get public meetings for
recruiting purposes is by putting
advertisements in the Press. During the
past fortnight the Parliamentary Secretary and I have been busily engaged
attending these public meetings and
advocating the recruiting of fire guards
who are so very essential. We cannot
attend all the public meetings and make
all the speeches for recruiting purposes,
and we are greatly indebted to a number
of prominent people in the community
for their assistance in that direction.
The hon. Member for Shankill suggests
that I should call all my officials together and let them make their speeches
in my presence before going out. I am
not prepared to accept that suggestion.
I think if I make my own speeches and
listen to those delivered in this House
I am doing quite well without listening
to more speeches. Though I might have
the best will in the world, the hon. Member for Shankill will admit, if I do
listen to those speeches in
Department I have no guarantee that the
officials will make the same speeches
when they go out. The hon. Member for
Shankill sometimes says things when he
is on his feet that he did not intend to
say when he got up. I am not finding
fault with him for that, because I
I only
probably do the same myself.
want to point out that this was a public
meeting held for recruiting purposes.
own
I would do a great disservice if I
created in the public mind any feeling of
alarm or any occasion for panic. There
is no ground for that. But I should do
a still greater disservice to the public if
I said anything which would induce a
habit of wishful thinking or a feeling of
complacency that we were now out of the
wood so far as air attack is concerned.
We know enough of our enemy to
appreciate that this lull in his barbarous
policy of bombing women and children is
due not to any change of heart on his
part but to the necessities of the
military situation in which he finds
himself. If it should suit the policy on
which he is fighting this war, to resume
these attacks, then resume them he will.
I understand that the hon. Member
has some misgivings that the words used
by Colonel Davies, in his address at a
Fire Guard meeting last night, may give
rise to some disquiet in the public mind,
by suggesting that the Government had
certain information pointing to the
imminence of an aerial attack on Belfast
which it had not disclosed to the public.
I am prepared to agree with the hon.
Member that the words are capable of
that interpretation, but they were not
intended to convey that impression. We
have no information of the enemy's intentions. It is not his habit to tell us in
advance what he proposes to do. I do
not know when, if ever, another attack on
Belfast will come, but I should be remiss
in my duty if I failed to see that the
plans of my department were based on
the assumption that the attack might
happen to-night.
Colonel Davies used the phrase "German
aeroplanes have been circling round here
and down the coast." It has been pointed
out to me that only on one occasion,
namely, on Saturday last, was a public
statement issued by my department and
the Royal Air Force mentioning enemy
air activity over Northern Ireland. It is
desirable, therefore, that I should explain
to the House what our policy is in regard
to this matter. Aerial navigation is not
an exact science. Often a pilot is lost;
finds himself over a particular locality
without knowing where he is. If, therefore, we published in the Press information about the presence of enemy aircraft
over Northern Ireland we might be giving
the enemy information which would
be of substantial use to him. At
the request of the R.A.F. we have
made it a rule to make specific
references in the Press to the presence of
enemy aircraft over Northern Ireland only
in certain circumstances. I am unable
for security reasons to inform the House
what these circumstances are, but they
arose on Saturday in relation to
the enemy air activity over Northern
Ireland. Merely because many months
have elapsed since the presence of
enemy aircraft over Northern Ireland
was the subject of an official statement
it should not be assumed that enemy
aircraft have not been over Northern
Ireland on other occasions. In fact
they have been, and no official mention has been made of their presence for
security reasons.
Speech by Colonel Davies
Speech by Colonel Davies

2 DECEMBER 1941-
I have, I hope, said enough to convey
the two points which the Government
wishes should be conveyed to the public,
on the one hand, that the Government has
got no information up its sleeve pointing
to any imminent danger to Belfast or the
Province, or that there is any undue
cause for panic or alarm, and on the other
hand that we cannot afford to indulge
either in wishful thinking or in complacency, and that we should follow that
old adage, "Hope for the best, but expect
the worst."
I think this was what Colonel Davies
wished to convey, and if he spoke with
rather more directness than I myself
should have done on the same occasion, it
was probably because he has been trained
as a soldier, and not as a Parliamentarian.

Exported Animals (Compensation)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): This Bill which I
bring before the House is to give legal
effect to a procedure which in fact has
been carried on for a considerable number
of years.
It arises out of a Bill passed
in 1928, which had to deal with the
slaughter of animals on arrival at English
ports where a case of foot and mouth
disease had broken out. A small payment has to be made on each beast going
across Channel, and that goes into a fund,
for which there are trustees. When an
animal has been slaughtered on arrival
at an English port on account of foot and
mouth disease, these trustees can pay
compensation on the value of the animal.
The trustees, and in fact everyone in
connection with this matter, are
appointed from the exporters of cattle.
on this side. Supposing beasts are
shipped to a port like Bristol, where,
on arrival, it is found they have foot and
mouth disease and are ordered to be
slaughtered, it is quite obvious that this
particular committee of assessors, who
live in Northern Ireland, could not
possibly, if I may use a legal term, view
the body in time, because the animal has
been slaughtered and probably burned
before they hear of it. The procedure
they have adopted has been to appoint
agents at the ports in England, and when
slaughter has taken place these agents
value the animal, and on that valuation
the owners have been paid compensation.
There is nothing in the Act which permits
that, and this little Bill is simply to
permit the trustees to appoint agents at
the different ports in Great Britain to
value the cattle before slaughter. On
the valuation the compensation is paid.
out of the moneys collected from the
levies paid by the men who ship the
cattle to the other side. There is a small
increase in the salary of the secretary.
That is all that this Bill contains and
I hope the House will pass it.

Air Raid Precautions (Postponement of
Financial Investigations) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): This is a very
brief measure and one which does not
raise any point of policy. The question
at issue is purely administrative. When
the original Air Raid Precautions Act
was passed by Parliament in 1938, the
intention of Parliament clearly was that
in such a novel departure as air raid
precautions any financia! arrangement
laid down in the Act must of necessity be
experimental. The Act therefore contained a section placing an obligation
upon the Ministry to conduct an investigation into the financial working of the
Act before the expiration of three years
from the date upon which it became law.
Those three years have now expired.
But to hold an investigation of the
nature contemplated by the Act of 1938
would entail much detailed work, both
on the part of my Ministry and the local
councils, and absorb a considerable
amount of time, which can be more profitably used in dealing with the many
more important and urgent tasks which
are on hand.
The Air Raid Precautions Act laid it
down that the Government should contribute to all approved air raid precautions expenditure on a grant-aided basis
according to a certain formula. The rate
of grant varied from 70 per cent. to 85
per cent.
$
As time went on, it became clear that
this arrangement placed too heavy a

burden upon the local rates in respect of
certain services, and so from time to time,
and for various reasons, certain classes
of expenditure have, with the approval of
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, been reimbursed in full by the,
Government. I refer to such matters as
whole-time paid personnel, the erection of
shelters, welfare arrangements, demolition
of dangerous buildings, and clearance of
débris amongst others. On all these the
Government now pays 100 per cent. of
the cost.
I mention that point in order that the
House may realise that the financial
relations between the Government and
the local authorities in this matter of
civil defence have not been stabilised, and
that where it has been found that adjustments are necessary to ensure an equitable
division of the cost, they are made.
In case any hon. Member has doubts
in his mind about the effectiveness of the
control of air raid precautions expenditure, I think I ought to explain that
local government auditors scrutinize the
accounts of the councils, and final settlement of claims for grant is held over
until the auditors' reports are available
to my Ministry.
In conclusion, let me say that a few
weeks ago my Ministry consulted with
representatives of the General Council of
Municipal Authorities and of the Association of Rural District Councils, who
expressed their
with the
proposal to postpone the investigation, on
the understanding that the door remained
open to discussion on any financial point
which might arise. That assurance was
given. I beg to move.
concurrence

is used in all these big Government cars I
see dashing about the town with one or
two people in them? Is there any
control there? In the Corporation at the
present time the "Big Six" are going
into this question of petrol. They are
recommending small 10 h.p. cars and
taking the cars from some people altogether. I am not blaming the Minister.
I am one of the few men of any little
prominence belonging to any party who
has stood for the Minister's appointment
behind his back and before his face. I
am not sorry yet, though he made a weak
enough speech yesterday. I expected
something better from him. I would
have made a speech of four words: "It
won't happen again."

Mr. GRANT: It will not occur again.
Mr. NIXON: If you had said that I
would not have asked you to say one
word more. When I make a complaint I
make it sincerely because I believe there
is something that has to be changed.
am not looking for anyone's blood, but I
am looking for strict instructions that if
a thing is wrong it will not happen again.
That satisfies me. That is a rule I have
always followed myself when I had a
little power. I would say, "Do not let
that occur again," and if it did occur
again there was no excuse.
I know this Bill will pass, and I know
the Minister was really not a party to it
more than that he was Minister. These
councils met and made a recommendation,
and that recommendation was embodied
in a Bill extending these investigations
for a year and the Minister accepted it.
It was difficult probably for him to do
anything else under the circumstances.
I would not like him to do that too often,
but the fact that the recommendation
came from the representatives of the
General Council does not prove anything,
because there are very few of these bodies
that have not some of their relatives stuck
into some of the top jobs.
That was established here by a question
to the Minister in regard to the city of
Belfast. Another could be put down
that would bring us much further in that
direction. A recommendation coming
from people using these services and using
the misery of the people and of the nation
to invent jobs for their own relatives is a
thing I cannot think of very highly. I
would be far more popular if I said
nothing about it. I am not brought to
any of their functions because I would
find out too much about them. But I
hear enough. You see a man in a high
position and he has there his cousin who
is a partner in the same trade-and he
knows a good deal about bricks himself—
and another man a little higher up who
has his brother in much the same trade.
Then they all get together and make a
recommendation which is put into a Bill.
That is going too far.
We have to win this war, and it is not
by wasting money we are going to do
it. When I say that I am not attacking
the Minister. I expect the Minister will
give orders, and our finances will be
looked into a little bit better. There
should be no waste of money. No fellows
who were never in a car in their lives
before should be allowed to dodge about
in a big 25 h.p. or 30 h.p. car simply
because they had got a job. Cut all that
kind of thing out and get a supply of
tram tickets. Give them a supply for a
month, and make them account for those
used. When you see a man in a 30 h.p.
car, with a driver to drive him about
300 yards and back, on a little errand
that could be done by tram, well-a
straw shows how the wind blows.

Adjournment
3 DECEMBER 1941
That is what is going on, and I appeal
to the Minister and to the Government
to cut out all this unnecessary expense.
A patriot will not do that. But the
people who have to pay for this, and they
do not grudge it, are the ordinary citizens
-the shopkeepers, property holders, and
working men. Every penny squandered
is equivalent to a present to Hitler.
When the Government are going about
urging the people to save for victory, they
should set an example themselves in every
department. I often think, when I see
a save for victory meeting, I should go
and turn the tables on them; in fact, I
have done it. They may come to the
meeting in a big public car to tell other
people to save for victory. They are
burning petrol and wasting as much
money as they can, and at the same time
are stuffing their relatives into jobs.
That has gone too far. People cannot
say a word to anyone, because if they do
they will offend someone who has given
them a lift. That is why so many people
have their mouths shut. They placed
themselves under an obligation to get
something done that should not have been
done, and then they cannot talk. They
are closured. They are not independent.
I would not be independent if I was
running round after them trying to get
my relatives into jobs. If I did that I
could not get up here, because I would be
guilty myself. But I am not guilty,
notwithstanding the fact that years ago,
before I had any children, Glengall
Street reported that my son and daughter
had jobs at Stormont. But that does not
do any good.
When you are preaching to save for
victory, save, and save in this respect.
I say to the Minister, "Keep your eye
on expenditure, and if you feel it
necessary bring your private secretary in
and dictate an order. Send that order
round and make the head of every branch
of the department sign it, 'Copied for
compliance.' Then when you get it
back file it, and that man can never deny
he got the order. If he breaks the order,
produce it and put him on the carpet.
Then your Department will work well
and you will have no trouble." As far as
my little support goes the Minister if he
does that will get it. It may not be
much here, but I can gather a crowd any
time I like. No man in this city, as you
know, can do it as well. I am not gathering one now because I want one thing
only-I want Hitler downed before we
are downed.

4. Professor CORKEY asked the Prime

prevent speculation in land in towns and
cities that have been blitzed, and

hampered in rehousing and town-planning

The PRIME MINISTER: My hon.
Friend will be glad to know that we are
in close touch with the Imperial Government who have under consideration the
introduction of legislation to give effect

at an early date.

Ulster's War Effort
Ulster's War Effort
9 DECEMBER 1941
Ulster's War Effort.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move,
"That in the opinion of this House
a Select Committee should be appointed
to devise ways and means to increase
Ulster's war effort, to eliminate waste,
and increase efficiency in war production, and generally abolish unnecessary
expenditure and extravagance.'
""
This Motion is very simple; it sets out
what I believe the majority of the people.
outside require to be done. It asks the
Government to set up a Committee of this
House with a view to bringing about
economy, and urges a greater national war
effort. I have been very closely associated
with the expenditure of this Government
since I entered Parliament, and I must
say that, while each department has an
accounting officer who is always anxious.
to try to save the public purse, there has
been a relaxation of control since the war
began, a relaxation not only on the part
of the heads of the departments, but right
through the departments, with the result
that there is an increase in the Estimates
for this year that could not be justified
before the public.
As Chairman of the Public Accounts
Committee, I may state that that body
cannot exercise the control necessary, because it examines the accounts only after
the money has been spent. What is
required is a Committee to examine the
amount of money asked for by each
department, and to say whether the
demand from each department is justifiable or not and is required in the national
interest. Eighteen months ago I asked
for a Committee on Estimates, but my
request was turned down. Since then I
have had the pleasure of reading the
reports of the Select Committee
National Expenditure set up in Great
Britain. I have followed that Committee's work very closely, and I believe it
has been the means of saving millions of
pounds in Great Britain.
on
Anyone who wishes to confirm these
remarks of mine can have the use of the
reports showing the items in which public.
has been saved.
money
Economy in
public expenditure will not injure our
national effort. I think we will all agree
that to-day is a day of surprises. This
day week we thought we were seeing the
light, but to-day the horizon is darker.
I personally feel satisfied that the darkness will be cleared away at a very early
date, but it is up to me and to every man
and woman, boy and girl, in this Province
to see that the clearness is restored as
soon as possible.
The Motion is in two parts. The first
part, as I have told the House, seeks to
regulate the spending of public money by
the various departments. This Committee could be useful in that direction.
Civil servants are trained to carry out
very highly skilled work in their respective departments, and they have to carry
out their work in a perfect manner. That
I agree they do, but the civil servant
never takes into account the question of
cost. If the Prime Minister had to apply
the methods of the Civil Service to the
expenditure in his own business, I am
satisfied that at an early date he would
call a halt. We all realise that no matter
what article or commodity is required by
the Government, a higher price is always
demanded than would be demanded from
a private purse. Therefore, we must have a
regulating factor in national expenditure.
The right hon. Gentleman may oppose
the setting up of this Committee, but I
am sure that he, in his day and generation, recognises that what I am sayng is
in accordance with the facts. Again, he
cannot very well oppose the setting up of
this Commitee and remain consistent,
because he has found against the Belfast
Corporation, and the Government have
declared that a Committee of Six must
be set up to go into the affairs of the
Corporation. The Government approved
of that step, and I think wisely approved
of it. If the affairs of the Corporation
were all right, and if everything were
above board, then the Corporation and its
officials need have neither fear nor doubt
in their minds about the findings of the
Committee.
The Government cannot say that their
actions have had greater safeguards than
those of the Belfast Corporation. If it
goes by past experience, then I say the
knowledge I have gained in 16 years as
a member of the Public Accounts Committee shows that the Government's state
of affairs is worse than the state of affairs
found to exist in the Belfast Corporation
up to date. We have a certain amount
of political control throughout the
Departments, but political control is not
up to the hundred per cent. standard,
and that is quite natural when one
Ulster's War Effort
Ulster's War Effort
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
remembers that control changes hands
and new political heads are brought in
from time to time. During the transitional period there is a certain amount
of slackness, and one political head may
take a deeper interest in the affairs of a
Department than another. I will give
you the illustration of the Home Office.
The Home Office is an example in itself.
I am not going to speak in disrespectful
terms of any right hon. Gentleman.
In the early years of the Home Office
there was a certain strict supervision by
the head, and every unit under that head
was thoroughly examined from the point.
of view of cost. But in recent years
certain units of the Home Office have
branched out as authorities on their own
and they seem to have got away from the
political control and to be working as a
civil head of control. I refer to the
police, run solely now by the Inspector-
General, and the expenditure on the
police is carried out just in accordance
with the dictates of that head. That
branch of the Home Office in itself has
increased two-fold since its inception. I
am not saying that it has increased and
has had any less efficiency. The police
force has increased in cost and I believe
it is now at its highest standard of
efficiency, but the increase in cost to the
public purse is too great for the amount
of efficiency that has been established.
The right hon. Gentleman will hardly
believe this story when I tell him that we
have a man at the present time receiving
£850, going about the towns and villages
buying in second-hand motor-cars. Will
he believe that that is a fact? In any
second-hand motor market you may visit
if you ask do they know this particular
gentleman they will say, "Yes, he is a
customer of ours." Well, I never
visualised under the 1922 Act that the
duty attaching to a policeman of high
rank was the purchasing of second-hand
motor-cars. I am only giving you that
as an example of one unit of the service
that requires special attention. Then
again I say you have the dual position of
maintenance branch and establishment
branch. Since the establishment of the
police there has been growing expenditure
in the headquarters. They have now at
headquarters in Waring Street a fully
staffed maintenance branch carrying out
the maintenance services for the R.U.C.
They have also down there a fully staffed
establishment branch carrying out the
establishment duties attached to the
R.U.C.
I want the right hon. Gentleman
clearly to understand that we in this
Parliament have exactly the same departments operating as the two which are
operating in Waring Street. We have
the maintenance branch and the establishment branch in this building. But
the growth in these two branches in
Waring Street has only come to light in
its full glory in the past two years.
Surely we could save by the amalgamation of the duties attached to each of
these two units and give back to the
public purse what should never have been
taken away. I should also like to ask the
Minister of Commerce why he is spending anything from 1 to 2 millions in a
certain part of Northern Ireland, whilst
the services for which that money is being
spent, or the plant for them, is sitting
500 to 600 yards away competent to deal
with requirements of that description.
Did Parliament ever authorise the right
hon. Gentleman to stårt on the erection
of that plant which he is now having
carried out, putting on the taxpayers an
expenditure of £2,000,000 or over it?
Not only that, but our war effort is
suffering as the result. We have men on
machinery highly skilled and all classes
of labour employed thereon, and that
labour is required on work of national
importance. That is not a patriotic
gesture at all-taking away men required
in the national interest and placing them
on work that could be very well carried
out in the post-war period. We have got
the facilities at our disposal if we require
any more power to be used in Northern
Ireland towards the national interest. We
have got the essential things at our very
door, and can apply ourselves in that
direction for the duration of the war. In
view of the expenditure of the amount
which I say is being spent on the firm
which is employed in carrying out the
work for that plant, very essential men
that Britain is crying out for to-day are
being employed on this work.
The latter part of the resolution is to
eliminate waste and to increase efficiency
in war production. I have spoken so
often on our war effort that I am really
getting tired speaking to the Government
benches. There is not a firm in Northern
Ulster's War Effort

Ireland pulling its weight, and I make

who are in the employment of the
majority of firms in this city. One important firm, whose every effort should be

You would really think, as some of the

There are other proofs. Both stumped

Not content with that rebuff they started

blood introduced, to give other men a
chance to see what they can do. That is
all it is. We know that the men working in the factories had a mass meeting
to tell the world that owing to the
organisation they could not get on with
their work. They want to do more.
the workmen I meet want to do more,
but they are being kept back. I have
been told by patriotic working people

emphasise that to-day. In the reply of

Since this Motion has been so long

many cases, and I have endeavoured to

this most

has been going on during the past month
into the subsequent history of persons
who had been disallowed assistance. It
was, of course, impossible to examine
every such case and so the following procedure was adopted.
The Board took the disallowances
imposed during the first quarter of this
year which had not been reversed as the
result of appeal, and they marked every
fifth case for inquiry. 282 cases have
been investigated; and of these it has
been learned that 170 found work within
a month from the date of disallowance;
36 more within another month; and 30
more at later periods. That is to say,
more than 83 per cent. have found work.
The remaining 46 cases were accounted
for in other ways-some were evacuated;
others went on sickness benefit.

This Motion stands for fair play for
the men and women of this country. Does
this House stand for justice for the men
who made this country? Conditions in
Northern Ireland are altogether different
from the conditions prevailing
England. There is nobody unemployed
in England. They have had to resort to
conscription of labour in order to get
sufficient workers for their industries.
Here our Government export 29,000 or
30,000 unemployed to Great Britain, and
the Minister of Labour, that great standard bearer, instead of bringing those
men back, brings men from Eire. I have
no objection to their coming from
America or from Eire, or from any other
country, provided there is not a solitary
worker of our own out of employment.
They can come from wherever they like

26).

Mr. BEATTIE: I had not the pleasure
of being here on the Second Reading,
and I should like to have some definitions
of the merits of this Bill which the
House is being asked to pass. I see that
the first Clause is really one under
which compensation has to be granted
equal to the value of the animals. As I
was not present I would like the noble
Lord to give some explanation. The
principle of compensation, I think, for
all things appertaining to State control
is a very important point. We may be
called at some future date, and perhaps
earlier than some of us think, to take
over much property and stuff of private
owners to give the State the necessary
results from those concerns. I would
like to know what the State intends to
do in the form of compensation in regard
to exporting animals. I understand the
animals are the property of the State,
and under control by the State. Is the
State going to act more generously to exporters of animals under the State compensation scheme than under the private
- scheme of insurance which they were
called upon to bear at their own expense ?
I am putting these points forward with
the object of getting something from the
noble. Lord. I hope he will pardon me
for not being aware of the purport of
Clause one owing to my absence from the
House.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am very glad
to assist the hon. Member. Under the
1928 Act levies were charged on each
animal crossing the Channel. The total
amounts of these levies were put under
trustees, and those trustees, out of these
levies paid by the cattle owners themselves, paid compensation for the beasts.
which were slaughtered on arrival for
having foot-and-mouth disease in the
port.
I just want to make this point clear.
It was part of the duty of the assessors
to view the body, if I may put it that
way, before they assessed the price of
the animal. My hon. Friend can quite
understand if a shipment of cattle was
sent to Bristol and an outbreak occurred
at that port these animals would be
promptly slaughtered and burned, so it
would be quite impossible for the
assessors to get over in time to value.
Therefore the custom has been for the
assessors to have agents at the ports in
Great Britain actually to see these
animals before they were slaughtered and
assess their value. That was not legalised
under the 1928 Act, and this little Bill is
to legalise that and permit the assessors
here in Northern Ireland to appoint
agents at Liverpool and Bristol where the
cattle are shipped to. These agents will
then have authority to assess the value of
the cattle. That value is then paid by
the Committee on this side out of the
levies.
Mr. BEATTIE: That explanation is
very satisfactory up to a point. It is a
very practical outlook to have in the
cattle trade. The one point not answered
is, who bears the responsibility for the
value of the animal, that is, the compensation amount?
Lord GLENTORAN: The levies go
into a fund for that purpose and that
fund has trustees. The trustees appoint
assessors who assess the value of the cattle
and the amount comes out of that central
fund.

CONTROLLER OF ELECTRICITY
PRODUCTION.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state the name of the controller of electricity production in Northern Ireland, and
the salary he is to be paid for this work.
The
MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I assume that the
hon. and gallant Member refers to the
appointment of a controller for the
Belfast Corporation electricity undertaking. For this post, I am glad to say
I have secured the services of Mr. Hugh
Boyd, F.C.A. Mr. Boyd has intimated
to me his desire that the appointment
should carry no remuneration, and while
I gladly accept this public-spirited
attitude, I have thought it well to make
it clear to Mr. Boyd that, should his new
duties interfere seriously with his professional work, I shall be ready to reopen
the question of remuneration.
FEES OF A TECHNICAL ADVISER.
2. Lieut-Colonel GORDON asked the

that the technical adviser to the Ministry

being paid a fee of approximately

Sir BASIL BROOKE: On the 2nd
September, 1941, I stated, in reply to a
question from the hon. Member for
Woodvale, that the fees for the services
rendered by Messrs. Kennedy & Donkin,
who are employed as the Ministry's consultants in connection with the provision
of emergency electricity supplies, have
been approved by the Imperial Treasury,.
and are related to the actual cost of providing such supplies. The hon. and
gallant Member will appreciate that it
would not be in the national interest to
state the amount of these fees, as such
disclosure would be an indication to the
enemy of the nature of the/work involved.
The fees are paid to the firm and Mr.
Kennedy does not receive any remuneration for acting in an advisory capacity to
my Ministry.

Arising out of the Minister's reply may

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. MIDGLEY: Would I be in order
in saying that I give notice that I will

WITHHOLDING OF BILLETING
ALLOWANCES.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the deep-seated discontent arising from
the withholding or the discontinuance of
billeting allowances, and whether representations have been made to him of the
hardships involved in Ballymena and other
districts because of this, and what steps he
proposes taking in this matter.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I should like to take
this opportunity of clearing up some misunderstanding which appears to exist in
regard to the payment of billeting allowances and the issue of billeting notices.
From the implication in the hon. Member's question it is clear that the
principles underlying the issue of these
notices are not generally appreciated.
Billeting allowances may be paid in
respect of two different classes:
(1) persons rendered homeless by
enemy action; and
(2) persons of the priority classes
evacuated to reception areas.
In regard to the first class, the allowances
are intended to be only of a
temporary character until the persons
rendered homeless are able to make their
own arrangements for accommodation.
The billeting notice may, however, be
extended if the housing situation is acute,
or if, in the opinion of the authorities,
the circumstances are such that the homeless persons could not reasonably be
expected to be in a position to make their
own arrangements. The free billeting is
intended to apply only for an initial
period of two weeks, and any person
billeted after that period is expected to
recoup the authorities either in full or in
part for his accommodation.
In view of the particular circumstances
prevailing in Belfast after the two major
raids many individuals were billeted for
a considerable period beyond the initial
two weeks, and it was some time before
the Ministry was in a position to ascertain
who exactly were billeted and the circumstances of each case. These circumstances
have now been investigated and, as a result, it has been found that a large
number of people are no longer entitled
to be billeted. I may say in the majority
of cases which have been disallowed no
appeal has been received from the individuals concerned. I can quite understand that there may be discontent as a
result of this withholding or discontinuance of billeting allowances on the
part of those individuals who were
apparently of opinion that they were
entitled to be billeted at Government expense for the duration of the war.
With regard to the second class,
namely the priority class, who have been.
evacuated to reception areas, a similar
investigation has been proceeding and
many persons have been struck off the
scheme because they did not belong to
one of the priority classes, and, therefore,
there was no authority to billet them in
a reception area.
Representations have been made to my
Department from time to time in regard
to these individual cases, but I can assure
the hon. Member that every case is carefully considered and no billeting allowance is stopped if the person concerned
is legally entitled to be billeted.

of silage from the point of view of the

Vote of No Confidence.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move:
That this House, having before it the
published statements of the Prime
Minister clearly defining the issue in
the North Down and Willowfield byelections as a test of confidence in the
Northern Ireland Government, and
believing that the overwhelming
majority of the people of Northern
Ireland concurs in the repudiation of
the Government now expressed by the
voters in these constituencies, calls for
the immediate resignation of the Prime
Minister and his colleagues in order to
make way for a more virile Government composed of all sections, and
charged with the duty of saving Northern Ireland from the deplorable position
in which it now finds itself.
I move this Motion with a sense of
responsibility to the people I represent. I
feel that a Motion of this kind is overdue;
but in taking upon myself the responsibility of moving it I have no illusions
as to the result of the division which will
follow. I want that clearly understood.
The Prime Minister will receive the usual
majority. But it will only be an empty
victory this time. It will convince
nobody, for there is a rising tide of opinion.
outside this House which is beginning to
assert itself, and which will sweep this
Government from office, perhaps sooner
than we realise.
I warned the Prime Minister before to
take heed of the writing on the wall, and
I warn him again to-day. The game is
up, and the sooner he and his followers
realise it the better. The platoon of paid
voters and "Yes-men" who occupy the
Government benches to-day will vote
against this Motion, but they, too, are
nearing the end of their tether. They
have still time to take heed of the lesson
of Chamberlain and company. He, too,
fondly imagined a party majority in the
House of Commons would save him from
the wrath of the people. He and his
supporters soon found their mistake. The
people were not impressed by his machinemade majority, and in a few weeks he was
hounded from office. The same thing will
happen here I can see it coming-but in
Northern Ireland the crash will be all the
greater for having been delayed so long.
If any person doubts this just go out into
the highways and byways of Northern
Ireland to-day. Just listen to what the
people of all sections are saying. One of
the Unionist sayings is: "This Government is rotten. Why doesn't it resign!"
They are saying, "The Prime Minister is
a failure. We have no confidence in
him. Why doesn't he get out?"
These are not the words of a few. It
is common talk all over this area. The
Government knows it too, but is trying
to turn a deaf ear in the hope that the
storm will blow over. Using a slang
phrase, might I say the limpets are hanging on like grim death to the last. They
know in their heart of hearts that they
are doomed men, but they will not move.
They are waiting until the people can
stand them no longer, and will rise up
and put them out. At the present
moment it seems the Government has
scarcely a friend left in the world.
entire Unionist Press of Ulster seems to
have turned against the present Cabinet
since the North Down and Willowfield
disasters. The Willowfield result was
The
one of the most amazing events that has
taken place here in twenty years. The
conversion took a long time, and it looks
now as if the age of miracles is not past.
In the midst of these extraordinary
happenings is the Cabinet going to play
the part of the ostrich with its head
stuck in the sand, pretending that
nothing has happened?
If we are compelled to continue as we
have done for the past twenty years then
something drastic is bound to happen.

soldiers who have thrown off their
uniform to serve the King sleeping on
the back benches. Add to these a few
linen lords who have made a mess of
their own businesses, a few grasping
landlords, and you have the whole
Stormont combination.
We have had enough of these selfseekers. We want some men of principle
and high ideals, and there are certainly
plenty of them in Northern Ireland, but
they will not enter here until the timeservers have been cleared out. With such
men Northern Ireland's affairs have
some chance of straightening themselves.
But there is no future for this area until
this gang opposite have been chased from
office.

on the things that matter, and to leave

It is outside this House's authority and I
think you have had a statement from the
British Cabinet Ministers giving you the
assurance, which I believe you did or
should accept, and you should not be found

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 17th December, 1941.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Sittings of the House.
Resolved, "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until 12 noon
on Tuesday, 30th December, and that
after the Royal Assents to Bills agreed
upon by both Houses, Mr. Speaker do
adjourn the House without Question put
until Tuesday, the 20th January, 1942,
provided that in the event of any Bill or
Bills being returned from the Senate with
amendments, the House shall meet on
Monday, the 29th December and shall
transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date, and at its rising.
shall adjourn until 12 noon on Tuesday,
the 30th December."-(Lord Glentoran.)
BILL PRESENTED.
Education (Emergency Provisions) Bill,
"to make provision for additional grants
in respect of air raid protection at schools
and colleges; to amend certain provisions
of the Education Acts (Northern Ireland), 1923 to 1940, in their application
to evacuated children and the assignment
of school teachers; and for purposes connected with the said matters." Presented
by the Minister of Public Security; to be
read a Second time on 20th January, and
to be printed.
The Orders of the Day were read and
postponed.
Resolved, "That this House do now
adjourn." (Lord Glentoran.)
Adjourned accordingly at Five
Minutes past Two until
Tuesday, 30th December, in
pursuance of the Resolution
of the House of this day.

Ballynafie, Portglenone; Mr. R. G.
Nelson, Ballylumnin, Ahoghill; Mr. S.
Overend, Castle Street, Bellaghy; The
Central Fish and Poultry Market, 38
Bridge Street, Ballymena.
Since the introduction of the Live Stock
Control Scheme on 15th January, 1940,
the only types of fresh meat which may
be
shipped through the normal trade channels
are goat meat, horseflesh and offals from
abattoirs. Three licences have been issued
since that date, but one has been revoked
as the licencee committed a breach of the
regulations.
Fourteen applications for licences to
ship goat meat have been received since
June, 1941, but licences have not been
issued to any of the applicants.
In June of this year it was discovered,
as a result of inquiries following complaints from Great Britain, that a number
of unlicensed persons were shipping goat
meat. After this traffic was stopped the
fourteen applications referred to were
received-six of them (including those to
which the hon. Member refers) being from
traders who had been found to be shipping
goat meat illegally. It was clear, from the
manner in which these shipments were
consigned, that this trade would inevitably
result in a waste of food, as much of the
meat would be in a condition unfit for
human consumption when delivered.
FEMALE AGRICULTURAL
WORKERS.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will consider the
position of female workers on the land
and bring in a wages scheme on similar
lines as that applying to male agricultural
workers; whether it is a fact that female
workers in England engaged on the land
are paid wages fixed by an Agricultural
Wages Board, and, if so, whether he will
include female workers in Northern
Ireland under the Wages Board now in
operation in this area.
Lord GLENTORAN: The Agricultural Wages Board at present has power
to fix minimum rates of wages for female
agricultural workers in Northern Ireland.
In England the wages of female agricultural workers are fixed by agricultural
wages committees in the various districts.
The question of the inclusion of female
agricultural workers in the Northern
Ireland wages scheme is one for the Agricultural Wages Board.
LICENSING SCHEME FOR
POULTRY.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
result of negotiations concerning a licensing scheme governing poultry and rabbits;
whether it is the intention of his department to adopt such a scheme, and, if so,
whether he will be prepared to discuss the
scheme with shippers, packers and collectors before adoption.
2549 Sympathy and Support-

30 DECEMBER 1941
United States of America
Lord GLENTORAN : As the hon.
Member is no doubt aware, the introduction of the proposed scheme for the control
of poultry and rabbits exported from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain has
been indefinitely postponed. If any such
scheme is contemplated in the future, my
Ministry will certainly be prepared to discuss the working of it with the interests
concerned.
Message to United States of America.
Mr. NIXON: With the permission of
the House and the consent of Mr. Speaker,
I think it would be very appropriate to
send a message of sympathy and support
to the U.S.A.
I may say that I know in
advance that I have the support of the
Prime Minister in this matter, and that
he had contemplated moving a Motion
himself, only I happened to have this one
in first. It reads:
"That this House, on behalf of the
people of Ulster, tenders its sincere
sympathy to the President, Government
and people of the U.S.A. in connection
with the vicious and treacherous attack
made on them by Japan, and pledges
itself to support by every means in its
power the war effort until Japan and
her allies are overthrown. The House
also thanks the U.S.A. for their great
assistance in the past, and feels proud
and honoured that among the citizens
of the U.S.A. there are millions of our
kinsmen who helped in no small way to
shape the destinies of the great
Republic, and directs Mr. Speaker to
convey this
to the U.S.A.
message
through the appropriate channels."
I know it is not necessary for me to
say anything in this House or in Ulster
in support of this Motion in order to have
it passed. Ninety-nine per cent. of the
people of Ulster are behind this Motion.
At the present time we are at the parting
of the ways, and you are either on one
side or on the other. We are in the
struggle with all we have. All our
resources-and they are very considerable,
particularly our strategic position are at
the disposal of America and her allies.
I may say this.
There is no room in
Northern Ireland for the Japanese
ambassador. He will not be harboured
here. Lip sympathy is not worth much
-in fact, it is worth nothing at all. In
Northern Ireland and Ulster there is
practical sympathy for the cause.
Ulster has given some very distinguished
men to the U.S.A., and Ulster emigrants
have found homes, happiness and kindness in the U.S.A. This morning I came
by Eden; that is where the ancestors of
Stonewall Jackson came from; and in my
own little way I am proud to tell you what
you know, that it was my kinsman and
namesake, John Nixon, who read the first
Declaration of Independence publicly on
the 8th of July, 1776.
I may also say that this Motion was
signed by the hon. Member for North
Down who, I think, is here to speak for
himself, and also by the hon. Member for
Willowfield, who cannot be here owing to
circumstances over which he had no control.
I only mentioned that to prove that,
although we may have differences in
certain other matters and probably will
continue to have them, so far as the war
is concerned and the winning of the war
there is nothing between us.
(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We are all in
this conflict, and all we have is at the
disposal of the U.S.A. if they want to use
it against their enemy.
I am proud again to say that there is
no room in Northern Ireland for the
Japanese ambassador. I was surprised
to hear and could hardly accept it,
although it came from Mr. De Valera
himself in his message of sympathy to
America, that if the Free State went into
this struggle it would only cause disunion.
I did not know that. I did not think
there was an Irishman worthy of the name
who would take exception to Ireland joining with America in the defence of liberty
and justice. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the Prime
Minister makes his statement, I think I
should explain the procedure to the
House. This is really a suggestion by the
hon. Member for Woodvale that a message
should be sent unanimously from this
House of Commons to the American
Ambassador in London, with a view to his
sending it forward to the American
Government. There is no question of a
Motion, no question of a division, and no
Question can be put from the Chair.
Under these circumstances, the usual procedure is that the hon. Member who makes
the suggestion makes a short statement,
such as has been made by the hon. Member
for Woodvale. The Leader of the House
also makes a short statement, but over and
above that there can be no speeches and
Sympathy and Support-
United States of America
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Speaker]
no debate. There can be objections,
which I do not anticipate.
:
(Mr.
The PRIME MINISTER
Andrews) I feel sure that the proposal
made by the hon. Member for Woodvale
will receive the unqualified support and
approval of every Member of the House.
I entirely agree with him that in Ulster
we are all of one mind as regards the
prosecution of the war until victory comes.
If I may do so, I would like to refer to
the fact that we have in this House to-day
a distinguished representative of the great
Republican Democracy of the West.
Every right-thinking person must have
been struck with horror on hearing of the
savage onslaught of the Japanese forces
upon the outposts of American defence in
the Pacific Ocean. Without a word of
warning, and even while negotiations were
still proceeding at Washington, the
Japanese, taking their lead from that
master in the technique of treachery-
Hitler himself-showered their bombs on
the citizens of a country with which they
were then at peace. Nothing, I suppose,
has stirred the American public so much
to a realisation of the evil of the so-called
"New Order" as this act of aggresssion.
We are now proud to have as allies our
cousins across the seas. There are close
ties of kinship between Ulster and the
great Republic of the West, and the links
which bind the English-speaking nations
of the world will be forged even closer in
the ordeal which we are all facing.
I feel it may be of interest to the House
if I mention that some time ago I communicated with the President of the
United States conveying our profound
admiration and gratitude for the everincreasing aid which, under his gifted
and inspiring leadership, the United
States was giving to our Empire, and I
said that I felt justified in expressing to
him the deep conviction that, with the
moral and material help which he and his
country were giving, liberty and justice.
would ultimately triumph. I also pointed
out that, as part of the United Kingdom,
Ulster was striving to give all the support
within her powers to our great leader, Mr.
Churchill, and the Imperial Government
in the prosecution of the war.
To this letter I received an acknowledgment from the President himself bearing
testimony to the part which the Government and the people of Northern Ireland
were playing in the struggle against
Hitlerism, and I think the House will be
thrilled with Mr. Roosevelt's closing
words. He said:
"I share your conviction that the
spiritual and material forces of freedom
must and will triumph. For our part,
we will not rest until we have done
everything in our power to help bring
about that final victory."
arms.
The British Empire and the United
States of America are now partners in
Arrayed against us are powerful
forces, but we are not dismayed. When
the resources of our two democracies and
allies reach their full development the
British Empire, the
the United States.
Russia, China, and the other associated
nations will strike at their enemies with a
power that will be irresistible. Then those
evil things against which we are fighting
will be swept away, and the nations, in
safety and security, will be free to apply
themselves once more to the arts of peace.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. SPEAKER: In accordance with
the usual custom, I will forward this
message to the Foreign Secretary for
transmission to the American Ambassador, who will communicate it direct to the
United States of America. I will also
supply a copy to the American Consul-
General in Belfast, explaining to him
the proceedings which took place in
this House to-day. Further, the
message will be entered upon the Votes,
